stories.title: Snowbird replacements ‘extremely manoeuvrable, powerful,’ Rcaf commander says
stories.summary: The Royal Canadian Air Force welcomed its new trainer aircraft, the CT-157 Siskin II, which will replace the old Tutor jets flown by the Snowbirds aerial demonstration team.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan
stories.content:
The Royal Canadian Air Force welcomed on Thursday the first two of its new trainer aircraft, the CT-157 Siskin II — the same planes that will replace the old Tutor jets flown by the Snowbirds aerial demonstration team.

The turboprop planes will soon be headed to 15 Wing Moose Jaw, where the air force eventually will station 19 of them to serve as its main training fleet.

Acquiring the Siskin II, also known as the Pilatus PC-21, is part of the RCAF’s plan to modernize its fleets and overhaul its training.

RCAF Commander Lt.-Gen. Jamie Speiser-Blanchet said the modern aircraft are well suited both to aerial acrobatics and to preparing pilots for the more advanced aircraft the air force is bringing online.

“It has an advanced cockpit and capabilities and the design is just a very contemporary one that is used by other allies as well. We’re very excited that we’re able to bring this on board,” she said.

The commander made the comments just after one of the new planes buzzed overhead in a ceremonial first flypast at the airport in Gatineau, Que.

The current Snowbirds will hold their last show in the National Capital Region in Gatineau, Que., this weekend. After their final flight at the Grey Cup in Calgary in November, the Snowbird team will start a hiatus that could last until 2030.

As the RCAF brings in the new planes for pilot training, the federal government is still working on procuring extra Siskins for the Snowbirds team.

Speiser-Blanchet said these are “excellent” stunt planes that shouldn’t be underestimated — even though some have questioned whether a propeller aircraft is a suitable replacement for jets.

“It is extremely manoeuvrable and capable, and powerful, actually. More so than perhaps people’s understanding of other propeller aircraft from the past,” she said.

While the Siskin II has a slower top speed than the CT-114 Tutor and is not as loud as a jet, Speiser-Blanchet said “it’s not a quiet aircraft” and it will “really wow Canadians” once the shows are up and running.

The federal government announced this spring it would replace the roughly 60-year-old Tutor jets, which have encountered various problems with upgrades meant to extend their lifespans out to 2030. Costs, timelines and the growing scarcity of replacement parts threw a wrench into plans to keep them in the air longer.

The Swiss Air Force has been training its pilots on the Pilatus aircraft since about 2008, and Australia’s Roulettes aerial demonstration team also flies the same planes.

Speiser-Blanchet said that because so many Canadian pilots will be training on this aircraft, the air force will have a much larger pool of potential candidates for the Snowbirds. Having the multi-purpose aircraft based out of Moose Jaw will also make servicing and support easier to manage, she said.

The RCAF has never before used a Pilatus aircraft. The new planes will replace the air force’s CT-156 Harvard II trainers, also known as the T-6 Beechcraft.

Ioannis Papachristofilou, deputy CEO of Pilatus in Switzerland, said the aircraft are advanced, high-performance machines that use Pratt and Whitney’s powerful PT6A-68B turboprop engine, which is made in Canada.

“This aircraft has an embedded mission-simulation suite, which allows you to simulate, for example, sensors like radar,” he said, adding the technology allows pilots to train faster on fighter jets in later phases of training.

The fleet of Siskins will work alongside other types of trainers under the new Future Aircrew Training program, which covers 71 training aircraft split up across five fleets.

SkyAlyne, a partnership between CAE and KF Aerospace, won a contract in 2024 for the 25-year, $11-billion training program, referred to within the air force as FAcT. It will replace the commercial pilot training aspects of the RCAF program.

stories.title: St. Thomas residents, councillors push for greenspace in railway lands development
stories.summary: Plans are slowly taking shape for what could be a new community within a community in downtown St. Thomas.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Plans are slowly taking shape for what could be a new community within a community in downtown St. Thomas.

But many residents have ideas of their own as to what they’d like to see happen with the railway lands south of Talbot Street.

“I would love to see greenspace. The city is growing. It’s got like, 40,000 people, and we need as much greenspace as we can get,” said David Van Pelt.

“I’d like to see some parks come in here, some affordable housing. Nothing like the $2,000, $3,000 dollar apartments that they’re building in corners of the city. A dog park would be nice, and more centrally located. We also need a centrally located high school,” said resident Tasha Reid.

“I’m just looking for it to be developed into really nice parkland for families,” said resident Andrew Knowlton.

This week, St. Thomas council had a look at the Railway Lands Area Master Plan Preliminary Concepts.

The former rail lands downtown between Talbot and Wellington streets behind the Caso Station are being proposed for mixed use residential and commercial development.

Some councillors are pushing for an abundance of parkland at the site, including Coun. Joan Rymal.

“It’s a wonderful opportunity to have this downtown space central to downtown,” said Rymal at the Monday council meeting. “There’s so many things that could happen. I’m just thinking of, you know, Harris Park in London, where they have Rock the Park. You could have Rock the Rails, and have a wonderful concert venue there,” she suggested.

Concept 1 for the Railway Lands is Status Quo with Moderate Intensification, including up to 1,325 housing units.

Concept 2 is High Mixed Use and Connectivity Scenario with up to 3,550 units.

And Concept 3 is Hybrid Intensification Scenario with up to 1,325 units.

St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston says while council can guide the project, ultimately it will be up to private landowners as to what they do with the property.

“So, are we going back to the owner of the land and buying it back to make our parks? You’re asking a developer just to develop a park. There’s no income there,” he told CTV News.

Developing the brownfield site is no easy or inexpensive task. According to the mayor, remediation will cost millions of dollars per hectare- which would be picked up by both property owners and taxpayers.

“I frown a little bit about how the railways left our community in a contaminated state that we now have to deal with,” said Mayor Preston.

“When it’s costing us millions of dollars to repair what they left us, then that will also contribute to how much we can do,” he added.

Preston expects council will approve necessary zoning changes in 2027. In the meantime, public meetings are being planned for November.

The mayor is also encouraging people to share their views on the project through the Speak Up St. Thomas web page .

I’m just thinking of, you know, Harris Park in London, where they have Rock the Park. You could have Rock the Rails, and have a wonderful concert venue there,” she suggested.
Concept 1 for the Railway Lands is Status Quo with Moderate Intensification, including up to 1,325 housing units.
Concept 2 is High Mixed Use and Connectivity Scenario with up to 3,550 units.
And Concept 3 is Hybrid Intensification Scenario with up to 1,325 units.
St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston says while council can guide the project, ultimately it will be up to private landowners as to what they do with the property.
“So, are we going back to the owner of the land and buying it back to make our parks? You’re asking a developer just to develop a park. There’s no income there,” he told CTV News.

Developing the brownfield site is no easy or inexpensive task. According to the mayor, remediation will cost millions of dollars per hectare- which would be picked up by both property owners and taxpayers.
“I frown a little bit about how the railways left our community in a contaminated state that we now have to deal with,” said Mayor Preston.
“When it’s costing us millions of dollars to repair what they left us, then that will also contribute to how much we can do,” he added.
Preston expects council will approve necessary zoning changes in 2027. In the meantime, public meetings are being planned for November.
The mayor is also encouraging people to share their views on the project through the Speak Up St. Thomas web page .

stories.title: Ford says glowing comments about Chow were not an endorsement
stories.summary: Ford was asked about work on a new funding deal for Toronto and whether he'd be endorsing anyone in the Toronto election.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is walking away from his near-endorsement of Olivia Chow in Toronto’s mayoral race, saying his glowing words earlier this week were misinterpreted.

Ford was asked about work on a new funding deal for Toronto and whether he’d be endorsing anyone in the Toronto election.

“The mayor and I have a phenomenal relationship, phenomenal,” he told reporters.

“We’ve given the City of Toronto more money than they’ve ever seen in their lives — over $9 billion. We’re going to continue supporting the mayor. She’s doing an incredible job, so read between the lines.”

The glowing words were interpreted by Brad Bradford, Chow’s closet rival in the race, as an endorsement.

“Of course the premier endorsed Olivia Chow,” his team wrote in a news release immediately afterwards. “She is the easiest negotiation he has ever had. Everything she told Torontonians she would fight and oppose, she handed over on a silver platter.”

The premier’s office was silent on the issue for more than a day, suddenly issuing a statement to clarify that Ford hadn’t endorsed Chow some 30 hours after he made the comments.

“We would like to clarify that Premier Ford did not endorse Olivia Chow and will not endorse any candidate in the Toronto mayoral race,” Ford’s office wrote in a 6:30 p.m. statement on Thursday.

“The premier has demonstrated that he will work with anyone no matter their political stripe to advance the interests of the people of Ontario.”

stories.title: Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock formally resigns from House of Commons
stories.summary: MP for Brantford-Brant South announced his plans to step down last month, saying he planned to return to the office of the Crown prosecutor
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Conservative Larry Brock says he has resigned from the House of Commons, ending five years as the MP for Brantford-Brant South.

Brock announced his plans to step down last month , saying he planned to return to the office of the Crown prosecutor.

A by-election will be called in the Ontario riding, along with five others that are currently vacant, in the coming months.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is planning to hold a rally in Brantford on the weekend.

Brock is the sixth MP to leave Poilievre’s caucus over the past year.

Four members defected to the Liberal government and Richard Martel joined the Senate this summer.

stories.title: Canadian dollar extends weekly decline, weighed by wider yield spreads
stories.summary: Currency is on course for its eighth straight ​daily decline
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar added to its weekly ​decline against its U.S. counterpart ‌on Friday as recent widening of the gap between U.S. and Canadian bond yields weighed on the loonie.

The loonie was trading 0.1 per cent ⁠lower ​at 1.4010 per U.S. dollar, or 71.38 U.S. cents, after touching its weakest intraday level since August 7 at 1.40144. It left the currency on course for its eighth straight ​daily decline, which would be the longest ‌such streak since May.

For the week, the currency was down 1 per cent, as the Federal Reserve hiked interest rates and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in coming months.

“Wider front-end U.S.-Canada yield ‌spreads account ​for much of the ‌Cad’s slippage over the past few days, according to ​our correlation matrix,” Shaun Osborne and Eric Theoret, strategists ⁠at Scotiabank, said in a note.

The Canadian ⁠2-year yield was trading about 142 basis points below the U.S. equivalent, ​marking the widest gap since July 28.

The U.S. dollar rose on Friday against a basket of major currencies, including the yen, after two policy makers at the Bank of Japan dissented from a widely expected decision ⁠to raise interest rates.

U.S. crude oil futures were trading 0.5 per cent higher at US$102.43 a barrel as markets assessed Saudi supply alongside concerns about a widening Middle East conflict. Oil is one of Canada’s major exports.

Bank of Canada Governor ⁠Tiff Macklem is due to speak ​on Monday on economic developments.

“His comments May reaffirm the hawkish ⁠tone adopted following the Bank’s meeting earlier this month,” the Scotiabank strategists said.

Investors see ‌a roughly 60-per-cent chance the BoC would hike at its next policy ​announcement on October 28.

Canadian bond yields rose across the curve, tracking moves in U.S. Treasuries.

* The 10-year was up 5.5 basis points at 3.878 per cent but remained below ​the nearly 3-year high touched on Monday at 3.987 per cent.

stories.title: Ottawa mayoral candidate charged for alleged death threats against Sutcliffe, Ford
stories.summary: Ottawa — Ottawa mayoral candidate Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas has been charged with harassment and threats to cause death related to online posts about Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe, left, and Ontario Premier Doug Ford take part in a press conference at Ottawa City Hall on Monday, April 29, 2024. THE Canadian Press/Sean Kilpatrick

By The Canadian Press

Posted September 18, 2026 11:50 am.

Last Updated September 18, 2026 12:04 pm.

Ottawa — Ottawa mayoral candidate Geoffrey Nicholas Griplas has been charged with harassment and threats to cause death related to online posts about Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe.

The Kingston Police say they were made aware of “concerning behaviour and comments” made on Sept. 13.

Griplas was arrested on Sept. 15 in Ottawa and has been charged with two counts each of criminal harassment and uttering death threats, along with several weapons-related offences.

The accused has been remanded into custody in Kingston, Ont., after a bail hearing and is due back in court on Sept. 21.

Griplas is listed as a certified candidate in Ottawa’s mayoral election under the name “Geoff Nicholas” and is one of 14 mayoral candidates.

Ottawa’s civic election is set to take place on Oct. 26.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Sarnia police seize more than $300,000 in drugs, charge local man
stories.summary: Police say more than $300,000 worth of illegal drugs have been seized in Sarnia this week, resulting in charges against a 42-year-old man.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Police say more than $300,000 worth of illegal drugs have been seized in Sarnia this week, resulting in charges against a 42-year-old man.

Police said the operation led to the seizure of approximately four kilograms of crystal methamphetamine, one kilogram of cocaine, prescription hydromorphone pills in various strengths and 120 oxycodone tablets.

Investigators estimate the street value of the seized controlled substances at more than $300,000.

Officers also seized drug trafficking paraphernalia, including scales and packaging materials, along with $151,452 Canadian and $94 US in cash.

A 42-year-old Sarnia man was arrested and charged with possession of cocaine for the purpose of trafficking, possession of methamphetamine for the purpose of trafficking, possession of oxycodone for the purpose of trafficking, possession of hydromorphone and possession of proceeds of crime over $5,000.

The accused has appeared before the courts and the charges have not been proven in court. Police said the investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Pitching in: Friends retrace Toronto subway line on foot, raising money for unhoused people
stories.summary: Amanda Gracia and Samantha Ruth have walked along portions of the TTC, discovering the city while supporting Out of the Cold
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizers: Samantha Ruth and Amanda Gracia

The pitch: Raising $2,800 and climbing

The cause: Out of the Cold

A couple of years ago, Amanda Gracia came across a social-media post about someone who had walked from Union to Finch station along Toronto’s Yonge-University subway line.

She wanted to try the walk for herself and turned to her friend Samantha Ruth. “I asked Sam, ‘Hey, do you want to do this thing with me?’ Because we both like walking and we thought, well, there’s really nothing better to do anyway.”

So, last year they walked from Finch to Union station, a roughly 16-kilometre route that took them about seven hours. They enjoyed the walk so much they decided to make it an annual tradition. “We thought, ‘Okay, we did half of Line 1 last year. Maybe we’ll do Line 2 this year,’” recalled Ms. Gracia, a 23-year old dietician. “I don’t know, weird idea, but it was a lot of fun.”

This summer they set out from Kennedy station and walked to Kipling, a distance of 30 kilometres in total. Along with walking, the pair raised money for Out of the Cold, a Toronto-based charity that provides a range of services for unhoused people. Ms. Ruth, 26, has been volunteering with the organization for the past year.

“I’ve gotten to know that community really well. I’ve gotten to talk to people and see what they need in terms of food and housing,” she said. “And with the food costs rising and the amount of people who are using food banks increasing, I thought it would be a good idea to raise money for more hot meals for people in the city.”

The walk was a challenge, but it also gave the friends a different view of the city. They stopped in a variety of ethnic neighbourhoods and discovered new enclaves. “The walk just really reminded me of how diverse Toronto is and how beautiful it is,” Ms. Ruth said.

They’ve raised $2,800 so far and both have been humbled by the support and encouragement they’ve received. “We’re really proud that we’re able to do something for our neighbours and our community,” Ms. Gracia said.

They’ve already started thinking about next year’s walk and they’re considering Line 3, which has been closed, or the Ontario line. “We don’t really have a strict plan yet,” Ms. Gracia added. “We kind of just see where the summer takes us.”

stories.title: Canada and the EU want an energy alliance. What would it look like?
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Strasbourg, France, this week where he and European Union leadership discussed strengthening ties on several fronts.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Canada has the potential to bolster Europe’s energy security through a new alliance, but experts say it doesn’t necessarily mean tankers crossing the Atlantic Ocean laden with oil or liquefied natural gas.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was in Strasbourg, France, this week where he and European Union leadership discussed strengthening ties on several fronts amid strained relations with the United States.

Werner Antweiler, an economist at the University of British Columbia, says Europe is in a “precarious situation” as it aims to pivot away from Russian energy imports following that country’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Canada has pipelines and port infrastructure to export oil and gas from the West Coast to Asia, but no such option exists in the east, and any such project could take a decade or more to come to fruition.

In the meantime, Antweiler says European companies have the ability to secure a stable gas supply from Canada through what’s known as swap contracts, where a cargo headed for Asia, for instance, could be traded with another one bound for its shores.

Rachel Doran, executive director at Clean Energy Canada, sees a promising opportunity to supply critical minerals to Europe, helping it transition away from fossil fuels and grow its clean power supply.

stories.title: Man charged after alleged machete threats in Owen Sound
stories.summary: The Owen Sound Police Service says officers responded to a report of a man threatening individuals with a machete near 9th Street West and 1st Avenue West at about 11 p.m. on Sept. 17.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 63-year-old Wiarton man is facing several charges after police say he threatened people with a machete in Owen Sound late Thursday night.

The Owen Sound Police Service says officers responded to a report of a man threatening individuals with a machete near 9th Street West and 1st Avenue West at about 11 p.m. on Sept. 17.

Police said officers arrived within a minute of receiving the call, identified the suspect and arrested him without incident.

Investigators allege the man was in possession of a machete and a quantity of methamphetamine at the time of his arrest.

The accused has been charged with possession of a weapon for a dangerous purpose, uttering threats to cause death, assault with a weapon and possession of a Schedule I substance.

Police said no injuries were reported in connection with the incident.

The accused is scheduled to appear in court on Dec. 10.

stories.title: A paid skilled trade placement program is coming for Canadian youth
stories.summary: Ottawa plans to spend $880 million for the plan, which will begin in early 2027 and be available for young Canadians looking for on-the job experience in the trades.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The federal government is rolling out a plan to provide paid, four-month long placements for young people Canadians to build a career in the skilled trades , Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu said on Friday.

Ottawa plans to spend $880 million over the five years for the plan, which will begin in early 2027 and be available for young Canadians looking for on-the job experience in the trades.

This is part of a larger $8 billion financial commitment the Liberals made in the spring economic statement to promote skilled trades.

“By helping more young Canadians pursue careers in skilled trades, we are opening the door to meaningful work that will help build the homes, infrastructure and major projects Canada needs,” Hajdu said.

Additionally, those tradespeople who complete an apprenticeship and earn certification in an eligible Red Seal trade will be able to apply for a $5,000 completion bonus later this fall, she added.

The bonus will also be available to those who received their certification on or after April 1, 2025, Employment and Social Development Canada said.

A new program called Build Canada Apprenticeship Service will launch later this fall, connecting jobseekers to small and medium-sized businesses offering apprenticeships.

Businesses that offer apprenticeships under this program could receive up to $10,000 in grants to support hiring, the department added.

Hajdu also announced the Apprenticeship Training Grant, which will launch in spring 2027 and provide apprentices attending mandatory in-class technical training with a $400 weekly top-up in addition to Employment Insurance.

The federal government is also in “discussions” with provinces and territories on bilateral agreements that would provide them with $2 billion in federal funding to expand access to pre-apprenticeship and technical training, she said.

Canada will have more than 1.4 million job openings in the skilled trades between 2024 and 2033, according to the federal government’s estimates.

stories.title: Third Marineland beluga dies after move, this time in Spain
stories.summary: The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., along with four bottlenose dolphins.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died.

Jelly Bean, 19, died “suddenly and unexpectedly” on Friday, said Oceanografic Valencia.

The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., along with four bottlenose dolphins.

“In recent days, Jelly Bean had experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring,” Oceanografic said in a statement.

“During this period, she showed signs of improvement and remained responsive to her caregivers, while continuing to receive around-the-clock monitoring.”

Two Marineland belugas, Rain and Peekachu, and a resident beluga, Beethoven, at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move. The aquarium’s investigation remains ongoing.

Nineteen belugas and Marineland’s lone killer whale, Kiska, died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

The park had the largest collection of captive beluga whales in the world with 30. Former owner Marie Holer put the park up for sale in 2024 before closing for good after that summer. She died days after the closure after taking over the helm from John Holer, who founded the park in 1961 and died in 2018.

Sources say the park has been tentatively sold on the condition all the animals are gone before closing. Several hundred deer remain at the park.

Marineland and Oceanografic moved the two belugas along with four dolphins to Spain in a 20-hour odyssey on Aug. 27.

“At this time, it is not possible to determine the cause of death,” Oceanografic said.

“Oceanografic’s veterinarians will conduct a necropsy together with the pathology team at CEU Cardenal Herrera University to try to determine the factors that May have contributed to her death.”

Marineland has said its whales were healthy at the time they left the park. Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also cleared the whales and dolphins to move.

Marineland moved its whales and dolphins to five parks in the course of six weeks: SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and Oceanografic in Valencia.

“We were deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Jelly Bean,” Marineland said in a statement.

“Our thoughts are with the people who cared for her – the staff and caretakers who knew her daily, and everyone who followed her story.”

In 2019, the federal government banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s animals. It also forbade breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its males and females. The law also banned performances.

The park blames some of its deaths, in part, ON those changes.

That was the beginning of the end for Marineland .

Last year, Marineland had a deal to sell all its whales and dolphins to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, an aquarium in China with a Guinness Book of World Records for the world’s largest aquarium. It was the only place in the world Marineland could find that would take them all.

But Thompson nixed the deal, saying it wasn’t in the best interest of the whales because they would be subject to different laws, including breeding and performing tricks.

In response, Marineland made international headlines when it said it was running out of money and needed an injection of federal funds, otherwise it would euthanize all its whales.

That threat of euthanasia remained on the table unless it could get the whales out.

It turned to a consortium of aquariums from the United States and Spain for help. Thompson eventually approved that move, despite the fact the whales and dolphins ended up in spots where breeding and performances were allowed.

The last captive whale in Canada, Tofino, left Marineland’s waters on Aug. 31.

content_blocks.text: A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died.
Jelly Bean, 19, died “suddenly and unexpectedly” on Friday, said Oceanografic Valencia.
The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont., along with four bottlenose dolphins.
“In recent days, Jelly Bean had experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring,” Oceanografic said in a statement.
“During this period, she showed signs of improvement and remained responsive to her caregivers, while continuing to receive around-the-clock monitoring.”
Two Marineland belugas, Rain and Peekachu, and a resident beluga, Beethoven, at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move. The aquarium’s investigation remains ongoing.
Nineteen belugas and Marineland’s lone killer whale, Kiska, died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

The park had the largest collection of captive beluga whales in the world with 30. Former owner Marie Holer put the park up for sale in 2024 before closing for good after that summer. She died days after the closure after taking over the helm from John Holer, who founded the park in 1961 and died in 2018.
Sources say the park has been tentatively sold on the condition all the animals are gone before closing. Several hundred deer remain at the park.
Marineland and Oceanografic moved the two belugas along with four dolphins to Spain in a 20-hour odyssey on Aug. 27.
“At this time, it is not possible to determine the cause of death,” Oceanografic said.
“Oceanografic’s veterinarians will conduct a necropsy together with the pathology team at CEU Cardenal Herrera University to try to determine the factors that May have contributed to her death.”
Marineland has said its whales were healthy at the time they left the park. Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson also cleared the whales and dolphins to move.

Marineland moved its whales and dolphins to five parks in the course of six weeks: SeaWorld locations in San Diego and San Antonio, the Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and Oceanografic in Valencia.
“We were deeply saddened to learn of the passing of Jelly Bean,” Marineland said in a statement.
“Our thoughts are with the people who cared for her – the staff and caretakers who knew her daily, and everyone who followed her story.”

In 2019, the federal government banned whale and dolphin captivity, but grandfathered in Marineland’s animals. It also forbade breeding, which forced Marineland to separate its males and females. The law also banned performances.
The park blames some of its deaths, in part, ON those changes.
That was the beginning of the end for Marineland .

content_blocks.text: Last year, Marineland had a deal to sell all its whales and dolphins to Chimelong Ocean Kingdom, an aquarium in China with a Guinness Book of World Records for the world’s largest aquarium. It was the only place in the world Marineland could find that would take them all.
But Thompson nixed the deal, saying it wasn’t in the best interest of the whales because they would be subject to different laws, including breeding and performing tricks.
In response, Marineland made international headlines when it said it was running out of money and needed an injection of federal funds, otherwise it would euthanize all its whales.
That threat of euthanasia remained on the table unless it could get the whales out.

It turned to a consortium of aquariums from the United States and Spain for help. Thompson eventually approved that move, despite the fact the whales and dolphins ended up in spots where breeding and performances were allowed.
The last captive whale in Canada, Tofino, left Marineland’s waters on Aug. 31.

stories.title: Hudson Williams and Yaga premiere leave Tiff crowd buzzing
stories.summary: Heated Rivalry star talks about the show’s second season, Yaga’s ‘witchy feminist rage’ and working in Canada
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
Yaga , the upcoming Crave show starring Hudson Williams, Noah Reid and Carrie-Anne Moss, premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival on Thursday evening in a cloud of fandom for another project entirely: Heated Rivalry , which 10 months ago vaulted Williams to stratospheric levels of fame for his portrayal of closeted hockey player Shane Hollander.

While some premiere-goers sported Baba Yaga-inspired fashion – a chicken-feet handbag for Yaga creator and showrunner Kat Sandler, an ethereal black-and-gold robe for Heated Rivalry author Rachel Reid – a large percentage of fans showed up to the Tiff Lightbox in garb connected to a certain gay hockey romance, whose second season is expected to land on Crave in spring of 2027.

Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams sends fans into a flurry over this $2 Canadian Tire tote bag

But by the end of Yaga ’s screening, which featured the first two episodes of Sandler’s half-hour thriller, the audience was buzzing – and not only about Williams, who plays two people in Sandler’s folklore-inspired whodunit. As the audience slowly filtered out of the screening room, fans lamented having to wait until Oct. 23 for the series to land on Crave: “Yagaween” quickly became the vernacular of choice for the show’s release date.

First conceived as a play at Toronto’s Tarragon Theatre in 2019, Yaga follows a private detective (Reid) and a local cop (Clark Backo) as they investigate the disappearance of fishery heir Henry Park (Williams) in the fictional coastal town of Whittock.

Before long, the story morphs from a True Detective -style mystery to something more magical – and sinister.

Thursday’s premiere ended on a cliffhanger (no spoilers here), but during the first two episodes, the audience got a taste of Sandler’s quirky sense of humour and highly feminist approach to storytelling. (Moss, best known for her work as Trinity in The Matrix series, plays a middle-aged professor “with a taste for younger men,” per Crave’s marketing materials.)

It was a triumphant conclusion to a Williams-themed day that kicked off with an afternoon Q&A at the Royal Alexandra Theatre. In the leadup to the event, hosted by Tiff’s vice-president of public programming Keith Bennie, long queues snaked around the theatre, with some Heated Rivalry aficionados reporting standing in line since the early morning to try and score a rush ticket. (Some fans on King Street were rewarded for their patience when Williams showed up to the theatre early, offering autographs to a lucky few members of the enormous crowd.)

Bennie’s questions covered a wide range of topics, from Williams’s coming-of-age as a young actor in Kamloops, B.C., to his early career making indie films with friends at Langara College in Vancouver.

In the Q&A, Williams shared intimate details from the Heated Rivalry set, exploring at length scenes where Shane comes out to a girlfriend and sees Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) win a championship game on TV. He also recalled being unsure what the show could lead to – while he remembered appreciating its writing during the audition process, he didn’t anticipate just how strongly Heated Rivalry would resonate with audiences.

“It’s weird that our memory of season one isn’t just our memory of showing up and doing the scenes,” he said. “It’s having watched them cut together. It’s fan reactions. Our memory isn’t ours, it’s everyone’s. It’s been abstracted and twisted, and it’s become this weird amalgamation of a memory.”

Heated Rivalry trounces competition with 13 Canadian Screen Awards

That feeling has made returning to Shane for Heated Rivalry ’s second season harder than expected, he said. (Filming is ongoing.) Both he and Storrie had a tough first day on set this year, but “it came back, thankfully,” he added. “Jacob [Tierney] does a really good job of making this set feel as tiny as it was in season one. It’s all the same crew, which is really great. But it was surreal to step into it. The only other character I’ve had to return to was Land Leopard,” he continued with a laugh, referring to his 2025 indie films Super Support and Super Support 2.

The Q&A soon pivoted to Apparatus, his upcoming film opposite Dylan O’Brien, and Yaga. Williams praised Yaga ’s “witchy feminist rage,” and recalled wondering “how the hell did they greenlight this?” Stylistically, the show is markedly different from Heated Rivalry : It’s “obviously a different world” in terms of genre, he said.

“Those were all exciting things,” he remembered. “I was constantly on the edge of my seat reading it, and I remember my team reading it, and we were like, ‘We’re almost near the end. Do you know what’s happening? No, neither do I.’ And a 30-minute episodic thriller is really interesting.”

Williams called Sandler “uncompromising” as a showrunner, and highlighted her trust in the Yaga cast to find their characters. Williams and Sandler traded voice memos and texts about his two characters, and overall, he said, the experience was highly collaborative. “That’s sort of your dream as an actor,” he said.

And the best part? Both Yaga and Apparatus , booked after the global success of Heated Rivalry , are Canadian. When posed the question of what being Canadian means to him, he quipped, “being American with manners?” before speaking more seriously.

“I was getting a lot of scripts, obviously, and when the show’s blow-up was happening, Yaga and Apparatus were just two of the coolest things that came in. It was sort of a no-brainer to simultaneously choose good projects and also get to be in Canada.”

stories.title: Third Marineland beluga dies after moves, this time in Spain
stories.summary: A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died. Jelly Bean died “suddenly and unexpectedly” on Friday, said Oceanografic Valencia. The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont. Two Marineland belugas […]
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Trainer Taylor-Lee Dell says goodbye to beluga whale "Tofino," the last whale in captivity in Canada, before being transported by a group of experts from Marineland and several U.S. aquariums onto a truck via a sling before being moved to an aquarium in the U.S., in the final transfer of whales out of the closed park, in Niagara Falls, Ont., ON Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Carlos Osorio

By Liam Casey, The Canadian Press

Posted September 18, 2026 9:01 am.

A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died.

Jelly Bean died “suddenly and unexpectedly” on Friday, said Oceanografic Valencia.

The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August from the shuttered theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont.

Two Marineland belugas and a resident beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move.

“In recent days, Jelly Bean had experienced feeding difficulties, prompting the veterinary team to intensify her monitoring,” Oceanografic said in a statement.

“During this period, she showed signs of improvement and remained responsive to her caregivers, while continuing to receive around-the-clock monitoring.”

‘Bittersweet’: Canada’s last captive whales leave Marineland for U.S. aquariums

Marineland had the largest collection of captive beluga whales in the world with 30. But the park had been put up for sale in 2024 before closing for good after that summer.

Nineteen belugas died at the park between 2019 and 2025.

Marineland said it was running out of money and needed the whales gone otherwise they would be euthanized.

stories.title: Ottawa to fund paid placements in skilled trades at a cost of $880-million
stories.summary: Program funding to come from $8-billion pot set aside to support the sector
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government is putting $880-million behind a plan to get young workers paid, ON-the-job experience in the skilled trades.

Starting early next year, young Canadians will be able to access paid job placements for up to four months to get hands-on experience before beginning an apprenticeship.

The funding comes from a bigger pot of $8-billion in spending that the Liberals have set aside since the spring economic update to promote the skilled trades across Canada.

‘The trades are having a real moment’: As perceptions change, more young workers are choosing this path

The federal government has stressed the importance of recruiting and training a new generation of skilled tradespeople – such as carpenters, electricians and welders.

As part of that regime, later this fall, any tradesperson who has completed an apprenticeship and earned a certification in a Red Seal trade since April, 2025, will also receive a $5,000 bonus.

The federal government will roll out a program over the fall to help small- and medium-sized businesses offer more apprenticeships and Ottawa also plans to top up employment insurance payments for apprentices during training starting next spring.

stories.title: Liberals will not compromise right to strike or bargain, jobs minister vows
stories.summary: Ottawa — Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government will not interfere with workers' right to strike as Ottawa considers legal changes to improve labour relations.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

Posted September 18, 2026 8:28 am.

Last Updated September 18, 2026 11:28 am.

Ottawa — Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says the federal government will not interfere with workers’ right to strike as Ottawa considers legal changes to improve labour relations.

Hajdu’s department held months of consultations with unions, employers and other stakeholders over the spring and summer about the state of the Canada Labour Code. Feedback from those sessions is meant to inform future legislation.

A report summarizing what the government heard during that review found that unions and employers were split over the degree of power Ottawa should have to intervene in disputes.

Most employers argued the government should have the ability to step in to quash a labour action when Canada’s national interests are at risk. Unions were staunchly opposed to any measure that could threaten their right to strike.

Hajdu was asked Friday in Ottawa whether she would respect unions’ concerns.

She said the government heard in the review that Canada needs a stronger labour regime to foster better relationships between workers and employers. The focus of the review was to find new supports for both parties, with an eye to leveraging the federal mediation service to maintain industrial peace.

“I can stand here and say that we will never interfere with a worker’s right to bargain or to strike, but we do all agree that there are circumstances where better tools are needed,” Hajdu said.

The minister would not say whether legislation to change the Canada Labour Code will come in the fall session of Parliament, which is set to begin Monday.

Canadian Labour Congress president Bea Bruske said in a media statement that the government’s labour review report did reflect what unions told Ottawa about its priorities.

“Canada needs stronger labour laws that protect the right to strike, support free collective bargaining and hold employers accountable when they break the rules,” Bruske said.

A Senate committee report published in June argued that labour disruptions in critical industries like transportation can harm Canada’s reputation as a reliable trading partner at a time when Ottawa is trying to diversify its trade beyond the United States.

Bruske said in her statement that worker protections, decent wages and collective bargaining are critical to making Canada’s economy more resilient in the face of U.S. trade aggression.

Hajdu was at Algonquin College on Friday to explain the federal government’s plan to get young workers paid, ON-the-job experience in the skilled trades.

Starting early next year, young Canadians will be able to access paid job placements for up to four months, giving them hands-on experience before beginning an apprenticeship.

The $880 million in funding for that program comes from a bigger pot of $8 billion the Liberals have set aside since the spring economic update to promote the skilled trades across Canada.

The federal government has stressed the importance of recruiting and training a new generation of skilled tradespeople, such as carpenters, electricians and welders.

Later this fall, any tradesperson who has completed an apprenticeship and earned a certification in a Red Seal trade since April 2025 will also receive a $5,000 bonus.

The federal government will roll out a program over the fall to help small- and medium-sized businesses offer more apprenticeships and Ottawa also plans to top up employment insurance payments for apprentices during training starting next spring.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

The federal government has stressed the importance of recruiting and training a new generation of skilled tradespeople, such as carpenters, electricians and welders.
Later this fall, any tradesperson who has completed an apprenticeship and earned a certification in a Red Seal trade since April 2025 will also receive a $5,000 bonus.

The federal government will roll out a program over the fall to help small- and medium-sized businesses offer more apprenticeships and Ottawa also plans to top up employment insurance payments for apprentices during training starting next spring.

stories.title: Barenaked Ladies bring ‘O Canada’ to Buffalo Bills home opener amid deepening cross‑border tensions
stories.summary: The Canadian anthem drew loud cheers inside the new Highmark Stadium, where the Bills have been emphasizing their southern Ontario fan base.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto

Posted September 18, 2026 8:26 am.

Last Updated September 18, 2026 8:31 am.

The Buffalo Bills turned their home opener into a rare moment of cross‑border unity Thursday night, inviting Toronto’s Barenaked Ladies to perform “O Canada” before kickoff against the Detroit Lions.

The Canadian anthem drew loud cheers inside the new Highmark Stadium, where the Bills have been emphasizing their sizable southern Ontario fan base — roughly 10,000 Canadian season‑ticket holders — even as political relations between Washington and Ottawa continue to sour.

O Canada! ???????? @barenakedladies | #DETvsBUF pic.twitter.com/eBxgaGjLmK — Buffalo Bills (@BuffaloBills) September 18, 2026

The performance came just days after the White House confirmed President Donald Trump had signed a memorandum targeting Canadian‑origin goods for removal from U.S. federal procurement , the latest in a series of tariff escalations and retaliatory moves that have strained bilateral ties.

Hawaiian‑born singer Auli’i Cravalho performing The Star‑Spangled Banner after Canada’s national anthem.

This isn’t the first time the Bills have played both anthems during games at Orchard Park. Under former owner Ralph Wilson, the Bills once hosted an annual Canadian fan appreciation game scheduled near Canadian Thanksgiving.

The Buffalo Sabres perform both national anthems before every home game, regardless of opponent, a tradition tied to Buffalo’s proximity to the border and its strong Canadian fan base. In April, fans helped finish “O Canada” after the singer’s microphone failed during a Stanley Cup playoff game against Boston.

Bills quarterback Josh Allen threw for three touchdowns and rushed for two more as Buffalo beat the Lions 41-31 on Thursday night to improve to 2-0 on the season.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney to address Liberal caucus after return from Europe
stories.summary: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday she wants Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to address his Liberal caucus in Ottawa on Friday.

The Liberal caucus retreat comes just before the fall sitting of the House of Commons gets underway on Monday.

Among the Liberals’ first bills of the sitting will be legislation to enact the fuel excise tax extension that Carney announced on Sept. 2.

On Thursday, Carney returned from Strasbourg, France, where he looked to secure a stronger alliance with Europe focused primarily on trade, defence and people-to-people ties — the latest move in his campaign to reduce Canada’s reliance on the United States.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday she wants Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union.

In a historic address to the European Parliament on Thursday, Carney said he welcomes von der Leyen’s ambition to see Canada become the first associate member of the EU.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Third Marineland beluga dies after being moved
stories.summary: Two Marineland belugas and a resident beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A third beluga that was a part of a massive move of whales from Marineland has died.

Oceanografic Valencia says Jelly Bean died suddenly on Friday.

The Spanish aquarium took in Jelly Bean and another beluga named Cleopatra in late August.

Two Marineland belugas and a resident beluga at Chicago’s Shedd Aquarium died within weeks of their move.

Marineland said it was running out of money and needed the whales gone otherwise they would be euthanized.

The closed Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction moved all 30 of its belugas and four dolphins to five aquariums in Chicago, San Antonio, San Diego, Atlanta and Valencia in Spain.

stories.title: Parole hearing for Hamed Shafia, convicted of murdering his sisters and woman
stories.summary: A man convicted of murdering his three sisters and another woman more than 17 years ago is set to have a parole hearing Friday.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A man convicted of murdering his three sisters and another woman more than 17 years ago is set to have a parole hearing F.

It wasn’t immediately clear what type of release Hamed Shafia is seeking from the Parole Board of Canada.

Shafia and his parents were found guilty in January 2012 of four counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of his teenage sisters and his father’s first wife in a polygamous marriage.

The four bodies were found in a car at the bottom of the Rideau Canal in Kingston, Ont., in June 2009.

The trial judge had described the killings as being motivated by the Shafia family’s “twisted concept of honour.”

The family had immigrated to Canada from Afghanistan and settled in Montreal, where the father was a successful businessman.

After his conviction, the younger Shafia argued that he was too young to be tried as an adult in the case, but Ontario’s top court rejected his appeal.

The Supreme Court of Canada declined to hear the case in 2017.

stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
When the fourth Toronto Biennial of Art launches next week, participants will be growing plants and harvesting vegetables along the Erie Canal in upstate New York, in the city of Detroit and on the Caribbean island of Martinique. The biennial aims for a North American reach this year, and the far-flung gardens and farms are the work of artists who are investigating the intersection of art and climate change.

“The projects are dealing with food insecurity, food sustainability, looking at the rupture of not having access to healthy food and proposing solutions,” said Allison Glenn, the American curator who picked Things Fall Apart as the title and theme for the 2026 exhibition.

The continental scope also fulfills the Toronto Biennial’s original ambition: to place Canadian art on the world stage. From its inception in the 2010s and its launch in 2019, the biennial has striven to bring global art to Toronto while showing the international art community what Canada can produce. By bringing in Glenn, after three iterations organized by Canadian teams, the exhibition is turning to the international model of hiring a prestigious outsider to curate a global gathering.

“We need a reoccurring international platform that can convene global and local voices, at scale,” said Patrizia Libralato, the biennial’s founding executive director. Back then, Canada was the only G7 country without an art biennial, to the clear disadvantage of Canadian artists, she said. “Successful biennials shape how a place sees itself and how it’s also seen globally.”

This year, one-third of the 34 participating artists are Canadian and, with a sense that the 12-week event must showcase the country’s senior talents, it features several well-known Indigenous artists – Kent Monkman, Bonnie Devine and Rebecca Belmore – who have not been included before.

After three iterations in borrowed spaces – 2019 featured an old car dealership on Lake Shore Boulevard and a former munitions factory in Mississauga, while the main venue for 2024 was a City of Toronto building in the Queen and Dovercourt neighbourhood – the biennial has entered into a partnership with the Art Museum at the University of Toronto, using its two galleries as the main venues.

Meanwhile, other institutions, including the Art Gallery of Ontario, the Royal Ontario Museum and Mercer Union, are once again contributing programming to the lineup.

“We don’t have a permanent home or a permanent space like some other biennials, so it’s nice to change up the model,” Libralato said.

The collaboration with U of T, and the collaboration among institutions in general, she added, has been driven by the financial constraints of an art scene where many public galleries are still trying to recover from the closings imposed by the pandemic.

She looks with envy to Australia, where the government of New South Wales invested $100-million to renovate an old power plant that now houses the Biennale of Sydney. The possibility of showing huge installations – like those displayed in the old naval warehouses used by the Venice Biennale – is tempting, Libralato acknowledged.

But instead the Toronto Biennial is looking for geographic scale, especially across water.

The Notebook of Return is a collaboration between two artists brought together by Glenn, the biennial’s curator: Jean-Marc Bullet is an innovative designer who runs a market garden in Martinique and Céline Semaan is a Lebanese-Canadian multidisciplinary artist based in Nyack, N.Y., and founder of the Slow Factory, a foundation dedicated to culture and climate education. She is also contributing a rewilding project entitled Slow Forest .

For their joint project, Bullet and Semaan have distributed seeds and notebooks to various groups, including the Toronto Black Farmers and Food Growers Collective and multidisciplinary Detroit artist and Wayne State professor Allana Clarke, who runs an organic garden. Elsewhere, New York artist Mary Mattingly has mounted a floating garden on a repurposed barge in the Erie Canal (in a collaboration with the 2026 Medina Triennial in Medina, N.Y.). The students of Sumner High School in St. Louis, Mo., who tend the garden of the Antioch Baptist Church in a historic Black neighbourhood, are also participating (in a collaboration with Counterpublic, a triennial in their city). All the participants are to plant the seeds, share the harvest and record the season.

The groups are all located along the Great Loop, a 9,700-kilometre navigable water route that covers the eastern United States and part of Ontario, and includes the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River. The watery theme is no coincidence: Glenn grew up in Detroit, near Lake St. Clair and the Detroit River, and now lives in New York in sight of the East River. Toronto, meanwhile, is busy re-establishing its connection to Lake Ontario with development in the Port Lands.

“I sometimes gaze out over the East River and wonder if it’s connected to Detroit,” Glenn said. “And that really started me on this journey of thinking about international waterways, trade routes and voyages.

“I was keenly aware that the inaugural biennial looked at the geographies of Toronto, and so I wanted to be sure that I was honouring that work,” she added, referring to the 2019 exhibition that included several waterfront venues and addressed the Indigenous history of the lakefront as a meeting place.

Glenn, who focuses on special art projects, has a Canadian great-grandparent and remembers travelling to Toronto and Montreal as a child while living in Detroit and also Rochester, just across the lake from Toronto.

“I grew up on the border,” she said. “My whole life has been spent gazing up at Canada.”

Her theme of rupture or collapse – or resilience in the face of them – extends beyond water. The Art Museum at U of T will exhibit paintings by California artist Cameron Harvey, three of which will also be shown at the Anchorage Art Museum in Alaska. The paintings are based on chaparral, the fire-resistant shrubs native to Southern California, and were inspired by the artist’s evacuation from her home to her studio during the Eaton and Palisades fires of 2025.

Of course, all this planning around Great Lakes geography and climate change took place long before U.S. President Donald Trump complained about Canadian wildfire smoke or attempted to rename Lake Ontario. Today, Glenn’s emphasis on a shared continent seems prescient.

The Toronto Biennial takes places at multiple locations until Dec. 20. Admission is free at most sites.

stories.title: A CEO’s family home close to the ski hills
stories.summary: The the estate, called Winterbrook, sits on a two-acre site next to the Osler Brook Golf course
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
2710 Nottawasaga 10 Concession N, Clearview, Ont.

Asking price: $3,975,000

Lot size: 290 by 300 feet

Property Taxes: $14,046 (2026)

Listing agents: Mark Veer, Mary Riopelle, Re/Max Four Seasons Realty Limited

In most families, what your home is like plays a big role in defining who you are and what you want as you get older. Sometimes, a second home (or a third) can play that same role.

For Canadian business veteran Joe Canavan, family is a foundational motivation. When he was building Fidelity Investment Canada in the 1990s and at other stops in his career, he says he has been driven by a commitment to helping Canadians build wealth since money is so often at the root of what breaks up families. When you build wealth, you reinvest in family.

Which is why it was an easy decision for him to build a ski chalet near Osler Bluff Ski Club in Collingwood, Ont. “That chalet was really built for our boys,” he said, referring to his three sons who have had almost unfettered access to skiing over the last 16 years. “Our family bonds are so much stronger, so much better because of our affiliation with the club.”

He was also driven by the role sports played in his own life and career.

“Playing hockey and football at a high level made me very competitive; that changed my character, my nature,” said Mr. Canavan. “I was never the most gifted athlete, but I was usually the captain of my team. My job was to be the guy who brought people together.” He’s been a CEO seven times over his career in finance and philanthropy, and still credits many of those lessons and experiences for his approach.

Home of the Week: Clapboard house is oldest documented wooden structure in Nova Scotia

It was friend and former National Hockey League Players’ Association boss Bob Goodenow who told him not to put the boys in hockey, which was his inclination.

“He essentially forbid me from putting my boys in hockey; he said our chances of having a boy in the NHL is 0.02 per cent. Goodenow said we should look at ski clubs. My wife Larissa, she was elated: she didn’t want to sit in hockey arenas all winter,” said Mr. Canavan.

So the boys began training for ski racing from a young age, and after a few years of renting chalet’s for the winter near Osler, Mr. Canavan found a two-acre site next to the Osler Brook Golf course and began construction in 2008 on the estate home now called Winterbrook. The design had a bit of everything the family wanted in a country getaway and at-home training facility: a full gym, boot and equipment room, hot tub, steam room and cold plunge tub (not to mention heated garage, which is a great perk when you’re running out to the lift on a cold morning) all of which reduces the friction to and from the slopes.

Mr. Canavan is proud of their accomplishments; his middle son was asked to join Canada’s national team (he declined, and has made a mark in Ironman competitions instead) and his youngest has coached in the sport. But they are grown up now, either in university or finished their degrees, and a full-season skiing hub isn’t as necessary for the family now.

Mr. Canavan said he and his wife were inspired by Belgian country homes featuring lots of stone and white oak for the motif of their chalet. Working with custom-builder Dalton Beachli, they came up with a series of spaces that emphasize natural materials and a connection with the landscape.

The front porch portico is made from big, chunky beams of Douglas fir from British Columbia, and those huge beams are used for structure and emphasis as you enter the main floor.

This central section of the house is a massive volume of space that’s open to the vaulted second-floor ceiling that is clad in Douglas fir. Directly across from the front foyer is a two-storey tall bank of windows that fill the great room with light and look out toward the golf course.

On the left from the foyer is a set of stairs (more chunky beams) that climb to a loft/bridge that connects the wings on the second level, and also descends to the partially above-grade basement. Passing under the bridge the great room opens up, with the wall on the right dominated by a chimney of mixed cut and raw stone, and to the left an entrance to the kitchen and dining area.

Home of the Week: A Brockville home steeped in history

The kitchen is built around a long stone-topped island prep space with induction cooktop built in, with an equally long dining space alongside it, all under more of the chunky wood beams and cladding. At the far end of the room is a set of double doors to a side patio with a built-in fire pit.

Back through the main room, the other wing of the house features a wood-panelled library/office, main-floor powder room, a large laundry room and the equipment rooms and garage access.

On the second level the primary suite is an airy space above the kitchen and its ensuite bathroom features double-sized walk-in shower, dual vanity and soaker tub. Three bedrooms for the boys and a shared bathroom fill the wing above the garage.

The basement rec room features another distinctive fireplace with huge stone slabs, and in addition to the gym on this lower level there are two guest suites (or nanny suites) and a full bath.

There are four fireplaces in the home, if you include the outdoor firepit, no accident since Mr. Canavan is a self-proclaimed fire fanatic.

“I wanted fire everywhere because my parents at home we didn’t have anything like that,” said Mr. Canavan, who shared that while his parents provided for the family, they were both new Canadians and often worked two jobs. When his career in finance began to take off, Mr. Canavan felt compelled as the oldest child to help support his parents.

“I bought my first cottage when I was 25, one of the reasons that place won out over other places, the beautiful stone fireplace, it was stunning and the centre of the home,” he said, and the effect this space had on his parents was profound. “I used to see my mother and father nattering at each other in the city but as soon as they went north of the 401 they were like lovebirds … it was crazy.”

He eventually gave that first cottage to his parents, and the gift he continues to give himself is spaces designed for his family to bond and connect. They host all the Thanksgivings and Christmases, the big anniversaries and birthdays. They never intended to sell this home, but the plan is to reconstruct a more modest version of it nearby.

When Mr. Canavan is at Winterbrook, he likes to start his day in that first-floor study, turn on the fireplace and get his morning reading done. If the kids are up for a ski run he’ll put together breakfast before they head out. When the day is done, winding down in the great room with the landscape shining through the windows and a fire roaring in the large fireplace is his idea of being at home.

When you build wealth, you reinvest in family.

Which is why it was an easy decision for him to build a ski chalet near Osler Bluff Ski Club in Collingwood, Ont. “That chalet was really built for our boys,” he said, referring to his three sons who have had almost unfettered access to skiing over the last 16 years. “Our family bonds are so much stronger, so much better because of our affiliation with the club.”
He was also driven by the role sports played in his own life and career.

“Playing hockey and football at a high level made me very competitive; that changed my character, my nature,” said Mr. Canavan. “I was never the most gifted athlete, but I was usually the captain of my team. My job was to be the guy who brought people together.” He’s been a CEO seven times over his career in finance and philanthropy, and still credits many of those lessons and experiences for his approach.
Home of the Week: Clapboard house is oldest documented wooden structure in Nova Scotia
It was friend and former National Hockey League Players’ Association boss Bob Goodenow who told him not to put the boys in hockey, which was his inclination.

“He essentially forbid me from putting my boys in hockey; he said our chances of having a boy in the NHL is 0.02 per cent. Goodenow said we should look at ski clubs. My wife Larissa, she was elated: she didn’t want to sit in hockey arenas all winter,” said Mr. Canavan.

So the boys began training for ski racing from a young age, and after a few years of renting chalet’s for the winter near Osler, Mr. Canavan found a two-acre site next to the Osler Brook Golf course and began construction in 2008 on the estate home now called Winterbrook. The design had a bit of everything the family wanted in a country getaway and at-home training facility: a full gym, boot and equipment room, hot tub, steam room and cold plunge tub (not to mention heated garage, which is a great perk when you’re running out to the lift on a cold morning) all of which reduces the friction to and from the slopes.

Mr. Canavan is proud of their accomplishments; his middle son was asked to join Canada’s national team (he declined, and has made a mark in Ironman competitions instead) and his youngest has coached in the sport. But they are grown up now, either in university or finished their degrees, and a full-season skiing hub isn’t as necessary for the family now.
The house today

Mr. Canavan said he and his wife were inspired by Belgian country homes featuring lots of stone and white oak for the motif of their chalet. Working with custom-builder Dalton Beachli, they came up with a series of spaces that emphasize natural materials and a connection with the landscape.
The front porch portico is made from big, chunky beams of Douglas fir from British Columbia, and those huge beams are used for structure and emphasis as you enter the main floor.

This central section of the house is a massive volume of space that’s open to the vaulted second-floor ceiling that is clad in Douglas fir. Directly across from the front foyer is a two-storey tall bank of windows that fill the great room with light and look out toward the golf course.

On the left from the foyer is a set of stairs (more chunky beams) that climb to a loft/bridge that connects the wings on the second level, and also descends to the partially above-grade basement. Passing under the bridge the great room opens up, with the wall on the right dominated by a chimney of mixed cut and raw stone, and to the left an entrance to the kitchen and dining area.
Home of the Week: A Brockville home steeped in history

The kitchen is built around a long stone-topped island prep space with induction cooktop built in, with an equally long dining space alongside it, all under more of the chunky wood beams and cladding. At the far end of the room is a set of double doors to a side patio with a built-in fire pit.
Back through the main room, the other wing of the house features a wood-panelled library/office, main-floor powder room, a large laundry room and the equipment rooms and garage access.

On the second level the primary suite is an airy space above the kitchen and its ensuite bathroom features double-sized walk-in shower, dual vanity and soaker tub. Three bedrooms for the boys and a shared bathroom fill the wing above the garage.
The basement rec room features another distinctive fireplace with huge stone slabs, and in addition to the gym on this lower level there are two guest suites (or nanny suites) and a full bath.
Fire when ready
There are four fireplaces in the home, if you include the outdoor firepit, no accident since Mr. Canavan is a self-proclaimed fire fanatic.

“I wanted fire everywhere because my parents at home we didn’t have anything like that,” said Mr. Canavan, who shared that while his parents provided for the family, they were both new Canadians and often worked two jobs. When his career in finance began to take off, Mr. Canavan felt compelled as the oldest child to help support his parents.

“I bought my first cottage when I was 25, one of the reasons that place won out over other places, the beautiful stone fireplace, it was stunning and the centre of the home,” he said, and the effect this space had on his parents was profound. “I used to see my mother and father nattering at each other in the city but as soon as they went north of the 401 they were like lovebirds … it was crazy.”

He eventually gave that first cottage to his parents, and the gift he continues to give himself is spaces designed for his family to bond and connect. They host all the Thanksgivings and Christmases, the big anniversaries and birthdays. They never intended to sell this home, but the plan is to reconstruct a more modest version of it nearby.

When Mr. Canavan is at Winterbrook, he likes to start his day in that first-floor study, turn on the fireplace and get his morning reading done. If the kids are up for a ski run he’ll put together breakfast before they head out. When the day is done, winding down in the great room with the landscape shining through the windows and a fire roaring in the large fireplace is his idea of being at home.

stories.title: White Rock home sells $150,000 below 2021 purchase price
stories.summary: House sold for $1.5-million in 2021
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
2168 165B St., White Rock, B.C.

Asking price: $1,397,000 (June 8)

Selling price: $1,350,000 (June 27)

Previous selling price: $1.5-million (2021)

Taxes: $6,923.25 (2025)

Days on market: 19

Buyer’s agent: Jeremy Sellmer, Oakwyn Realty

The sellers had purchased the property for $1.5-million in 2021, so the sale price shows the market adjustment under way, said the buyer’s agent Jeremy Sellmer.

“The clients loved the neighbourhood; they wanted something newer, they wanted a detached house, and they wanted to keep it under $1.36-million,” said the agent. “And this one fit the bill.”

His clients didn’t have any competition, he added.

“We put in an offer, and we went back and forth, and then sort of stalled out on this one for like a day or two. And then, probably an hour before our offer expired, they just sent it back signed. I guess they had a change of heart.”

This two-storey, 2,400-square-foot house is only nine years old, with five bedrooms, four bathrooms, air conditioning and a covered patio.

The design is open concept with a fireplace and large outdoor entertaining space. The floors are engineered hardwood, the countertops are quartz and the all-white kitchen includes a walk-in pantry.

The bedroom has vaulted ceilings with a walk-in closet and ensuite bathroom, and the basement includes a one-bedroom suite with a separate entrance. Shops, schools and parks are within walking distance.

“Buyers, they’re going to be very selective right now. And if you’re the same as three or four other places that are in your direct area, and you’re all priced relatively the same, the buyer is just going to get the best deal,” said the agent.

Mr. Sellmer said that, for sellers, it’s all about the number of private bookings that they get. Those are the best indicator that they’ve priced their house correctly.

The sale completed on Sept. 10.

stories.title: Lake Huron town turns to grazing goats for eco-friendly attack on invasive species
stories.summary: Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Goderich has temporarily become ‘Goaterich’ as grazing goats take on a week of eating, in the name of infrastructure access.

“So back in 2008 or 2009, we had a piece of the underground water infrastructure fail. And when we came in to make the repair, the disturbance to the soil let the invasive species, the Japanese knotweed and the Himalayan blackberry get established,” said Director of Operations, Infrastructure, and Community Services, Sean Thomas.

“Over the last decade, we’ve tried different options or different methods to address the issue. This is the newest one, and so far it seems to be the most successful,” he added.

Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.

Other options were considered to clear the utility corridor, but this unique approach won the day, says Goderich Deputy Mayor Leah Noel.

“Mechanical solutions aren’t great, right? The slope is steep and the area is wet, so it makes it really hard to get equipment in, and we don’t want to use herbicides so close to the lake obviously. So, this opportunity presented itself to bring in a herd of goats to graze,” said Noel.

The goat grazers have attracted a crowd each day as the chewing crew works its way from Sunset Park down to Cove Road near Goderich’s waterfront.

“Goats are built for this. They love steep hills, they love vegetation, they love everything leafy, so they’re going for it, they eat everything, said the owner of Big Crunch Grazing, Florentine Maathuis, from Caledon East.

“And because they’re relatively small and lightweight, their hooves are not a danger for erosion or anything. So they’re still respectful of the natural bluffs here,” said Maathuis.

According to Maathius, her goats and sheep have been booked all summer, travelling across southern Ontario, chewing up hard to reach areas of the province. She stays on site with her herding dogs, while her herd works away behind an electric fence.

They herd has until Sunday to complete Phase 1 of the job.

“It will likely take a couple of times of bringing the goats and sheep back in order to completely manage the site. But this is step one, and this is how we assess moving forward in an environmentally friendly way,” said Noel.
