stories.title: London civic election: Ward 14 all-candidates debate
stories.summary: The race to represent Ward 14 on London city council is wide open, with incumbent Steve Hillier not seeking re-election.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
The race to represent Ward 14 on London city council is wide open, with incumbent Steve Hillier not seeking re-election. The ward is huge, taking in about a third of the city by land area. Two candidates gathered for a debate on Thursday night and LFP city hall reporter Jack Moulton was there.

Ward 14 under the new city ward boundaries will remain the largest ward by area in the city. It includes the Pond Mills, Westminster, Summerside, Brockley, and Wilton Grove neighbourhoods.

Ubaid Bhatti (absent)

Jason King: 52, intelligence analyst/investigator, part-time professor

Sarah Lehman: 35, executive assistant

Gurinder Pal Singh (absent)

Speaking to a crowd of about 60 at Chalmers Presbyterian Church, located at Commissioners Road East and Pond Mills Road, King spoke of his canvassing on his home turf to build his platform.

“It is important to me that no conversation is rushed, so that I can be a good listener. As time went on, my campaign platform evolved and developed from what I was learning from you,” he said. “From that, I formed an actionable and realistic vision for Ward 14. My ideas bear the fruit of our engagements at the door.”

Lehman unsuccessfully ran for the ward in 2022, finishing with 40 per cent of the vote to Hillier’s 45 per cent. She was recently endorsed by the London and District Labour Council and on Thursday night touted her public- and private-sector experience and also pledged to be a constituency-focused councillor if elected.

“London is growing, and the decisions we make now will shape the city for decades to come. I want to see real progress in affordable housing and homelessness, reliable public transit to Ward 14, safer, more connected neighbourhoods, inclusion and accessibility to those neighbourhoods, and enhancing our existing green spaces as London grows,” she said.

Several residents who put questions to King and Lehman were eager to hear how well they know their ward, asking if they lived in the ward or were familiar with areas like Brockley and Glanworth. King said he lives in Summerside and Lehman, a longtime Pond Mills resident, said she lives across the boundary at Commissioners.

One question dealt with how to make the largely rural Ward 14 more prominent in the city, with King suggesting it’s a matter of an available councillor to respond to residents, and Lehman saying it’s a matter of better communication through the office on what is happening in the ward and city.

“I think that Ward 14 is suffering from being neglected for so long because we’ve not had a strong voice and strong representation at city council,” King said. “It’s also a political job. The work is to be political at making agreements with people, like other councillors, and drawing them into finding solutions.”

The first question involved homelessness, with King expressing his opposition to harm reduction in drug addiction, and Lehman suggesting more preventive measures through housing protections and provincial support, explaining “property taxpayers cannot be expected to solve a housing crisis, a mental health crisis, an addiction crisis, and an income support crisis on their own.”

On property tax increases, King suggested aiming for a tax freeze by bringing in more revenue through commercial development, while Lehman suggested reviewing city budgets for waste and duplication.

King dismissed the city’s Indigenous reconciliation action plan as something he’s never heard as a priority from residents, while advocating for city-building to everyone’s benefit. Lehman suggested better accountability and reporting for the city’s strategy.

When it came to climate action, King said the city should prioritize flood protection and downplayed climate change, saying the city has experienced “ quite typical and normal weather behaviour in the past few years.” Lehman’s answer took a different direction, acknowledging climate change while advocating for better transit and active transportation options to reduce emissions, and a robust tree canopy.

“Climate change isn’t something that’s happening somewhere else or decades from now – Londoners are already experiencing extreme heat, flooding, poor air quality from the wildfire smoke, and increasingly severe weather,” she said. “I would prioritize investments that make our neighbourhoods and infrastructure more resilient.”

Voters will head to the polls to elect their next city council on Oct. 26, with several advance voting days on Oct. 1, 3, 8, and 10.

There are 81 candidates running for London mayor and the 14 ward councillor positions — read what most of them have to say, in their own words, right here .

content_blocks.html: WHAT WERE THE HIGHLIGHTS?

content_blocks.text: Several residents who put questions to King and Lehman were eager to hear how well they know their ward, asking if they lived in the ward or were familiar with areas like Brockley and Glanworth. King said he lives in Summerside and Lehman, a longtime Pond Mills resident, said she lives across the boundary at Commissioners.

One question dealt with how to make the largely rural Ward 14 more prominent in the city, with King suggesting it’s a matter of an available councillor to respond to residents, and Lehman saying it’s a matter of better communication through the office on what is happening in the ward and city.

“I think that Ward 14 is suffering from being neglected for so long because we’ve not had a strong voice and strong representation at city council,” King said. “It’s also a political job. The work is to be political at making agreements with people, like other councillors, and drawing them into finding solutions.”

The first question involved homelessness, with King expressing his opposition to harm reduction in drug addiction, and Lehman suggesting more preventive measures through housing protections and provincial support, explaining “property taxpayers cannot be expected to solve a housing crisis, a mental health crisis, an addiction crisis, and an income support crisis on their own.”
On property tax increases, King suggested aiming for a tax freeze by bringing in more revenue through commercial development, while Lehman suggested reviewing city budgets for waste and duplication.

King dismissed the city’s Indigenous reconciliation action plan as something he’s never heard as a priority from residents, while advocating for city-building to everyone’s benefit. Lehman suggested better accountability and reporting for the city’s strategy.

When it came to climate action, King said the city should prioritize flood protection and downplayed climate change, saying the city has experienced “ quite typical and normal weather behaviour in the past few years.” Lehman’s answer took a different direction, acknowledging climate change while advocating for better transit and active transportation options to reduce emissions, and a robust tree canopy.

content_blocks.text: “Climate change isn’t something that’s happening somewhere else or decades from now – Londoners are already experiencing extreme heat, flooding, poor air quality from the wildfire smoke, and increasingly severe weather,” she said. “I would prioritize investments that make our neighbourhoods and infrastructure more resilient.”

stories.title: Is Canada’s future European?
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses why Canada and the EU are reaching for each other, and what its future might be in the age of President Trump.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney looks towards European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, seated left, as he addresses the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, ON Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted September 18, 2026 7:43 am.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has made history in Europe. On Sept. 16, he became the first foreign world leader to ever attend the State of the European Union (EU) address, delivered by President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen. During that address, von de Leyen invited Canada to become the first ever “associate member” of the EU. On Sept. 17, Carney himself addressed the European parliament, acknowledging the invitation and expressing Canada’s desire to become closer to Europe.

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Dr. Kurt Hübner, professor in the European studies department at the University of British Columbia, about what it might mean to be an associate member, why Canada and the EU are reaching for each other, and what the future of Canada and Europe might be in the age of U.S. President Donald Trump.

stories.title: Goderich becomes ‘Goaterich’ during weeklong grazing goat program
stories.summary: Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Goderich has temporarily become ‘Goaterich’ as grazing goats take on a week of eating, in the name of infrastructure access.

“So back in 2008 or 2009, we had a piece of the underground water infrastructure fail. And when we came in to make the repair, the disturbance to the soil let the invasive species, the Japanese knotweed and the Himalayan blackberry get established,” said Director of Operations, Infrastructure, and Community Services, Sean Thomas.

“Over the last decade, we’ve tried different options or different methods to address the issue. This is the newest one, and so far it seems to be the most successful,” he added.

Since Tuesday, 52 goats and 20 sheep have been eating undesirable vines and bushes covering a key corridor for Goderich’s water and natural gas pipes.

Other options were considered to clear the utility corridor, but this unique approach won the day, says Goderich Deputy Mayor Leah Noel.

“Mechanical solutions aren’t great, right? The slope is steep and the area is wet, so it makes it really hard to get equipment in, and we don’t want to use herbicides so close to the lake obviously. So, this opportunity presented itself to bring in a herd of goats to graze,” said Noel.

The goat grazers have attracted a crowd each day as the chewing crew works its way from Sunset Park down to Cove Road near Goderich’s waterfront.

“Goats are built for this. They love steep hills, they love vegetation, they love everything leafy, so they’re going for it, they eat everything, said the owner of Big Crunch Grazing, Florentine Maathuis, from Caledon East.

“And because they’re relatively small and lightweight, their hooves are not a danger for erosion or anything. So they’re still respectful of the natural bluffs here,” said Maathuis.

According to Maathius, her goats and sheep have been booked all summer, travelling across southern Ontario, chewing up hard to reach areas of the province. She stays on site with her herding dogs, while her herd works away behind an electric fence.

They herd has until Sunday to complete Phase 1 of the job.

“It will likely take a couple of times of bringing the goats and sheep back in order to completely manage the site. But this is step one, and this is how we assess moving forward in an environmentally friendly way,” said Noel.

stories.title: Ontario trucker sent to prison in U.S. for hauling cocaine allegedly for Ryan Wedding's cartel
stories.summary: Iqbal Singh Virk admitted that he helped knit a drug transportation network in Canada to an immense cocaine cartel in Mexico and US.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
An Ontario truck driver who was caught at the border trying to smuggle cocaine from the United States into Canada — allegedly for Ryan Wedding, the Canadian Olympic snowboarder named as an international narco mastermind — was sentenced to nine years in a U.S. prison after court proceedings draped in secrecy.

Iqbal Singh Virk, 58, an owner-operator of a transport truck based in Brampton, Ont., admitted to a judge in Los Angeles that he helped knit a drug transportation network in Canada to an immense cocaine cartel in Mexico and the United States.

In keeping with the high stakes and high profile of the Ryan Wedding investigation — including the murder of a government witness who was cooperating with U.S. authorities in the case — Virk’s hearings featured more secretiveness than usual.

Several documents entered into the court record were ordered sealed by the judge and cannot be read or reported on.

Judge Sherilyn Peace Garnett issued protective orders over court filings that could reveal the identities of confidential informants, cooperating witnesses and cooperating defendants “who participated in the government’s investigation and provided information relevant to defendant’s sentencing,” the order says.

The orders were to protect sensitive information from unauthorized dissemination while allowing defence lawyers with enough information to adequately represent Virk. The order also refers to material marked “Attorney’s Eyes Only,” which the lawyers cannot even show their client.

Garnett also granted a secrecy motion requested by Virk to have his response to the government’s sentencing position filed under seal and not available for public viewing.

John Hanusz, Virk’s lawyer, declined to comment on the case or on how Virk was taking the sentencing decision issued against him on Wednesday.

Virk signed a plea agreement last August admitting he was part of a cocaine conspiracy comprised of members of a drug-trafficking organization who arranged with a drug transportation network to move more than 1,800 kilograms of cocaine from the Los Angeles area into Canada.

Virk was part of the transportation network and drove his long-haul truck from Ontario to California specifically to collect cocaine and hide it in a secret compartment in his truck.

He and his partner, Ranjit Singh Rowal, shared the driving, then tried to mask the purpose of their trip by loading legal goods into the truck for the return to Canada.

Virk and Rowal, however, were caught in an elaborate sting operation the FBI was running after infiltrating the ring. The man with whom Virk was arranging the cocaine pick up was really a confidential source secretly working with the FBI.

When the pair pulled their tractor-trailer up to the customs post on the U.S. side of the Blue Water Bridge, connecting Ontario and Michigan, ON Aug. 28, 2024, Virk was behind the wheel and Rowal in the passenger seat.

They didn’t stand a chance of getting across as authorities were waiting for them. Customs officers were soon pulling cocaine bricks wrapped together in cellophane from a hidden slot at the rear of their trailer just above their Ontario licence plate. Stacking them on the loading bay floor, they counted 115 bricks weighing slightly more than 124 kilos. An officer estimated it was worth close to US$4 million.

The arrests of Virk and Rowal were a sign of things to come.

It turned out that they were small fry in the scheme of things as U.S., Canadian and Mexican authorities targeted an international criminal enterprise — a violent and prolific cartel authorities said was headed by Wedding.

Wedding, who competed for Team Canada in the 2002 Winter Olympics, was named the mastermind behind a deluge of cocaine flowing from Colombia to Mexico and then to California where it was loaded in trucks for the drive to Canada.

Two months after the arrests of the two drivers, Wedding’s name was the first on a long list of accused in a U.S. indictment. The FBI called Wedding a modern-day Pablo Escobar or El Chapo Guzman, naming two of history’s most notorious drug lords.

The last two names on the indictment were Virk and Rowal.

Both men pleaded guilty, 10 days apart, to two charges: conspiracy to distribute cocaine and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. Rowal was sentenced in November to 37 months in prison.

In return for Virk’s guilty plea on two drug charges, prosecutors agreed to drop other charges and asked the judge to reduce his sentence. Since Virk faced a maximum penalty of life in prison and an $11-million fine, nine years and no fine might seem a good deal, despite it being significantly longer than his partner’s punishment.

Virk’s conviction makes it almost a certainty that he will be deported from the United States upon his release from prison. Both men are citizens of India and travelled on an Indian passport but had immigrated to Canada, where they had permanent resident status.

Wedding remains in U.S. custody, also in California, after his arrest in Mexico in January. He pleaded not guilty to multiple drug trafficking and murder charges and is awaiting trial.

He and his partner, Ranjit Singh Rowal, shared the driving, then tried to mask the purpose of their trip by loading legal goods into the truck for the return to Canada.

They didn’t stand a chance of getting across as authorities were waiting for them. Customs officers were soon pulling cocaine bricks wrapped together in cellophane from a hidden slot at the rear of their trailer just above their Ontario licence plate. Stacking them on the loading bay floor, they counted 115 bricks weighing slightly more than 124 kilos. An officer estimated it was worth close to US$4 million.
The arrests of Virk and Rowal were a sign of things to come.

It turned out that they were small fry in the scheme of things as U.S., Canadian and Mexican authorities targeted an international criminal enterprise — a violent and prolific cartel authorities said was headed by Wedding.

Wedding, who competed for Team Canada in the 2002 Winter Olympics, was named the mastermind behind a deluge of cocaine flowing from Colombia to Mexico and then to California where it was loaded in trucks for the drive to Canada.

Two months after the arrests of the two drivers, Wedding’s name was the first on a long list of accused in a U.S. indictment. The FBI called Wedding a modern-day Pablo Escobar or El Chapo Guzman, naming two of history’s most notorious drug lords.
The last two names on the indictment were Virk and Rowal.
Both men pleaded guilty, 10 days apart, to two charges: conspiracy to distribute cocaine and possession with intent to distribute cocaine. Rowal was sentenced in November to 37 months in prison.

In return for Virk’s guilty plea on two drug charges, prosecutors agreed to drop other charges and asked the judge to reduce his sentence. Since Virk faced a maximum penalty of life in prison and an $11-million fine, nine years and no fine might seem a good deal, despite it being significantly longer than his partner’s punishment.

Virk’s conviction makes it almost a certainty that he will be deported from the United States upon his release from prison. Both men are citizens of India and travelled on an Indian passport but had immigrated to Canada, where they had permanent resident status.

stories.title: Sweden consistently outperforms Canada on universal health care despite similar spending: new study
stories.summary: Sweden maintains a higher physician-to-population ratio than Canada, with 4.4 physicians per 1,000 population, compared with 2.8 in Canada.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Sweden and Canada operate publicly financed universal health-care systems, but access to care in the Nordic country is “markedly better,” according to a new report from the Fraser Institute.

In 2024, wait times leading to unmet medical needs affected two per cent of Swedes, compared with 9.1 per cent of Canadians, says the report’s author, Yanick Labrie.

The study argues that the difference between the two national systems can be found in the way they are organized. Labrie states that almost half (46.9 per cent) of primary care centres in Sweden are privately operated, while still fully funded by public dollars.

Labrie notes that private providers in Sweden perform more than 40 per cent of publicly funded hip and knee replacements and over 70 per cent of cataract procedures.

Private providers have also expanded surgical capacity, rather than displacing it, he suggests. Between 2001 and 2019, the share of cataract patients treated within 90 days increased from 36.9 to 88.2 per cent while median waiting times fell from 6.2 to 1.8 months.

More particularly, 85 per cent of patients receive a medical assessment within three days when needed, the study states.

Labrie states that European health-care systems have attracted an increasing level attention among Canadian policymakers. For example, he states that in May 2026, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith led a delegation to Sweden to learn more about the country’s approach to organizing and delivering health care within a universal system.

Labrie notes that similar to Canada, Sweden’s health-care system is founded on the principle that access to medically necessary care should depend on need rather than ability to pay. But discussions of health-care reform in Canada often become highly polarized when it comes to expanding the role of private providers, says Labrie.

“As a result, health-care policy discussions in Canada often focus primarily on preserving existing financing arrangements rather than examining alternative models for organizing and delivering care to Canadians.”

The primary responsibility for organizing health care falls under Sweden’s 21 regions, governed by local political assemblies. Regional authorities are responsible for organizing hospitals, primary care, specialist services, and provider-reimbursement systems. Municipal governments are primarily responsible for long-term care, home care, rehabilitation support, and services for older adults and individuals with disabilities.

In contrast, says Labrie, beginning in the early 2000s several provinces (Quebec, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia and Alberta) merged regional health authorities into larger provincial organizations, reducing the autonomy of intermediary bodies.

Meanwhile, in Sweden patients commonly pay modest co-payments for primary care visits, specialist consultations, emergency department visits and prescription drugs. Annual caps substantially limit total out-of-pocket exposure.

Sweden permits duplicate private health insurance for services already covered under the public system, whereas in most Canadian provinces, such insurance remains heavily restricted or prohibited. By the end of 2024 over 800,000 Swedes held duplicate health insurance coverage (15.8 per cent of the working-age population). Most insurance policies are financed by employers as part of workplace benefits.

“In Sweden, privately insured patients continue to contribute to the public system through income taxation. They do not opt out financially,” says Labrie.

One of the greatest health-care needs – physician access – seems to be better met in Sweden, which according to Oecd data cited by Labrie, maintains a higher physician-to-population ratio than Canada, with 4.4 physicians per 1,000 population, compared with 2.8 in Canada. Sweden also has a national waiting-time guarantee aimed at improving timely access to care throughout the country.

Sweden’s Primary Care Choice Act was implemented between 2007 and 2010. The new legislation introduced patient choice among accredited primary care providers, whether publicly or privately operated. Private providers were allowed to establish new clinics and compete for patient enrolment under the country’s regional reimbursement systems.

Overall, says Labrie, the study’s findings indicate that greater private-sector participation necessarily reduces publicly financed health-care system capacity. “In several areas of Sweden, private providers expanded the overall volume of publicly funded services rather than simply displacing activity from public providers.”

stories.title: ‘He’s a fighter’: Mayich family opens up about son, brother Matthew
stories.summary: Matthew Mayich came to Arizona State last month, joining the Sun Devils after four seasons with OHL Ottawa and another at Ncaa Clarkson.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Elliotte Friedman, Sportsnet

Posted September 18, 2026 6:47 am.

John and Christina Mayich have two requests.

First, they want the world to learn more about their son, Matthew.

“Matthew is a boy’s boy,” Christina said. “He’s a guy’s guy. He is a simple, simple guy who has an infectious smile. Anybody you talk to will tell you about his smile. He loves to fish. He fishes almost every day, every chance he can get. He loves his family. He likes to hang out at home. He doesn’t like to go out partying … he just likes to be with us. He loves his girlfriend, his siblings, funny guy, chirper.

“And he, as a teammate, he obviously loves hockey. That’s his world. He likes to stand up for his teammates. He has your back. I wish you got to meet him as the Matthew we all know and love.”

“He brings joy to a room, bottom line,” John added, before Christina continued.

“When he’s away for hockey, our house is different. When he is there, there is so much, so much life, so much energy. He brings a different vibe to our home, to our family, and to the neighbourhood.”

Their second request is this: no matter where you are from or what faith you follow, you pray for their 21-year-old son.

Matthew Mayich came to Arizona State last month, joining the Sun Devils after four seasons with OHL Ottawa and another at NCAA Clarkson. Days after his arrival, on Aug. 20, Mayich collapsed during an outdoor workout and has been hospitalized since. The university is reviewing the circumstances, and a spokesman emailed Wednesday that “we expect to be able to update everyone on our review process in the coming days.”

“We’ve been told there was a workout scheduled for early (that day), and I guess it was hot, and the conditions weren’t good for working out,” John said. “(Matthew) basically got heat stroke. (It) had nothing to do with his heart. He came in shape. He was 100 per cent ready to go this season. He worked all summer, and he was ready.

“And I guess just the heat … just snowballed from there. He ended up collapsing and is still in a coma. Considering the situation, I think we’re somewhat strong in just trying to push through. We’ve got no choice.”

What have doctors told the family about the prognosis?

“We’re taking it day by day,” Christina answered. “We’re here praying hard, praying to our Lord for a miracle.”

“He’s a fighter,” added John. “So we know that, and we’re giving him every chance to survive.”

John and Christina have a strong support group in Arizona, including daughter Stephanie and son Josh — two and three years younger than their brother, respectively — and Matthew’s girlfriend of four years, Alexa. But what’s really helped in immeasurable ways is support from the most unexpected places, including priests who reached out from Kenya.

“There’s so many countries that we were very shocked to hear,” Christina said. “Matthew is a simple boy from Stoney Creek, Ont., and we don’t know how he made it that far that people are praying for him. It’s just proof that there’s a lot of great people out there. We’ve seen a different side of humanity that we would have never seen if we didn’t go through this.”

The Mayich family is hugely thankful to the doctors, nurses and hospital staff; Anthony Houston, who oversees eight Arizona hospitals, making sure Matthew received proper care. They were embraced by the local Lebanese community after the family visited one of their churches to pray to St. Charbel, a Lebanese-born monk revered for his powers of healing.

Among many from the hockey community: Utah coach Andre Tourigny, who scouted Matthew back when he coached the Ottawa 67’s, Auston Matthews, Clayton Keller and the Xhekaj family. John and Jack Xhekaj — Arber and Florian’s father — have a long friendship.

“If we don’t speak one Sunday, we’ll speak the next,” John laughed. “We never go more than two Sundays without talking.”

And the Thompson family, led by Kim, Tage’s mother.

“Kim set up a lovely vigil for Matthew that included his (Arizona State) teammates, their family, and anybody who wanted to come out and pray for Matthew, which was very lovely and means so much to us,” Christina said.

“I think there was about 25, 26 current players and ex-players,” John said. “It was very nice to see.”

“For me, it was emotional seeing them,” Christina continued. “When you saw the team, it was like, ‘Matthew, you should be sitting there with them right now. You shouldn’t be up here.’ So it was tough, but it was also very warm, very … I can’t explain. It’s all in my heart, so I’m thankful to everybody.”

John Mayich has a message for Matthew’s Sun Devil teammates.

“I feel for them. I don’t want them to feel guilty at all that this happened. They had to see some ugly stuff, and I just hope they can push through. I wish them nothing but the best.”

If his parents are most proud of one thing, it’s that their son had an ability to make friends of all ages, from putting together a three-year-old neighbour’s bicycle to helping Alexa’s octogenarian grandfather with his garden tomatoes. John Mayich smiled reminiscing about Ring video of young kids from the neighbourhood asking Matthew to come out and play street hockey with them, a request rarely — if ever — refused.

“He was, just … he lived life,” John said. “That’s it. He really did live life and he didn’t judge anybody. Never.”

Thanks to old friends and newfound supporters worldwide, Matthew’s hospital room is personalized with unique items.

“Five of his friends flew down when they heard the news, and they bought him fishing paraphernalia,” Christina said. “Went to Bass Pro, just kind of decorated his room, which was very nice, surrounding him with the things that he loves.”

By his head there is a stone in a pouch. On his body, there’s a small medallion, called the Miraculous Medal. Christina describes the Mayiches as devout Catholics; the Miraculous Medal reminds you to keep the faith, never lose your trust in the power of prayer.

“A man from England found us, and he had sent the package, which was the rock and a Miraculous Medal. When he sent it, (with) a picture of a Sister, I didn’t quite know who the Sister was. She’s an Irish nun who had just passed, and she’s on her way to being Canonized.

“And he took a chance, and he said, even if you don’t believe, there’s nothing to lose if you put this by Matthew’s head. So I did, because I was just so touched. And the next day I reached out to him, and he explained to me that he felt in his heart when he heard Matthew’s story that he needed to deliver this to us, to somehow find us. “It was blessed by Our Lady, which to me meant the world,” Christina continued. “And I could not believe that was happening. And it was a sign that Mary, our mother, is with us. And she is leading us to her son and giving us that peace and calm. So, we thank you from the bottom of our heart that you found us all the way from England.

“There’s just so many, so many people we’ve met along the way that have touched our hearts and that are showing us the goodness of humanity, and they all give us hope and faith.”

“Seeing the support back home and all over the world, it’s like, unexplainable,” added Josh, the younger brother. “It’s something I never imagined and it’s honestly a blessing.”

“All the kids here with us all put their crosses on here,” she said. “His siblings’ crosses are here, his cousin Vicky, her husband, Owen. “It seems like it started on our street with the yellow ribbons and then just spread,” John added. “And that’s Matthew. That’s his personality. You meet him once. Someone wants to introduce him to someone else and it just spreads.”

“It actually started in Canada in there’s an Instagram group,” Christina added. “It’s called ‘Yellow Ribbons for Matthew.’ So people are tying yellow ribbons on their trees outside. And the kids are wearing yellow ribbons. And there was just a soccer tournament in Ottawa … they were honouring Matthew by wearing “M.M” (and the) number nine, his soccer number when he was little.

“So this yellow ribbon has grown.”

There are three yellow ribbons on his hospital room window.

The family realized Matthew’s hockey dreams had a chance to become reality when Tourigny, then head coach and vice-president of hockey operations for the OHL 67’s, started showing up to Matthew’s games and practices.

“People are driving six, seven hours to just watch him skate for an hour,” John said. “So to me, that’s pretty cool.”

Christina: “We were excited for Matthew because he was excited.”

“I just remember dropping Matthew off the first time in Ottawa,” John smiled. “He’s 16 years old so we’re driving up and we get to the house. It was COVID so you couldn’t meet the billet family who are super people. I just remember this red door. I’m getting Matthew’s stuff out of the car and he goes to the front porch and the door’s closed. I started putting the stuff away, like what was left over back in the trunk. I look, he already shut the door. He was in the house, ready to go.”

“Yeah, we met the billet family and they’re like, ‘We’re new to this,’” Christina added while also smiling. “And I’m like, ‘So are we.’ And we’re like, ‘Okay, bye, Matthew.’”

John added: “But he wanted to be there.”

Was he ever homesick or anything like that? Both parents immediately jump in.

“No. No. No.”

“Yeah, he missed us,” Christina continued. “But he was, you know, this is his job. This is his dream. And he loved it. And he loved all his billet families. He was very close with all of them.”

Then came the lead-up to the 2023 NHL Draft. The calls were coming to Matthew’s phone.

“All sorts of teams were reaching out,” John said.

“Matthew would go in a room and I’d be at the door listening to him talk to the teams,” Christina laughed.

John grew up a Maple Leafs fan in the era of Wendel Clark and Doug Gilmour, his favourite players.

“I think when the Leafs called him, it kind of … kind of hit home a bit.”

Christina: “Yeah, they called a couple of times.”

John continued: “And, you know, when they call, you’re just like, ‘Wow. Like, how far (Matthew has) come with this sport. It’s unreal.”

The St. Louis Blues selected Matthew in the sixth round, 170th overall, in the 2023 NHL Draft. The family went to Nashville and saw it first-hand. John said they knew the Blues were a possibility, but “the reason why we went to the draft was because Tampa Bay told him to bring his skates, so you know there’s interest there.”

“So we’re like, ‘We better go,” Christina added.

“It’s surreal, right?” John continued. “You just think of all the work … You think of all the work that we did, all the work, his grandparents, his brother and sister, and his friends.

“One thing I’ll give Matthew: he surrounded himself with good people. He really has good people around. You can’t name them all, but that’s one thing he did right, is he surrounded himself with very good people.”

Good people attract good people.

John paused before answering: “Yeah.”

“Just seeing his dreams come true in that moment,” sister Stephanie remembered. “There was a point where I was … I don’t even know, but I was getting a little nervous. I was like, ‘What’s happening over here?’ When they finally called his name and you see that relief it’s kind of a blur. But, at the same time, it sticks with you. You see all his hard work. At that point, it was worth it.”

“Me and Matthew would always grow up watching the draft,” Josh added. “That was always our thing. We love the draft, and to be there and for him to be a part of it was surreal, and when I came to that moment where his name got called it’s something I’ll never forget, ever. For St. Louis picking him — and I grew up a Boston fan — the first thing I joked about was when St. Louis beat Boston. It was a dream come true seeing my older brother get drafted.”

“When we were leaving,” Christina continued, “we were out at the corner, and there was a group of guys also drafted as well. And I see a man walk by, and he went through the crowd … and I see him go over to tap Matthew.

“And I said, ‘Johnny, who is that guy? I know him. I’ve seen him before.’ And he’s like, ‘Oh, that’s Shane Doan.’ We asked Matthew, “What did he say to you?”

John, now: “(Doan) said, ‘Congratulations. We’ll be watching you.’”

“I don’t know if he just said that randomly, but to Matthew, that meant a lot,” Christina said.

Last spring, at a Buffalo Sabres playoff game to cheer on son Josh, Shane saw Matthew in the crowd. He walked over, tapped Matthew on the shoulder and said hello.

“It meant a lot to Matthew that he just found him in the crowd, tapped him and said that,” Christina added.

“He went out of his way to get a hold of him,” John emphasized. “It wasn’t just by fluke. He went out of his way to talk to this kid.”

Since Matthew has been in hospital, Doan has reached out several times to make sure the family is okay and offer whatever help is necessary.

John and Christina also wanted to recognize Matthew’s girlfriend, Alexa. There is a joke that the “official” relationship is four years, but they’ve known each other longer than that. She carries with her a scrapbook of great photos from their times together.

“So Alexa’s our special angel,” Christina said. “I met her at hockey. She came to support and watch Matthew. And ever since that date, she’s been part of the family. We had just met, but we were going on a road trip right away to Ottawa so she got a crash course into the family. Her family is Matthew’s family, too. Her dad’s one of his best friends. They’re so supportive and (Matthew) loves her so much.

“And I am so thankful, so thankful, so thankful for everyone and to share the story. If we can get prayers, more prayers for Matthew, it would mean so much to us.”

Last word to Matthew’s sister Stephanie.

“He brought light everywhere he went. He brought noise, but the best type of noise. He’s so humorous, and that’s something we hope and pray we can hear again. And I believe that we will.”

stories.title: B.C. Premier Eby to address local politicians amid snap election speculation
stories.summary: His annual speech to delegates at the Union of British Columbia Municipalities convention comes days after he warned Elections BC and his caucus to be ‘election ready’
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia Premier David Eby will speak to local politicians at their annual convention today just as he contemplates disrupting their upcoming municipal elections with his own provincial vote.

The premier’s annual speech to delegates at the Union of British Columbia Municipalities convention comes days after he said he warned Elections BC and his caucus to be “election ready” amid disruptions posed by the U.S. trade war.

A vote just two years into the NDP government’s mandate could overlap with the municipal election campaign that runs from Sept. 19 to Oct. 17, and the union’s president, Cori Ramsay, says that would be a disservice to citizens.

B.C. Conservative leader vows to stay as allegations emerge party funds were used to spy on critics

The Prince George city councillor says provincial leaders must uphold the principle of separate periods for local and provincial campaigns, so residents can properly consider the issues as they choose among 3,500 candidates running in local races.

Eby’s speech comes a day after B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay told delegates that she wasn’t going anywhere after being asked to resign by two members of her Opposition caucus, which has suffered nine defections in recent weeks.

Findlay called the prospect of a snap election a “cynical move” by a premier who knew she would win a Sept. 26 by-election in Abbotsford-Mission.

stories.title: Is there a design for Toronto’s parks?
stories.summary: Urban green spaces deserve care, attention and planning from design professionals
stories.author: Alex Bozikovic
stories.content:
Christie Pits is a melting pot of urban humanity. On an August Saturday there, hundreds of spectators watched the Toronto Maple Leafs baseball team get thrashed, lounging on the steep slopes above the diamond. To the south, down in the deep vale of the park, young people rested on the grass listening to reggaeton, while others sprawled on picnic tables or did kickturns on the skateboard ramps.

It was easy, ON an evening like this, not to notice that the park is a mess.

Benches are broken. The main pedestrian path is crumbling into a sinkhole, as it has been for years. A picnic shelter and a century-old washroom building are shedding peeling paint.

As Toronto approaches a municipal election on Oct. 26, its Parks and Recreation division has no design vision. The division will spend $440-million this year on construction projects. But much of that money trickles out in piecemeal fixes and alterations that do not generate great places.

Take Christie Pits. This 8.9-hectare space at Bloor and Christie streets was once a sand and gravel pit, spanning the old Garrison Creek. It has been a park for a century and is among Toronto’s busiest. People come to play, work out, watch baseball, enjoy festivals and just hang out in a crowd. This intense activity demands careful co-ordination. But no dedicated manager watches over the park.

And no plan shapes it. The city is planning or enacting seven different capital projects here. At least three more have been finished in recent years: Altered pathways, a new skate park and semicircular concrete pads billed as “lookouts.” Those lookouts, carved into the hill on the park’s south side, have brought about erosion, generating a zone of hard-packed mud. That’s not in the plan; it’s what happened.

In this chaos, basic amenities of a busy urban park are missing. There are few places to sit. There is little shade. There is no café or restaurant, where the thousand-plus people in the park on a busy day could get a sandwich or a coffee. Like most of the city’s downtown parks, it is chronically ignored.

The solution is clear. Major parks should each have a manager, and a comprehensive 20-year plan drawn up by excellent landscape architects. Not a shrub should be planted without reference to that design. This would offer a guideline: What kind of place is this? What do we want to happen here?

The mess has been building for decades. Since the Pits became a park in the early 20 th century, then named Willowvale Park, it has seen a subway go through its south side, and a pool and rink be added to its west. A 1922 drawing by city parks engineer R.B. Evans shows curling paths typical of Victorian green space. Their remnants remain, a vision never fully realized.

A decade ago, Christie Pits almost got a new vision. Back then, Toronto’s new downtown plan included a brilliant parks and public realm strategy. In it, landscape architects Public Work envisioned a specific “park district” here.

But that did not result in a design. Instead, stuff happened. The parks consultation department and a non-governmental organization conducted a “public life study” asking park users what they wanted to see. Dog owners said there should be more amenities for their pets.

Skateboarders were using the ice rink in the summer months and disturbing neighbours. So the city paved some grass to create a skate park. This brought activity; it also damaged the adjacent trees and removed a rare place to sit in the shade. And it works against the Parks and Recreation division’s goal of increasing green space – toward which the city will spend millions this year acquiring land and demolishing buildings.

But why is there no specific design for this place? Because Toronto Parks doesn’t really do design. Occasionally they create a “master plan,” which involves years of consultation and spits out vague principles. (Queen’s Park North has had two in 10 years.)

Mostly the division has plans and “strategies” that apply to many sites at once, like the washrooms plan they announced a year ago. Playgrounds, pickleball – everything citywide is imagined from 10,000 feet up.

That is backward. When you deal with a place, especially a park, you need to get down in the dirt. Socially, economically, ecologically, there are tradeoffs and constraints. Solving those challenges is what landscape architects and architects do. It requires conscious choices and demands imagination.

Instead Parks opts to solve issues bit by bit over time, with little or no input from design professionals. (Their staff includes a few landscape architects, whose power is limited.) Then politicians have their own ideas. Last year, city councillor Dianne Saxe proudly announced she and city staff had planted 22 new trees. Who decided where they should go? Who knows?

In this election year, change is possible. The general manager of Parks and Recreation, Terry Ricketts, is new to the job and hasn’t yet signalled a direction. The division’s “Facilities Plan” is in the middle of a review, ripe to be rewritten. The head of the powerful parks consultation unit has left for another job. And the head of capital projects is also leaving. To replace him, the city is looking for an engineer. The job posting says nothing about design or vision for public space.

That is unacceptable. Parks building should be led by a distinguished design professional who has a vision. Parks strategy and its biggest projects should get external design review and council debate. What are the priorities? How and where are we building great parks?

Toronto has seen in recent years that this is possible, as great landscape architects and the agency Waterfront Toronto gave the city Love Park and Biidaasige Park. City parks can’t all be masterpieces, but they shouldn’t be the pits.

stories.title: London's 1st Hussars raise $100K for veterans' supportive housing project set to open this fall
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London·Video
A local London, Ont., Canadian Forces reserve regiment has raised $100,000 for Homes for Heroes' London Veterans' Village.
· Posted: Sep 18, 2026 6:14 AM EDT | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
London's 1st Hussars present their $100,000 cheque to Homes for Heroes.
7 hours ago|

A Canadian Forces reserve regiment raised $100,000 to support the London Veteran's Village, a transitional, supportive housing community for veterans built by Homes for Heroes. The project is nearly complete, and the first residents are expected to move in later this fall.
Members of London's 1st Hussars, presented the cheque at the nearly-completed site on Thursday afternoon.

"When we heard this project was coming to London, we knew we had to get behind it," said Honorary Lieutenant Colonel Bob Buchanan. "We had to support former members from our membership, our friends and family, our veterans."
"We know how important it is to get behind service members who are living rough for various reasons."

The London Veterans' Village, a transitional, supportive housing community for veterans, has been under construction on the Parkwood Institute grounds in south London since the spring. It consists of 25 single-dwelling tiny homes, including five fully accessible units, set up around a common resource centre, community garden and wraparound supports for the veterans that live there.

It's being built by the Homes for Heroes Foundation, a Calgary-based charity that has built similar supportive housing communities in Calgary, Edmonton, and Kingston, with another underway in Winnipeg. The London village is set to welcome its first residents later this fall.
Q&A A tiny home village for veterans is coming to London. Here's how it will work
Members of the 1st Hussars, along with their friends, families and the wider community came together "in a very impressive way" to raise the $100,000, Buchanan said.
"It was just a fantastic experience to see the energy behind the fundraising for this," he said. "It's more than a cheque to us, it's a commitment."

Patrick O'Hagan, a member of the 1st Hussars who sits on the Homes for Heroes steering committee for London, said it didn't take long to raise the money through initiatives like dinners and luncheons.
"The people of London are incredible," he said.
In a show of appreciation for the donation, one of the houses in the village will be named after the regiment, O'Hagan said, with a memorial to some of their lost veterans outside.
Kim Shippey, the Vice President for Advancement at Homes for Heroes, accepted the cheque from the 1st Hussars in what she called "a really heartfelt moment" of collective impact and action.
"That's what a check like that represents," she said. "It's a group of people that are coming together that want to do good within their own community and beyond."
"It really makes your heart feel full, and it becomes the why of what we do."

stories.title: Northlander train still being repaired months after crash during testing
stories.summary: In early July, one of the Northlander trains ploughed into a vehicle at the rail crossing on High Falls Road when the lights were active to stop cars entering the track.
stories.author: Isaac Callan, Colin D'Mello
stories.content:
One of the new Northlander trains ordered by the Ford government to restart rail service to northern Ontario has been out of commission for two months, since it crashed into a tow truck near Bracebridge, Ont.

In early July, during a testing and commissioning run, one of the Northlander trains ploughed into a vehicle at the rail crossing on High Falls Road when the lights were active to stop cars entering the track.

Although nobody was injured in the collision, the train has been out of service and under repair for the two-and-a-half months that followed the crash.

“Repairs to the trainset will be completed soon and testing and commissioning activities are advancing as we prepare the service for launch,” a spokesperson for the Ministry of Transportation told Global News.

Reopening the Northlander train was a 2018 election promise by Ontario Premier Doug Ford. It is set to run from Toronto’s Union Station to Timmins and Cochrane.

The train route was originally decommissioned by the Ontario Liberals in 2012.

Although the Ministry of Transportation did not confirm if, or how much, the July crash had delayed testing and therefore the date for the line, Ontario NDP MPP Guy Bourgouin said locals were growing frustrated.

“The people of the north, we want the Northlander back, of course,” he told Global News.

“This is a service that we need in northern Ontario. We’ve been asking questions to the government, to the appropriate people; we can’t get an answer. We heard it was supposed to start at the end of August, then the end of September.”

The government has not set a specific opening date for the train line, but has said it will be operational in 2026.

stories.title: Warm, sunny Friday ahead before weekend rain
stories.summary: Friday is shaping up to be the best day of the next few, with a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 22 C, according to CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Friday is shaping up to be the best day of the next few, with a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 22 C, according to CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison.

Winds will be light from the north, with comfortable conditions expected throughout the afternoon.

“We have a beautiful Friday on the way. I hope you make it a great day under a mix of sun and cloud,” said Atchison.

Rain is expected to arrive Saturday night and continue into Sunday, with daytime highs of 19 to 20 C over the weekend.

Fall officially arrives Monday night shortly after 8 p.m. Tuesday, the first full day of fall, will bring a mix of sun and cloud with a high of 17 C and a chance of rain overnight.

Showers are also expected Wednesday.

stories.title: Riopelle retrospective among highlights of fall art lineup
stories.summary: Black folk art and Caribbean culture form another powerful theme on the fall calendar
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
More fall culture: Film | Albums | Stage | TV | Concerts

The big event of the fall season is the opening of the Espace Riopelle – Michael Audain Pavilion at the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec (Mnbaq) in Quebec City. Festivities begin Oct. 22 to celebrate a new wing of the museum dedicated to Quebec painter Jean-Paul Riopelle, who died in 2002. Exhibitions include a 130-work retrospective of Riopelle’s career from his early involvement with the Automatiste movement in Montreal to his role as a leading abstractionist in Paris in the 1940s and 50s and his return to Quebec and representation in the 1970s.

There will also be a reinstallation of Mnbaq’s collection of modern art to put Riopelle in context, and a new presentation of Tribute to Rosa Luxemburg , the 1992 fresco the artist created in reaction to the death of his former companion, the American painter Joan Mitchell. An interactive exhibition, Art and Emotions, will investigate reactions to Riopelle’s work from both those who knew him and the public. Timed tickets for the Oct. 22-25 events, which also feature dance and musical performances, are available on the museum website .

The new pavilion is named for British Columbia art collector Michael Audain, who along with Quebec philanthropists André Desmarais, France Chrétien Desmarais and Pierre Lassonde, helped fund its construction. Audain, his wife, Yoshiko Karasawa, and Lassonde have also donated 60 works from their personal collections.

It’s an unusual cross-Canada collaboration that reveals the impact of collectors’ tastes and interests on major institutions. Back in Audain’s home province, Griffin Art Projects in North Vancouver specializes in exhibiting private collections. On Sept. 12, it opened Found in Translation: The Michael and Inna O’Brian Collection, featuring the historic and contemporary Indigenous art, and contemporary Canadian and international work, collected over 40 years by the O’Brians. (Michael O’Brian died in 2023.) The collection covers a century’s worth of work and includes such contemporary Indigenous artists as Shawn Hunt, Lawrence Paul Yuxweluptun and Michael Nicoll Yahgulanaas. It runs until Dec. 13.

The Art Gallery of Alberta in Edmonton figures this is a good moment to investigate the influence of the Automatistes, the seminal Montreal abstractionists of the 1940s and 50s led by Paul-Émile Borduas and including Riopelle. Les Automatistes and Automatic Painting in Alberta focuses on the movement’s core concept of spontaneity, letting the subconscious mind direct creativity to seek truth and liberation in the intuitive, the random and the serendipitous. The show features work by Quebec artists and automatic painting from the West. The ideas arrived in Alberta thanks to Jock Macdonald, later a member of the Painters Eleven, who was influenced by the British Surrealists and introduced automatic painting to Alberta artist Marion Nicoll in the 1940s. It runs from Oct. 31 to Jan. 24.

Black folk art and Caribbean culture form another powerful theme on the fall calendar. Contemporary Calgary is now showing the work of Curtis Talwst Santiago in an exhibition titled worlds, worlds, worlds. The Canadian artist, who lives in Germany, makes miniature dioramas showing scenes of life in the Caribbean diaspora. The Infinity Series , started in 2008, features tiny figures mounted in cardboard and cloth jewellery boxes, scenes of people waiting for a haircut or enjoying a dance party, with themes of migration and territorialism emerging from these seemingly toy-like creations. The exhibition runs until Jan. 3.

The Art Gallery of Nova Scotia in Halifax is currently showing the work of Harold Cromwell with its first-ever solo show devoted to the neglected Black folk artist, who died in 2008. Cromwell was born in the Black Loyalist community of Weymouth Falls, N.S., in 1919, and developed a meticulous, highly detailed style, drawing in pen and ink on lowly materials such as cupboard doors, scraps of paper and paper plates. His subject was daily life in a rural community, including his youthful memories of the Depression years. On the Matter of Memory: The Drawings of Harold Cromwell continues to July 4.

The Art Gallery of Ontario in Toronto considers the role of self-fashioning in Black culture from the 1880s to the present with Sunday Best: The Power and The Glory of Black Style. Co-organized with the Philadelphia Museum of Art, the exhibition includes fashion, visual art and video. It’s open to members Oct. 7 and the general public Oct. 13, and continuing to Feb. 28.

stories.title: Style Magazine Autumn 2026: Download the full issue
stories.summary: We pay tribute to Canada’s most stylish dressers. Plus: makeup goes bold, and reimagining the classic Chanel blazer
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
With her first photography exhibition in Toronto, Melissa Auf der Maur considers the indie energy of 1990s music with a new exhibit at the AGO. We caught up with the musician to talk nostalgia, rock music and the power of excavating the past.

Also in the Autumn 2026 issue:

Style: Canada’s best-dressed list showcases seven stylish Canadians who have embraced their sartorial evolution as they get older (pg. 8)

Fashion: We unpack the utilitarian toppers and bejewelled blazers that are redefining the Chanel jacket (pg. 36)

Personal Style: Saying goodbye to the Paris apartment that taught a lesson in style (pg. 46)

Download the full issue of Style Magazine Autumn 2026 issue here .

For the Summer 2026 issue, we sit down with actor Whitney Peak, who’s set to star in the Hunger Games prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping in the fall. Peak is also the face of Chanel, a partnership that’s allowed her to travel the world and experiment with the clothing and accessories she once admired from afar. On set, she says, “I get to play dress up in the most beautiful clothes, which always feels surreal.”

Also in this issue:

Design: Our annual roundup of Canada’s best architecture and interiors illustrates how to live creatively at home (pg. 10)

Travel: Mandarin Oriental’s Vienna outpost distills the city’s design ethos (pg. 42)

Personal Style: Online shopping has disconnected us from the importance of how a garment feels (pg. 46)

In the Spring 2026 issue, we catch up with Anna Lambe , the breakout star of the hit show North of North (pg. 26); And our first-ever portfolio of names to know focuses on the creative journeys of those in visual arts , furniture retail , conceptual dining and jewellery design (pg. 8).

Design: The enduring appeal of Birkenstock (pg. 40)

Travel: Don’t skip New Brunswick on your foodie journey (pg. 44)

Personal Style: You’ll never guess this season’s fail-proof accessory (hint: You already own it.) (pg. 46)

In the Holiday 2025 issue, we catch up with singer Alex Porat (pg. 28), who’s joined a growing cohort of 20-something pop stars who are dominating music streaming and wielding enormous cultural influence. And whether you’re looking to give the perfect gift (pg. 8) or host an over-the-top holiday party (pg. 38) we’ve got you covered.

Fashion: The grand finale of the latest round of runway shows was Matthieu Blazy’s debut at Chanel, which placed the house on a bold new path (pg. 34)

Travel: At La Minerva in Rome, Orient Express chicly steps into luxury hotels (pg. 42)

Personal style: It’s time to ignore the influence of online algorithms and go back to basics to cultivate good taste (pg. 46)

In the Autumn 2025 issue, we pay tribute to our man in London, Montreal-born fashion designer Erdem Moralioglu (pg. 28). As Moralioglu marks the twentieth anniversary of his mononymous independent fashion house, we take a look at his unshakeable style.

Style: Meet the best-dressed Canadians, the creative types who are making their mark with their chic sense of style. (pg. 8)

Fashion: This season’s knit standouts range from delicate pieces to chunky layers. (pg. 30)

Travel: On her first-ever cruise, writer Maryam Siddiqi discovers the magic of Greenland. (pg. 44)

In the May 2025 issue, we highlight the growing interest in archival fashion, which is prompting designers to embrace their own greatest hits. Also in this issue:

Travel: Shop the spoils of Mexico City’s local maker boom (pg. 38)

Accessories: Bold pieces take on a sculptural quality (pg. 42)

Design: Lessons from a design lover’s first new build (pg. 46)

Download the full issue of Style Advisor May 2025 here.

The March 2025 issue celebrates the joy of travel and discovery, from wine to fashion to grand hotels. Also in this issue:

Wellness: Take the plunge at Prince Edward County’s new Nordic spa (pg. 20)

Beauty: Globetrotting perfumes are the ultimate souvenir of your next trip abroad (pg. 21)

Accessories: Glashütte, Germany is a small town with an outsized role in the watchmaking world (pg. 22)

The November 2024 issue is about holiday style, trends and inspiration. Also in this issue:

Gift Guide: The most over-the-top gift ideas for that special person in your life (pg. 15)

Travel: A preview of 2025’s buzziest destinations (pg. 26)

Fashion: Chanel’s cruise collection tries to evoke the magic of Marseilles (pg. 40)

This issue is all about fall fashion, from pinstripes to plush coats. Also in this issue:

Film: Costume designer Mara Zigler explains how vintage clothing elevates storytelling on screen (pg. 10)

Travel: Architect Omar Gandhi’s personal retreat is now open to guests who want to experience ‘the best sleep of their lives’ (pg. 26)

Shopping: The joy of shopping in real life is making a comeback (pg. 42)

In summer fashion this month, a garden variety of greens gives this season’s collections a lush look (pg. 28). Also in this issue:

Accessories: Artful hair tools and ‘90s minimalism (pg. 18)

Wine: A look at how Sideways changed the California wine scene, two decades later (pg. 26)

Travel: New British design in historic Bath (pg. 42)

In the March 2024 issue, we celebrate the joys of travel, from the dramatic drive up California’s central coast (pg. 26) to exploring creativity in Japan’s cultural capital (pg. 42) to soaking up the slower side of Spain’s party island, Ibiza (pg. 38). Also in this issue:

Art: A look at the joyous work of Quebec artist Jeraume (pg. 21)

Wine and Spirits: Australia’s wine leader thinks global (pg. 29)

Fashion: Vacation must-haves, from statement sandals to beach-ready totes (pg. 16)

In the November 2023 issue, we celebrate lavish holiday baubles and haute couture. Plus, our gift guide has the best picks in dreamy watches and jewellery for lavishing on your loved ones. Also in this issue:

Winter fashion: Statement coats elevate utilitarian elements (pg. 28)

Travel: New Year escapes to Antigua, Bodrum and Mykonos (pg. 42)

Food: Trifle captures how holiday entertaining can be both nostalgic and resourceful (pg. 46)

The September 2023 issue is all about fashion’s next act: high drama. We look at designers who are creating theatrical counterpoints to the quiet luxury frenzy. Also in this issue:

Beauty: New cosmetics inspired by beautiful gardens and wild landscapes (pg. 38)

Travel: Fogo Island Inn celebrates 10 years of outport design (pg. 42)

Retail: On Madison Avenue, a new boutique captures a designer’s roots and a sense of home (pg. 46)

In the May 2023 issue, we track the rise of a more grown-up fashion sensibility, and explore weekends in the country house, from Prince Edward County to the British Isles. Also in this issue:

Wine & Spirits: Warm-weather sips, from chilled gamay to zero-proof rosé. (pg. 26)

Technology: Is a well-connected home all it’s cracked up to be? (pg. 22)

Fashion: The summer’s best neck ties and loafers (pg. 18)

In the March 2023 issue, we take you on a coastal escape in Turks and Caicos, where spring’s holiday-ready fashion is set amid a dazzling backdrop. Also in this issue:

Wine & Spirits : These 9 souvenir bottles are hyper-local gems (page 28)

Beauty: Pack easy with these carry-on cosmetics that are meant to travel (page 20)

Design : A crash course in good taste in Sweden (page 22)

In our November 2022 issue of Style Advisor, we capture the fun and glamour of the holiday season. From playful gifts to shimmering face jewels, this month is all about the spirit of self expression. Plus: we explore how caviar got to be so casual, and offer a first look at resort collections.

For our September 2022 issue of Style Advisor, visual art takes centre stage. In our main fashion spread, we look at how the season’s top styles are influenced by some of history’s most famous art movements, with a striking backdrop: an original mural created by artist Sarah Alinia Ziazi, which she created while we shot this year’s cover model. Plus, photographer Adetona Omokanye goes beyond the ‘poverty gaze’ to celebrate West African fashion, Caitlin Agnew explains how you can get the most from a good night’s sleep, and more in this month’s issue, which you can download below.

In May, men’s wear went high-voltage, and we looked at how vintage Ikea has the resale market cornered, plus we checked in at a few hotels that are elevating the enjoyment of art.

In March, we took you on a stylish tour around the world, from Prince Edward County’s revamped Royal Hotel to sustainable travel-focused New Zealand to Tuscany, where olives are harvested for oil production under cover or darkness.

In November, we presented a gift guide to sculptural perfume bottles, quirky bags, handmade ceramics and crafty ornaments, plus plenty of other stylish suggestions including made-in-Canada and sustainable gifts.

In April, we looked at Quonset houses that offer loft-like airiness with more affordable construction, plus summer design trends, men’s spring fashion and the playful world of dollhouse design.

In the March issue we spotlight the chintz prints and botanic lacework of the new collections, take a farm-to-flaçon journey across France to mark the 100th anniversary of Chanel No. 5, and trace how designers are working with artists to bring us closer to their creative process.

The November holiday issue highlighted gifts that give back, new twists on holiday pastries and festive decor, makeup and wardrobes.

The people profiled in the April issue devote their time to inspiring a sense of wonder in their audiences, from National Ballet of Canada artistic director Karen Kain to artist Jen Mann, who paints portraits that look deep into selfie culture.

stories.title: Fall theatre season bets big on made-in-Canada productions
stories.summary: Audiences will find a notable uptick in homegrown and international theatre in the months to come
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
More fall culture: Film | Albums | TV | Concerts | Visual Art

For the past year-and-a-half, many Canadians have opted for local or international goods and experiences over American ones. This fall, major Canadian theatre companies – which plan their seasons far in advance – have started to catch up with the shift in demand, just in time for an escalating trade war. Audiences will find a notable uptick in homegrown and international theatre in the months to come.

From an adaptation of a Mona Awad novel to a Canadian musical about a performer with more than 35 siblings around the world, here are five shows to look out for in Toronto and beyond this fall.

Ins Choi, best known for writing the 2011 play Kim’s Convenience and its TV adaptation, is back this fall with Son of a Preacherman , a funny drama that combines Choi’s experiences of growing up in a family of clergy with his trademark wit.

An intimate snapshot of this country’s Korean-Canadian communities – and Choi’s own faith – Son of a Preacherman runs at the National Arts Centre until Sept. 26, then tours to Toronto, Vancouver and Kamloops in October and November.

When Our Little Secret: A True New Musical first premiered at the 2023 Toronto Fringe, the show was subtitled “the 23andMe musical.” And rightly so: The piece, written and performed by Noam Tomaschoff, examines the actor’s experience of finding out he’s not really an only child and instead has at least 35 siblings around the world.

I left the U.S. for Canada a decade ago. These plays and musicals taught me what it means to be Canadian

Our Little Secret has adjusted its title, but after a successful run at Montreal’s Segal Centre last year, the show is just as buzzy as it was three years ago. This fall, a new production directed by Broadway’s Adam Pascal will play at Edmonton’s Citadel Theatre in October and at Toronto’s CAA Theatre in November.

Operation Mincemeat , the centrepiece touring production of Mirvish’s subscription season, will play at the Royal Alexandra Theatre for a lengthy run from October to December.

First conceived by British musical comedy group SpitLip, Operation Mincemeat May offer a compelling change of pace for Mirvish audiences: The show is neither a jukebox musical nor an adaptation of an existing film. Instead, it’s a hilarious, award-winning spy thriller about the successful 1943 British operation to disguise the Allied invasion of Sicily.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a bookish twentysomething in this country who hasn’t read anything by Mona Awad, and particularly Bunny. (Hey, guilty as charged.)

But this fall, Crow’s and Soulpepper theatres in Toronto will tackle another Awad title: All’s Well , which follows theatre professor Miranda Fitch as she struggles to manage chronic pain, a fiery temper and a crop of underinspiring drama students in equal measure. Maev Beaty will play Miranda in the adaptation, penned for the stage by the ever-busy Erin Shields , and former Shaw artistic director Jackie Maxwell will direct. After its premiere run in Toronto this fall, the production will transfer to Theatre Aquarius in Hamilton in early 2027.

Monks , another Toronto Fringe success story, first premiered in 2024 and almost immediately acquired a cult following in the city. The clown show, about two friars tasked with counting lentils, has popped up around Ontario for short runs since that first Fringe run, and this summer, the show travelled abroad to the Edinburgh Fringe, where it was showered with praise from audiences and critics alike.

Named one of the best new Canadian works of 2025 by the Toronto Theatre Critics’ Awards, Monks , created and performed by Annie Luján and Veronica Hortigüela, returns to Toronto this October with a two-and-a-half-week run at Tarragon Theatre.

stories.content:
More fall culture: Film | Albums | Stage | TV | Visual Art

In 2021, concert promoter Live Nation opened the 2,500-capacity History club in Toronto, filling the need for a mid-size venue in the city.

Sleek, ultramodern and built specifically for music, the two-level facility has extra cachet for its association with local rapper Drake, who had a hand in the design. By any reasonable standard, the venue has been a success.

Now History has repeated itself. Last month, Live Nation opened a 2,000-capacity sister club with same branding in Ottawa, a city that had seen the shuttering of Barrymore’s Music Hall and the rock bar Mavericks.

Ottawa’s History complements the 900-capacity Bronson Centre and the National Arts Centre’s soft-seater, Southam Hall.

While History welcomes such artists as melodic singer-guitarist Bahamas, funky fusionist Thundercat, indie rockers Modest Mouse and the pop star Talk this fall, the Bronson Centre has Daniel Lanois, the Skydiggers and Protest the Hero on its schedule. Southam Hall hosts the likes of Begonia, Bruce Cockburn, Rheostatics, k.d. lang, Loreena McKennitt, Charlotte Cornfield and, for something completely different, Monty Python comedian John Cleese.

stories.title: Robinhood grows Toronto work force to 200 as trading giant ramps up Canadian expansion
stories.summary: The Toronto office is now the company’s third-largest globally by head count and one of its fastest-growing
stories.author: Meera Raman
stories.content:
Robinhood Markets Inc. Hood-Q has grown its Canadian work force to more than 200 employees and moved into a new Toronto office with room for roughly twice that number, as the U.S. trading giant ramps up its expansion into Canada just months after officially launching in the country.

The Toronto office, which opened in August, is now Robinhood’s third-largest globally by head count and one of its fastest-growing, according to Chris Pollock, general manager of Robinhood Canada. The space has capacity for about 400 employees, and the office currently has more than 20 job openings listed as of mid-September. The company declined to provide a hiring target.

“It’s not just Robinhood launching in Canada. It’s also Robinhood investing in Canada,” said Johann Kerbrat, Robinhood’s senior vice-president and general manager of crypto. Robinhood first established its Canadian headquarters in Toronto in 2024.

The company is preparing to expand its Canadian offering beyond cryptocurrency. Mr. Kerbat did not say which product will come next but said Robinhood’s next phase will focus on more trading and investment products.

Robinhood entering Canada after closing WonderFi deal

The hiring push offers an early look at Robinhood’s ambitions in Canada after its roughly $250-million acquisition of Canadian crypto company WonderFi Technologies Inc. Wndr-T closed in June. The deal gave Robinhood an immediate regulatory foothold in the Canadian market and access to more than 300,000 funded WonderFi customers at the time it was announced.

Robinhood’s arrival also adds another competitor to a Canadian self-directed investing market that includes homegrown companies such as Questrade and Wealthsimple.

“There is a lot of room for competition here,” Mr. Kerbat said. He said that he has seen Canadian companies “trying to imitate” Robinhood’s features and user experience.

“We have a product innovation that is quite different from a lot of these companies,” he said, referencing products available in the U.S. such as 3-per-cent cash-back credit cards. “I think they will follow what we are trying to do.”

For now, Robinhood’s Canadian offering remains considerably narrower than its U.S. platform, where customers can trade stocks, options, cryptocurrencies and prediction-market contracts, among other traditional banking products. Canadian customers currently have access to cryptocurrency trading across 50 assets.

Robinhood’s trading fees will range between 0.5 per cent and 1.85 per cent on Canadian-dollar crypto trades. In comparison, Wealthsimple’s fee is 2 per cent for its clients with less than $100,000 in assets investing less than $1,000.

“We are unique because we are one of the largest retail platforms in the U.S. and in other places, and so the type of pricing we’ll be able to offer and the type of features we’ll be able to offer should give us a large advantage,” Mr. Kerbat said.

The company is currently offering zero-fee crypto trading until the end of September, a promotion it is using to migrate previous WonderFi customers, and new customers, to the Robinhood app.

The company is inviting the 300,000 WonderFi customers in phases to the new platform. As of mid-September, approximately 160,000 WonderFi customers had been invited and roughly 25,000 had completed the process, according to Mr. Pollock.

The Robinhood acquisition was originally expected to close in the second half of 2025. But, WonderFi said late last year that it would be pushed into the first half of 2026 while the company sought regulatory approvals.

The deal was delayed amid a difficult period for the company. WonderFi has reported large losses in recent years, while one of its largest shareholders, Vancouver-based Orion Digital Corp., sold half of its shares at a loss in August, 2025, before exiting its position entirely earlier this year.
