stories.title: OHL 2026-27 season preview: Our team-by-team guide
stories.summary: Ryan Pyette takes an in-depth look at all 20 Ontario Hockey League teams.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The puck drops this week on the 2026-27 Ontario Hockey League season. LFP sportswriter Ryan Pyette, who has been covering the OHL for 25 years, has in-depth previews for all 20 teams.

Last year: 28 wins, 61 points. Seventh. Lost to Windsor in 1st round.

New: Plenty, but pencil in Londoner Ryan Roobroeck (Blackhawks) for 50 goals. The former IceDog has Auston Matthews-like qualities.

Good stuff: Sophomore forward Jaakko Wycisk will be one of the NHL’s top prospects for the next draft . . . Former Frontenac Tyler Hopkins (Maple Leafs) will be a dominant force up front . . . Over-age goalie Ben Hrebik backstopped Barrie to the OHL final last spring.

Big question: Will they win it all at home?

Outlook: Top of the heap.

Last year: 26 wins, 60 points. Eighth. Lost to Kitchener in 1st round.

New: Coach Brendan Taylor took the reins from 2024 Memorial Cup winner Chris Lazary, now an assistant at University of Michigan.

Good stuff: NHL draft prospect Dima Zhilkin had 36 goals and 100 penalty minutes last year. Expect more this time . . . Nikita Klepov (Ducks) could become repeat scoring champ for first time since Ottawa’s Corey Locke (2002-04) . . . Levi Harper will be well over a point per game from the back end.

Big question: Can they improve in their own end?

Outlook: They’ll outscore some issues.

Last year: 40 wins, 85 points. Fourth. Lost to Sault Ste. Marie in 1st round.

New: Swedish scorer Marcus Nordmark (Ducks) will bring high-end skill to a team banking on a big offensive surge.

Good stuff: London boasts three NHL first-rounders, including shifty Cayman Islander Jaxon Cover (Senators), giant d-man Maksim Sokolovskii (Flyers) and Nordmark . . . Second-generation Knight Kane Barch, Finnish forward Luca Santala and rearguard Cooper McAslan are all potential high NHL picks in 2027.

Big question: Will Aleksei Medvedev finally secure the No. 1 job in net?

Outlook: Grappling with Guelph for top perch.

'Blue-collar' centre Carson Harmer on trade to London Knights: 'An honour'

Marcus Nordmark gives London Knights major firepower up front

Last year: 27 wins, 63 points. Sixth. Lost to Flint in 1st round.

New: Nearly everything but their rink. President/GM Tyler Nother and head coach Keenan Reynolds are both 28 years old.

Good stuff: Harry Nansi (Maple Leafs) primed for a big offensive jump . . . Pierce Mbuyi (Penguins) has 40-goal potential and Cole Zurawski (Panthers) led the OHL preseason with 15 points in six games . . . Former Brantford stopper Ryerson Leenders (Sabres) is on the cusp of 100 OHL wins (94 in 168 career games).

Big question: Have they put last spring’s playoff meltdown behind them?

Outlook: Bears should be considerably better.

Last year: 21 wins, 51 points. Ninth. Missed playoffs.

New: Sting ownership, led by Ryan Finch, pumped $2.5 million-plus into the city-owned Progressive Auto Sales Arena for a ‘more consistent (fan) experience.’

Good stuff: Captain Alessandro Di Iorio (Blue Jackets) needs to be at the top of his game . . . What will Easton Walos (25 goals as a rookie) do for an encore? . . . Brenner Lammens should be a super scoring sophomore and rack up more than 100 PIMs.

Big question: Can Ivan Tkach-Tkachenko provide a steady hand in net?

Outlook: Bees on the rise.

Last year: 44 wins, 95 points. Third. Lost to Windsor in 2nd round.

New: U.S. national team development program d-man Nick Bogas (Blues) will help after rights acquired from Sarnia.

Good stuff: Freshly minted captain Jimmy Lombardi (Kings) should score 40 goals . . . Goalie Mason Courville shut out Erie last fall before his 16th birthday and is only getting better . . . Outscored Owen Sound 35-3 in one of the most lopsided playoff series in junior hockey history last spring.

Big question: Can they build on last year’s resurgence?

Outlook: Replacing elite talent on the fly.

Last year: 47 wins, 101 points. First. Won OHL title and Memorial Cup.

New: Jeff Kyrzakos moves to the middle of the bench for impactful Jussi Ahokas, now the AHL Colorado Eagles boss.

Good stuff: Luca Romano (Islanders) and Tanner Lam will provide veteran scoring . . . Alexander Bileki (Maple Leafs) will log a lot of blue-line time after breakout playoffs (two goals, 11 points in 18 games) . . . Blueshirts need third-year goalie Jason Schaubel to shine.

Big question: Was dealing for a London Knight (Sam O’Reilly) last year the best move in franchise history?

Outlook: Down, but not for long.

Last year: 18 wins, 45 points. 10th. Missed playoffs.

New: Second-overall pick Colin Kennedy has quite the family tree – dad Craig played in the OHL and grandfather Craig Hartsburg is a pro and junior puck legend.

Good stuff: Goalie David Egorov brings top-tier experience after Brantford run . . . D-man Ty Henry (Blackhawks) will be hungry after missing an entire season with knee woes . . . Michael Dec led the offence with 25 goals and 53 points in 46 games after trade with Owen Sound.

Big question: Will they score enough this season?

Outlook: Need more time.

Last year: 44 wins, 97 points. Second. Lost to Kitchener in conference final.

New: Michael Newlove takes over main crease duty from graduated Joey Costanzo.

Good stuff: Brass believe in NHL draft prospect Johnny McLaughlin, who will boost scoring totals in sophomore season . . . Caden Harvey (Oilers) can score and has some jam along the boards . . . Anthony Cristoforo is hard to stop from the back end.

Big question: How will the Spits replace Ethan Belchetz (Michigan State) and Jack Nesbitt (Michigan)?

Outlook: So much first-rate talent gone.

Last year: 39 wins, 84 points. Fifth. Lost to Kitchener in 2nd round.

New: Drew Bannister, tied to so much great Hounds history, replaces John Dean as coach.

Good stuff: Captain Brady Martin is gone, but Jeremy Martin (29 goals last year) remains . . . There are big hopes for rookie forward Trevor Daley, Jr., whose NHL father played for the Greyhounds . . . Czech goalie David Vermirovsky had a promising preseason.

Big question: How large will the hole be on D with Chase Reid (Kraken) at Michigan State?

Outlook: Dog days this time around.

Last year: 47 wins, 100 points. Third. Lost to Barrie in 2nd round.

New: Third-year Jaeden Nelson gets his starting goalie chance with Ryder Fetterolf heading to Penn State.

Good stuff: Swedish forward Filip Ekberg (Hurricanes) has 35-goal chops . . . Nic Whitehead can score and was plus-36 last season . . . Veteran boss Dave Cameron coming off coach of the year performance.

Big question: Was last year’s turnaround a one-hit wonder?

Outlook: Battling for the top.

Last year: 27 wins, 57 points. 8th. Lost to Brantford in 1st round.

New: Talented Tanner Adams will look to impress after eye-popping 15-pick trade from Brampton.

Good stuff: Slovaks Jan Chovan (Kings) and Adam Nemec (Senators) will lead the offence . . . Artem Gonchar (Rangers) racked up 51 points from the back end last year . . . Busy blue-liner Luca Blonda received an Ontario Provincial Police commissioner’s citation for saving a woman from drowning a few years ago.

Big question: Will the Pack win it all before ancient Sudbury Community Arena meets the wrecking ball in 2028?

Outlook: No longer pretenders.

Last year: 33 wins, 71 points. Sixth. Lost to Ottawa in 1st round.

New: Towering first-round centre Logan Prud’homme could be a game-changer early.

Good stuff: Matthew Minchak (Golden Knights) and Gavin Betts form one of league’s best goalie tandems . . . Slovak winger Alex Misiak can be a power-play demon . . . Sophomore Matthew Henderson posted six points in five games at the 2025 U17 worlds and won gold with Canada at the recent Hlinka Gretzky Cup.

Big question: Are they still too young to get it done?

Outlook: Moving on up.

Last year: 38 wins, 80 points. 5th. Lost to Brantford in 2nd round.

New: Seven-footer Alexander Karmanov (Sharks) gets his first full season on an OHL blue line.

Good stuff: Parker Vaughan’s double-overtime series winner against Peterborough is a sign of clutch things to come . . . Sophomore centre Cam Warren’s six points in the playoffs showed he’s ready for prime time . . . Troops coach Ryan Oulahen led Canada to Hlinka Gretzky Cup gold.

Big question: Will overager Mike McIvor be in the conversation for league’s best goalie?

Outlook: A sturdy group.

Last year: 40 wins, 84 points. 4th. Lost to North Bay in 1st round.

New: Cooper Dennis arrives from Brantford on heels of 34-goal, 74-point rookie campaign.

Good stuff: Czech forward Adam Novotny (Canucks) scored 65 points in 58 games in first season with the Petes . . . Adam Levac (Red Wings) can mix it up and put the puck in the net . . . Carson Cameron will bring calming influence to the back end in second season as captain.

Big question: Who will shine between the pipes?

Outlook: Plenty to like.

Last year: 48 wins, 106 points. First. Lost to Barrie in conference final.

New: Michael Babcock, whose dad Mike coaches the Oilers, will try to keep the wins flowing.

Good stuff: Forward Jeremy Freeman is Bulldogs’ most experienced OHL player – with 57 games under his belt . . . Jason Musa could be a nice offensive pick-up after 25 goals in the Ushl . . . Swedish goalie Vilmer Salen Forsberg brings nice size (6-foot-4) to the crease.

Big question: Will 2025 first-overall pick Kaden McGregor flourish after trade from Peterborough?

Outlook: A step back.

Last year: 19 wins, 48 points. Ninth. Missed playoffs.

New: New strength coach Alex Fontana was a Canadian Football League offensive lineman with Ottawa and Hamilton.

Good stuff: Finnish goalie Oskari Ahmajarvi, the 18-year-old No. 7 pick in the 2026 import draft, was backbone of Kiekko-Espoo’s under-20 domestic title last season . . . Reliable centre Troy Patton won 603 faceoffs last season . . . Russian forward Stepan Kuryachenkov put up 28 points in 47 games with Swift Current at age 16 last year.

Big question: How will they utilize the draft pick bounty from the Tanner Adams trade with Sudbury?

Outlook: Swimming upstream.

Last year: 19 wins, 42 points. 10th. Missed playoffs.

New: First-overall pick Kane Cloutier. If the skilled scorer owns the intensity of his father (Dan, the former NHL goaltender), he’ll be an immediate force.

Good stuff: 6-foot-7 American forward Brooks Rogowski (Canucks) needs to dominate consistently . . . 2025 first-rounder Sam Roberts will get the chance to do some damage . . . Swedish defender Linus Funck (Avalanche) will get big minutes after London trade.

Big question: Is this a playoff team yet?

Prediction: Still searching.

New: Too much. Respected Jake Grimes is club’s seventh coach in five years.

stories.title: Judge sends Hamilton fentanyl dealer to prison despite 'immigration consequences'
stories.summary: The judge handed the permanent resident, who emigrated from Jamaica at the age of five, two years behind bars and three years of probation.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A judge in Hamilton, Ont., has resisted a drug dealer’s attempt to get a lighter sentence because he might be deported to Jamaica.

Hopeton McFarlane pleaded guilty in the Ontario Court of Justice to possession of fentanyl for the purpose of trafficking. His lawyer argued unsuccessfully for a conditional sentence, the Crown recommended three years in prison.

The judge handed the 28-year-old permanent resident, who emigrated from Jamaica at the age of five with his mother, two years behind bars and three years of probation.

“I am concerned about the immigration consequences that May result from the sentence imposed on Mr. McFarlane,” Justice Joe Patrick Paul Fiorucci wrote in a recent sentencing decision.

“However, having regard to the seriousness of the offence and Mr. McFarlane’s degree of responsibility, I am satisfied that a penitentiary sentence is required notwithstanding those immigration consequences.”

McFarlane’s immigration lawyer filed a letter with the court advising “that a conviction for possession of fentanyl for the purpose of trafficking renders Mr. McFarlane inadmissible to Canada on grounds of serious criminality under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and would likely result in admissibility and removal proceedings,” said the judge’s Sept. 9 decision.

“Counsel also advises that a custodial sentence of six months or more would eliminate Mr. McFarlane’s right to appeal any resulting removal order to the Immigration Appeal Division, whereas a conditional sentence would preserve that right,” Fiorucci said.

“Given that Mr. McFarlane has lived in Canada since childhood and that his family and support network are located here, I accept that these potential immigration consequences are significant.”

The Supreme Court of Canada “has recognized that immigration consequences May properly be considered in crafting a fit sentence,” the judge noted.

“However, the court also cautioned that collateral immigration consequences cannot be permitted to dominate or skew the sentencing process and that sentencing judges must not impose artificial sentences designed to circumvent Parliament’s immigration regime.”

The court heard that police officers were conducting a foot patrol on James Street South on July 2, 2024, just before 10 a.m., when they spotted McFarlane on the north side of a building.

“He was kneeling beside a working digital scale on which fentanyl was visible,” said the decision.

“He was speaking with a female who was seated a few feet away on nearby steps. Based on their observations, the officers believed that Mr. McFarlane was in the midst of a drug transaction.”

stories.title: Tree planters cultivate community deep in Northern Alberta
stories.summary: During a gruelling summer, nights at camp turn a crew into a family
stories.author: Aidan Clark
stories.content:
Underexposed is a photojournalism series dedicated to shedding light on the unseen lives of Canadians in every province and territory. Learn more and share your thoughts with The Globe.

For the past three years, I have spent my summers deep in the bush of Northern Alberta.

With a small spade in hand and heavy planting bags on my hips,

I have sunk in mud, climbed over logs and waded through thick greenery.

Laughing together, planters get settled for a long ride into Peace River on a day off. Short on laundry, beer, and other supplies after an extra-long shift, planters will resupply in town

Like generations of young Canadians and international workers before me, I have spent the last few summers in the bush, planting trees for reforestation companies.

For the duration of the season, we live out of tents and RVs, spending our days deep in remote forests.

Ryan McNaughton and Mak Dzonlic wait for a turn in the camp showers at the end of a planting shift.

Nate Mackenzie is shaved bald as a remedy for a recently botched haircut.

It is, in many ways, a Canadian rite of passage.

Among these workers, I count my friends, people whom I have come to know through seasons spent living and working alongside each other.

In the dry summer months, fire bans in the bush are common. When the ban is lifted, nights around the campfire feel like a special treat.

This past summer was my third with a company called Outland. Our crew of 14 was part of a larger camp of 50, based just outside of Manning, a small farming town four hours south of the Northwest Territories.

Jeremy Young appears as no more than a splinter dwarfed by a vast surrounding cut block. Left alone with their thoughts for 10-plus hours, planters often see the crew boss only once a day.

Each day we were helicoptered into clearcuts deep in the forests to plant trees.

“I’ve said this to almost every rookie that I’ve hired or every rookie that I’ve interviewed: You don’t understand how mentally difficult this job is,” says Jeremy Young, from Revelstoke, B.C.

After six seasons of planting, he has spent the last three as a crew boss.

I, like thousands of other planters, have earned my wage in every condition, from sweltering heat waves to hailstorms that sting.

I have been chased by wasps, stared down by a grizzly bear and swarmed by black flies.

My knees have buckled from dehydration and lungs burned from thick wildfire smoke.

“In the first year I cried almost every day,” says Emma Sutcliffe, from Gravenhurst, Ont.

Despite the tears, she has returned each season since 2024.

Emma tells me a large reason for coming back was her drive to be a better planter.

“Knowing what I could do was motivating.”

“And I just had so much fun on party nights and meeting all these people.”

Later in our conversation, she shares a sentiment that I believe rings true for many planters.

“I just feel like a better person out there.”

The community aspect of tree planting is, for many, a major draw.

“When you don’t have Wi-Fi, you don’t have cell connection and you are all just out in the woods with each other, you can get up to some shenanigans that are just memories for you and the people present there,” says Jeremy.

Halloween (in June) is a revered camp holiday. Dante Amato kept his costume a secret until the big reveal on the Halloween-themed party night.

“Everyone’s performance kind of falls, and you do feel freer to be yourself.”

For seven years, Lucas Morgani had been working what he described as a “dead-end” restaurant kitchen job in Oakville, Ont.

Before being convinced to come out planting, he didn’t consider himself an “outdoorsy person.” But the social aspect enticed him.

Back home after the season, he reflects with me on the unique tangible community of camp.

“At any moment of time, you can just zip down your tent, walk outside and there are going to be people you can just converse with.”

After a 10-plus-hour day, planters return beaten and exhausted, but together.

Evenings unfold in the mess tent with friends and hot food.

Laughter about the good, but mostly the bad, of the day helps to alleviate the pain.

My first year, for the most part, sucked. I largely dreaded the work and the monotony that came with it, but I kept pushing.

Each planter’s body undergoes a transformation at the beginning of the season as it acclimates to the conditions. The frequent workdays, however, make healing sores and blisters nearly impossible, as they are ripped open again each day.

I pushed because I was sure this would be my first and last year.

Then, all of a sudden, it was over. The contract wrapped. We tore down camp and said our long goodbyes.

All that time in the land, all the pain and frustration, all I wanted to do was leave. But in the end, while driving away with a lump in my throat, I knew I was coming back.

A newly planted seedling on a clear-cut block.

“Dude, I just want to plant a tree,” Lucas tells me.

“Once we left, that’s all I could think about.”

Aidan Clark is a documentary photographer and visual storyteller based in Toronto. His work explores themes of connection, community, and relationships between individuals, their pasts and their environments. Completing a BFA in Photography Studies at Toronto Metropolitan University, his work has been recognized through various awards -- most recently, the Edward Burtynsky Studio Award.

Photography and story by Aidan Clark

Photo editing by Clare Vander Meersch

Editing by Lisan Jutras

Visuals editing by Solana Cain and Liz Sullivan

Digital presentation by Mackenzie Lad

Interactive design and development by Christopher Manza

stories.title: Second Alzheimer’s-treating drug should be publicly covered, Canada’s Drug Agency recommends
stories.summary: Recommendation sets the stage for possible government funding of the medication
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Canada’s Drug Agency is recommending that a second disease-modifying medication used to treat people with early Alzheimer’s disease should be publicly covered, with conditions.

The agency, which offers non-binding recommendations for drug reimbursement through its expert committee, released draft recommendations on the medication donanemab on Thursday.

In a report, the Canadian Drug Expert Committee found donanemab provided clinical benefits by “slowing cognitive and functional decline.”

Alzheimer’s, a progressive and irreversible disease, is characterized by worsening cognitive decline and functional impairment. It is the most common cause of dementia. As of January, 2025, it was estimated 771,939 people in Canada live with dementia.

The drug expert committee’s recommendation, supported by 11 of its members while three voted against, sets the stage for possible public funding of the medication, not currently captured by provincial or territorial drug plans.

Health Canada approves second drug targeting underlying cause of Alzheimer’s disease

The medication carries a costly sticker price: $47,250 annually, per patient.

The majority recommended there be conditions for public coverage, including limiting it to adult patients who are 50 and older with a clinical diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia owing to Alzheimer’s disease.

As well, patients must not be homozygous for the APOE4 gene variant, which is the highest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s. It also said pricing must be significantly reduced before public reimbursement.

Donanemab, which is administered as an infusion therapy and marketed under the brand name Kisunla, is part of a new class of disease-modifying drugs used to treat early Alzheimer’s.

Previously, medications used to treat the disease could only address symptoms. However, new medication options are designed to target and clear beta-amyloid, a protein that turns into clumps in the brain, which sets off a series of events that leads to brain-cell death.

Canada’s Drug Agency reverses course, now recommends public drug plans cover Alzheimer’s drug

Mathilde Merlet, president and general manager of Lilly Canada Inc. , the pharmaceutical company that makes donanemab, applauded the committee’s positive recommendation.

She said it recognizes the importance of offering patients who are diagnosed with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease a treatment option, at a time when intervention matters.

“Timely intervention for patients with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s can have the greatest impact to slow the progression of this devastating disease,” she said in a statement.

Ms. Merlet said for more than 30 years, the company has led research to pursue a treatment for Alzheimer’s disease.

“Today, we celebrate a historic milestone,” she said. “We are committed to working with the government and broader healthcare ecosystem to accelerate access for eligible patients.”

The drug was approved by Health Canada in May, more than two years after the federal department responsible for regulating drugs began reviewing the medication in February, 2024.

Age of breakthroughs: The gift of care for people with Alzheimer’s disease

The Alzheimer Society of Canada said at that time it could still take more than a year to become accessible through private drug plans and more than two through public plans. It added that this underscores the importance of receiving a timely diagnosis because the medication is effective only for those in the earliest stages of the disease.

The society also pointed to World Alzheimer Report 2024 , which found more than 90 per cent of respondents would pursue a dementia diagnosis if they knew a disease-modifying treatment was available.

Donanemab is one of two recently approved disease-modifying Alzheimer’s treatments in Canada; the other is lecanemab.

In July, the CDA reversed a previous recommendation and said public drug plans should cover lecanemab’s cost.

The expert committee’s report said lecanemab “May address a significant unmet clinical need to a degree that justifies a positive recommendation despite the uncertainty in the clinical value.”

Health Canada approved the medication last October. However, it also carries a high price tag. The annual cost of it is around $30,000.

Neither donanemab nor lecanemab are considered to be cures for Alzheimer’s disease. The medications are designed to slow cognitive decline to allow patients to stay in mild stages of the disease for longer.

With reports from Alanna Smith and Kelly Grant

stories.title: A trailblazer at Tiff and beyond: Clement Virgo’s stories of tenderness and desire
stories.summary: Filmmaker “tells stories that are uniquely Canadian in a uniquely Clement Virgo way”
stories.author: Sarah Laing
stories.content:
As the 51st Toronto International Film Festival takes over the city Sept. 10-20, this series of articles examines some of the Canadian directors whose lives and careers have been shaped by Tiff.

The setting is Toronto, sometime in the mid-90s. Garvia Bailey – now a veteran broadcaster and arts journalist – was part of a collective of artists and musicians who all hung out on Queen Street West. A friend introduced her to an acquaintance.

“They said, ‘This is Clement Virgo. He’s a filmmaker. Do you know the film Rude ?” recalls Bailey. “And I was like, ‘What?!’, because I remember Rude being the type of film that felt like no one else had really done anything like it; something that was raw, gritty and unapologetically Toronto.”

Rude, released in 1995, tells three interconnected tales of Black Canadian life in Toronto’s economically disadvantaged Regent Park neighbourhood. It was the first full-length dramatic film helmed by a Black Canadian director and features an all-Black cast. Bailey says it reminded her of the kind of stories Spike Lee and John Singleton were telling in the U.S.

“But nobody [before Virgo] was telling the story of what it was like in Regent Park, the story of immigrants and the children of immigrants, with kind of a West Indian slang to it, with an incredible soundtrack,” she says. “I was blown away by the film, and then I was blown away by Clement Virgo himself. He was the humblest, sweetest, nicest person.”

Bailey wasn’t the only person to be struck by Virgo’s directorial debut, made in partnership with collaborator Damon D’Oliveira. It played at the Cannes Film Festival and went on to receive an honourable mention at Tiff from the Best Canadian Film jury. In 2017, Tiff screened the film again as part of its Cinematheque program, which is dedicated to showcasing Canadian and international films.

“It is such a singular work,” says Robyn Citizen, director of programming, Festival and Cinematheque at Tiff. She points out that the film introduced many Virgo signatures, most notably his unique perspective on Black diasporic masculinity.

“It’s quite tender. It’s also quite bold. It’s infused with this desire,” she says. “All of his work has this through line of evolved masculinity and concerns with desire that is really fascinating.”

Bailey uses almost identical vocabulary to describe Virgo’s directorial credits, which span 30 feature films and shorts and notable television series like The Wire and The Book of Negroes .

“There is a very real tenderness to the way that he makes a film, the way he directs, the way he writes,” she says. “As soon as you see it, you can see the poetry and the tenderness of it, even though he sometimes deals with super hard, gritty topics or super sexy topics.”

Whether he’s telling a story about two young men in the early days of Toronto’s hip hop scene in Brother , a couple embarking on an intense intimate relationship in Lie With Me , or two half-brothers struggling in the wake of childhood trauma in Love Come Down , there is “this soft little heart at the centre of all of the work, even with characters that seem at first to be aggressive or closed off,” says Citizen. “Quite quickly that unravels, and you see the tender soul.”

She notes that he was an early trailblazer in this regard. “The vulnerability of his characters was something I wasn’t seeing in other cinemas.”

In addition to screening several of his films at Tiff, Virgo has maintained a close relationship with his hometown film festival. He’s given talks and mentored aspiring filmmakers through Tiff events. “There’s a continuing mutual support from the organization for his work, and he’s a big advocate for Tiff as well,” says Citizen.

Over the years, Virgo’s films and series have won numerous awards, including 12 Canadian Screen Awards for Brother and 11 for The Book of Negroes . Yet more than thirty years into his career, he continues to evolve and experiment. His latest film, Steal Away , is an Afrofuturist thriller that explores the complex racial and power dynamics between two young women. Co-written by Virgo and his creative and life partner Tamara Faith Berger, the film has a feminist bent.

“That’s in keeping with his ability to always be pushing the envelope,” says Bailey. “He’s ahead of the game all the time, ahead of what people are thinking about and putting on the screen.”

For Bailey, Virgo’s name belongs in the same pantheon of great Canadian storytellers as Leonard Cohen, Margaret Atwood and Lawrence Hill.

“He tells stories that are uniquely Canadian in a uniquely Clement Virgo way,” she says. “He’s not afraid of busting it open, and that lack of fear is something that young Canadian filmmakers can look to as a North star.”

In Steal Away , Fanny (Angourie Rice) is a sheltered teenager from a wealthy family and Cécile (Mallori Johnson) is a refugee seeking asylum who comes to live at Fanny’s house.

Early on, there is a scene where Fanny takes the stage to sing Edith Piaf’s “Non, je ne regrette rien” at a party while Cécile watches her from the crowd.

“Everyone is around them, but the connection between the two characters is so pregnant that it feels like those deep exhales when you’re reading a piece of poetry and one line just stops you in your tracks,” Bailey says.

This is signature Virgo, she adds. “There’s a lot of that in his filmmaking, where he just allows the viewer to breathe into the moment.”

stories.title: The investment summit made the pitch, but the sale isn’t closed
stories.summary: As attendees disperse, questions will arise about Ottawa’s ‘productivity mega deduction,’ and Carney will need answers
stories.author: William Robson, Mawakina Bafale
stories.content:
William Robson is a fellow-in-residence at the C.D. Howe Institute, where he is also president emeritus, and holder of the William Robson Chair in Public Sector Governance and Accountability.

Mawakina Bafale is a research officer at the C.D. Howe Institute

A big question going into the first-ever Canada Investment Summit held in Toronto this week was whether Prime Minister Mark Carney could bolster his pitch for fund managers to invest more in Canada with a major policy change? He did. The exclamation point in his speech to the summit was a “productivity mega deduction” (PMD) that will allow business to write off new investments in most capital assets immediately. The Department of Finance calculates that the PMD will cut the economy-wide marginal effective tax rate on new capital investments in half – to 6.4 per cent, compared with 16.9 per cent in the United States and an average of 19 per cent in other Oecd countries. Its estimated fiscal cost is also impressive, at $36-billion over the next five years. This is a major policy initiative.

The Prime Minister needed something big. After a decade of indifference, a federal government putting capital formation at the centre of its economic strategy was a welcome change. Business investment in non-residential capital has been so weak since 2015 that the average Canadian worker today has roughly 9 per cent less capital to work with than a decade ago. That fact, and the stagnation of productivity and incomes that went with it, have made Canada a less inviting place to invest.

Canadian investment per worker has always been somewhat lower than in the United States and other Oecd members. From the mid-1990s to the mid 2010s, however, the gaps were narrowing. By 2014, the average Canadian worker was backed by about 98 cents of new capital for every dollar received by the average worker across the Oecd, and about 89 cents for every dollar the average American worker had. Projections from the Oecd this spring implied that the average Canadian worker would see only 64 cents of new capital for every dollar per Oecd worker in 2026, and only 50 cents per American worker.

Ottawa gets it on tax policy, gamechanger ‘mega deduction’ shows

These numbers matter not only as indicators of declining attractiveness but because they affect prospects for the future. Investment and productivity move together. In the 1990s, Canadian workers produced less than their U.S. counterparts and slightly more than their peers in other advanced economies. Today, the gap with the United States has widened, and Canada has slipped down the international rankings. For Canadians, that means disappointing growth in earnings and living standards; for international investors, it means a less dynamic and inviting economy.

The PMD is big enough to make a difference. Forecasters will be raising their estimates of investment and growth in Canada, and businesses considering responding to U.S. President Donald Trump ’s trade aggression by serving more of the North American market from production in the United States now have better reason to produce in Canada. Importantly, the PMD applies to most capital assets; unlike the more targeted accelerated depreciation it will replace, it looks less like industrial policy favouring particular activities and more like a boost to investment across the board.

Now that the Prime Minister has put the PMD exclamation point on the investment summit and the attendees are dispersing, questions will arise. Immediate expensing of capital favours capital-intensive industries over others. Calculations from the Department of Finance show that the economy-wide marginal effective tax rate of 6.4 per cent is an average of dramatically different rates: close to 20 per cent in retail and wholesale trade, and rates that are actually negative in agriculture and fishing, manufacturing and processing, and transportation and storage.

List of announcements coming out of the Canada Investment Summit

Immediate expensing does nothing about the widening gap between small- and large-business rates that locks capital into smaller, less productive companies. High general corporate income-tax rates discourage reporting income in Canada and encourage leverage – too many new PMD-inspired investments May be financed by debt. And it does nothing to address Canada’s high personal income tax rates, which encourage talent – and the investment that follows it – to locate in the United States or more welcoming jurisdictions overseas. The Prime Minister needs answers for those as well.

The next challenge is to reintroduce Canada to domestic and foreign investors as a place where economically motivated projects generate solid returns over the long haul – past the horizon affected by fast write-offs. Lower, simpler taxes on businesses and people would show that Canada is not just a good host for a summit, but a good destination for their next investment in capital that will produce competitive products – and raise Canadians’ productivity and living standards – for many years to come.

The Department of Finance calculates that the PMD will cut the economy-wide marginal effective tax rate on new capital investments in half – to 6.4 per cent, compared with 16.9 per cent in the United States and an average of 19 per cent in other Oecd countries. Its estimated fiscal cost is also impressive, at $36-billion over the next five years. This is a major policy initiative.

The Prime Minister needed something big. After a decade of indifference, a federal government putting capital formation at the centre of its economic strategy was a welcome change. Business investment in non-residential capital has been so weak since 2015 that the average Canadian worker today has roughly 9 per cent less capital to work with than a decade ago. That fact, and the stagnation of productivity and incomes that went with it, have made Canada a less inviting place to invest.

Canadian investment per worker has always been somewhat lower than in the United States and other Oecd members. From the mid-1990s to the mid 2010s, however, the gaps were narrowing. By 2014, the average Canadian worker was backed by about 98 cents of new capital for every dollar received by the average worker across the Oecd, and about 89 cents for every dollar the average American worker had. Projections from the Oecd this spring implied that the average Canadian worker would see only 64 cents of new capital for every dollar per Oecd worker in 2026, and only 50 cents per American worker.
Ottawa gets it on tax policy, gamechanger ‘mega deduction’ shows

These numbers matter not only as indicators of declining attractiveness but because they affect prospects for the future. Investment and productivity move together. In the 1990s, Canadian workers produced less than their U.S. counterparts and slightly more than their peers in other advanced economies. Today, the gap with the United States has widened, and Canada has slipped down the international rankings. For Canadians, that means disappointing growth in earnings and living standards; for international investors, it means a less dynamic and inviting economy.

The PMD is big enough to make a difference. Forecasters will be raising their estimates of investment and growth in Canada, and businesses considering responding to U.S. President Donald Trump ’s trade aggression by serving more of the North American market from production in the United States now have better reason to produce in Canada. Importantly, the PMD applies to most capital assets; unlike the more targeted accelerated depreciation it will replace, it looks less like industrial policy favouring particular activities and more like a boost to investment across the board.

Now that the Prime Minister has put the PMD exclamation point on the investment summit and the attendees are dispersing, questions will arise. Immediate expensing of capital favours capital-intensive industries over others. Calculations from the Department of Finance show that the economy-wide marginal effective tax rate of 6.4 per cent is an average of dramatically different rates: close to 20 per cent in retail and wholesale trade, and rates that are actually negative in agriculture and fishing, manufacturing and processing, and transportation and storage.
List of announcements coming out of the Canada Investment Summit

Immediate expensing does nothing about the widening gap between small- and large-business rates that locks capital into smaller, less productive companies. High general corporate income-tax rates discourage reporting income in Canada and encourage leverage – too many new PMD-inspired investments May be financed by debt. And it does nothing to address Canada’s high personal income tax rates, which encourage talent – and the investment that follows it – to locate in the United States or more welcoming jurisdictions overseas. The Prime Minister needs answers for those as well.

The next challenge is to reintroduce Canada to domestic and foreign investors as a place where economically motivated projects generate solid returns over the long haul – past the horizon affected by fast write-offs. Lower, simpler taxes on businesses and people would show that Canada is not just a good host for a summit, but a good destination for their next investment in capital that will produce competitive products – and raise Canadians’ productivity and living standards – for many years to come.

stories.title: Frank Stronach to be sentenced for indecent assault conviction
stories.summary: Hearing is set as prosecutors challenge post-verdict mistrial on the billionaire businessman’s sexual assault conviction
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A sentencing hearing is scheduled today for Canadian auto parts mogul Frank Stronach on the historical offence of indecent assault.

The hearing is set to take place even as prosecutors are challenging the judge’s decision to declare a rare post-verdict mistrial on Stronach’s sexual assault conviction.

Stronach, who is 94, was found guilty in June of both charges, which relate to separate allegations brought by two of the women in his Toronto criminal trial.

Weeks later, Superior Court Justice Anne Molloy granted the mistrial on the sexual assault conviction after e-mails from the complainant’s lawyer in a separate civil case were presented in court.

Stronach’s lawyer argued those e-mails told a story that was inconsistent with the woman’s testimony in the criminal trial.

At the time, Leora Shemesh told The Canadian Press that the court did not hear from the complainant before the judge made her decision.

Analysis: Erosion of case against Frank Stronach spotlights challenges of prosecuting historical sexual assaults

The Crown’s appeal argues the guilty verdict on the sexual assault charge should be restored and the case sent back to Superior Court for sentencing.

The billionaire businessman initially faced 12 charges related to allegations brought by seven complainants and dating as far back as the late 1970s.

The Crown later withdrew one charge and agreed Stronach should be found not guilty on four more.

Soon after, Molloy said she couldn’t convict Stronach on two charges related to one complainant whose evidence she deemed unreliable.

Five charges related to three complainants remained, and Stronach was found guilty of two, until the mistrial was granted.

He is set to stand trial before a jury in Newmarket, Ont., next year in a sexual assault case involving six complainants.

stories.title: 911 outages reported by officials in several Canadian provinces
stories.summary: Police forces in multiple provinces reported issues with 911 services early Thursday.
stories.author: Devika Desai, Kendra Mangione
stories.content:
A spate of 911 outages across the country early Thursday has been confirmed to be due to a technical issue with Bell.

The telecommunications provider confirmed that “an issue with the next-generation 9-1-1 network” was detected at 3:13 a.m ET.

An email statement says the provider used backup systems to route calls to emergency services and has confirmed that 911 services have been fully restored.

“We are investigating the root cause of the issue and will have further details once available,” the statement reads.

Police officers in Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia reported the outages early Thursday and advised residents to contact them through non-emergency numbers or Wi-Fi calling.

Officers in Toronto said the 911 emergency line was unable to receive calls at one point, but posted on social media at 6:20 a.m. local time that service was being restored.

The Ontario Provincial Police similarly warned of “intermittent 911 outages” in parts of the province, as did municipal forces in areas including Durham Region and Kingston.

By about 6 a.m., most police services confirmed that their lines are back up and running, including Peel, York and Durham.

For other regions where service has not yet been restored, residents are urged to contact non-emergency lines to access emergency services.

The Sûreté du Québec (SQ) and some local forces in the province issued similar warnings early Thursday.

Montreal police (Spvm) confirmed that it was also affected by the outage, but noted its service was operational as of 4:45 a.m. local time.

Other municipal forces like the Quebec City police and the Thérèse-De Blainville police confirmed the same.

Provincial police attributed the outage to a “technical issue” affecting the transfer of certain calls, according to a statement on social media.

Perturbation DES Appels 911 Une problématique technique affecte actuellement le transfert de certains appels entre les centres 911 et les centres de gestion des appels de la SQ. https://t.co/mGXeiwaZ7D pic.twitter.com/5S9sIumTEZ — Sûreté du Québec (@sureteduquebec) September 17, 2026

Although calls were still being received, it’s possible that they were being routed to police forces elsewhere in the country, a provincial police spokesperson told The Canadian Press.

On social media, police forces urged the public to call non-emergency phone lines to report an emergency.

Quebec Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière stated on social media that the issue was being investigated.

“Overnight, we experienced a 911 service disruption that lasted over an hour,” he wrote. “Although extremely rare, the police have contingency measures in place, including increased visibility, public announcements via social media and alternative telephone numbers.”

He added that the Government Operations Centre (COG) was also activated.

“We are still investigating and verifying what appears to be a technical fault with call routing,” Lafrenière said. “The extent of the fault is believed to extend beyond Quebec. Service is reported to have largely been restored.”

Residents of Nova Scotia woke up to an advisory of “intermittent 9-1-1 service outages across Canada,” and were told to try a landline or Wi-Fi calling in the event of an emergency.

“For emergencies, seek immediate assistance from emergency personnel or the nearest police, fire, or medical facility if 9-1-1 is unavailable,” the advisory added.

Truro Police said people can contact their 24-hour dispatch centre directly at 902-895-5351.

Police in Saint John, N.B., also said some cellphone users May be unable to connect to 911.

Winnipeg police also reported service outages Thursday.

In a public advisory, residents were asked to call the non-emergency number, if needed.

The advisory has since been updated to reflect that the service has been restored.

stories.title: Concerns over pickleball courts divide Port Stanley, Ont. neighbourhood
stories.summary: Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's all because of pickleball. While the public courts are popular with players, some neighbours consider them a nuisance.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's all because of pickleball. While the public courts are popular with players, some neighbours consider them a nuisance.
· Posted: Sep 17, 2026 6:46 AM EDT | Last Updated: 36 minutes ago
Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's because of pickleball.

Kokomo Park is a quiet neighbourhood, with a condo building, a block of single-family homes, a playground and four public pickleball courts that are popular with some of the residents and their friends.

"We hang out together, we laugh together, we joke together," said Ashley Hennesey, who plays at the courts regularly. "The good thing about pickleball is it brings you out so that you're getting good healthy workout, good community and get to know people you didn't know before."
But for others, the courts are a source of constant noise.
After receiving a number of complaints, the Municipality of Central Elgin decided in July that the courts could only be used from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., a change from the previous policy of dawn to dusk.

At a municipal council meeting on Monday the players submitted a petition with 130 signatures, asking to change the hours to 8 a.m. to dusk, and for the municipality to conduct a noise study and to include the players in future discussions.

At the same meeting, St. Catharines-based lawyer J. Patrick Maloney submitted a letter on behalf of Richard Robson, one of the condo owners, and "Kokomo Affected Neighbours," a group of condo residents.

The letter threatened legal action if the courts are not removed, claiming the use of the pickleball courts would exceed provincial noise guidelines and would "contravene the general legal principles associated with the tort of nuisance."

"We understand that the pickleball users are pushing for expanded hours, which demonstrates they are not concerned with such nuisance impacts or our clients legal right to the quiet enjoyment of their property," Maloney wrote.
Maloney did not respond to a request for a statement. CBC News spoke with two of the "Kokomo Affected Neighbours" but neither wished to comment.
The municipality received both communications at Monday's meeting, but no decision has been made regarding either the players' or the residents' requests.

Hennessey, who started the players' petition, said he and the others want the courts to remain open earlier in the morning due to concerns over the heat and humidity, noting the "advanced age" of many of the people who frequent the courts.
"Playing in 30 to 35 degree weather is not healthy," he said. "So we come out, we play earlier in the day and to us that is a reasonable alternative."

The disagreement has led to tensions between neighbours, he said, describing multiple occasions on which condo residents have yelled at him and other players if they arrive at the courts too early or leave too late.

Hennessey and the other players are willing to work with the community to find a way to reduce the disruption, he said, and he was surprised to read the lawyer's letter asking for the courts to be closed outright.

"That is absolutely not fair because what we want to hear is the joy...the laughing, the joking, chirping each other back and forth," he said. "This is what life is about, it's supposed to be about getting along, being peaceful and having a good time."

In 2025, Lloyd Mulroney moved into the home directly in front of the pickleball courts, fully aware they existed and were a part of the community, he said, adding that he's even taken to sitting and watching from his porch some mornings, and he and his wife occasionally play.
But the courts can get busy, he said, particularly in the evenings, with upwards of 20 people playing, and 15-20 cars in the small parking lot.
"There's a lot of cheering and activity that's happening," he said. "But if it closes down by 8 p.m., people are respectful, then that works for everybody, right?"
He said there are a lot of "camps" in the community, where the courts are concerned. Some want them gone, some don't care, and some, like him, "kind of lay in the middle."
"I think it could have been dealt with a little bit better," he said. "A little bit more collaboration and a little bit more folks concerned for their neighbour."

Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's all because of pickleball. While the public courts are popular with players, some neighbours consider them a nuisance.

· Posted: Sep 17, 2026 6:46 AM EDT | Last Updated: 36 minutes ago

Tensions are rising between residents of the Kokomo Park community in Port Stanley, Ont., and it's because of pickleball.

Kokomo Park is a quiet neighbourhood, with a condo building, a block of single-family homes, a playground and four public pickleball courts that are popular with some of the residents and their friends.

"We hang out together, we laugh together, we joke together," said Ashley Hennesey, who plays at the courts regularly. "The good thing about pickleball is it brings you out so that you're getting good healthy workout, good community and get to know people you didn't know before."

But for others, the courts are a source of constant noise.

After receiving a number of complaints, the Municipality of Central Elgin decided in July that the courts could only be used from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., a change from the previous policy of dawn to dusk.

At a municipal council meeting on Monday the players submitted a petition with 130 signatures, asking to change the hours to 8 a.m. to dusk, and for the municipality to conduct a noise study and to include the players in future discussions.

At the same meeting, St. Catharines-based lawyer J. Patrick Maloney submitted a letter on behalf of Richard Robson, one of the condo owners, and "Kokomo Affected Neighbours," a group of condo residents.

The letter threatened legal action if the courts are not removed, claiming the use of the pickleball courts would exceed provincial noise guidelines and would "contravene the general legal principles associated with the tort of nuisance."

"We understand that the pickleball users are pushing for expanded hours, which demonstrates they are not concerned with such nuisance impacts or our clients legal right to the quiet enjoyment of their property," Maloney wrote.

Maloney did not respond to a request for a statement. CBC News spoke with two of the "Kokomo Affected Neighbours" but neither wished to comment.

The municipality received both communications at Monday's meeting, but no decision has been made regarding either the players' or the residents' requests.

Hennessey, who started the players' petition, said he and the others want the courts to remain open earlier in the morning due to concerns over the heat and humidity, noting the "advanced age" of many of the people who frequent the courts.

"Playing in 30 to 35 degree weather is not healthy," he said. "So we come out, we play earlier in the day and to us that is a reasonable alternative."

The disagreement has led to tensions between neighbours, he said, describing multiple occasions on which condo residents have yelled at him and other players if they arrive at the courts too early or leave too late.

Hennessey and the other players are willing to work with the community to find a way to reduce the disruption, he said, and he was surprised to read the lawyer's letter asking for the courts to be closed outright.

"That is absolutely not fair because what we want to hear is the joy...the laughing, the joking, chirping each other back and forth," he said. "This is what life is about, it's supposed to be about getting along, being peaceful and having a good time."

In 2025, Lloyd Mulroney moved into the home directly in front of the pickleball courts, fully aware they existed and were a part of the community, he said, adding that he's even taken to sitting and watching from his porch some mornings, and he and his wife occasionally play.

But the courts can get busy, he said, particularly in the evenings, with upwards of 20 people playing, and 15-20 cars in the small parking lot.

"There's a lot of cheering and activity that's happening," he said. "But if it closes down by 8 p.m., people are respectful, then that works for everybody, right?"

He said there are a lot of "camps" in the community, where the courts are concerned. Some want them gone, some don't care, and some, like him, "kind of lay in the middle."

"I think it could have been dealt with a little bit better," he said. "A little bit more collaboration and a little bit more folks concerned for their neighbour."

stories.title: Carney welcomes EU's 'associate member' plan, while Trump lashes out
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the European Unions' invitation to become its first ever "associate member" Thursday.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Strasbourg, France — Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the European Unions’ invitation to become its first ever “associate member,” and pitched it as deepening ties between two allies who face threats of retaliation from U.S. President Donald Trump.

On Thursday morning, Carney delivered a speech to hundreds of members of European Parliament (MEP) members as well as EU chief Ursula von der Leyen at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France.

The prime minister confirmed Canada’s interest in becoming the first ever “associate member” of the union, an invitation extended the previous day by von der Leyen.

While what that means remains to be seen, Carney used his speech to pitch Canada as a natural ally for the block of 27 European countries in the face of international upheaval — a “tremendous storm,” in his words — and the creation of the next world order.

He sold Canada as a reliable partner in the face of increasing trade violence and volatility by U.S. President Donald Trump. To hundreds of European lawmakers, he proposed Canadian energy and critical minerals in exchange for knocking down trade and travel barriers as well as deeper integration on tech, defence and artificial intelligence.

The speech came on the heels of new tit-for-tat tariffs between Canada and the U.S. after trade negotiations between both countries once again failed to deliver a new deal.

On Thursday, the prime minister set out to make it clear to Trump that the budding partnership with the E.U. was not intended as a hostile effort to supplant the U.S., a fear expressed by the American president Wednesday evening that came with a threat of significant trade retaliation.

“I am not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great-power rival, only with better manners,” Carney said. Dozens of EU parliamentarians laughed and clapped in response.

“We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience, so no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity, or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

Already close, Canada and the European Union should cooperate even more to build up their defence industrial bases, develop sovereign compute but also regulate artificial intelligence, and make it easier for students to move between them, Carney argued.

“We are not fair-weather allies. We do not pursue zero-sum deals,” he told hundreds of European lawmakers. “Our commitment to the rule of law and our unyielding defence of human dignity, individual freedom, and democracy share the same deep roots, the same unwavering dedication.”

Canada has loads of energy, including natural gas and hydrogen, and critical minerals that Europe will need for decades, he argued. On the flip side, Canada can contribute to Europe’s military procurement and development and would like to pool “sovereign compute power” to break away from foreign tech giant dependence.

He would also like Canada to join Erasmus+, a 26.2 billion Euro program student mobility and exchange program.

“Canada and Europe should consider exploring an integrated market for financial services to broaden choice and reduce costs for our citizens,” he added.

Despite all the buzz around the EUˋs associate membership offer to Canada, negotiations on the new alliance are in early stages, both parties say.

When the deal is done, Carney promised it would be debated in Parliament and put to a vote. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said it would be studied by European committees as well.

“That the overwhelmingly positive reaction of members in plenary just a few moments ago will be reflected in a similar reaction in the committees, that I have no doubt,” Metsola said.

Much like his headline-grabbing speech at the World Economic Forum at Davos in January, Carney’s speech repeatedly took aim at Trump’s administration without naming the president. This time, he focus his criticism on the U.S.’s growing use of tariffs and trade threats to ply longtime allies like Canada.

“Today, our societies are being shaken by new storms: the upheavals linked to climate change, the erosion of democratic norms, and the use of trade as a weapon,” said the prime minister.

“Economic integration is now being used as a weapon, and tariffs as a means of pressure. Financial mechanisms are being used for coercive purposes,” he added in French.

Carney’s star power in Europe was on full display before and after his speech. In fact, the start of his talk was delayed roughly ten minutes as dozens of European lawmakers huddled around the prime minister to shake his hand, exchange some words and, occasionally, take a selfie.

Terry Reintke, a German politician and co-president of the Greens–European Free Alliance Group, wore a Sidney Crosby Team Canada jersey and was all smiles as she posed for a picture with Carney before he spoke.

Then, as Carney took the stand, Siegbert Droese — one of the few MEPs from the populist right wing Europe of Sovereign Nations Group attending the speech — chanted “USA! USA!” earning himself groans from other lawmakers and a laugh from the prime minister.

His speech was frequently interrupted by applause and received a hearty standing ovation, hoots and hollers from nearly all MEPs in the room. Only members of the most right wing political group remained silent.

von der Leyen’s invitation for Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU attracted Trump’s ire Wednesday evening, with the president lobbing a bevy of threats against Europe if he perceives the new Canada-EU alliance as a “hostile act.”

“If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” Trump told reporters, calling the notion of an associate membership for Canada “laughable”.

In a press conference after his speech, Carney argued that the U.S. would in fact benefit from Canada deepening its ties to Europe.

“It will make Europe stronger. It will make Canada stronger. It will make… Canada a better partner with the United States,” he told reporters.

stories.title: Frank Stronach to be sentenced today for 1977 indecent assault
stories.summary: The conviction is the only guilty finding out of 12 offences initially alleged involving seven women in a trial that went badly sideways.
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Canada

The conviction is the only guilty finding out of 12 offences initially alleged involving seven women in a trial that went badly sideways over the course of the spring

Last updated 48 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/frank-stronach-to-be-sentenced-today-for-1977-indecent-assault#comments-area)

Canadian businessman Frank Stronach leaves the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Toronto, ON June 19, 2026.Photo by Nick Kozak for Postmedia News

Autoparts billionaire Frank Stronach, 94, is due in a Toronto courtroom Thursday morning for a sentencing hearing for the crime of indecently assaulting a woman in a Toronto apartment in 1977.

Justice Anne Molloy, who found Stronach guilty in June, is to hear Crown and defence arguments before sentencing him for a crime that technically no longer exists, as it was rewritten in 1983 into the broader Criminal Code offence of sexual assault.

An offender can only be charged with a crime that was in force at the time of the alleged offence. Today’s legal arguments will be based on the law of indecent assault as it then was for the substance of the offence, guided by more recent precedent and comparable sentences.

Get a dash of perspective along with the trending news of the day in a very readable format.

The next issue of NP Posted will soon be in your inbox.

We encountered an issue signing you up. Please try again

All were historic complaints, some older than the modern law of sexual assault itself, most in the 1980s. The charges were laid in 2024.

The trial started provocatively, as the Crown sought to use each case to bolster the credibility of the others. But by trial’s end, only three complainants remained. One woman had an emotional breakdown on the witness stand and gave evidence so garbled and disjointed the judge decided no conviction could flow from it. Another gave such self-contradictory evidence, especially over the year the alleged crime occurred, that Molloy decided she could not convict. One woman tried to apologize after lying on the witness stand about whether she had read another complainant’s account in the media. Another was revealed in cross-examination to have an extensive history of controversial business litigation involving what a judge described as her deceit and dishonesty, and a more recent instance of allegedly falsely reporting to police that a man she had a dispute with threatened to kill her. All those charges failed.

Two guilty findings were recorded in June involving two women. Then a few days later with the trial still in the hands of Molloy, a civil lawyer for one of them made an attempt to extract money through Stronach’s lawyer, but ended up sharing information that contradicted the woman’s testimony under oath. That led Molloy to declare a surprise mistrial over the woman’s charge, leaving only the indecent assault conviction involving the other woman. Chronologically, it was the first of the 12 crimes initially alleged.

This woman was also the alleged victim in another charge of attempted rape, which is likewise a historic charge that no longer exists in criminal law, but Molloy found Stronach not guilty on that count.

Now 74, the woman was a 25-year-old legal secretary at the time of the offence in 1977. When she testified, she said she knew Stronach from Rooney’s, the Toronto bar he owned.

“After dinner there, she agreed to go to a nearby apartment with him. He came up from behind her, flipped her forwards over the upholstered arm of a chair, lifted her skirt, and ground his groin into her pelvic area over her panties. There is no evidence that he took his penis out of his pants. At law, this cannot be attempted rape, as alleged in Count 5, but it indecent assault under Count 6,” Molloy wrote.

“It happened so quickly. I was just pushed forward, face first, from behind, fairly forceful. The conviction is the only guilty finding out of 12 offences initially alleged involving seven women in a trial that went badly sideways over the course of the spring
Last updated 48 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/frank-stronach-to-be-sentenced-today-for-1977-indecent-assault#comments-area)
Canadian businessman Frank Stronach leaves the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Toronto, ON June 19, 2026.Photo by Nick Kozak for Postmedia News
Autoparts billionaire Frank Stronach, 94, is due in a Toronto courtroom Thursday morning for a sentencing hearing for the crime of indecently assaulting a woman in a Toronto apartment in 1977.

Justice Anne Molloy, who found Stronach guilty in June, is to hear Crown and defence arguments before sentencing him for a crime that technically no longer exists, as it was rewritten in 1983 into the broader Criminal Code offence of sexual assault.

An offender can only be charged with a crime that was in force at the time of the alleged offence. Today’s legal arguments will be based on the law of indecent assault as it then was for the substance of the offence, guided by more recent precedent and comparable sentences.

All were historic complaints, some older than the modern law of sexual assault itself, most in the 1980s. The charges were laid in 2024.

The trial started provocatively, as the Crown sought to use each case to bolster the credibility of the others. But by trial’s end, only three complainants remained. One woman had an emotional breakdown on the witness stand and gave evidence so garbled and disjointed the judge decided no conviction could flow from it. Another gave such self-contradictory evidence, especially over the year the alleged crime occurred, that Molloy decided she could not convict. One woman tried to apologize after lying on the witness stand about whether she had read another complainant’s account in the media. Another was revealed in cross-examination to have an extensive history of controversial business litigation involving what a judge described as her deceit and dishonesty, and a more recent instance of allegedly falsely reporting to police that a man she had a dispute with threatened to kill her. All those charges failed.

Two guilty findings were recorded in June involving two women. Then a few days later with the trial still in the hands of Molloy, a civil lawyer for one of them made an attempt to extract money through Stronach’s lawyer, but ended up sharing information that contradicted the woman’s testimony under oath. That led Molloy to declare a surprise mistrial over the woman’s charge, leaving only the indecent assault conviction involving the other woman. Chronologically, it was the first of the 12 crimes initially alleged.

This woman was also the alleged victim in another charge of attempted rape, which is likewise a historic charge that no longer exists in criminal law, but Molloy found Stronach not guilty on that count.
Now 74, the woman was a 25-year-old legal secretary at the time of the offence in 1977. When she testified, she said she knew Stronach from Rooney’s, the Toronto bar he owned.

“After dinner there, she agreed to go to a nearby apartment with him. He came up from behind her, flipped her forwards over the upholstered arm of a chair, lifted her skirt, and ground his groin into her pelvic area over her panties. There is no evidence that he took his penis out of his pants. At law, this cannot be attempted rape, as alleged in Count 5, but it indecent assault under Count 6,” Molloy wrote.

“It happened so quickly. I was just pushed forward, face first, from behind, fairly forceful. It wasn’t violent but it was firm… Frankly, it was kind of bizarre,” the victim testified. “It was kind of pathetic… I have to say I felt betrayed… I freed myself from this bizarre event and I gathered up my things and I left.”
Stronach faces a separate trial with similar charges and six complainants in York Region that is not yet scheduled.

stories.title: Blue Jays staying loose with 9 games left in season and a playoff spot on the line
stories.summary: The 42-year-old Scherzer (3-8) pitched five innings of one-run ball, allowing three hits and three walks but striking out three.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By John Chidley-Hill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 17, 2026 6:27 am.

If the Toronto Blue Jays are nervous about reaching the post-season, it doesn’t show.

Myles Straw wore small, silver 1990s-style sunglasses as he answered questions from reporters following a 2 for 4 performance in Wednesday’s 5-1 win over the Detroit Tigers. As he spoke, Blue Jays teammates like Louis Varland and Shane Bieber stopped to take photos or videos, while Andres Gimenez stood near the media scrum shaking his head ruefully.

“I think they look good. I’m not sure. I got these guys over here laughing at me,” said Straw who drove in a run in the fourth inning. “I don’t know why they’re all looking.

“I mean, (infielder) Josh Smith. He gave them to me, so he’s got the same pair. I’m not the only one.”

The Cleveland Guardians beat Chicago 6-3 earlier in the day to take the lead in the American League Central. The White Sox now hold the AL’s third and final wild-card berth and the Blue Jays are 1 1/2 games behind them.

The Texas Rangers defeated the Boston Red Sox 7-3 later in the day to sit one game back of Chicago.

“Today was huge. Obviously, that was like a must-win,” said Straw. “Obviously, we’ve got, what, nine more (games), so anything can happen.

“That’s plenty of baseball, but I think today was a good one to get, for sure.”

Toronto’s rookie class like centre-fielder Brett Bateman and relief pitchers Spencer Miles and Brendan Cellucci were all duded up in short jean shorts, sleeveless plaid shirts and cowboy hats for the Blue Jays trip down to Texas for a critical three-game series against the Rangers.

“That was (veteran pitcher) Max Scherzer. He was excited to show me that a couple days ago,” said Straw. “I saw it, and I thought it’d be great.

“Hopefully, there’s some pictures. I’m sure there will be pictures posted, and you guys will definitely like it.”

The 42-year-old Scherzer (3-8) pitched five innings of one-run ball, allowing three hits and three walks but striking out three. Mason Fluharty, Miles and Varland combined for four scoreless innings to preserve the win.

It was Scherzer’s best start in three outings, keeping Toronto in the game long enough for shortstop Ernie Clement and Straw to drive in some runs. Scherzer had given up six runs over five innings in a 7-4 loss to the Baltimore Orioles on Sept. 11 and three runs over 5 2/3 innings in a 4-3 win over the Kansas City Royals on Sept. 5.

“It’s great when you have to come to the field, and it’s must-win baseball. That’s how we’ve felt for a while now,” said Scherzer. “We know this position that we’re in. We’re aware of the standings, but at the end of the day, you’ve got to come here and win ball games.

“You can’t worry about everything else. You’ve got to worry about yourself. Today we had a good game, and everybody did their job.”

Blue Jays manager John Schneider said that he was going to try and relax on Thursday, the team’s off day, by golfing with his wife. He said he encouraged all of his players to also spend time with their families or think about anything other than baseball.

“I’ve been scoreboard watching for a while,” said Schneider. “I May take a break and just try to focus on going 1-0 every day with the Blue Jays.

“Whatever’s going to happen is going to happen. There’s a lot of moving pieces, and there’s going to continue to be a lot of moving pieces. I think if we can kind of worry about us, that’s the best thing to do.”

Before Wednesday’s win over Detroit, Schneider said that pitcher Trey Yesavage felt good after a conditioning start with the triple-A Buffalo Bisons and could pitch for the Blue Jays as soon as Sunday.

Schneider said that the rookie’s physical readiness was more important than his stat line for the Bisons after he threw 2/3 of an inning, giving up two hits and two runs, one earned, against the Rochester Red Wings.

Yesavage has a 5-5 record for Toronto this season with a 3.65 earned-run average over 18 starts. He’s struck out 91 batters over 93 2/3 innings pitched. He had been out after having surgery on his left knee to repair a meniscus injury suffered Aug. 4 against the Houston Astros.

Bieber, a former Cy Young Award winner, had a setback, however, and will have to delay his next side session. Bieber (5-2) has a 4.37 ERA, striking out 44 over 55 2/3 innings this year.

With nine games left in the regular season, Bieber’s runway to return from inflammation of the right teres major muscle is getting very short.

stories.title: MP Leslyn Lewis sues her alma mater, and professor for 'traumatizing' job interview
stories.summary: Leslyn Lewis is seeking $3 million after failing to get a scholar position reserved for a Black person of African descent
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
Canada

Lewis claims York University prof Sean Rehaag derailed her candidacy for a scholar position by allegedly alerting decision makers to defamatory claims she was racist, anti-gay and anti-refugee

Last updated 25 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/MP-leslyn-lewis-sues-her-alma-mater-and-professor-for-traumatizing-job-interview#comments-area)

Conservative MP Leslyn Lewis speaks during question period in the House of Commons in Ottawa, April 20, 2026.Photo by Blair Gable/Postmedia

Seeking damages of more than $3 million, Leslyn Lewis, the MP for Haldimand-Norfolk in rural southern Ontario and a former leadership candidate for the Conservative Party of Canada, has brought a defamation claim against her alma mater law school at York University and a professor of refugee law over Lewis’s failed application to a scholar position reserved for a Black person of African descent.

Lewis claims Sean Rehaag derailed her short-listed candidacy from the start, by allegedly scheming behind the scenes to alert academic decision makers to his defamatory allegations that Lewis was racist, anti-gay, anti-refugee and opposed women’s reproductive freedom.

In her statement of claim filed in Ontario Superior Court, Lewis also alleges the school was negligent in exposing her to a “traumatizing” job interview process by allowing a “toxic culture” of “wokeism” and “groupthink” to develop at Osgoode Hall law school.

She claims Rehaag “blindsided” her with these defamatory allegations about her politics as she gave a presentation about her candidacy, “ganged up” on her with other academic decision makers to verbally abuse her, and that he did this to “embarrass and humiliate” her in public and in front of academic colleagues.

She claims she has been “de facto vetted-out of any future prospect in academia.”

She claims Rehaag told her that people like her had no place at Osgoode and she was not welcome.

In a statement of defence, Rehaag specifically denies this. York denies the environment was “dangerous, hostile, or abusive.” Both deny there was ever any campaign of “vetting out” or “lobbying” against Lewis.
