By Lucas Casaletto

Posted September 16, 2026 12:18 pm.

Premier Doug Ford says he is fully supportive of the federal government’s move toward privatizing major Canadian airports, signaling he intends to push Ottawa to extend the same approach to Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport.

Ford made the comments at an unrelated press conference in Toronto on Wednesday, responding to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s proposal to maintain ownership but allow for private investment and operations at four of Canada’s largest airports, including Toronto Pearson International Airport.

“I have to give credit where credit is due: the PM is on fire,” Ford said.

Carney wants private investors to run Canada’s four largest airports

Federal government rejects Ford’s Billy Bishop airport expansion plan

Construction to begin on Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport runway safety buffer zones

“He’s moving. He’s lowering taxes like we have done for years. He’s privatizing airports, which should have been done years ago, but there’s one airport that has to be privatized and that’s Billy Bishop.”

On Tuesday, Carney said Canada must rethink how airports are funded and operated. He stated his government is examining ways to bring private capital into airport operations to help fund expansions, improve passenger experience, and reduce bottlenecks.

“We will reinvest the tens of billions of dollars of capital that we raise into infrastructure that Canada needs for the next generation,” Carney said in his speech, noting new funding would support more regional airports in the country.

The federal plan includes exploring private‑sector involvement at Toronto Pearson International Airport, Vancouver International Airport, Montréal‑Trudeau International Airport, and Calgary International Airport.

Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport has been at the centre of political debate for more than a decade with past disputes involving runway expansion, waterfront development, and noise concerns.

“It’s shovel ready,” Ford said on Wednesday.

“$5 to $7 billion of private investment, not costing the taxpayers anything, creating thousands and thousands of jobs, so I look forward to sitting down with [Carney] when he gets back.”

Ford also expressed his confidence in “more effective, more efficient airports.”

“That was the prime minister’s decision that I support 1,000 per cent,” the premier continued.

“Hopefully, at lower cost. I always believe the market dictates. The people will determine. There’s nothing better than competition.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford speaks at an event at Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport on Monday March 23, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Frank Gunn

stories.title: Alberta separation could cost up to $170-billion over first five years, report estimates
stories.summary: University of Calgary authors present two scenarios for secession – ‘smooth’ and ‘difficult’ paths – in report commissioned by province
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Abandoning Confederation and setting up a sovereign country would cost Alberta up to $170-billion over the first five years of independence and would devastate the economy of a shrunken Canada, a report commissioned by the provincial government estimates.

And even in the best-case scenario, the report says secession would provide only minimal economic gains for Alberta. In a more painful separation, wages would plummet, GDP would decline precipitously and government debt would balloon.

The province on Wednesday published the report, which was produced by an independent panel of experts at the University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy.

The report provides a wide range of estimated costs to separation, painting one relatively rosy scenario in which Ottawa co-operates in negotiations and gives the province a favourable deal, and another in which Alberta and Canada enter hostile, prolonged talks that bring the country’s economy to a standstill.

Alberta is currently in the midst of a heated campaign over provincial separation, with voters preparing to decide on Oct. 19 whether to remain in Canada or lay the legal groundwork for a second, binding referendum.

Support for separation in Alberta, estimated to be between 25 and 30 per cent, has remained steady for years. The referendum arrives at a time of heightened concerns over national unity and threats to Canadian sovereignty in response to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation rhetoric.

Quebec voters, meanwhile, are roughly three weeks from a provincial election. The sovereigntist Parti Québécois has led in the polls for the better part of three years but currently seems unlikely to form a majority government. In June, the party published its 524-page Livre bleu – its latest blueprint for independence.

Martha Hall Findlay, director of the UofC’s School of Public Policy, wrote in the Alberta report that the document is non-partisan. It “neither advocates for, nor opposes, separation,” she wrote.

Tim Sargent, the report’s lead author, said in an interview that one of the biggest challenges during the exercise was finding real-world scenarios that could accurately inform the outcomes of a possible Alberta divorce from Canada.

Over the past year, numerous groups and voices in Alberta’s separatism debate have jockeyed to pin down the consequences of secession; the report is the first comprehensive analysis published by an academic institution.

“You’re really staring in the crystal ball,” Mr. Sargent said.

The report says that establishing a separate Alberta could cost between $50-billion and $170-billion in the first five years. It also says Alberta’s debt would hit roughly $324-billion in the best-case scenario and $442-billion if negotiations between the province and Canada aren’t friendly.

The rest of Canada, meanwhile, would be economically devastated by Alberta’s departure. The authors predict that Canada’s global economic standing would fall, its currency would weaken and that there would be major challenges to interprovincial and international trade routes.

The panel said its findings underline two key points: that separation would involve significant short-term costs, and that the long-term economic and fiscal consequences would be highly uncertain.

Alberta Finance Minister Jason Nixon pointed to that uncertainty in a Wednesday statement responding to the report.

“The panel’s assessment emphasizes that both the scenarios outlined in the report highlight how costly it would be for Alberta to separate from Canada in the short term and also highlight the substantial amount of uncertainty Alberta would face in the long term,” he wrote.

NDP finance critic Court Ellingson said in a statement that the report demonstrates that separatism is a “terrible idea for Alberta’s economy and families” and shows that the Oct. 19 referendum is a “waste of money.”

Alberta’s path to secession would largely rest on Ottawa’s reaction and its negotiation strategy, the report says. A “smooth” departure would require the Canadian government – in this case, motivated by providing certainty and limiting the economic damage – to quickly conclude negotiations with Alberta.

The “difficult” scenario, meanwhile, would likely see Ottawa limit its concessions to Alberta to discourage other provinces from leaving, which the authors say motivated the European Union’s approach when Britain voted to leave the bloc.

Prolonged negotiations would weigh on investment, interest rates and the exchange rate because investors would be hesitant to put money into Alberta and Canada until they had a clear picture of the future, the report says.

The vast range of potential outcomes is reflected in some of the estimates.

Under the “smooth” scenario, the authors expect that the Alberta government’s surplus over a 20-year horizon would be around $7.8-billion, while GDP would increase by about three per cent more than if Alberta had stayed in the country. The “difficult” scenario estimates that the province’s deficit would grow to $31-billion and GDP would contract by 16 per cent.

The report also ponders Alberta’s relationship with the U.S., things the new country would not need to spend money on – such as a Coast Guard – and how it would set up a military.

Alberta wouldn’t inherit assets such as fighter jets, which would “need to be acquired quickly,” the report says, and as a new country it would need to spend about $10-billion to meet Nato’s requirement that members spend 2 per cent of gross domestic product on defence. That would increase to $25-billion as Nato countries last year committed to investing 5 per cent of GDP annually on defence by 2035.

Keith Wilson, leader of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, said he feels that the report is “unrealistically pessimistic” because it ignores the province’s leverage in negotiations with the rest of Canada. Even the best-case scenario dismisses the province’s economic levers, he said.

“Canada does not have that economic strength. Alberta holds the cards here,” said Mr. Wilson, who recently published his own economic projections under what he called the Alberta Transition Council.

The relatively minor benefits outlined in the “smooth” scenario are highly unlikely and underline the limited upside of separation, Adam Legge, president of the Business Council of Alberta, said in an interview.

“The highest probability is that we would be landing somewhere in negative economic territory,” said Mr. Legge, a member of the report’s advisory panel.

Mr. Legge added that the best-case scenario was included to “insulate” the report from criticism that it only looked at the negative consequences of separation.

“It was really about ensuring that we enabled the report to stand the test of a challenge and not being a predetermined conclusion.”

stories.title: Max Domi fails physical, out indefinitely: Leafs’ GM Chayka
stories.summary: The Leafs' Max Domi underwent a procedure to deal with an injury that hampered him throughout the 2025-26 campaign.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
Posted September 16, 2026 12:17 pm.

The Toronto Maple Leafs medical staff had a busy off-season.

General manager John Chayka announced Wednesday that Max Domi failed his physical and will be out indefinitely.

Chayka added that the 31-year-old would address the situation publicly “at the right time in the near future.”

Domi underwent a procedure to deal with an injury that hampered him throughout the 2025-26 campaign. The team did not reveal the nature of the injury or surgery.

Domi has two years remaining on his contract with a $3.75-million cap hit.

In positive news for Leafs fans, veteran defenceman Chris Tanev has been given the green light from the medical staff to be on the ice to start training camp.

Tanev had core muscle surgery in March that forced him to miss the rest of the season. He struggled with injuries, which limited him to 11 games and 17:58 average ice time, the lowest since the 2012-13 season.

stories.title: Trump criticizes Canada over drugs but leaves it off list of drug-producing countries
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump is again accusing Canada of not doing enough to clamp down on drugs but did not include it in a list of major drug-producing countries released today.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington — U.S. President Donald Trump is again accusing Canada of not doing enough to clamp down on drugs but did not include it in a list of major drug-producing countries released today.

The list, which is published each year, cites Afghanistan, China, Colombia, Guatemala, Haiti, Mexico and other nations deemed major drug producers.

In a declaration submitted to Congress, Trump praised the efforts of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum’s administration to stop the flow of drugs and shut down labs but said Mexico and Canada still need to do more.

Trump alleged that fentanyl is being made in clandestine Canadian labs and transported south into the United States, and claimed Chinese gangs are operating along the border.

U.S. government data shows a minuscule volume of drugs is seized at the northern border compared to the boundary with Mexico.

Trump used fentanyl as a reason to hit Canada with tariffs last year before the U.S. Supreme Court struck down those duties.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta separation could cost $170 billion in first 5 years: report
stories.summary: A report on Alberta’s separation from Canada finds establishing a new country would cost several tens of billions of dollars and as much as $170 billion in the first five years. However, the report also shows some long term benefits for Albertans. In addressing the report, the province says in a news release “the short-term […]
stories.author: Darren Rathwell
stories.content:
Posted September 16, 2026 12:03 pm.

A report on Alberta’s separation from Canada finds establishing a new country would cost several tens of billions of dollars and as much as $170 billion in the first five years.

However, the report also shows some long term benefits for Albertans. In addressing the report, the province says in a news release “the short-term impacts of potential separation would result in significant economic disruption and costs for Albertans.”

They add the report was commissioned by the Danielle Smith government to “provide Albertans with reliable, transparent information ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum”, and examine potential the potential economic impact of separation.

The University of Calgary’s School of Public Policy report says the cost of establishing a new country could range from $50 billion to $170 billion in the first five years following separation, and would be in addition to the impact on economic growth and Alberta’s fiscal position.

The report outlines a pair of scenarios for separation, a “smooth” and “difficult” transition, both of which are expected to be economically troublesome.

In the difficult case, the report anticipates limits on trade and market access that could create lasting economic challenges for both Alberta and Canada.

“Even after 20 years, employment could be nearly five per cent lower and Alberta’s economy more than 16 per cent smaller than if the province remained in Canada. Despite higher taxes, the government could face an ongoing annual budget deficit of more than $30 billion.”

stories.title: Teen in critical condition after e-scooter collides with SUV in Winnipeg
stories.summary: A teenager was taken to hospital in critical condition after a collision between an e-scooter and an SUV at Waverley Street and Lake Crest Road.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A teenager is suffering from life-threatening injuries after being struck by an SUV while riding an e-scooter in Winnipeg, police said.

The teen was crossing Waverley Stret at Lake Crest Road with their e-scooter Monday, when a 2010 Honda CRV heading southbound struck them, the Winnipeg Police Service (WPS) said in a news release. Officers responded to the reported collision around 9:30 p.m.

The e-scooter operator was taken to hospital in critical condition, where they remain as of Wednesday morning, WPS continued. The driver of the CRV, a person in their late teens, remained on the scene and spoke with investigators.

Anyone with dashcam or cell phone video is being asked to contact Winnipeg police’s traffic division.

stories.title: Montreal AI research institute denounces violence after office vandalized
stories.summary: Montreal — Hours after the office of a Quebec artificial intelligence institute was vandalized Tuesday night, the founder of the organization warned that violence would not resolve public concerns about the rapidly evolving technology.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Posted September 16, 2026 11:48 am.

Last Updated September 16, 2026 3:35 pm.

Montreal — Hours after the office of a Quebec artificial intelligence institute was vandalized Tuesday night, the founder of the organization warned that violence would not resolve public concerns about the rapidly evolving technology.

Mila’s Yoshua Bengio made the comments Wednesday morning at the opening of All In, a major artificial intelligence conference in Montreal, where he and federal Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon were set to announce new funding for research into the potential dangers of AI systems.

“Violence is not an answer to these risks and fears, which I can understand,” Bengio said at the AI and tech summit.

Montreal police say a group of about 10 people targeted the building at the corner of Saint-Urbain and Saint-Zotique streets at around 11:45 p.m. on Tuesday, smashing several windows and spray-painting graffiti on its walls.

A 25-year-old woman was arrested near the scene. Johany Charland, a spokesperson for Montreal police, said the woman was released Wednesday afternoon after being interviewed by investigators. Charland would not say if the woman was still considered a suspect in the investigation.

Mila says its central mission is to develop ethical and safe artificial intelligence that serves the public interest. It also says it focuses its mission on core research areas such as health, environment and climate change and that it carries out research using an open science approach to promote collaboration and foster the transfer of knowledge.

At the conference, Bengio said he has spent years examining the responsibilities of researchers, companies and governments as increasingly powerful artificial intelligence systems raise ethical and safety questions.

“How can we make sure that ethics are at the centre of our decisions?” Bengio said, adding that doing so isn’t necessarily easy amid market competition and geopolitical pressures.

He said raising public awareness can lead to democratic debate about the choices society wants to make — “certainly not through violence.”

Solomon also condemned the vandalism, calling it unacceptable in a democracy and saying researchers and students have the right to work in peace and safety.

“There are real questions about technology, and we welcome them in our democracy,” Solomon said. He added that people should be able to ask questions and protest peacefully.

Mila separately condemned what it described as acts of vandalism and intimidation targeting its premises.

“While we respect the fundamental right to express differing opinions and social criticism, we strongly condemn any use of violence, property damage and tactics aimed at intimidating our staff and researchers,” the research institute wrote in a statement Wednesday.

Montreal police said investigators were reviewing surveillance footage and gathering evidence in an effort to identify other suspects. ”The investigation is ongoing,” said Charland.

Montreal police also said their presence at the city’s main convention centre, where the conference is taking place, had not been increased in response to the vandalism. Police said deployments had already been planned and no additional officers were assigned as a result of the overnight incident.

The comments from Bengio and Solomon came as the federal minister announced $150 million in funding for LawZero,a non-profit AI safety research organization founded by Bengio and incubated at Mila.

German federal Minister for Digital Transformation and Government Modernization Karsten Wildberger also announced plans to provide up to 100 million euros for the project, subject to approval by the European Commission.

Bengio said the money will help researchers demonstrate how artificial intelligence can be trained with safety guarantees.

Bengio also said some of the most serious risks posed by advanced AI are difficult to predict, but that doesn’t mean they should be ignored.

“The more powerful it is, the more beneficial it can be — and also the more dangerous,” Bengio said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Charlotte Glorieux, The Canadian Press

The comments from Bengio and Solomon came as the federal minister announced $150 million in funding for LawZero,a non-profit AI safety research organization founded by Bengio and incubated at Mila.

German federal Minister for Digital Transformation and Government Modernization Karsten Wildberger also announced plans to provide up to 100 million euros for the project, subject to approval by the European Commission.
Bengio said the money will help researchers demonstrate how artificial intelligence can be trained with safety guarantees.
Bengio also said some of the most serious risks posed by advanced AI are difficult to predict, but that doesn’t mean they should be ignored.
“The more powerful it is, the more beneficial it can be — and also the more dangerous,” Bengio said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.
Charlotte Glorieux, The Canadian Press

stories.title: A list of Ontario cities that are weighing restrictions on AI data centres
stories.summary: Mississauga city council is set to vote Wednesday on a one-year data centre moratorium
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The boom in artificial intelligence has put Ontario municipalities on the front lines of a major debate over how to regulate a new wave of large, energy-hungry data centres.

Several municipalities have voted in recent months on temporary data centre moratoriums while they study possible guardrails, and at least one has amended its bylaws to specifically permit them on industrial lands.

Under pressure from local lawmakers, the Ontario government released a draft framework last month to deal with an influx of proposals that are causing some municipalities to consider temporary bans on constructing these facilities.

Here’s a brief look at what some Ontario municipalities have done, and plan to do.

Mississauga city council is set to vote Wednesday on a one-year data centre moratorium. The proposed citywide moratorium would apply to data centres with energy demands over 10 megawatts. It comes as Prologis, a major U.S.-headquartered firm, pursues a two-storey data centre in a business park in the city’s northwest.

The city was the first in Canada to vote on a one-year data centre freeze, what’s called an interim control bylaw. The proposed moratorium easily cleared committee but was voted down by council in July after a closed-door session with the city’s legal team. City staff are still carrying out a data centre planning study to look at possible guardrails, from energy demand to noise pollution.

What is happening with AI data centre development in Canada, according to our experts

The town became the first in Ontario to get a moratorium past the finish line last month, while staff carry out a planning study. While Oakville officials said it had no formal data centre applications, developer Hive Digital Technologies in May announced plans for a 320-megawatt AI facility in the Greater Toronto Area targeted for the second half of 2027.

Council directed staff last month to draft a moratorium on data centres with energy demands over 50 megawatts. A vote on that moratorium is expected on Sept. 21.

The municipality in eastern Ontario passed a bylaw in February to include data centres as a permitted use in the town’s industrial lands.

Council directed staff in July to review the city’s planning policies around data centres and pressed the province to come up with an Ontario-wide framework. Staff were also told to alert city councillors about any large data centre applications.

City council directed staff last month to study and develop an assessment framework for data centres, including possible amendments to city policy. Until that framework is brought to council, staff were told to make council aware of any large-scale data centres to allow for the city to potentially consider case-by-case moratoriums to manage community impacts.

What to know about Ottawa’s push for more data centres

The town on Monday directed staff to study data centres, but voted down an interim control bylaw.

Council in July voted down a bid to pursue a temporary moratorium but directed staff to study the city’s rules around data centres.

The regional municipality in August directed staff to report back to council early next year on possible data centre development implications.

The Ontario government says data centres in the province will need to cover all their energy costs and could pay more for electricity than other industrial users. The province released a data centre framework as it faces pressure to bring in guardrails around the facilities powering the artificial intelligence boom.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ottawa gets it on tax policy, gamechanger ‘mega deduction’ shows
stories.summary: Initiative will address Canada’s lagging productivity by reducing the after-tax cost of investment
stories.author: Steve Suarez
stories.content:
Steve Suarez is a partner in the Toronto office of BLG, and the co-chair of the Taxation and Economics Committee of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s announcement Tuesday of the “ productivity mega deduction ” is one of the most consequential Canadian tax policy initiatives of the 21st century. At a stroke, the Canadian government has signalled to the business community “we get it.”

In simple terms (and simplicity is one of this measure’s virtues), this new “immediate expensing” deduction is a timing measure: It allows businesses to deduct for tax purposes the cost of eligible expenditures much sooner than would be the case under existing rules. The taxpayer doesn’t get a bigger deduction or more tax savings: just the same tax savings faster.

This is because while current rules require these business expenditures to be deducted for tax purposes over a period of years even if paid for up front, the productivity mega deduction allows the taxpayer to deduct the entire expenditure in the year in which the property in question becomes “available for use” (basically installed and capable of operation). Generally this means that taxpayers are much less likely to pay tax on profits before recovering their costs, which is eminently fair.

What is truly remarkable is the breadth of what qualifies. Most new investments in capital property acquired on or after Sept. 15 are eligible. Taken together with a 2025 federal budget measure for other property, the government estimates that some two-thirds of business investments in capital assets are now eligible for immediate expensing, with the Prime Minister’s Office describing the expanded scope as including “fibre-optic cable, mining property, oil and gas pipelines, software, research and development, computer equipment, aircraft and vehicles, patents, rail track, bridges, and roads.”

Opinion: Mark Carney’s investment moment

This initiative is vitally important to Canada’s economy for many reasons. Most importantly, it directly addresses Canada’s dreadful productivity record over the past 25 years. In March, 2026, Statistics Canada estimated that our labour productivity relative to the U.S. has fallen 26 per cent since the late 1990s, much of which occurred in the past five years.

Immediate expensing on this scale moves the needle on this problem by reducing the after-tax cost of badly needed investment. Measured by marginal effective tax rate (tax imposed on an additional dollar of business investment), the government estimates that Canada’s Metr on eligible investment will be reduced to 6.4 per cent, well below the comparable U.S. rate of 16.9 per cent. Making investments in productive assets cheaper in this way and on this scale was the Canadian Chamber of Commerce’s first recommendation in its 2026 prebudget submission to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne this summer, prompting president and CEO Candace Laing to describe this measure as “a launchpad to make Canada globally tax competitive.”

While this measure is not limited to any particular industry, Pierre Gratton, president and CEO of the Mining Association of Canada, described it as “transformative” in the resource sector. Building new mines is a high-risk, capital-intensive exercise often stretching over several years. Under current rules, only 30 per cent of most mine development costs can be deducted in the year incurred. Under immediate expensing, they would be 100-per-cent deductible when incurred: a huge difference.

Also critical is the fact that broad-based immediate expensing responds to a wave of 2025 U.S. business-friendly tax changes. Lisa Baiton, president and CEO of the Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers, acknowledged this on Tuesday, observing that “Canada’s largest competitor for upstream oil and natural gas investment is the United States, and the productivity mega deduction closes a significant competitive gap between the two countries in terms of capital cost expensing.” Canadian business deserves a level playing field to compete on.

Broad-based immediate expensing hopefully signals a larger and long-overdue shift in Canada’s tax policy toward actively investing in our economy and its tax base, which is needed to fund the social programs that are part of what makes us Canada. Tuesday’s Department of Finance release described immediate expensing as representing “a sea-change in how Canada intends to stimulate business investment decisions,” which is exactly what our tax policy should be doing in these circumstances: actively supporting our larger economic strategy.

Reduced tax revenue today will generate much more tax revenue later, based on the estimated increased economic activity of 1.4 to three times the government’s cost of these measures and long-term employment increases of up to 80,000 jobs annually 10 years from now. Apart from these businesses, the workers building these investments today and those using them in the future are themselves taxpayers, who will add to our tax base.

The productivity mega deduction is a powerful and welcome statement of the federal government’s intention to make the cost of doing business in Canada much cheaper (hopefully the provinces follow suit). Canada just became a much more interesting place for Canadians and foreigners alike to invest in.

stories.title: Élections Québec ordered to mail bilingual voter information by Quebec judge
stories.summary: The judge said there is serious concern that a large number of English-speaking seniors could be unable to exercise their right to vote due to a lack of understandable information.
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
A Quebec Superior Court judge has ordered Élections Québec to mail voting reminder cards in both French and English.

This was the first year the elections authority sent out voter guides in French only, to comply with new provincial language legislation. The guides included a QR code to access information in English online.

Groups representing anglophones in the province heavily criticized the move, saying it infringes on the right to vote.

Justice Sylvain Lussier wrote in his 23-page decision that there was concern of serious and irreparable prejudice against Quebecers who do not understand French.

Geoffrey Chambers, a Westmount resident and the former president of an anglophone rights group, was the lead plaintiff in the case.

He had asked the judge to grant an emergency order to get the elections agency to provide English copies of the provincial election guide, a notice sent to electors, and a reminder card.

He argued that the QR code isn’t an adequate substitute because many people can’t access them, including some seniors and people without cellphones or reliable internet.

“The proof raises concerns that a large number of English-speaking seniors could be unable to exercise their right to vote due to a lack of understandable information,” Lussier wrote.

According to Lussier, there is also concern that election results could be invalidated if the right to vote is infringed on.

He pointed to the result of the 2025 federal byelection in Terrebonne, which was invalidated because of a clerical error on the return address for some mail-in ballots.

A recount handed the win to Liberal Tatiana Auguste by a single vote.

The one-vote result triggered a challenge after a Bloc voter’s mail-in ballot was returned because of an incorrect postal code on an Elections Canada return envelope

“It is clear that the loss of the right to vote in an election is permanent,” wrote Lussier. “The loss of a single vote was enough to invalidate the federal election in Terrebonne.”

However, lawyers representing the elections authority said it was impossible to reprint all documents to include English information given the time and budgetary constraints, which Lussier acknowledged in his decision.

He nonetheless asked Élections Québec to send the voter reminder card in both official languages. The list of candidates on the cards is finalized at 2 p.m. on Sept. 17, and the agency had already planned to print out reminder cards to mail out after that deadline.

Lussier’s ruling suspends provisions of the Charter of the French Language for 10 days to allow the printing of bilingual reminder cards.

Élections Québec had asked the government to be exempt from provisions forcing government institutions to issue public communications in French only as early as 2023. It raised concerns that it could not fulfil its mission to make elections accessible to all Quebecers as a result of the law.

Quebec voters go to the polls on Oct. 5.

stories.title: Cohere, Aleph Alpha combine to target enterprise AI market
stories.summary: Merged company will operate as Cohere, have headquarters in Toronto and Berlin
stories.author: Leo Marchandon
stories.content:
Canada’s Cohere and Germany’s Aleph Alpha signed a definitive merger agreement on Wednesday, the AI companies said.

The combined business will operate as Cohere, with dual headquarters in Toronto and Berlin, while Aleph Alpha’s Heidelberg office will focus on research. Aleph Alpha co-chief Ilhan Scheer will become chief operating officer of Cohere.

The merger brings together a Canadian AI model developer and a German company that has increasingly focused on helping governments and businesses deploy artificial intelligence. The companies said demand was growing for AI systems that can operate within a customer’s own infrastructure and comply with local regulatory requirements.

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said the tie-up aimed to meet demand for AI “powerful enough to compete, but secure and governable enough to trust.”

Cohere, Open Text to pitch Canadian-made AI agent tools to enterprises

The plan was first disclosed in April, a combination valued at about US$20-billion at the time. Lidl-owner Schwarz Group is investing €500-million (US572-million) in the new entity. The companies did not disclose updated financial terms and said the transaction remained subject to regulatory approvals.

The deal comes as European AI companies attract fresh investment. Mistral, Europe’s lead model maker, last week raised €3-billion (US$3.46-billion) at a valuation of more than €21-billion (US$24.2-billion).

Cohere develops Command, a family of open source AI models designed to run inside a customer’s own computing environment, positioning the company to serve businesses, governments and public administrations rather than consumers.

Aleph Alpha, once touted as Germany’s AI champion, stepped back from developing frontier AI models and refocused on AI integration software. Co-founder Jonas Andrulis left the company earlier this year after relinquishing the chief executive role in 2025.

Cohere reported US$240-million in annual recurring revenue last year, while Aleph Alpha reported revenue of less than €1-million (US$1.15-million) in 2023, according to its latest public accounts.

The companies said Schwarz Group would provide computing capacity through its cloud arm StackIT. The retailer is investing between €11-billion (US$1.15-million) and €13-billion (US$15-billion) in a German data-centre campus expected to house up to 100,000 AI chips.

stories.title: Danny Boyle defends use of AI in new film ‘Ink’ at Tiff screening
stories.summary: Toronto — Danny Boyle says he tried to be responsible with the small amount of artificial intelligence used in the making of his new film “Ink.”
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Danny Boyle says he tried to be responsible with the small amount of artificial intelligence used in the making of his new film “Ink.”

At a Tuesday screening of the movie at the Toronto International Film Festival, the British director said he was careful to think about potential job losses when deciding to use the technology for about 30 seconds in the movie.

His remarks were met with jeers by some in the audience.

“We try to be very responsible and make sure that no actors were out of work because of it,” he explained during a panel after the screening, when an audience member asked about his use of AI. “We would always employ actors if we were going to use a bit of it.”

AI helped Boyle animate old photographs used in a montage and add mice to another scene in the movie about the sensationalism of U.K. tabloid the Sun under owner Rupert Murdoch.

Boyle didn’t explain why he felt it necessary to rely on the technology but said it’s an issue both the industry and humanity need to explore in the future.

“The wider question of It and its place in our society, of course, including our profession is a huge and complicated one, which I don’t think we could probably go into here,” he said. “But we will need to go into it more.”

As he wrapped up answering the question, an audience member shouted that he should never use AI in his film again. A Tiff employee who was moderating the panel with Boyle and stars Guy Pearce and Jack O’Connell then ended the question session.

Boyle is best known for “Slumdog Millionaire,” a rags to riches film that won Tiff’s People’s Choice Award in 2008 and then an Academy Award for best picture.

“Ink” screened at Tiff about a week after its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Toronto — Danny Boyle says he tried to be responsible with the small amount of artificial intelligence used in the making of his new film “Ink.”

At a Tuesday screening of the movie at the Toronto International Film Festival, the British director said he was careful to think about potential job losses when deciding to use the technology for about 30 seconds in the movie.
His remarks were met with jeers by some in the audience.

“We try to be very responsible and make sure that no actors were out of work because of it,” he explained during a panel after the screening, when an audience member asked about his use of AI. “We would always employ actors if we were going to use a bit of it.”
AI helped Boyle animate old photographs used in a montage and add mice to another scene in the movie about the sensationalism of U.K. tabloid the Sun under owner Rupert Murdoch.
Boyle didn’t explain why he felt it necessary to rely on the technology but said it’s an issue both the industry and humanity need to explore in the future.

“The wider question of It and its place in our society, of course, including our profession is a huge and complicated one, which I don’t think we could probably go into here,” he said. “But we will need to go into it more.”

As he wrapped up answering the question, an audience member shouted that he should never use AI in his film again. A Tiff employee who was moderating the panel with Boyle and stars Guy Pearce and Jack O’Connell then ended the question session.
Boyle is best known for “Slumdog Millionaire,” a rags to riches film that won Tiff’s People’s Choice Award in 2008 and then an Academy Award for best picture.
“Ink” screened at Tiff about a week after its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.
Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Annual pace of housing starts dips in August, Cmhc says
stories.summary: Modest gains in Quebec and Alberta only partially offset decline in other provinces
stories.content:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. reports the annual pace of housing starts for August edged lower compared with July.

The national housing agency says the seasonally adjusted annual rate of housing starts came in at 229,046 units for August, down from 229,360 in July.

The result came as actual monthly housing starts in centres with a population of 10,000 or more totalled 17,691 in August, down from 18,112 units in August 2025.

The annual pace of rural starts was estimated at 11,224 units.

The six-month moving average of the seasonally adjusted annual rate of total housing starts for all areas in Canada was 244,149 in August, down 1.3 per cent from July.

Cmhc deputy chief economist Kevin Hughes says housing starts continued to trend slightly down in August, as modest gains in Quebec and Alberta only partially offset the decline in other provinces, most notably, Ontario.

stories.title: Western Propel Fund invests in next generation of entrepreneurial leaders
stories.summary: The Western Propel Fund will invest up to $150,000 in early-stage companies founded by Western students, faculty, staff and alumni.
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
A landmark $5-million institutional venture fund launched at Western University will invest directly in early stage companies founded by entrepreneurs in the campus community.

In a first for the university, the Western Propel Fund will offer up to six investments of $150,000 per year for five years to startup businesses with at least one founder who is a Western student, faculty or staff member or graduate.

“The fund signals to the entrepreneurial community, here at Western and beyond, that we are serious about our entrepreneurs’ success,” said Eric Morse, executive director of Western’s Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship, powered by Ivey.

Western and Ivey Business School are each committing $2 million to the Propel Fund, while Morrissette Entrepreneurship will contribute another $1 million. Together, their investments will power the fund through 2030.

The Propel Fund is designed to fill a specific gap – companies far enough along to show promise but too small to attract institutional venture capital. To be eligible, companies must have raised less than $1 million in total capital.

Eric Morse, executive director of Morrissette Institute for Entrepreneurship, says the new Western Propel Fund demonstrates the university’s commitment to helping founders grow and succeed. (Brandon MacIntosh/Ivey Communications)

“We see the Propel Fund as a way to help Western-founded ventures bridge that investment gap,” Morse said. “The fund is just one part of Morrissette’s ongoing support for founders through every stage of their business journey.”

Founders can apply to the Propel Fund through Morrissette’s twice-yearly Angels’ Demo Day. Each cycle, six to eight companies make their pitch before a live audience of investors, mentors and alumni. After pitching, each company will be assigned to a team of student volunteers who will conduct formal due diligence under guidance from the Propel leadership team and external subject-matter experts.

Their findings will be reviewed by an investment committee, which will make the final decision about which companies to fund. Up to three founders from each Demo Day will receive funding, giving Western equity in each company.

Propel leadership will track the companies’ milestones, revenue and jobs created through quarterly check-ins. The program also trains student volunteers in the skills needed to conduct due diligence. While many are business students, other volunteers come from faculties across campus.

Zachary Kanemy

Zachary Kanemy, a fourth-year student in management and organizational studies who’s volunteering on the due diligence team, says it provides meaningful exposure to venture capital in a real-world setting, while allowing students to contribute fresh perspectives during the review.

“A large part of the process is stress-testing assumptions, evaluating markets, determining a company’s potential to scale up and understanding founder dynamics,” he said.

Volunteers did that due diligence on the first round of applicants this summer – seven startups that pitched their businesses at Demo Day on June 3.

“What stands out is how much emphasis is placed on the team itself, especially at the seed stage where products and financial models can still evolve significantly,” Kanemy said.

Recipients will be supported through Morrissette’s full suite of programming, including mentorship, makerspaces, workshops and alumni connections. Morse said the university ecosystem gives the fund an edge a standalone investor couldn’t easily replicate.

“We are able to put additional resources into the ventures that come through our programming, including access to industry and startup expertise from our large network of alumni mentors and experts,” he said.

Entrepreneurship is a priority for Western, with about 20 student clubs and nearly 30 courses across campus adding to Morrissette’s formal programming.

Across the university, entrepreneurs are supported through every stage of their journeys, from idea to real-world impact. Students and researchers from all faculties can learn the basics of entrepreneurship before developing their ideas through various programs, courses, mentors, workshops and competitions.

As ideas grow, entrepreneurs can opt in to commercialization support through Innovation and Strategic Partnerships at Western Research, including the Technology Transfer Office that collaborates with inventors and industry partners.

The Western Accelerator is a critical component of the cross-campus entrepreneurship ecosystem, offering an immersive, full-time opportunity to advance high-potential ventures run by students, faculty, staff and recent alumni. Since its inception in 2017, more than 150 companies have passed through the program, including success stories such as Marlow, TerraOptima, Apricotton and Tenomix.

PitchBook included Western among the top 50 schools for undergraduate and MBA entrepreneurship for the second year in 2026, ranking the university 36th globally for undergraduate entrepreneurs who have raised venture capital over the last decade, ahead of prestigious institutions like Cambridge and Oxford.

Since 2018, more than $6.5 billion has been raised by Western entrepreneurs. With the Propel Fund, Western will now play a direct role, investing in promising early stage companies financially, in addition to the support provided through entrepreneurial programming and expertise.

“Western produces some exceptional entrepreneurial quality, both the entrepreneurs themselves and the companies they start,” Morse said. “This is just the beginning of more ambitious possibilities.”

stories.title: London police seek man after suspect fled from stolen vehicle
stories.summary: London police say that officers arrested one man and are looking for two other suspects after recovering a stolen vehicle.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
A London police vehicle responds to a call on Tuesday, June 16, 2026. (Geoff Robins/The London Free Press)

London police say that officers arrested one man and are looking for two other suspects after recovering a stolen vehicle.

Officers were at a home near Wharncliffe Road and Oxford Street on Sept. 11, last Friday, when they spotted three people running away, police said in a news release on Wednesday.

Police say that they later located the three suspects inside a vehicle that had been reported stolen by another police force. The three suspects ran away, but officers arrested one and recovered the stolen vehicle, police said.

Two London men, 24 and 38, are charged with possession of property over $5,000 obtained by crime. The 24-year-old man is charged by warrant and police are asking the public for help finding him. The identity of the third suspect remains unknown, police said.

A pedestrian is dead after a Saturday crash on Walpole Island First Nation, provincial police say.

Walpole Island police, Ontario Provincial Police officers and paramedics responded after a sport utility vehicle and pedestrian collided on Chiefs Road, between Tecumseh and Austin roads, about 11:30 p.m., a Lambton OPP news release said.

The pedestrian, a Walpole Island resident, 48, was pronounced dead at the scene, police said.

The road was closed for several hours for the investigation, which continues with help from the West Region OPP traffic incident management and enforcement team, police said.

Anyone who saw the crash, or has information or dashcam footage from the area around the time of the collision, is asked to call Walpole Island police at 1-888-310-1122 or submit an anonymous tip to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477) orsarnialambtoncrimestoppers.org.

stories.title: Clement on Blue Jays’ wild-card chase: ‘Every game’s a playoff game at this point’
stories.summary: It wasn’t just that the Toronto Blue Jays lost badly. The timing was bad too. Alejandro Kirk’s RBI single was all the offence Toronto could muster in a 10-1 loss to the Detroit Tigers on Tuesday. The defeat put the Blue Jays two games back of Cleveland for the third and final wild-card spot in […]
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Ernie Clement #22 of the Toronto Blue Jays singles in the second inning during Game Seven of the 2025 World Series presented by Capital One between the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Toronto Blue Jays at Rogers Centre on Saturday, November 1, 2025 in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images) 2025 Major League Baseball Photos

By John Chidley-Hill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 16, 2026 9:39 am.

It wasn’t just that the Toronto Blue Jays lost badly. The timing was bad too.

Alejandro Kirk’s RBI single was all the offence Toronto could muster in a 10-1 loss to the Detroit Tigers on Tuesday. The defeat put the Blue Jays two games back of Cleveland for the third and final wild-card spot in the American League after the Guardians rallied past the Chicago White Sox 7-6.

The Texas Rangers’ 4-2 win over the Boston Red Sox later Tuesday moved them half a game ahead of Toronto in the playoff chase.

“I think you just have to find a way,” said Blue Jays second baseman Ernie Clement on how to stay positive with 10 games left in the regular season. “You have to find a way to come back with energy tomorrow and just take one game at a time right now.”

Toronto (75-76) lost the first two games of its three-game series with Detroit (71-79) with the finale on Wednesday afternoon. After climbing back into the AL’s wild-card hunt, the Blue Jays stumbled and have lost five of their last eight.

“I think we’re playing pretty good baseball,” said Clement in the quiet of Toronto’s clubhouse at Rogers Centre. “Today, obviously, it was not our best, but we’re fighting back. We’re swinging the bats well. We’re pitching really, really well. We’re playing great defence.

“I think you just flush this one and get back to it tomorrow.”

Reliever Braydon Fisher was the opener for Toronto’s scheduled bullpen day. He was followed to the mound by Brendan Cellucci, Michael Lorenzen (3-13), Brendon Little, Spencer Arrighetti and Joe Mantiply.

Manager John Schneider had said pre-game that he hoped Arrighetti would have the day off but, with a pivotal series starting in Texas on Friday, he decided to think big picture.

“You’re asking a lot out of guys in the bullpen, so looking ahead, we kind of pivoted a little bit, and Dylan (Cease) is going to start first game in Texas, and then Jose (Soriano),” said Schneider of his bullpen management strategy. “So it put Spencer available today, and we needed a couple innings out of him tonight.”

Max Scherzer (2-8) will take the mound Wednesday when Toronto concludes its series against Detroit. Keider Montero (9-8) was named the Tigers’ starter.

“Every game’s a playoff game at this point,” said Clement.

stories.title: No injuries reported after small plane’s emergency landing east of Edmonton: RCMP
stories.summary: RCMP say the Cessna 172 was blocking southbound lanes of Highway 21, between Highway 16 and Baseline Road, in Strathcona County, east of Edmonton.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
Mounties east of Edmonton say a small plane made an emergency landing on a highway early Wednesday.

RCMP say the Cessna 172 was blocking southbound lanes of Highway 21, between Highway 16 and Baseline Road, in Strathcona County.

They say traffic was to be re-directed until emergency crews could clear the scene.

Police say two people were on board the aircraft at the time of the landing, but no injuries were reported.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada has been notified.

The Cessna 172 Skyhawk is a popular single-engine aircraft commonly used to train student pilots.

stories.title: Ford, Eby approval grows since June amid escalating U.S. trade war: poll
stories.summary: As the Canada-U.S. trade war intensifies, a new poll finds approval for Ontario Premier Doug Ford and B.C. Premier David Eby has grown.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Shachi Kurl, President: 604.908.1693 shachi.kurl@angusreid.org @shachikurl

Dave Korzinski, Research Director: 250.899.0821 dave.korzinski@angusreid.org

Jon Roe, Senior Research Associate: 825.437.1147 jon.roe@angusreid.org

Kinew tops rankings as the only premier with majority approval

September 16, 2026 – Some might say the U.S.-Canada trade war has become a renewed source of political leverage for this country’s politicians . But unlike last year, when the non-profit Angus Reid Institute found rising personal popularity for a majority of provincial premiers, few of the provincial first ministers appear to be benefiting this fall, even as trade animosity between Canada and the U.S. intensifies.

New data from ARI shows big bumps in approval for B.C.’s David Eby (+10 to 41% approval) and Ontario’s Doug Ford

(+10 to 31%) but little movement elsewhere in the country. For both Eby and Ford, this represents a recovery in what had been flagging assessments from constituents. However, the latter is still facing deep disapproval across Ontario as plane and hotel spending scandals dog the governing Progressive Conservatives.

With key votes looming in October, eyes are turned to Quebec and Alberta where both Premiers Christine Fréchette (39%) and Danielle Smith (38%) are approved of by approximately two-in-five in their respective provinces. Both have seen no statistically significant change from the previous quarter. Smith’s status quo comes as the governing UCP sorts through the aftermath of a surprise byelection defeat in a conservative stronghold and just weeks ahead of the Alberta referenda on separation and other issues. Fréchette has evidently built little momentum as the governing Coalition Avenir Québec to fend off the resurgent Parti Québécois in next month’s election.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s honeymoon period continues with approval of approaching two-thirds (63%) in the province. The second most approved-of premiers in the country are Newfoundland and

Labrador’s Tony Wakeham (48%) and Saskatchewan’s Scott Moe (48% ).

Note: Because its small population precludes drawing discrete samples over multiple waves, data on Prince Edward Island is not released.

METHODOLOGY:

The Angus Reid Institute conducted an online survey from Sept 8-15, 2026, among a randomized sample of 4,310 Canadian adults.

Respondents are drawn from the Angus Reid Forum , a large-scale online panel developed to include Canadian residents in each of the 343 federal ridings in Canada and representative of the Canadian population by age, gender, family income, ethnic status and education. The sample was weighted to be representative of adults nationwide according to region, gender, age, household income, and education, based on the Canadian census. Provincial margin of errors are found at the end of the release. The survey was self-commissioned and paid for by ARI.

For more information on our polling methods, click here. Page 2 of 10

CONTACT: Shachi Kurl, President: 604.908.1693 shachi.kurl@angusreid.org @shachikurl Dave Korzinski, Research Director: 250.899.0821 dave.korzinski@angusreid.org Jon Roe, Senior Research Associate: 825.437.1147 jon.roe@angusreid.org

The Angus Reid Institute (ARI) was founded in October 2014 by pollster and sociologist, Dr. Angus Reid. ARI is a national, not-for-profit, non-partisan public opinion research foundation established to advance education by commissioning, conducting and disseminating to the public accessible and impartial statistical data, research and policy analysis on economics, political science, philanthropy, public administration, domestic and international affairs and other socio-economic issues of importance to Canada and its world.

• B.C.: Eby ’s approval recovers

• Alberta: Smith approved of by two-in-five

• Saskatchewan: Moe approval hovers around half

• Manitoba: Kinew endorsed by two-thirds

• Ontario: Ford rebounds, but still lowest in country

• Quebec: Frechette unchanged at 39 per cent as campaign underway

• New Brunswick: Holt holds at 41 per cent

• Nova Scotia: Houston bucks negative trend

• Newfoundland and Labrador: Wakeham approved of by half

The Trump tariffs may be the source of economic anxiety for Canadians, but they have also sown fertile ground for the nation’s politicians. B.C. Premier David Eby’s strong words in response to Trump’s tariff and annexation threats last year helped boost his personal popularity in March 2025. For the only time in his tenure, a majority of British Columbians approved of his performance.

The escalation of the trade war is perhaps to Eby’s political benefit, as his approval gains ten points from 31 per cent in June to 41 per cent now. Eby headlined at a recent “ Rally for Canada ”, during which he revealed new signs to be erected at U.S. border crossings in the province that say “Strong, proud and will never be the 51 st state. Sorry!”

Eby may also benefit by being seen as better option than the alternative, B.C. Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay. Barely three months into the job, her caucus has splintered. Stay tuned for a coming release outlining the latest on the B.C. political scene. Page 3 of 10

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith was dealt a surprise political blow during a crucial period for her in advance of the referendum when the NDP upset the UCP in the Calgary-Shaw byelection, claiming a historically conservative stronghold . It perhaps further highlights the challenges facing Smith in holding together the UCP coalition that is bifurcated by the separatist issue . The UCP candidate in Calgary-Shaw was endorsed by a separatist who ran as a pro-independence candidate for the position of UCP board president . The loss saw UCP yield half of its voters from the 2023 election , while the NDP managed to bring out 70 per cent of their support from the previous election.

Still, while there will be questions surrounding the surprise defeat in Calgary-Shaw, Smith ’s approval is unchanged compared to last quarter, with 38 per cent appraising her positively. A majority of Albertans (56%) say they disapprove of her performance, including 43 per cent who strongly do so, the highest such level of strong disapproval in the country.

46% 48% 45% 48% 46% 48% 43% 46% 46% 53% 46% 41% 40% 37% 31% 41%

Approval of B.C. Premier David Eby Page 4 of 10

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe is equally approved of (48%) and disapproved of (48%) this quarter.

He’s been a relatively consistent presence in the top half of ARI’s premier rankings, but this quarter’s high ranking is more about other premiers’ decline than an especially high approval for Moe himself.

Still, as the longest tenured premier, Moe’s relative popularity for a provincial leader is remarkable considering the fall other leaders elected in 2018 – Ontario’s Doug Ford and Quebec’s François Legault .

Moe has waded into the trade war by levelling a retaliatory tariff on U.S. alcohol coming into the province, a notable change since Saskatchewan, alongside Alberta, were among the first to reverse U.S. alcohol bans last year. But it would seem the U.S. tariff issue is not a major factor for approval of Moe, who was among the premiers who did not receive a Trump bump in approval last March , at the previous peak of

Trump’s 51 st state rhetoric.

42% 46% 45% 47% 47% 47% 45% 46% 45% 46% 51% 46% 44% 46% 39% 38%

Approval of Alberta Premier Danielle Smith Page 5 of 10

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s perch at the top of the premier rankings is uncontested once again .Kinew is the only premier with majority approval and is a full 14 points clear of second place. Kinew has made a strong push on economic development, touting the potential benefits of year-round shipping at the Port of Churchill .

Meanwhile, Kinew’s government enacted a policy it says will help address the key issue of affordability: cutting the provincial sales tax on store-bought food on July 1 . Manitobans get tax relief on rotisserie chickens, chips, and baked goods, which were previously subject to a seven-per-cent tax.

Approval of Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe

57% 63% 66% 66% 67% 65% 68% 61% 58% 61% 62% 63%

Approval of Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew Page 6 of 10

The trade war between Canada and the United States has become a key platform for Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has perhaps been the premier most in the spotlight with his U.S. TV appearances and controversial ad. Ford, who has been nicknamed “ Captain Canada ”, was one of the biggest beneficiaries last March when many provincial leaders saw nationalism-fueled boost to their popularity.

The intensified hostilities between Canada and the U.S. on the trade front has coincided with another improvement for assessments of Ford, but not to the same extent as last year. Three-in-10 (31%) of

Ontarians approve of Ford’s performance, as he’s used colourful languag e in a literal war of words with

U.S. President Donald Trump, who is deeply unpopular among Canadians .

But two-thirds (64 %) of Ontarians say they disapprove of their premier’s performance . At issue is perhaps the lingering effects of spending scandals by Ford government MPPs. Twenty PC caucus members came under fire for expensing hotels during government sittings despite living nearby . The hotel scandal comes on the heels of a private plane kerfuffle earlier this year .

stories.title: Mississauga city council to vote on one-year data centre pause
stories.summary: It’s the latest Ontario city to weigh a moratorium as it studies possible guardrails on development
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mississauga city council is set to vote today on a one-year data centre moratorium.

The city is the latest in Ontario to consider a pause as it studies what guardrails it could place on energy-intensive data centres fuelling the artificial intelligence boom.

The proposed citywide moratorium would apply to data centres with energy demands over 10 megawatts.

It comes as Prologis, a major U.S.-headquartered firm, pursues a two-storey data centre in a business park in the city’s northwest.

Ontario proposes data-centre framework, including higher electricity rate for large projects

Opinion: How Canada can overcome the backlash against AI data centres

Under pressure from local lawmakers, the province last month released a draft framework that pledged new data centres would cover all their electricity costs and could be charged more than other industrial users.

Oakville last month became the first Ontario municipality to enact a pause after failed bids in Hamilton and Burlington.

The proposed citywide moratorium would apply to data centres with energy demands over 10 megawatts.
It comes as Prologis, a major U.S.-headquartered firm, pursues a two-storey data centre in a business park in the city’s northwest.
Ontario proposes data-centre framework, including higher electricity rate for large projects
Opinion: How Canada can overcome the backlash against AI data centres

Under pressure from local lawmakers, the province last month released a draft framework that pledged new data centres would cover all their electricity costs and could be charged more than other industrial users.
Oakville last month became the first Ontario municipality to enact a pause after failed bids in Hamilton and Burlington.

stories.title: A gentle paddle through Toronto’s new Don River mouth
stories.summary: My host, who canoed here last year when the riverbanks were still lined with piles of earth, is amazed at the transformation: ‘It all looks established’
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
It is the morning of Sept. 4. Local news outlets, including The Globe and Mail, are rife with frightening photographs of a flooded Don Valley Parkway, a partially collapsed Rogers Stadium and descriptions of “ping pong-sized hail with gusts up to 110 kilometres an hour.”

As architect Rick Galezowski of Great Lake Studio – a fitting name for this morning’s activity – prepares to hoist his 16-foot, Evergreen Prospector canoe over his head and portage it to the new, pebble-lined “Canoe Cove” in Biidaasige Park West, I silently curse Canada’s troubadour, Gordon Lightfoot, for his woeful account of that ill-fated ore freighter, the Edmund Fitzgerald, and my propensity to look up old newspaper articles.

“The gales of November can pile up mountainous waves,” Derik Hodgson wrote in The Globe on Nov. 12, 1975. “The ore carrier suddenly vanished from sight and radar … [and] although much debris has been found, the searchers failed to find any bodies or parts of the ship.” Thanks to Mr. Lightfoot’s song, we all know the rest of the story.

And despite the tree debris on the surface of Lake Ontario – which has turned brown due to last night’s churning – Mr. Galezowski assures me we won’t suffer the same fate. He’s consulted windy.com “all week” and he’s just returned from 16 days canoeing with his wife, architect Maggie Bennedsen, and their 12-year-old son, at Wabakimi Provincial Park (north of Thunder Bay), so he’s ready to take on anything Lake Ontario can throw at us.

However, in my mind, too much time in the wilderness can lead to Colonel Kurtz Syndrome; Mr. Galezowski is sporting an enormous vacation beard, and beards are good for hiding malevolent smiles.

We push out into the water. I am in the front seat (probably to prevent me from seeing Mr. Galezowski ruddering us into a freighter) and, after admiring the restored, 300-ton Atlas crane (installed in 1961), which Mr. Galezowski agrees is a “fantastic landmark,” I dip my oar into the water. While I haven’t been in a canoe for, perhaps, 20 years, I quickly find the rhythm. Before long, we are exiting the newly naturalized mouth of the Don River into open water (have you seen the 2003 movie of the same name? Thankfully there are no sharks here).

“One of the cool things about touring this area, particularly from the water,” he says, “is it’s such a weird mishmash of competing interests, of old stuff and new stuff, and things on the rise and things in decay.”

I agree, and add that I’m surprised at how far away the urban realm seems. One of Jerome Markson’s red-brick buildings of the St. Lawrence neighbourhood – a place that feels pretty far south – is way up there to the north, and looks pretty tiny.

The water is a little choppy as we paddle beside Polson Pier, so Mr. Galezowski steers us into the long, much calmer Ship Channel. As we pass a few sleeping – and tired-looking – pleasure boats and slip under the Cherry Street Strauss Trunnion Bascule Bridge (built in 1930, it has 750-ton concrete counterweights that allow it to raise), the architect lulls me into a false sense of security by allowing me to talk about my time as a failed rock star in the late 1980s and my current 1980s cover band. But, when I look up, I realize he’s positioned our little boat dangerously close to the enormous anchor of the McKeil Spirit (according to the McKeil site, it’s a “newly converted, shallow-draft pneumatic cement carrier” with four holds that combine for a 13,770 metric ton capacity).

“That anchor could kill us,” I stutter nervously as I look back to see Mr. Galezowski grinning under that beard.

Luckily, the lure of looking at landscape architect Claude Cormier’s Leslie Lookout Park overtakes my host, so we paddle away. After inspecting GH3’s lovely lookout tower – which mimics the silos nearby – we notice three painted ‘banners’ trumpeting Emma Robinson’s achievements on the concrete wall of the channel. Typing her into Google, I learn she is a medal-winning rower who won many world championships in the 1990s, as well as a silver during the 1996 Olympic Games in Atlanta and a bronze in Sydney in 2000. Did she practice here?

We paddle back to the mouth of the Don, but this time venture to where it begins to zig and zag. Mr. Galezowski, who canoed here last year when the riverbanks were still lined with piles of earth, is amazed at the transformation: “It all looks established,” he says as we glide past ducks and a father and son standing in a clearing, fishing lines dangling in the water.

“How did the city make it look so natural so quickly?” I wonder aloud.

New Toronto condo will feature porcelain tile handpicked in Italy

Women take the reins in family-friendly condo project

Arriving at the twin bridges of Commissioners Street, we pause for water and snacks. Talk, which has been rather philosophical so far, turns to politics. While mostly in agreement on Canada-U.S. relations, when talk turns to local politics, Mr. Galezowski warns that “canoes have been known to tip over,” so I immediately change the subject and ask him about Great Lake Studio.

“I’ve always got three or four projects on the go,” he says. “I’ve got a new build in Swansea that is about halfway through construction right now … and a wonderful client, which makes all the difference.” Is there a benevolent smile behind that beard? Was Rick Galezowski’s plan to rid this city of one of its architecture writers just a fiction in my head?

“Welcome to dry land,” he says after three hours on the water. My junior by only one year, Mr. Galezowski’s back and shoulders are fine, but, since mine are aching, he generously helps me out of the canoe.

“It was a fiction,” I think to myself as I wash my hands in the robot-voiced, self-cleaning bathroom.

But as he narrows his eyes, snarls and aggressively ratchets the straps to secure the canoe to his car’s roof-rack, I know I can’t be entirely sure.

My alter ego, Irma Girdle, drag queen/architecture expert, will be reading from my book, Hidden Toronto , at Book Bar (600 Markham St., Toronto) on Sunday, Sept. 27. For tickets, visit: bookbarto.CA/events .

stories.title: Wealthy family adviser Forthlane Partners acquires June Inc. to build $2-billion platform
stories.summary: Firms’ outsourced chief investment officer model provides independent financial advice to families that want personalized service without hiring a CIO
stories.author: Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Wealth manager Forthlane Partners Ltd. acquired rival June Inc. on Wednesday to scale up a platform that serves the country’s richest families.

Toronto-based Forthlane and June both offer a relatively new service to wealthy Canadians called outsourced chief investment officers or OCIOs. The concept is meant to help those who have made a fortune preserve that wealth with investment management approaches previously reserved for billionaires.

Led by former TD Securities head of investment banking Robbie Pryde, Forthlane will have more than $2-billion of assets under management now that founder June Ntazinda and her clients at June are in the fold.

Forthlane had $500-million of assets two years ago, when Mr. Pryde and Robert Vanderhooft, former chief investment officer at TD Asset Management, joined the firm.

Its clients typically have between $10-million and $1-billion in investable assets. They tend to be entrepreneurs and those with second-generation wealth. Mr. Pryde said these clients want to avoid market volatility and the risks that come with having their wealth tied up in a family business.

Forthlane has 28 employees after the June acquisition and the team often partners with advisers such as lawyers and accountants to oversee a family fortune.

June decided to join forces with Forthlane to give clients better access to the alternative asset managers, risk management expertise and sophisticated tax planning required by wealthy families, said Ms. Ntazinda in an interview.

“Forthlane gives clients access to the best managers in the world, something you can only achieve with scale,” said Ms. Ntazinda. She will be a partner and vice-chair of Forthlane, which has offices in Calgary and the Cayman Islands and plans to expand to Vancouver.

Ms. Ntazinda launched her company 12 years ago by purchasing a wealth management business she ran, called i3 Advisors Inc., from Ernst & Young.

Mr. Pryde said acquiring June “represents an important step in Forthlane’s growth and enhances our ability to serve ultra-high-net-worth families and foundations with increasingly complex investment needs.”

The white-glove services wealthy families receive from an outsourced chief investment officer include strategic asset allocation, global manager research and selection, and portfolio risk management. Mr. Vanderhooft said a typical client might have investments in eight funds, chosen to balance the risks of exposure to any one asset class.

Forthlane founders Ken Grewal, a former banker at UBS Securities, and Wayne Kozun, a former executive at the Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, launched the platform in 2018.

The Ocio concept has been around for several decades in the U.S. and Europe. In a recent study, consulting firm Cerulli Associates estimated American OCIOs will manage US$5.6-trillion by 2030, up from US$1-trillion in 2015.

The approach traces its roots to the role of chief investment officers who run the holdings of large family offices for those with more than $1-billion.

Last year, the federal Parliamentary Budget Office published a study showing the approximately 170,000 families in the top 1 per cent of the Canadian population by wealth had assets of at least $7.4-million each.

Forthlane and June did not disclose financial terms of the transaction.

Forthlane and June hired investment banks TD Securities Inc. and Origin Merchant Partners as financial advisers, along with law firms Wildeboer Dellelce LLP and Ccsb Law.

stories.title: Mississauga, Ont. council set to vote on temporary data centre moratorium
stories.summary: The city is the latest in Ontario to consider a pause as it studies what guardrails it could place on energy-intensive data centres fuelling the artificial intelligence boom.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Mississauga city council has voted unanimously to put a one-year freeze on new data centre projects.

The moratorium is framed as a chance for the city to study what guardrails to place around those projects as the artificial intelligence boom fuels demand for larger, more energy-intensive facilities.

Mississauga joins neighbouring Oakville, which last month passed the province’s first moratorium, as local lawmakers grapple with how to respond to the possible energy, water and noise concerns tied to the new wave of data centres.

The pause applies to data centres with energy demands over 10 megawatts, or enough electricity to power roughly 10,000 homes.

The vote appears to put in limbo a 40-megawatt data centre project in a business park in the city’s northwest pursued by Prologis, a major U.S.-headquartered firm.

In a statement, the company says it’s disappointed by the vote and was considering its next steps, but it remains committed to Mississauga.
