stories.title: EU wants Canada as its first ‘associate member,’ von der Leyen says
stories.summary: The two sides will move from Ceta to an Alliance for the Future, European Commission President Urusla von der Leyen said in her State of the Union address.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The European Union wants Canada as its first “associate member” and to “urgently reimagine” their relationship, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said during her annual State of the Union address in France on Wednesday.

“Dear Mark, I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen told Prime Minister Mark Carney , who was attending the speech.

“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well – thank you for being here,” she said.

“In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible,” she added.

Carney and von der Leyen met on Wednesday, after which Carney said in a statement he “welcomed” her proposal to move towards a “a far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future.”

Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU have already increased their volume of trade by 75 per cent in less than a decade since the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) was signed.

While the trade deal has been provisionally implemented, it isn’t yet fully ratified as some European Union member states still need to ratify the agreement in their individual legislatures.

Belgium, Bulgaria, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Poland and Slovenia are the states that haven’t yet ratified Ceta.

In Strasbourg to deepen Canada’s relationship with the EU. We see the benefits of a stronger partnership — to our economies, our security, and our mutual sovereignty. We’re working fast to forge it. pic.twitter.com/JFy9fMpcGx — Mark Carney (@MarkJCarney) September 16, 2026

The European Union and Canada would move from Ceta to an Alliance for the Future, von der Leyen said.

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project. We will work on energy, critical minerals and batteries. On AI, quantum, cyber and economic security,” von der Leyen said.

The talk of Canadian membership comes as the U.S. escalates its trade war against Canada and the U.S. escalates and as U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly asserted the Nato military alliance, of which Canada is a member, is not pulling its weight.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said.

Dear @MarkJCarney we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the EU. And create a common prosperity and economic security space. pic.twitter.com/GqIjGBz6aY — Ursula von der Leyen (@vonderleyen) September 16, 2026

However, it is unclear whether the proposal for including Canada as an “associate member,” a category that does not exist so far and would have to be specifically created for Canada, has wide support from EU member states.

A German government spokesperson told Reuters that while they support deeper integration with Canada, the term “associate member” should be “reconsidered.”

“Canada is a particularly close partner for Europe. That is why we are open to discussing new models of partnership,” the spokesperson said.

“But as for the terminology — the label attached to it — we ought to reconsider that,” they added.

Carney has previously said that Canada was “not looking” to gain EU membership but was working to develop a “unique alliance” with Brussels.

–With files from Reuters

stories.title: With tariff tit-for-tat, builders get the carpet pulled out from under them
stories.summary: Target of opportunity for retaliation against U.S. can be found beneath the feet of most Canadians living in apartment buildings
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
As Canada fights a trade war with the United States, one of the targets of opportunity for counter-tariff retaliation can be found under the feet of most Canadians living in apartment buildings, as well as many visiting hotels or working in offices: carpet.

While most of us walk all over carpet without noticing it, those who work with the stuff are having déjà vu from a year ago when U.S. President Donald Trump’s global tariff policy kicked off, and Canada released a raft of retaliatory tariffs targeted at politically sensitive states and companies.

Last time around, the tariffs May have been more bark than bite. Not so much this time.

“Nobody paid carpet tariffs the last time,” said John Margaritis, vice-president of sales and estimating with Armourco Solutions, a condominium refurbishing company that buys a lot of commercial carpet. He said that while carpets were listed among the tariffed goods by the federal Department of Finance, it was one of several imports that, so long as it was compliant with the free trade deal between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico, in most cases the extra taxes were not actually applied. “It slipped under the tariff code: Carpet that was produced in the U.S. in nylon that was extruded in the U.S., you were exempt under Cusma,” he said.

This time, there is no exemption under Cusma for the 25-per-cent tariff on these kinds of carpet. That means buyers are having to look to other international suppliers, since there are no domestic Canadian makers of the most in-demand high-grade broadloom commercial carpet.

Mike Moffatt: Canada should lower pointless tariffs on goods from countries other than the U.S.

Experts expect the tariffs on a variety of construction inputs will be another unwelcome headwind for the already downtrodden new-home building market.

“I would say that it’s going to have a pretty dampening effect on people wanting to build,” said Ben Haythornthwaite, director of Toronto-area market analytics for real estate data company CoStar Group. “To have such a huge sway of a potential 50 per cent on appliances, heat pumps. Heat pumps are massive things; it’s about $10,000 for one unit that might do 1,000 square feet. And you’re putting 50-per-cent tariff on? It’s not an extra couple hundred bucks. That’s the sort of money that stops people making decisions.”

Trade retaliation against carpet May seem random, but most of the carpet produced by the multibillion-dollar American flooring industry comes from one place: Georgia, a politically sensitive state that leans Republican but has swung to Democrats statewide in recent election cycles.

“I knew it was coming,” said Lisa Parise, who runs the Toronto-based design company Matter & Co. “As a carpet girl, I was like, here we go.” Ms. Parise’s company is now primed to fill the gap created by tariffs on carpeting, since two years ago she struck a deal to distribute carpeting from the French company Balsan, one of the few international brands that can compete with U.S. producers. Balsan was founded in 1751 and is now part of the global carpet and flooring giant Belgotex International.

At the time that she cut the deal with Balsan, Ms. Parise said, it was simply about having more options for her clients. Now it looks like prophetic foresight.

“We went to Europe out of necessity; it just so happened that Donald Trump decided to go insane,” she said. “We picked up a major American mill to complement our offering, and now nobody wants it. We’re trying our best to mitigate the losses.”

Ms. Parise used to work for one of the big Georgia companies, Interface Inc., and said that, just a few years ago, the Toronto market was one of the biggest for the carpet industry, representing close to $30-million a year in sales.

American carpeting is made using solution-dyed nylon, a process that keeps the colours from fading, and woven on Card-Monroe ColorPoint machines. That combination has become the gold standard in commercial carpeting, and Balsan was the only European supplier she could find that used the same technology and product.

“Ironically, the European prices were a little bit less, about 5 to 10 per cent less even factoring the euro. Now, with the tariff, we’re looking at huge, huge savings,” Ms. Parise said. Early in 2025, she received a similar flurry of interest from clients turned off by Mr. Trump’s 51st state rhetoric who were looking for non-U.S. options: “It wasn’t financial; it was a principles thing; they didn’t want to do it.”

When tariff fears waned in early 2025, many Canadian buyers went back to the well-established Georgia producers. Now, those U.S. companies are having mixed reactions about how to manage the tariff costs.

“There’s one project we had with a Shaw product, they hurried up and got it across the border in time,” said Mr. Margaritis, referring to Shaw Industries Group Inc., headquartered in Dalton, Ga. “I have another project where we’re shortlisted, so I reached out to my Shaw dealer; they are absorbing 5 per cent [of the existing 25-per-cent tariff].”

He’s proposing to the client that they each pay half of the remaining 20 per cent to keep the project on track. Still, it can be a big pill to swallow when a carpet order for updating hallways in a condominium building could cost $150,000 in material alone. As the trade war deadline approached, many of the U.S. companies took a “wait and see” approach to figuring out how to handle the extra costs, he said.

For example, another supplier is arguing with Mr. Margaritis about an order placed weeks ago that’s supposed to be delivered in October. “This dealer told me I couldn’t cancel, even though it hadn’t gone into production; I’m not sure what I’m going to do with that,” he said.

The smallest condos are being hit hardest by the market decline

Russ DeLozier, president of The Carpet and Rug Institute, the industry’s trade organization, pointed to the decades-long stability and predictability of supplies from Georgia and the U.S. in an e-mailed statement. “As new policies take effect, the industry will remain committed to ensuring Canadian consumers have access to the carpet products they need,” he said.

Ms. Parise recently booked a deal with a senior living facility for Balsan carpeting, and she’s relieved she won’t have to go back and tell them it might cost 25 per cent more. If she has one message to Canadian policy-makers it’s to make it easier to import from Europe. “Our stuff goes into customs hold all the time, versus bringing it in from Georgia,” she said. Still, delivery timelines are about the same: eight to 10 weeks from order time. Despite it all, she bears no ill will toward her American suppliers.

“I would love it to be over; we love our American factories,” she said. “We hope the tariffs die because our customers are suffering and so are our friends across the border.”

However, Mr. Haythornthwaite argues that if certainty of supply is the goal for businesses looking to import goods, it’s long past time to consider diversifying from U.S. suppliers.

“Look at who you’re dealing with: Knowing what’s coming around the corner is not what we’ve been used to for the last couple of years,” he said.

While most of us walk all over carpet without noticing it, those who work with the stuff are having déjà vu from a year ago when U.S. President Donald Trump’s global tariff policy kicked off, and Canada released a raft of retaliatory tariffs targeted at politically sensitive states and companies.
Last time around, the tariffs May have been more bark than bite. Not so much this time.

“Nobody paid carpet tariffs the last time,” said John Margaritis, vice-president of sales and estimating with Armourco Solutions, a condominium refurbishing company that buys a lot of commercial carpet. He said that while carpets were listed among the tariffed goods by the federal Department of Finance, it was one of several imports that, so long as it was compliant with the free trade deal between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico, in most cases the extra taxes were not actually applied. “It slipped under the tariff code: Carpet that was produced in the U.S. in nylon that was extruded in the U.S., you were exempt under Cusma,” he said.

This time, there is no exemption under Cusma for the 25-per-cent tariff on these kinds of carpet. That means buyers are having to look to other international suppliers, since there are no domestic Canadian makers of the most in-demand high-grade broadloom commercial carpet.
Mike Moffatt: Canada should lower pointless tariffs on goods from countries other than the U.S.
Experts expect the tariffs on a variety of construction inputs will be another unwelcome headwind for the already downtrodden new-home building market.

“I would say that it’s going to have a pretty dampening effect on people wanting to build,” said Ben Haythornthwaite, director of Toronto-area market analytics for real estate data company CoStar Group. “To have such a huge sway of a potential 50 per cent on appliances, heat pumps. Heat pumps are massive things; it’s about $10,000 for one unit that might do 1,000 square feet. And you’re putting 50-per-cent tariff on? It’s not an extra couple hundred bucks. That’s the sort of money that stops people making decisions.”

Trade retaliation against carpet May seem random, but most of the carpet produced by the multibillion-dollar American flooring industry comes from one place: Georgia, a politically sensitive state that leans Republican but has swung to Democrats statewide in recent election cycles.

“I knew it was coming,” said Lisa Parise, who runs the Toronto-based design company Matter & Co. “As a carpet girl, I was like, here we go.” Ms. Parise’s company is now primed to fill the gap created by tariffs on carpeting, since two years ago she struck a deal to distribute carpeting from the French company Balsan, one of the few international brands that can compete with U.S. producers. Balsan was founded in 1751 and is now part of the global carpet and flooring giant Belgotex International.

content_blocks.caption: Matter & Co is Toronto's sole importer of European carpets. Ms. Parise works with operations manager Luke Forhan, top, and fellow founder Jordan Molson. Nic Hotchkiss/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: At the time that she cut the deal with Balsan, Ms. Parise said, it was simply about having more options for her clients. Now it looks like prophetic foresight.

“We went to Europe out of necessity; it just so happened that Donald Trump decided to go insane,” she said. “We picked up a major American mill to complement our offering, and now nobody wants it. We’re trying our best to mitigate the losses.”

Ms. Parise used to work for one of the big Georgia companies, Interface Inc., and said that, just a few years ago, the Toronto market was one of the biggest for the carpet industry, representing close to $30-million a year in sales.

American carpeting is made using solution-dyed nylon, a process that keeps the colours from fading, and woven on Card-Monroe ColorPoint machines. That combination has become the gold standard in commercial carpeting, and Balsan was the only European supplier she could find that used the same technology and product.

“Ironically, the European prices were a little bit less, about 5 to 10 per cent less even factoring the euro. Now, with the tariff, we’re looking at huge, huge savings,” Ms. Parise said. Early in 2025, she received a similar flurry of interest from clients turned off by Mr. Trump’s 51st state rhetoric who were looking for non-U.S. options: “It wasn’t financial; it was a principles thing; they didn’t want to do it.”

content_blocks.caption: The Matter & Co. team workshop project palettes on the floor of their Toronto showroom. Nic Hotchkiss/The Globe and Mail

content_blocks.text: When tariff fears waned in early 2025, many Canadian buyers went back to the well-established Georgia producers. Now, those U.S. companies are having mixed reactions about how to manage the tariff costs.

“There’s one project we had with a Shaw product, they hurried up and got it across the border in time,” said Mr. Margaritis, referring to Shaw Industries Group Inc., headquartered in Dalton, Ga. “I have another project where we’re shortlisted, so I reached out to my Shaw dealer; they are absorbing 5 per cent [of the existing 25-per-cent tariff].”

He’s proposing to the client that they each pay half of the remaining 20 per cent to keep the project on track. Still, it can be a big pill to swallow when a carpet order for updating hallways in a condominium building could cost $150,000 in material alone. As the trade war deadline approached, many of the U.S. companies took a “wait and see” approach to figuring out how to handle the extra costs, he said.

For example, another supplier is arguing with Mr. Margaritis about an order placed weeks ago that’s supposed to be delivered in October. “This dealer told me I couldn’t cancel, even though it hadn’t gone into production; I’m not sure what I’m going to do with that,” he said.
The smallest condos are being hit hardest by the market decline

Russ DeLozier, president of The Carpet and Rug Institute, the industry’s trade organization, pointed to the decades-long stability and predictability of supplies from Georgia and the U.S. in an e-mailed statement. “As new policies take effect, the industry will remain committed to ensuring Canadian consumers have access to the carpet products they need,” he said.

Ms. Parise recently booked a deal with a senior living facility for Balsan carpeting, and she’s relieved she won’t have to go back and tell them it might cost 25 per cent more. If she has one message to Canadian policy-makers it’s to make it easier to import from Europe. “Our stuff goes into customs hold all the time, versus bringing it in from Georgia,” she said. Still, delivery timelines are about the same: eight to 10 weeks from order time. Despite it all, she bears no ill will toward her American suppliers.
“I would love it to be over; we love our American factories,” she said. “We hope the tariffs die because our customers are suffering and so are our friends across the border.”
However, Mr. Haythornthwaite argues that if certainty of supply is the goal for businesses looking to import goods, it’s long past time to consider diversifying from U.S. suppliers.
“Look at who you’re dealing with: Knowing what’s coming around the corner is not what we’ve been used to for the last couple of years,” he said.

stories.title: Trade tensions likely to hold back aspiring home buyers this fall
stories.summary: Market slowdown likely caused by uncertainty surrounding the Canada-U.S. trade war
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Real estate buyers, sellers and market watchers in Toronto and cities across Canada are entering the key fall selling season with trepidation as trade tensions linger in the background.

Daren King, senior economist at National Bank of Canada, remains hopeful that Canada and the United States will reach a deal that ends trade war turbulence.

If so, the economic uncertainty May turn out to be a short-term phenomenon, Mr. King said in an interview.

In the meantime, the disruption is a major headwind likely to hold back aspiring home buyers across the country in September.

In August, sales across Canada decreased 0.7 per cent from July on a seasonally adjusted basis, data from the Canadian Real Estate Association show.

New listings surged 3.3 per cent in the same period.

Mr. King notes there is a very strong correlation between consumer confidence and the home resale market in Canada.

Many consumers are likely wondering about the prospects for the economy in general and their own job security, he notes.

“The situation is very fluid.”

He won’t be surprised to see real estate sales in the Greater Toronto Area and many cities remain flat or decline in September after a lacklustre August.

What the trade war and U.S. policy mean for Canadian mortgage rates

Sales in the Vancouver area rose in August compared with July, but the cooling in the GTA and Calgary offset that rise, notes National Bank senior economist Alexandra Ducharme.

Sales in Vancouver and the GTA remain well below their long-term averages, Ms. Ducharme points out.

Sales in the GTA in August slipped 0.3 per cent from July on a seasonally-adjusted basis, according to Crea.

Although it is not uncommon for the market to take a breather after a string of gains, Mr. King says, he does not believe the decline in August represents a temporary blip.

Realtors hoping for a rebound get side-swiped by trade war

The slowdown was likely caused by the uncertainty surrounding trade, which intensified during the month.

Meanwhile, some of the potential buyers still waiting to purchase a first home or trade up to a more desirable one are fretting about the strength of the economy, the health of the labour market and the direction of interest rates.

Mr. King sees no rush for the Bank of Canada to raise its benchmark rate, despite policy-makers’ concerns about an upside risk to inflation. A prolonged trade war might even justify a decline in short-term interest rates, he says.

“We’ll have to see where all this is going.”

The dynamic at the long end of the curve is a different story.

Like many financial market mavens, Mr. King is keeping an eye on the rise in long-term bond yields in the United States.

Spiking oil prices recently pushed the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield above the psychologically important threshold of five per cent.

At the same time, the burgeoning U.S. government deficit is spooking investors and raising questions about fiscal sustainability.

The massive play on AI has technology companies issuing huge amounts of debt, creating lots of crowding in the bond market, he points out.

“Everything is pushing interest rates higher,” Mr. King says, adding that the trends will create significant headwinds for housing in the medium term.

For now the impact remains limited, he says.

On the front lines of trade war, cities begin to reckon with its financial toll

Climbing U.S. Treasury yields influence borrowing costs in this country, including those for fixed-term mortgages and consumer debt.

While he watches those forces, Mr. King notes that housing affordability has been improving in Canada with the decline in prices in many markets.

The second quarter of 2026 brought a tenth consecutive quarterly gain in affordability, which marks the longest streak on record in this country.

In Toronto, that trend could tempt some of the plentiful home buyers who remain on the sidelines, Mr. King notes.

“There are people who want to jump into that market,” the economist says.

The tariff situation can change overnight, he notes, and hesitant home buyers are likely to perk up if a deal comes together.

“If there is negotiation, we have seen it can go pretty fast.”

“It’s the same story we’ve seen in a loop – for the past two years – every time the trade discussion starts up.”

Tariffs on U.S. homebuilding materials will raise costs, industry warns

So far in September, buyers do not appear to be in any rush in Toronto, says Dino Capocci, real estate agent at Royal LePage Real Estate Services.

On one recent day, for example, he counted 100 new listings for detached houses in midtown Toronto on the Multiple Listing Service of the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board.

The same day, nine sales were recorded.

“I am seeing a lot more listings than I am sales,” says Mr. Capocci.

Mr. Capocci says properties are changing hands, but the pace is sluggish.

“There are sales out there. It’s not dire.”

Mr. Capocci listed a two-bedroom row house in Cabbagetown in August, figuring he would get a jump on the fall market.

The house at 7 Bowman St. is listed with an asking price of $1.895-million, which is slightly below the price the homeowner paid before the top-to-bottom renovation.

“Even at that, I’m not feeling the love,” says Mr. Capocci. “August was definitely slower than expected.”

In August, sales in the GTA dipped 2.1 per cent compared with the same month last year, while new listings fell a sharp 14.1 per cent in the same period.

Active listings dropped 11.3 per cent last month from August, 2025.

Mr. Capocci believes many sellers who put properties up for sale in the spring and failed to sell pulled their listings last month. Some of the September bump is likely coming from relistings, he says.

The condo segment remains bleak, in Mr. Capocci’s view.

At mid-September, he trimmed the price for a renovated unit at the Lonsdale at 619 Avenue Rd. to $1.479-million.

“With condos, it’s a constant adjustment,” he says of the price reductions.

Mr. Capocci recently talked with an agent who listed a condo in the hard loft conversion at 90 Sumach St.

The owner paid $1.2-million a couple of years ago, Mr. Capocci says, and the unit was listed with an asking price of $998,000.

He learned that the seller was hoping for a higher price but now the lender is moving to sell the property under the process known as “power of sale.”

“The “power of sale has started,” he says. “The bank is going to take over.”

The single-family market is brisk in some brackets, he adds.

Houses do sell with multiples offers, he notes, but they tend to be in most sought-after neighbourhoods in the popular price range around $1.5-million.

The buyers are rarely investors or builders, he says, but “end users” who plan to live in the home.

Those who do enter bidding contests are careful to stick to a budget, he adds.

“They are not losing their minds any more. We’re seeing a lot more restraint with buyers. There’s not that fear of missing out.”

Mr. Capocci says most sellers he has spoken with who decided to list this fall intend to stick with their plan.

Many realize that a rebound in prices is not likely to happen soon.

He points to the example of a Deer Park house he estimated would sell for about $2.2-million when the sellers called on him to evaluate the property just over three years ago.

Now he plans to bring the property out in a few weeks with an asking price of $1.7-million.

“If you’re postponing because of price, I would strongly suggest against that,” Mr. Capocci says. “There’s no certainty in putting it on hold.”

stories.title: Outbid buyers on Mississauga home called back to forge a deal
stories.summary: Buyers get a second chance and finalize deal for $1,331,000
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
431 Naomi Cres., Mississauga

Asking price: $1,425,000 (May, 2026)

Previous asking prices: $1,449,000 (April, 2026); $1,485,000 (March, 2026); $1,499,000 (September, 2025)

Selling price: $1,331,000 (June, 2026)

Previous selling price: $350,000 (June, 1989)

Taxes: $10,535 (2025)

Days on the market: 27

Property days on market: 169

Buyers’ agent: Pradip Nag, Right at Home Realty

This spring, a homeowning couple looking for a larger property combed through 40 to 50 detached houses with three bedrooms and three bathrooms, primarily in a community south of Square One mall in Mississauga, Ont. One of their favourite homes was this four-bedroom house, listed for $1,449,000 when they first saw it, and reduced to $1.425-million the next month. As they were compiling their offer, another buyer submitted their own offer, which the seller quickly accepted.

“I showed them this property four times because they were not sure if they should go with it or not,” said the buyers’ agent Pradip Nag.

“It was bad luck another offer came in.”

Fortunately for Mr. Nag’s clients, their rivals failed to waive a condition on their offer, giving them a second chance. Satisfied by their inspection of the 37-year-old home, they finalized a deal for $1,331,000.

“They really liked this one, especially since it was in their budget,” Mr. Nag said.

“The schools are also good in that area.”

This two-storey house has four bedrooms upstairs, three bathrooms and a laundry room with access to the double garage.

The main floor has an office, a dining area and two entertaining areas, including one with a fireplace and an exit to a two-tiered deck.

stories.title: Q+A: Rapper Shad on being Museum London's first musician-in-residence
stories.summary: London-born rapper Shad will be Museum London’s first musician-in-residence this fall.
stories.author: Allison Young
stories.content:
London-born rapper Shad is set to become Museum London’s first musician-in-residence this fall. Officials say the year-long post will explore themes of memory, storytelling and belonging through performances, public programs, educational initiatives and collaborations with local artists. The 44-year-old spoke with LFP reporter Allison Young.

Q: What was it like growing up in London and where did you first become interested in making music?

A: “I went to École Frère-André, that was elementary school, and then Monseigneur-Bruyère. I was in the French system. Then I went to Central for high school. At the time the French public high school that is now Gabriel-Dumont was inside of Central. So, that brought me over there. When I was in high school, I was just freestyling with friends. It wasn’t anything too serious. I also learned how to play guitar in high school, but it wasn’t something I really imagined myself doing at all for a career. It just didn’t seem possible. I had no idea how someone would even go about that. (In the) mid-2000s, a world of independent music opened up because it became more feasible for ordinary people to record and play shows and there’s just an exciting scene sort of around independent music and the internet obviously starting to open up possibilities as well. When I was away at school at Laurier (University) was when I started to make a bit more music with friends from London, guys I used to rap with in high school, we had a group. Also while I was away at school was when I recorded my first album. . . . There was a radio station called 91.5 that was based in Kitchener, but it broadcast down to London as well . . . and they had an unsung talent competition and the winners got money to record an album. That gave me the opportunity to record and was also an encouragement as well, probably the first time people that weren’t my family or friends were telling me that I was good. When I graduated, I came back to London for a couple of years and that was when I was getting my career started.”

Q: Were there any London musicians who inspired you when you were starting out, or who you worked with and looked up to at the time?

A: “This would be around the mid-2000s, when I moved back to London after school. There was a fun scene. A lot of other independent artists, hip hop and outside of hip hop. In terms of artists, the first that comes to mind is Matthew Johnson, who’s one of my best friends. He was doing his solo stuff at that time and also playing drums for me. We would watch each other play at the Embassy and there were other rappers, but it was also punk and different genres because the scene wasn’t that big, but there was excitement because people were making things and people were playing shows.”

Q: You’ve taken on so many different opportunities throughout your career, including hosting CBC’s Q and the documentary television series Hip-Hop Evolution. Now you are taking on this residency. What draws you to these different roles and makes you put yourself out there in different ways?

A: “As a general rule, if someone says ‘do you want to do this cool thing?’ I just say ‘yes,’ because I think from the very beginning this journey of putting more time and energy into music, part of the goals for me was to have interesting experiences. That’s always been one of the goals because success, so to speak, is not guaranteed and to a great extent is outside of my control. What I can really try to do is have fun experiences, do different things. I think on some level, I’m also just a curious person and I like to try different things. I’ve never really been someone who, for better or worse, only wants to do music. Music is the core of what I do and it’s my best way of explaining who I am at different points in time, but I also get curious and I get a bit restless and when opportunities present themselves at the right time, I’m keen to say yes.”

Q: This residency is new for both you and Museum London. How did the opportunity come about, and what was it like being chosen as the museum’s first musician-in-residence?

A: “The Museum approached me with the idea and again, as a general rule, when someone says, you want to do something cool, I say ‘yes,’ but we did have a lot of conversations before I said ‘yes,’ because I really wanted to get a sense of what might be involved and to try to be a little bit confident that I could fulfill the responsibilities. I love the opportunity to make new stuff and be inspired by my own history and regional histories. That’s cool from a creative standpoint, but also at this point, I really am interested in education and mentorship. Also the challenge of doing something new, like visual arts, I’ll be helping to curate the atrium wall at a certain point and that’s entirely new for me. . . . It just lines up with where I’m at and also the opportunity to look back a little bit. I’ve been putting out music for 20 years now and I don’t want to be sentimental and nostalgic about that, but I kind of am. This is an opportunity to indulge that little bit. Be reflective about my history in London, my own career and what I’ve been trying to say for the last 20 years. It allows the space to do that.”

Q:What can people expect from this year-long residency?

A: “It is an interesting idea that they had to bring a musician into the museum because it is primarily a visual art space as well as a historical space. There’s a few things that we’re going to do. I’m going to create some new music, obviously. There’s some educational components. I’ll be doing something with student groups or youth groups. There’s the atrium wall. That will be visual arts and history-heavy, curating something for that big atrium wall space. There will be speaking events, There’ll be performances. I feel a bit of pressure because as the first person to do this program, I really want to do well so that there can be a lot more in the future.”

Q: You’re returning to London for the residency, and many younger and aspiring artists will be encountering your work, possibly for the first time. What does it mean to come back to the city where you started? What do you hope to share with the next generation?

A: “One thing at this point in my life and career that I’m passionate about is the next generation of artists. I remember quite vividly being 20, 21, 22 and just starting. All of the feelings that come with that, the excitement, but also the fear and the nerves and I’ve just become more and more passionate about speaking into that stage and helping younger artists feel like it’s possible. Not necessarily to make a career, it’s not guaranteed and you don’t control that, but you can make things. I really believe that and I want people to feel inspired and encouraged around the idea that you can make things. The outcome you don’t control, but you can make things. You can participate in the thing that you love. I’m really excited to just share that and hopefully pass on that encouragement and the inspiration that I got when I was at that age. That’s a big part of what this is for me.”

stories.title: Why the U.S. still needs Canadian lumber
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the impact of tariffs on Canada's lumber sector and what Canada can do to better support its wood business.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Lumber awaiting shipment is seen stacked at the Gorman Brothers Lumber sawmill, in West Kelowna, B.C., ON Tuesday, August 5, 2025. THE Canadian Press/Darryl Dyck

By Analysis by The Big Story podcast

Posted September 16, 2026 7:18 am.

Among the steel, aluminum, and auto sectors, Canada’s softwood lumber industry has also fallen victim to U.S. tariffs. But levies on Canadian lumber are nothing new, and neither are tensions between the two countries surrounding lumber exports.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Russ Taylor, a global wood business and market consultant, about the impact of tariffs on Canada’s lumber sector, how the industry has long been a point of tension between our two nations, and what Canada can do to better support its wood business.

stories.title: Canadians signing up to be deliberately infected with flu virus to aid vaccine research
stories.summary: In a Canadian first, scientists are exposing healthy volunteers to influenza to speed vaccine research in preparation for the next pandemic.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Canada

In a Canadian first, scientists are exposing healthy volunteers to influenza to speed vaccine research in preparation for the next pandemic

Last updated 23 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/canadians-flu-virus-vaccine-research#comments-area)

"It is a little bit on the edge to be working with these volunteers and trying to do good science and make sure we aren't doing any harm," said McGill University's Dr. Brian Ward, who is co-principal investigator of the influenza challenge study.Photo by Handout/McGill University Health Centre

Canadian scientists are purposely spraying an influenza virus into the noses of human volunteers, joining other nations in controlled human infection studies that, while speeding vaccine development in preparation for future pandemics, have also raised ethical uneasiness.

The experiment, one of the first of its kind in Canada, involves exposing consenting adults to a dose of a seasonal influenza virus, monitoring their symptoms and immune responses, administering antiviral drugs if necessary and keeping volunteers in special isolation “pods” for at least a week until they test negative.

The trials are designed to give researchers a better picture of how a pathogen behaves inside the human body to help fine-tune existing drugs or vaccines or develop new ones.

The experiments have a long history in other parts of the world, used for decades to test potential treatments or vaccines for diseases like influence and malaria.

In 2020, when COVID was spreading rapidly, British scientists led COVID-19 human challenge trials, injecting young, healthy adults with candidate vaccines and then infecting them with Sars-CoV-2 when no proven treatments against COVID existed, raising ethical concerns over “the twin risks of exploitation and coercion.” Volunteers were paid the equivalent of C$6,500 for agreeing to be infected with COVID and then quarantined.

In Canada, Liberal MP Marcus Powlowski, a former emergency room doctor, presented a petition to Parliament, signed by several Canadian infectious diseases experts, calling on the government to announce a plan for similar COVID-19 challenge trials. The government responded that doing so would be particularly risky, given the limited treatments and unknown long-term effects of a potentially “severe and deadly” virus.

“Because Sars-CoV-2 was really new — we were discovering its biology and side effects in real time — I think there was a very reasonable hesitation on the part of many virologists, myself included, to the idea we should start using it as a challenge strain,” said Dr. Brian Ward, co-principal investigator of the influenza challenge study.

In normal vaccine studies, volunteers are vaccinated or injected with a placebo, and then sent back out into the real world to see how many get naturally exposed to the circulating virus, an approach that’s lengthy and pricey, said Ward, director of the Muhc (McGill University Health Centre) Vaccine Study Centre.

By contrast, controlled human infection studies take fewer volunteers and far less time because they don’t rely on natural infections.

But Canada doesn’t normally run them. Ward and his co-investigator, Dalhousie University’s Scott Halperin, spent two decades on the background work getting them off the ground. Halperin recently led a controlled human infection study using Bordetella pertussis, the bacterium that causes whooping cough.

Canada first needed special isolation units, the challenge viruses and the expertise. “And then you have to convince everyone around you this is OK to do,” Ward said. “Each of those steps took a lot of time.”

The new project, in collaboration with the Canadian Center for Vaccinology at Dalhousie, began in June with the first eight volunteers in Halifax; two more participants have now started the study in Montreal. The research will eventually involve 32 people, 16 at each site, all healthy adults ages 18 to 45 who have no known risk factors for severe influenza, a disease that contributes to an estimated 3,500 deaths in Canada each year.

Researchers are using an attenuated, or weakened H3N2 virus that’s diluted in glucose and saline and sprayed into the nose as an aerosol. Volunteers are being intensively studied “from the moment that we infect them,” Ward said. H3N2 is a subtype of influenza A. Influenza A viruses are on the short list of viruses that can cause global pandemics, Ward said.

Half the volunteers are getting a low dose; the other half, a higher one. One out of every group of four is getting a saline placebo. At the higher dose, it’s expected 60 to 70 per cent will end up with mild to moderate symptoms.

All remain isolated for a minimum seven days in specially designed negative-pressure rooms that keep potentially contaminated air or other particles inside the room from circulating outside the room.

People are monitored 24/7 by one or two nurses and undergo regular blood tests and nasal swabs. Ward is on call 24-hours a day. “If these people show any signs of getting into trouble, we will be on top of it immediately and start antivirals,” he said.

The experiments will help better understand how the human body responds, even within the first few hours, to influenza, a “slippery family of viruses” that, unlike measles, “mutate like crazy,” Ward said.

“One of the big problems with understanding how our human body responds to any pathogen is that it’s awfully difficult to know when somebody got infected,” Ward said.

Some volunteers exposed to flu won’t show any symptoms at all. “What did their bodies do right that shut down that possible infection before it started,” Ward said. “We May find early biomarkers of a successful response.”

The team isn’t testing a vaccine this round but hope to create a model for future vaccine challenge trials, Ward said. “How do you recruit people to do this kind of study? How do you convince your research ethics board this is an OK thing to do?”

In the event of a deadly influenza pandemic, for example, “two, three, 10, 20 different vaccines” could be tested in a challenge trial to determine which offer the most by way of individual protection and reducing community transmission, Ward said.

In the influenza infection study, “You have to have a very frank conversations with the volunteers,” Ward said. “Because every now and then — extremely rarely, but every now and then — a healthy individual gets flu and ends up in the intensive care unit, because their body happens to react over-strenuously to that particular viral challenge.”

Ten per cent of the adult world gets infected every year with influenza. “It’s not like we’re doing something that is unlikely to ever happen to you otherwise,” Ward said, but added that “we do everything we can do to mitigate” risks.

While Ward said he’s excited the trials are happening, “I wouldn’t be honest if I didn’t say I was also really nervous.

“It is a little bit on the edge to be working with these volunteers and trying to do good science and make sure we aren’t doing any harm.”

Volunteers are being remunerated commensurate for giving up seven to 10 days of their lives, Ward said, though he declined to give exact amounts.

The work is being funded through a pandemic-preparedness grant from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research.

stories.title: 'Our neighbours, our friends': 8 U.S. celebrities who've thrown support behind Canada
stories.summary: The relationship between Canada and the U.S. continues to sour, and some American celebrities have thrown their support north of the border.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Amid tariffs , social media jibes and the renaming of lakes , the relationship between Canada and the U.S. continues to sour, with some public figures on both sides of the border expressing their support for Canadians.

Most recently, American actress Sally Field spoke out during the Emmy Awards on Monday night, saying, “Blessed Canada, our neighbours, our friends,” during her acceptance speech for best actress in a limited or anthology series or TV movie. She received the award for her role in the Netflix drama Remarkably Bright Creatures, which was filmed in Vancouver.

But while several Canadian celebrities have been vocal in their patriotism since the beginning of the trade war, such as rock band Blue Rodeo, who denounced Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario at their recent Toronto concert, fewer American celebrities have voiced their support for their Canadian neighbours.

And yet, Sally Field is not alone in her sentiment.

Trump and the current U.S. administration are frequently the butt of the joke for American late-night show hosts, but perhaps none have been as supportive of Canada as Seth Meyers, who said in a segment of his show in May 2025: “Congrats, Donald. You turned the most polite country on Earth into an enemy.”

Later on in the tongue-in-cheek segment, which focused on the first meeting between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump, Meyers said: “Let’s recap this very normal meeting with our closest ally and trading partner. Trump said he was imposing tariffs on Canada in order to negotiate a better trade deal, even though (he said) ‘we don’t do business with Canada.’ And the only concession he wants is ‘friendship’. But it doesn’t matter if they negotiate because he won’t lift the tariffs anyway. And when asked why not, he said ‘that’s just the way it is.'”

On a more serious note, he added that the Trump administration’s suggestion that Canada “has been feeding off the U.S.” is “insane.” He added: “They are close partners of ours. We buy stuff from them, they buy stuff from us and, in the process, our people cooperate and our nations come together.”

In more recent episodes of his show, Meyers called Trump’s trade war with Canada “one-sided lunacy” and criticized the renaming of Lake Ontario .

Among the other well-known TV hosts who have poked fun at Trump’s trade war with Canada is Jimmy Kimmel, who mocked Trump’s “51st state” remarks around the same time as Meyers, and praised Carney’s approach in the meeting.

“He handled it very well,” Kimmel said of the prime minister. “And in a friendly way he made sure Trump knows they have no intention of becoming our 51st state.”

Jimmy Kimmel is also the honorary mayor of the Canadian town of Dildo, in Newfoundland and Labrador, after he began to feature it repeatedly on his show in 2019 due to its eye-catching name.

The town threw their support behind Kimmel when his show was temporarily cancelled last year after comments he made about the murder of right-wing political activist Charlie Kirk.

“Jimmy Kimmel’s got a fallback job, h e can always come here and be our mayor,” one resident told CBC at the time.

Meanwhile, American rapper and singer Jelly Roll joined Jimmy Kimmel Live! as a guest host last month. He took the opportunity to criticize Trump’s latest tariff threats against Canada, as well as the renaming of Lake Ontario.

“I hate to break it to the president, but we don’t have a problem with Canada, you have a problem with Canada,” he said to loud cheers from the audience.

He also said on the show: “You can’t make the Great Lakes great again, they’re already great, it’s in the f—ing name!” referencing Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan.

In an interview with CBC on the red carpet of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff) opening weekend, American actor Ed Helms, best known for his roles in NBC sitcom The Office and The Hangover trilogy, threw his support behind the Canadian film scene.

“This is an incredible film community and I’m super proud to be part of it,” he said.

Helms stars in a new film titled The Stunt Driver, which premiered at Tiff on Thursday and follows the story of a Canadian stuntman.

“The reason I’m in these projects is because they’re incredible stories and they happen to be Canadian stories,” he said, adding, “the crews that I worked on in Edmonton and Montreal were just the best.”

Also speaking to CBC at Tiff, Sarah Paulson, who stars in the movie Closing Night, which premiered on Saturday, said “I love Canada.”

Responding to a question asked by a reporter on the red carpet, she added: “I love Canada more and more every day,” while looking down the lens of the camera.

Paulson is best known for her roles in the TV shows American Horror Story, All’s Fair and Ratched, among others, and also starred in the films Ocean’s 8 and Birdbox.

Closing Night was filmed in Montreal.

Ex-NFL star Jason Kelce previously insulted Canada in an episode of his podcast, New Heights, which he hosts with brother Travis Kelce. But, making up for his comments, he said in a social media apology: “I love Canada.”

Speaking about the 2025 World Series between the Toronto Blue Jays and the Los Angeles Dodgers, he said on the podcast: “You’re telling me I’m supposed to get excited about a Canadian baseball team and a team that spends more money than everybody else? Who the fuck cares about either?”

His comments were met with criticism, particularly from Canadians, leading him to share an apology outlining several things he “loves” about Canada.

paragraphs: Amid tariffs , social media jibes and the renaming of lakes , the relationship between Canada and the U.S. continues to sour, with some public figures on both sides of the border expressing their support for Canadians.

Most recently, American actress Sally Field spoke out during the Emmy Awards on Monday night, saying, “Blessed Canada, our neighbours, our friends,” during her acceptance speech for best actress in a limited or anthology series or TV movie. She received the award for her role in the Netflix drama Remarkably Bright Creatures, which was filmed in Vancouver.

But while several Canadian celebrities have been vocal in their patriotism since the beginning of the trade war, such as rock band Blue Rodeo, who denounced Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario at their recent Toronto concert, fewer American celebrities have voiced their support for their Canadian neighbours.
And yet, Sally Field is not alone in her sentiment.

Trump and the current U.S. administration are frequently the butt of the joke for American late-night show hosts, but perhaps none have been as supportive of Canada as Seth Meyers, who said in a segment of his show in May 2025: “Congrats, Donald. You turned the most polite country on Earth into an enemy.”

Later on in the tongue-in-cheek segment, which focused on the first meeting between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump, Meyers said: “Let’s recap this very normal meeting with our closest ally and trading partner. Trump said he was imposing tariffs on Canada in order to negotiate a better trade deal, even though (he said) ‘we don’t do business with Canada.’ And the only concession he wants is ‘friendship’. But it doesn’t matter if they negotiate because he won’t lift the tariffs anyway. And when asked why not, he said ‘that’s just the way it is.'”

On a more serious note, he added that the Trump administration’s suggestion that Canada “has been feeding off the U.S.” is “insane.” He added: “They are close partners of ours. We buy stuff from them, they buy stuff from us and, in the process, our people cooperate and our nations come together.”
In more recent episodes of his show, Meyers called Trump’s trade war with Canada “one-sided lunacy” and criticized the renaming of Lake Ontario .

Among the other well-known TV hosts who have poked fun at Trump’s trade war with Canada is Jimmy Kimmel, who mocked Trump’s “51st state” remarks around the same time as Meyers, and praised Carney’s approach in the meeting.
“He handled it very well,” Kimmel said of the prime minister. “And in a friendly way he made sure Trump knows they have no intention of becoming our 51st state.”
Jimmy Kimmel is also the honorary mayor of the Canadian town of Dildo, in Newfoundland and Labrador, after he began to feature it repeatedly on his show in 2019 due to its eye-catching name.
The town threw their support behind Kimmel when his show was temporarily cancelled last year after comments he made about the murder of right-wing political activist Charlie Kirk.
“Jimmy Kimmel’s got a fallback job, h e can always come here and be our mayor,” one resident told CBC at the time.

Meanwhile, American rapper and singer Jelly Roll joined Jimmy Kimmel Live! as a guest host last month. He took the opportunity to criticize Trump’s latest tariff threats against Canada, as well as the renaming of Lake Ontario.
“I hate to break it to the president, but we don’t have a problem with Canada, you have a problem with Canada,” he said to loud cheers from the audience.
He also said on the show: “You can’t make the Great Lakes great again, they’re already great, it’s in the f—ing name!” referencing Trump’s “Make America Great Again” slogan.

In an interview with CBC on the red carpet of the 2026 Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff) opening weekend, American actor Ed Helms, best known for his roles in NBC sitcom The Office and The Hangover trilogy, threw his support behind the Canadian film scene.
“This is an incredible film community and I’m super proud to be part of it,” he said.
Helms stars in a new film titled The Stunt Driver, which premiered at Tiff on Thursday and follows the story of a Canadian stuntman.

“The reason I’m in these projects is because they’re incredible stories and they happen to be Canadian stories,” he said, adding, “the crews that I worked on in Edmonton and Montreal were just the best.”
Also speaking to CBC at Tiff, Sarah Paulson, who stars in the movie Closing Night, which premiered on Saturday, said “I love Canada.”
Responding to a question asked by a reporter on the red carpet, she added: “I love Canada more and more every day,” while looking down the lens of the camera.

stories.title: Head of EU invites Canada to become 'associate member'
stories.summary: European Union President Ursula von der Leyen invited Canada to become the union's first ever "associate member" Wednesday.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

Carney has firmly denied that Canada was seeking EU membership, instead referring to a new 'unique alliance'

Last updated 3 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/politics/head-of-eu-invites-Canada-become-associate-member#comments-area)

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney, EU Parliament President Roberta Metsola and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen arrive for a speech during European Commission President's annual State of the Union address at a plenary session of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, eastern France on September 16, 2026. Photo by Jean-Christophe Verhaegen /AFP via Getty Images

Strasbourg — European Union President Ursula von der Leyen extended an invitation to Canada on Wednesday to become the European Union’s first ever “associate member.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was seated just a few feet to her left, was beaming while European Parliamentarians erupted in applause.

The rest of von der Leyen’s speech in the EU Parliament on Wednesday would ring strangely familiar in Canadians’ ears.

As global crises abound, the European Union must cut down on red tape and “massively accelerate” project permitting, she said. Europe must double its energy production by 2040. It must boost its defence investments and production and learn to better harness artificial intelligence while managing its inevitable human and social impacts, she argued.

The words she used could have been ripped straight from any number of Carney’s speeches about Canada in the past year.

“We see the world with the same eyes, from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics, and we have stood together on Ukraine, ON defence, ON raw materials and supply chains,” von der Leyen said to Carney.

“But above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy.”

On Sunday, Carney firmly denied that Canada was seeking EU membership, instead referring to a new “unique alliance” with the block of 27 countries.

Asked about the new status proposed by the EU head, PMO spokesperson Audrey Champoux said the government welcomed van der Leyen’s invitation to build a deeper alliance in a statement that did not mention associate membership.

van der Leyen’s announcement comes as Carney doubles down on efforts to pivot the Canadian economy away from its dependence on the United States amid an escalating trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump.

The EU head’s speech did not detail what that would entail, but she argued Canada and the EU needed to bring their relationship “to the highest level possible”.

She said that meant going well above and beyond the decade-old Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) deal between Canada and the European Union, which 10 European countries have not yet ratified.

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project. We will work on energy critical minerals and batteries on AI, quantum, cyber, and economic security,” she said.

The announcement was greeted with enthusiastic applause from the hundreds of members of European Parliament attending her speech.

But notably absent from her announcement was talk of boosting mobility between both countries, something Carney alluded to repeatedly in the days leading up to his trip to France.

Specifically, Carney has mentioned easing mobility for labour (facilitating workers’ movement between countries), students and researchers. But the possibility of increased labour mobility from the EU — a key irritant in the U.K.’s Brexit debate — raises hackles in Canada.

For example, Conservatives said Carney “must be absolutely clear that he will not make matters worse by importing Europe’s immigration crisis.”

Carney is scheduled to deliver his own speech to the European Parliament on Thursday in which he is expected to flesh out his vision of what he called a “unique alliance” with the European Union.

Carney is the first non-European leader to be invited to attend a European Union president’s “state of the union” speech.

von der Leyen’s speech Wednesday showed just how aligned her vision for the EU is with that of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s for Canada.

She called for the European Union to slash it’s administrative burden and “move much faster”. She argued that the block needed to better manage record heatwaves and wildfires that tore across the continent this summer. She called out Russia’s ongoing threat to Europe and promised a new security union to better respond to military threats.

But where the EU president’s speech diverged from Carney was on China. Whereas the prime minister has quickly thawed diplomatic relations and advocated for a new “strategic partnership” with the Asian behemoth to boost bilateral trade, von der Leyen called on Europe to do the opposite.

“Our trade deficit with China is now 1 billion euros a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she said. “This is unsustainable, and this is why we are engaged in a dialog with China to rebalance our trade.”

She also insisted that Europe would stay the course on its climate targets, whereas Carney has thrown many of the objectives set by his predecessor Justin Trudeau by the wayside.

Carney — a well known entity in Europe since his days as governor of the Bank of England — received a warm welcome and a standing ovation from the hundreds of Members of European Parliament (MEP) gathered to hear von der Leyen’s speech.

Carney walked into the massive circular Parliamentary chamber alongside von der Leyen and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola.

Just before the speech, Carney met with both European politicians in a trilateral meeting.

Carney is expected to travel briefly to the United Kingdom on Wednesday afternoon for a first bilateral meeting with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham before returning to Strasbourg.

It must boost its defence investments and production and learn to better harness artificial intelligence while managing its inevitable human and social impacts, she argued.
The words she used could have been ripped straight from any number of Carney’s speeches about Canada in the past year.

“We see the world with the same eyes, from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics, and we have stood together on Ukraine, ON defence, ON raw materials and supply chains,” von der Leyen said to Carney.
“But above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy.”
On Sunday, Carney firmly denied that Canada was seeking EU membership, instead referring to a new “unique alliance” with the block of 27 countries.

Asked about the new status proposed by the EU head, PMO spokesperson Audrey Champoux said the government welcomed van der Leyen’s invitation to build a deeper alliance in a statement that did not mention associate membership.

van der Leyen’s announcement comes as Carney doubles down on efforts to pivot the Canadian economy away from its dependence on the United States amid an escalating trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump.
The EU head’s speech did not detail what that would entail, but she argued Canada and the EU needed to bring their relationship “to the highest level possible”.

She said that meant going well above and beyond the decade-old Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) deal between Canada and the European Union, which 10 European countries have not yet ratified.

“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project. We will work on energy critical minerals and batteries on AI, quantum, cyber, and economic security,” she said.
The announcement was greeted with enthusiastic applause from the hundreds of members of European Parliament attending her speech.
But notably absent from her announcement was talk of boosting mobility between both countries, something Carney alluded to repeatedly in the days leading up to his trip to France.

Specifically, Carney has mentioned easing mobility for labour (facilitating workers’ movement between countries), students and researchers. But the possibility of increased labour mobility from the EU — a key irritant in the U.K.’s Brexit debate — raises hackles in Canada.
For example, Conservatives said Carney “must be absolutely clear that he will not make matters worse by importing Europe’s immigration crisis.”
Carney is scheduled to deliver his own speech to the European Parliament on Thursday in which he is expected to flesh out his vision of what he called a “unique alliance” with the European Union.
Carney is the first non-European leader to be invited to attend a European Union president’s “state of the union” speech.
von der Leyen’s speech Wednesday showed just how aligned her vision for the EU is with that of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s for Canada.

She called for the European Union to slash it’s administrative burden and “move much faster”. She argued that the block needed to better manage record heatwaves and wildfires that tore across the continent this summer. She called out Russia’s ongoing threat to Europe and promised a new security union to better respond to military threats.

But where the EU president’s speech diverged from Carney was on China. Whereas the prime minister has quickly thawed diplomatic relations and advocated for a new “strategic partnership” with the Asian behemoth to boost bilateral trade, von der Leyen called on Europe to do the opposite.

“Our trade deficit with China is now 1 billion euros a day. It has reached a tipping point,” she said. “This is unsustainable, and this is why we are engaged in a dialog with China to rebalance our trade.”
She also insisted that Europe would stay the course on its climate targets, whereas Carney has thrown many of the objectives set by his predecessor Justin Trudeau by the wayside.

Carney — a well known entity in Europe since his days as governor of the Bank of England — received a warm welcome and a standing ovation from the hundreds of Members of European Parliament (MEP) gathered to hear von der Leyen’s speech.
Carney walked into the massive circular Parliamentary chamber alongside von der Leyen and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola.
Just before the speech, Carney met with both European politicians in a trilateral meeting.
Carney is expected to travel briefly to the United Kingdom on Wednesday afternoon for a first bilateral meeting with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham before returning to Strasbourg.

stories.title: Warm temperatures hold Wednesday with breaks of sunshine
stories.summary: Waking up to showers and thunderstorms Wednesday, especially along the northern shoreline of Lake Erie.
stories.author: Fiona Robertson
stories.content:
A warm and humid day in London is set to start cooling off heading into the overnight as a cold front moves through southern Ontario. Wednesday began with some rainfall, but only a small chance of rain at 30 per cent into the evening.

“Still feeling like 32 C in London, but look to the north. So, that’s where the northernly flow is starting to dry things out,” said CTV London Meteorologist Julie Atchison. “The cold front that’s making the move through will be stalling south of the Great Lakes and that could be a bit problematic for our Thursday morning.

The reason, we’ll see a little wave of low pressure develop along that front as that wave comes in, it’ll bring the chance for some showers.” Atchison added a chance of light rain will clear out by Thursday afternoon. Here’s a look at the rest of the forecast Wednesday night: Mainly cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers.

A few showers beginning before morning. Low 16 C. Thursday: A few showers ending in the afternoon, then clearing. High 23 C, humidex 28 C. Friday: Sunny. High 23 C. Saturday: Cloudy with 60 per cent chance of showers. High 17 C.

Sunday: Cloudy with a 70 per cent chance of showers. High 20 C.

stories.title: Environmental advocates ask Sask. Court of Appeal to review coal decision
stories.summary: Environmental advocates are asking Saskatchewan's Court of Appeal for a judicial review of their case against the province's decision to extend coal-fired power plants.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
A non-profit environmental group had its concerns regarding the Saskatchewan government’s decision to extend coal-fired power plants heard by the province’s highest court Tuesday.

The Saskatchewan Environmental Society (SES) is asking the court to review a January decision by the Court of King’s Bench that dismissed its challenge to the province’s coal-power extension plans.

Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison announced the decision via a letter distributed to SaskPower employees in June 2025.

One month later, SES, along with three individuals and Citizens for Public Justice, filed for judicial review of the decision, claiming the government’s decision is unlawful and conflicts with a federally mandated coal phase-out deadline of 2030.

Earlier this year, the lower court struck down the case on procedural grounds, saying it concerns a high-level policy decision that is not suitable for judicial review.

“I’m hoping that we will get a judicial review of this case,” said Peter Prebble, board member with SES.

“There are lots of reasons why this case should be looked at on its merits, which so far we haven’t had a chance to present,” Prebble said.

At the centre of the Tuesday appeal is whether the lower court has jurisdiction to hear the case, with the appellants arguing that it is justiciable.

“What we’re talking about is that this coal decision puts us on a path that defies federal law and will breach our own provincial law,” said Glenn Wright, a lawyer representing the appellants.

“For these reasons, we think it is unreasonable, and it warrants a second look to make sure we’re doing the right thing,” Wright said.

The provincial government, one of the two respondents in the case, argues that it is allowed to make laws related to energy production, with any judicial review overstepping its policymaking freedoms.

In a statement to Global News, the province says it will continue to defend its decisions to “ensure reliable and affordable power for our province,” adding it is reserving further comment as the matter is before the courts.

The government is also seeking costs on behalf of taxpayers for time spent in court over the case.

Among the dozens of people in attendance were members of the United Mine Workers of America (Umwa), a union that represents coal workers in southeast Saskatchewan, including the Estevan and Bienfait areas.

A lawyer representing labourers’ views was the second respondent in the case.

“At the end of the day, it’s all about reliable power and jobs,” said Jody Dukart, a representative of the Umwa.

“It makes a lot of income down there in the communities, and it’s their livelihood, right?” he said.

The three-judge panel is reserving its decision, which will be issued in writing at a later date.

stories.title: Brampton machete killer approved for independent living with less supervision
stories.summary: “If (Jermaine) Wood stopped taking medication it would be a matter of weeks before deterioration,” said the Ontario Review Board.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Canada

'If (Jermaine) Wood stopped taking medication it would be a matter of weeks before deterioration,' said the Ontario Review Board

Last updated 31 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/brampton-machete-killer-approved-for-independent-living-with-less-supervision#comments-area)

Jermaine Wood reported that he stopped taking his mental health medications a few months before killing his upstairs neighbour in a Brampton, Ont., apartment building in 2015.Photo by Handout/Toronto Sun/Postmedia

An Ontario man found not criminally responsible for murdering his neighbour with a machete has moved to independent living, only has to report to his handlers once every two weeks and is free to go on longer international trips with a minder even though he still presents a significant risk to public safety.

Jermaine Wood’s lawyer had asked the Ontario Review Board (ORB) for a conditional discharge for his client, and that Wood’s international travel passes not require supervision. But the Centre for Addictions and Mental Health and the Crown argued successfully to maintain a detention order for the 40-year-old, and Wood was not approved for unaccompanied international travel.

“Significant threat to the safety of the community was not in issue and is plainly evident in the serious index offence, the history of violence, the serious mental health condition and the history, including recent history, concerning issues surrounding housing conditions,” said a new decision from the independent tribunal that regularly reviews the status of individuals found not criminally responsible due to mental disorder.

The case raises the question of how the board balances protection of the public with the rights of an accused.

Recently Wood moved from a transitional rehabilitation housing program in North York to independent housing sponsored by the Canadian Mental Health Association.

“While there is housing staff attached to the new accommodation, forensic staff are not on site,” said the Sept. 4 decision. “This is a change from his last housing where the forensic staff were on site.”

He “ruminated for about a month” about the necessity of changing the locks.

“Eventually he accepted that they had indeed been changed.”

Wood’s brooding about the locks worried his psychiatrist, who told the ORB that housing changes constitute significant stressors for his patient. He refused to support a conditional discharge for Wood and the ORB agreed with him.

“The ruminations about the locks were a concern given past difficulties with housing stability and a history of aggression and violence in relation to co-tenants culminating in the fatality to a co-resident during the index offence,” said the ORB decision. “The lock issue required significant reassurance that indeed they had been changed.”

While the psychiatrist was interested in seeing how Wood performed with less site supervision, the panel had concerns about whether Wood would voluntarily return to hospital if necessary.

“There is a history of assault and threatening that preceded the index offence,” said the Orb’s decision.

“If Mr. Wood stopped taking medication it would be a matter of weeks before deterioration.”

Wood, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia in his early 20s, immigrated to Canada from Guyana with his family at the age of 17. He was bullied in school, used cannabis and was homesick, the board said.

“He was disappointed in life in Canada, the financial strain on the family and his need to work night shift full time while attending high school.”

He has previous convictions for assault, uttering threats, theft and carrying a concealed weapon

“He saw a psychiatrist through the probation office for a while,” said the decision. “He would hear voices, was paranoid and had no insight. He reluctantly took medication and his symptoms improved with treatment.”

Wood reported that he stopped taking his medications a few months before killing his upstairs neighbour in a Brampton, Ont., apartment building in 2015.

In the months prior to the murder, Wood had “developed delusions about his neighbour and complained about him repeatedly,” said the decision.

Early in the afternoon of June 30, 2015, 61-year-old Robert McCollum was walking up the stairs of their low-rise building carrying a load of groceries. As he climbed toward the building’s third floor, Wood attacked him from behind with a machete and fled.

“Jermaine Wood sliced open (McCollum’s) neck with one swift chop of the machete and killed him,” the decision said.

Wood was found not criminally responsible on a charge of first-degree murder in January 2019.

The panel did increase the length of his international travel passes to 21 days from 14 days. But he must travel with an approved person.

Wood “enjoyed a positive trip to Guyana last Christmas with his mother,” said the decision. “He continues to see his mother regularly.”

His psychiatrist discussed unaccompanied travel with Wood, “who stumbled when confronted with what he would do if the flight was cancelled,” said the decision.

His psychiatrist “stated Mr. Wood’s problem-solving was not at a level to support unaccompanied travel. Mr. Wood still relies heavily on his case manager to navigate different bus routes in Toronto.”
