stories.title: Confederation’s PEI birthplace gets a new face in a fraught time
stories.summary: A decade-long renovation of Province House nears completion just as symbols of federal unity are top of mind
stories.author: Lindsay Jones, Photography by Vanessa Tignanelli
stories.content:
The stately sandstone building in Charlottetown where the idea of Canada was born has been fenced off from the public eye for more than a decade.

Province House National Historic Site, home to Prince Edward Island’s legislative assembly, had been at risk of crumbling to the ground.

The story of the building’s restoration and conservation should perhaps go down in the history books itself – for the near 12 years it took to complete, its giant, taxpayer-funded, $138-million price tag and the secrets that were unearthed inside its stone walls. The finishing touches are now under way and provincial politicians, some of whom have never walked its halls as lawmakers, will soon move in for the fall sitting of the legislature.

The newly restored building where a united Canadian state was first imagined is returning to the public sphere at an inflection point, when the foundations of that idea are being tested by separatist sentiments and an economic assault by the United States.

It was around midday on Aug. 31, 1864, when the S.S. Queen Victoria dropped anchor in Charlottetown Harbour, with $13,000 of champagne in its hold. Pei’s colonial secretary William Henry Pope rowed out to meet the delegates.

They included Sir John A. Macdonald, the man who would soon become Canada’s first prime minister; his nemesis George Brown, publisher of the Toronto Globe, an early incarnation of this newspaper before it merged with the Mail and Empire; and Sir George-Étienne Cartier, who would lead Quebec and eventually the Northwest Territories, British Columbia and Manitoba into Confederation.

Mr. Pope brought the group to the seat of Pei’s legislative assembly, the Colonial Building, as it was called at the time.

It was here, ON the second storey of the right wing, between the faux marble pillars and around a long mahogany table, that 36 leaders from the colonies of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and PEI, along with the Province of Canada (Ontario and Quebec) laid the groundwork for Confederation.

Within these walls, now freshly painted in Benjamin Moore Bryant Gold, the leaders forged an agreement in principle for a federal union. Their discussions – lubricated by boozy seafood banquets and balls held over a week – later became known as the Charlottetown Conference.

It led to the Quebec Conference that October, where 72 resolutions were drafted to form the foundation of the British North America Act, now referred to as the Constitution Act. That was signed into law in London by Queen Victoria on July 1, 1867.

While many different peoples form the fabric of the Canadian state, including Indigenous nations whose voices were not included or considered at the time, Confederation is still the template within which those relationships are negotiated, said Edward MacDonald, a professor emeritus of history at the University of Prince Edward Island.

More than any other building in Canada, he said, Province House is a symbol of that foundational pact. “It’s a physical emblem of the relationship that defines us as a nation, and all of the complexities, all of the challenges, and all of the accomplishments of Canada,” Prof. MacDonald said.

Designed by Isaac Smith and built between 1843 and 1847, Province House is Canada’s second-oldest legislature after Nova Scotia’s. Like many state buildings of the day, the design is neoclassical, influenced by Roman and Greek architecture with massive columns, symmetrical fronts and smooth stone walls.

When the restoration project began in January, 2015, the building smelled musty. Soot from decades of coal-burning heating systems and grit from disintegrating sandstone and plaster collected in every crevice. More than a tonne of dust was carted out before work even started.

Engineers discovered the mortar that held the walls together had disintegrated over the decades due to moisture. The walls had essentially become blocks of dry stone stacked one on top of one another.

Without the use of modern reinforcements such as steel beams or columns, workers meticulously rebuilt the walls from the top down, stone by stone, using red sandstone from PEI. They replaced 124 cubic metres in total using hammers and chisels – the same tools as the masons who helped build Province House. They spread 11 kilometres worth of mortar by hand and trowel.

True to how it was in the 1800s, there is no drywall to be seen – just plaster. It was made out of 78 tonnes of sand, carried inside in five-gallon buckets, along with lime and goat hair shipped from Wisconsin, which came packaged like sheaves of wheat.

Heritage plaster experts used a centuries-old technique to recreate walls and ceilings, and more than 600 metres of cornices, the decorative moulding located along the top of interior walls. They also recast hundreds of plaster embellishments for the ceiling’s medallions, which form ornate bases around light fixtures.

To restore the massive medallion on the Legislative Chamber ceiling, four heritage plasterers each hand-sculpted replicas of the flower, shell and acanthus-leaf embellishments out of clay. These were used to create silicone moulds to recast the embellishments in plaster. In an effort to preserve a historic look and to avoid a cookie-cutter appearance, the replicas were interspersed around the medallion at random.

Lead plasterer Kieran Reid of the architectural restoration firm Heritage Grade said the project was the biggest full historic plaster restoration project in history in Canada, even bigger than the work required for West Block on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, which he is about to start working on.

The most difficult room was also the most decorative and perhaps the most famous – the Confederation Chamber where the idea of Canada was hammered out, with its curved ceiling, arches and three large medallions. Mr. Reid said he spent a lot of late nights and early mornings over the two-and-a-half years he worked on the building to figure out how to “respect what happened in that room before.”

“There’s a lot of history in the building, but in that one room in particular, you can almost feel it when you walk in,” Mr. Reid said in an interview from his home in Ottawa.

The builder likely felt it would become an important place, too.

One of the most treasured finds during the project was Isaac Smith’s signature, found scrawled in chalk on a structural beam along the underside of the southwest balcony in the Confederation Chamber. While there was some doubt at first about whether it was authentic, his descendants helped verify it with a copy of his personal Bible. The signature inside the Bible matched the one on the beam.

The exterior of the building was also in rough shape. Much of it was rebuilt using sandstone from Wallace, N.S., from the same vein of stone that was originally used to build Province House.

Stonemason Robert Morrison of RJW Stonemasons spent 250 hours to rebuild one of the building’s eight Ionic capitals – massive decorative scrolls at the top of the columns in the façade.

Mr. Morrison, who previously worked on the Palace of Westminster and Buckingham Palace, has said it was one of the most technically challenging projects of his 41 years as a stonemason.

There has been much criticism about the length and cost of the project, which ballooned from an initial five-year timeline and $20-million budget to a near 12-year renovation that cost the federal government $138-million.

Parks Canada, which operates the site jointly with the province, oversaw the restoration. It said the delays were mainly due to the extent of the building’s deterioration, some of which remained hidden until work began. As a result, design plans had to be continuously adapted. The intricacy of the masonry and sourcing stones also caused delays.

In addition, the timeline was set back because two firms involved in the project went into receivership, requiring new tendering processes. On top of that, the COVID-19 pandemic slowed work and interrupted supply chains.

“You can pinpoint small little things as you go along that always delay,” said Ryan McGuire, senior project manager for Public Services and Procurement Canada, which is managing the project for Parks Canada. “But globally, the project itself has been a 10-plus-year project, and it’s those reasons that just accumulate and accumulate.”

Parks Canada acting project manager Chantelle MacDonald said the project came in on budget, despite the expanding cost. “It was just that it was allotted incrementally as the project evolved,” she said.

One aspect of the project that isn’t complete for the reopening is an interpretive exhibit meant to include perspectives of Black and Indigenous people, whose voices were not represented at the Charlottetown Conference. Black people lived in a historic neighbourhood in Charlottetown known as The Bog starting in the 1780s. Mi’kmaq have lived on the island for more than 12,000 years.

Ms. MacDonald said in a statement that the exhibit is on pause for now.

“To prioritize the reopening of the building for legislative use following the unforeseen challenges encountered late in the conservation project, Parks Canada put a hold on the interpretive exhibit for Province House National Historic Site to ensure full focus on the building’s completion,” she said.

Though the legislature will use the building beginning Nov. 3, there is still no official opening date for the public to visit the site. Ms. MacDonald said it’s difficult to identify a precise reopening date with a project of this complexity, though she added, “we expect the building to reopen to the public this fall.”

Despite the delays and setbacks, Prof. MacDonald, from the University of PEI, said the timing of the reopening is poignant.

Reflecting on pre-Confederation times, he said one of the factors driving the union of the colonies was fear of American invasion or annexation – a threat that’s dominating Canadian headlines thanks to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

“For the first time in generations, we have to think about the future of our nation-state with America, the neighbour and friend who suddenly appears to be a bully, talking about annexation, talking about the 51st state,” he said.

Even as a strong vein of nationalism presents itself in the wake of President Trump’s threats and punitive economic measures, those in some parts of the Confederation are voicing displeasure to the extent that they might consider leaving, Prof. MacDonald added.

In Alberta, a segment of the population is dissatisfied enough about their relationship with Ottawa to contemplate separation, with a referendum scheduled for the fall on whether a binding vote should be held.

And Quebec, which has held two such referendums and whose relationship with the rest of Canada remains at times tenuous, could put the sovereigntist Parti Québécois in power after an October election.

“It’s an important moment in Canada and, again, a building is a building, but a building is also a symbol,” said Prof. MacDonald.

“This building is a symbol of all those things, and for it to reopen at a time when reopening some of those debates is happening is a coincidence, but a significant coincidence.”

Heritage conservation is a hot topic in Canada as cities, racing to build new homes, reassess what older buildings are worth. Two years ago, City Space took a deeper look at one famous case – Montreal’s Van Horne mansion – and how its demolition in 1973 still shapes our debates about preserving the past.

They replaced 124 cubic metres in total using hammers and chisels – the same tools as the masons who helped build Province House. They spread 11 kilometres worth of mortar by hand and trowel.

content_blocks.caption: This sandstone, part of the original exterior, was kept exposed inside the building. Workers found many carved signatures and drawings left in the stone over generations.

content_blocks.text: True to how it was in the 1800s, there is no drywall to be seen – just plaster. It was made out of 78 tonnes of sand, carried inside in five-gallon buckets, along with lime and goat hair shipped from Wisconsin, which came packaged like sheaves of wheat.

Heritage plaster experts used a centuries-old technique to recreate walls and ceilings, and more than 600 metres of cornices, the decorative moulding located along the top of interior walls. They also recast hundreds of plaster embellishments for the ceiling’s medallions, which form ornate bases around light fixtures.

To restore the massive medallion on the Legislative Chamber ceiling, four heritage plasterers each hand-sculpted replicas of the flower, shell and acanthus-leaf embellishments out of clay. These were used to create silicone moulds to recast the embellishments in plaster. In an effort to preserve a historic look and to avoid a cookie-cutter appearance, the replicas were interspersed around the medallion at random.

Lead plasterer Kieran Reid of the architectural restoration firm Heritage Grade said the project was the biggest full historic plaster restoration project in history in Canada, even bigger than the work required for West Block on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, which he is about to start working on.

The most difficult room was also the most decorative and perhaps the most famous – the Confederation Chamber where the idea of Canada was hammered out, with its curved ceiling, arches and three large medallions. Mr. Reid said he spent a lot of late nights and early mornings over the two-and-a-half years he worked on the building to figure out how to “respect what happened in that room before.”
“There’s a lot of history in the building, but in that one room in particular, you can almost feel it when you walk in,” Mr. Reid said in an interview from his home in Ottawa.

content_blocks.caption: The view of St. Dunstan’s Basilica would be unfamiliar to the Fathers of Confederation: The stone cathedral, also a National Historic Site, was built later.

content_blocks.text: The builder likely felt it would become an important place, too.

One of the most treasured finds during the project was Isaac Smith’s signature, found scrawled in chalk on a structural beam along the underside of the southwest balcony in the Confederation Chamber. While there was some doubt at first about whether it was authentic, his descendants helped verify it with a copy of his personal Bible. The signature inside the Bible matched the one on the beam.

content_blocks.caption: One of the architect’s descendants helped confirm that this ‘Mr. I. Smith’ inscription was genuinely his.

content_blocks.text: The exterior of the building was also in rough shape. Much of it was rebuilt using sandstone from Wallace, N.S., from the same vein of stone that was originally used to build Province House.
Stonemason Robert Morrison of RJW Stonemasons spent 250 hours to rebuild one of the building’s eight Ionic capitals – massive decorative scrolls at the top of the columns in the façade.
Mr. Morrison, who previously worked on the Palace of Westminster and Buckingham Palace, has said it was one of the most technically challenging projects of his 41 years as a stonemason.

content_blocks.caption: Getting the stonework right has been a challenge: Workers had to hand-carve a new capital on the left column to match the original one on the right.

content_blocks.text: There has been much criticism about the length and cost of the project, which ballooned from an initial five-year timeline and $20-million budget to a near 12-year renovation that cost the federal government $138-million.

Parks Canada, which operates the site jointly with the province, oversaw the restoration. It said the delays were mainly due to the extent of the building’s deterioration, some of which remained hidden until work began. As a result, design plans had to be continuously adapted. The intricacy of the masonry and sourcing stones also caused delays.

In addition, the timeline was set back because two firms involved in the project went into receivership, requiring new tendering processes. On top of that, the COVID-19 pandemic slowed work and interrupted supply chains.

“You can pinpoint small little things as you go along that always delay,” said Ryan McGuire, senior project manager for Public Services and Procurement Canada, which is managing the project for Parks Canada. “But globally, the project itself has been a 10-plus-year project, and it’s those reasons that just accumulate and accumulate.”

content_blocks.caption: This basement corridor was part of the housekeeper’s quarters. The restored version has washrooms for the public and service rooms for water and power utilities.

content_blocks.text: Parks Canada acting project manager Chantelle MacDonald said the project came in on budget, despite the expanding cost. “It was just that it was allotted incrementally as the project evolved,” she said.

One aspect of the project that isn’t complete for the reopening is an interpretive exhibit meant to include perspectives of Black and Indigenous people, whose voices were not represented at the Charlottetown Conference. Black people lived in a historic neighbourhood in Charlottetown known as The Bog starting in the 1780s. Mi’kmaq have lived on the island for more than 12,000 years.
Ms. MacDonald said in a statement that the exhibit is on pause for now.

“To prioritize the reopening of the building for legislative use following the unforeseen challenges encountered late in the conservation project, Parks Canada put a hold on the interpretive exhibit for Province House National Historic Site to ensure full focus on the building’s completion,” she said.

Though the legislature will use the building beginning Nov. 3, there is still no official opening date for the public to visit the site. Ms. MacDonald said it’s difficult to identify a precise reopening date with a project of this complexity, though she added, “we expect the building to reopen to the public this fall.”

content_blocks.caption: Chantelle MacDonald from Parks Canada, right, says a public reopening is expected this fall, but pinning down an exact date is complex.

content_blocks.text: Despite the delays and setbacks, Prof. MacDonald, from the University of PEI, said the timing of the reopening is poignant.

Reflecting on pre-Confederation times, he said one of the factors driving the union of the colonies was fear of American invasion or annexation – a threat that’s dominating Canadian headlines thanks to U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

“For the first time in generations, we have to think about the future of our nation-state with America, the neighbour and friend who suddenly appears to be a bully, talking about annexation, talking about the 51st state,” he said.

Even as a strong vein of nationalism presents itself in the wake of President Trump’s threats and punitive economic measures, those in some parts of the Confederation are voicing displeasure to the extent that they might consider leaving, Prof. MacDonald added.

In Alberta, a segment of the population is dissatisfied enough about their relationship with Ottawa to contemplate separation, with a referendum scheduled for the fall on whether a binding vote should be held.

And Quebec, which has held two such referendums and whose relationship with the rest of Canada remains at times tenuous, could put the sovereigntist Parti Québécois in power after an October election.
“It’s an important moment in Canada and, again, a building is a building, but a building is also a symbol,” said Prof. MacDonald.
“This building is a symbol of all those things, and for it to reopen at a time when reopening some of those debates is happening is a coincidence, but a significant coincidence.”

Heritage conservation is a hot topic in Canada as cities, racing to build new homes, reassess what older buildings are worth. Two years ago, City Space took a deeper look at one famous case – Montreal’s Van Horne mansion – and how its demolition in 1973 still shapes our debates about preserving the past.

stories.title: Canada’s investment problem won’t be solved in a hotel ballroom
stories.summary: The summit’s main achievement May have been to serve as a platform for investors to explain to government officials why they won’t invest in Canada
stories.author: Andrew Coyne
stories.content:
I confess to a certain skepticism about the Canada Investment Summit, the two-day confab of company executives, institutional investors and politicians which has just wrapped up in Toronto.

Why such a conference was needed, or what it would accomplish, has never been entirely clear, despite all the hype about “catalyzing” a trillion dollars in investment.

To imagine a mere conference was the key to unlocking all those hundreds of billions of dollars – that it was all just a matter of getting the people with money and the people with projects together in the same glitzy hotel – stretches credulity.

International asset managers like BlackRock and Macquarie employ brigades of people whose whole job is to find good investments. The people who run Canadian mining and energy companies are highly skilled at separating investors from their money.

It has been especially strange to see the parade of Canadian banks, in the days leading up to the summit, announcing plans to provide tens of billions of dollars in financing to Canadian businesses over the next several years, as if this were some extraordinary departure. Lending money to businesses is what banks do.

Read the full transcript of Mark Carney’s speech at the Canada Investment Summit

Nonetheless, there was the government press release after the event crowing that the summit had “unleashed” nearly $500-billion of new investment. Of this sum $325-billion was in financing from Canadian banks for businesses in “key sectors” over the next five years or more – roughly $60-billion a year. Gross business lending by Canadian banks already runs to about $2-trillion annually, so that’s not quite the torrent it appears.

More to the point: Are we really to believe that this was all new money? That none of it was already in the works? Canadian banks are not known for their adventurousness, but if the industries to which they are committing (promise!) to lend are indeed so “key,” possibly even they can see it, without the help of a government matchmaker.

This is such obvious guff that I can’t think even the government believes it. What might be the actual rationale for such a conference? One clue lies in the types of projects listed in the prospectus handed out to conference attendees.

They tend to be big, complicated resource and/or infrastructure plays, involving multiple levels of regulatory approval, lots of “stakeholder” consultation, and tons of political risk – and consequently are typically undertaken only by consortiums of large investors, who can collectively shoulder risks none of them could individually. Gathering all those players under one roof might actually have some use.

Teck CEO calls for more investment in crucial mining infrastructure at investment summit

But it also comes with risks of its own. This was not just a conference of private businesses, with their own money at stake. Also in attendance were a number of politicians, trembling with excitement at all the projects they could announce – and desperate to avoid the embarrassment of coming away empty.

Any time people in power let it be known that they need private capital to make something happen – and that they cannot allow it not to happen – they hand private capital the opportunity to exploit them. What went on behind closed doors at the conference will not be known for some time, but I suspect a good deal of it consisted of potential investors setting out the conditions on which they would put money at risk – the political conditions, that is.

That’s not necessarily all to the bad. Part of the reason the government felt compelled to put on such a conference was undoubtedly that Canada had acquired such a bad reputation as a place to invest. If the summit served as the platform for potential investors to spell out for government officials the kinds of tax and regulatory impediments that were deterring them from investing, all to the good.

Opinion: Mark Carney’s investment moment

If, ON the other hand, the demands were about protecting investors, not from political risk, but from the economic risks that naturally attend any such large project – if the “de-risking” took the form of subsidies, of one kind or another – that is a very different matter.

Indeed, many of the 167 projects listed in the prospectus – along with those that were already more or less done deals long before it, and those that will remain twinkles in their promoters’ eyes long after – explicitly advertise their dependence on government money to proceed.

How much government money remains to be seen. But to the extent that private capital is “mobilized” behind these projects by the prospect of subsidy, it will not be because of their subtle economic benefits, which could only properly be explained in the intimacy of a conference hotel room. It will be because it has been bought with taxpayers’ money.

stories.title: Reimaging the classic Chanel jacket
stories.summary: At Nimmo Bay in B.C.’s Coast Mountains, we unpack the utilitarian toppers and bejewelled blazers that are redefining the Chanel jacket
stories.author: Andrew Sardone
stories.content:
At Nimmo Bay in B.C.’s Coast Mountains, we unpack the utilitarian toppers and bejewelled blazers that are redefining the Chanel jacket

In The Little Black Jacket , a collectable compendium of portraits of celebrities and fashion figures sporting Chanel tweeds that was published in 2012, there are 100 images but only 12 words. An opening quote, attributed to Argentine poet Roberto Juarroz, succinctly sums up the magic of its subject matter: “There are clothes that keep rejuvenating themselves instead of getting worn out.”

The collectible tome was a collaboration between Chanel’s designer at the time, Karl Lagerfeld, and über-stylist Carine Roitfeld. In graphic black and white, bold faces from Sarah Jessica Parker to Linda Evangelista to Roitfeld herself illustrate why the softly tailored blazer exists as one of high fashion’s evergreen essentials, a century-old example of Juarroz’s musings about sartorial immortality.

Today, the house’s current artistic director, Matthieu Blazy, is in the middle of his own reinvention of the definition of a Chanel jacket. “Chanel is a paradox. Chanel is function, Chanel is fiction. Chanel is sensible, Chanel is seductive. Chanel is day, Chanel is night,” he is quoted as saying in the fall/winter 2026 collection’s show notes.

As outerwear, that versatility is translated into suede blouson bombers, drop-waist blazers and evening suits knit with thousands of pearls. They maintain many of the classic jacket’s signature details – flap pockets, gilt buttons and a discreet chain sewn into the inside of the hem to help maintain its silhouette – but play with shape, material and colour.

The most casual example is what Blazy calls a “work shirt,” an oversized piece that evokes the ease of a flannel button up worn around an early autumn campfire. Where better than the Nimmo Bay wilderness resort in the Great Bear Rainforest to capture it and every other rejuvenated option in the wild?

The first hint that a Nimmo Bay guest is in for a once-in-a-lifetime adventure sits on the tarmac at the little airport in Port Hardy, B.C. The eight-passenger Grumman Goose that makes the 30-minute flight into the Great Bear Rainforest is as much a boat as a plane. As you cruise toward K’we mountain, the resort’s array of six Monopoly game piece tidal cabins appears below (three other cottages are shaded in the woods nearby). After a quick U-turn, the pilot glides down to the shimmering water of Mackenzie Sound, skipping the aircraft along the sea. When the amphibious wonder slows down, it gently tilts to the left on one of its retractable floats, and the engine revs down to a gurgle as you pull up to a wide dock lined with the resort’s smiling staff.

The second hint is the angular architecture of the dining pavilion that stands behind them. Its contemporary façade is a far cry from the humble fishing camp that founder Craig Murray and his wife Deborah opened here in 1981, taking advantage of a thundering waterfall on the property to power their dreams of an immersive wilderness escape. Over the next couple of days, it will become your clubhouse: a space for hearty breakfasts, evening martinis shaken with ocean brine or boarding a Bond villain-worthy catamaran destined for a day on a floating sauna.

That type of experience is the third hint. These moments can be as elaborate as you can dream – helicoptering to the top of the Klinaklini glacier; spending the day diving for urchins and sea cucumbers that a chef incorporates into a private meal served at an open-water dining table. They can also be a simple surprise like being invited to quietly boat across the bay with a set of binoculars to spy on a mother grizzly and her pair of cubs.

For many of Nimmo Bay’s guests, all these elements mean a visit isn’t, in fact, a once-in-a-lifetime experience at all. According to Fraser Murray, Craig and Deborah’s son, and his wife, Becky, who assumed management of the resort in 2011, a quarter of visitors who make the flight from May to October are returning guests. While the vistas remain remarkably untouched, the on-site perks are updated each season. A floating massage room debuted this summer and a sauna that can be airlifted into remote landscapes is in the works for 2027. “I like to make a place that’s welcoming and comfortable for someone who’s not used to this environment,” Fraser says. “And then allow them to slowly inch their way into the wild.”

For more, visit nimmobay.com

All clothing and accessories by Chanel (chanel.com). Makeup and hair by Julie Cusson for Chanel using Les 4 Ombres eyeshadow in shade 308 Clair-Obscur, Rouge Coco lipstick in shade 106 Deauville and Le Vernis nail polish in shade 103 Légende, all available at Chanel (chanel.com). Model: Elaina Winslow-Hansen at Family Management. Photo assistant: Yohan Kim. Photographed at the Nimmo Bay resort in BC (nimmobay.com).

The Globe and Mail Style Magazine travelled as a guest of Chanel and Nimmo Bay, which did not review or approve this article. Stories are based on merit; The Globe does not guarantee coverage.

content_blocks.text: At Nimmo Bay in B.C.’s Coast Mountains, we unpack the utilitarian toppers and bejewelled blazers that are redefining the Chanel jacket

In The Little Black Jacket , a collectable compendium of portraits of celebrities and fashion figures sporting Chanel tweeds that was published in 2012, there are 100 images but only 12 words. An opening quote, attributed to Argentine poet Roberto Juarroz, succinctly sums up the magic of its subject matter: “There are clothes that keep rejuvenating themselves instead of getting worn out.”

The collectible tome was a collaboration between Chanel’s designer at the time, Karl Lagerfeld, and über-stylist Carine Roitfeld. In graphic black and white, bold faces from Sarah Jessica Parker to Linda Evangelista to Roitfeld herself illustrate why the softly tailored blazer exists as one of high fashion’s evergreen essentials, a century-old example of Juarroz’s musings about sartorial immortality.

Today, the house’s current artistic director, Matthieu Blazy, is in the middle of his own reinvention of the definition of a Chanel jacket. “Chanel is a paradox. Chanel is function, Chanel is fiction. Chanel is sensible, Chanel is seductive. Chanel is day, Chanel is night,” he is quoted as saying in the fall/winter 2026 collection’s show notes.

content_blocks.caption: FLIGHT SUIT The palette of a work shirt’s open tweed evokes the colour scheme on the amphibious Grumman Goose that delivers guests to Nimmo Bay’s dock.
BRANCH OUT With its jewel-like buttons and rich texture, this look camouflages into the forest landscape.

SEA WORTHY In home decor circles, the suede sofa in Gabrielle Chanel’s Paris apartment is as legendary as the founder’s fashionable tweeds. Here, its supple texture inspires a cropped style with trench-coat-like flaps.

content_blocks.text: As outerwear, that versatility is translated into suede blouson bombers, drop-waist blazers and evening suits knit with thousands of pearls. They maintain many of the classic jacket’s signature details – flap pockets, gilt buttons and a discreet chain sewn into the inside of the hem to help maintain its silhouette – but play with shape, material and colour.

The most casual example is what Blazy calls a “work shirt,” an oversized piece that evokes the ease of a flannel button up worn around an early autumn campfire. Where better than the Nimmo Bay wilderness resort in the Great Bear Rainforest to capture it and every other rejuvenated option in the wild?

content_blocks.caption: SOFT FOCUS For the ultimate après-plunge warm-up at one of Nimmo Bay’s floating saunas, a shearling coat is an example of how Blazy layers a clean design language into an often playful lineup.
FOREST BATHED With its jewel-like buttons and rich texture, this look camouflages into the forest landscape.
KNIT AND PEARL For this skirt suit, miniature orbs are incorporated into the body material, braid details and fringed trim.
Little River Restaurant and Lounge at Nimmo Bay Wilderness Resort. Supplied

content_blocks.text: Nimmo Bay

The first hint that a Nimmo Bay guest is in for a once-in-a-lifetime adventure sits on the tarmac at the little airport in Port Hardy, B.C. The eight-passenger Grumman Goose that makes the 30-minute flight into the Great Bear Rainforest is as much a boat as a plane. As you cruise toward K’we mountain, the resort’s array of six Monopoly game piece tidal cabins appears below (three other cottages are shaded in the woods nearby). After a quick U-turn, the pilot glides down to the shimmering water of Mackenzie Sound, skipping the aircraft along the sea. When the amphibious wonder slows down, it gently tilts to the left on one of its retractable floats, and the engine revs down to a gurgle as you pull up to a wide dock lined with the resort’s smiling staff.

The second hint is the angular architecture of the dining pavilion that stands behind them. Its contemporary façade is a far cry from the humble fishing camp that founder Craig Murray and his wife Deborah opened here in 1981, taking advantage of a thundering waterfall on the property to power their dreams of an immersive wilderness escape. Over the next couple of days, it will become your clubhouse: a space for hearty breakfasts, evening martinis shaken with ocean brine or boarding a Bond villain-worthy catamaran destined for a day on a floating sauna.

That type of experience is the third hint. These moments can be as elaborate as you can dream – helicoptering to the top of the Klinaklini glacier; spending the day diving for urchins and sea cucumbers that a chef incorporates into a private meal served at an open-water dining table. They can also be a simple surprise like being invited to quietly boat across the bay with a set of binoculars to spy on a mother grizzly and her pair of cubs.

For many of Nimmo Bay’s guests, all these elements mean a visit isn’t, in fact, a once-in-a-lifetime experience at all. According to Fraser Murray, Craig and Deborah’s son, and his wife, Becky, who assumed management of the resort in 2011, a quarter of visitors who make the flight from May to October are returning guests. While the vistas remain remarkably untouched, the on-site perks are updated each season. A floating massage room debuted this summer and a sauna that can be airlifted into remote landscapes is in the works for 2027. “I like to make a place that’s welcoming and comfortable for someone who’s not used to this environment,” Fraser says. “And then allow them to slowly inch their way into the wild.”
For more, visit nimmobay.com

stories.title: Blue Jays’ bullpen falters in 10-1 loss to Tigers
stories.summary: The Blue Jays dropped to two games back of Cleveland for the third and final wild-card spot in the American League.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Toronto Blue Jays pitching coach Pete Walker visits pitcher Michael Lorenzen (55) and catcher Alejandro Kirk (30) on the mound during fourth inning MLB baseball action against the Detroit Tigers in Toronto on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Jon Blacker.

By John Chidley-Hill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 16, 2026 5:40 am.

Spencer Torkelson smashed a three-run homer as part of a four-run inning and the Detroit Tigers routed the Toronto Blue Jays 10-1 on Tuesday.

Max Clark had a one-run double earlier in the fourth inning as Detroit (72-79) won its sixth straight. Riley Greene and John Peck had RBI singles in the fifth and sixth innings respectively.

A throwing error by Blue Jays catcher Alejandro Kirk in the eighth allowed two more runs to score and Hao-Yu Lee hit a solo home run in the ninth.

Drew Anderson (5-6) struck out four over five scoreless innings in which he allowed just two hits and three walks. Relief pitchers Jacob Waguespack, Kyle Finnegan and Brant Hurter followed him to the mound.

Kirk had an RBI single in the eighth for Toronto’s (75-77) only offence.

The Blue Jays dropped to two games back of Cleveland for the third and final wild-card spot in the American League after the Guardians rallied past the Chicago White Sox 7-6.

Reliever Braydon Fisher was the opener for Toronto’s scheduled bullpen day. He was followed to the mound by Brendan Cellucci, Michael Lorenzen (3-13), Brendon Little, Spencer Arrighetti and Joe Mantiply.

Spencer Miles has been a go-to option for manager John Schneider this season when Toronto has a scheduled bullpen day, but he wasn’t available to pitch against Detroit after throwing two innings on Saturday. Miles has a 2.71 earned-run average and 86 strikeouts over 89 2/3 innings pitched in his rookie season and his arm was missed.

Max Scherzer (2-8) will take the mound as Toronto concludes its series against Detroit with a matinee.

stories.title: Kenneth Law, who admitted to aiding at least 93 suicides, says he is not a ‘diabolical madman’
stories.summary: The Canadian engineer who sold toxic substances online said ahead of his sentencing that ‘we all learn from our mistakes’
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Kenneth Law, the Canadian man who has admitted that he helped end the lives of at least 93 suicidal people by selling toxic salts and other deadly paraphernalia online, has told a psychiatrist that he considers himself a “pathfinder” and not a psychopath.

“I was just trying to serve a need that I thought was humane,” Mr. Law said during interviews with psychiatrist Jonathan Rootenberg conducted in a Lindsay, Ont., jail this July.

“I’m not a diabolical madman.”

Summations of Mr. Law’s post-conviction medical interviews have been filed in court ahead of sentencing hearings scheduled to start later this month. In these recent discussions, the 60-year-old describes his upbringing and his crimes in his own words, while arguing that much of what he did was morally defensible even if it violated the law.

“Now I can look back and say that what I was doing was legally wrong ... that’s why I pled guilty. It’s about taking ownership and responsibility for your actions,” Mr. Law told the psychiatrist. “We all learn from our mistakes.”

The former engineer has been jailed for more than three years since his May, 2023, arrest on criminal charges of aiding suicide. This past May, Mr. Law admitted guilt in court, agreeing that his online businesses generated about $300,000 from a vulnerable and global clientele that included young teenagers.

In his psychiatric interviews, he said the businesses were not profitable. “I’m not a serial killer lurking around trying to kill people,” he said. “I made enough to sustain the business.”

Mr. Law’s wares were repurposed industrial goods – such as potent meat-preserving salts, as well as hoods, masks and lethal gas cylinders – that could be legally purchased but used to induce deaths.

He has pleaded guilty to Canadian charges that he aided in the suicides of 14 people in Ontario, including two minors. As part of his plea deal, he has also admitted that he aided in the suicides of another 79 people in Britain after police and prosecutors there sent evidence to Canada rather than start a separate prosecution.

Mr. Law is facing a substantial prison term in the range of 20 years, according to some experts. But the length of his incarceration and the conditions of his jailing have yet to be set.

Ontario Justice Michelle Fuerst will preside over several hearings this fall aimed at determining those details. It is anticipated that prosecutors – who withdrew premeditated murder charges against Mr. Law as part of this spring’s plea deal – will start the proceedings on Sept. 23 with victim impact statements.

Last week, lawyers acting for Mr. Law submitted a 600-page sentencing evidence brief with findings that he is not dangerous, but rather redeemable, especially if programming is made available to him while he is in prison. The reports in the submission describe him as a man who “should be able to effectively participate in psychological treatments and programs aimed at rehabilitation.”

In an agreed statement filed in court, Mr. Law admitted to shipping more than 1,000 packages between 2021 and 2023 from a Canada Post office near his Mississauga home.

Who is Kenneth Law, the Ontario man accused of selling lethal substances to aid in suicides? A timeline of events

Prosecutors named dozens of countries that received these deadly shipments, but said most went to the United States (431 packages), Britain (330) and Canada (157). Half of the Canadian packages ended up in Ontario, where Mr. Law lived and operated. Ontario Premier Doug Ford has said his government will not convene an inquiry into the crimes.

There is no known tally of the overall number of victims killed by Mr. Law’s products, but the scale is staggering by his own account.

“The suicide rate is around 10 per cent and I sold around 1,200 products,” Mr. Law is quoted as telling a psychiatrist.

In the court-filed reports, he said suicide is not a crime and that he saw himself as someone who provided a legitimate service: “Maybe I’m a pathfinder to find the best medium for this type of behaviour.”

stories.title: Some farmers are opposed to proposed trail connecting Ilderton to London
stories.summary: A transportation plan going to the Municipality of Middlesex Centre council proposes the Ilderton Rail Trail extend an additional 5 km to north London. However, that would require the new part of the trail would need to cross into several landowners' private property.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A transportation plan going to the Municipality of Middlesex Centre council proposes the Ilderton Rail Trail extend an additional 5 km to north London. However, that would require the new part of the trail would need to cross into several landowners' private property.
· Posted: Sep 16, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 16
Middlesex Centre council will review the municipality's new active transportation plan, which includes a proposal to extend the Ilderton Rail Trail into London.(Submitted by Jean Coles)

Some southwestern Ontario landowners are voicing their concerns about a proposed walking and cycling trail expansion project that will make it easier for the public to move between two neighbouring communities.
A transportation plan going to the Municipality of Middlesex Centre council on Wednesday proposes the Ilderton Rail Trail extend an additional 5 km to reach north London.
In order to do that, the new part of the trail would need to cross into several landowners' private property.
"The extension of this trail, while beneficial to some, poses significant challenges for landowners," a letter to council, signed by nearly 40 local residents, said.
"Expropriating private land not only disrupts the lives of those who have invested their resources into their land, but it also undermines the sanctity of private property," the letter added.
A map shows the proposed area of the Ilderton Rail Trail expansion, which would enter into north London. (Middlesex County)

The Rail Trail, which is currently 3.4 km between Twelve Mile Road and Ten Mile Road in Ilderton, primarily follows the path of former train tracks in the rural community. The municipality sold the rest of the rail corridor land to residents years ago.
However, the plan suggests buying back some of that land from homeowners who live along the proposed expanded trail path.
Middlesex Centre Ward 1 Coun. Jean Coles, whose area includes Ilderton, says residents have been coming to her with their opinions on the proposal.
Middlesex Centre Ward 1 Coun. Jean Coles says walkers, runners, cyclists and other non-motorists currently use the Ilderton Rail Trail to get around the rural community. (Submitted by Jean Coles)
"I'm hearing both sides of the coin. I'm hearing the positive and the negative," she said.
"People really do like to walk, run and all of those things along our trail. They like to get outside. People like living in our healthy community ... but there's also some legitimate concerns."
Coles said she's primarily heard from people who work in Ilderton's agriculture industry about their opposition to the project, specifically those with farmland along the proposed pathway.

"If you are the landowner and this is being proposed on your parcel of land, you don't really want it to be cut up," she said. It would interrupt their work causing farmers to have to drive around the trail to get to the other side of their land, she added.
She said landowners have also expressed concerns about how this could affect the sale of land down the road.
Some of the current Ilderton Rail Trail is covered with pavement, while other parts are a dirt path. (Submitted by Jean Coles)

The municipality's transportation plan highlights a slew of other landowner concerns, which came up during a feedback process. Some people expressed worries about trespassing, litter, stolen property and homeless encampments appearing along the trail, the report said, adding there is a lack of evidence that any of these issues will materialize.
It suggests ways to mitigate possible concerns with signage, marked boundaries and collaboration with police.
Preliminary estimates put the project cost at $3.23 million, the plan said, and it could take until 2038 for the extension to be complete.
Coles says she uses the current rail trail on a regular basis, often walking her dog along the path, which has both pavement and dirt sections.

"Having the opportunity to not use a car to get where I'm going would be so beautiful, but on the flip side, I don't want to make changes to actively-farmed fields," she said. "Agriculture is an important business in our area and a livelihood for many of our residents."
Coles said she wants residents to attend Wednesday's council meeting to share their thoughts, adding that nothing is set in stone yet.
"It is a long-term plan so we want to make sure we get it right before there is development that May happen in this area," she said.

stories.title: London romance book convention moves venues days before event
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 16, 2026 9:00 AM | Last Updated: September 16
Some vendors are organizing a separate event after Love Among the Pages moved from RBC Place to Citi Plaza
Two events aimed at romance book fans are scheduled for London this weekend after the organizer of a planned three-day convention moved the event to a new venue just days before it was set to begin.
Love Among the Pages was originally scheduled to run Sept. 18 to 20 at RBC Place London. The event was first announced in July 2025, with proceeds intended to support animal rescues in Canada.

Tickets remained on sale through the event's website as of Tuesday afternoon, with the site still listing RBC Place as the venue. However, the event was removed from the venue's website over the weekend.
RBC Place event planning manager Rochelle Stone told CBC News in an email that Love Among the Pages “is no longer taking place at RBC Place London.”

an Instagram post on Sunday , organizer Haustier Events executive director and CEO Nicole Ramsdale said the event had not been cancelled but that she was facing financial challenges because of low ticket sales and members of her volunteer team being unable to continue helping with the planning.
She said the event had about $17,000 still to raise, while ticket sales and sponsorships had been lower than expected.
Ramsdale said the event was intended to be funded through ticket sales, sponsorships, and vendor booth fees, with any leftover money donated to animal rescues.
“It was never meant to be a one-person event to plan,” she wrote, adding that she did not want to cancel the event because people had already invested in tickets, booths, inventory and travel.

Ramsdale's Instagram post did not mention RBC Place or a potential change of venue. But in an email to vendors obtained by CBC News, she said she had an outstanding balance with the venue and had been told the event could still go ahead at RBC Place if she raised enough money to cover it.

Ramsdale said RBC Place had marked the event as cancelled on its administrative system until the outstanding amount was paid. She said she spent the following days trying to raise the money while also looking for an alternative venue.
“I planned on informing all my guests and attendees when I had things figured out, as I did not want to create panic over something that I could resolve,” Ramsdale wrote.
CBC News spoke to Ramsdale for comment on Tuesday, but she declined to be interviewed. She was also given an opportunity to provide a written statement, but none was received before publication.
More than 50 romance authors were previously advertised as participating in the event, along with close to a dozen audiobook narrators and 17 craft vendors.
Some vendors had planned to travel from outside Canada to attend. Several have since announced on social media that they will no longer participate.
Kitchener-Waterloo author Sara Clement said she paid $400 for a vendor table. She said she is no longer planning to attend because of the venue change.

“It feels like very much being tugged along and being expected to just wait her out, which feels very unfair to the amount that we have all invested into this,” Clement said, adding the decision also affected her personally because she had made plans around the convention.
“I make sacrifices,” she said. “I give up time with my kids. My daughter has a hockey tournament this weekend that I can't go to because I was booked already for this.”

Some previously advertised activities have also been scaled back. Narrator panels and the “A Night of a Thousand Tropes Ball,” which had been scheduled for Saturday night, no longer appear to be part of the event schedule.
Brittany Cameron, who paid $400 for a vendor table for her London-based crochet business Fox Flair, said she was concerned about the lack of public information about the changes.
“There was no public announcement made,” Cameron said. “That does not sit well with me.”
Ticket prices have also changed, with some tickets advertised for as little as $10. Friday tickets were no longer listed on the event website as of Tuesday afternoon.
Its FAQ says tickets are non-refundable, but also says Haustier Events will refund ticket purchases if the event is cancelled because of “extreme circumstances.”
It was not clear whether VIP ticket holders would receive refunds following the programming changes.
On Monday, Ramsdale told vendors that Citi Plaza had been secured as the new venue.
The downtown shopping centre is a block away from RBC Place, but some vendors told CBC News they do not intend to participate at the new location.
Clement said she believes the venue change could affect the contracts vendors signed with the organizer. CBC News obtained a copy of a vendor contract that lists RBC Place as the event venue.
“We are not obligated to show up to a place because any amendments to a venue would need to be agreed upon by both parties,” Clement said.

stories.title: Grifols permitted donors to give plasma despite punctures, bruising on arms, Health Canada finds
stories.summary: The safety of drugs made from plasma has not been compromised, says Canadian Blood Services
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
A Health Canada inspection of a facility in Regina run by Grifols, the country’s only major private collector of blood plasma, found multiple plasma donors with punctures and bruising on their arms who were allowed to donate without proper medical assessments, newly obtained documents show.

The inspection report also found a donor who had disclosed to Grifols that they had sexual contact with someone who had HIV/Aids was inappropriately allowed to donate twice.

These details, which have not been previously published, explain why Health Canada found the clinic to be “non-compliant” with federal regulations in February, although the regulator allowed the centre to keep operating.

Graham Sher, the chief executive officer of Canadian Blood Services, which has a partnership with Grifols and distributes the company’s plasma-derived products, said the safety of medicines made from the plasma of Grifols’ donors has never been compromised.

Grifols temporarily closed all of its collection centres in Canada as of Aug. 14, after a series of critical inspections from Health Canada and public scrutiny following the deaths of two donors in Winnipeg. The company said it is using the temporary closure to retrain staff and work with Health Canada and CBS to improve its operations. It has not announced a reopening date.

Spanish parent company of Grifols takes full ownership of Canadian operations

Plasma is a golden-coloured fluid found in blood that is used to make medicine, particularly for patients with immune deficiencies.

Grifols, a Barcelona-headquartered company, operates in Canada as part of an agreement signed in 2022 with Canadian Blood Services, the national charity that manages the country’s blood supply. CBS relies on volunteers for blood and plasma donations, while Grifols pays donors. CBS spends more than $1-billion per year on supplying hospitals with drugs made from plasma and other related products.

Health Canada’s inspection of the Regina location, which ran from Jan. 13 to 23, found a series of deficiencies, including with how the facility screened donors and followed operating procedures.

The report, dated Feb. 20 and obtained by The Globe and Mail, found that “multiple donors presenting with punctures and bruising near the venipuncture site were permitted to proceed with donation without documented additional assessment.” The report does not specify how many donors this observation applied to.

It cites an example of a donor on Jan. 13 who “presented with bruising and puncture marks on both arms” and was deemed eligible for donation by a Grifols staff member without an assessment by someone acting under the supervision of a physician. (That role, referred to as a “physician substitute” in federal regulations, is often performed by a nurse at Grifols collection centres.)

Grifols said in a response filed with Health Canada on March 20 that there is “no established guidance for what constitutes an acceptable forearm check by donor screeners to differentiate markings that result from frequent donations compared to high-risk activities or injury.” The company said it would update its screening procedures with examples of “acceptable versus unacceptable forearm checks.”

A high-risk activity that could lead to forearm bruising and puncture marks is intravenous drug use. Cbs’s website says those who have injected drugs must wait 12 months from the date of last use before donating blood to the charity.

What we know so far about Grifols’s plasma pause and Health Canada’s safety concerns

Health Canada inspectors also wrote that a donor in November, 2025, was permitted to donate twice despite answering “yes” to the question of whether they had “ever had sexual contact with anyone who has ever had HIV/Aids or has ever had a positive test for HIV/Aids virus.” The report says such a response should cause someone to be barred from donating. However, a staff member at Grifols, who was a “physician substitute in training,” changed the response to “no,” allowing the person to donate.

Grifols said in its response to Health Canada that the error was discovered on the donor’s third visit. The company told Health Canada it then “rejected” the plasma collected during the prior two visits and applied an indefinite ban on the donor. The Grifols report said that staff member was no longer employed by the company.

Other observations from the inspection of the Regina centre included a person donating twice within 48 hours even though donations are supposed to be more than two days apart, and the process for verifying donors’ addresses as being “ineffective.”

Health Canada inspections of other Grifols locations have raised concerns about staff failing to properly respond to alarms on donation machines and physicians (or physician substitutes) not always being present .

Grifols told The Globe Tuesday that the safety of plasma and plasma-derived medicines is the company’s number-one priority. “At no point donor safety or the quality and safety of plasma collected at our Regina centre – or at any of our other Canadian centres – has been compromised,” Grifols said in an unsigned statement.

It said collected plasma goes through rigorous tests to detect infectious agents, including syphilis, hepatitis B and C and HIV.

The company said that, since January, 2026, no donors at its Canadian centres have tested positive for HIV or hepatitis B virus, though two donors were confirmed positive for hepatitis C virus and two had indeterminate results. Grifols said that in 2025, one donor was confirmed positive for HIV, one for hepatitis B and two for hepatitis C.

Grifols revises reports of serious injuries or death at its centres down to six from 25 since 2018

“Overall, the number of confirmed positive donors remains very low and well below Grifols Canada’s established epidemiological alert limits,” the company said.

Strict screening of blood and plasma donors for diseases is an important part of managing health and safety. In the 1980s, tens of thousands of Canadians contracted hepatitis and HIV in a tragedy that came to be known as the tainted blood scandal. Afterwards, an exhaustive commission overseen by Justice Horace Krever into the crisis led to an overhaul of Canada’s blood system and the creation of Canadian Blood Services.

Dr. Sher said in an interview Tuesday that advances in manufacturing processes and testing have meant no cases of HIV, hepatitis B or hepatitis C have been transmitted through blood products since the organization’s founding.

He said he could not address specific findings of Health Canada’s report on the Regina centre. He said inspections are point-in-time observations and that a focus on specific findings ignores the wider context of the safety of products made from human plasma.

“I’m not disputing that there have been a set of systemic findings across many of the Grifols sites,” Dr. Sher said.

But he said he believes the company will use its current collection pause to improve its entire operations.

“I am assured and I am confident that Grifols is taking this very seriously,” he said.

stories.title: EU chief Ursula von der Leyen says she wants Canada to become the bloc’s 1st associate member
stories.summary: Strasbourg, France (AP) — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed opening a path for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member, a striking overture as U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs drive Ottawa closer to Europe.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Rob Gillies, The Associated Press,

Posted September 16, 2026 4:11 am.

Last Updated September 16, 2026 8:57 am.

Strasbourg, France (AP) — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union’s first associate member, a striking overture as U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats drive Ottawa closer to Europe.

Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have soured the relationship between the North American neighbors. Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on the United States, the destination for roughly 70% of its exports, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU.

In her annual State of the European Union address, von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as Ceta, with a broader “Alliance for the Future” aimed at creating “a common prosperity and economic security space.”

She cast that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values.

“Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said to Carney, who received a standing ovation at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He is due to address the Parliament on Thursday.

Canada seeks a relationship just short of EU membership

A Canadian official familiar with the discussions told The Associated Press last week that Ottawa was exploring ties with the EU that could stop just short of membership. The official said Canada would seek an arrangement allowing its citizens to live and work in Europe without visas as part of a broader strategic partnership.

Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said Wednesday that Ottawa had discussed associate membership with European officials before von der Leyen’s speech and “knew that that was something that was on the table.” He said Canada had talked to the EU about an “Alliance for the Future,” while European officials had raised associate membership.

Wilkinson said Canada is not seeking full EU membership because it would require surrendering some sovereignty. Instead, Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc in a way that strengthens Canadian sovereignty rather than diminishes it, he said.

Carney’s office welcomed von der Leyen’s proposal, saying Canada was deepening ties with the EU “to strengthen our sovereignty” and supported a move beyond Ceta.

Canada has already joined the EU’s defense procurement program

Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.

“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”

Because Canada joining the EU as an associate member would be a first, there is no rulebook on how that would work or what it would mean in practice. It is unclear who would need to approve membership, and how long that could take.

Wilkinson said Ottawa and Brussels are deliberately focusing first on the substance of the relationship rather than what to call it. “Before you actually get to the point where you decide what you’re going to call something, you should actually know the shape,” he said.

He said the shape is likely to become clearer at the Canada-EU summit in October, when the two sides expect to make an announcement and May settle on how to describe it.

Currently, all steps toward EU membership must be approved unanimously by the 27 member countries.

The idea of associate membership has been floated in the past for Ukraine , or for post-Brexit Britain, but no concrete steps have been taken.

Beyond trade: Canada and EU explore a broader alliance

The relationship between Canada and the European Union has reached a point where the two sides need to move beyond rhetoric and start building something more substantive, said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament.

“Now is the time to stop sending each other love letters and put meat on the bone,” said Cremer, from the center-left Social Democrats.

He argued that any new arrangement should be more ambitious than another trade or defense agreement, describing the goal as a more holistic strategic alliance between Canada and the EU.

Existing frameworks such as Ceta could provide a foundation, Cremer said, but should be used more fully and expanded. The case for closer ties, he said, is increasingly being driven by geopolitics as much as economics.

The aim, he said, should ultimately be bigger than a bilateral arrangement — potentially positioning the EU as a convener of middle powers, an idea Carney has also raised.

Canada this year became the first non-European country to join the EU’s 150-billion-euro ($173-billion) Safe defense program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe seeks to increase its defense readiness.

Iratxe García Pérez, president of the Socialists & Democrats group in the European Parliament, praised Carney for showing “great courage confronting Donald Trump” and said allies were needed to defend “sovereignty, solidarity and international law.”

Carney said Tuesday that economic integration, once viewed largely as an asset, is increasingly “being used as a weapon by certain countries.” Discussions will ramp up at the Canada-EU summit in late October, he said.

Trump rupture accelerates Canada’s turn toward Europe

Canada has retaliated against U.S. tariffs and rejected trade terms Carney says would weaken its sovereignty.

The EU has taken a different course with Washington, reaching a trade agreement that set a 15% U.S. tariff ceiling on the vast majority of EU exports while Europe eliminated tariffs on U.S. industrial goods.

That contrast has loomed over Carney’s push for closer European ties. In a closely watched speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, he urged middle powers to work together to increase their leverage in an era of great-power rivalry.

“When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered,” Carney said.

“This is not sovereignty,” he said. “It is the performance of sovereignty while accepting subordination.”

Carney’s Davos speech drew a personal rebuke from Trump, and von der Leyen’s overture to America’s neighbor could raise the temperature again.

Associated Press writer Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report.

Rob Gillies, The Associated Press

stories.title: Taxpayer group calls for Carney to cut the cord on CBC, Senate, past GGs
stories.summary: Canada’s leading taxpayers’ watchdog is calling on the Carney government to make about $60-billion in annual spending cuts.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Penticton, B.C. — Canada’s leading taxpayers’ watchdog is calling on the Carney government to make about $60-billion in annual spending cuts, including the end of taxpayer support for corporations, the CBC, the Senate and expense accounts for past governors general.

In its pre-budget recommendations to the federal government, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation (CTF) also calls for slashing the costs of the federal bureaucracy and Parliament itself as part of a plan to make government more affordable and to reduce the costs of the fast-growing federal debt.

“The massive accumulation of debt is due to a government spending problem, not revenue problem,” the Ctf’s submission states.

The document, obtained by National Post, is to be released later this month. The non-profit’s roster of recommendations marks one of the boldest pre-budget submissions to date.

The Ctf’s suggested plan also includes (with projected annual savings where available) cutting the government’s planned high-speed rail project, campaign reimbursements for political parties and candidates ($85 million) and the corporate carbon tax.

It also recommends returning salaries and benefits for federal politicians to 2020 levels, cutting pensions for new MPs and second pension for prime ministers, and budgets for governor generals and their offices, down by 50 per cent, including reducing the GG’s salary to that of cabinet ministers ($264,000). It would also cut tax credits for political contributions ($35 million)

The CTF plan also calls for the public service to be cut to pre-2020 levels, plus inflation ($16 billion), to cut consultants, contractors and other outsourcing to 2015-16 levels, plus inflation ($16 billion), along with regional development agencies ($1.9 billion) and to cut crown corporations, down by 25 per cent ($3 billion). The government is trying to achieve a delicate push-and-pull where it increases spending, particularly on infrastructure, defence and other priority items, while making the economy more competitive through tax cuts and other efforts to boost growth and investment.

As Prime Minister Mark Carney meets this week with international investors in Toronto to try to spark more interest in the Canadian economy, sky-high federal deficits, and the accumulated debt, are adding extra pressure on the government to cut costs.

stories.title: Élections Québec asked government to change French-language laws in 2023
stories.summary: Montreal - Élections Québec knew it would not be allowed to send voter information in English over a year before the electoral campaign, The Canadian Press has learned.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Élections Québec knew it would not be allowed to send voter information in English over a year before the electoral campaign, The Canadian Press has learned.

The provincial election authority had tried to pressure the government to amend its language laws – even providing proposed wording – but the government refused, according to correspondence sent between April 2023 and June 2025.

The deadline for Élections Québec to finalize its voting reminder cards in English is rapidly approaching, with a court process underway to force the agency to mail information in English.

The provincial elections authority had to comply with 2022 language legislation making French the sole language of communication for public institutions. Earlier this month, it sent out unilingual voter documents for the first time in its history.

The agency’s director, Jean-François Blanchet, had told the government as early as April 2023 he worried the new rules would encroach on Charter rights and Élections Québec’s core mission.

Blanchet raised concerns around the right to vote, the right to representation, and the possibility that results could be contested in his correspondence with the French-language commissioner.

Over two years, the Élections Québec, the commissioner and the ministry of the French language corresponded and met several times to address the issue.

Ultimately, voter guides and information cards were only printed and mailed out in French. The guide includes a QR code to access information in English online.

Advocacy groups for anglophone rights denounced Elections Quebec’s decision to send unilingual documents, and a group of lawyers launched a legal challenge.

The case was heard last week and a decision is expected to come in shortly.

In court, Henrick Lavoie, the lawyer representing Élections Québec, said it might still be possible to send out a voting reminder card in English if the court issues an order to that effect by Sept. 16. The list of candidates is finalized at 2 p.m. on Sept. 17 and the agency had already planned to print out reminder cards to mail out after that deadline.

Here is a timeline of the conversations that led to the case.

About a month after Benoît Dubreuil became Quebec’s French-language commissioner in March 2023, Blanchet sent him an email requesting a meeting. In his letter dated April 6, 2023, Blanchet wrote that Élections Québec was working to ensure it met its responsibilities under the Charter of the French Language.

“This work raises questions that we would like to discuss, particularly in light of our institution’s mission, which is to ensure that all voters can exercise their right to vote,” wrote Blanchet.

Dubreuil’s assistant wrote back that same day to organize a meeting to brief Blanchet on the latest guidelines.

Subsequent correspondence indicates there were at least two meetings held in May, with Dubreuil and the heads of various government institutions, including Blanchet, in attendance.

Dubreuil suggested those who attended those meetings name a representative to form a working group on the implementation of the Charter of the French Language in their institutions.

The law says the commissioner of the French language “must support and assist the parliamentary institutions to which the state’s language policy applies in fulfilling their obligations,” wrote Dubreuil.

According to his agenda, the committee would also discuss possible exceptions to the rules.

Blanchet happily agreed and reiterated his concerns surrounding the right to vote and the right to representation.

“How can we reconcile the application of the provisions of the Charter of the French Language while ensuring that citizens can fully exercise their rights to vote or run for office?” he wrote.

While discussions were underway, a byelection was scheduled for Oct. 2, 2023, in the riding of Jean-Talon. Blanchet once again wrote to Dubreuil, telling him Élections Québec would use temporary provisions in the legislation that would allow it to mail bilingual documents.

“All voters must be able to understand the information they need to fully exercise those rights,” Blanchet wrote.

He added he hoped to discuss exempting Élections Québec from some provisions of the law to “balance the fulfilment of our mission with the provisions of the Charter of the French Language” in the coming months.

An adviser for the commissioner emailed the members of the working group, saying the ministry of the French language was seeking their input on draft legislation.

The ministry was looking to amend the language regulation for government agencies and had sent a form for them to fill out.

A few days later, Blanchet sent his form back to Dubreuil, which was mostly redacted in the documents obtained by The Canadian Press, to be forwarded to the ministry.

Blanchet had requested the ministry permanently exempt the elections agency from its laws forcing it to communicate in French only. A temporary provision allowing it to send bilingual documents was set to expire in June 2025, but was later extended.

Blanchet suggested the ministry amend its regulation to allow government agencies to deviate from the Charter of the French Language “to ensure respect for the right to vote and the right to run for office in a provincial, municipal, or school election or a referendum.”

Blanchet also requested a meeting with Jean-François Roberge, the minister of the French language. Later correspondence indicates the two spoke on March 11, 2025.

Blanchet reached out to Roberge directly, a few weeks after the government made public its amendments to the French-language laws. Those amendments would not exempt Élections Québec from having to issue all communications in French only.

The temporary provisions allowing it to send bilingual documents expired in December 2025 – after the Montreal municipal election and before the 2026 provincial election.

In his email, Blanchet said he anticipated “significant consequences” that could affect Quebec’s democracy. He worried that anglophones and allophones May not show up at the ballot “because of the extra efforts and steps they would have to take” to obtain and understand crucial information.

“Encouraging the public to exercise their right to vote is already a challenge,” he wrote.

He added that there could be legal challenges regarding the validity of the election as a result.

Blanchet received an answer from Roberge’s deputy ministers, saying he would not extend the temporary provisions allowing it to provide bilingual voter information.

“Elections can no longer be conducted in both French and English, as was previously the case,” wrote deputy minister Nathaly Marcoux. “This is a decision made by the legislature.”

She said the government and Élections Québec would continue discussions to find solutions that would respect French-language laws.

Élections Québec announced it would mail out voter information in French only, and that those eligible to receive English education and Indigenous people could contact the agency for English information.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.

stories.title: Secrecy and accountability 'can coexist': groups push for Tumbler Ridge gun details
stories.summary: Ottawa - Five gun control advocacy groups are renewing pressure on the RCMP to disclose information about the firearms used in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., saying public discussion of the details could help prevent another tragedy.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
People attend a vigil for the victims of a mass shooting, in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., Friday, Feb. 13, 2026.

Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press file photo

Canada

Ottawa - Five gun control advocacy groups are renewing pressure on the RCMP to disclose information about the firearms used in the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., saying public discussion of the details could help prevent another tragedy.
