stories.title: Read Stephen Harper's full speech on the need for Canada to defend its sovereignty against the U.S.
stories.summary: Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper delivered the closing speech at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper delivered the closing speech at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday. The summit was organized by the Liberal government and hosted in partnership with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments). Harper, who currently serves as chairman of the Alberta Investment Management Corporation and is co-founder of the investment fund Vision-One Management, said that Canada was right to walk away from trade talks “must pursue diminished reliance upon the United States” to maintain its sovereignty. Read the full text of the English portions of Harper’s speech, below.

Thank you very much…. Distinguished guests from Canada and around the world, it is an honour to address you today and to formally conclude this summit. I want to express my appreciation on behalf of myself, and on behalf of the 20th prime minister of Canada, the Right Honourable Jean Chrétien. I want to express our appreciation to the organizers at CPP, at PSP, and the Government of Canada for inviting us here, and also for giving me the podium today.

The prime minister said to me yesterday, “I really want to thank you for doing this.” I said, “Well, you May want to wait and see what I’m going to say, first.” I used a line from from that famous British TV show, I said, “You know, I am a partisan appointment. Your decision to give me a microphone is a courageous decision, prime minister.”

In any case, I’ve been delighted to attend this event, and even more pleased to see so many familiar faces in this room today. I have met with many of you in your own countries these past few years, and I consider you friends. And I thank you, each and every one of you, for making the journey to spend this time here with us in Canada. I consider your attendance an act of friendship and a vote of confidence in our country at a crucial time.

Now I know that, as board chair of the Alberta Investment Management Corporation, you expect me to speak about Canada as an investment destination, and I will. I tell people at AIMCo, we are not an economic development fund. We are global investors. We seek the best returns from anywhere that we can for our clients. And for all those reasons, we have over 40 per cent of our investments in this country, so we see lots of opportunity in Canada. That’s my AIMCo hat.

However, I am also a former prime minister, and as such, I cannot help but address the current situation that Canada faces. It is a situation in which, given the ongoing violations of our trade agreement by the United States and the current impasse in negotiations, our country felt compelled to walk away and to see a trade war commence in earnest…. This had to be a very difficult decision, but I do believe that our government had no choice but to take this path.

I say that, as one who has long been, and known to be, a great admirer of America, and one who believes that our close proximity and close relationship to the United States has been among this country’s most precious assets.

However, it is clear that the current U.S. administration views our level of economic integration as incompatible with our separate sovereignty. Thus, to maintain that sovereignty, we must pursue diminished reliance upon the United States. There will be significant costs to this effort, but those are costs that I hope and believe Canadians are able and prepared to accept.

I find this all, I do find this all very sad, just as equally necessary. And I believe that, in this necessity, our country will also discover, and is discovering, opportunity…. It is an opportunity for Canada to rediscover a long-term agenda for economic prosperity, an opportunity to realize our true potential as a country, which I believe, to be frank, we have come nowhere close to achieving.

We in this room all know very well that this is a competitive world, fraught with shifting politics, fragile supply chains, and other transactional pressures, now more so than recent decades. In the face of such change, Canada cannot simply blame external factors or make other excuses to explain away the difficulties that we face. Leadership is defined by taking accountability for what you can control.

And today, more than ever, Canada must become more internally competitive, more externally connected, and more truly sovereign than it has been. That is the opportunity.

And obviously, I do want to speak about the Canadian economy. Canada possesses — I know you’ve heard it throughout the conference — Canada possesses a unique economic structure and therefore unique opportunities.

We have a healthy economic presence across the full range of economic activities: primary, secondary, tertiary, advanced technology. We must be committed to retaining this incredible economic diversity, and we cannot allow the Trump administration to hollow out our industrial capacities.

Yet, despite this economic diversity, it remains my view that our resource endowment is our special comparative advantage. We have abundant resources, renewable and non-renewable, of every type, way beyond our conceivable needs in almost every category.

Further, these resources are found in an unmatched rule of law business environment with the highest of environmental standards and far removed from conflict zones. That is a comparative advantage.

Now, I’m going to keep my comments brief, so I want to focus on one thing. I know that at AIMCo we are rightly known as one of the Maple 8, but dare I say that we are also the Wild Rose 1. That is, the sole major fund based in the province of Alberta. So allow me to speak a bit from that perspective, particularly from the perspective from Alberta’s position as the centre of the country’s energy industry…. As I said repeatedly when I was Canada’s prime minister, Canada should be an energy superpower. Whatever the energy mix of the future, Canada should be a major and a global supplier.

We are fifth largest in the world in natural gas production, fourth in the production of oil. Notes say fourth in oil reserves — (Suncor Energy CEO) Rich Kruger says third, I’ll take that. He knows more than I do.

We are third in hydroelectricity. We are second in uranium. All of it today from Saskatchewan, which, with the development of new mines there, will make us the largest global producer within a few years. Great credit for that is, by the way, due to Premier (Scott) Moe and the government of Saskatchewan.

And by the way, we are not just a uranium miner; we are a builder and refurbisher of nuclear reactors with a world-leading regulatory review agency for the development of SMRs (small modular reactors).

And of course, as a country, we have plenty of investments in biofuels and renewables, and we possess the raw materials necessary for further development of those sectors.

In 2015, Canada was poised to become that energy superpower. Today, we are not. Why? Because of deliberate policy choices that followed over the next decade.

But there is no point bemoaning what is past, especially because the opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again.

I do congratulate our current federal government on the measures it has taken to fast-track major project approvals, especially for projects in the oil sands. These changes are welcome and they are very important.

However, more does need to be done. The burdens and restrictions that do not exist elsewhere simply must be removed in Canada. And we need to provide comprehensive reform, regulatory reviews, and permitting processes, so that Canada can provide investors with the certainty of a science-based decision on both resource and related infrastructure projects within a fixed and reasonable time frame, as we had set up a decade ago.

The opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again

Ironically, if we do not do these things as a country, the Americans will continue to be our sole customers, and they will not lack the urgency that we have lacked here in Canada. Nor will many others in the world.

That is why I have to say that I am very encouraged by the detailed comments the prime minister made today on doing just some of these things, and I welcome them.

I believe that Canada’s new government is committed to further reforms in these areas, and committed to their urgency. And I know that our premier, Premier (Danielle) Smith, will continue using that what we call “Alberta diplomacy” to remind our federal government of that.

Because becoming that energy superpower is no longer just good business. Not only, my view, good politics. It is critical to our prosperity and indeed to our survival as a country. Critical to raising our horizons beyond narrow domestic considerations to address global opportunities and imperatives.

And to be blunt, we need not worry about demand from either customers or investors, as I have been reminded by many of you in this room and others around the world for a decade. The world is developing an unprecedented demand for energy in all its forms, and they want it from Canada, provided we want to get it out of the ground and sell it.

But this is not just about other markets. We need this energy not only for its export potential. We also need it right here in Canada for our own reindustrialization and technological innovation, as well as, of course, as a critical signal that Canada is indeed once again a serious investment destination.

And that brings me back to the purpose of this conference.

As I’ve said, we are honoured that you have joined us. I congratulate the federal government for holding this conference — I believe the first of its kind in Canada.

It is such a great innovation that I wish I had thought of it. But we all know that it is only a start, and to realize its potential, we need ongoing determination and urgency here in Canada.

I do hope that this conference, I do hope that this conference is not a one-off. I think this conference needs to become regular, and we need your input, delegates from everywhere. We need your input to make it bigger and better going forward.

Now, just in conclusion, I know that you all have come here to discuss commercial opportunities, but it is my hope that in these conversations, you have deepened the trust and affirmed the values upon which commercial partnerships are built.

Because friends, this country offers something even more precious than our abundant raw resources and our plentiful business opportunities. It offers a mindset of respect, of collaboration, and of partnership.

No matter their industry, Canadians are fundamentally in the business of building trusted partnerships that benefit both sides. This orientation for partnership has been in Canada’s DNA since our confederation was first established In 1867.

It is chiseled in our national character, like the granite of the Canadian Shield, and it flows across the boundless expanse of our fresh water. It is also the cornerstone of real value creation, and in that vein, I hope that this gathering is merely the beginning of building such partnerships.

In the meanwhile, I really do want to thank all of you once again, each and every one of you, for coming here. Godspeed wherever your travels May take you next.

Merci beaucoup…. God bless Canada.

I have met with many of you in your own countries these past few years, and I consider you friends. And I thank you, each and every one of you, for making the journey to spend this time here with us in Canada. I consider your attendance an act of friendship and a vote of confidence in our country at a crucial time.

Now I know that, as board chair of the Alberta Investment Management Corporation, you expect me to speak about Canada as an investment destination, and I will. I tell people at AIMCo, we are not an economic development fund. We are global investors. We seek the best returns from anywhere that we can for our clients. And for all those reasons, we have over 40 per cent of our investments in this country, so we see lots of opportunity in Canada. That’s my AIMCo hat.

However, I am also a former prime minister, and as such, I cannot help but address the current situation that Canada faces. It is a situation in which, given the ongoing violations of our trade agreement by the United States and the current impasse in negotiations, our country felt compelled to walk away and to see a trade war commence in earnest…. This had to be a very difficult decision, but I do believe that our government had no choice but to take this path.

I say that, as one who has long been, and known to be, a great admirer of America, and one who believes that our close proximity and close relationship to the United States has been among this country’s most precious assets.

However, it is clear that the current U.S. administration views our level of economic integration as incompatible with our separate sovereignty. Thus, to maintain that sovereignty, we must pursue diminished reliance upon the United States. There will be significant costs to this effort, but those are costs that I hope and believe Canadians are able and prepared to accept.

I find this all, I do find this all very sad, just as equally necessary. And I believe that, in this necessity, our country will also discover, and is discovering, opportunity…. It is an opportunity for Canada to rediscover a long-term agenda for economic prosperity, an opportunity to realize our true potential as a country, which I believe, to be frank, we have come nowhere close to achieving.

We in this room all know very well that this is a competitive world, fraught with shifting politics, fragile supply chains, and other transactional pressures, now more so than recent decades. In the face of such change, Canada cannot simply blame external factors or make other excuses to explain away the difficulties that we face. Leadership is defined by taking accountability for what you can control.
And today, more than ever, Canada must become more internally competitive, more externally connected, and more truly sovereign than it has been. That is the opportunity.

And obviously, I do want to speak about the Canadian economy. Canada possesses — I know you’ve heard it throughout the conference — Canada possesses a unique economic structure and therefore unique opportunities.

We have a healthy economic presence across the full range of economic activities: primary, secondary, tertiary, advanced technology. We must be committed to retaining this incredible economic diversity, and we cannot allow the Trump administration to hollow out our industrial capacities.

Yet, despite this economic diversity, it remains my view that our resource endowment is our special comparative advantage. We have abundant resources, renewable and non-renewable, of every type, way beyond our conceivable needs in almost every category.
Further, these resources are found in an unmatched rule of law business environment with the highest of environmental standards and far removed from conflict zones. That is a comparative advantage.

Now, I’m going to keep my comments brief, so I want to focus on one thing. I know that at AIMCo we are rightly known as one of the Maple 8, but dare I say that we are also the Wild Rose 1. That is, the sole major fund based in the province of Alberta. So allow me to speak a bit from that perspective, particularly from the perspective from Alberta’s position as the centre of the country’s energy industry…. As I said repeatedly when I was Canada’s prime minister, Canada should be an energy superpower. Whatever the energy mix of the future, Canada should be a major and a global supplier.

We are fifth largest in the world in natural gas production, fourth in the production of oil. Notes say fourth in oil reserves — (Suncor Energy CEO) Rich Kruger says third, I’ll take that. He knows more than I do.

We are third in hydroelectricity. We are second in uranium. All of it today from Saskatchewan, which, with the development of new mines there, will make us the largest global producer within a few years. Great credit for that is, by the way, due to Premier (Scott) Moe and the government of Saskatchewan.

And by the way, we are not just a uranium miner; we are a builder and refurbisher of nuclear reactors with a world-leading regulatory review agency for the development of SMRs (small modular reactors).
And of course, as a country, we have plenty of investments in biofuels and renewables, and we possess the raw materials necessary for further development of those sectors.
In 2015, Canada was poised to become that energy superpower. Today, we are not. Why? Because of deliberate policy choices that followed over the next decade.
But there is no point bemoaning what is past, especially because the opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again.

I do congratulate our current federal government on the measures it has taken to fast-track major project approvals, especially for projects in the oil sands. These changes are welcome and they are very important.

However, more does need to be done. The burdens and restrictions that do not exist elsewhere simply must be removed in Canada. And we need to provide comprehensive reform, regulatory reviews, and permitting processes, so that Canada can provide investors with the certainty of a science-based decision on both resource and related infrastructure projects within a fixed and reasonable time frame, as we had set up a decade ago.
The opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again

Ironically, if we do not do these things as a country, the Americans will continue to be our sole customers, and they will not lack the urgency that we have lacked here in Canada. Nor will many others in the world.
That is why I have to say that I am very encouraged by the detailed comments the prime minister made today on doing just some of these things, and I welcome them.

I believe that Canada’s new government is committed to further reforms in these areas, and committed to their urgency. And I know that our premier, Premier (Danielle) Smith, will continue using that what we call “Alberta diplomacy” to remind our federal government of that.

Because becoming that energy superpower is no longer just good business. Not only, my view, good politics. It is critical to our prosperity and indeed to our survival as a country. Critical to raising our horizons beyond narrow domestic considerations to address global opportunities and imperatives.

And to be blunt, we need not worry about demand from either customers or investors, as I have been reminded by many of you in this room and others around the world for a decade. The world is developing an unprecedented demand for energy in all its forms, and they want it from Canada, provided we want to get it out of the ground and sell it.

But this is not just about other markets. We need this energy not only for its export potential. We also need it right here in Canada for our own reindustrialization and technological innovation, as well as, of course, as a critical signal that Canada is indeed once again a serious investment destination.
And that brings me back to the purpose of this conference.
As I’ve said, we are honoured that you have joined us. I congratulate the federal government for holding this conference — I believe the first of its kind in Canada.
It is such a great innovation that I wish I had thought of it. But we all know that it is only a start, and to realize its potential, we need ongoing determination and urgency here in Canada.

I do hope that this conference, I do hope that this conference is not a one-off. I think this conference needs to become regular, and we need your input, delegates from everywhere. We need your input to make it bigger and better going forward.

Now, just in conclusion, I know that you all have come here to discuss commercial opportunities, but it is my hope that in these conversations, you have deepened the trust and affirmed the values upon which commercial partnerships are built.

Because friends, this country offers something even more precious than our abundant raw resources and our plentiful business opportunities. It offers a mindset of respect, of collaboration, and of partnership.

No matter their industry, Canadians are fundamentally in the business of building trusted partnerships that benefit both sides. This orientation for partnership has been in Canada’s DNA since our confederation was first established In 1867.

It is chiseled in our national character, like the granite of the Canadian Shield, and it flows across the boundless expanse of our fresh water. It is also the cornerstone of real value creation, and in that vein, I hope that this gathering is merely the beginning of building such partnerships.
In the meanwhile, I really do want to thank all of you once again, each and every one of you, for coming here. Godspeed wherever your travels May take you next.
Merci beaucoup…. God bless Canada.

stories.title: Harper lauds Carney government’s efforts to diversify trade in closing speech at investment summit
stories.summary: The former prime minister also praised Ottawa for course-correcting Canada’s bid to become an energy superpower
stories.author: Stephanie Levitz, Bill Curry
stories.content:
Former prime minister Stephen Harper said Canada had no choice but to walk away from trade talks with the United States as he endorsed the Carney government’s efforts to diversify the economy while taking a swipe at the past Liberal government’s energy policies.

Mr. Harper said it was clear to him that the U.S. views economic integration between the two countries as incompatible with Canada’s sovereignty, a state of affairs he described as “sad,” in his remarks to close out a global investment summit, organized by the Carney government to boost the economy.

“It leaves no choice but for Canada to pursue diminished reliance on the U.S.,” Mr. Harper said.

“There will be significant costs to this effort, but those are costs that I hope and believe Canadians are able and prepared to accept.”

Canada Investment Summit Day 2: Carney announces corporate tax ‘mega deduction’ and plan to open airports to private investors

Mr. Harper’s comments were made during a rare public appearance at the end of a full day’s worth of discussions among global and domestic private and public sector investors, CEOs and other high-profile financiers about investment opportunities and challenges for Canada.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a goal to raise $1-trillion in new investment over the next five years and said the Toronto summit resulted in nearly $500-billion in new commitments.

Mr. Carney said earlier in the day Mr. Harper was invited because he holds influence with business leaders and investors, and because he is also a patriot – a nod to the spirit of national unity organizers have tried to infuse into the event at the Four Seasons Hotel.

“The world’s looking at Canada differently, and we should look, I’d suggest, at ourselves differently too,” Mr. Carney said.

Mr. Harper, who is also board chair for the Alberta Investment Management Corp., said the summit was such a good idea, he wished he’d thought of it first.

Former prime minister Stephen Harper says the federal government had no choice but to walk away from trade talks with the United States. While delivering closing remarks at Canada's first-ever national investment summit, Harper said the move was necessary and that Canada needs to reduce its reliance on the United States.

The Canadian Press

The aside captured the continuing like-mindedness of Canada’s 22nd prime minister and its current one; Mr. Carney was appointed as the Bank of Canada governor by Mr. Harper, and the two speak regularly.

Mr. Harper also lauded Mr. Carney for course-correcting Canada’s bid to become an energy superpower, something Mr. Harper had tried to do until his party lost power in 2015 to the Trudeau Liberals.

“In 2015, Canada was poised to become that energy superpower. Today, we are not. Why? Because of deliberate policy choices that followed over the next decade,” Mr. Harper said.

Foreign investors optimistic about changing Canadian investment environment

He noted that the Carney government is now changing its approach, citing an announcement Tuesday about ensuring approvals will only take a year as an example, but he said he believes the government is committed to do more.

The Trudeau-era approach to natural resources development is routinely cited by the Alberta separatist movement as one of the reasons they believe the province should break off from Canada. Mr. Carney has sought to reset that narrative by embracing oil and gas development and is working with the Alberta government toward a new pipeline.

Mr. Harper did not explicitly reference the Oct. 19 referendum on separation in his home province, but said Premier Danielle Smith would continue to push Ottawa for more reforms to energy policy.

“Becoming that energy superpower is no longer just good business. Not only, in my view, good politics,” he said.

“It is critical to our prosperity.”

Current Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has continuously questioned the Carney government’s promises for regulatory reform and commitment to energy development.

He was asked earlier Tuesday by reporters in Vancouver whether Mr. Harper’s appearance at the summit undercuts his own message.

“No, it doesn’t,” he said, adding that he had spoken to Mr. Harper about the event a few days earlier.

“Conservatives are always willing to put Canada first and will work with anybody.”

List of announcements coming out of the Canada Investment Summit

Last week, Mr. Poilievre travelled to the U.S. to pitch Americans on stronger ties with Canada.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew told reporters that Mr. Harper’s appearance at the event signals national unity.

“I think Donald Trump is a reminder that the differences between Canadians when it comes to politics are pretty minor compared to what’s going on around the world,” Mr. Kinew said at a news conference in Toronto on Tuesday.

Former Liberal prime minister Jean Chrétien was also spotted in and around the event.

Critics of the investment summit, however, have argued that Mr. Carney’s government is undermining national unity by selling out to global investors.

“You don’t save Canada by selling it off piece by piece,” NDP Leader Avi Lewis said in a statement e-mailed to reporters.

“Protecting our sovereignty means keeping our airports in public hands.”

B.C. Premier David Eby said the discussions happening at the summit come at a crucial time.

Opinion: Mark Carney’s investment moment

“This is a discussion that’s taking place about investment in Canada to build up jobs, opportunity, and Canada’s resources to raise the prosperity of the entire country, and to defend us against an unjustified attack from the United States and Donald Trump,” he said at a news conference outside the summit.

“This is about diversifying away from the United States. It is inspirational.”

Mr. Harper told the attendees he hopes the take-away from the event is not just the commercial discussions but the change to deepen the trust and values upon which business relationships are built.

“This country offers something even more precious than our abundant raw resources and our plentiful business opportunities,” he said.

“It offers a mindset of respect, of collaboration, and of partnership.”

– with a report from Laura Stone

stories.title: Foreign investors optimistic about changing Canadian investment environment
stories.summary: CEOs say the country’s trusted reputation is intact, but are waiting to see tangible signs of the country’s economy waking up
stories.author: James Bradshaw, Stefanie Marotta
stories.content:
Chief executives from powerful global investors say Canada’s efforts to attract capital have captured their attention, and now the country needs to deliver quickly on its promises.

The CEOs emerged from two days of frenetic meetings at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto signalling their optimism that the cumbersome Canadian investment environment they had encountered in previous deals is on the cusp of changing for the better.

“Canada is a bit of a sleeping giant, economically,” Blackstone Inc. president and chief operating officer Jon Gray, who oversees US$1.3-trillion of assets, said during a panel discussion on Tuesday.

In comments on and offstage, several CEOs said the country’s trusted reputation is intact, and contrasts well against a backdrop of volatility and uncertainty sweeping through trade relationships and financial markets.

Executives are eyeing ways to invest capital in coveted Canadian resources, such as critical minerals, natural gas and clean energy, as well as in the country’s untapped capacity to build and power data centres.

Canada Investment Summit Day 2: Carney announces corporate tax 'mega deduction'; Harper closes with optimistic keynote

But those CEOs are waiting to see tangible signs of Canada’s economy waking up, including a deeper pipeline of investable projects, regulatory and permitting barriers coming down, and a more generous tax framework.

“The regulation, the permitting, the taxation – all well-intended,” Mr. Gray said, “but people didn’t think about the cumulative impact.”

The summit, led by Prime Minister Mark Carney and two of the country’s largest pension funds, drew roughly 250 CEOs and top executives to Toronto for two days of meetings, dinners and receptions.

It was also a platform for Ottawa to announce tax incentives, such as an expanded, upfront “mega deduction” on investment costs, and launch a process to allow private investment in airports .

“There’s a level of urgency and there’s a level of ambition,” said John Graham, CEO of the $864-billion Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and a summit co-organizer, in an interview. “The most important thing is now we’ve got to maintain this momentum.”

Opinion: Mark Carney’s investment moment

BlackRock Inc. CEO Larry Fink, sitting next to Mr. Gray on stage on Tuesday, said the demand to build new infrastructure is increasingly outpacing available investment capital, ramping up already fierce competition for dollars.

And BlackRock, which manages US$15.3-trillion, has historically “been challenged in finding deals within Canada itself,” he said.

But if Mr. Carney and Canadian CEOs can deliver on what they promised at the summit, “even in this more challenging world for supply of capital, Canada will be a large beneficiary,” Mr. Fink said.

In particular, surging demand to build AI infrastructure and computing capacity presents an opportunity for Canada that the country has not yet fully tapped.

“We’re waiting to see those projects. We’re ready to put the money in the ground,” Mr. Fink said.

List of announcements coming out of the Canada Investment Summit

Annette Mosman, the CEO of €639-billion Dutch pension fund APG Group, said she was impressed by Mr. Carney’s narrative linking politics and policy “in terms of getting things done.”

Energy, advanced technology and defence are familiar themes for European investors, Ms. Mosman said in an interview. “I think Canada now is a bit quicker compared to Europe, making it more tangible,” she said.

The federal government’s openness to private investment in its four largest airports – in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and Calgary – is early proof “there are more concrete, investable assets” on the table, she said.

Christian Sewing, CEO of Germany’s largest bank, Deutsche Bank AG, said on a panel that Canada’s efforts to attract investment and bolster the economy have been “heroic.” He took notes from the summit on what the German government needs to do to “top” Canada when it holds its own investment summit next month.

As geopolitical turmoil has escalated, global investors have shifted their approach in the past year, emphasizing democratic values, independent institutions and reliability – all of which they can find in Canada. The country is “on the map” and more important than ever as investors seek out new opportunities to diversify their portfolios, he said.

Read the full transcript of Mark Carney’s speech at the Canada Investment Summit

This is a major reason Deutsche Bank and major German investors, including state-owned development bank Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau, travelled to Canada to attend the summit, he said. However, the ability to execute is the greatest hurdle that Canada faces.

“You have the capital, you have the skills, you have the resources, and in my view, you have something which the Prime Minister again and again emphasized – you have trust and values. In the times we are living, the latter point is so important,” Mr. Sewing said.

“What you really need to show over the next four months is delivery.”

Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the rupture in Canada-U.S. trade and bilateral relations is likely to be felt in border states in the U.S., and that political discussions are taking place in states including Vermont, Maine and Michigan. Ultimately, he said, this is a chance for Canada to make improvements to trade.

“This is an opportunity to correct an imbalance,” he said on a panel.

French asset manager Ardian SAS already has about $7-billion invested in Canada and a Montreal office with 30 staff. Co-CEO Mark Benedetti, who is Canadian-born and based in New York, said in an interview he is “really seriously” considering launching a fund to invest in Canada’s middle market.

“What I found about this summit today is a real sense of optimism,” he said.

And that was “not just from the top down, from the government, from Prime Minister Carney,” he said, “but from all of my peer investors.”
paragraphs: Chief executives from powerful global investors say Canada’s efforts to attract capital have captured their attention, and now the country needs to deliver quickly on its promises.

The CEOs emerged from two days of frenetic meetings at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto signalling their optimism that the cumbersome Canadian investment environment they had encountered in previous deals is on the cusp of changing for the better.
“Canada is a bit of a sleeping giant, economically,” Blackstone Inc. president and chief operating officer Jon Gray, who oversees US$1.3-trillion of assets, said during a panel discussion on Tuesday.

In comments on and offstage, several CEOs said the country’s trusted reputation is intact, and contrasts well against a backdrop of volatility and uncertainty sweeping through trade relationships and financial markets.

Executives are eyeing ways to invest capital in coveted Canadian resources, such as critical minerals, natural gas and clean energy, as well as in the country’s untapped capacity to build and power data centres.
Canada Investment Summit Day 2: Carney announces corporate tax 'mega deduction'; Harper closes with optimistic keynote

But those CEOs are waiting to see tangible signs of Canada’s economy waking up, including a deeper pipeline of investable projects, regulatory and permitting barriers coming down, and a more generous tax framework.
“The regulation, the permitting, the taxation – all well-intended,” Mr. Gray said, “but people didn’t think about the cumulative impact.”
The summit, led by Prime Minister Mark Carney and two of the country’s largest pension funds, drew roughly 250 CEOs and top executives to Toronto for two days of meetings, dinners and receptions.
It was also a platform for Ottawa to announce tax incentives, such as an expanded, upfront “mega deduction” on investment costs, and launch a process to allow private investment in airports .

“There’s a level of urgency and there’s a level of ambition,” said John Graham, CEO of the $864-billion Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and a summit co-organizer, in an interview. “The most important thing is now we’ve got to maintain this momentum.”
Opinion: Mark Carney’s investment moment

BlackRock Inc. CEO Larry Fink, sitting next to Mr. Gray on stage on Tuesday, said the demand to build new infrastructure is increasingly outpacing available investment capital, ramping up already fierce competition for dollars.
And BlackRock, which manages US$15.3-trillion, has historically “been challenged in finding deals within Canada itself,” he said.
But if Mr. Carney and Canadian CEOs can deliver on what they promised at the summit, “even in this more challenging world for supply of capital, Canada will be a large beneficiary,” Mr. Fink said.
In particular, surging demand to build AI infrastructure and computing capacity presents an opportunity for Canada that the country has not yet fully tapped.
“We’re waiting to see those projects. We’re ready to put the money in the ground,” Mr. Fink said.
List of announcements coming out of the Canada Investment Summit
Annette Mosman, the CEO of €639-billion Dutch pension fund APG Group, said she was impressed by Mr. Carney’s narrative linking politics and policy “in terms of getting things done.”

Energy, advanced technology and defence are familiar themes for European investors, Ms. Mosman said in an interview. “I think Canada now is a bit quicker compared to Europe, making it more tangible,” she said.

The federal government’s openness to private investment in its four largest airports – in Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal and Calgary – is early proof “there are more concrete, investable assets” on the table, she said.

Christian Sewing, CEO of Germany’s largest bank, Deutsche Bank AG, said on a panel that Canada’s efforts to attract investment and bolster the economy have been “heroic.” He took notes from the summit on what the German government needs to do to “top” Canada when it holds its own investment summit next month.

As geopolitical turmoil has escalated, global investors have shifted their approach in the past year, emphasizing democratic values, independent institutions and reliability – all of which they can find in Canada. The country is “on the map” and more important than ever as investors seek out new opportunities to diversify their portfolios, he said.
Read the full transcript of Mark Carney’s speech at the Canada Investment Summit

This is a major reason Deutsche Bank and major German investors, including state-owned development bank Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau, travelled to Canada to attend the summit, he said. However, the ability to execute is the greatest hurdle that Canada faces.

“You have the capital, you have the skills, you have the resources, and in my view, you have something which the Prime Minister again and again emphasized – you have trust and values. In the times we are living, the latter point is so important,” Mr. Sewing said.
“What you really need to show over the next four months is delivery.”

Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan said the rupture in Canada-U.S. trade and bilateral relations is likely to be felt in border states in the U.S., and that political discussions are taking place in states including Vermont, Maine and Michigan. Ultimately, he said, this is a chance for Canada to make improvements to trade.
“This is an opportunity to correct an imbalance,” he said on a panel.

French asset manager Ardian SAS already has about $7-billion invested in Canada and a Montreal office with 30 staff. Co-CEO Mark Benedetti, who is Canadian-born and based in New York, said in an interview he is “really seriously” considering launching a fund to invest in Canada’s middle market.
“What I found about this summit today is a real sense of optimism,” he said.
And that was “not just from the top down, from the government, from Prime Minister Carney,” he said, “but from all of my peer investors.”

stories.title: How deal making gets done at the Canada Investment Summit, a ‘massive catalyst’ for growth
stories.summary: If good relationships were seeded in Toronto, that could influence power players from around the globe to take ideas to their investment committees
stories.author: Tim Kiladze
stories.content:
Early on the first morning of the inaugural Canada Investment Summit, a senior executive at one of the country’s Big Six banks sauntered over to share some advice, informed by his experiences at global conferences such as the World Economic Forum in Davos.

“You don’t even need to watch the panels,” he said in a private conversation. “The lobby is where it’s at.”

In this case, it was the wood-panelled lobby outside the Park Hyatt ballroom in Yorkville, the ritzy Toronto neighbourhood that hosted hundreds of institutional investors this week.

The event that morning was a mini-forum put together by the Milken Institute and its speaker lineup was legitimate, including Jenny Johnson, the CEO of Franklin Templeton Investments, and Jack Neumark, the co-CEO of Fortress Investment Group. But everyone there seemed to be thrilled about getting lost in the sea of navy-blue and grey suits that formed at every break in programming.

Foreign investors optimistic about changing Canadian investment environment

In a way, it was a parable for the entire summit. Technically, the signature event was an all-day conference at the Four Seasons Hotel on Tuesday. But its guest list of foreign investors, Canadian CEOs and politicians was incredibly selective. So, there were spillover events, including a private dinner hosted by TD Bank on Sunday evening and a sushi-and-cocktail reception hosted by Torys LLP on Monday. In total, there were dozens of them, and they served a unique purpose.

In the old days, a billion-dollar deal might get hashed at the bar. In this era, sophisticated investment funds have risk and investment committees that prevent handshake deals from happening (often for good reason). The real draw of a conference like the Investment Summit, then, is bringing together power players and letting them cook.

The institutional investors that Canada hosted this week, including Singapore’s Temasek and Blackstone, a giant U.S. private equity investor, are pitched deals and ideas all the time. The goal of the Investment Summit, which was modelled off similar events in France and Saudi Arabia, wasn’t to inform these intelligent investors that Canada, a G7 country, exists – it was to allow them to break bread with more Canadians in person. If a good relationship is seeded, it could eventually influence them to take something back to their investment committees.

This year, the conference organizers also got some cherries on top, because even though the target audience was foreign investors, it had an influence on many Canadians who attended, fuelling an excitement that verged on giddiness.

List of announcements coming out of the Canada Investment Summit

Read the full transcript of Carney’s speech

It May not have seemed this way from the outside. The Summit looked like a staid event because suits and ties were the dominant outfit. Even at a forum held by the Canadian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association, which attracts tech investors who are more inclined to treat Patagonia vests as suit jackets, the attire was quite formal – mirroring Prime Minister Mark Carney’s sartorial style.

But the wardrobes were deceiving. There was a palpable pulse in the rooms. Canada has been bullied by the U.S. government for nearly two years, and the Summit dangled the prospect of growth again.

“I really do think the event is a massive catalyst,” said David Lewin, the lead senior partner at Quebec-based Novacap, which invests in Canadian technology companies.

Even though Ottawa’s primary goal is to attract billion-dollar cheques to fund infrastructure investments, he believes there were knock-on effects and that smaller funds can piggyback on the energy. “All the ripple effects around these large announcements will create a lot of opportunity,” Mr. Lewin said.

The Summit also permitted Canadians to do something they hardly ever do: Talk themselves up. Similar to Australia, Canada suffers from Tall Poppy Syndrome. Boasting about success is often seen as distasteful.

AI firms’ calls for co-ordinated slowdown amounts to ‘cartel’ behaviour, Cohere CEO says

At the Milken Institute forum on Monday, Aidan Gomez, one of the co-founders of Cohere, a homegrown artificial intelligence company that has the potential to compete with American and Chinese rivals, reminded the crowd that the technology behind American companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic came out of Canada.

Mr. Gomez worked with Geoffrey Hinton, a godfather of AI, in Toronto, and he co-authored a 2017 paper that introduced a pivotal concept that allowed AI to rapidly advance.

For a while, he told the crowd, he worked at Google Brain, one of the first research hubs for AI, and early in his time there he overheard colleagues speaking French with Québécois accents. Something clicked for him. “All of this was built by Canadians,” he thought to himself.

American and Chinese companies May dominate the conversation today, he went on to say, but Canada is just as relevant – something many Canadians don’t even know.

“We invented AI,” he boasted.

stories.title: ‘A true blessing’: This First Nation grew more than 1,000 pounds of food in its first community garden
stories.summary: Onion Lake Cree Nation grew more than 1,000 pounds of vegetables, including cauliflower, tomatoes, potatoes and cabbage, in a small, no-till garden plot that the community decided to trial this year.
stories.author: Allison Bamford
stories.content:
Onion Lake Cree Nation, Sask. – A Saskatchewan First Nation is cultivating its own solution to the growing problem of food insecurity.

Onion Lake Cree Nation grew more than 1,000 pounds of vegetables in a small, no-till garden plot that the community decided to trial this year.

The vegetables, which include cauliflower, tomatoes, zucchini, potatoes, cabbage and carrots, will be donated to the community’s group homes, Elders, food banks and schools.

“It’s a true blessing,” said Amanda Lameman, a policy analyst at the Onion Lake Health Centre.

For years, she and many others have been working to help bring the community garden to fruition.

“My late father was big into food sovereignty, and I do this work because of him,” she said.

A cross-country study of First Nations communities from between 2008 and 2018 found that nearly half of on-reserve households experience food insecurity.

Indigenous communities are also more likely to exhibit a high prevalence of nutrition-related chronic disease, including Type 2 diabetes.

The condition used to be common in adults, according to registered dietitian Ashley DeBusschere.

But recently, Onion Lake Cree Nation has seen a rise in Type 2 diabetes among children, she said. Poor access to healthy foods is a contributing factor.

“By increasing the amounts of fresh produce and healthy foods on reserve, we are really hoping that that gets more foods into kids’ mouths,” DeBusschere said.

Alicia Oliver, a driving force behind the no-till garden project, has been teaching people how to eat healthy for more than two decades.

“I have seen people struggle to get healthy vegetables on their plates,” the community dietitian said.

“Sometimes it can be an issue of transportation and the cost of fresh produce.”

Onion Lake sits on the Saskatchewan-Alberta border, about 330 kilometres northwest of Saskatoon. Fresh produce is often limited and expensive at the local store, and most people have to drive 30 minutes just to get groceries.

Oliver said people in the community are “struggling to make ends meet,” which results in food insecurity for many.

“It makes people feel like they are failing,” she said.

“Sometimes, people feel a sense of not being able to support their family. I want people to feel like having access to food gives them that. It empowers people.”

Low-maintenance gardening

Oliver first learned of no-till gardens through an online course she took with the University of Saskatchewan.

The low-maintenance method of gardening avoids digging up the ground. Instead, layers of compost and straw are piled onto mounds of soil, which helps retain moisture and prevent weeds from surfacing.

“We didn’t water even once,” Oliver said. “It was extremely minimal work.”

No-till gardens provide better soil structure and protect the microorganisms in the ground. They do not require fertilizer or pesticides.

Oliver admitted it took quite a bit of upfront work to set up the plot of land, but the payoff in yields has been worth it.

“We have grown over 1,000 pounds of produce,” she said. “We have not (harvested) any of the root vegetables, yet. We still have carrots, beets and potatoes.”

The no-till garden is part of a larger garden project in the community. This year, the First Nation planted hundreds of potatoes and fruit bushes in regular gardens next to the no-till plot.

The project reminds Elder Yvonne Carter of her own garden she used to grow. Carter, 81, would grow corn, raspberries and sunflowers taller than her.

“I just love gardening (and) growing something with my hands,” she said.

She’s helping with the community garden as much as she can – chopping fresh vegetables for soup to feed residents and learning how to make preserves.

“It’s good to see these gardeners doing everything,” she said. “Nobody goes hungry.”

The group hopes to see the no-till concept grow throughout the community and expand into schools.

“If each school had a patch this size, they could greatly reduce their food bills and ensure that there is healthier foods being served to the kids,” DeBusschere said.

The First Nation will finish harvesting the vegetables this week before distributing the rest of the bounty.

The project reminds Elder Yvonne Carter of her own garden she used to grow. Carter, 81, would grow corn, raspberries and sunflowers taller than her.
“I just love gardening (and) growing something with my hands,” she said.
She’s helping with the community garden as much as she can – chopping fresh vegetables for soup to feed residents and learning how to make preserves.
“It’s good to see these gardeners doing everything,” she said. “Nobody goes hungry.”
The group hopes to see the no-till concept grow throughout the community and expand into schools.
“If each school had a patch this size, they could greatly reduce their food bills and ensure that there is healthier foods being served to the kids,” DeBusschere said.
The First Nation will finish harvesting the vegetables this week before distributing the rest of the bounty.

content_blocks.text: Onion Lake Cree Nation, Sask. – A Saskatchewan First Nation is cultivating its own solution to the growing problem of food insecurity.
Onion Lake Cree Nation grew more than 1,000 pounds of vegetables in a small, no-till garden plot that the community decided to trial this year.
The vegetables, which include cauliflower, tomatoes, zucchini, potatoes, cabbage and carrots, will be donated to the community’s group homes, Elders, food banks and schools.
“It’s a true blessing,” said Amanda Lameman, a policy analyst at the Onion Lake Health Centre.
For years, she and many others have been working to help bring the community garden to fruition.
“My late father was big into food sovereignty, and I do this work because of him,” she said.

content_blocks.caption: Community dietitian Alicia Oliver picks potatoes from the no-till garden. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: A cross-country study of First Nations communities from between 2008 and 2018 found that nearly half of on-reserve households experience food insecurity.
Indigenous communities are also more likely to exhibit a high prevalence of nutrition-related chronic disease, including Type 2 diabetes.
The condition used to be common in adults, according to registered dietitian Ashley DeBusschere.
But recently, Onion Lake Cree Nation has seen a rise in Type 2 diabetes among children, she said. Poor access to healthy foods is a contributing factor.
“By increasing the amounts of fresh produce and healthy foods on reserve, we are really hoping that that gets more foods into kids’ mouths,” DeBusschere said.

content_blocks.caption: This plot produced more than 1,000 pounds of vegetables in its first year. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: Alicia Oliver, a driving force behind the no-till garden project, has been teaching people how to eat healthy for more than two decades.
“I have seen people struggle to get healthy vegetables on their plates,” the community dietitian said.
“Sometimes it can be an issue of transportation and the cost of fresh produce.”

Onion Lake sits on the Saskatchewan-Alberta border, about 330 kilometres northwest of Saskatoon. Fresh produce is often limited and expensive at the local store, and most people have to drive 30 minutes just to get groceries.
Oliver said people in the community are “struggling to make ends meet,” which results in food insecurity for many.
“It makes people feel like they are failing,” she said.
“Sometimes, people feel a sense of not being able to support their family. I want people to feel like having access to food gives them that. It empowers people.”

stories.title: London Street Outreach Continues to Serve its Community
stories.summary: London Street Outreach, a Christian based organization has been going strong for six years now, 4 days a week,...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
London Street Outreach, a Christian based organization has been going strong for six years now, 4 days a week, giving those in need clean clothes, as well as food, drinks and other essential items.

“On Bathurst Street we usually get over one hundred people” said the Co-Coordinator for London Street Outreach, Carol Butt. “Here at this location [Corner of King’s and Adelaide] we get around 60 or 80 people.”

The Director of London Street Outreach, Paul Presant, says that he was first struck with “divine inspiration” for this program during his time at “Ark Aid Mission”.

“It was in the middle of COVID.” said Presant. “I audibly heard from God to get out of your comfort zone and get out on the street.”

London Street Outreach is partnered with a variety of other church’s and stores, including, but not limited to, Delta Arms, the First Baptist Church, 519 Pursuit, Harvest Hands, among others.

stories.title: “Massively influential”: London and District Labour Council endorsements set possible stage for city elections
stories.summary: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RRMASPA4EYc With the recent candidate endorsements by the London and District ...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
With the recent candidate endorsements by the London and District Labour Council, a new layer has been added to the city of London’s ongoing election, one that one expert believes could potentially have a major impact on its outcome.

This past Saturday, the Labour Council made an announcement of who they endorse in each ward for the 2026 city elections, with names including incumbent mayor Josh Morgan. These endorsements were the product of a questionnaire given to each candidate for them to answer on a wide range of topics, including climate change; the housing crisis; the cost of living; Indigenous Truth and Reconciliation; and AI, among others.

“These are values-based questions,” says Mike Donachie, the editor-in-chief of the digital publication The London Ontario Online News ( The Loon ). “That makes it really interesting if people want to get to know their candidates.”

Donachie also believes that the values to be found in the questions posed by the Labour Council are meant to reflect those held by the unions that the Council serves as an umbrella group for.

Even so, the impact of the questions seems to hold a wider impact. Corrine Rahman, a candidate for Ward 5, says she has seen those values mentioned while canvassing door-to-door.

“I really value those conversations at the door,” she says, also adding that she has found the importance of the issues on the questionnaire matter differently to different people across the Ward she is campaigning in.

Rahman has been endorsed by the Labour Council for three elections, including the current one.

XFM News has reached out to all of the candidates for Ward 5 for comment on the endorsements. Mary Blake Rose says that while she is disappointed to have not received the endorsement, she respects the Labour Council’s process and remains confident in her campaign. Otherwise, as of publication, Simon Karikkassery, Abid Raza, and Charles Spina have not responded.

Beyond just the potential to gauge a candidate’s views, the Labour Council’s endorsements can hold a substantial amount of power for its recipients. In the 2022 election, 8 of the 15 candidates endorsed by the Labour Council won their race, including Rahman.

Campaign signs in Ward 5. The endorsements of the London and District Labour Council can have a major impact on the outcome of an election. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“If you have a recommendation from your union […] that answers the problem for you,” says Donachie, adding that the impact of these endorsements is greater in wards with low turnouts and large numbers of candidates.

“This is massively influential.”

Rahman adds that in her experience, “[the endorsement] just lends that extra credibility” in the eyes of the Labour Council and their interests.

The endorsements are not without controversy, however. In a recent thread on the London subreddit , several users questioned and voiced objections regarding the choices of candidates by the Labour Council.

“There will be push and pull in every Ward,” says Donachie. “Every candidate needs to be open to taking criticism on the regular.”

In the end, the endorsements and the values they reflect are still one part of the larger election as a whole, with Rahman saying that when the new City Council is elected, it decides for itself what to address.

“Part of it is coalescing around interests that are shared,” she says. “I think that’s a really important step in the process.”

stories.title: London has room for improvement when it comes to small business friendliness, report says
stories.summary: Small business owner Steve Hillier has been operating a make-your-own wine store on Wellington Road South, London for about ten years.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Small business owner Steve Hillier has been operating a make-your-own wine store on Wellington Road South, London for about 10 years.

He says dealing with the city of London has been mostly pain-free. That is, except for when it comes to construction of the rapid transit network outside his front door.

“It seems like the construction is causing issues for customers to, A, make it on time, or just to find how to get in here if you’re coming from a certain direction. And when a plan out here is going for three years or so, it really hinders,” explained Hillier.

Lack of supports for businesses affected by construction is one of several issues cited in a new report that rates business-friendliness across Canadian cities. In its Municipal Report Card, 2026, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (Cfib) ranks London 15th out of 66 cities. London scored an overall grade of D, considered below satisfactory. But the highest any city scored was C+.

Angela Drennan, Cfib Vice-President of Ontario Legislative Affairs, says London gets some things right, but other things, not so much.

“Lowest scoring category was in the regulatory burden section, reflecting an average number of permits required to start and operate a business. No publicly available license or permit approval timelines. And no dedicated red tape feedback portal.

Some of the strengths though, was actually the cost burden, driven by operating spending growth, that actually didn’t exceed population and inflation growth,” Drennan said.

And in a time of trade uncertainty, businesses large and small are always looking for a leg up. One business expert says the city could consider procurement policies that favour local companies.

“Businesses are often looking to government for grants and support and that type of thing,” said Steve Pellarin, Executive Director of the London Small Business Centre. “But a purchase order can go a lot further. Right? Purchase orders build businesses. And I think that the city of London needs to look closely at its procurement policies, and how do they make those inclusive of the small businesses,” he said.

Among the Cfib recommendations, the report card says municipalities should:

Address property tax unfairness

Cut red tape by getting rid of duplication

Post clear service standards and permit timelines

Create online portal for flagging unnecessary rules

stories.title: Health watchdog group warns of private clinic fees and alleges underutilization of hospital MRIs
stories.summary: Outside an independent eye care clinic in London, Ont., leaders within the London Health Coalition contend they are out to educate the public about any additional fees charged for Ohip-covered procedures.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Outside an independent eye care clinic in London, Ont., leaders within the London Health Coalition contend they are out to educate the public about any additional fees charged for Ohip-covered procedures.

“And it doesn’t matter if it’s under a scalpel or a laser; if you’re just getting a cataract lens, it’s covered, folks,” said Co-Chair Peter Bergmanis.

While the clinic targeted by the group has yet to respond to claims of any charges for cataract services outside of Ohip, Bergmanis tells CTV News that concerns about additional fees in private clinics across the province are part of a new report by the Ontario Health Coalition.

The document also calls on the public to be aware of what it calls the underutilization of surgical rooms and MRI machines.

It lists the operating hours of hospital resources, suggesting many facilities sit idle on weekends and evenings.

Bergmanis claims that if hospitals’ MRIs and operating rooms were funded for more hours, the need for private clinics would be reduced or eliminated.

“There would be no draining of the public purse of resources.”

In 2023, the Ford government passed a bill allowing some private clinics to conduct Ohip-covered surgeries.

At the time, the government maintained it was necessary to reduce the province’s surgical backlog.

Three years on, the Health Coalition argues too much money is spent on private clinics at the expense of hospitals.

Meanwhile, as the current tariff war continues with the United States, the coalition is contending that private US healthcare companies continue to find their way into the Ontario healthcare system.

“If we go towards privatization, we lose that ability to protect our national Medicare, which is arguably the biggest thing that separates us from the US, for our identity,” said Jeff Hanks, a registered nurse and co-chair of the London chapter.

While the province did not directly address private health care clinics in a statement sent to CTV News, a spokesperson for the minister of health said the “The Ontario Health Coalition’s claims are entirely misguided.”

The statement went on to read in part:

“Our government has increased funding for the hospital sector by a record 4% this year, for the third year in a row, bringing our total investment in hospitals to over 50% since 2018. This is in addition to the over $60 billion we are investing to get shovels in the ground for over 60 hospital development projects, that will add 3,000 new hospital beds across the province, the 50 new MRI and CT machines we have added in hospitals, including at London Health Sciences.”

In 2023, the Ford government passed a bill allowing some private clinics to conduct Ohip-covered surgeries.
At the time, the government maintained it was necessary to reduce the province’s surgical backlog.
Three years on, the Health Coalition argues too much money is spent on private clinics at the expense of hospitals.
Meanwhile, as the current tariff war continues with the United States, the coalition is contending that private US healthcare companies continue to find their way into the Ontario healthcare system.

“If we go towards privatization, we lose that ability to protect our national Medicare, which is arguably the biggest thing that separates us from the US, for our identity,” said Jeff Hanks, a registered nurse and co-chair of the London chapter.

While the province did not directly address private health care clinics in a statement sent to CTV News, a spokesperson for the minister of health said the “The Ontario Health Coalition’s claims are entirely misguided.”
The statement went on to read in part:

“Our government has increased funding for the hospital sector by a record 4% this year, for the third year in a row, bringing our total investment in hospitals to over 50% since 2018. This is in addition to the over $60 billion we are investing to get shovels in the ground for over 60 hospital development projects, that will add 3,000 new hospital beds across the province, the 50 new MRI and CT machines we have added in hospitals, including at London Health Sciences.”

stories.title: The role of school board trustees remains unclear. Here's why some Londoners want the job anyway
stories.summary: Dozens of Londoners are running to be school board trustees in the 2026 municipal elections next month, in spite of the Ontario government's sweeping changes that have taken away much of the position's power.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Dozens of Londoners are running to be school board trustees in the 2026 municipal elections next month, in spite of the Ontario government's sweeping changes that have taken away much of the position's power.
· Posted: Sep 15, 2026 6:05 PM EDT | Last Updated: 39 minutes ago

Dozens of people are running to be London-area school board trustees in the 2026 municipal elections next month, despite the Ontario government's sweeping changes that have stripped much of the position's power.

The Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) remains under provincial supervision, but candidates running for the positions are still hopeful they can make an impact if elected. There 18 people running and six elected public trustee positions with the board.
"It's not about the role, it's about a passion," said Lori-Ann Pizzolato, an incumbent TVDSB trustee for Wards 1, 11, 12 and 14 who is seeking re-election for another term.
"I have a passion to help students, to help support families, to make sure that students achieve the best that they can achieve."
Lori-Ann Pizzolato is seeking another term as the TVDSB trustee for Wards 1, 11, 12 and 14. (Submitted by Lori-Ann Pizzolato)

Ontario's Education Minister Paul Calandra dismissed the trustees at TVDSB back in April 2025 following a report that found the board demonstrated "extremely poor judgement" in the use of public funds.
'Momentous decision' as province takes over TVDSB operations from trustees

Other English-language boards not under supervision, such as the London District Catholic School Board, also saw trustee powers diminished by Bill 101, also known as the Putting Student Achievement First Act. Among other changes, Bill 101 significantly reduced the role of trustees, who are now limited to representing parents and students.
LISTEN | TVDSB trustee Sherri Moore is also seeking re-election:
London Morning 7:51 Why this London school board trustee is running for reelection
Despite the province's pushback and changes to the role of trustee at public school boards, Sherri Moore is running in London again. She joined London Morning to explain why.
Pizzolato said she and her fellow trustees at TVDSB have found ways to continue serving the community, and she wants to continue those efforts despite the uncertainty around the role.
"They can't take away the knowledge I learned for two terms at Thames Valley, so I'm happy to provide any knowledge I have to help parents and to support families and to help students," she said.
She said the trustees have also continued advocacy at the provincial level, meeting with elected officials and provincial trustee associations, and working to get information out to the public.
Smita Tajne, a first-time candidate, is running for TVDSB trustee in Wards 1, 11, 12 and 14. (Submitted by Smita Tajne)
The upheavals and uncertainty are not turning away first-time candidates such as Smita Tajne, who is also running for Wards 1, 11, 12 and 13 at TVDSB.

Tajne has an eight-year-old daughter who attends a TVDSB school. She also runs a parent support group where parents often share concerns with her, and she does her best to point them in the right direction.
But lately she feels in the dark since the board was placed under supervision, and wants to provide answers to families.
"I hope to be a trustee who advocates transparency and dedicates a proper channel to bring the parents' concerns to the board," she said.

She said she envisions a role in which she could continue to listen to parents while the trustees remain sidelined, so that if the supervision is eventually lifted and the trustees reinstated, she will already have information to share about parent concerns.
"Do they have any plans of reviving the board? I don't know, but we cannot just lose hope and give up," she said.
The Catholic board has eight candidates running to be trustees. Like the public boards, the trustees' role has been limited, but they will maintain responsibility over religious issues.

Linda Steel, the current vice-chair of the LDCSB Board of Trustees representing Wards 8, 9 and 10, has been acclaimed for another term with no opponents in the race. She said that while she has not noticed too many changes at the local level, there are uncertainties on the horizon.
London Catholic District School Board trustee Linda Steel has been acclaimed for another term, with no opponents running against her in the race. (Linda Steel/LinkedIn)
But Steel wanted to continue in her role all the same to represent the community and provide a local voice.
"Parents need someone to speak to," she said. "Sometimes the system doesn't work the way it's supposed to, and trustees are there to ensure that it works properly."
She said she will navigate the role over the next term by taking "a good, hard look at it" to understand exactly what her rights and responsibilities are as a trustee.
"I ask a whole lot of questions, and then I advocate as hard as I can for what I believe is right," she said.

"If you're truly committed to being a school board trustee, I say 'when the going gets tough, the tough get up and advocate even harder,' and that's what I would hope to see in all the boards across the province."

stories.title: 15k Londoners lose power following large-scale outages: London Hydro
stories.summary: London Hydro is reporting that roughly 15,000 people primarily in central and northwest areas lost power late Tuesday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: September 15, 2026 9:51 PM | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
London Hydro is reporting that roughly 15,000 people lost power late Tuesday afternoon.

The outages, the cause of which has yet to be reported, were mostly concentrated in the area surrounding Wonderland Road North, through the Medway, White Hills and Fox Hollow neighbourhoods, according to London Hydro's publicly available outage map .

"We're aware of 15,000 customers being out in the northwest area of London. We don't know the cause yet," said London Hydro spokesperson Kathryn Arnot shortly after the outages began. "We have crews out and they're assessing to find the problem. Once they locate it, they'll be able to start planning out what they'll need to fix it."
Other significant outages were reported in Oakridge and River Bend in the city's west end.
As of 5:50 p.m., London Hydro reported about 2,900 were still without power but the majority of the outages were solved.

stories.title: Power restored to most of 15k Londoners who lost power to large-scale outages
stories.summary: London Hydro initially reported that roughly 15,000 people primarily in central and northwest areas lost power late Tuesday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: CBC News | Posted: September 15, 2026 9:51 PM | Last Updated: 8 hours ago
London Hydro is reporting most customers have had their power restored after roughly 15,000 people lost power, late Tuesday afternoon.

The outages were mostly concentrated in the area surrounding Wonderland Road North, through the Medway, White Hills and Fox Hollow neighbourhoods, according to London Hydro's publicly available outage map .
"We're aware of 15,000 customers being out in the northwest area of London," said London Hydro spokesperson Kathryn Arnot shortly after the outages began.
Roughly an hour after the outages were first reported, officials noted an "animal contact" caused an equipment failure.
Other significant outages were reported in Oakridge and River Bend in the city's west end, and in the east London neighbourhood of Carling.

stories.title: ‘I felt duped’: COVID vaccine injury victim not impressed by inquiry into Canadian vaccine injuries
stories.summary: Maria Dunning lays out the multitude of pills she takes on a daily basis, just to manage the chronic pain she lives with.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Maria Dunning-Ballagh lays out the multitude of pills she takes on a daily basis, just to manage the chronic pain she lives with.

“So, from the second I wake up, by body is in this screaming pain, from my shoulders to my toes. I get electrical shocks all over my body, throughout the day. Restless legs. I’ve been diagnosed with Sjogren’s Disease, which means I make no moisture, no saliva, I can’t cry. I’ve also lost most of my teeth,” says the Walkerton woman.

The normally healthy Dunning-Ballagh, says all these symptoms started three weeks after she received her first COVID-19 vaccine, ON April 27, 2021. She was working three jobs at that time, but has had to quit them all, due to the constant, chronic pain.

“I’ve tried everything from ketamine injections, to Reset, and nothing has helped the pain,” she says.

A frustrated Dunning-Ballagh applied to the government’s Vaccine Injury Support Program back in January of 2023, but in three years hasn’t progressed past Phase I. Which is why, when Conservative MP Dean Allison invited COVID injury victims to share their stories, at an inquiry, she applied. She wasn’t one of the 50 picked to testify, but tuned in, only to be disappointed by, what she calls, the anti-vaccine, anti-mandate politicization of her injuries. Especially the testimony of two controversial American presenters."

“I was more than disappointed, I was disgusted, I felt betrayed, and duped,” she says.

Dunning-Ballagh says there isn’t currently a place for people like her, that were amongst the 12,000 Canadians who suffered serious adverse effects from the COVID vaccine, but who aren’t anti-vaccine, or anti-COVID mandates.

“I go into a doctor and I even hint that it might be a vaccine injury, and they automatically think I’m an anti-vaxxer, I’m against mandates, I’m against science, I’m against vaccines, but I am far from it. I had my initial vaccine, and then my doctor and I decided it was smart for me to continue to get vaccines, because now I’m immune compromised, and I’ve not got any reactions to any of the other vaccines. Because science does work. I’m a believer in it. I believe, overall, the vaccines helped most everybody,” she says.

She fears the Allison Inquiry set back her cause, and that of others, who are trying to get the government to help them, through the newly named, Vaccine Impact Assistance Program.

“The large number of people that were vaccinated in such a short time, there were bound to be injuries. That’s what we need to stay focused on, us injured, and ensuring we get the care and help that we deserve and need from the government.”

Dunning says while her physician supported her application to the Vaccine Injury Assistance Program, no doctor has directly diagnosed her chronic pain, as a direct result of the COVID vaccine. Approximately, 28 million Canadians received at least one dose of a COVID vaccine. 58,000 Canadians reported adverse effects, 12,000 of those were considered serious effects. 3500 Canadians have applied to the government’s Vaccine Injury Assistance Program, but only 252 claims have been approved for compensation, totalling a combined $21 million.

Conservative MP Dean Allison who launched the inquiry, said on the final day last week, that the inquiry “was intended to begin a conversation that should’ve begun years ago,” and that “no matter what people think about [COVID-19] or the vaccines or public policy, compassion should never be controversial.”

stories.title: Power outages hit parts of northwest London during rush hour
stories.summary: London Hydro said it was aware of the outage and had crews deployed “to quickly and safely understand the issue.”
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
London Hydro said it was aware of the outage and had crews deployed “to quickly and safely understand the issue.”

Last updated 25 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/news/local-news/power-outages-hit-parts-of-northwest-London-during-rush-hour#comments-area)

Power outages were reported across northwest London late Tuesday afternoon.

Pockets in the north on Wonderland Road and west on Wharncliffe Road were without power as of 5 p.m., during what is typically the height of the evening rush hour.

London Hydro’s outage map showed five outages affecting the Carling, Oakridge and Hyde Park areas as of about 5:45 p.m.

In a later update, the utility said it was using automation to complete partial restorations from adjacent circuits and urged customers to check its outage map for updates.
