stories.title: Western engineers investigate cracking in nuclear reactor pressure tubes
stories.summary: Western University engineers have taken a major step toward solving a long-standing challenge in nuclear power.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Western University engineers have taken a major step toward solving a long-standing challenge in nuclear power.A study, published in the high-impact journal Nature Communications, describes for the first time how hydrogen can combine with zirconium to form tiny, brittle structures that create intense stresses in Candu reactor pressure tubes. These stresses May cause the surrounding metal to deform and even crack.

Candu (Canada Deuterium Uranium) reactors are Canadian-designed, pressurized heavy-water nuclear reactors that use unenriched uranium as fuel and heavy water as a moderator and coolant. Inside the reactor, zirconium alloy pressure tubes (long, high-strength metal pipes) surround and hold fuel bundles and coolants for safety.

Over time, hydrogen can build up in the zirconium and combine with the metal to create a hydride (a chemical compound formed when hydrogen combines with another element). In this case, these tiny, brittle structures develop inside the zirconium and can create significant stresses in the pressure tubes.

The study, led by mechanical and materials engineering professor Hamid Abdolvand, offers a better understanding of how stresses develop and could help improve computer models used to predict fracturing in nuclear reactors. These findings May also be used to determine when reactor components are in need of replacement, helping improve their safety, reliability and lifespan.

“Nuclear engineers and scientists need to understand how these reactor components deform over time so they can accurately determine when they need to be replaced,” said Abdolvand. “This discovery proves why something happening at a scale invisible to the human eye matters to a reactor the size of a building.”

For the study, Abdolvand and his team used powerful X-rays at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France to examine zirconium and hydride structures at a resolution of about 200 nanometres in three dimensions. The researchers found significant stresses inside the hydrides, exceeding one gigapascal.

“That is significant because these stresses can influence how cracks initiate and grow in the material. Having a three-dimensional picture of those stresses gives us a much better understanding of what is actually happening inside reactor components, such as fuel cladding or pressure tubes,” said Abdolvand.

The zirconium-alloy pressure tubes in Candu reactors are only about four millimetres thick, yet they must withstand high pressures and temperatures while operating for decades. Hydrides can form repeatedly throughout a Candu’s lifetime, so their effects can add up over time.

“If there is a small flaw in the zirconium-alloy component, the associated localized stresses can cause hydrides to form around it. As they form, they change the state of the material and potentially contribute to cracking,” said Abdolvand.

These localized stresses within the reactor May lead to delayed hydride cracking, a phenomenon that has been the subject of extensive research since a pressure tube failure at Pickering Nuclear Generating Station in the 1980s.

The challenge with studying hydrides has always been seeing what is happening inside. Nuclear engineers have long had computer models that predict hydride stresses, but hydrides themselves are tiny – typically hundreds of nanometres to a few micrometres – making them extremely difficult to study experimentally, especially in 3D.

The experiment, led by Abdolvand, was conducted at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in France, which produces extremely bright and powerful X-rays that can probe materials at scales inaccessible to conventional imaging techniques. The Western team, which included Abdolvand and postdoctoral research associate Saiedeh Marashi, used a newly developed scanning 3D X-ray diffraction technique to map the grains and crystallographic structure within the zirconium alloy. The experiment generated about 10 terabytes of diffraction data and turning it into something meaningful required five years of analysis, computer modelling and collaboration.

Marashi, Masoud Taherijam and former PhD student Alireza Tondro, all contributed to the work, along with researchers at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility and Lund University in Sweden.

Overall, the new technique gave the researchers something they had never had before – direct experimental evidence of the intense stresses inside hydrides their models had predicted.

Marking the importance of the discovery, the research team is making the work available to others. Along with the paper, the researchers plan to publicly release the raw diffraction data, cleaned and processed data, numerical results and source code.

“We are here to make a better place for the next generation,” said Abdolvand. “The next person who wants to look at this problem doesn’t have to start from zero. They can begin where our work stopped and take the science somewhere new.”

Darlington Nuclear Generating Station (Robert T. Bell)

The five-year project also illustrates something Abdolvand considers just as important as the scientific finding: what happens to the students who do the work.

Marashi, a PhD student in Abdolvand’s Multiscale Deformation Lab when the project began, took on the extensive data analysis and numerical modelling. She ultimately led the project and wrote the paper. After working for more than a year as a postdoctoral research associate, she is now moving into the nuclear industry, joining Candu Energy Inc., part of AtkinsRéalis.

And Tondro is now a scientist at Canadian Nuclear Laboratories, a world leader in developing nuclear technology for peaceful and innovative applications.

For Abdolvand, seeing students move into jobs where they use the skills developed through their research is not simply a measure of academic success or validation of the work. It’s a sign of real-world impact.

“Students spend years developing difficult, highly specialized skills. When they graduate and industry wants those skills, that’s real impact,” said Abdolvand.

That connection is especially important as Canada looks to extend the life of its existing Candu fleet while developing new nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors for the Darlington New Nuclear Project.

Abdolvand has also seen knowledge move in the other direction – from industry into the university and back again.

“Researchers and engineers collaborate, students are trained on real problems, and the resulting knowledge can move into the next generation of reactor technology,” said Abdolvand.

Learn more about how Western is turning curiosity into solutions.

content_blocks.text: Western University engineers have taken a major step toward solving a long-standing challenge in nuclear power.A study, published in the high-impact journal Nature Communications, describes for the first time how hydrogen can combine with zirconium to form tiny, brittle structures that create intense stresses in Candu reactor pressure tubes. These stresses May cause the surrounding metal to deform and even crack.

Candu (Canada Deuterium Uranium) reactors are Canadian-designed, pressurized heavy-water nuclear reactors that use unenriched uranium as fuel and heavy water as a moderator and coolant. Inside the reactor, zirconium alloy pressure tubes (long, high-strength metal pipes) surround and hold fuel bundles and coolants for safety.

Over time, hydrogen can build up in the zirconium and combine with the metal to create a hydride (a chemical compound formed when hydrogen combines with another element). In this case, these tiny, brittle structures develop inside the zirconium and can create significant stresses in the pressure tubes.

The study, led by mechanical and materials engineering professor Hamid Abdolvand, offers a better understanding of how stresses develop and could help improve computer models used to predict fracturing in nuclear reactors. These findings May also be used to determine when reactor components are in need of replacement, helping improve their safety, reliability and lifespan.

“Nuclear engineers and scientists need to understand how these reactor components deform over time so they can accurately determine when they need to be replaced,” said Abdolvand. “This discovery proves why something happening at a scale invisible to the human eye matters to a reactor the size of a building.”

For the study, Abdolvand and his team used powerful X-rays at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France to examine zirconium and hydride structures at a resolution of about 200 nanometres in three dimensions. The researchers found significant stresses inside the hydrides, exceeding one gigapascal.

“That is significant because these stresses can influence how cracks initiate and grow in the material. Having a three-dimensional picture of those stresses gives us a much better understanding of what is actually happening inside reactor components, such as fuel cladding or pressure tubes,” said Abdolvand.
A problem hiding in plain sight

The zirconium-alloy pressure tubes in Candu reactors are only about four millimetres thick, yet they must withstand high pressures and temperatures while operating for decades. Hydrides can form repeatedly throughout a Candu’s lifetime, so their effects can add up over time.

“If there is a small flaw in the zirconium-alloy component, the associated localized stresses can cause hydrides to form around it. As they form, they change the state of the material and potentially contribute to cracking,” said Abdolvand.

These localized stresses within the reactor May lead to delayed hydride cracking, a phenomenon that has been the subject of extensive research since a pressure tube failure at Pickering Nuclear Generating Station in the 1980s.
Seeing inside

The challenge with studying hydrides has always been seeing what is happening inside. Nuclear engineers have long had computer models that predict hydride stresses, but hydrides themselves are tiny – typically hundreds of nanometres to a few micrometres – making them extremely difficult to study experimentally, especially in 3D.

The experiment, led by Abdolvand, was conducted at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in France, which produces extremely bright and powerful X-rays that can probe materials at scales inaccessible to conventional imaging techniques. The Western team, which included Abdolvand and postdoctoral research associate Saiedeh Marashi, used a newly developed scanning 3D X-ray diffraction technique to map the grains and crystallographic structure within the zirconium alloy. The experiment generated about 10 terabytes of diffraction data and turning it into something meaningful required five years of analysis, computer modelling and collaboration.
Marashi, Masoud Taherijam and former PhD student Alireza Tondro, all contributed to the work, along with researchers at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility and Lund University in Sweden.
Overall, the new technique gave the researchers something they had never had before – direct experimental evidence of the intense stresses inside hydrides their models had predicted.

Marking the importance of the discovery, the research team is making the work available to others. Along with the paper, the researchers plan to publicly release the raw diffraction data, cleaned and processed data, numerical results and source code.

“We are here to make a better place for the next generation,” said Abdolvand. “The next person who wants to look at this problem doesn’t have to start from zero. They can begin where our work stopped and take the science somewhere new.”
Darlington Nuclear Generating Station (Robert T. Bell)
From Western to the world
The five-year project also illustrates something Abdolvand considers just as important as the scientific finding: what happens to the students who do the work.

Marashi, a PhD student in Abdolvand’s Multiscale Deformation Lab when the project began, took on the extensive data analysis and numerical modelling. She ultimately led the project and wrote the paper. After working for more than a year as a postdoctoral research associate, she is now moving into the nuclear industry, joining Candu Energy Inc., part of AtkinsRéalis.
And Tondro is now a scientist at Canadian Nuclear Laboratories, a world leader in developing nuclear technology for peaceful and innovative applications.

For Abdolvand, seeing students move into jobs where they use the skills developed through their research is not simply a measure of academic success or validation of the work. It’s a sign of real-world impact.
“Students spend years developing difficult, highly specialized skills. When they graduate and industry wants those skills, that’s real impact,” said Abdolvand.

That connection is especially important as Canada looks to extend the life of its existing Candu fleet while developing new nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors for the Darlington New Nuclear Project.
Abdolvand has also seen knowledge move in the other direction – from industry into the university and back again.
“Researchers and engineers collaborate, students are trained on real problems, and the resulting knowledge can move into the next generation of reactor technology,” said Abdolvand.

stories.title: City of London marks half-century with Aaa credit rating
stories.summary: An independent evaluator has once again assigned the City of London a Aaa credit rating, which minimizes city hall’s cost of borrowing for one-time expenses and infrastructure projects.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
An independent evaluator has once again assigned the City of London a Aaa credit rating, which minimizes city hall’s cost of borrowing for one-time expenses and infrastructure projects.

On Tuesday, Moody’s Investors Service confirmed that city hall has maintained its top-tier credit rating for the 50 th consecutive year.

The highest rating possible, its an achievement that reflects longstanding strong financial management and sustainable financial planning.

According to a news release, “Moody’s noted that the City’s excellent governance and management, low reliance on debt and high levels of cash and investments provide increased bondholder security. While an upward pressure on debt levels from growth related capital projects is anticipated, Moody’s does not see this as a change in the City’s strong debt management policies.”

The annual credit evaluation is based on London’s audited financial statements, Multi-Year Budget, and meeting with Civic Administration, the mayor, and other independent research.

stories.title: Poilievre set to try to rally Conservative MPs ahead of Parliament’s return
stories.summary: The Conservative leader is trailing badly to Mark Carney’s Liberals, ties to shift political conversation from “speeches, summits” to results felt by Canadians.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre will try to rally his MPs after a summer of conservative movement infighting and polling that shows his party continuing to trail the federal Liberals by double-digits.

Poilievre and the Conservative caucus are gathering in Penticton, B.C., for a strategy session ahead of the House of Commons’ return next week.

The Conservative leader enters the fall sitting with his party trailing Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals. Polling aggregator 338 Canada has the Liberals with 46 per cent popular support, with the Conservatives at 33 per cent.

Poilievre has also faced continued questions about his leadership from within the Conservative family, after publicly taking what was seen as a shot at Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s campaign manager, Kory Teneycke.

While congratulating former MP Kerry-Lynne Findlay on winning the leadership of the B.C. Conservatives, Poilievre declared it a victory over “liberal lobbyists” from Eastern Canada, a comment widely interpreted as directed at Teneycke, who worked on a rival campaign.

Findlay went on to lose several MLAs, who left the party publicly due to her leadership. Teneycke also publicly shot back at the Conservative leader, suggesting Poilievre was not long for the job. Several prominent Conservative voices spent the summer publicly opining on the future of the party.

Despite the internal turmoil, Poilievre’s comments Tuesday ahead of the retreat sounded like they could’ve come from one of his 2025 election campaign speeches.

“The promise of Canada – that if you work hard, you get a great life, a home you can own, food you can afford, a safe street to live on – that promise is broken after 11 years of Liberal government,” Poilievre said.

“Our mission as Conservatives is to fight for you and to fight for Canada, to save you money. That is our single biggest immediate priority.”

Poilievre took a dig at Carney, accusing the prime minister of participating in “summits and signing ceremonies” – a reference to the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto this week, where the government is trying to lure $1 trillion in foreign investment to the country – rather than delivering results for Canadian voters.

The Conservative leader also questioned Carney’s push for stronger partnership with the European Union – suggesting that the Liberals could force Canadians to pay taxes to the EU or adopt the bloc’s immigration policies, neither of which has been suggested by the government.

“We want Canada to have free trade with Europe, cooperation with Europe, but we never surrender our independence and sovereignty over our laws, our tax money, and our immigration policies,” Poilievre said.

Polling released by Abacus Data Monday suggested that 80 per cent of Canadians support deepening cooperation with European nations on foreign policy, defence and economic priorities – including a strong majority of Poilievre’s own supporters.

“Ninety-two per cent of Liberal voters support deeper cooperation with the EU. So do 92 per cent of NDP voters and 86 per cent of Bloc voters,” Abacus CEO David Colletto wrote of the findings.

“Among Conservative voters, support is lower but still reaches 69 per cent.”

The House of Commons is set to return on Sept. 21.

stories.title: Local researcher champions holistic approach to concussion recovery in schools
stories.summary: A Western University professor is aiming to redefine concussion recovery for young athletes and students by focusing not just on physical healing, but on the critical, often overlooked, academic and social reintegration process.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
A Western University professor is aiming to redefine concussion recovery for young athletes and students by focusing not just on physical healing, but on the critical, often overlooked, academic and social reintegration process.

Professor Heather Shepherd has developed a comprehensive framework designed to bridge the gaps in how schools support students returning after a head injury.

While the physical symptoms of a concussion are well-documented and require treatment, the ripple effects on a young person’s life can extend far beyond the initial injury.

For students, concussions often lead to falling behind in learning, disrupted social connections, and significant anxiety about returning to the classroom.

Shepherd, from Western’s School of Occupational Therapy, highlights a significant challenge: “Things like who communicates with the school when a child has a concussion? Who within the school communicates with each other about the child’s accommodations, that the child is not the one who is now navigating their own kind of return to school support?”

This lack of clear communication pathways leaves students and their families struggling to navigate the complex return-to-school process.

Concussions can impede learning and isolate students from their peers. To combat this, Shepherd’s research proposes innovative solutions, including the establishment of a “buddy system.” This involves a fellow student who can help relay crucial information, such as homework assignments and classroom updates.

“The hope is that having peers there to help from that social support and peer support perspective will help alleviate some of that anxiousness with returning to school and help them from that more academic and support context,” Shepherd explained.

Teachers, often stretched thin, face unique difficulties in managing concussion recovery. Shepherd notes that the fluctuating nature of a student’s needs presents a constant challenge. “Concussions are unique in that the student’s needs are going to change on a day by day or week by week basis, which can be quite difficult for schools to accommodate,” she said.

This requires a flexible, gradual return to both classwork and extracurricular activities.

Shepherd experienced the profound impact of concussions firsthand, sustaining four during her first two years of high school, with three occurring within a single six-month period.

The severity of her third concussion led to her withdrawal from school for the remainder of that academic year, providing her with an intimate understanding of the challenges students face.

The prevalence of concussions among young people underscores the urgency of Shepherd’s work. She points out that approximately one in four adolescents will experience a concussion by age 18. Citing research from Dr. Carolyn Emery’s group at the University of Calgary, Shepherd noted that “about 11% of high school students will sustain a concussion each year in Canada, who play sports, which includes physical education class.”

It was during her doctoral studies at the University of Calgary that Shepherd first developed the Return to School Framework.

Created collaboratively with students, caregivers, educators, and fellow researchers, the Return to School Framework offers schools a practical toolkit of strategies to support students recovering from concussions. This approach aims to mitigate the impact on both learning and social connections.

Now a researcher in the Faculty of Health Sciences at Western University, Shepherd is focused on determining how this framework can be effectively implemented across school boards in Ontario, with the ultimate goal of a nationwide adoption. She emphasizes the collaborative nature of her work: “We’re working to identify, hopefully, a solution that has real world impact, and we’re doing it with the people that are actually living that life.”

Shepherd’s ultimate aim is to create a universal template that any school, regardless of its size or available resources, can utilize to ensure a smoother, more supportive return to school for students recovering from concussions, fostering both academic success and social well-being.

Shepherd’s ultimate aim is to create a universal template that any school, regardless of its size or available resources, can utilize to ensure a smoother, more supportive return to school for students recovering from concussions, fostering both academic success and social well-being.

stories.title: Halifax Wanderers pitch privately-funded $100M stadium and sports hub
stories.summary: The Halifax Wanderers are taking matters into their own hands when it comes to having a permanent soccer stadium in the city.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
The Halifax Wanderers are taking matters into their own hands when it comes to having a permanent soccer stadium in the city .

The owner of the football club, Derek Martin, has brought forward a proposal to Halifax Regional Council to build a stadium on municipal land, with the project privately funded by the Wanderers.

“What I’ve seen over the last 10 years of working on this project is coming up with that type of money is going to be incredibly difficult for HRM right now, so we’ve come up with a solution that we think can work,” Martin told reporters after Tuesday’s council meeting.

The Canadian Premier League team has been playing in a pop-up stadium at Wanderer’s Grounds in downtown Halifax since 2019. That pop-up is on municipal land and lacks amenities such as running water and permanent grandstands.

There have been years of discussions and debates about a permanent stadium .

Martin’s new proposal reimagines the Wanderers Block as a permanent, year-round stadium with the possibility of a winter bubble dome. It would have a 650-space parking area beneath the facility that could also be used by people visiting the nearby Qeii Health Sciences Centre. In addition, the plan has extra space for the Halifax Lancers horse riding school and a new lawn bowling green.

The proposal also includes a community sports hub at Maybank Field in Dartmouth, which would provide expanded facilities for soccer and community sports.

“I think we’ve done the best we can to find a solution that satisfies as many stakeholders as we can without it ever being perfect for anyone,” Martin said.

Martin told councillors the project will cost about $100 million and be privately funded.

HRM would still partner in the project through a 99-year lease.

Many on council were tentatively excited by the proposal.

“Now, I’ve been saying very plainly for quite a while that we need to seek partners in our large infrastructure and capital projects. And so that’s what the proponent in this case has done,” said Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore.

Coun. Tony Mancini called it a “creative approach.”

“Our normal approach is not working anymore because of a variety of different reasons. We need to be more creative. Here’s a creative approach in front of us. I think it’s worthy of the conversation,” he said.

However, there was concern expressed about the quick timeline. The initial plan is to break ground in January 2027.

As well, there are considerations about the use of private investment on public land.

“When we do it this way and when it’s privately owned, we lose that municipal opportunity. I think there’s a lot more to consider,” said Deputy Mayor Patty Cuttell.

Angie Holt, executive director and head coach with the Halifax Lancers, said they’ve had some consultation with the Wanderers and are interested to see where the project goes.

“We’ve been living in the state of uncertainty for a long time now, but I do think that due process is absolutely necessary and we have to make sure this is something that actually is going to work for everybody,” said Holt.

A motion for a staff report for HRM to consider the proposal’s implications passed 15-1.

stories.title: ‘It’s looking bleak’: Soaring fuel costs squeeze Southwestern Ontario farmers
stories.summary: Higher diesel prices are adding to already steep input costs for farmers across the region.
stories.author: Jonathan Juha
stories.content:
Kevin Cron is blunt in assessing whether his cash-crop operation will turn a profit this year: “It’s looking bleak.”

The Port Stanley-area grower said his lack of optimism stems from sharp increases in input costs, particularly crude oil-based products such as diesel and hydraulic oil, which are already eating into what he said are farmers’ slim profit margins.

“The daily costs are just killing us,” he said Tuesday at Canada’s Outdoor Farm Show in Woodstock, billed as the largest farm show in Eastern Canada and expected to attract more than 30,000 people from the agricultural sector.

The average price of diesel in Canada on Tuesday was $2.64 per litre, according to Natural Resources Canada, with prices in places such as Halifax just shy of $2.70, as the war in Iran has disrupted global supplies. About a year ago, Cron said he was probably paying about $1.50 per litre.

“Now that we’re coming into cropping season, a combine alone will use 300 to 400 litres a day, so when you see diesel prices at $2.60 a litre, it makes you shudder,” he said.

Brent crude, up more than 75 per cent this year, was trading at around US$106 a barrel Tuesday following reports that Saudi Arabia May take weeks to reopen its east-west pipeline, which was halted after it was struck by militants.

The pipeline had become Saudi Arabia’s most important workaround since the Iran war choked off exports from the Persian Gulf that normally move through the Strait of Hormuz.

Diesel futures were also trading at around US$200 a barrel, as fuel supplies have been disrupted in both the Middle East and Russia, where Ukrainian strikes have hindered refining capacity.

But high oil prices are far from the only concern on farmers’ minds, said Mark Reusser, a director with the Ontario Federation of Agriculture.

For the most part, agricultural products have continued to enter the United States tariff-free, but he said specific sectors such as dairy are closely following developments in the ongoing trade war between the two countries.

“The anxiety is probably higher in the supply management sector, simply because the U.S. has specifically targeted supply management and specifically dairy as being something that they want to see changed,” Reusser said. “Many are wondering, ‘How can I run a business when it’s under threat from my neighbour to the south?’”

The trade tensions, however, are also creating some silver linings and opening new opportunities, said Rob O’Connor, director of Canada’s Outdoor Farm Show.

For example, this year’s event attracted companies from 13 countries, up from seven last year, looking to bring farming equipment and other products into the country after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down, prompting the federal government to implement counter-tariffs on some farming equipment.

Though large machinery, such as combines and tractors, is excluded from the counter-tariffs, other components, including parts for balers and harvesting or threshing machinery, face levies of between 15 per cent and 25 per cent, according to a list from Canada’s Department of Finance.

“This is just the beginning,” O’Connor said. “I think it will continue to grow.”

Among the companies at the event was Germany-based Claas KGaA mbH, which used the trade show to launch a new line of products for the North American market.

Though the tractors the company sells in Canada all come from Europe, combines that used to be made in the U.S. are now also being brought from overseas to avoid tariffs on steel and other components.

Frans Reijmers, a Claas product manager, said this gives the company an edge over certain products from competitors produced south of the border, particularly big-horsepower tractors.

“The new lines that we are introducing here are all coming out of France, so that is outside of the scope of the U.S.-Canadian tensions,” he said. “In that sense, we have the benefit that it is not currently coming out of the U.S.”

With files from Bloomberg News jjuha@postmedia.com

The average price of diesel in Canada on Tuesday was $2.64 per litre, according to Natural Resources Canada, with prices in places such as Halifax just shy of $2.70, as the war in Iran has disrupted global supplies. About a year ago, Cron said he was probably paying about $1.50 per litre.
“Now that we’re coming into cropping season, a combine alone will use 300 to 400 litres a day, so when you see diesel prices at $2.60 a litre, it makes you shudder,” he said.

Brent crude, up more than 75 per cent this year, was trading at around US$106 a barrel Tuesday following reports that Saudi Arabia May take weeks to reopen its east-west pipeline, which was halted after it was struck by militants.
The pipeline had become Saudi Arabia’s most important workaround since the Iran war choked off exports from the Persian Gulf that normally move through the Strait of Hormuz.
Diesel futures were also trading at around US$200 a barrel, as fuel supplies have been disrupted in both the Middle East and Russia, where Ukrainian strikes have hindered refining capacity.
But high oil prices are far from the only concern on farmers’ minds, said Mark Reusser, a director with the Ontario Federation of Agriculture.

For the most part, agricultural products have continued to enter the United States tariff-free, but he said specific sectors such as dairy are closely following developments in the ongoing trade war between the two countries.

“The anxiety is probably higher in the supply management sector, simply because the U.S. has specifically targeted supply management and specifically dairy as being something that they want to see changed,” Reusser said. “Many are wondering, ‘How can I run a business when it’s under threat from my neighbour to the south?’”
The trade tensions, however, are also creating some silver linings and opening new opportunities, said Rob O’Connor, director of Canada’s Outdoor Farm Show.

For example, this year’s event attracted companies from 13 countries, up from seven last year, looking to bring farming equipment and other products into the country after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down, prompting the federal government to implement counter-tariffs on some farming equipment.

Though large machinery, such as combines and tractors, is excluded from the counter-tariffs, other components, including parts for balers and harvesting or threshing machinery, face levies of between 15 per cent and 25 per cent, according to a list from Canada’s Department of Finance.
“This is just the beginning,” O’Connor said. “I think it will continue to grow.”
Among the companies at the event was Germany-based Claas KGaA mbH, which used the trade show to launch a new line of products for the North American market.

Though the tractors the company sells in Canada all come from Europe, combines that used to be made in the U.S. are now also being brought from overseas to avoid tariffs on steel and other components.
Frans Reijmers, a Claas product manager, said this gives the company an edge over certain products from competitors produced south of the border, particularly big-horsepower tractors.

“The new lines that we are introducing here are all coming out of France, so that is outside of the scope of the U.S.-Canadian tensions,” he said. “In that sense, we have the benefit that it is not currently coming out of the U.S.”

stories.title: City launches annual resident satisfaction survey
stories.summary: The City of London’s resident satisfaction survey will be conducted starting today to September 30 in collaboration with Liaison Strategies.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
The City of London’s resident satisfaction survey will be conducted starting today to September 30 in collaboration with Liaison Strategies.

The survey gives Londoners the chance to voice their opinions and perspectives about key issues facing our community.

“The purpose is to help council and staff with prioritization and decision making. This information gets analyzed and synthesized and then shared with the council,” said Trevor Fowler with the city of London. “This will be going to council the results of the survey in 2026 in December and then that then feeds into some of the prioritization and decision making that the city would undertake in the subsequent year.”

500 residents aged 18 and older will participate in the survey.

stories.title: Carney says deepening ‘alliance’ with European Union is a work in progress
stories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is seeking to deepen ties with the European Union amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says discussions about deepening the “alliance” between Canada and the European Union are in early days yet, dialing back expectations as he departs for France to address the European Parliament.

Speaking to reporters in Toronto Tuesday, Carney said there are “strategic areas” that Canada can focus on with the 27-member political and trade bloc, including energy and critical minerals.

But while there is an “economic component” to those talks, Carney said Canada’s push to diversify away from dependence on the United States is ultimately about the country’s sovereignty.

“One of the lessons of the last few years is that integration, whether it’s trade or in a supply chain or in a technology, which used to be only an asset, is being used as a weapon by certain countries and others. So, a country like Canada that has many assets, we have to look at where we stand and who our partners are so that we are integrating, in other words, we’re trading with and connected to partners on which we can rely,” Carney told reporters.

“And that makes us more independent. So … yes, there’s an economic component, but it is about greater sovereignty, having partnerships.”

Carney made the comments after a speech at the Canada Investment Summit, an event aimed at bringing in $1 trillion in foreign investment to Canada over the next decade. Both the investment summit and Carney’s overtures to European leaders are set against the backdrop of ongoing tensions with the United States and President Donald Trump’s administration.

The prime minister left the summit Tuesday to travel to Strasbourg, France, where he will become the first world leader to attend the European Union’s “state of the union” debate on Wednesday and on Thursday will address the continent’s politicians.

The Wall Street Journal, citing unnamed sources, suggested that Canada was exploring becoming an “associate” member of the EU. That’s led to wide and varied speculation about what that would actually mean – there is no category for “associate” membership in the E.U.’s founding treaty, for instance.

But Carney cautioned against a “big reveal” about Canada’s future relationship with the European Union on the trip, noting that discussions about “deepening” ties began last June and will continue at a summit planned for Montreal next month.

“This is a process that has been underway for more than a year since we deepened our strategic partnership last June,” Carney said.

“This is the next stage of that process.”

stories.title: This nude Sydney Sweeney ad is causing major backlash from athletes around the globe
stories.summary: The backlash has been directed at the representation of women in sports and body image
stories.author: Sarah Wallace
stories.content:
Another advertisement featuring Sydney Sweeney causing controversy? Check.

The actress has found herself in hot water again, after promoting sports betting app Novig in an online ad campaign last Wednesday. The advertisement has sparked outrage from around the globe, with female athletes clapping back against the commercial’s messaging.

The Novig ad sees the Euphoria actress almost nude, covered only by her hands, hair or various sports equipment, while stating that the app allows users to bet on “just sports.”

“No betting on wars or deaths and no politics,” she says at one point. “Just you, your takes and sports.”

The video has more than 48 million views on the 29-year-old’s Instagram Reels, and another 1.3 million views on Novig’s YouTube channel.

In a press release on Wednesday, Sweeney – who is an equity holder and strategic partner in the company – said the campaign was “embracing a fun idea.”

“The concept is simple: cut through the noise and put the focus entirely on sports. The campaign brings that idea to life with confidence, humour and a playful edge.”

The chief executive officer and co-founder of Novig, Jacob Fortinsky, said Sweeney’s appearance in the ad “helped bring that message to life in a way that’s impossible to ignore.”

Novig declined to respond to The Globe’s request for comment. Sweeney has also not directly responded to the criticism.

The campaign has sparked intense social media blowback, including from professional female athletes. Much of the backlash has been directed at Sweeney and Novig’s representation of women in sports and body image, with various posts addressing Sweeney directly.

Hundreds of response videos and photo carousels from athletes have circulated showing “what a women in sports looks like.”

One popular post format showcases the user’s career highlights while British pop star Dua Lipa’s live performance of her song Training Season plays in the background. Former Ncaa gymnast Gracie Kramer initiated the trend on Saturday, writing “idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a women in sports looks like.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gracie Kramer (@gracie.kramer)

In a separate Instagram post , Kramer said that it was “SO much more than sports.”

“This is so much bigger than a moment or a trend,” she wrote. “It’s about inspiring real change in the way women are seen, valued, and represented and reminding the next generation of powerful girls that there is no limit to who they can become.”

Canadian high diver Molly Carlson posted on Instagram how the public should “focus less on how women Look and more on what they can DO.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Molly Carlson (@mollycarlson1)

“There were so many moments I wanted to walk away because I didn’t think I looked like the athlete I was ‘supposed’ to be. … Young girls deserve to grow up seeing female athletes celebrated for their strength, courage, talent and what their bodies are capable of.”

Olympic gold medallists including British cyclist Sophie Capewell and Australian swimmer Ariarne Titmus have also responded to the Sweeney ad and Novig’s sexualization of women.

British sprinter Amy Hunt, who finished fourth in the 200-metre final at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship on Sunday, directly called out Sweeney after the race.

“Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like,” Hunt said post-race to BBC Sport .

This is Sweeney’s second advertisement in two years that has prompted widespread reaction. The first – for American Eagle in the summer of 2025 – centred on blond-haired, blue-eyed Sweeney having great “jeans,” a play on “genes.”

The campaign faced social-media criticism that it promoted eugenics, but it also helped the company’s shares rise 77 per cent since July, 2025. Revenue jumped 37 per cent in the six months through January, compared with a 24-per-cent rise in the same period a year earlier.

“If Sydney Sweeney is a registered Republican, I think her ad is fantastic,” U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters last year.

Sweeney didn’t initially respond to the criticism, but noted in a November, 2025, video with GQ magazine that “when I have an issue I want to speak about, people will hear.”

With a report from Reuters

content_blocks.caption: The 'Sydney Sweeney has great jeans' ad campaign on display at an American Eagle Outfitters store in August, 2025. Ted Shaffrey/The Associated Press

content_blocks.text: This is Sweeney’s second advertisement in two years that has prompted widespread reaction. The first – for American Eagle in the summer of 2025 – centred on blond-haired, blue-eyed Sweeney having great “jeans,” a play on “genes.”

The campaign faced social-media criticism that it promoted eugenics, but it also helped the company’s shares rise 77 per cent since July, 2025. Revenue jumped 37 per cent in the six months through January, compared with a 24-per-cent rise in the same period a year earlier.
“If Sydney Sweeney is a registered Republican, I think her ad is fantastic,” U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters last year.
Sweeney didn’t initially respond to the criticism, but noted in a November, 2025, video with GQ magazine that “when I have an issue I want to speak about, people will hear.”

stories.title: The best Canadian moments from the 2026 Emmys
stories.summary: The show was imbued with Canadiana, from its honourees to a nod to Heated Rivalry
stories.author: Arisa Valyear
stories.content:
Throngs of Hollywood’s A-list television actors descended on Los Angeles’s Peacock Theater to celebrate their craft at the 78th edition of the Emmys last night. In true award show fashion, the evening spurred touching tributes, cringey jokes, meme-able stills (we’re looking at you Michelle Pfeiffer ) – and some truly Canadian moments.

Against the political backdrop of an intensifying trade war between Canada and the United States , the night of pop culture largely celebrated American talent. But a few noteworthy moments in the spotlight ensured Canada didn’t go unnoticed.

From Michael J. Fox receiving the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award to Sally Field praising “blessed Canada, our neighbours, our friends,” here were the top Canadian moments from the show.

The California-born actress was all about Canada last night, both on the red carpet and on stage. While accepting her award for outstanding lead actress in a limited or anthology series or movie for Netflix’s Remarkably Bright Creatures , she expressed admiration for her northern neighbours . It was a fitting remark considering the movie was filmed in several British Columbia locations including Vancouver, Richmond and Lions Bay.

Field shared more about her love for the country in a red carpet interview with Canadian entertainment program Etalk preceremony, even holding and waving a Canadian flag that was handed to her off screen. During the segment, she called Vancouver “one of the most spectacular cities on Earth.”

Save for a small mention in host Mariska Hargitay’s introductory segment , the Canadian juggernaut series – based on the novel by Nova Scotian author Rachel Reid – was passed over throughout the night. It didn’t receive any nominations, though Connor Storrie was nominated for outstanding guest actor in a comedy series for his Saturday Night Live hosting earlier this year .

Despite its global success, the show’s Canadian financing is what ruled it out of Emmy contention: Productions wholly financed outside of the U.S. are ineligible for nomination, according to the Television Academy’s rules .

Nonetheless, Canadian actor Stephen Amell, who presented at the ceremony with some of his castmates from the upcoming Baywatch reboot, reflected on the snub in a red carpet interview . “The Emmys should be a snapshot of what was relevant in television. And there was nothing more relevant in television this year than Heated Rivalry ,” he said.

Macaulay Culkin, Annie Murphy and Dan Levy delivered a heartfelt tribute to the actress ahead of the larger in memoriam segment. The trio, who all starred alongside O’Hara (Culkin in Home Alone and Murphy and Levy in the homegrown hit series Schitt’s Creek ) collectively praised the Toronto-born actress for her warmth, encouragement and sharp humour.

Murphy specifically injected a few hits of Canadiana into her portion of the tribute, remembering a time she was passed a note of condolences on an Air Canada flight and recalling “a drive up north” when she was embraced by a gas station attendant grieving O’Hara’s death. The Lcbo also popped up in Murphy’s address when she detailed a shopping trip interrupted by a passerby impersonating character Moira Rose by combining her “where’s the bébé” line with the show’s iconic “ew, David” phrase.

Perhaps the most touching moment of Canadian pride was when Michael J. Fox took the stage to receive the Bob Hope Humanitarian Award, becoming only the sixth person to ever receive the honour since its inception in 2002. Fox was given the award for his philanthropic efforts toward Parkinson’s research, made possible through his foundation dedicated to the cause, the Michael J. Fox Foundation .

With Fox’s Order of Canada pin fixed to his lapel , the Alberta-born actor and philanthropist received not one but two standing ovations during his acceptance speech. Along with thanking the Television Academy, his foundation partners, donors, staff and patient community, Fox thoughtfully remarked on Hope’s military support and championing of “military families like mine.”

Remembering his father’s time spent in the Canadian Armed Forces, Fox highlighted what he learned: “When it starts to get tough, you show up. You help. And if you can add a little joy while you’re doing it, that’s even better.”

Fox closed his acceptance remarks by thanking his wife and children, mom and dad, members of his family living in Canada, “army brats and Bob Hope fans.”

stories.title: Londoner Jovan Ivanisevic named to Canada men’s soccer team
stories.summary: The 21-year-old defender is one of eight named to Canada’s squad for three fall internationals against Chile, Peru and the United States.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The 21-year-old defender is one of eight named to Canada’s squad for three fall internationals against Chile, Peru and the United States.

Last updated 21 minutes ago[](http://lfpress.com/sports/londoner-jovan-ivanisevic-named-to-Canada-mens-soccer-team#comments-area)

Canada head coach Jesse Marsch celebrates after Stephen Eustaquio scores the team’s first goal during a Fifa World Cup round-of-32 match against South Africa at Los Angeles Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., ON June 28, 2026. (Fran Santiago/Getty Images)

Jovan Ivanisevic will wear Canadian colours again this fall.

The 21-year-old Londoner was named to Canada Soccer’s 26-man roster for the September-October Fifa international window, which includes a pair of home matches against Chile at Toronto’s BMO Field on Sept. 26 (7 p.m.) and Peru at Montreal’s Stade Saputo on Oct. 3 (2 p.m.).

The series will close against the United States on Oct. 6 at Allianz Field in St. Paul, Minn. The home leg is being billed as“The Homecoming,”a chance to welcome back the team that“inspired a nation”at the World Cup this summer.

“We’re excited to get the group back together following a historic summer,” national team head coach Jesse Marsch said. “This team left everything out there at the World Cup and now we get to do it again in front of the fans who were with us every step of the way. That’s what these matches are about. This summer changed what’s possible for this program and these matches are our chance to build on it.”

Ivanisevic, a local Alliance and TFC Academy grad, is one of eight defenders named to the squad. He attended Mother Teresa high school before making his senior and professional debut in 2023.

The 6-foot-3 centre-back has already played internationally for Canada as a member of the under-20 team two years ago. He is currently starting for Sarajevo in the Bosnian Premier League.

Ivanisevic joined that club last year on loan from Croatian Football League side Istra 1961, where he played for parts of two seasons starting in 2023. He also made 12 appearances with Bologna FC in Italy’s Serie A in 2025.

All three Canada matches will air live on TSN and online atOneSoccer.CA.

stories.title: Is the Western Fair still affordable for London Families?
stories.summary: For many London families, the Western Fair is an annual tradition, but rising costs are making some question h...
stories.author: Torey Joseph Legarrie
stories.content:
For many London families, the Western Fair is an annual tradition, but rising costs are making some question how affordable a day at the fair is.

Visitors packed the fairgrounds and lined up for rides and food on the opening weekend of the 149th Western Fair. But outside the gates on Tuesday, one passer by said the cost to bring a family was unaffordable.

“I’ve not been there, but I work close,” said Benjamin Agyeman who was walking by the fairgrounds Tuesday. “Last year, it wasn’t affordable and then it was very hard for you to come with all the kids and family.”

Benjamin Agyeman, (Photo: Torey Joseph Legarrie)

(Photo: Torey Joseph Legarrie)

Regular admission is $20, and then the SuperPass is $50 for unlimited rides, and ticket sales on the grounds start at $10 for 14 tickets.

But fair organizers say it’s important to remember that the admission pass alone covers a lot of activities, including concerts, farm animal viewing, exhibits and monster truck shows, inside the gates.

“It is pretty wild the amount of entertainment you actually get within your admission,” said Angela Hawkins, director of marketing and community relations.

She said it’s too early to measure the overall attendance and how prices have affected numbers, but noted there have been a number of discount options available since opening day, when they .

The fair also has a $6 before six special, which means every food vendor has to offer at least one item for $6 before 6 p.m., and timed specials for seniors, children and students. For example, Tuesday, Fanshawe and Western students could enter for $12 andride all day for $35.

Despite rising costs, the Western Fair continues to be a popular fall tradition in London, giving families a chance to enjoy rides, entertainment, and food while spending time together.

stories.title: Angine de Poitrine to perform at Polaris awards show in Toronto
stories.summary: Quebec rock duo will perform at concert and award ceremony in Massey Hall on Sept. 22
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Extraterrestrial rock band Angine de Poitrine is to land in Toronto next week.

The Polaris Music Prize says the duo from Saguenay, Que., will perform at its concert and award ceremony on Sept. 22 at Massey Hall.

The eccentric performers, who claim to be 333-year-old aliens, have been gaining global recognition and made their American TV debut Monday on Jimmy Fallon’s show.

CBC’s Eurovision head explains why bbno$ has a chance to represent Canada, but Angine de Poitrine is a no-go

Angine de Poitrine is among the 10 artists shortlisted for the prestigious prize that awards $30,000 to the best Canadian album based solely on artistic merit.

Organizers say two-time Polaris prizewinner Jeremy Dutcher has also been added to the bill as a special guest presenter.

Other scheduled performers include fellow nominees Aquakultre, Begonia, Bibi Club, Beverly Glenn-Copeland, Les Louanges and Tanya Tagaq.

stories.title: Lack of educational assistants hurting students, teachers and families at Thames Valley public schools, parent
stories.summary: | CBC News | Posted: September 15, 2026 7:21 PM | Last Updated: September 15
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 15, 2026 7:21 PM | Last Updated: September 15
Union and school board won't say how many educational assistants are working this year
Every time Sarah Lawrence drops her son Caleb, 8, off at his Thames Valley District School Board (TVDSB) school, she wonders if he'll run away and get hit by a car.

Alana Parker's daughter, Parker, 7, has to have a classmate accompany her to the bathroom. If Parker needs help, the classmate runs back to the classroom to tell the teacher, who can then page an educational assistant.
Jack Staiton, 15, is a curious kid who has just started Grade 9 at an East Elgin high school that offers courses such as carpentry, drama and music.

But he spends his days in a classroom with seven other students with disabilities. His mother says he can't take part in many of those courses because there's no one available to take the students to other classrooms.

The parents, whose children attend different Thames Valley schools, say the lack of educational assistants, or EAs, is leaving students without the support they need and putting additional pressure on teachers, other education workers and families.

"It feels like the staff who are doing a good job managing the crisis the school system is in are being punished for doing a good job — they're holding it together because they care about the kids, they want kids to get support, but nothing changes. They're the camouflage," said Lawrence, whose son is in Grade 4 and has autism, severe ADHD, and apraxia of speech.
Last year, the school had a safety plan for Caleb that required direct supervision "pretty much all of the time," she said.

"This year, they put him in a class with zero support, no safety accommodations. Every year it's like an experiment — how long can we make it until Caleb runs away and becomes a safety issue and we have to give him direct support. How many times can we get lucky? Is this the year he's going to be hit by a car and not come home from school?"
The concerns echo those raised by parents and unions across the Thames Valley board in recent years.
"There are never enough EAs, and there have never been enough," said Sherri Moore, a TVDSB trustee who is running for re-election.
"I'm hearing from a lot of parents that their child had an EA last year but doesn't this year. There's a lot going on and teachers are having to do more and more in the classroom with less support."

The number of EAs guaranteed by the collective agreement hasn't changed this year over last, even if there are more kids with special needs who need help, said Paul Nagy, the acting president of CUPE Local 7575, which represents EAs, instructional assistants and student supervisors in the Thames Valley board.
But school boards get funding from the province based on how many students are enrolled, and this year there are fewer Thames Valley kids than there were last year, which means less money.
The province told CBC News it knows there is a problem with the funding formula, and that it is working on a solution.
Nagy declined to disclose how many EAs the school board employs, as did Thames Valley officials.

EAs get moved to schools where they are needed throughout the year, a "taking from Peter to pay Paul" situation, Nagy said. The board also hires temporary EAs if it needs to or has the money to do so, he added.
"It's about underfunding, when it comes down to it. The province's funding formula just hasn't kept up with the pace of reality and with the increasing complexity of student needs," Nagy said.
"A school doesn't look like it did 10 or 15 years go. It's just not the same place."
Nagy said EAs are increasingly being asked to monitor several students who require one-on-one care, meaning some children are slipping through the cracks.
In many cases, classroom teachers are picking up the slack, Lawrence said.

Her other son, Mason, 10, has autism and has an intellectual disability. He is also non-verbal, and gets government-funded therapy at home during the mornings. In the afternoons, he goes to school and doesn't have an EA in his classroom.
"This is year two of no EA support. Nothing," said Lawrence.

"His teacher is amazing, and she has engaged his classmates to help him with different work tasks, and she does a great job of including him and bringing him into activities with other kids so he can participate."
Lawrence said teachers' dedication can make it seem like the system is functioning when, in her view, educators are holding it together by doing more than they should have to.

"Educators are the reason that my kids are successful and why kids aren't dying at school. But because she's doing such a great job with him, the system can say, 'See, the seams are stretched, the dress is ripping, but it hasn't ripped yet, so it's still good."
The Thames Valley District School Board predicted a $9.2 million budget shortfall in special education in 2026-2027.

The result is fewer EAs supporting more students, increased pressure on classroom teachers and other education workers, and greater concerns about student and staff safety," said Mike Thomas, who heads the union representing elementary school teachers.
"Our students deserve properly funded classrooms with enough qualified Educational Assistants to ensure every child can participate, learn, and thrive in Ontario’s public education system."
School board officials say they recognize that kids have complex needs and say they want them to get the support they need.

Staffing levels are dictated by enrolment, which has experienced a decline. However, these numbers will not be finalized for several weeks, as new students continue to register," the board said in an emailed statement.
"Our focus remains on maintaining safe and inclusive learning environments and responding to student needs in collaboration with families and school teams.
The newly appointed CEO of the school board, Kevin Auckland, was not available for an interview.
Staiton, whose son Jack just started high school and lost his one-on-one support, said every year has been a struggle to advocate for an education that other kids take for granted.

"Somehow, a little boy who can't talk or express himself has an EA all through elementary, and we enter high school, and it's, 'Nope, he'll be in a classroom with other people close to possibly his level and two EAs and a teacher who sits at a desk,'" she said.
"Do I think he can go to mechanics on his own? Absolutely not. But he's in a school with a wealth of opportunities and no one to take him to those opportunities."
Staiton said she isn't asking the school to create special opportunities for her son. She wants someone to help him access the opportunities already available to other students.
"All they have to do is take him to the room and show him this different stuff that's out there."
Parker, the seven-year-old who has to bring a classmate with her to the bathroom, has been told she has to wear a bright orange pinnie on the school yard because she runs away.
She's in Grade 2 and has autism, but her mom said she's been told Parker is doing "too well" to get assigned an EA.

"Last year, while Parker was in Grade 1, I watched her teacher essentially have to do two jobs: teach an entire classroom of children while simultaneously trying to meet Parker's individual support needs," her mother said.
"That isn't fair to Parker, and it isn't fair to her teacher or the other students."

The Thames Valley District School Board predicted a $9.2 million budget shortfall in special education in 2026-2027.

Alana Parker's daughter, Parker, 7, has to have a classmate accompany her to the bathroom. If Parker needs help, the classmate runs back to the classroom to tell the teacher, who can then page an educational assistant.

Jack Staiton, 15, is a curious kid who has just started Grade 9 at an East Elgin high school that offers courses such as carpentry, drama and music.

But he spends his days in a classroom with seven other students with disabilities. His mother says he can't take part in many of those courses because there's no one available to take the students to other classrooms.

The parents, whose children attend different Thames Valley schools, say the lack of educational assistants, or EAs, is leaving students without the support they need and putting additional pressure on teachers, other education workers and families.

"It feels like the staff who are doing a good job managing the crisis the school system is in are being punished for doing a good job — they're holding it together because they care about the kids, they want kids to get support, but nothing changes. Last year, the school had a safety plan for Caleb that required direct supervision "pretty much all of the time," she said.

"This year, they put him in a class with zero support, no safety accommodations. stories.title: London commercial real estate investment nearly doubles to $459M
stories.summary: Apartment and condo deals helped drive the second-quarter surge, with multi-family investment topping $387 million.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
London recorded nearly $460 million in commercial real estate investment in the second quarter, making it the eighth-best-performing market in Canada, according to a new report.

Commercial real estate investment across the country surged to $16.2 billion between April and June, a more than 50 per cent year-over-year increase, boosted by increased transactions and merger and acquisition activity, the Canada Investment Overview report from commercial real estate firm Cbre shows.

In London, 28 deals worth a combined $459.1 million were made in the second quarter, nearly double the investment recorded in the previous three months.

“Things are a little bit more buoyant than they have been in a while,” said Kevin MacDougall, vice-president of Cbre’s London office.

Multi-family home sales – a category that includes apartment and condo buildings – brought in $387.7 million, compared with $127.5 million the previous quarter, representing a 204 per cent increase.

“I think generally there’s a flight to more stable investments,” MacDougall said, noting multi-family investments bring in steady rental income.

“There’s still a lot of uncertainty in the market. Nobody likes uncertainty,” he said.

Real estate investment trusts (REITs) accounted for the bulk of London transactions at more than $250 million, followed by foreign investors at more than $100 million.

Across Canada, foreign investors accounted for nearly 44 per cent of acquisitions, followed by private Canadian investors with more than 33 per cent.

Cross-border investment into Canadian commercial real estate hit $4.3 billion, bringing the total for the first half of 2026 to $5.1 billion and surpassing the full-year totals of the previous two years.

“Despite some of the negative headlines, the momentum is real and investors believe in Canada,” Cbre Canadian capital markets president Peter Senst said in a release.

Could a long-empty downtown jewel soon be turned into apartments?

Large downtown London properties hit market again amid ‘stability’

“We are on a trajectory that could make 2026 a record year for Canadian commercial real estate investment. Global investors are increasingly viewing Canada as a market of safety and stability, and the capital flows back that up.”

Office : $5.5M ($11.5M)

Industrial: $23.7M ($39.8M)

Retail: $10.4M ($17.1M)

Multi-family: $387.7M ($127.5M)

ICI land : $31.9M ($50M)

Total: $459.1M ($245.8M)

stories.title: Carney says investment tax incentive expansion is a “mega deduction”
stories.summary: The federal government is expanding a tax incentive aimed at boosting new business investment.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The federal government is expanding a tax incentive aimed at boosting new business investment.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the “productivity mega deduction” during t he Canada Investment Summit underway in Toronto , building on a measure introduced in budget 2025 .

Ottawa is making immediate expensing permanent on a broader range of investments in a move that’s expected to have a fiscal cost of $36 billion over five years, starting this year.

Immediate expensing is a measure that allows businesses to fully write off the cost of an investment in the year that it becomes available for use.

The deduction will now apply to more than 65 per cent of investments in a wider array of eligible capital assets from roughly 15 per cent in the previous year’s budget.

The government says the move lowers Canada’s marginal effective tax rate on new business investment to 6.4 per cent from 13 per cent.

stories.title: 'Blue-collar' centre Carson Harmer on trade to London Knights: 'An honour'
stories.summary: Carson Harmer should fit in with Hunter Hockey just fine.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
Carson Harmer should fit in with Hunter Hockey just fine.

The 19-year-old centreman grew up on farmland 10 minutes south of Mitchell with a father in the concrete pumping business. He learned early what it’s like to roll up your sleeves and earn a day’s wage.

“I come from a blue-collar family,” the 5-foot-10, 195-pounder said. “You just work hard with whatever you do. Really, it was instilled in me at a young age and I just stuck with it. Working hard at everything you do is something I live by.”

Harmer didn’t report to Saginaw Spirit training camp this fall. This past weekend, he was dealt to London for 2024 OHL fourth-overall pick Braidy Wassilyn, who scored 17 goals and 41 points in 56 games with London last year.

The Knights used the former Niagara IceDog, who attended Montreal Canadiens rookie camp, sparingly in last spring’s playoff series against Sault Ste. Marie.

“We thought we needed more of a centreman,” London GM Mark Hunter said. “We should have lots of offence this year and this guy is a good two-way hockey player. Wassilyn is a good offensive player.

“Both teams wanted a little different mix, that’s all.”

Hunter was well-informed on Harmer’s situation. The Spirit’s 2023 third-rounder (44th overall) worked out with new London teammates Kane Barch and Eloan Le Gallic at Deon Keller’s gym in Lucan during the summer.

All three went on the ice routinely with Barch’s father Krys, who coached the IceDogs last year and is now helping out in skills development with the Knights.

“It’ll be exciting to play in front of my family and friends,” Harmer said, “and it’s an honour to play for this team. It’s close to home so I’m really happy to be here. It’s good (the trade happened) at the start of the season and not get thrown in during it.

“I think I’ll fit in with their style of game of working, having some grit and being able to produce offensively and being good defensively.”

Harmer was the top scorer for the Junior B Greater Ontario Hockey League’s Stratford Warriors (28 goals, 65 points) in 2023-24. He was called up to the Spirit for the end of the playoffs and watched Saginaw win a historic Memorial Cup final on home ice against the Knights.

He posted a combined 41 goals and 94 points over the past two seasons with the Spirit and has the ability to score 25-30 more goals with the serious talent London has assembled. He will head straight to the regular schedule against Windsor Friday (7 p.m. at Canada Life Place) with no exhibition tune-ups, but that’s nothing more hard work can’t fix.

“I worked on my shot a lot in the summer,” he said. “I’m confident coming in.”

Around THE Rink: The Knights’ roster is in its final stages of completion heading into the season opener Friday. London wants its younger players to get time in Junior B but will keep additional skaters around longer until the NHL campers return . . . Hunter explained his reasoning for trading 18-year-old defenceman Jacob Xu to Peterborough for a couple of draft picks. “We’re pretty strong down the left side,” he said. “We have Vandeven, Sokolovskii and Mitchell. Xu had to play on his right side (as a left-hand shot) and I don’t think he was comfortable there. He plays better on the left side and I didn’t think it was fair for him (to play on the right).” . . . Who’s getting the start in net for the opener? That depends on Aleksei Medvedev’s status with the Canucks this week. If he stays, it will be either 17-year-old Charlie Weiss (2.14 goals against average, .914 save percentage in three preseason appearances) or 18-year-old American Brian Cooke (6.53 GAA, .833 save percentage in five games) . . . Should London’s 2-4 preseason record and 31 goals surrendered be of concern? Not really. But it will be if the first six real games have similar numbers. Even with NHL first-rounders gone and rookies in the lineup, the Knights should ice enough talent early for a solid start.

stories.title: A terminal diagnosis is sending me on a whirlwind world tour
stories.summary: I want to inspire people to stop putting off cool experiences until later - to travel now while they’re healthy
stories.author: Lauren Smith
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

My dad’s death was a brutal reminder of how short life is and how little control we really have in the end. Cancer didn’t care what he’d achieved or what type of person he was. It was aggressive and moved with an unfeeling decisiveness.

My dad was a charismatic man who was generous with his time. I’d listen intently to stories about his early career and the adventures that he had in Germany and France. He made travelling sound so exciting. But despite his bold youth, he found himself content as a family man and he loved the mountains where we live in British Columbia. “Why would you ever leave here?” he’d say as we watched the sun setting behind the nearby ski resort.

I could think of a million reasons.

Yet after he died, I stayed in the small city of Rossland and got a good retirement-oriented job at a company with a pension – the same company he used to work for. He had left me some money (about two times my annual salary) and I channelled my grief into growing the windfall for my own retirement.

It was difficult adapting to life without his encouragement. When I got upset, he wasn’t there to coach me to breathe. Tearful moments turned into tearful nights; they didn’t end in minutes anymore with me laughing at myself for being so dramatic. But time marched on.

Four years later I was forced to accept the next part of my inheritance – the cancer gene. In September, 2024, my mom and I sat in the oncology unit in Trail, B.C., and listened to the doctors about an unresectable melanoma that had spread to my spine.

At 41, no one gave me a prognosis, but my body felt like I didn’t have much time.

Google told me less than a year.

I tried to calm myself and hear my Dad’s voice in my head: “In with the good, out with the bad,” I’d repeat as I breathed deeply. Simultaneously, I berated myself because my body was moving at a geriatric pace and still I hadn’t really lived.

Bypass surgery scarred me. But years spent worrying about my heart took a greater toll

I felt so stupid for prioritizing work, for being so timid. I had not travelled but I had maxed out my employee share purchase plan and Rrsp every year, content with waiting until I was 60 to start living. I mourned those 20 years that I was no longer going to get with so much ferocity that I became unhinged.

The day I was diagnosed as terminal, I made a decision to spend everything before I died. I bought a motorized bed to help me get up in the mornings, but otherwise I spent money recklessly. I gave away most of my office clothes because I wasn’t going to need them. I bought expensive gifts for most of my friends and family. I booked a trip to Ottawa to visit my aunt and brought my new boyfriend on a whim without even telling her.

I May have been a bit manic but I followed doctors’ orders closely that whole time and took the targeted therapies as prescribed. Within six months, I no longer needed the bed to help me get up and the cancer had stabilized. This was a gift. I was going to live longer than the year that my research had suggested.

So I started planning my travel.

Since my diagnosis, I’ve been to Italy, Spain, Portugal and the Bahamas. I’m grateful that my dad left me the means to chase famous sights such as the Colosseum in Rome or the ruins of Pompeii. Except for nausea and lack of appetite, my stamina held up well until April. My mom and I went to Barcelona, but side effects left my feet aching and callused. I also needed more naps.

My inheritance has given me some control over an illness that’s unpredictable. My current commitment is to spend what’s remaining on travel and unique experiences. If I take someone with me, I have the budget for at least seven more trips. I’ll be able to do even more if I want to brave solo travel.

I have also started a blog about my travels. I want to inspire people to stop putting off cool experiences until later - to travel now while they’re healthy. Also, I hope to empower people who are sick to seek out solutions so they can see the world instead of living life solely by the rhythm of monthly bloodwork and doctor’s appointments.

The best of times for some can be the worst for others

My next trip is to Ireland and France. My boyfriend and I are going to capture this adventure on video and create a miniseries on YouTube . For now, I’m keeping a positive frame of mind. I’m treating the world like I’m going to live, but the memory of my dad’s death keeps me grounded.

I know my expiration date is still sooner than it should be. When I’m too weak to leave my bed and when the pain can’t be medicated, I’ll breathe in deeply and hang onto the good memories.

I’ll know I lived a life that sought out exceptional and pivotal experiences. I want everyone to be able to say the same.

Lauren Smith lives in Castlegar, B.C.

stories.title: Federal public service has lost 23,000 staffers in two years: budget watchdog report
stories.summary: The federal public service has shed more than 23,000 staffers over the last two years, says Canada's parliamentary spending watchdog.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A person passes a Health Canada office at Tunney's Pasture, in Ottawa on Wednesday, Jan. 29, 2025. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

Posted September 15, 2026 2:40 pm.

Last Updated September 15, 2026 3:13 pm.

Ottawa — The federal public service has shed more than 23,000 staffers over the last two years, says Canada’s parliamentary spending watchdog.

A new online tool released by the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer estimates there were 344,970 federal employees in the second quarter of this year, down 6.5 per cent from two years ago.

The departments and agencies that gained the most staff over the last two years were National Defence, the Communications Security Establishment, Elections Canada, Housing, Infrastructure and Communities Canada and the Canadian Space Agency.

The departments that lost the most employees were the Canada Revenue Agency, Employment and Social Development Canada, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada, the Public Health Agency of Canada and Health Canada.
