stories.title: London-area school board elections: Who’s running and what’s changed
stories.summary: Despite reduced trustee powers, candidates are still lining up across London and the surrounding region ahead of the Oct. 26 vote.
stories.author: Heather Rivers Davey
stories.content:
In the run-up to the Oct. 26 election, LFP reporter Heather Rivers Davey takes a deep dive into the school board trustee races to see who is running and why they are seeking office at a time of significant change.

It May not be what you think.

Despite a very different role than in the past, candidates are still widely signing up in London, with just one acclamation and 18 candidates competing for six positions.

That runs contrary to “a common misconception” that school board trustee elections are characterized by widespread acclamations and vacancies, the Ontario Public School Boards’ Association said in a release this week.

Across the province, 673 candidates are vying for trustee positions in public school boards, including 519 new candidates.

“The fact that so many people are prepared to take on that responsibility tells us that local education governance continues to matter deeply to Ontarians. It’s clear that democracy is not outdated,” association president Kathleen Woodcock said.

It’s a different story across the wider region, where positions have been acclaimed except in Middlesex County, where two candidates are challenging a veteran trustee.

Basically, much of trustees’ former powers have been suspended.

Earlier this year, the provincial government rolled out major changes to the school trustee system in English public and Catholic boards, stripping elected officials of budgetary power and placing it under the purview of a new chief executive role.

When it comes to the budget, trustees can only provide feedback and advice, while the chief executive makes the final decision.

For example, the London District Catholic school board voted down a proposed budget for next year that included job cuts, but the chief executive advanced it to Queen’s Park for approval anyway.

Both new and familiar faces have thrown their hats into the ring in the Thames Valley District school board, including former Thames Valley chair Lori-Ann Pizzolato, Sheri Polhill and Sherri Moore.

Others running for office include Christine Morgan, Smita Tajne, Durgeshwar Tiwari, Andrew Bawden, Mike Bloxam, Paul Gray, Veena Joshi, Paras (Pat) Mehta, David Ross, Nisha Sharma, Manojkumar Chakkanthara Viswanathan, Sarvarinder Singh Dohil, Lincoln McCardle, Archana Patel and Ron Royal.

In Elgin County, Melissa Knott and Bob Pate have been acclaimed.

In Oxford, Benjamin Lampkin and William McKinnon have also been acclaimed.

It’s a different story in Middlesex, where veteran trustee Christian Sachs is being challenged by Bev Noble and Bill Tichenoff.

In the London District Catholic school board, newcomers running for office include Sibu Joseph, Michael Wickett, Tarish Roy, Sujeesh Chacko, Joanne Andrews and Swapna Simon. Veteran trustees hoping to keep their seats are Sandra Cruz, Gabe Pizzuti and Linda Steel, who has been acclaimed.

In Elgin County, Stephen Huver and Mary Intven Wallace have been acclaimed.

Veteran trustees Mary Holmes in Oxford County and Josh Lamb in Middlesex have also been acclaimed.

Marianne Larsen, a Thames Valley trustee and scholar specializing in education policy, calls the number of candidates running in London “a good thing.”

“These folks (who were trustees previously) are committed to public education, they want to serve, they want to give back to their communities, and they know something about what it is to be a trustee,” she said.

“I have heard Sherri Moore say ‘the TVDSB is under supervision now but we want to be ready with a full team of elected representatives for when supervision ends.’ I get that.”

The Thames Valley District school board has been under provincial supervision since the spring of 2025 over financial mismanagement and other issues.

But for Larsen, the lure of returning to a trustee’s seat just isn’t there. She is not running again.

“For me, the changes that happened with Bill 33 . . . that expanded the powers of minister of education to basically direct what goes on in school boards, I see that as a progression of what has been happening over the years,” she said.

“There are very little substantive powers or responsibilities that trustees now have. Any powers they do have can be overridden by the minister of education.”

Hrivers@postmedia.com

stories.title: Date set for coroner’s inquest into 2020 death of Toronto woman that led to protests
stories.summary: The inquest will begin on Oct. 13, with Dr. David Cameron as the presiding officer, and is expected to last 14 days.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The date has been set for a coroner’s inquest into the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet , a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

The inquest will begin on Oct. 13, with Dr. David Cameron as the presiding officer, and is expected to last 14 days.

Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment.

Her death came days after the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, and further fuelled protests and calls to defund the police.

The case also brought greater scrutiny to how police deal with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death, finding that it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

stories.title: London film director premieres the Stunt Driver at Tiff
stories.summary: A London-based director's film is premiering at the Toronto Independent Film Festival. The Stunt Driver, direc...
stories.author: Kelly Nicol
stories.content:
A London-based director’s film is premiering at the Toronto Independent Film Festival. The Stunt Driver, directed by London’s Michael Dowse, follows the story of stunt driver and daredevil Ken Carter, as he attempts to drive a car across the Saint-Laurent river from a 30-metre-high ramp.

The film will also open London’s Forest City Film Festival (Fcff) next month.

“It’s a Canadian film through-and-through,” says Ethan Hickey, Fcff executive director. “Shot in Canada, made by Canadians.”

Michael Dowse, and Jay Baruchel, who plays Ken Carter in the film, are expected to do a Q&A panel after the Fcff showing, he says.

Launched by Dorothy Downs in 2016, the Forest City Film Festival plans to show 141 films over the course of 11 days. “The films range from extremely local and regional films, to films that have premiered at Tiff and [conventions],” says Hickey.

The co-ordinator for Fanshawe College’s Television and Film program, Joel Merritt, says he’s hopeful the film will draw in more work for the London film industry. “We always appreciate when some of our locals out there are able to show we are generating talent for film making and the community. […] What I hope is that we keep attracting more and more people that are interested in producing their films in this community.”

The Stunt Driver will be shown as the opening film for the Forest City Film Festival on October 15th.

stories.title: Family of missing Canadian skyrunner Kalie McCrystal accepts that she died on the Matterhorn
stories.summary: Search teams have failed to locate Kalie McCrystal after a two-week effort
stories.author: Eric Reguly
stories.content:
The family of Kalie McCrystal has acknowledged that the Canadian mountaineer and star skyrunner met a tragic death on the Matterhorn, ON the Italian-Swiss border.

Ms. McCrystal , a 38-year-old lawyer from Squamish, B.C., went missing Sept. 1 during a practice run aimed at setting a record for ascending and descending the 4,478-metre-high mountain, one of the highest peaks in the Alps. She was alone at the time.

In a statement, her sister Jody McCrystal and their mother, Wendy Cooper, thanked the search-and-rescue teams for their two-week effort, which included helicopter and drone flights, AI analysis of images taken below the peak and on-foot patrols over the treacherous rocks and debris where she May have disappeared. The RCMP were also involved in the attempt.

“Despite Kalie’s exceptional skill and experience in technical mountain terrain, including her previous experience on the Matterhorn itself, everything we now know suggests she fell while descending,” their statement said. “Despite the efforts of so many over the past weeks, the search has not led us to Kalie. This is not the outcome any of us had hoped for and is very difficult to accept.

“While we desperately wish we could have found her, we find peace in knowing that she was doing what made her feel most alive until her very last moments, and that she remains among the mountains where she was most at home.”

Kalie’s family was in the Italian alpine village of Cervinia, at the base of the Matterhorn, while the search was under way. They found the hotel room where she was staying, including her luggage and clothing.

The Matterhorn is considered a formidable mountain for even well-trained hikers and climbers, including skyrunners. Skyrunning is a relatively new sport that requires athletes to run up high-elevation mountain trails and slopes with inclines of as much as 30 per cent. Sometimes, they rely on chains fastened to the rock faces to assist their climbs.

Various Matterhorn records say that 500 to 600 climbers have lost their lives on the mountain since the first recorded ascent in 1864. A Finnish climber went missing on the Matterhorn in late July. His body has yet to be located. Ms. McCrystal’s disappearance marks the second presumed fatality on the mountain so far this year.

In an interview Monday, Valerio Segor, director of civil protection for the Aosta Valley region in Italy’s northwest, near the French-Swiss border, said, “We are very sad and disappointed” that the rescue teams, including those of Italy’s quasi-military Guardia di Finanza, could not find any trace of the Canadian climber.

“We did everything that was possible to locate her,” he said. “Even AI analysis of the images taken by the drones could not find any new information.”

Two Polish climbers saw Ms. McCrystal ascending and descending from Pic Tyndall, a “sub-summit” about 200 metres below the Matterhorn’s peak on the Italian side of the mountain, ON the afternoon of Sept. 1. The two women shot a video, which the rescue teams have seen, of Ms. McCrystal ascending the mountain. “They said she was going up the mountain very fast,” Mr. Segor said.

The initial searches concentrated on that area of the Matterhorn. The Guardia di Finanza learned that the last signal from the electronic SIM on Ms. McCrystal’s phone came that afternoon.

Ms. McCrystal was a seasoned, trophy-winning skyrunner who has trained and competed in mountain races across South America and in Europe, typically finishing among the top-five competitors.

As a lawyer, she specialized in international arbitration. She was an instructor in the school of legal studies at Capilano University, which has a campus in Squamish, where she lived. She was a graduate in law of the University of British Columbia.

stories.title: Law Enforcement Torch Run rolls through downtown St. Thomas
stories.summary: St. Thomas Special Olympics male athlete of the year Gordie Michie proudly held the torch as local athletes made their way through downtown St. Thomas, Ont. Tuesday.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
St. Thomas Special Olympics male athlete of the year Gordie Michie proudly held the torch as local athletes made their way through downtown St. Thomas, Ont. Tuesday.

As traffic stopped to cheer on the athletes, they made their way from the west end of the city to City Hall, then onto the St. Thomas Police Station for a barbeque as part of the Law Enforcement Torch Run (Letr).

“It’s fun to hold the torch and being part of this special day and I like to run to keep healthy to have fun for the day,” said Michie.

Michie is coming off a strong performance at the national games where he won 3 gold medals, one silver and one bronze.

He likes the torch run because it raises awareness to help with fundraising for his peers.

“The support and the money helps for sure,” said Michie.

“I get to meet a lot of people, it’s always fun to have field cheer me on and it’s a special day”.

The St. Thomas Police Service was joined by the OPP and Aylmer Police who escorted the athletes during the route.

“It just warms our heart and our athletes that mean so much to us,” said Staff Sgt. Kim Manuel, the law enforcement coordinator with the Letr.

“The law enforcement torch run supports some athletes across the province. The funds that we raise actually go back to Special Olympics Ontario and different events that they’re involved in. These athletes compete both at local, provincial and national levels as well”.

stories.title: Mark Carney’s investment moment
stories.summary: Only now, in the era of Trump, could a Prime Minister welcome the world’s investors this way
stories.author: Campbell Clark
stories.content:
“What incredible timing, huh?”

That was John Toomey, CEO of Boston-based private equity firm HarbourVest Partners, speaking at an event hosted by the Canadian Venture Capital and Private Equity Association on the eve of the Canada Investment summit as foreign investors touched down in Toronto.

It is a unique moment. Mere weeks ago, the Canada-U.S. trade war was bumped up another notch with new tariffs and new threatening memes from President Donald Trump. Now investors controlling trillions in assets are here to be pitched on Canada.

There’s coincidence, in that this week’s summit had been planned for many months. But it wouldn’t have happened without Mr. Trump and the trade war he launched last year. It’s hard to imagine this kind of event happening at any other time, under any other Prime Minister – at least, not like this.

The deals and dealmakers to watch at the Canada Investment Summit

Justin Trudeau organized his own investment summit in 2016, but with less hoopla and a lesser guest list. Conservatives criticized him for being too cozy with foreign investors. And Mr. Trudeau wouldn’t have dreamed of proposing selling off concessions to operate Canada’s biggest airports, as Mr. Carney announced Tuesday – an idea once so controversial that prime ministers wouldn’t go there.

This time around, there was a gala. There were so many black Escalades and Suburbans in Yorkville that you had to wonder how movie stars would get to the Toronto International Film Festival.

The deal book Mr. Carney’s government sent out offers more than 160 projects in mining, energy, port infrastructure, manufacturing and technology, laid out in little rectangles like old hockey cards, but with projects and CapEx instead of players. West Coast Oil Pipeline, $35-billion. Nicola Wind Energy Project in British Columbia, $1.4-billion. And so on.

No other prime minster ever brought the global finance bros to this kind of party to buy Canada’s assets.

That’s in part because Mr. Carney has the contacts in global finance to fill the guest list.

But there is also the moment – the incredible timing.

Read the full transcript of Mark Carney’s speech at the Canada Investment Summit

In one sense, the summit is at odds with the trade war. Investors are sizing up Canadian operations when their access to the U.S. market is particularly uncertain. Some foreign investors aren’t keen on publicizing their interest in Canada for fear it might annoy Mr. Trump’s administration.

But if it wasn’t for Mr. Trump taking aim at Canada, a summit wouldn’t be happening this way.

Mr. Carney talked about that in his opening address Tuesday. How could he not? He spoke about great powers – he meant the U.S. – weaponizing economic integration and using tariffs as leverage.

He said Canada has responded by moving to build projects bigger, deregulate and make investment attractive. Before an audience of foreign investors, he also held out hope about U.S. trade, saying Canada is the U.S.’s best partner and suggesting “those opportunities” will return one day.

But right now, Mr. Trump, the global “rupture,” and the threat to Canada’s economy and sovereignty are the factors that give Mr. Carney the political licence with Canadians to do a summit like this, and to take risks – to announce a big new write-down on capital assets for business, advance Canada Revenue Agency rulings for billion-dollar investments. And airport deals.

Other prime ministers at other times wouldn’t have put on this show.

It would have been too on the nose for pro-corporate Brian Mulroney, who incidentally had to backpedal on stabs at privatizing airports in the eighties. Stephen Harper didn’t do it, though he showed up for Mr. Carney’s summit. Jean Chrétien led Team Canada trade missions, but the little guy from Shawinigan wouldn’t have thrown a love-in for the masters of the financial universe. Mr. Carney didn’t get elected to be an everyman.

There were protests at this summit, but small ones. Eight premiers attended, including two New Democrats and four conservatives of various party labels.

Yet it is Mr. Carney’s moment, and a defining one. It will be his to answer for.

He has some time, despite the opposition Conservatives’ call for results now.

Foreign investment is certainly important to Canada, but the public consensus isn’t a hankering for foreign firms’ mergers and acquisitions, or banks and funds creating pools to invest. Most don’t share Mr. Carney’s optimism about asset managers operating airports. “Recycling capital” from infrastructure or funding regional airports with the proceeds from leasing big-city airports is abstract. The political test will be about greenfield investment in projects that create jobs.

Mr. Carney has set this summit as a crucial antidote to crisis.

The moment won’t last forever.

“Now they don’t lock their doors in Fort Smith so I’m not sure what the advantage of it is,” he joked. “But it was very nice… it was an emotional moment.”

He then contrasted the moment with one he had after a meeting with President Donald Trump during a visit to the White House in Washington in the spring of 2025.

Carney, gesticulating in Trump’s signature style, explained that the President said “Mark I want to give you something really special.”

“So special Mark, so special,” said Carney, once again moving his palms inwards and out in a gesture that is unmistakably Trumpian, which elicited a big laugh from Orida and the audience.

“I opened this box and it’s this big gold key. I was like ‘wow Mr. President, that’s fantastic.’ He’s like ‘yeah, it’s a key to the White House. You just bring it, they’ll let you in’ and then he says ‘maybe they’ll shoot you,'” he said followed by a big laugh.

“And that sort of sums up the relationship that we have. And that’s kind of Canada and the U.S. – Canada you get the key, you’re in and the U.S. – they might shoot you,” Carney joked adding “It was very nice, I have them both and I’m very grateful – Donald if you’re listening – I am very grateful, it was a very good gesture. He’s a very good host.”

After he wrapped up the story, Carney once again added jokingly “just to be clear, if we give you a key to Canada, we’re not going to shoot you, we’re going to welcome you,” which elicited more laughter from the audience.

The Canada Investment Summit is Carney’s attempt at attracting billions of dollars in capital to Canada and court the world’s investors as part of his lofty goal to attract $1 trillion in investments over the next five years.

While Carney did not directly address the ongoing trade war with the U.S. while opening the summit on Monday, he spoke of large investment’s like the one Bell is making in Saskatchewan for a massive data centre expansion as the kind of infusion Canada needs to pivot the economy to growth.

“The tone of Canadians is, let’s get on with it. Let’s build. Let’s control our future. Let’s be positive. Let’s come together. This is a fantastic example of that,” Carney said during the announcement at the Fairmont Royal York in downtown Toronto.

stories.title: Steal the look: the Canadian midcentury ‘Scoop’ chair from Sterling Point
stories.summary: The midcentury modern chair by Toronto manufacturer R. Huber is an in-demand vintage find
stories.author: Nathalie Atkinson
stories.content:
Created by Canadian Megan Park, Prime Video’s Sterling Point is set and filmed in Ontario’s Muskoka cottage country. The coming-of-age drama follows two privileged New Yorkers: 17-year-old Annie (Ella Rubin) and her twin brother, Connor (Keen Ruffalo), who inherit an island from their estranged grandfather.

The setting is pure, unfiltered Canadiana. Canadian design aficionados, in particular, May have sat up a little straighter during an early episode that features a midcentury modern chair by Toronto manufacturer R. Huber. Spotted at a thrift store by Annie (and name-checked twice), the 1968 Huber lounge chair is known as the “Scoop” because of its curved, cocoonlike seat.

The storyline was in the script, but the idea to use the Huber lounge chair came from production designer Zazu Myers. “I loved the idea of including an iconic Canadian midcentury piece for this storyline, and the name is particularly fun to say,” she said. “We wanted something that could bring a pop of vivid colour to the cottage,” Myers, who grew up in Muskoka herself, credited the set decorating team led by Kerri Wylie with sourcing and reupholstering the chair in a blue shade that stands out against the dramatic Canadian Shield.

Spying the Scandi-inspired chair in episode three, Annie gasps, “Peacock blue Huber Scoop chair! This would be, like, five thousand dollars in New York.”

Would it, really? Yes, according to Denville, N.J., vintage dealer Eva Goldfarb of Mod City Madness. She listed sculptural accent chairs by Adrian Pearsall and Vladimir Kagan as items of similar vintage. Comparatively the Scoop is “priced very well” in the tri-state area she services. “With vintage furniture it’s like collecting cars or coins – it’s collecting history,” she said.

Sterling Point is one of summer’s most talked-about shows

If Sterling Point local Ellis (Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie), who accompanies Annie to the thrift store, is nonplussed by her furniture find, it’s because he’s grown up seeing plenty of the chairs. The Huber chair, usually sold with an ottoman as a set, isn’t particularly scarce.

Dealer William Pritchard of Victoria, B.C.’s Pray for Modern said he finds the chairs fairly regularly and has probably sold a hundred of them, even as he’s watched their popularity steadily rise. When he started his career 15 years ago, the Scoop was seen as a “cool vintage chair you would sell for $500 to $600.” In the past five years, he’s noticed an uptick in interest in vintage and in the Scoop in particular. It’s currently on the wish list of an overseas client, an architectural firm in Switzerland.

For Kate Eisen of Toronto furniture store INabstracto, the Scoop was one of the first pieces that piqued her interest in Canadian design. She was among the first to reintroduce it to the market in the early 2000s, paying roughly $100 for the first one. The store’s most recent set sold for $5,500.

“Everyone wants one, everyone’s got to have an original,” she said, though most are restored and upgraded with new foam and fabric. A factor in the chair’s current price point is its distinctive, deep button-tufting, which makes it challenging (and expensive) to reupholster. Still, it’s what dealers like Pritchard call a “very keepable” chair.

How likely would it be to stumble upon a Scoop at a rural vintage shop, as Annie does in Sterling Point ? “Value Village? Zero per cent,” said Paul McManus of Decade Five Furniture in Whitby, Ont. “If you were in an old cottage-country thrift place, there’s a chance. But it’s fairly unlikely.” The dealer was about to hit an estate sale in Gananoque, in the Thousand Islands, and he joked that odds were he would find a Scoop chair in the basement rec room.

How Marissa Schwartz brought Muskoka to life with the costumes in Sterling Point

For the most part, he’s buying from the original owners, who are either downsizing or have come to discover the chair is valuable, “and it’s been in their basement for more than 30 years and hasn’t been sat in,” he said.

McManus noticed the tide turn during COVID-19 lockdowns. In the early 2000s “they would have been at the bottom of people’s driveways – there was no market.” Later when he started dealing, he would buy them for $200 to $300 and sell them for $700. By his estimate, he has restored and sold more than 65 sets since 2020. Some have gone for as little as $2,000, with $5,000 being the peak price for restored and reupholstered Scoops.

“It’s become more valuable than the average imported Danish lounge chair from that era,” he said, including those by Grete Jalk or Arne Vodder. In recent weeks, he’s fielded queries from as far away as California.

What’s more scarce is the Huber Scoop’s documented history. The consensus among Canadian midcentury modern experts is that the chair first appeared in 1968, but the story of its design, production and distribution is little-known.

Prior to the Scoop, R. Huber was known for its teak side chairs. In 1963, Globe reporter Mary Jukes credited “the growing appreciation of domestic Scandinavian-influenced furniture” to the work of Canadian manufacturers including R. Huber. In 1965, another Globe article on the emerging taste for accent chairs praised Canadian-made examples, including a “Scandinavian-style” armchair by the Toronto manufacturer.

A Simpsons sales flyer from July, 1968, advertised a version in black vinyl or fabric for $179.98 (about $1,600 today). The department store touted the Scoop again the next year, “for the sleek, uncluttered look of teak furniture by Huber” – now with a matching moulded sofa. Swivel and rocking chair variations would soon follow.

The enduring affection for the Huber Scoop seems to be about nostalgia and memories – and great design, McManus pointed out. The chairs are famously comfortable, with the enveloping coziness of an Eames lounge chair. There’s also the aspect of their longevity.

“By the time we restore them, there’s no reason they can’t go on for another 60 years,” he said.

Good Canadian Value

We asked vintage experts for other midcentury Canadian pieces that won’t break the bank.

Kate Eisen of INabstracto favours Canadian-made Lotte lamps . Created by Danish immigrants Lotte and Gunnar Bostlund in 1957, the tri-lite table lamps feature beautifully glazed ceramic bases with spun fibreglass shades that cast a pretty light at night. The pieces regularly command four figures on e-commerce sites such as 1stDibs but cost less in Canada (around $375 to $1,500 for larger models). ( INabstracto.com )

William Pritchard at Pray for Modern said one of the most slept-on Canadian midcentury designs is A.J. Donahue’s “Winnipeg” chair , which many have likened to George Nelson’s more famous Coconut lounge chair. ( prayformodern.com )

Paul McManus recommended the dining set pieces by Deilcraft, from Kitchener, Ont., for their great value (the chairs are a favourite of his collector clients). Decade Five also refinishes the classic sideboard Deilcraft became known for, stripping the dark brown lacquer finish to reveal a walnut with lighter ash accents. ( decadefivefurniture.CA )

Canadian interior stylist and designer Arren Williams’s collection with Quebec studio Renwil draws on midcentury design in pieces such as the Noto table lamp, which has similar proportions to the smaller Lotte lamp and comes in brown marble or beige travertine. ( renwil.com )

If thrifting isn’t your thing, Ottawa upholstery firm Kessels has revived the Huber name, offering a new version crafted by Amish and Mennonite makers. ( huberscoopchair.com )

In the early 2000s “they would have been at the bottom of people’s driveways – there was no market.” Later when he started dealing, he would buy them for $200 to $300 and sell them for $700. By his estimate, he has restored and sold more than 65 sets since 2020. Some have gone for as little as $2,000, with $5,000 being the peak price for restored and reupholstered Scoops.

“It’s become more valuable than the average imported Danish lounge chair from that era,” he said, including those by Grete Jalk or Arne Vodder. In recent weeks, he’s fielded queries from as far away as California.

What’s more scarce is the Huber Scoop’s documented history. The consensus among Canadian midcentury modern experts is that the chair first appeared in 1968, but the story of its design, production and distribution is little-known.

Prior to the Scoop, R. Huber was known for its teak side chairs. In 1963, Globe reporter Mary Jukes credited “the growing appreciation of domestic Scandinavian-influenced furniture” to the work of Canadian manufacturers including R. Huber. In 1965, another Globe article on the emerging taste for accent chairs praised Canadian-made examples, including a “Scandinavian-style” armchair by the Toronto manufacturer.

A Simpsons sales flyer from July, 1968, advertised a version in black vinyl or fabric for $179.98 (about $1,600 today). The department store touted the Scoop again the next year, “for the sleek, uncluttered look of teak furniture by Huber” – now with a matching moulded sofa. Swivel and rocking chair variations would soon follow.

The enduring affection for the Huber Scoop seems to be about nostalgia and memories – and great design, McManus pointed out. The chairs are famously comfortable, with the enveloping coziness of an Eames lounge chair. There’s also the aspect of their longevity.
“By the time we restore them, there’s no reason they can’t go on for another 60 years,” he said.
Good Canadian Value
We asked vintage experts for other midcentury Canadian pieces that won’t break the bank.

Kate Eisen of INabstracto favours Canadian-made Lotte lamps . Created by Danish immigrants Lotte and Gunnar Bostlund in 1957, the tri-lite table lamps feature beautifully glazed ceramic bases with spun fibreglass shades that cast a pretty light at night. The pieces regularly command four figures on e-commerce sites such as 1stDibs but cost less in Canada (around $375 to $1,500 for larger models). ( INabstracto.com )

William Pritchard at Pray for Modern said one of the most slept-on Canadian midcentury designs is A.J. Donahue’s “Winnipeg” chair , which many have likened to George Nelson’s more famous Coconut lounge chair. ( prayformodern.com )

Paul McManus recommended the dining set pieces by Deilcraft, from Kitchener, Ont., for their great value (the chairs are a favourite of his collector clients). Decade Five also refinishes the classic sideboard Deilcraft became known for, stripping the dark brown lacquer finish to reveal a walnut with lighter ash accents. ( decadefivefurniture.CA )

Canadian interior stylist and designer Arren Williams’s collection with Quebec studio Renwil draws on midcentury design in pieces such as the Noto table lamp, which has similar proportions to the smaller Lotte lamp and comes in brown marble or beige travertine. ( renwil.com )
If thrifting isn’t your thing, Ottawa upholstery firm Kessels has revived the Huber name, offering a new version crafted by Amish and Mennonite makers. ( huberscoopchair.com )

content_blocks.text: Created by Canadian Megan Park, Prime Video’s Sterling Point is set and filmed in Ontario’s Muskoka cottage country. The coming-of-age drama follows two privileged New Yorkers: 17-year-old Annie (Ella Rubin) and her twin brother, Connor (Keen Ruffalo), who inherit an island from their estranged grandfather.

The setting is pure, unfiltered Canadiana. Canadian design aficionados, in particular, May have sat up a little straighter during an early episode that features a midcentury modern chair by Toronto manufacturer R. Huber. Spotted at a thrift store by Annie (and name-checked twice), the 1968 Huber lounge chair is known as the “Scoop” because of its curved, cocoonlike seat.

content_blocks.caption: A leather reupholstered Scoop chair recently sold for $2,950 by B.C.'s Pray for Modern. Pray For Modern/Supplied

content_blocks.text: The storyline was in the script, but the idea to use the Huber lounge chair came from production designer Zazu Myers. “I loved the idea of including an iconic Canadian midcentury piece for this storyline, and the name is particularly fun to say,” she said. “We wanted something that could bring a pop of vivid colour to the cottage,” Myers, who grew up in Muskoka herself, credited the set decorating team led by Kerri Wylie with sourcing and reupholstering the chair in a blue shade that stands out against the dramatic Canadian Shield.
Spying the Scandi-inspired chair in episode three, Annie gasps, “Peacock blue Huber Scoop chair! This would be, like, five thousand dollars in New York.”

Would it, really? Yes, according to Denville, N.J., vintage dealer Eva Goldfarb of Mod City Madness. She listed sculptural accent chairs by Adrian Pearsall and Vladimir Kagan as items of similar vintage. Comparatively the Scoop is “priced very well” in the tri-state area she services. “With vintage furniture it’s like collecting cars or coins – it’s collecting history,” she said.
Sterling Point is one of summer’s most talked-about shows

If Sterling Point local Ellis (Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie), who accompanies Annie to the thrift store, is nonplussed by her furniture find, it’s because he’s grown up seeing plenty of the chairs. The Huber chair, usually sold with an ottoman as a set, isn’t particularly scarce.

content_blocks.caption: Jacob Whiteduck-Lavoie as Ellis in Sterling Point. The Huber Scoop chair and ottoman were reupholstered in a blue shade to stand out against the dramatic Canadian Shield. sabrina lantos/Supplied

When he started his career 15 years ago, the Scoop was seen as a “cool vintage chair you would sell for $500 to $600.” In the past five years, he’s noticed an uptick in interest in vintage and in the Scoop in particular. stories.title: UCP by-election loss sends strong message ahead of separation vote, Kenney says
stories.summary: Conservative voices link upcoming separation vote to Ucp’s surprise loss in Calgary stronghold riding
stories.content:
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney and other conservative voices are linking the upcoming separation vote to the governing United Conservative Party’s shocking by-election loss in one of its Calgary stronghold ridings.

Kenney, in posts on social media, says the Opposition Ndp’s victory Monday night in Calgary-Shaw sends a strong message about the Oct. 19 referendum’s impact on conservative supporters.

He says the debate on quitting Canada is alienating conservative voters who also love Canada while pushing disaffected nationalist supporters into the arms of left-centre opponents such as the NDP.

“Folks planning to vote ‘to send a message’ by starting the separation process: please take note of the Ndp’s win tonight in the most conservative part of urban Canada,” Kenney wrote on X early Tuesday.

“A vote to separate is a vote to help the NDP win the next provincial election, and for the Liberal Party of Canada to win far more Alberta seats.”

Alberta NDP wins by-election in longtime Conservative riding

Kenney, who won multiple elections representing the people of south Calgary as both a provincial and a federal politician, said the one thing he knows for sure is that “the overwhelming majority (of them) are proud, patriotic Canadians.”

Other prominent conservatives also weighed in on social media.

Ken Boessenkool, a long-time conservative strategist, said he reads the by-election result as voters being unhappy they’re dealing with separatism at a time when more serious issues need addressing.

The UCP loss, he wrote on X, is “a welcome rebuke for distracting Albertans with a foolish, dangerous and undemocratic referendum.”

Boessenkool was a signatory of the famous 2001 Alberta firewall letter calling for more autonomy from Ottawa.

Michael Solberg, a former staffer to former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper, said on X that the NDP win sends a compelling message.

“The growing brand of rage-farming ‘conservative’ who supports separation and pushes conspiracy theories and fake narratives is Unelectable anywhere,” said Solberg.

“The people are never wrong.’

Cory Morgan, a conservative commentator who leads a third-party advertising outfit pushing for the province to separate from Canada, said the results show Premier Danielle Smith has angered her base, prompting many to stay home for the by-election.

“What I see here is the result of Smith trying to play on both sides of the unity issue,” Morgan wrote on X.

Smith has said she had no choice but to put separation on the referendum ballot and put the contentious issue to rest.

The question asks voters whether Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a second binding referendum on setting up the process to quit Confederation.

Opponents say Smith has no mandate to quit Canada, that there is no raging public debate to leave, and that she is just doing it to hold at bay separatist hardliners in her party.

The next provincial election is set for Oct. 18, 2027, and Calgary is considered the linchpin.

The NDP has dominated Edmonton in recent elections while the UCP takes the smaller cities and the rural areas, making Calgary the critical path to electoral success.

In the 2023 general election, won by the UCP under Smith, Calgary was a heated battleground. The UCP won 12 of the 26 seats — a stark turnaround after the NDP captured just three seats in the city in 2019.

During the by-election campaign, NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said voters should choose his party and send a message to the premier that they don’t want a government that caters to separatists.

The new legislature member for Calgary-Shaw is Kyle Campbell. In unofficial results Monday night, the NDP candidate received 7,461 votes, while Mike Derry with the UCP received 6,879.

The riding, created in 1986, has long voted Conservative. The NDP has won the seat only once, in 2015, as part of the “orange wave” that brought former premier Rachel Notley into government.

The by-election was called after former UCP cabinet minister Rebecca Schulz resigned in May.

Progressive Tory candidate Kyle Joseph came in third place with 978 votes.

Political scientist Lori Williams called the result a “significant loss” for Smith, but also said it’s difficult to take firm lessons from by-elections.

Williams, with Mount Royal University in Calgary, said that since forming government isn’t on the line, voters have more freedom to send a message than they would in a general election.

“It’s some combination of endorsement of or support for the NDP, and sending a message to the government that voters aren’t happy with the job that they’re doing currently,” Williams said in an interview.

Williams agreed that the upcoming referendum played a role in the Ndp’s win, adding that the UCP candidate being endorsed by some in the independence movement could have been an additional liability.

But she also said perceptions of Smith’s performance on long-standing priorities for Albertans like health care and affordability played a significant role.

“I think it’s that sort of one-two punch that’s really generated the result in this by-election,” she said.

“Voters have sent a message that they don’t think she’s performing on the files.”

stories.title: 10/3 podcast: Canada-U.S. trade war: How did two neighbours become rivals?
stories.summary: Canada and the U.S. are locked in a trade war. How did two friendly neighbours become rivals, and can their relationship be repaired?
stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
Flags of Canada and the United States fly across the international border on the Gordie Howe International bridge that connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Michigan on September 6, 2026.Photo by Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images

If Canada and the U.S. were homes on a street, they’d be locked in what could be politely called one of the worst neighbour disputes their quiet town of North America has ever seen.

One neighbour complains about how the other treats their kids, while the second neighbour is worried the first is going to unilaterally move the fence into their yard. And tensions are on the rise.

But how did two friendly neighbours run into such problems?

stories.title: Owner seeks access to building that housed alleged unlicensed pot shop
stories.summary: Owner of a downtown London building that allegedly housed an unsanctioned pot shop says she thought the business was legal
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The owner of a downtown London building that allegedly housed an unsanctioned pot shop raided by police last year says she thought the business was legal and is asking police to allow her to return to her property.

Erin Barletta, the owner of the building at 264 Dundas St., and husband Vincent, who manages the property, have filed an application asking the OPP-led cannabis enforcement team to grant them permission to access the downtown building.

Police searched Indi Exotics on Nov. 25, 2025. Officers seized cannabis products valued at more than $4,000 and charged a 44-year-old London man with possession of illicit cannabis, possession of cannabis for the purpose of selling and possession of property obtained by crime, the OPP said at the time.

The dispensary was operating without authorization from the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario, the province’s pot regulator, police said.

Police placed an interim seizure order on the building that requires anyone wanting to enter it to apply to the Superior Court for permission.

A tenant who had rented the main-floor commercial space since 2022 began subletting it to another man, who operated the dispensary, for $2,965 per month beginning in July 2024, the Barlettas say in the application filed last month.

“At all times the applicants understood the marijuana dispensary was legal, that the premises were appropriately zoned . . . and that all necessary insurance was in place to cover the operation,” the application says.

Vincent Barletta conducted due diligence prior to the sublease, the application says. He contacted the city’s zoning department and confirmed the proposed use was allowed, and visited nearby licensed and unlicensed dispensaries “all of which reported positive experiences with respect to traffic and the absence of issues,” the document says.

But it wasn’t long before there were issues at the Dundas Street pop shop.

The backdoor to the business was riddled with bullets in an overnight shooting on Nov. 24, 2024. Nobody was injured and two Toronto-area men were later charged in the gunfire. The dispensary reopened weeks later.

On Nov. 25, 2025, less than two weeks before the police search, a man was shot at the dispensary in broad daylight. The pot shop reopened three days later and no arrests have been made in the case.

Police have been engaged in a whack-a-mole style battle with black market cannabis shops, most of them claiming to be Indigenous-run and exempt from federal cannabis laws, in recent years. These illegal businesses source their products from the black market, rather than through the Ontario Cannabis Store, the government-run pot wholesaler.

The Barlettas contend it was the alleged unlawful acts by the sub-tenant that led to the police raid and they had no knowledge of the police operation. The couple also terminated the tenancy of the man who had been renting the upstairs apartment for the past five years for $1,250 per month, the application says.

Court records show the man was charged with six gun and drug-related offences in connection with a shootout involving two vehicles near Oxford and Talbot streets on Aug. 22, 2025. Nobody was injured. The charges against the man were later stayed, an outcome that halts a prosecution without a finding of guilt or innocence.

The seizure of the Dundas Street property has resulted in a loss of $20,755 for the Barlettas as of July, the application says.

“Since being denied access to the ground floor, the applicants have been unable to inspect the premises to assess damage from several floods or to carry out clean-up or repairs,” the application says.

Salvatice Barletta, the mother of Vincent, bought the building in 2000, and transferred the ownership to her daughter-in-law in 2003, the application says.

The longtime owner of the now-closed Beef Baron strip club, Vincent Barletta is the brother of Robert Barletta , an alleged high-ranking member of the Hells Angels who narrowly survived a attempt on his life in 2020.

A lawyer representing the Barlettas didn’t respond to a request for comment.

A hearing for the application is scheduled for Friday.

stories.title: New Brunswick lawyer disbarred over professional misconduct charges
stories.summary: Fredericton lawyer Stephen Hill has been disbarred following a series of complaints about professional misconduct.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
Fredericton lawyer Stephen Hill owes more than $1 million following a series of complaints about professional misconduct, says the registrar of complaints at the Law Society of New Brunswick.

The law society’s discipline committee released a notice last week saying Hill was disbarred as of Aug. 31.

As part of their decision, the committee ordered Hill to pay approximately $1.4 million to cover compensation payments the law society made to his clients, as well as legal fees, investigation costs and custodial costs, said Joleen Dable, registrar of complaints and deputy executive director of the law society.

Hill is required to pay the money within a year of the decision date, she said.

The decision comes after the committee found Hill guilty of 29 professional misconduct complaints in May, Dable said.

These included misappropriating client funds, failing to complete work for clients and failing to respond to the law society about complaints filed against him on time.

“[Clients] would have paid Mr. Hill for services and either the services weren’t rendered or part of the services were rendered, or he would have kept the money,” Dable said.

“There’s a pattern there in all complaints.”

Dable said the society used its compensation fund to reimburse a number of Hill’s clients. These included people who gave the former lawyer hundreds of thousands of dollars to complete mortgage transactions.

The law society said he misappropriated those funds.

“There are significant amounts we’re talking about,” she said. “One complainant was out $400,000, another one $300,000.”

Dable said the amount of money provided to Hill’s clients through the compensation fund is the highest she’s seen during her six years working at the law society.

Dable also said that Hill made multiple requests for extensions during the disciplinary process, contributing to delays in the law society’s review of the complaints.

According to the documents released by the law society, the discipline committee granted Hill’s initial adjournment request and postponed his hearing from November 2025 until March 2026.

The documents also revealed that in March 2026, a lawyer for Hill requested an adjournment saying his client had been incarcerated for five days after being sentenced for civil contempt.

However, the committee denied that request for an adjournment and proceeded with a hearing.

The discipline committee concluded Hill admitted his guilt by failing to respond to the complaints by its deadline.

It initially suspended Hill from practising law in February 2025 after receiving complaints about his conduct.

stories.title: Carney eyes ‘unique alliance’ with EU, but there are legal limits to his plan
stories.summary: The PM is pitching a closer strategic partnership with the EU, but experts say the bloc has no ready-made path to his “unique alliance.”
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney has suggested that deeper integration and a “unique alliance” between Canada and the European Union (EU) could be the answer to the souring of the Canada-U.S. relationship amid the trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump.

“We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union ,” he said on Sunday.

“What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — [is] a unique alliance with the European Union. We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths.”

Strategically, Canada offers Europe a like-minded G7 partner with natural resources, defence capacity, and similar values — as well as a shared interest in being less dependent upon an increasingly unpredictable Washington. But the policy content of Carney’s proposal remains undefined — and scholars on EU law say that the EU has no ready-made legal route for granting Canada a membership-like status.

Under Carney especially, Canada is a “key player” and “highly respected,” said Cambridge professor Catherine Barnard, who specializes in EU law.

But trade watchers are also skeptical that Carney’s gambit for a “ unique alliance ” will lead to a new formal, membership-like arrangement anytime soon. The first hurdle is that no such EU category currently exists.

When asked what a “unique alliance” might look like, Barnard said nobody knows and pointed to the difference between the political and legal dimensions.

“The EU wants to be close to Canada and supportive of Canada — that’s the political side,” she said.

Legally, however, “there is just no possibility (of that) as the EU stands,” she said, pointing to the Michel Barnier staircase of the available models. At the top is full membership, followed by looser forms of economic integration — European Economic Area (EEA) participation, Swiss-style bilateral accords, customs-union arrangements, and free-trade agreements. Canada is already on the bottom step with the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta), an EU-Canada free-trade agreement provisionally in place since 2017.

Simon Usherwood, professor of politics and international studies at The Open University, also pointed to the lack of “off-the-shelf relationships with other countries.”

While Carney has said he’s not seeking it, full membership would simply not be feasible under the EU treaties as they stand.

“People jokingly say, ‘Oh, yes, Canada could join, join the EU,’” Barnard said. “Well, legally that’s impossible because Article 49 of the treaty says you’ve got to be a European state, and Canada is not that.”

Even if the focus is just on a bespoke partnership, the political room for this remains uncertain as it’s not just a question of what Canada hopes to obtain but also what privileges — and demands — the EU is willing to extend to Ottawa.

The EU could, in theory, devise a new arrangement for a country it wants to draw closer. But Barnard said Brussels would be wary of creating a precedent because any generous concession to Canada could prompt Britain, Switzerland, the EEA states, Ukraine and other countries outside the bloc to demand comparable treatment.

Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House, was more enthusiastic about institutional innovation and said the debate about Canada comes at an interesting time — when the EU is considering whether to create more flexible, intermediate forms of association.

“Europe is asking itself where it wants to go in terms of enlargement,” he said, noting that it will depend on whether the EU is willing to create a broader set of intermediate relationships between full membership and outsider status.

While a bigger relationship with Canada could upset other countries, Roos argued that the risks of institutional innovation should not deter Europe.

“In the realm of politics and policymaking, any kind of audacity is risky. But this is exactly what Europe needs,” he said.

But if a new formal status is unlikely anytime soon, what exactly can Ottawa and Brussels achieve?

On that point, the experts agree that the clearest — and least legally questionable — way forward is on defence, Ukraine support, and industrial cooperation.

Usherwood, for example, expects Canada’s support for Ukraine to continue to expand and believes its participation in Security Action for Europe (Safe), the EU’s defence financing programme, could “bear some fruit pretty quickly on defence procurements.”

Both the EU and Canada have incentives given U.S. unpredictability and the need to diversify their defence supply chains.

Other areas for strategic cooperation could include critical minerals, energy security — including potential undersea electricity interconnections — and technology.

Carney has also suggested that a deal could include greater mobility for Canadians, specifically “enhanced labour mobility… enhanced educational opportunities, enhanced research co-operation.”

Usherwood said a youth-mobility scheme would be more realistic than unrestricted free movement. But Barnard cautioned that EU member states would retain control over admission numbers and could, in principle, set Canadian quotas at zero.

Roos was more optimistic and said freer movement for Canadians to work and live in the EU would not be difficult in practical or political terms. He even believes Canada’s positive image in Europe could help mute populist opposition to such mobility arrangements, at least for now.

When it comes to deeper trade integration between Canada and the EU, however, the experts were more cautious.

Usherwood said Ceta itself illustrates how difficult deeper integration can be.

“Ceta … is still not fully in effect because we’ve still got 10 member states that haven’t done the ratification because they’re worried about access of Canadian agricultural imports into the EU,” he said.

The EU can readily make separate agreements with Canada on defence and security, Barnard said. But WTO rules generally prevent Brussels from offering Canada selective preferential access to parts of the EU market without extending the same treatment to other WTO members. The principal exception is a free-trade agreement or customs union under Gatt Article Xxiv, which must cover “substantially all” trade between the parties — not a narrow, Canada-specific economic arrangement.

Even if a more generous arrangement were legally feasible, Barnard said, the politics would remain difficult. If Brussels devised a new Canada-specific relationship, countries with stronger geographic or accession claims could demand comparable treatment.

“It’s difficult to see quite what cozy relationship the EU might have with Canada unless they invent something new,” Barnard said. “And if they invent something new, then Ukraine, Bosnia, Serbia, the U.K. all will say, ‘Well, we want some of that, and we have much greater claim than Canada does because we’re on the EU borders.’”

For that reason, Barnard and Usherwood see the “unique alliance” language as more rhetorical than immediately realistic.

“People jokingly say, ‘Oh, yes, Canada could join, join the EU,’” Barnard said. “Well, legally that’s impossible because Article 49 of the treaty says you’ve got to be a European state, and Canada is not that.”

Even if the focus is just on a bespoke partnership, the political room for this remains uncertain as it’s not just a question of what Canada hopes to obtain but also what privileges — and demands — the EU is willing to extend to Ottawa.

The EU could, in theory, devise a new arrangement for a country it wants to draw closer. But Barnard said Brussels would be wary of creating a precedent because any generous concession to Canada could prompt Britain, Switzerland, the EEA states, Ukraine and other countries outside the bloc to demand comparable treatment.

Grégoire Roos, director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House, was more enthusiastic about institutional innovation and said the debate about Canada comes at an interesting time — when the EU is considering whether to create more flexible, intermediate forms of association.

“Europe is asking itself where it wants to go in terms of enlargement,” he said, noting that it will depend on whether the EU is willing to create a broader set of intermediate relationships between full membership and outsider status.
While a bigger relationship with Canada could upset other countries, Roos argued that the risks of institutional innovation should not deter Europe.
“In the realm of politics and policymaking, any kind of audacity is risky. But this is exactly what Europe needs,” he said.
But if a new formal status is unlikely anytime soon, what exactly can Ottawa and Brussels achieve?
On that point, the experts agree that the clearest — and least legally questionable — way forward is on defence, Ukraine support, and industrial cooperation.

Usherwood, for example, expects Canada’s support for Ukraine to continue to expand and believes its participation in Security Action for Europe (Safe), the EU’s defence financing programme, could “bear some fruit pretty quickly on defence procurements.”
Both the EU and Canada have incentives given U.S. unpredictability and the need to diversify their defence supply chains.
Other areas for strategic cooperation could include critical minerals, energy security — including potential undersea electricity interconnections — and technology.
Carney has also suggested that a deal could include greater mobility for Canadians, specifically “enhanced labour mobility… enhanced educational opportunities, enhanced research co-operation.”

Usherwood said a youth-mobility scheme would be more realistic than unrestricted free movement. But Barnard cautioned that EU member states would retain control over admission numbers and could, in principle, set Canadian quotas at zero.

Roos was more optimistic and said freer movement for Canadians to work and live in the EU would not be difficult in practical or political terms. He even believes Canada’s positive image in Europe could help mute populist opposition to such mobility arrangements, at least for now.
When it comes to deeper trade integration between Canada and the EU, however, the experts were more cautious.
Usherwood said Ceta itself illustrates how difficult deeper integration can be.

“Ceta … is still not fully in effect because we’ve still got 10 member states that haven’t done the ratification because they’re worried about access of Canadian agricultural imports into the EU,” he said.

The EU can readily make separate agreements with Canada on defence and security, Barnard said. But WTO rules generally prevent Brussels from offering Canada selective preferential access to parts of the EU market without extending the same treatment to other WTO members. The principal exception is a free-trade agreement or customs union under Gatt Article Xxiv, which must cover “substantially all” trade between the parties — not a narrow, Canada-specific economic arrangement.

Even if a more generous arrangement were legally feasible, Barnard said, the politics would remain difficult. If Brussels devised a new Canada-specific relationship, countries with stronger geographic or accession claims could demand comparable treatment.

“It’s difficult to see quite what cozy relationship the EU might have with Canada unless they invent something new,” Barnard said. “And if they invent something new, then Ukraine, Bosnia, Serbia, the U.K. all will say, ‘Well, we want some of that, and we have much greater claim than Canada does because we’re on the EU borders.’”
For that reason, Barnard and Usherwood see the “unique alliance” language as more rhetorical than immediately realistic.

stories.title: Carney says he's 'pleased' with Stephen Harper's support during investor summit
stories.summary: Carney said he is pleased with former prime minister Stephen Harper's support during his government's Canada Investment Summit in Toronto.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Harper said more comprehensive reforms are needed to speed up Canada's permitting processes

Ottawa — Former prime minister Stephen Harper said Canada lost its potential to become an energy superpower after he left office, blaming the policies of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, while congratulating Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government on its efforts to revive that opportunity.

“In 2015, Canada was poised to become that energy superpower,” said Harper, during the closing speech at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday.

“Today, we are not. Why? Because of deliberate policy choices that followed over the next decade, but there is no point bemoaning what is past, especially because the opportunity of becoming that global energy superpower is fortuitously offering itself to us once again,” he added.

The former Conservative prime minister, who currently serves as chairman of the Alberta Investment Management Corporation and is co-founder of the investment fund Vision-One Management, congratulated Carney’s government on the measures it has taken to fast-track major projects, including in the oil sands.

Harper also referred to the government as “Canada’s new government,” which is a common refrain from Carney in an effort to distinguish himself from the policies of the Trudeau government.

“Ironically, if we do not do these things as a country, the Americans will continue to be our sole customers, and they will not lack the urgency that we have lacked here in Canada,” said Harper.

Harper said the U.S. administration views Canada’s economic integration as incompatible with our separate sovereignty.

“Thus, to maintain that sovereignty, we must pursue diminished reliance upon the United States,” he said. “There will be significant costs to this effort, but those are costs that I hope and believe Canadians are able and prepared to accept.”

Harper’s presence at the Liberal government’s investor summit raised some questions for Carney earlier Tuesday. Carney said he was “pleased” with Harper’s support.

“I’ve taken advice from Mr. Harper, I’ve taken advice from Mr. Chrétien, Mr. Trudeau, as I should in this role,” said Carney, during a press conference at the summit on Tuesday. “I’m pleased that he’s here supporting…this effort.”

Carney said like other former prime ministers, Harper is a Canadian patriot and is well positioned in the global investment landscape.

“I’m aware that…in his current role, he’s influential, and he’s influential with a number of investors and businesses around world, and it’s helpful for Canada,” said Carney. “So, I thank him for those contributions.”

Just over year ago during the 2025 federal election, Harper endorsed Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre for prime minister and took aim at Carney’s record, particularly his role in the global financial crisis as the governor of the Bank of Canada.

Still, Harper’s presence at Carney’s investment summit could be interpreted as an endorsement of the prime minister’s strategy to attract more global capital investment in Canada. Carney hopes to attract $1 trillion in investment over the next five years.

When asked on Tuesday whether Harper’s participation in the summit undermines his economic criticisms of Carney, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said it doesn’t.

“I spoke to prime minister Harper about this a few days ago, and of course Conservatives are always willing to put Canada first, and will work with anybody just like I did last week in New York when I went there and I fought for Canada and stood side by side with Canadians of all political backgrounds to fight for tariff-free trade with the United States,” said Poilievre, during a press conference in Vancouver.

“I’m encouraged that prime minister Harper is doing the same thing,” he added.

Poilievre said his party is asking for results that will help Canadian pocketbooks.

“Summits, signing ceremonies, speeches — they’re all fine,” said Poilievre. “But what we need from the Liberals right now are results to save you money, to save Canadians’ jobs.”

The two-day summit will wrap up Tuesday with several announcements, including the government’s intention to privatize operations at Canada’s four largest airports, a decrease in the marginal effective tax rate on new business investment from 13 per cent to 6.4 per cent, a $50-billion investment by Bell Canada to expand its AI data centre project in Saskatchewan and a $50-billion “Maple Fund” partnership between the CPP Investments and Brookfield Asset Management.

Present at the two-day conference were some of the world’s largest global investors, including BlackRock CEO Larry Fink, Blackstone president Jon Gray, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Hong Kong Monetary Authority and China International Capital Corp.

stories.title: Carney says Trump's White House gift came with odd warning: 'Maybe they'll shoot you'
stories.summary: Mark Carney says a ceremonial key to the White House gifted to him by Donald Trump would let him in the presidential home, or he might get shot.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Canada

World

'That's kind of Canada and the U.S. It's like in Canada, you get the key, you're in, and the U.S., they might shoot you. No, I’m just kidding,' the PM said

Last updated 22 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/carney-trump-white-house-gift-warning-shoot-you#comments-area)

Prime Minister Mark Carney and U.S. President Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, May 6, 2025.Photo by Handout/The White House

It’s common for heads of government and state to exchange gifts when they meet, but Prime Minister Mark Carney says an offering from U.S. President Donald Trump last year came with a curious caveat.

“‘I want to give you something very special, so special, Mark, so special,” Carney recounted of his May 6, 2025 meeting with Trump at the White House, mimicking Trump’s speaking style and a signature open-palmed hand gesture to the delight of some members of the Canada Investment Summit audience in Toronto Tuesday.

Carney told moderator Deborah K. Orida, CEO of Public Sector Pension Investments, that Trump presented him with a box containing a “big gold key.”

“And I was like, ‘Wow, Mr. President, this is fantastic.’ He said, ‘Yeah, it’s a key to the White House. You just bring it, they’ll let you in,’” he recounted, still making the hand gestures but dropping the speaking inflections.

“And then he says, ‘maybe they’ll shoot you.’”

As the audience and Orida burst into laughter, Carney added: “And that sort of sums up the relationship that we have.”

“That’s kind of Canada and the U.S. It’s like in Canada, you get the key, you’re in, and the U.S., they might shoot you. No, I’m just kidding.”

The subject of keys arose when Orida asked him a personal question about the two ceremonial keys he mentioned having during their conversation the night before.

The first, he said, was a key to his hometown, Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories, presented to him when he became Governor of the Bank of Canada.

“Now, they don’t lock their doors in Fort Smith, so I’m not sure the advantage of it, but it’s very nice and it sits very proudly and it was an emotional moment,” he said.

The White House key from Trump, too, was “very nice,” according to Carney.

“Donald, if you’re listening,” he said, glancing to the camera, “I am very grateful. It’s a very good gesture. He’s a very good host.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks with Deborah Orida, President and CEO of PSP Investments at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday.Photo by Peter J Thompson/National Post

But he reiterated that if someone’s given a key to Canada, they won’t be shot.

“We’re going to welcome you,” Carney finished.

As reported by National Post at the time, Carney’s meeting in the Oval Office swung between praise and discussions about whether Canada would ever become the 51st state.

When Carney made it clear Canada, like Buckingham Palace or the White House, “won’t be for sale, ever,” Trump responded: “Time will tell. It’s only time. But I say never say never.”

stories.title: Teck CEO calls for more investment in crucial mining infrastructure at investment summit
stories.summary: More funding is needed for electricity grids and transportation corridors, Jonathan Price says
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Mark Carney’s government is moving in the right direction to strengthen Canada’s critical minerals sector, but more investment is needed in crucial mining infrastructure, Teck Resources Ltd. Teck-B-T chief executive Jonathan Price said Tuesday at the Canada Investment Summit.

In a panel discussion at the summit alongside Cameco Corp. CEO Tim Gitzel and Agnico Eagle Mines Ltd. CEO Ammar Al-Joundi, Mr. Price called for more money to be put into electricity grids, and transportation corridors, a move that will benefit many mining companies.

Mr. Price pointed to the Ring of Fire in Northern Ontario and British Columbia’s Golden Triangle as remote areas of the country where such infrastructure investment is particularly needed.

Live updates from the Canada Investment Summit

“To unlock those deposits, we need access either by road or rail, we need power solutions, we need a route to port, and we need port capacity to get those products to market,” he said.

“When that infrastructure comes, and the Major Projects Office is working on this right now, particularly in B.C., that will allow multiple proponents to develop multiple mines.”

Several infrastructure projects that would benefit the mining sector have already been referred to the MPO, which was created last year by Mr. Carney to both reduce red tape and potentially facilitate funding.

Those projects include the North Coast Transmission Line in northwestern British Columbia, the Taltson Hydro Expansion in the Great Slave Lake region of the Northwest Territories, and the Arctic Economic and Security Corridor in the NWT, a 400-kilometre all-season road through the Slave Geological Province to the Nunavut border.

The deals and dealmakers to watch at the Canada Investment Summit

Carney sees chance to tap into Asian, European markets at investment summit

The goal of the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in Toronto is to help attract hundreds of billions of dollars of investment into Canada to help cushion the blow of the continuing trade war with the United States. The event, which kicked off Monday evening and continued into Tuesday, is being led by Mr. Carney and co-hosted by big Canadian pension funds.

In a speech on Tuesday morning at the summit, Mr. Carney said that building resource projects faster by removing federal red tape is one of the ways to make Canada the most attractive country in the G7 to invest.

“For projects and supply chains, our standard will be simple: One project. One review. One year,” he said.

“Canada will remain a country of high standards. But high standards do not require slow decisions. Speed, certainty and predictability are themselves competitive advantages.”

stories.title: Calgary man charged after alleged threats against Carney
stories.summary: The 31-year-old allegedly made threats on a YouTube account to kill the Prime Minister
stories.content:
Mounties say a Calgary man has been charged after he allegedly made threats on a YouTube account to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney.

RCMP say its federal policing division received information about the alleged threats on July 28.

A 31-year-old Calgary man was arrested and charged with uttering a death threat.

He was in custody and scheduled to appear in court Tuesday.

The RCMP’s federal policing division is responsible for safeguarding designated Canadians and select foreign diplomatic personnel residing in Canada.

It’s also mandated to investigate criminal offences, including terrorism, espionage, cyberattacks, nuclear security risks and foreign influenced activities.

RCMP say the investigation is ongoing and it won’t be providing further information as the case is before the courts.

“The security environment in which public figures operate continues to evolve both within Canada and abroad, and we recognize this is a time for increased vigilance,” RCMP said in a news release Tuesday.

stories.title: Construction contract awarded for Ceeh redevelopment
stories.summary: Bluewater Health has given a $14-million construction contract to K&L Construction Ltd. for the redevelopment of the emergency department and diagnostic imaging areas at the Charlotte Eleanor Englehart Hospital (Ceeh).
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Bluewater Health has given a $14-million construction contract to K&L Construction Ltd. for the redevelopment of the emergency department and diagnostic imaging areas at the Charlotte Eleanor Englehart Hospital (Ceeh).

This work will be done to modernize the emergency department and associated clinical and support spaces. Construction is expected to begin in late October or early November, taking 36 to 42 months to complete.

“This is an exciting milestone for Ceeh and for the Petrolia and Central Lambton community,” said Bob Bailey, Sarnia-Lambton MPP.

“Our government is proud to support this important investment in modernizing the hospital’s emergency department and diagnostic imaging spaces. Today’s announcement reflects the tremendous progress that has been made on this long-awaited project and our government’s continued commitment to strengthening rural healthcare in Sarnia-Lambton.”

In order to choose a construction company, a procurement process and Ministry of Health approval were required.

“Awarding the construction contract is an incredibly exciting milestone for Ceeh of Bluewater Health and the Petrolia and Central Lambton community,” said Paula Reaume-Zimmer, president and CEO of Bluewater Health.

“Selecting our construction partner brings us closer than ever to seeing years of planning, advocacy, and community support take shape. This investment further solidifies our commitment to rural health for decades to come. We are grateful to the Ministry of Health, local elected officials, Bluewater Health Foundation, and its donors, staff and physicians, and the entire community for their continued commitment to the future of rural healthcare in Petrolia.”

The Bluewater Health Foundation is raising $5 million to put towards the redevelopment. So far, $2 million has been raised.

stories.title: Calgary man charged for alleged threat to kill Carney on YouTube, RCMP says
stories.summary: A Calgary resident is facing criminal charges for allegedly issuing threats to Prime Minister Mark Carney on YouTube, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A Calgary man is facing criminal charges for allegedly issuing threats to Prime Minister Mark Carney on YouTube , the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said on Tuesday.

Jamie Dacosta, 31, of Calgary was charged under Section 264.1(1)(a) of the Criminal Code for “uttering a threat to Prime Minister of Canada Mark Carney to cause death” in a video posted to YouTube, the RCMP’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (Inset) said in a statement.

“On July 28, 2026, the RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (Inset) received information that a YouTube account had posted threats to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney,” the statement says.

Working with the Calgary Police Service, law enforcement arrested and charged Dacosta.

Dacosta remains in custody and is scheduled to appear at the Alberta Court of Justice in Calgary on Sep. 15, the RCMP said.

stories.title: Nova Scotia family horrified to learn they buried a stranger’s remains
stories.summary: Several other people on social media are sharing similar stories about the remains of their loved ones.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Nova Scotia woman says she doesn’t know who her family buried eight years ago after the new owners of an Annapolis Valley funeral home recently revealed that her father’s remains were still in storage.

Amanda Sabean says her family buried what they were told were the cremated remains of her father Hendrik (Hank) Sabean alongside other late family members in the spring of 2018.

Last week, her sister received an email from East Coast Memorial, which recently acquired the assets of the former Serenity Funeral Home.

The new owners asked the family to pick up Hank Sabean’s remains.

Several other people on social media are sharing similar stories about the remains of their loved ones.

Provincial officials confirmed today they are investigating the mix-up.

The former and current owners of the funeral home could not be immediately reached for comment.

“We aren’t certain what to do, but know that someone May be missing the displaced remains of a family member,” Amanda Sabean said in a text message Tuesday.

“Our father didn’t deserve the error, and storage like some sort of dusty (collection of) books.”
