stories.title: Former B.C. Conservative Donegal Wilson joins Milobar’s new party
stories.summary: Wilson, member of the legislature for Boundary-Similkameen, is the seventh B.C. legislator to join the as-yet unnamed party
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
The new party formed by British Columbia legislators who have defected from the provincial Conservatives in recent weeks gained a seventh member on Monday, with interim leader Peter Milobar calling it an exciting development as the fledgling caucus works toward official recognition when the legislature resumes next month.

Donegal Wilson, member of the legislature for Boundary-Similkameen, said she made the decision after spending the last week talking with residents of her southern Interior riding.

Wilson said she did not plan to join the new party when she quit the Conservatives on Sept. 2 but found many areas of agreement with its members.

“When I left the B.C. Conservative caucus, I left because I could no longer support the leadership of Kerry-Lynne Findlay. I said then that I was leaving a caucus, not my principles, and that has not changed,” she said in a statement.

Wilson said both the governing NDP and Opposition B.C. Conservatives are largely focused on ideological issues, leaving many voters politically homeless.

“As a fiscal conservative, I saw an opportunity to get in and help form the new party,” she said in an interview. “So, that is why I chose to go now.”

Five ex-B.C. Conservative legislature members join newly formed party

Milobar said the legislators were close to finalizing the constitution and foundational principles for the as-yet unnamed party.

He said the party was working with Elections BC, but the agency was in a “holding pattern” until after the Sept. 26 by-election in Abbotsford-Mission, where voters will decide whether Findlay, the Conservative leader, will have a seat in the legislature.

“We’re still on track and aiming to be ready and recognized with our name approved by Oct. 5,” when the legislature resumes, he said.

Milobar, a former Opposition finance critic who had run for the B.C. Conservative leadership, said Monday there wouldn’t be a “massive gulf” between the Conservatives and the new party he was forming on every issue.

“We are coming up with policy and direction and a set of principles that resonate with the broader public that people will see themselves reflected in, regardless of how they voted in the past.”

The party’s stance would reflect the concerns of “a modern British Columbia family,” including the cost of living, housing and health care, he told reporters in Vancouver outside the Union of B.C. Municipalities annual convention.

Milobar said the name of the new party would not include the terms “Liberal” or “Conservative,” detaching it from any association with unrelated parties at the federal level.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s shambolic reign has handed the B.C. NDP a gift

Milobar founded the party with Ian Paton, another legislator who quit the Conservative caucus last month, and it has since been joined by Bruce Banman, A’a:liya Warbus, Rosalyn Bird, Teresa Wat and now Wilson.

They are among nine legislators who have defected from the Conservatives under Findlay, who narrowly won the party’s leadership contest in May.

Two remaining former Conservatives, Scott McInnis and Brennan Day, have said they will sit as Independents.

Milobar said he and other members of the new party have had conversations with sitting Conservatives.

“Some, you know, are maybe closer to potentially leaving or not. Others want to see what happens in the by-election or not,” he said.

Asked about possible collaboration with Centre BC and other potential right-of-centre alternatives, Milobar said there was room to continue having discussions.

But he said the new party he has helped form is the only option with sitting legislators and the benefits and resources they bring.

Wilson said former and current Conservative caucus members will have to make their own decisions for their own reasons in choosing a direction.

“But I do think we are building something exciting, and hopefully, they will want to come and be part of it.”

Wilson said she’s not interested in rebuilding an old, failed party.

“The new party has made significant strides in a matter of weeks and I am so thrilled to join this team and help build a credible alternative to the NDP that British Columbians can choose in the next election, whenever that May be.”

Those who have quit the B.C. Conservatives have cited issues around Findlay’s leadership and strategies.

Banman has said that Findlay is “unelectable” and levelled scathing criticism about the direction of the party under her leadership, calling out those around her for creating a “purity test” of whether legislators were “hard right enough.”

Findlay is scheduled to speak at the Union of B.C. Municipalities convention on Thursday, with Premier David Eby set to speak the next day.

stories.title: How can the Canadian health care system better care for its patients? Ask us your questions
stories.summary: This summer, we highlighted the work of volunteers across the country who devote their time to helping Canadian patients
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
The Q&A is happening on Thursday, Sept. 17. Submit your questions now.

This summer, we featured the stories of volunteers in Canadian health care in our Care Between the Lines series.

From a non-profit organization in Saskatchewan that drives locals to their medical appointments , stylists giving free haircuts in a Charlottetown hospital , cyclists taking seniors out for outdoor excursions and many more stories, the series celebrated these volunteers while highlighting the gaps in a system that can feel isolating for patients.

On Thursday, Sept. 17 at 1 p.m. ET, health editor Caroline Alphonso and national health reporter Alanna Smith will be answering your questions on the series, what volunteers are doing across the country, and how the Canadian health care system can better care for its patients.

Submit your questions in the box below, or send an e-mail to audience@globeandmail.com .

stories.title: TC Energy urges co-operation on growing natural gas network to meet ‘generational’ demand
stories.summary: A leaked UCP cabinet report raised concern over TC Energy's ability to serve Alberta's nascent A.I. data centre industry, oilsands projects and other sources of demand growth.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The pipeline company that moves three quarters of Western Canada’s natural gas says it’s prepared to keep investing in its vast Alberta network to meet “generational demand” for the fuel.

TC Energy Corp. released its statement days after the leak of an Alberta cabinet report that raised concern over the Calgary company’s ability to serve the province’s nascent artificial intelligence data centre industry, oilsands projects and other sources of demand growth.

The report says TC’s future expansion plans for its Nova Gas Transmission Ltd. pipeline are “misaligned” with the province’s projected demand growth and that the company’s dominant position has led to a “market failure” that has left key growth regions unable to access gas.

The Ngtl network , in operation since 1957, forms a vast web stretching across Alberta and connecting into northeastern British Columbia , shipping an average of 15 billion cubic feet per day of gas.

TC says natural gas demand is growing faster than infrastructure can be built, but it has invested “more than anyone” to grow is system.

It says it’s spent $15 billion in the last decade on expansion projects and is continuing to grow the system with another $1 billion in planned projects.

“TC Energy is prepared to keep investing in Ngtl and expand the system to meet the scale of opportunity in front of Alberta and Canada. This will require all of us — industry, customers, regulators, governments, stakeholders and rightsholders — to come to the table and improve the conditions to get infrastructure built,” the company said.

“The key is working together to bring forward credible solutions, capital and capacity quickly enough to support Alberta’s growth and enable Canada to unlock the opportunity to meet the moment.”

The Canadian Press has viewed the Alberta cabinet report, which The Narwhal first reported on last week.

The report included a recommendation that the province create two Crown corporations to spur new natural gas transmission lines. Premier Danielle Smith told her “Your Province Your Premier” radio call-in show Saturday that it’s “unlikely” the province will make such a move as there should be enough private-sector interest.

Court challenges from TC Energy and potentially Atco Gas and Pipelines Ltd. were flagged as “legal considerations” in the report.

stories.title: Canadian teens ranked 9th in science in global student performance survey
stories.summary: According to a new survey of more than 760,000 teenagers, student performance in science, reading and math is declining worldwide – and Canada is no exception.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Student performance in science, reading and math is declining worldwide – and Canada is no exception.

But despite the downward trend, Canadian teens are still well above the global average and only slightly behind the world’s top academic performers, ranking No. 9 in science, No. 11 in math and No. 12 in reading.

The data comes from the latest report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (Oecd) Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) . Pisa assesses 15-year-old students worldwide every three years in areas such as knowledge, skills and attitudes towards learning. The largest survey of its kind, more than 760,000 students from 91 countries and economies participated in Pisa’s 2025 assessment, including roughly 24,600 Canadian teens from 897 schools.

On average, the top-performing students in science, reading and math came from parts of China, Singapore, Taiwan and Japan. Other countries that cracked the top 10 in all three subjects included South Korea, Estonia and the United Kingdom. But even the highest-ranking countries saw declines in most measures of academic performance.

“Following the unprecedented drop in performance recorded in Pisa 2022, learning outcomes have largely stagnated or continued to decline in many countries,” the Pisa report stated. “In all three subjects, Pisa 2025 results are the lowest ever observed in Pisa in Canada, and are significantly below results from a decade earlier, in 2015.”

Despite its falling scores, Canada still ranked well above the Oecd average in all three subjects. The Oecd’s 38 member nations include the world’s most advanced and developed democracies.

Canada also did well in other measures , including student engagement, computational problem solving and socioeconomic performance gaps.

“Average 2025 results in Canada were lower than in 2022 in mathematics and reading, and about the same as in 2022 in science,” Pisa’s profile on Canada said. “Over this period, performance declined to a larger extent among advantaged than among disadvantaged students.”

Globally, academic performance declines in 2025 were the most precipitous in reading and math and more modest in science.

“In reading, increased digitalisation, longer screen time and falling rates of reading for enjoyment have coincided with weaker literacy outcomes,” the report explained. “Countries with the largest declines in reading also tended to record the largest drops in mathematics and science.”

Some countries, however, are bucking the trend, including Costa Rica, Turkiye and the United Kingdom, which all saw average science scores improve.

The Pisa report points to disruptions from the COVID-19 pandemic as a contributing factor to the global decline in educational performance, but it also notes that the downward trend was already in progress in many countries before the pandemic struck.

“The long-term declines in performance suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level,” the report said. “These include changing attitudes towards reading, the impact of digital distractions on students and rising levels of absenteeism.

“Overall, the data suggest weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change,” the report added.

But despite the downward trend, Canadian teens are still well above the global average and only slightly behind the world’s top academic performers, ranking No. 9 in science, No. 11 in math and No. 12 in reading.

The largest survey of its kind, more than 760,000 students from 91 countries and economies participated in Pisa’s 2025 assessment, including roughly 24,600 Canadian teens from 897 schools.

“Following the unprecedented drop in performance recorded in Pisa 2022, learning outcomes have largely stagnated or continued to decline in many countries,” the Pisa report stated. “In all three subjects, Pisa 2025 results are the lowest ever observed in Pisa in Canada, and are significantly below results from a decade earlier, in 2015.”

stories.title: Lawyer says new bill could cause ramped up surveillance of vulnerable Nova Scotians
stories.summary: The existing act allows people to submit anonymous complaints about a property in their neighbourhood that they believe is linked to criminal activity.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Halifax-based legal aid agency is urging the provincial government to scrap proposed legislative changes that one of its lawyers says could ramp up surveillance and investigations targeting vulnerable Nova Scotians.

Nadia Shivji, a lawyer with Dalhousie Legal Aid, told the provincial legislature’s public bills committee Monday that an expansion of the Safer Communities and Neighbourhoods Act could disproportionately harm Black, Indigenous and immigrant communities.

The existing act allows people to submit anonymous complaints about a property in their neighbourhood that they believe is linked to criminal activity. Amendments introduced in an omnibus bill tabled last week would allow complaints to be made by residents who don’t live in the area.

“The complaints outside of the community, I think that raises the most risk for marginalized communities and for complaints to be weaponized on the basis of prejudice,” Shivji said in an interview after the meeting.

Shivji told the committee that statistics gathered by various civil liberties organizations across Canada show that populations who are typically subject to over-policing, Indigenous and Black people as well as immigrants, are “the most vulnerable to the negative effects of state action.”

“This law opens an avenue for targeted harassment that is driven by racism and prejudice,” Shivji told the committee, adding that it’s an unnecessary measure because police already have the power to investigate concerns about potential criminal activity.

Justice Minister Scott Armstrong said the proposed changes are aimed at helping police tackle higher level crime, because the proposed changes also call for increasing the scope of criminal activity.

“We’ve seen a sort of a resurgence of organized crime in Nova Scotia. So the amendments, what they do is expand (the act) … to be able to look into organized crime, gang activity, retail theft and human trafficking,” Armstrong said in an interview after the committee meeting.

Armstrong, who is also the minister responsible for equity and anti-racism, said he takes Shivji’s concerns seriously. However, Armstrong said he does not believe the proposed changes will disproportionately affect marginalized people.

“These are amendments to existing legislation, targeting more high level things (crimes) that really aren’t attributed to racial minorities,” he said.

During the committee meeting, the NDP critic for justice, Suzy Hansen, said Armstrong should have anticipated the concerns about the bill since he is also the minister responsible for equity and anti-racism.

“We want tools to address criminal activity, but we also know there’s unintended consequences that could happen to marginalized communities, to Indigenous folks, to African Nova Scotians,” Hansen said in an interview after the meeting.

Shivji also told the committee she’s concerned that perpetrators of intimate partner violence could potentially take advantage of the proposed amendments to issue bogus complaints against their victims.

“What is to stop an abuser from making reports under Scan (Safer Communities and Neighbourhoods Act) to have their survivor who is fleeing, followed, surveilled, investigated, and possibly evicted? Nothing,” she said.

Armstrong said complaints made through the legislation are reviewed and verified to ensure they are credible before any action or investigation is taken.

Since 2006, there have been 2,100 complaints that met the bar for an investigation, and 22 were brought to the Supreme Court and resulted in property closure, he said.

stories.title: How Kate and Rooney Mara prepared for unique roles in ‘Bucking Fastard’
stories.summary: Werner Herzog’s film, which premiered at Tiff, follows two sisters who speak in unison, dress alike and, eventually, fall in love with the same man
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Kate and Rooney Mara walked the red carpet together at the Toronto International Film Festival, mirroring the in-sync characters in the buzzy Bucking Fastard , which premiered on Monday.

From renowned filmmaker Werner Herzog, the film follows sisters who speak in unison, dress alike and, eventually, fall in love with the same man.

Rooney Mara said playing sisters felt natural to the real-life siblings, but Kate Mara said they still did simple things to prepare for the unique roles such as wearing the same clothes to set and eating the same food at the same time.

“But we would have been eating the same thing anyway,” Rooney Mara said, interjecting.

“Because we like the same foods,” Kate Mara added.

Werner Herzog's 'Bucking Fastard' made its Canadian premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, with Kate and Rooney Mara explaining they would sing together, dress alike, and eat the same foods to get in the right headspace for their unique roles as sisters who speak in unison.

The Canadian Press

“It was really fun to be able to find all of the ways in which we’re similar as people. It was such a fun experiment and something that was really vital to the story and to playing these sisters,” said Kate Mara.

Orlando Bloom and Domhnall Gleeson also attended the Toronto premiere on Monday, the halfway point of the festival. Although King Street has reopened to traffic and many of the vendors on “Festival Street” are gone, the star-studded events are set to continue through next weekend.

Martin McDonagh is bringing his latest, Wild Horse Nine , along with stars John Malkovich – who just won the best actor award at the Venice Film festival – and Sam Rockwell.

At Tiff, and in Washington, Quebec’s film industry finds itself in the hot seat

Meanwhile, Fleabag star Andrew Scott was in town promoting his new film Elsinore , which tells the real-life story of Chariots of Fire actor Ian Charleson, who pushed through his Aids diagnosis while playing Hamlet at London’s National Theatre.

Other films premiering on Monday include the animated In Waves starring Will Sharpe and Stephanie Hsu and Helen Mirren’s thriller A Talent For Murder . Mirren was honoured at Tiff’s Tribute Awards on Sunday with an award inspired by Tiff’s women’s empowerment initiative, Share Her Journey.

stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadian border authorities say they have deported 111 people since August last year in efforts to combat extortion violence in South Asian communities.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Canadian border authorities say they have deported 111 people since August last year in efforts to combat extortion violence in South Asian communities.

DD[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/british-columbia/border-authorities-have-deported-111-due-to-extortion-violence-since-last-August/article_9da07240-288d-51c7-8a5d-d32e9c2f2ae9.html)

By The Canadian Press

The Canada Border Services Agency says 58 cases were in the Pacific region, 30 were removed from the Prairies and 23 from Greater Toronto.

The agency began dedicating resources to identifying immigration and refugee cases linked to extortion violence in August 2025 in Western Canada and expanded operations to Ontario last November.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 9Image 10Image 11

The Cbsa says its operation is to investigate if foreign nationals implicated in extortion violence have also violated Canadian immigration and refugee laws, removing those with known links to organized crime or other criminal activity.

It highlights recent cases where four men were deported for violating the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act with “firearms-related activity,” “serious criminality” and “a pattern of criminal activity.”

A total of 188 removal orders have been issued by the Cbsa relating to foreign nationals linked to extortion violence, with 91 in B.C., 47 in the Prairies and 50 in the Greater Toronto Area.

“These investigations are built on information from law enforcement partners, other government agencies, Cbsa-led investigations, and public reporting,” the agency release says.

“The Cbsa places the highest priority on enforcement and removal of cases involving criminality, organized crime and individuals who pose a risk to public safety.”

A tip line is in place to share information on such cases with border agents.

Surrey, B.C., has been among the hardest hit by the extortion violence in Canada.

Police there say there have been 139 reported extortions so far this year, with 21 cases of shots fired, two arsons and 74 victim.

The Cbsa did not identify the home countries of deportees, but authorities across Canada have cited the role of the India-based Lawrence Bishnoi gang in extortion crime, with the federal government designating it a terrorist group in September last year.

“The Bishnoi gang generates terror in the communities in which they operate through their involvement in extortions and intimidation,” Public Safety Canada says in its listing of the group, which it says “engages in murder, shootings and arson” as it targets diaspora communities.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

stories.title: Canada’s 2026 census participation was among highest ever, says StatCan
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says the response rate for this year's census of the population was 98.4 per cent, one of the highest ever recorded.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 14, 2026 2:52 pm

Statistics Canada says the response rate for this year’s census of the population was 98.4 per cent, one of the highest ever recorded.

The data is collected every five years and the questionnaire includes age, gender, marital status and language use.

That information is used to determine electoral maps, plan social programs and determine funding for municipal and provincial governments.

This spring, some people posted photos of their forms marked “return to sender” and made claims that the questions violated their privacy rights, prompting Liberal MP Mark Gerretsen to urge people to fill out the form.

StatCan says it’s begun the work to compile the data it collected and it will release seven batches of information beginning in February 2027.

The agency says more than 88 per cent of Canadians chose to fill out the census online, more than have ever used that option before.

stories.title: Manitoba offers to waive sales tax on major Port of Churchill investments
stories.summary: The Manitoba government is offering to waive the provincial sales tax on capital spending for the Port of Churchill as it tries to attract investments.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Winnipeg — The Manitoba government is offering to waive the provincial sales tax on major capital spending for the Port of Churchill as it tries to attract international investment.

Premier Wab Kinew made the announcement Monday at a major investment summit in Toronto organized by the federal government.

“We are here in Toronto to tell global investors that the Port of Churchill is open and ready to expand,” Kinew said in a statement.

Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA

The province said the new tax measure would apply to proposals for a new energy corridor and liquefied natural gas facilities, upgrades to the railway that runs to the port and icebreaking capacity to support year-round shipping.

Kinew is to meet with global investment firms while in Toronto to pitch the Port of Churchill as well as mining, infrastructure and agriculture projects totalling more than $85 billion.

Hundreds of executives and global asset managers have descended on Toronto for Canada’s first investment summit.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, his ministers and premiers from across the country are pitching investors on opportunities in multiple sectors, including energy, critical minerals and defence, over the next two days.

Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.CA

Kinew has championed the Port of Churchill as the province’s best bet for transformative economic growth.

The port has seen little activity in recent years, but in early September it loaded the first grain cargo in six years as well as its first potash shipment.

The province also released studies in August showing that receding ice levels are helping make the arctic shipping route more accessible with much cheaper ships than previously thought.

Ian Bickis, The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘My dad was always very generous’: family honours father with foundation to combat seniors scams
stories.summary: John Parkinson was a beloved father and grandfather, who was born in Ireland, but called Canada home for the majority of his life, ending his days at the age of 95, at a nursing home in Stratford.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
John Parkinson was a beloved father and grandfather, who was born in Ireland, but called Canada home for the majority of his life, ending his days at the age of 95, at a nursing home in Stratford.

To honour his memory, his family has started a foundation to help seniors from being scammed out of their hard earned money, like he and his family were.

“My dad was always a very generous and loving person, and anyone who knew him never had a negative word to say about him. So, in order to honor my father’s memory, we wanted to reach out to the public, and make sure that other families and individuals out there don’t have to go through the same turmoil in their time of grieving,” says Dave Parkinson, John’s son.

Canadians lost nearly $1 billion to fraud last year. Dave hopes the John Parkinson Family Foundation can help lower that number through education, advocacy, and simply not shying away from the uncomfortable subject.

“Many individuals don’t realize that after this has happened, it can be very difficult to find relief through legal circles. And if it ends up in civil courts, you’re looking at tens, if not hundreds of thousands of dollars, and years of litigation in order to recover lost funds. So, it’s important to put a stop to this before it actually starts,” says Parkinson.

Parkinson says fraudsters are preying on seniors, like his late father, and it has to stop.

“We’re seeing the financial predators up their game to a level that we’ve never seen before. We have these AI grandparent scams where you can actually clone the image of a loved one and reach out to them. We see the C.R.A scams, with people calling up. Bitcoin, everyone wants to pay in Bitcoin. So there’s many red flags that people need to look out for, especially in this day and age,” says Parkinson.

The Foundation was just launched in January, but they’ve already been in touch with banks, credit unions, and the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, to try and advocate for improved fraud protections.

“We’re seeing a major demographic shift that we haven’t seen in Western history before, and a wealth transfer to the extent that we haven’t seen before. So, it’s important to educate the public and the other stakeholders out there about the necessity to ensure that our seniors are kept safe and that financial predators are stopped in their tracks,” says Parkinson.

stories.title: Police investigate fatal collision involving a pedestrian in London
stories.summary: A man has died after being struck by a vehicle in London Monday morning.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
A man has died after being struck by a vehicle in London Monday morning.

London police say emergency crews were called to Hale Street, between Hamilton Road and Ellsworth Crescent, shortly after 7 a.m. for a report of a pedestrian being struck.

The adult male was taken to hospital with injuries but later died.

Police say although the investigation remains in its early stages, video surveillance was obtained, and officers determined that the pedestrian had been struck by a motor vehicle. The driver of the vehicle remained on scene.

The area was closed to traffic while emergency crews responded to the collision and police investigated. Roads have since reopened.

No further details have been released at this time.

stories.title: Doctor at centre of licensing controversy found guilty of assault, counselling to commit offence
stories.summary: Dr. Sanjeev Sirpal still faces five sexual-assault charges in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia
stories.author: Tu Thanh Ha
stories.content:
Sanjeev Sirpal, the doctor behind a controversy about Atlantic Canada’s physician licensing registry, has been found guilty by a Quebec court of having assaulted his then-girlfriend and counselling her to forge a diary entry that falsely portrayed a patient as a Nazi sympathizer.

In rendering his verdict Monday, Quebec Court Justice Frédéric Bénard, however, acquitted Dr. Sirpal of two other charges: dangerous driving and obstruction of justice.

Taking the stand in his defence in April, Dr. Sirpal had denied that he assaulted his then-girlfriend, a nurse named Mélina Harrisson, and that he had asked her to write a fake document.

Justice Bénard said he didn’t find the doctor’s testimony credible. “He’s not sincere … the court does not believe the accused,” the judge said, reading his decision in court.

Dr. Sirpal’s defence lawyer, Charles Levasseur, told The Globe and Mail that he was assessing a potential appeal of the ruling.

Dr. Sirpal is still awaiting trial on five counts of sexual assaults on patients in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. He has pleaded not guilty to those charges.

Sexual-assault allegations against doctor spur review of cross-province licensing system

His case has raised questions about the screening process for physicians in Atlantic Canada.

Dr. Sirpal obtained the right to practise medicine in New Brunswick in 2022, at the time when the Quebec College of Physicians was in the process of revoking his licence for failing to disclose that he had been dismissed from a U.S. medical school before eventually obtaining his degree in St. Lucia. New Brunswick’s College of Physicians and Surgeons wasn’t aware that Quebec regulators initially opened their investigation because of a complaint of sexual assault by one of his patients.

At his trial, held in Laval, Que., Ms. Harrisson described him to the court as a volatile, ill-tempered partner who shoved her violently while she was at his home, and on another occasion punched her, bent her index finger and bruised her arm.

Ms. Harrisson also testified that in early 2021, Dr. Sirpal disclosed to her that he was facing a complaint for sexual misconduct.

According to documents filed in the probe by the Quebec College of Physicians, a female patient reported that Dr. Sirpal examined her vagina and breasts when she consulted him for a concussion at the Westmount Square medical clinic in February, 2020.

Ms. Harrisson said that Dr. Sirpal asked her to write a bogus diary entry where she claimed to have dropped by the clinic that day and noticed that the female patient was in the waiting room, wearing a bandana with a Nazi insignia and uttering racist slurs.

The six-page false diary entry was entered into the trial evidence.

“The accused’s objective was to undermine the credibility of the said person in the event of a case before the College … What is found in this document is pure invention,” Justice Bénard said in convicting the doctor of counselling a criminal offence that was not committed.

However, Justice Bénard acquitted Dr. Sirpal of a count of obstruction of justice. He noted that ultimately, the fake diary was not sent to anyone.

The judge noted, however, that Ms. Harrisson’s account of the two assaults was supported by a Snapchat messaging exchange between her and the 39-year-old doctor in which she described the two incidents.

The judge said the messages undermined Dr. Sirpal’s denials. “The complainant’s testimony is not perfect, does not have to be, but the court considers it to be trustworthy in accordance with the truth.”

During the second incident, which took place in her car while she drove Dr. Sirpal to work, Ms. Harrisson said that, while he hit her, he also grabbed the steering wheel, making the car veer out of its lane.

Justice Bénard acquitted Dr. Sirpal of a charge of dangerous operation of a vehicle. “It has not been established that the accused driving style was objectively dangerous to the public,” he said.

The New Brunswick College said it could not comment specifically about Dr. Sirpal’s case.

In a written statement sent to The Globe, the college said that criminal convictions don’t automatically result in the revocation of a physician’s licence, but the regulating body could consider a range of disciplinary measures.

The college suspended Dr. Sirpal’s license in August, 2025, a day after the RCMP charged him with sexual assault in Nova Scotia.

The six-page false diary entry was entered into the trial evidence.

“The accused’s objective was to undermine the credibility of the said person in the event of a case before the College … What is found in this document is pure invention,” Justice Bénard said in convicting the doctor of counselling a criminal offence that was not committed.
However, Justice Bénard acquitted Dr. Sirpal of a count of obstruction of justice. He noted that ultimately, the fake diary was not sent to anyone.

The judge noted, however, that Ms. Harrisson’s account of the two assaults was supported by a Snapchat messaging exchange between her and the 39-year-old doctor in which she described the two incidents.

The judge said the messages undermined Dr. Sirpal’s denials. “The complainant’s testimony is not perfect, does not have to be, but the court considers it to be trustworthy in accordance with the truth.”

During the second incident, which took place in her car while she drove Dr. Sirpal to work, Ms. Harrisson said that, while he hit her, he also grabbed the steering wheel, making the car veer out of its lane.
Justice Bénard acquitted Dr. Sirpal of a charge of dangerous operation of a vehicle. “It has not been established that the accused driving style was objectively dangerous to the public,” he said.
The New Brunswick College said it could not comment specifically about Dr. Sirpal’s case.

In a written statement sent to The Globe, the college said that criminal convictions don’t automatically result in the revocation of a physician’s licence, but the regulating body could consider a range of disciplinary measures.
The college suspended Dr. Sirpal’s license in August, 2025, a day after the RCMP charged him with sexual assault in Nova Scotia.

stories.title: Unsettled weather with on and off showers
stories.summary: The temperatures are climbing as we see some sun and cloud in Midwestern Ontario.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The temperatures are climbing as we see some sun and cloud in Midwestern Ontario. “Today [Monday] we’ll see increasing amounts of cloud heading through the overnight,” said meteorologist Julie Atchison. “Our next pressure system will move in as we head into tomorrow with the chance of showers in the short term.

There will be some fog developing overnight as this low-pressure system starts to pull this cloud cover eastward.” There’s a possibility of thunderstorms as the system moves through. Here’s a full look at your forecast: Monday night: A few clouds.

Fog patches overnight. Low 10. Tuesday: A mix of sun and cloud with 60 percent chance of showers. Risk of a thunderstorm late in the afternoon. Wind becoming southwest 30 km/h gusting to 50 in the morning. High 24. Humidex 26.

UV index 6 or high. Wednesday: A mix of sun and cloud with 40 percent chance of showers. High 26. Thursday: A mix of sun and cloud with 60 percent chance of showers. High 26.

stories.title: Detainee releases raise concerns over Chinatown being used as a ‘dumping ground’
stories.summary: Security footage, obtained by Global News, is raising concerns as to why detainees being released from custody are being dropped off at all hours in Edmonton's Chinatown area.
stories.author: Kabi Moulitharan
stories.content:
People living and working in Edmonton’s Chinatown are speaking out over how people leaving correctional custody are being released into the inner city neighbourhood.

It comes after Global News obtained surveillance video showing several people getting out of corrections transport vans at different locations in the area north of downtown, where much of the city’s social services and homeless supports are concentrated.

Community leaders say the concern is not that people are being released from custody, but where and how those releases are happening — particularly when social service providers are closed.

2:10 Detainees released on sidewalks and in parking lots in Chinatown raises concerns for officials

One incident happened late Friday night near Kim Fat Market near 99 Street and 107 Avenue.

Kathryn Luu, interim executive director of the Chinatown Business Association, provided Global News with security footage showing a white corrections transport van pulling up near the business shortly before 10 p.m. Friday.

The video shows several people getting out of the van and walking onto the street.

Luu says she approached the corrections officer to ask what was happening, but the man refused to engage in conversation.

“He looked at me, and then he drove off,” she explained.

“That was very unprofessional and very dismissive in some ways.”

Luu questions why people were being released in the area late on a Friday night — a time when services were not open.

She said she would have preferred to see people handed over directly to a service provider, such as Hope Mission, the King Thunderbird Centre or the province’s Navigation and Support Centre.

“I do think that there is a better system that can help do handovers for people to get the necessary help that they need,” Luu suggested.

The situation adds another challenge for a neighbourhood already dealing with issues such as fires, vandalism, theft, people defecating and urinating in public, and other forms of social disorder.

Community leaders say the drop-off near Kim Fat Market does not appear to be isolated.

Earlier this month, surveillance video provided by the Yorkton Equity Group showed another person being released from a corrections van.

That incident happened in the morning hours in a private parking lot near Pacific Mall, just off 97 Street and 105 Avenue.

Karl Miu with Yorkton Equity says he had heard reports of people being released in the area, but was shocked when he saw it happen himself.

“We need change,” Miu said.

“We don’t want Chinatown to be a dumping ground for everything.”

Community leaders say they are concerned Chinatown could increasingly become a destination for people leaving custody without a clear connection to supports.

Sandy Pon, co-chair of Chinatown Transformation Collaborative Society, says it’s created a lot of frustration.

“What are the owners of these buildings going to do for them? Nothing.

“People dropped off in the middle of the night when everything is shut down? How are they going to get help?”

Pon says there needs to be better coordination between corrections and service providers to ensure people leaving custody can connect with appropriate supports.

“There’s a big disconnect in communication between the Ministry of Safety and Correctional Services. That is provincial and federal,” Pon said.

“Where’s the decency for everyone? For the businesses, for the people that live in the area and also for the people that have been released?”

In a statement, the Alberta government said it has met with Chinatown representatives and support services and procedures are in place to help create transition plans for people being released from custody.

“Approximately 80 per cent of the individuals in custody are on remand status, release dates May not be known ahead of time, and therefore Corrections works with the individuals to assist in coordinating release planning, recognizing the individual cannot legally remain in custody and must be released,” a spokesperson for the Ministry of Public Safety and Emergency Services stated.

Community leaders say they want a system that ensures people are not simply left on the street without a clear path to support.

stories.title: Capital Power CEO says Canada still needs to remove regulatory roadblocks
stories.summary: Transforming business enthusiasm into final investment decisions will be the real challenge at Carney’s summit, Avik Dey says
stories.author: Emma Graney
stories.content:
Transforming the enthusiasm of business and political leaders into final investment decisions will be the real challenge at the Canada Investment Summit this week in Toronto, says Capital Power chief executive officer Avik Dey.

Prime Minister Mark Carney first announced plans for the summit in April, saying it will focus on attracting new investment from domestic and global players for nation-building projects. It is part of his stated effort to broaden Canada’s economic ties in order to reduce its dependence on trade with the United States.

The business community is on board with that ambition and committed to big projects, but catalyzing it into final investment decisions and shovels in the ground means busting through Canada’s multiple layers of bureaucracy and regulation, Mr. Dey told The Globe on Monday.

Live updates: Mark Carney's investment summit

Ottawa’s Major Projects Office goes some way toward doing that, but lacks the teeth to say, “These are the projects we’re supporting, and here’s how we’re going to push them through to approval,” he said.

Mr. Dey spent Sunday evening at an invite-only reception at the Royal Ontario Museum. There, nearly 500 guests from sectors such as banking, mining, pension funds and technology rubbed shoulders with federal and provincial politicians ahead of the summit.

He described the event as something of a “rallying cry;” a chance to say, “Let’s put our game face on, and let’s not lose this opportunity” to get major projects built.

“I’ve been in finance and energy my entire career, working around the globe, and I’ve never seen a room like that assembled last night of Canadian business leaders, policymakers, the federal government,” Mr. Dey said.

“It was very inspiring as a Canadian to be in that room.”

Mr. Dey comes to the event in something of a unique position. When he meets with investors, he’ll be tapping his experience on their side of the table from when he worked in private equity and pension investments.

He expects conversations between CEOs and global investors will outline not just potential projects, but the benefits of being in Canada; namely, the country’s security of law, proximity to markets and a regulatory body that, “if you can navigate it, gives you security of outcomes.”

Officials organizing the Canada Investment Summit identified more than 160 projects in various stages of development that are open for investment, including a proposed $10.9-billion high-speed rail link between Edmonton and Calgary and a planned $57-billion Port of Churchill expansion project.

Capital Power was on that list for a proposed US$2-billion to US$6-billion expansion of its Genesee electricity generation station site near Edmonton. The project would make the site a “major power generation and energy storage hub capable of supporting large industrial and data centre demand.”

The 66-page “prospectus” booklet, shared with summit attendees ahead of the event, was framed as “a snapshot of the diverse opportunities available across multiple asset classes, sectors and stages of development.”

Yet the next two days are “just the tip of the iceberg,” Mr. Dey said.

Global investors will be in Toronto “excited and ready” about major projects, he said. “But the deliverability of them is going to be on us.”

stories.title: New Brunswick aiming to attract $30 billion in investment at Toronto summit
stories.summary: The New Brunswick government is hoping to attract billions of dollars from investors at a major conference this week.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt says the top executive from Bank of Montreal Financial Group is one of several business leaders she’s meeting with this week as her government looks to attract billions of dollars of spending.

Hundreds of executives and global asset managers descended on Toronto on Monday for Canada’s first-ever national investment summit — and, like many of her counterparts, Holt is hoping to attract some of that capital to her province.

The provincial Liberal government said it will pitch investors on a new nuclear development, the Sisson Mine, a proposed data centre, an expansion to the Belledune port and four other projects.

All eight projects represent $30 billion in capital investment opportunities in New Brunswick and demonstrate the province’s potential in sectors critical to Canada’s economic and industrial future, government officials said.

Holt said she’s pitching New Brunswick’s value to would-be investors in a series of closed-door meetings. She said that while the summit has brought in many foreign investors, there are domestic players who could be good partners, too.

That includes Bank of Montreal Financial Group CEO Darryl White.

“We’re talking about the kind of growth that New Brunswick is seeing and making sure that he’s aware of the kind of mineral assets that we’re developing,” she told The Canadian Press by phone.

Holt noted her government’s ongoing efforts to reinvigorate the Maritime province’s once-thriving mining sector, as Canada and its allies look for secure, trusted sources of minerals critical to the production of semiconductors, batteries and other everyday products.

“They have capital that we’d like to see deployed towards some of these projects. And we learn more about what kinds of things they like to invest in, what kind of businesses (and) what kind of projects,” she said.

The premier added that after an initial conversation, her team can connect a potential investor with the appropriate government department or private firm involved in a capital project, such as the Port of Belledune expansion.

“The team at Opportunities New Brunswick and I follow up on those and continue the work to grow our economy (and) produce the kind of good-paying jobs that New Brunswickers are looking for.”

The country is hosting the Canada Investment Summit as it aims to improve its reputation in the eyes of investors after years of stagnant business investment. It comes also amid an unpredictable trade war with the United States.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a lofty goal of attracting $1 trillion in investment over the next five years and has reoriented federal spending priorities to focus on critical infrastructure and other major projects.

Herb Emery, political science department chair at the University of New Brunswick, said the summit amounts to “great political theatre” in the way it appears to show co-ordinated action on attracting new cash flow to the country.

“It does advertise and aggregate the range of opportunities that the world could be looking at in Canada,” Emery said in an interview Monday afternoon.

“But it doesn’t get around our fundamental problem, which is for over a decade Canada has been seen as a poor return place to invest.”

And he questioned why the premier and her government would need to be so hands-on as a marketer if New Brunswick’s energy and mineral projects are the great opportunities her government says they are.

Holt said it was important for investors to see a jurisdiction they can trust will be reliable long-term.

“Evaluating the political stability of a country, of a province and of a project is a piece of investors’ due diligence, and this is where Canada shines and where New Brunswick shines as well,” she said.

“We know how to develop resources in this province and this country, and we can show that we’ve had the kind of political stability … that is attractive to investors.”

But even if New Brunswick were to get an influx of new public and private cash boosting its large-scale energy and resource projects, Emery said it May not be enough to have the impact taxpayers are looking for.

“These projects would generate GDP too far down the road,” he said.

“And the growth that it would generate isn’t enough to close the hole that they’ve created with the spending,” he added, referencing New Brunswick’s budget deficits.

The eight projects the New Brunswick government has chosen to highlight are among those being pitched by Canada at the Toronto conference.

Holt said she wouldn’t have any deal to announce right away, instead describing the meetings Monday and Tuesday as “first connection points” as they evaluate whether they are a good fit for New Brunswick.

“Our ultimate goal is to get investment into our key projects and to do so in the near term,” she said.

“And we’ll certainly be sharing with New Brunswickers the outcomes and the successes from this effort.”

Meanwhile, Holt said she’ll join about 100 other officials and investors at the Art Gallery of Ontario for a gala dinner that is closed to the public and the media.

On Tuesday, attendees will huddle at the downtown Four Seasons Hotel for presentations on Canada’s investment landscape.

Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper is expected to deliver closing remarks at the summit, according to a source with knowledge of the planned events.

stories.title: London Majors’ Roop Chanderdat dissects disappointing playoff exit
stories.summary: The Majors dropped eight of their final 10 games, including four straight to end their semifinal series against Welland.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The London Majors crumbled in the clutch when the games mattered most.

That was the immediate takeaway from what had been a promising first Canadian Baseball campaign. The local club couldn’t close out the pennant in the final two weeks of the regular season and couldn’t put a stranglehold on the Welland Jackfish after taking a 2-0 lead in the semifinal series.

The Majors were sent to the sidelines in six games – culminating in a crushing 15-6 loss this past weekend at Welland, fuelled by an eight-run seventh inning – and will watch the Jackfish face the Hamilton Cardinals in the championship series starting Friday.

“It’s disappointing,” London co-owner and manager Roop Chanderdat said. “Our goal is always to win a championship. I had to rebuild almost the entire roster and I knew that was a difficult task. We didn’t have many returnees and I liked the roster I put together.

“We went into a slump at the wrong time with roughly two weeks left in the season.”

The Majors dropped eight of their final 10 games overall. They were outscored 33-9 in pivotal Games 4-6 against Welland and outhomered 8-2 in the series.

“You don’t want to put the blame on the pitching alone,” Chanderdat said. “Our offence just never got firing on all cylinders. We had a big-time offence and they just couldn’t put it together like they did in the regular season.”

Only Tucker Zdunich (.435) and Maikol Escotto (.360) hit consistently among the London regulars in the lineup. But big hits with runners in scoring position were few and far between.

“We were leaving runners on with less than two outs,” Chanderdat said. “In Game 5, we had runners on third twice and didn’t capitalize. I know the offence isn’t going to be as good in the post-season because the pitching is better, but it didn’t come together when needed.

“We did expect to get out-hit (in the series) with our offence.”

The Majors brought in speedy outfielder Jordan Lewis specifically to be a table-setter at the top of the order. He managed to score only once in four games against Welland.

“He was our speed guy, which we didn’t have a lot of, and then he got hurt,” Chanderdat said. “He tried to play through it, but when you hurt your leg and you’re fast, it’s tough.”

The turning point was the near-comeback in Game 3 at Labatt Park. London trailed 6-0 in the ninth, but rallied to score five runs and then stranded a runner at third.

They never won another game in the series.

“When you reflect on it, their second baseman made a helluva play to get a force out at second on a ball up the middle that would’ve tied the game,” Chanderdat said. “We lost Game 5 in the ninth with our closer (Skylar Janisse) on the mound. We knew it would be a tight series. You had a three-way tie for first (London, Hamilton, Welland with 31-17 records) and that says a lot.”

Two of those teams will decide the title. The Majors will try to construct a championship pedigree again.

The London organization felt the first year of pro-style ball was a positive experience. The league naturally improved with the move to eight import players.

“There were no headaches in the first year with the (salary) cap,” Chanderdat said. “It took some adjusting and balancing of the budget. The crowds were strong for us.”

Could CBL teams expand on their 48-game schedule?

“It’s something we’ll have to really assess,” he said. “We’re one mid-week game now, so it would mean adding another mid-week game. Financially, can everyone handle that? There’s the possibility but you would need another team in the league to make it work.”

The first-time playoff format of five teams with a one-game wild card will also be scrutinized in the winter. There was a clear separation between the top five and the bottom four clubs this season.

“You hear maybe the wild card should be a two-of-three series or you even go to six teams (qualifying),” Chanderdat said. “In the major leagues, you have more teams making playoffs. There’s a business aspect to it.

“Looking how the season ended, that top five might turn into seven fighting for those spots next year.”

stories.title: Here’s why employers say university degrees are still worth it, but not on their own
stories.summary: As roughly two million students return to Canadian colleges and universities this month, some are questioning whether a degree is still worth the time and money, as grads face a job market that is rapidly changing in the age of artificial intelligence.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
As roughly two million students return to Canadian colleges and universities this month, some are questioning whether a degree is still worth the time and money, as grads face a job market that is rapidly changing in the age of artificial intelligence.

Leeroy Mudhikwa, a Simon Fraser University student studying data science, is trying to broaden his skill base in case he is unable to secure a job after graduation. He has one year left in the program but spent his summer running a painting business, looking for ways to broaden his experience beyond his education.

“I learn how to hire people, you know, to recruit, learn how to run a business,” he said. “I really have enjoyed that aspect of it all.”

At the University of British Columbia, economics student Aiden Thomas says he is questioning whether continuing his studies is the best use of his time and money. “I feel like the worth of a degree is becoming less and less, of course, dependent on the specific degree,” he said.

A university education, plus something else

Tara Parry, a hiring expert and director of permanent services with Robert Half, says a university degree still has value, but increasingly it needs to be accompanied by practical experience and job-specific skills.

“A university degree is still worth it, but not on its own,” Parry said. “It doesn’t guarantee a job the same way it used to.”

A degree can demonstrate qualities employers value, including time management, managing a workload and being prepared and reliable, she said.

But employers are looking for more than education.

“It’s not just education alone, it’s skills,” Parry said. “It’s technical skills, it’s practical experience, it’s applicable experience as well as foundational knowledge.”

That could mean internships, co-op placements, apprenticeships or other opportunities to gain experience while studying.

For those pursuing a more general arts degree, Parry suggests looking for ways to gain relevant experience.

A degree will now cost you more

A university education is now more expensive than it was a generation ago.

Statistics Canada data for the 2025/26 school yea r shows Canadian undergraduate students are now paying $7,734 a year in tuition. 20 years ago, for the school year 2006/07, the average cost was $4,400. That’s an increase of nearly 76 per cent, which has outpaced inflation.

Roughly half of graduates have debt when they complete their studies, according to Statistics Canada, owing an average of more than $38,000.

With that in mind, does the investment pay off? The answer, at least in terms of average earnings, is still yes.

Statistics Canada data shows employees aged 25 and older with a bachelor’s degree or higher earned an average of $44.67 an hour in 2024. That’s about 55 per cent more than workers with a high school diploma or less, who earned an average of $28.82 an hour.

Workers with post-secondary education below a bachelor’s degree earned an average of $34.38 an hour.

Bottom line, Parry says, is a degree still sets candidates apart. “If it’s apples to apples, down to two candidates, they will nine times out of 10 take the candidate that has the bachelor’s degree versus the one who doesn’t,” she said.

stories.title: No incumbent, just four candidates and the quietest race for London city council
stories.summary: One race stands out in the London's south end – mainly for how relatively quiet it is.
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
With Londoners just weeks away from heading to the polls to elect their next city council, one race stands out in the city’s south end – mainly for how relatively quiet it is.

The city’s ward boundaries are seeing their first substantial change in a decade, and nowhere else is that more apparent than Ward 14, which will grow to represent roughly a third of the city’s land area after taking in all land south of Highway 401.

Add in a wide open race as the incumbent Coun. Steven Hillier bows out of civic politics, and voters might expect a heated battle. But with just four candidates – two of whom signed up late in the nomination period – it’s arguably the quietest race for a spot on city council.

“I think partly it speaks to the nature of that ward. It’s a pretty unusual ward,” said Western University political scientist Martin Horak. “It has very large rural area, it has a lot of industrial land, and then it does have some residential neighbourhoods as well. Most wards in London have more of a kind of residential base.”

Within London’s 14 races for city councillor, three are guaranteed to elect new politicians – Wards 4, 7, and 14 to replace Susan Stevenson, Corrine Rahman (who is running in Ward 5 to replace outgoing Jerry Pribil), and Hillier.

Wards 4 and 7 in particular are heated races, boasting nine and eight candidates, respectively. Ward 14, though, has only four and none with any significant community profile. In fact, two signed up within the final week of the nomination period, which closed last month.

Despite seemingly being one of the paths of least resistance to city hall, the dynamics of the ward likely make it daunting to prospective candidates, Horak said.

“It May be a little more intimidating for new candidates because how do you canvass all of those interests beyond the residential areas? What do you do with that in terms of campaign promises?” he said.

“My point is that there’s less of a sense of established identity, I think, in Ward 14 than there is in a lot of the other (wards). And if you’re a new candidate, you’re looking for something to hang your hat on, and I think it’s more difficult.”

Jason King is one of the candidates seeking that seat – having signed up on the first day of the nomination period.

The 52-year-old says he is running to be a champion of the many priorities of the ward, taking in the suburban Westminster and Pond Mills areas, new growth in Summerside, much of the city’s industrial southeast, and much of the rural land up to the city’s southern border.

“As I’ve been knocking on doors, it’s become more of my mission to help everybody in Ward 14, and they really do need a champion here in Ward 14 because the consensus at the doors is Ward 14, and specifically the southeast corner of the city, has been neglected,” he said.

Some of the top issues he’s been hearing depend on the area, with traffic calming dominating the Westminster region while construction and its traffic resonate elsewhere.

Sarah Lehman signed up as a candidate on the first day of the nomination period, taking another shot at the Ward 14 race after losing by 228 votes to Hillier in the 2022 election. She netted 40 per cent of the vote to Hillier’s 45 per cent.

She says she’s heard concerns at the door about residents being left behind when it comes to representation and receiving city services, and she agrees there’s no shortage of priorities.

“It has rural issues, it has urban issues, we have a huge industrial park in the east end, we also now have the city landfill, which is an issue for people,” the 35-year-old said. “There are a lot of different issues that you have to kind of compile and then prioritize.”

She does see common threads, however, hearing at the door concerns about public safety and police response, property taxes, along with proper infrastructure for growth in the Jackson and Summerside areas – especially transit. Lehman hopes the open race can drive voter turnout, and says she’s eager to hear from her opponents and constituents at the planned all-candidates debate set for Thursday evening at Chalmers Presbyterian Church.

Also running in the Ward 14 race is Ubaid Bhatti and Gurinder Pal Singh, both of whom signed up within the last week of nomination period. Singh told reporters on Aug. 21 that his first priority is to make sure the voices of the ward are heard.

“Their interests, or their concerns, or their problems, they should feel confident that somebody is going to bring it before the city. And whatever I can do as in my capacity, I will pursue that,” Singh said.

Bhatti has not registered any campaign contact information and could not be reached for comment. Neither Bhatti nor Singh replied to a Free Press survey of all the candidates running in London’s Oct. 26 civic election.

stories.title: How London’s youth are disengaged from municipal politics. And how they could return
stories.summary: Across London, the signs of a city election are clear to see - literally. Coming in all shapes and sizes, bear...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Across London, the signs of a city election are clear to see – literally. Coming in all shapes and sizes, bearing one of 111 possible different names, competing for positions as mayor, city council, or school board trustees, election signs adorn street corners, lawns, and boulevards around the city, reminding Londoners to get out and vote.

But it seems the youngest among the voting public often miss that reminder, e ven though youth engagement has the potential to shape the election outcome, said one political scientist.

Recent interviews conducted with Fanshawe College students about which issues are important to them in the city election suggest awareness of the municipal elections, and key information surrounding them, is at a low among youth in London.

“I’m not sure who is getting elected,” says Fanshawe College nursing student Raphael Alvis. “There’s not information going about it. All I see are the signs in the streets.”

During “people on the street” interviews last week, Alvis was one of a number of Fanshawe students who told XFM News they knew little about the municipal election.

Jasmine Bo, a student in the Autism Sciences & Behavioural Studies program, says that many students haven’t stayed informed on the election because they aren’t getting information on it.

“The election itself should be broadcast more because […] we barely know about it,” she says.

According to a 2020 survey done by Statistics Canada, youth demographics (identified as being between the ages of 18-24) across the country are less invested in politics than other age groups.

This trend among municipal politics to be relatively overlooked is a larger one. Matt Farrell, a political science professor at Fanshawe College, goes so far as to call the municipal level the “forgotten child” of politics.

Farrell says the reason for this is twofold: Firstly, municipal politics lack the presence of political parties.

“The average person doesn’t pay a lot of attention to politics, but they can remember who they voted for,” he says. “That connection is gone at the municipal level.”

Farrell also states that it is more difficult for voters to gather information on municipal candidates, and that together with the lack of partisanship the result is a sense of apathy towards municipal politics.

With the youth demographic, there are further reasons for a lack of engagement in London’s election. Despite a large decrease in international students since 2024 at Fanshawe, many members of the school’s student population are still from outside the city of London.

“They might not necessarily have an attachment to the community that they’re in,” says Farrell.

However, this doesn’t mean there are no young Londoners engaged in municipal politics.

Twenty-four year-old mayoral candidate Mustafa Zeboon has garnered attention for his social media-focused campaign . As well, at 19, Ward 12 candidate Ribal Zebian is the youngest person running for any position in the city.

Campaign sign for Ward 12 candidate Ribal Zebian. Despite the ubiquity of signs such as this in London, youth engagement in the election remains low. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

Zebian is a student in the engineering program at Western University, and is running in Ward 12 against Alexander Main and incumbent Elizabeth Peloza. When asked about the lack of youth engagement in municipal politics, he blames communication issues.

“When you have hundreds of pages for a policy that has a bureaucratic approach or written in legal language, the youth […] don’t have the time or background to decipher all of that information,” he says.

Both Farrell and Zebian also see a generational gap as being a key issue with youth engagement. Zebian considers this gap to be “significant,” while Farrell says that older generations are more connected to their communities than youth voters.

Though the disconnect between the youth demographic and city politics is prevalent, both Zebian and Farrell believe that if youth were more involved, it could change the political landscape of London.

“If [young people] throw their voice into the polls and they just vote, there’s a high chance we could make a change,” says Zebian. “You’d be very surprised how quickly we can get your ideas out there.”

Farrell says it’s important to recognize that elections can make a difference on local issues that affect Fanshawe and Western communities, such as the housing market and the cost of living.

“If one of [the candidates] makes a concerted effort to try and increase the number of younger folks that do come out and vote, there’s a lot of potential there,” he says.

With low voter turnouts and close races in London, attracting the youth vote could mean the margin of victory for a candidate who does so.

Campaign signs outside of Fanshawe College. Experts believe that if youth voters were focused on as a demographic, the political landscape of London could be changed. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

Ultimately, both Farrell and Zebian have similar answers to the question of how to engage the youth demographics and get out the vote. Farrell believes that municipal politicians putting in the effort to appeal to youth voters is the key, while Zebian believes that better communication of issues could attract the demographic.

“If we could properly, adequately, and clearly communicate and show them ‘hey, if you come, you can be heard in this way,’ we can get results and that builds trust,” he says.

Zebian is confident that the presence of young candidates such as himself and Mustafa Zeboon suggests younger generations are becoming engaged in city politics.

“It’s gonna make a big difference,” Zebian says. “Right now it might not show as much, but the more we get in, the more momentum we’re gonna have, [and] the more we can do.”

Coming in all shapes and sizes, bearing one of 111 possible different names, competing for positions as mayor, city council, or school board trustees, election signs adorn street corners, lawns, and boulevards around the city, reminding Londoners to get out and vote.
But it seems the youngest among the voting public often miss that reminder, e ven though youth engagement has the potential to shape the election outcome, said one political scientist.

Recent interviews conducted with Fanshawe College students about which issues are important to them in the city election suggest awareness of the municipal elections, and key information surrounding them, is at a low among youth in London.
“I’m not sure who is getting elected,” says Fanshawe College nursing student Raphael Alvis. “There’s not information going about it. All I see are the signs in the streets.”
During “people on the street” interviews last week, Alvis was one of a number of Fanshawe students who told XFM News they knew little about the municipal election.
Jasmine Bo, a student in the Autism Sciences & Behavioural Studies program, says that many students haven’t stayed informed on the election because they aren’t getting information on it.
“The election itself should be broadcast more because […] we barely know about it,” she says.
According to a 2020 survey done by Statistics Canada, youth demographics (identified as being between the ages of 18-24) across the country are less invested in politics than other age groups.

“The average person doesn’t pay a lot of attention to politics, but they can remember who they voted for,” he says. “That connection is gone at the municipal level.”

stories.title: Quebec doctor convicted of assault, counselling an offence
stories.summary: Laval - A doctor in Quebec has been found guilty of two counts of assault and one count of counselling a person to commit an offence that was not committed.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Laval - A doctor in Quebec has been found guilty of two counts of assault and one count of counselling a person to commit an offence that was not committed.

Updated at 4:05 p.m.

CMU[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/quebec/quebec-doctor-convicted-of-assault-counselling-an-offence/article_429fd93c-3bb8-5e62-bd4f-7e36a72a0b2e.html)

By Morgan Lowrie The Canadian Press

Quebec Court Judge Frédéric Bénard found that Sanjeev Sirpal asked his then-girlfriend to create a false diary entry suggesting that she’d witnessed one of his patients wearing a Nazi symbol and making a racist remark in a Montreal-area waiting room.

Bénard told a courtroom in Laval, Que., that Sirpal had urged the woman to fabricate the story to discredit the patient, who had complained about him to the province’s doctor’s college.

Article continues below

The judge said Sirpal bought the notebook used to create the diary, and reviewed a draft version of the story in order to make suggestions.

As the woman later testified, “what is found in this document was pure invention and was not true,” he told the court.

”(The complainant) explained that she had done this to help him, while specifying that she has felt a lot of pressure,” the judge said.

The patient ultimately decided not to move forward with a complaint, and therefore the diary was never used in Sirpal’s defence or viewed by anyone besides the accused, the judge said.

He acquitted Sirpal of a charge of obstruction of justice, noting that the “material evidence of the offence was therefore not committed.”

The judge also concluded that Sirpal assaulted the ex-girlfriend in August and December 2020.

The first assault happened at Sirpal’s home, where the complainant testified that he grabbed her shoulders and pushed her after hearing that a colleague had expressed interest in her.

The second happened while she was driving him to work later that year. The woman testified that he lost his temper and grabbed and pulled at the steering wheel on two occasions, before punching her in the chest and grabbing and bending her finger hard after she stopped the vehicle.

The judge acquitted Sirpal of a charge of dangerous driving.

Bénard said Sirpal and the complainant presented opposing versions of the events in question. Sirpal had denied any wrongdoing and had tried to paint the accused’s testimony as inconsistent, but the judge found her to be credible.

“The complainant’s testimony is not perfect, it does not have to be, but the court considers it to be trustworthy in accordance with the truth,” the judge said, adding that “the court does not believe the accused.”

Prosecutor Nicolas Désilets-Laforge said he welcomed the judgment, noting that the judge “considered that the complainant was credible and reliable.”

Sirpal’s lawyer listened to the decision by video conference, and did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment. Sirpal, who wore a grey suit and sat in front of the judge as the verdict was read, did not comment.

The case returns to court for a sentencing hearing on Oct. 15.

Documents from Quebec’s doctor’s college say he was born in the United States and studied in Canada, the U.S. and St. Lucia before joining the province’s order of doctors in 2019.

The college revoked Sirpal’s permit in 2022, after concluding that he had provided fraudulent information when applying. He appealed the decision but lost.

Sirpal has also worked as a doctor in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

He was removed from the interprovincial Atlantic Registry as of March 20, 2025. A few months later, the College of Physicians and Surgeons of New Brunswick also suspended his licence.

Nova Scotia RCMP charged Sirpal with sexual assault in August 2025 after officers received a complaint about an alleged assault during an assessment in an emergency room at Cumberland Regional Health Care Centre near Amherst in northern Nova Scotia.

Sirpal was released on conditions after his arrest, Nova Scotia RCMP said.

The case in Nova Scotia is due to return to court on Tuesday for a decision on pretrial applications. The trial is scheduled to be heard by a judge at the Amherst Provincial Court in November.

While practising in northwestern New Brunswick, Sirpal worked at the Edmundston Regional Hospital, according to the province’s physician registry.

Sirpal graduated from the Spartan Health Sciences University School of Medicine in St. Lucia in 2013. The school is no longer accredited by a regional health education authority in the Caribbean after failing to meet standards.

The Caribbean Accreditation Authority for Education in Medicine and Other Health Professions gave provisional accreditation to the school in 2013, while flagging numerous issues of concern. The authority revoked the school’s accreditation in 2024.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

With files from Tori Fitzpatrick and Michael MacDonald in Halifax

The Canadian Press

stories.title: TC Energy urges co-operation on growing network to meet 'generational' gas demand
stories.summary: Calgary - The pipeline company that moves three quarters of Western Canada's natural gas says it's prepared to keep investing in its vast Alberta network to meet "generational demand" for the fuel.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - The pipeline company that moves three quarters of Western Canada’s natural gas says it’s prepared to keep investing in its vast Alberta network to meet “generational demand” for the fuel.
