Todd Korol/The Canadian Press[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/alberta/tc-energy-urges-co-operation-on-growing-network-to-meet-generational-gas-demand/article_0082c789-9036-5b15-a9d8-d33e40c444db.html)

By Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press

TC Energy Corp. released its statement days after the leak of an Alberta cabinet report that raised concern over the Calgary company’s ability to serve the province’s nascent artificial intelligence data centre industry, oilsands projects and other sources of demand growth.

The report says TC’s future expansion plans for its Nova Gas Transmission Ltd. pipeline are “misaligned” with the province’s projected demand growth and that the company’s dominant position has led to a “market failure” that has left key growth regions unable to access gas.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

The Ngtl network, in operation since 1957, forms a vast web stretching across Alberta and connecting into northeastern British Columbia, shipping an average of 15 billion cubic feet per day of gas.

TC says natural gas demand is growing faster than infrastructure can be built, but it has invested “more than anyone” to grow is system.

It says it’s spent $15 billion in the last decade on expansion projects and is continuing to grow the system with another $1 billion in planned projects.

“TC Energy is prepared to keep investing in Ngtl and expand the system to meet the scale of opportunity in front of Alberta and Canada. This will require all of us — industry, customers, regulators, governments, stakeholders and rightsholders — to come to the table and improve the conditions to get infrastructure built,” the company said.

“The key is working together to bring forward credible solutions, capital and capacity quickly enough to support Alberta’s growth and enable Canada to unlock the opportunity to meet the moment.”

The Canadian Press has viewed the Alberta cabinet report, which The Narwhal first reported on last week.

The report included a recommendation that the province create two Crown corporations to spur new natural gas transmission lines. Premier Danielle Smith told her “Your Province Your Premier” radio call-in show Saturday that it’s “unlikely” the province will make such a move as there should be enough private-sector interest.

stories.title: Canadians are 'overwhelmingly open' to closer EU ties as Carney heads to Europe: poll
stories.summary: Support for Canada's relationship with Europe is growing, as Mark Carney prepares to travel to Strasbourg to strengthen ties with the EU.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Support for Canada deepening its relationship with Europe is growing, a new poll has found, as Prime Minister Mark Carney prepares to travel to Strasbourg, France, to strengthen ties with the European Union.

An Abacus Data survey , which was conducted from September 4 to 9, found that 80 per cent of Canadians say Canada should deepen strategic cooperation with the European Union on foreign policy, defence, and economic priorities — up six points since February.

The European Union itself is viewed positively by 71 per cent of Canadians, up five points since February, compared to 16 per cent who have a negative impression of it, which is unchanged from February.

Elsewhere, 81 per cent support closer integration with the EU, including making it easier to trade, travel, work and study and to cooperate on security, while 56 per cent say Canada has more in common with the countries of the EU than with the United States. Just 16 per cent say Canada has more in common with the United States.

The survey found that support for Canada deepening strategic cooperation with the EU is broad, and crosses provincial boundaries. It reaches 84 per cent in British Columbia, 79 per cent in Alberta, 74 per cent in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, 80 per cent in Ontario, 82 per cent in Quebec, and 73 per cent in Atlantic Canada.

The partisan difference is more marked, but a majority across party affiliations are in support. Among Liberal voters, 92 per cent support deeper cooperation with the EU, as do 92 per cent of NDP voters and 86 per cent of Bloc Québécois voters. Among Conservative voters, support is lower but still reaches 69 per cent.

The findings come ahead of Carney’s trip to Europe from September 15 to 17, where he is scheduled to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address, and meet with members of the European Parliament.

Canada seeking 'unique alliance' with EU, not membership: Carney

Ben Woodfinden: The EU is an economic disaster. What exactly is Mark Carney after?

On Sunday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Carney wishes to make Canada the first-ever “associate member” of the EU, which would allow Canada’s goods, services and workers in defence, energy, AI, and critical minerals to move freely in Europe.

However, the prime minister poured cold water on the claim later that day while on the red carpet of the Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff). The Globe and Mail reports that Carney said, “We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” but that Canada is starting talks with the EU about forming a “unique alliance.”

It comes as the federal government continues to frame closer ties with Europe as part of a broader effort to diversify Canada’s economic and security relationships and reduce its vulnerability to an increasingly unpredictable U.S. under president Donald Trump.

On that topic, the Abacus Data survey found that when Canadians are asked what concerns them more about the future of Canada’s relationships with both Europe and the U.S., 39 per cent point to Canada continuing to rely too heavily on the U.S. Just 16 per cent are concerned that closer ties with the EU could weaken Canada’s relationship with the U.S.

Meanwhile, only 21 per cent of Canadians now have a positive impression of the U.S., down three points since February, while 75 per cent have a negative impression, an increase of six points. It means the gap between positive impressions of the EU and positive impressions of the United States now stands at 50 points.

There is a much larger partisan divide, but even there, Europe is viewed positively by a majority of voters across party affiliations.

Among Liberal supporters, 85 per cent have a positive impression of the EU, as do 79 per cent of NDP supporters and 80 per cent of Bloc Québécois supporters. Among Conservative voters, 58 per cent have a positive impression.

By comparison, only 37 per cent of Conservative voters have a positive impression of the U.S. Among Liberal voters the number is 12 per cent, among NDP voters 11 per cent, and among Bloc voters just 3 per cent.

That said, Canadians are divided when asked about becoming a member of the EU. Nearly half of Canadians (49 per cent) say they would support Canada becoming a member state of the European Union, while another 30 per cent are opposed to the idea and 21 per cent are unsure. Support is up slightly from 48 per cent in February and from 46 per cent in 2025, while the share who are unsure has fallen from 25 per cent in 2025.

The majority of Liberal voters (64 per cent) support EU membership, as do 56 per cent of NDP voters and 57 per cent of Bloc Québécois voters, while only 33 per cent of Conservative voters support it and 51 per cent are opposed.

Nevertheless, Abacus Data says the survey results paint a clear picture: “Canadians are increasingly positive about Europe, overwhelmingly open to deeper cooperation, supportive of a much broader economic and security relationship, and more worried about continued dependence on the United States than they are about the consequences of moving closer to Europe.”

The survey authors add that the public increasingly appears to see Europe as part of the solution to how Canada can become more resilient, more economically independent, and less vulnerable to the decisions of any one country.

The Abacus Data survey was conducted with 1,479 Canadian adults from September 4 to 9, 2026. The margin of error for a comparable probability-based random sample of the same size is approximately plus or minus 2.5 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec party leaders are preparing for two debates this week in the provincial election campaign.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The first debate is scheduled on Tuesday evening and will feature all five party leaders.

Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette and Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon have both paused their public activities until the first debate.

The PQ is set to unveil the financial framework of its platform during the day on Tuesday.

stories.title: Man, 21, killed in animal attack on Manitoba First Nation
stories.summary: A man was killed in an animal attack in Western Manitoba last week, according to the Manitoba RCMP. The type of animal has not been identified.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A man has been found dead in Manitoba after being attacked by an animal, according to the RCMP.

The 21-year-old’s body was located on a community road in the Sapotaweyak Cree Nation last Wednesday, police said.

The RCMP said its major crime service investigated, and an autopsy determined his preliminary cause of death was an animal attack.

The office of the Sapotaweyak Cree Nation’s chief and council said it was aware of the fatal animal attack in a community-wide notice issued Thursday. The bulletin advised residents to avoid walking outside alone and to ensure their children are supervised while outdoors. Locals were also urged to be aware of their surroundings.

Manitoba’s Conservation Officer Service predator attack team is working alongside police to investigate the animal involved in man’s death, it said.

“While work is continuing to make a determination on what kind of animal May have been involved, the preliminary investigation has been able to rule out a bear attack,” the conservation service said in an email statement for Global News.

Sapotaweyak Cree Nation is located northeast of Swan River on the shores of Lake Winnipegosis.

stories.title: Porsche owners come together to raise money for Make-A-Wish Foundation
stories.summary: Dozens of Porsche’s lined up with a backdrop of aircraft at the London International Airport.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
It was a car show unlike many others.

Dozens of Porsche’s lined up with a backdrop of aircraft at the London International Airport.

“This is celebrating Sports Car Together Day for Porsche,” said Lakmina Ebbinghaus who is in charge of events for Porsche Club of America’s Upper Canada region.

“It’s a worldwide event celebrating both the brand and the car culture in every country that we represent around the planet”.

This event had race cars, sports cars and ones that have been in Germany, Italy and from across North America.

Londoner Jarod Arand brought five of his personal cars.

“You are looking at 2010, GT3 RS which is kind of a cool car,” said Arand a former employee at Porsche London who now owns his own business, Jcars Inc.

“There are not very many of them. So that’s a 1991 911 and a 1989 911. We’ve tried to have a few different generations to show off today.”

The event partnered with Flyxcite to use the airport hangar as well as the area next to the runway.

This event supported the Make-A-Wish Foundation and its work supporting children with serious illnesses and their families.

“It helps raise money so we can grant wishes for every child waiting for a wish,” said Demetria Drakos, a long-time volunteer with Make-A-Wish.

“It also helps raise awareness. It gets our name out to new people who might not be aware of us. There are lots of kids who love cars, and some of their wishes could be to sit in a porch or get a ride in a Porsche.”

The event had food trucks, airplanes taking off and cars representing every brand of Porsche in all 78 years.

“You’ve got air cooled, you’ve got water cooled, you’ve got GT3, you’ve got 911. every single flavour,” said Ebbinghaus.

“We’ve got cars representing every era of Porsche and also representing every value of Porsche. We’ve got a couple Porche’s here that are worth over $250,000.”

Arand has five different cars he’s collected over the years. He says this brand has entry-level cars at a price point of $20,000-$30,000 all the way up to multi-million-dollar cars.

“The other cool thing about most Porsches is they hold their value really, really well,” said Arand.

“You can buy this car, drive it for years, and you usually kind of get your money back out of it and the same can’t be said about a lot of other sports cars. You can own the car, enjoy the car, go to events like this and then it’s not maybe as expensive as I think a lot of people think that it might be”.

stories.title: Expert explainer: Why can’t we make a perfect map?
stories.summary: Western University GIS expert Liz Sutherland explains the Mercator map projection, Equal Earth maps and why no map is perfect.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Earlier this month, United Nations member states voted nearly unanimously to encourage the use of maps“that more accurately reflect the true size of continents” in response to an African-led campaign raising awareness of the flaws of the Mercator map projection, the most widely used map in the world.

Liz Sutherland, GIS research scientist at the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory,spoke with Western News to help untangle why the Mercator became the default, what the Equal Earth map does differently and why different maps are needed for different purposes.

Liz Sutherland (LS):The Mercator Projection was invented in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator, who invented this revolutionary (at the time) world map to make it easier for ships to navigate the seas. It preserves a constant compass direction, or rhumb line, but grossly exaggerates the sizes of countries near the poles (not your fault, Mercator! Every map needs to distort something).

An example of a Mercator projection map (Strebe/Wikimedia Commons)

LS:It happened gradually.As maps moved from ships and navigation charts into classrooms, atlases, textbooks, newspapers and eventually digital mapping, we became accustomed to seeing the world presented this way. And once something becomes familiar, it can be difficult to question it. Many people trusted, or never really questioned the Mercator Map so it became somewhat difficult to show its flaws. The Mercator map outlived the original problem it was trying to solve – seafaring – and became embedded in our society.

LS:Absolutely not! The Mercator projection is an incredibly useful projection for certain purposes, particularly navigation. The problem isn’t Mercator, the problem is using any projection without thinking about what you’re trying to represent. Unsure? Ask your local neighbourhood geographer! And if you want to learn more about maps and map projections, visit GIS Days on Nov.18 a free, ON campus open house exploring digital maps and mapping projects.

LS:In the world of cartography there are many categories of maps, each focuses on preserving a different quality such as area, distance, direction or shape. An equal-area projection is simply making a different choice than the Mercator (or conformal projections in general). Equal-area projections (maps like Equal Earth or the really cool Goode Homolosine or Mollweide) preserve relative size, or area, of features on Earth. But the decision to preserve area means the maps distort other properties – like distance or direction.

The Mercator Map Projection, which is part of a category of map projections called conformal projections, preserves local shape and direction, making them great for navigation,which is why we’ve used them so often historically.

Equal Earth map showing country boundaries (Wikimedia Commons)

LS:One of my favourite ways to demonstrate this is withThe True Size, which lets you move countries around the map and see how their apparent size changes with latitude.

The rule of thumb is that as you move towards the North or South poles,countries are going to distort more dramatically. Greenland is probably the most famous example,it looks comparable to Africa on a Mercator Projection,but in reality it can fit into Africa 14 times.Africa is the second largest continent in the world,though it doesn’t appear that way on a Mercator map.

The “Greenland effect” is prevalent elsewhere on the Mercator Map as well, Brazil is actually larger than the lower 48 states. Canada is also a great example. Because so much of our country extends into the high northern latitudes, the land area is substantially exaggerated.

LS:A map is the first place we’re introduced to the world and our place in it. It forms our own mental map, a perspective we carry with us into adulthood. When the same world map is shown to us over and over again, we naturally become familiar with its shapes, proportions and the relationships we see. We start to build our view of what the world “looks like” without seeing it.

That’s what makes map projections really interesting: a Mercator Map doesn’t intentionally tell us that countries near the equator are less important, but when we repeatedly see representations with certain places dramatically enlarged, it can influence our perception of the world around us.

LS:The mathematical problem of flattening the earth is one massive, complex puzzle.

The fundamental problem here is that you can’t flatten a sphere without distorting it. And the Earth actually isn’t a perfect sphere. It’s an irregular, constantly changing shape that we model as an ellipsoid for mapping purposes.

Think about trying to peel an orange and lay the peel completely flat: you’ll have to stretch, tear, cut or otherwise alter it in order to make it work. The same thing happens when we make a map of the Earth. You can’t preserve everything perfectly at the same time. But that’s why we have hundreds of map projections! They’re all different solutions, and different tools work for different projects.

LS:There are hundreds of different map projections, and they can look wildly different depending on what they’re designed to do.

Anyone can visit theWestern Libraries Map and Data Centre, including its Map Collectionto see some of these maps in real life. There are some really beautiful and creative projections,some designed for very specific purposes.

A world map from the Nuremberg Chronicle, an illustrated encyclopedia combining religion, myth, history and science published in 1493. (Schedel, Hartmann, 1440-1514, cartographer)

And this is just the conversation about global map projections. Once you start working at a regional or local scale, the question changes again. For example, the projection I would use to map all of Canada might not be the projection I would choose to map Southwestern Ontario, and neither would necessarily be the best choice for mapping a small neighbourhood.

That’s one of the things I love about GIS: there isn’t one map projection that does everything. The projection you choose should depend on your data, your geographic area and what you’re trying to communicate.

Mercator and Equal Earth are really just the beginning of the conversation.

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.

LS:The mathematical problem of flattening the earth is one massive, complex puzzle.

The fundamental problem here is that you can’t flatten a sphere without distorting it. And the Earth actually isn’t a perfect sphere. It’s an irregular, constantly changing shape that we model as an ellipsoid for mapping purposes.

Think about trying to peel an orange and lay the peel completely flat: you’ll have to stretch, tear, cut or otherwise alter it in order to make it work. The same thing happens when we make a map of the Earth. You can’t preserve everything perfectly at the same time. But that’s why we have hundreds of map projections! They’re all different solutions, and different tools work for different projects.
Are there other notable maps besides the Mercator and Equal Earth?
LS:There are hundreds of different map projections, and they can look wildly different depending on what they’re designed to do.

content_blocks.alt: A world map from the 1400s

content_blocks.text: Anyone can visit theWestern Libraries Map and Data Centre, including its Map Collectionto see some of these maps in real life. There are some really beautiful and creative projections,some designed for very specific purposes.
A world map from the Nuremberg Chronicle, an illustrated encyclopedia combining religion, myth, history and science published in 1493. (Schedel, Hartmann, 1440-1514, cartographer)

And this is just the conversation about global map projections. Once you start working at a regional or local scale, the question changes again. For example, the projection I would use to map all of Canada might not be the projection I would choose to map Southwestern Ontario, and neither would necessarily be the best choice for mapping a small neighbourhood.

That’s one of the things I love about GIS: there isn’t one map projection that does everything. The projection you choose should depend on your data, your geographic area and what you’re trying to communicate.
Mercator and Equal Earth are really just the beginning of the conversation.

stories.title: Politicians, CEOs pitch Canada’s fundamentals in bid to attract investment
stories.summary: Business leaders and politicians say an investment supercycle is taking hold in Canada, as investors flock to Toronto for large summits and conferences.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Business leaders and politicians say an investment supercycle is taking hold in Canada as investors from around the world flock to Toronto this week for a summit pitching the country as an attractive investment for foreign money.

Speaking at Global Dialogues Toronto, hosted by the Milken Institute think tank, TD chief executive Raymond Chun said he is seeing a more streamlined approval process for strategic projects and is encouraged by the progress thus far.

“The investment supercycle is beginning to take shape,” he said.

Chun’s comments come as TD Bank announced it’s committing $150 billion over five years to accelerate investment in the country. The other major banks have made similar announcements in recent days outlining their own lending plans for Canadian projects.

Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.CA

Chun highlighted specific industries including energy, critical minerals, infrastructure, as well as defence and aerospace, as potential investment targets.

“The early signs of this opportunity are extremely encouraging. We’re seeing streamlined approval processes, strategic projects moving from concept to execution faster, and policies encouraging progress and investment,” Chun said.

“The evidence is clear. Canada is beginning to move at the speed this moment requires.”

RBC president and CEO Dave McKay said during a panel discussion that foreign investors have underallocated funds in Canada for more than a decade due to a perception the country wasn’t getting projects to market fast enough.

However, he said circumstances are changing.

“Those are the old tapes. Investors now believe that there’s been a pivot and a change in philosophy,” McKay said, pointing to tax changes and the government’s major projects office.

McKay also said that as Canada pushes to diversify its economy beyond the United States, international players can capitalize on that.

Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne also spoke at the Global Dialogues conference, saying a few key factors position the country as a good target for investment.

One thing that sets Canada apart, he said, is its stability.

“I would say Canada inspires trust in the world today,” Champagne said.

“People (who) are making big bets are certainly looking for countries that can offer them stability, predictability, rule of law (and) trust over the long term.”

Selling the country as a trustworthy partner has been part of the federal government’s messaging ahead of the summit and a key component of their to pitch to the investment managers and corporate executives in town for the summit.

Amid a changing global trade order, he said investors are looking for places to allocate capital for the next 40 to 50 years, pitching Canada as a stable jurisdiction.

He said Canada has strong fundamentals, including an educated workforce, a robust manufacturing sector and proximity to resources.

Champagne said the energy industry will also be a significant driver for the country, both in the conventional and renewable power sectors.

Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA

“Those who house the energy, whether it’s conventional, renewable or nuclear, will certainly be having a head start in the economy in the 21st century.”

He also said that Canada is one of the “very few” countries that has all the critical minerals needed to support efforts for reindustrialization.

The federal government said in a news release Monday that investors putting $1 billion or more into the Canadian economy will now get priority access to a program that offers binding decisions from the Canada Revenue Agency.

Through the existing Advance Income Tax Rulings (Aitr) program, qualifying investors can get clarity on how income tax law will apply before they commit capital.

“This is one of the best practices that I’ve seen to provide additional certainty ... people who are going to invest in large projects among the billion, we’re going to provide them (with) an advanced tax relief to provide certainty,” Champagne said.

Daniel Johnson, The Canadian Press

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

stories.title: ‘One of the highest in the world’: StatCan applauds 2026 census response rate
stories.summary: The 2026 census saw record high response rates despite a “return to sender” social media trend.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen, Aarjavee Raaj
stories.content:
The 2026 census saw record high response rates despite a “return to sender” social media trend.

Statistics Canada reports the 2026 census having a general response rate of 98.4 per cent, surpassing the 98 per cent recorded in 2021 and matching the rate seen in 2016.

Meanwhile, the online and self-response rates broke records with 88.6 per cent and 91.2 per cent respectively.

“Our overall response rate for the Census of Population is one of the highest in the world for such an exercise, making the data it provides as accurate and reliable as can be,” chief statistician of Canada Andre Loranger said in a Monday press release.

“The information obtained from the census provides invaluable insights into the evolving characteristics of our country that are needed to make well-informed, fact-based decisions.”

The director general of the Census Program called the 2026 census a “success” in an interview with CTVNews.CA Monday.

“(The) majority of Canadians did it actually right away, as soon as they received their census invitation letter by mail, and we’re grateful for that,” Patrice Mathieu said. “So, we’re grateful to Canadians for that extraordinary participation.”

Is there a penalty for not completing it?

Mathieu confirmed that completing the census is required by law, and those who don’t fill out the census May get up to two reminder letters, phone calls, a visit by a StatCan employee and potential fines of up to $500 .

However, StatCan itself does not issue the fines, the director general clarified. The fines will be enforced by the Public Prosecution Service of Canada (Ppsc).

StatCan is currently compiling information on those who haven’t filled the 2026 census, and a small portion of them will be referred to the Ppsc in the next few weeks. However, Mathieu said not all are composed of refusals, as some May be away from their homes or otherwise unavailable during the window of collection.

“These referrals represent a very small number, (a) small fraction of the non-response that we have received. So, that reflects our approach, which is to prioritize communications with Canadians and making sure that they understand the value of the census,” he added.

“And the strong response rates demonstrate that a majority of Canadians believe in that.”

‘Return to sender’

The 2026 census was challenged by a social media trend where Canadians mailed their census form back with “return to sender” on it. Some burned or otherwise destroyed their form as an act of protest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was occasionally personally targeted in messages on the returned envelopes.

Mark Gerretsen, Liberal MP for Kingston and the Islands, took to social media in May to explain how the census helps Ottawa determine where to invest resources.

View this post on Instagram

“When people refuse the census, they’re not sticking it to Ottawa. They’re sticking it to their own community,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mathieu said such “criticisms” around the census aren’t new and have not impacted the information collection operation.

“We have seen them before,” he said, adding that it May have been more visible this time around due to social media.

“But it was still minority of cases … (a) minority of the population was expressing such negative comments about the census. For a majority of Canadians, the census is a positive thing.”

The federal Statistics Act mandates a census every five years. One in every four households receives what is known as the long-form census, while the rest get the short-form census.

The 2026 census results will be shared next year in seven separate releases covering a range of topics from population, gender, and income to citizenship, cultural and religious diversity, language, and homelessness.

With files from The Canadian Press and CTV News’ Heather Wright

stories.title: Ontario minister pledges better communication during wildfire season
stories.summary: Ontario's natural resources minister has pledged better communication on wildfires going forward.
stories.author: Liam Casey The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s Natural Resources Minister Mike Harris pledged Monday better communication on wildfires after many First Nations communities said they received little to no warning about approaching flames this summer.

Updated at 2:40 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

CHY/[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Ontario/Ontario-minister-pledges-better-communication-during-wildfire-season/article_e84faedb-272e-584c-ada0-1ddf0b4c0075.html)

By Liam Casey The Canadian Press

The government has been roundly criticized for its approach to the devastating wildfire season in northwestern Ontario. First Nations said warnings from the province to evacuate due to fast-moving fires either came too late or not at all.

Residents of Namaygoosisagagun, also known as Collins First Nation, fled on boats before a massive blaze destroyed the community in July. Whitewater Lake First Nation was also ravaged by fire.

Article continues below

Residents of more than a dozen northern communities were forced to leave their homes as about 200 fires raged in July.

Wildfire smoke drifted across much of southern Ontario and into the United States, leaving Toronto, New York City and parts in between in a smoky haze that glowed orange.

“One of the things just looking back that we can already learn is we’ve got to do a little bit better job on communication,” Harris said in Sault Ste. Marie, where he announced a $20-million investment to upgrade two major wildfire attack bases in northwestern Ontario.

First Nations leaders have also called for a public inquiry into the province’s response to the wildfires, a request that Harris has not committed to fulfilling.

The ministry reviews the wildfire season every year and earlier in the summer, Harris said he May not release those reports. He changed that tune on Monday.

“We’ll be able to do that deep dive to look at some of the challenges that we did face,” he said.

“And then when we get a bit of a formal plan together, then we’ll be looking to, of course, share that with communities that were affected to make sure that we are able to, in the coming seasons, have better relationships and make sure we’re getting information out to them as quickly ... as possible.”

The upgrades to the two bases will mean quicker firefighting deployments, Harris said. The province is looking to upgrade other wildfire bases as well, he added.

The province said there have been 786 wildfires in 2026 that burned nearly 750,000 hectares of land.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.summary: ST. John's - A four-day debate about a draft energy agreement with Quebec began with a member of Newfoundland and Labrador’s Progressive Conservative party crossing the floor.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - There was turmoil in and outside the Newfoundland and Labrador legislature Monday as a four-day debate about a tentative deal to share Labrador energy with Hydro-Québec got underway.

Updated at 4:50 p.m.

GAC[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/quebec/newfoundland-and-labrador-tory-leaves-party-as-debate-about-quebec-energy-deal-begins/article_ee73eecd-42c6-5cc7-9ece-2dc2bafe85f4.html)

By Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press

Government member Keith Russell rose to tell his colleagues he was leaving the governing Progressive Conservatives to represent his Labrador district as an Independent. He did not explain why he was walking away from the party and he refused to speak to reporters after his announcement.

“This is not a decision I make lightly, but there are moments in public life when we must listen to our conscience and put the people we represent first,” he told the legislature.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Russell’s departure was a surprise to Premier Tony Wakeham.

“Mr. Russell was in our caucus this morning,” Wakeham told reporters. “But Mr. Russell has made his choice.”

The Tories now hold half of the legislature’s 40 seats, though they retain a working majority.

Outside the Confederation Building, more than 100 people opposed to the proposed energy agreement sang the “Ode to Newfoundland” — the province’s official anthem — and applauded Russell’s move.

“This deal is absolutely not in Newfoundland and Labrador’s best interest,” said William Wells, who was CEO of Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro from 1996 until 2004.

Wells said the 50-year framework agreement gives Hydro-Québec the lion’s share of the power from the Churchill River in Labrador, with little in return for Newfoundland and Labrador.

“No deal is better than this deal,” Wells said.

The province’s former Liberal government first unveiled a draft deal in 2024, but Wakeham sent negotiators back to work after he was sworn in as premier last year. He unveiled the latest iteration of the agreement last month, alongside Prime Minister Mark Carney, who touted it as the “largest clean energy investment in North American history.”

The framework agreement outlines plans for Hydro-Québec and Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro to divvy up power from the Churchill Falls generating station and launch new hydro, wind and transmission projects worth more than $50 billion, officials said.

The two provinces’ electric utilities co-own and operate the 5,428-megawatt Churchill Falls hydroelectric plant through a 1969 contract described by critics in Newfoundland and Labrador as lopsided in favour of Hydro-Québec.

The Tories opened the legislature on Monday for four days of debate, after walking back their promise to subject any final agreements to a referendum. Outside, at least one protester held up a sign saying, “Tony lied,” denouncing the broken referendum promise.

Des Sullivan said the proposed agreement was a “travesty” because it gives Quebec decades of energy at rates below market value, just as the 1969 contract did. Sullivan is well known in the province for his energy blog, called Uncle Gnarly.

“I don’t think that’s well understood by Newfoundland and Labrador people.” Sullivan said.

Kaitlyn Duff said the memorandum of understanding surrenders too much control over the Churchill River to Hydro-Québec.

“Fifty years is too long,” she said. “We’re acting out of desperation because Newfoundland is in a deficit. We should be acting for our future, not in desperation.”

Inside the legislature, Lloyd Parrott, the province’s energy minister, took a swipe at some critics of the draft deal, particularly those online. “The price tag for your self-righteousness means that everybody else stays poor,” Parrott said.

Wakeham told reporters he was confident his party stood behind the tentative deal, despite Russell’s sudden exit. Russell was a member of the government’s Team Labrador group, which Wakeham assembled last month to advocate for Labrador’s interests in the Churchill River deal. The premier said the team would proceed as planned.

The Tories continue to control the legislature because the Speaker — who only votes in the case of a tie — is an Independent, and that means the Progressive Conservatives still have 20 regularly voting members.

Meanwhile, lead negotiator Barry Parry addressed calls from some critics to wait until the 1969 contract ends in 2041 before negotiating with Hydro-Québec.

He said Hydro-Québec would have to agree to pay 18 cents per kilowatt hour for Churchill Falls power in 2041 in order to compensate for money left on the table if Newfoundland and Labrador walked away from the current draft deal.

“With no deal, there is no money coming to Newfoundland and Labrador in the next 15 years,” he said.

Under the current contract, Hydro-Québec gets the lion’s share of the power from the Churchill Falls plant, at the basement-bottom rate of 0.2 cents per kilowatt hour. About 15 per cent of Québec’s electricity comes from Churchill Falls.

The new agreement proposes higher rates from Churchill Falls and a new, 2,700-megawatt generating station at Gull Island on the Churchill River. It also includes plans for feasibility studies for a second powerhouse at Churchill Falls and a 2,000-megawatt wind farm in the Churchill River area.

The arrangement would earmark about 2,750 megawatts of power for Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro and 8,515 megawatts for Hydro-Québec, though the figures could increase if the partners proceed with the expansion of the Churchill Falls plant.

Officials have said the expected return for Newfoundland and Labrador over the 50-year agreement is an estimated $49 billion.

The federal government would kick in about $10 billion in financing for several proposed projects including transmission lines and the Gull Island development, according to a news release last month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sport notes: Huge Western Mustangs comeback; London Nationals start slow
stories.summary: The Western football team scored 31 second-half points to beat the Windsor Lancers 44-37 this past weekend in Windsor.
stories.author: Ryan Pyette
stories.content:
The Western football team scored 31 second-half points to beat the Windsor Lancers 44-37 this past weekend in Windsor.

Mustangs quarterback Jerome Rancourt went 18-for-32 for 312 yards and three touchdown passes in the come-from-behind victory. Running back Jack Kelly rushed for 151 yards and a touchdown on six carries and Jackson Taylor added eight catches for 140 yards and a major.

New kicker Mateo Pasquini continued his perfect start with three field goals, including a 44-yarder, and was 5-for-5 on converts.

Western (2-0) takes on the Toronto Varsity Blues (0-2) on the road Saturday. Kickoff is 1 p.m.

Podium Finish: D.J. Kennington finished the Nascar Canada Series season with a third-place result in the NTN BCA 200, presented by APC, at Delaware Speedway this past weekend.

Donald Theetge drove the No. 80 Vulcain/Max Leclerc Construction Chevy for the win and Quebec native Marc-Antoine Camirand was crowned the series points champion for a historic third consecutive year.

Camirand’s fourth title in five seasons tied the series’ all-time record. L-P Dumoulin was second place in points while Kevin Lacroix was third. Connor Bell, who drives for Jason Hathaway’s Ed Hakonson Racing team, earned Jostens rookie of the year honours.

Nats Drop TWO: The London Nationals are 0-2 out of the gate in Greater Ontario Hockey League play after weekend losses to Chatham and Elmira this past weekend.

Sheldon Alexander, a 20-year-old from California, scored London’s only goal in a 4-1 defeat to the Chatham Maroons in the Nationals’ home opener at Western Fair on Saturday. London defenceman Henry Austin provided both Nats goals in a 6-2 defeat to Elmira Sunday at Dan Snyder Arena in Woolwich.

Former Knights prospect Brendan Gerber recorded a hat trick for the Sugar Kings. London’s lone game this week is Saturday (7:15 p.m.) on the road against the winless Komoka Kings.

Nash CUP: The 18th Nash Cup tournament features 31 of the world’s top 100 male and female professional squash players at London Squash & Fitness (76 Albert St.) this week through Saturday.

The event features four returning champions – two-time winner Auguste Dussourd, Zeina Zein, David Baillargeon and Hollie Naughton – and the field has representation from 22 countries, including first-timers from Croatia and Slovenia.

The Jack Fairs Open PSA challenger will run for a third straight year and feature 16 of Canada’s rising stars and five members of Western University’s current and past men’s squash dynasty.

The full event schedule can be found at www.nashcup.com rpyette@postmedia.com

stories.title: Canada seeking 'unique alliance' with EU, not membership: Carney
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is not seeking to become a member of the European Union, as a Wall Street Journal report alleged.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
After a Wall Street Journal exclusive created a small firestorm of controversy on Sunday when it revealed Mark Carney has reportedly been racing towards making Canada an “associate member” of the European Union, the prime minister poured cold water on the idea later that day.

“Look, we’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” he said on the red carpet of the Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff) Sunday night, per The Globe and Mail.

Rather, he said, Canada is starting talks with the EU about forming a “unique alliance.”

“We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths,” he continued.

“We’re stronger together and this is at a time when the world’s more dangerous and divided and friends need to stick together at these times.”

The Journal article, citing unnamed officials on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, claimed Carney has been eyeing the EU and its “$21 trillion single market” since securing government in 2025.

The EU doesn’t technically have any “associate members,” but the concept reportedly being pitched, per the Journal, would allow Canada’s goods, services and workers in defence, energy, AI and critical minerals to move freely throughout the 27 EU states.

They’ve also reportedly had discussions about trans-Atlantic sub-sea communications and energy corridors, new satellite networks that don’t involve U.S. tech giants, and potentially shipping Canadian fertilizer through a ice-breaker-cleared Northwest Passage.

The Journal also reported that Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron have discussed the possibility of Canadians living and working in EU member nations without requiring a visa, and that Carney wants access to an EU study-abroad program.

Sources indicate the concept is still in its bureaucratic infancy, but Carney has been clear with his officials that the result “will be the reorienting of an economy and a society that for half a century has been dominated by the U.S.”

Leader Pierre Poilievre added his voice to the chorus of Conservative voices who decried Carney’s reported moves and said Canadians deserve to know if their government is actually pursuing “associate membership.”

“If so, will European border policies apply in Canada, further overwhelming our immigration system while our youth can’t find homes? Will Canadian waitresses struggling with rent have to pay tax dollars to the bloated EU bureaucracy? Will Canadian small businesses be buried under the red tape of Eurocrats that have never met a Canadian entrepreneur,” he asked, noting he would ask these questions were it not for a shuttered Parliament.

“And one more: who decides for Canada?”

Carney wants Canada to be an ‘associate member’ of the EU: report

Ben Woodfinden: The EU is an economic disaster. What exactly is Mark Carney after?

Poilievre said the existing Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement already allows for free trade and more would happen were it not for the Liberals.

Like some of his MPs, Poilievre said just as Canada won’t acquiesce to U.S. President Donald Trump’s desire to make it the 51st state, nor will it become the “28th EU state.”

paragraphs: After a Wall Street Journal exclusive created a small firestorm of controversy on Sunday when it revealed Mark Carney has reportedly been racing towards making Canada an “associate member” of the European Union, the prime minister poured cold water on the idea later that day.
“Look, we’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” he said on the red carpet of the Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff) Sunday night, per The Globe and Mail.
Rather, he said, Canada is starting talks with the EU about forming a “unique alliance.”
“We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths,” he continued.
“We’re stronger together and this is at a time when the world’s more dangerous and divided and friends need to stick together at these times.”
The Journal article, citing unnamed officials on both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, claimed Carney has been eyeing the EU and its “$21 trillion single market” since securing government in 2025.

The EU doesn’t technically have any “associate members,” but the concept reportedly being pitched, per the Journal, would allow Canada’s goods, services and workers in defence, energy, AI and critical minerals to move freely throughout the 27 EU states.

They’ve also reportedly had discussions about trans-Atlantic sub-sea communications and energy corridors, new satellite networks that don’t involve U.S. tech giants, and potentially shipping Canadian fertilizer through a ice-breaker-cleared Northwest Passage.

The Journal also reported that Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron have discussed the possibility of Canadians living and working in EU member nations without requiring a visa, and that Carney wants access to an EU study-abroad program.

Sources indicate the concept is still in its bureaucratic infancy, but Carney has been clear with his officials that the result “will be the reorienting of an economy and a society that for half a century has been dominated by the U.S.”

Leader Pierre Poilievre added his voice to the chorus of Conservative voices who decried Carney’s reported moves and said Canadians deserve to know if their government is actually pursuing “associate membership.”

“If so, will European border policies apply in Canada, further overwhelming our immigration system while our youth can’t find homes? Will Canadian waitresses struggling with rent have to pay tax dollars to the bloated EU bureaucracy? Will Canadian small businesses be buried under the red tape of Eurocrats that have never met a Canadian entrepreneur,” he asked, noting he would ask these questions were it not for a shuttered Parliament.
“And one more: who decides for Canada?”

stories.title: Ottawa says it ended refugee residency sponsor exemption over ‘integrity concerns’
stories.summary: Ottawa — The immigration department says it ended a permanent residency sponsorship exemption for some refugees over unnamed "potential integrity concerns."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — A permanent residency sponsorship exemption for some refugees was allowed to expire earlier this month due to unspecified “potential integrity concerns,” an Immigration Department spokesperson said in an email.

Three years ago, a memo drafted for the immigration minister said the exemption policy posed a “minimal risk” to program integrity.

The Canadian Press has asked the government what has changed since then, and whether applicants were misusing the exemption, but has not yet received a response.

The temporary policy, which was introduced in 2019 and ended on Sept. 10, allowed certain refugees to sponsor family members who were not initially declared on their own applications.

Those family members could include children who were not born when the initial application was made. Advocates said the policy also was used by Lgbtq+ refugees to sponsor partners in countries where those relationships are criminalized.

The now-expired policy was last extended in September 2023, after the memo to the minister was drafted. That memo also said there had been about 2,000 applications under the policy and about 90 per cent had been approved.

All permanent resident applicants are required to give the government a list of family members for security and medical screening purposes — even if those family members aren’t coming to Canada. Permanent residents are barred from sponsoring family members who were not initially listed.

In an email sent by an Immigration Department spokesperson Friday — after The Canadian Press first reported on the policy change — the government said exemptions can still be granted on humanitarian or compassionate grounds.

The current wait time for humanitarian and compassionate applications is estimated at more than 10 years on the government’s online portal.

Jamie Liew is a University of Ottawa law professor who co-authored a 2017 study that contributed to the creation of the now cancelled exemption policy. She called the government’s stated reasoning “extremely vague.”

“There are two things that concern me about this. First, is there evidence or data that shows that there is a misuse of this program? And secondly, (humanitarian and compassionate applications) are basically non-functional,” Liew said.

“Our research is very clear, even before the increase in the wait times, but now it is virtually impossible to bring people through a (humanitarian and compassionate) application.”

Refugee advocates were informed of the policy’s end on Sept. 9 but were given no explanation.

The Canadian Council for Refugees sent a letter to Immigration Minister Lena Diab last week asking her to restore the policy.

Gauri Sreenivasan, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees, said in an emailed response that the organization worked with the Immigration Department for years to bring in the expired policy. She said the exemption addressed “a clear and present danger for refugee children and families.”

“If there were any issues to resolve with the temporary policy, we are and would have been ready to engage on those for longer-term solutions,” she said.

“As it stands, the decision to rescind the policy suddenly and go back to relying on (the humanitarian and compassionate claim process) to resolve issues, given its known inaccessibility, is a poor and cruel choice that we know will hurt many families. There is a better way forward and it starts with consultation.”

The government spokesperson said the department will continue to monitor the effect of the change and encouraged all permanent resident applicants “to declare their family members, which is the best way to prevent lengthy or permanent family separation.”

Liew said an applicant might not list family members for a number of legitimate reasons. In some cases, she said, applicants from strife-torn regions May not be aware that their children are still alive when they make their application. They also May lack literacy skills or be forced to rely on a translator, she added.

Liew warned the increasing embrace of digital automation in Immigration Department systems will lead to more refugee families being kept apart.

“The form is meant to be a gateway for inquiry and assessment. And then to punish people for that seems really, really unreasonable and harsh,” Liew said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Why now? Canada’s new sanctions on West Bank settlers
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the Canada-Israel relationship and whether or not Israel could announce counter sanctions on Canada.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Canada recently joined the UK and France in sanctioning all settler trade with the West Bank.

In a joint-statement written by the three prime ministers, Israel’s advancement of the E1 settlement, as well as the ongoing violence in the occupied strip, jeopardizes the possibility of a two-state solution.

Host Maria Kestane speaks to Jon Allen, the former Canadian ambassador to Israel and a senior fellow at the Bill Graham Centre for Contemporary International History at the University of Toronto. They discuss whether or not Israel could announce counter sanctions on Canada like they did with the UK, and how the Canada-Israel relationship has hit an all-time low.

stories.title: Two pulled from water near B.C. Lower Mainland after fishing vessel sinks
stories.summary: British Columbia's ferry operator says two people were pulled from the waters between the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island after their fishing vessel sank.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
British Columbia’s ferry operator says two people were pulled from the waters between the Lower Mainland and Vancouver Island after their fishing vessel sank.

BC Ferries spokesperson Sheila Reynolds says the marine rescue happened Sunday afternoon following reports of people in the water.

Reynolds says two ferry boats — the Spirit of British Columbia and Coastal Renaissance — launched separate rescue craft and the two boaters were brought to the Tsawwassen terminal on the mainland.

The ferry service did not have details on the condition of those rescued.

The rescue operation delayed sailings, and Reynolds says delays were to be expected on other sailings late Sunday.

She adds that the ferry operator appreciates customers’ understanding for any resulting delay.

stories.title: Indigenous legislation among top issues at Union of B.C. Municipalities convention
stories.summary: An annual gathering of municipal leaders from across British Columbia opens in Vancouver Monday with the province's Indigenous rights legislation high on the agenda.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
An annual gathering of municipal leaders from across British Columbia opens in Vancouver Monday with the province’s Indigenous rights legislation high on the agenda, along with housing and public safety, among other topics.

The Union of B.C. Municipalities convention runs until Friday and president Cori Ramsay says the future of B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act will be top of mind for many of the nearly 2,000 expected delegates.

Ramsay says local governments are highly committed to reconciliation and have been working for years to build relationships with First Nations.

But the city councillor from Prince George, B.C., says uncertainty has stemmed from recent court rulings, including a successful challenge by First Nations to B.C.’s mineral tenure system

The B.C. Court of Appeal ruled in that case that B.C.’s Indigenous rights legislation, known as Dripa, should be interpreted to incorporate the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples into provincial laws with immediate effect.

Premier David Eby backed down on a plan to suspend or amend Dripa in April amid strong opposition from many Indigenous leaders, while members of the provincial Conservatives have called for the law to be scrapped altogether.

Ramsay says delegates will also ask Eby’s government to reverse clawbacks in funding for community housing, deal with unprecedented mental health and addiction issues in communities across B.C., and renew funding for the FireSmart program aimed at boosting resilience to worsening wildfires.

Both Eby and B.C. Conservative Party Leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay and scheduled to attend the conference later this week.

stories.title: Inflation stayed at 3% in August as travel costs soared, says StatCan
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says the annual rate of inflation was unchanged at three per cent in August as a slowdown in rising gas prices was offset by higher rent and travel tour costs.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
Consumer inflation held steady at three per cent last month compared to a year earlier as higher rent and travel costs offset a slowdown in rising prices for gas and groceries.

Statistics Canada says the annual rate of inflation, as measured by the consumer price index (CPI) , was unchanged from July .

The agency says gasoline costs continued to increase in August but at a slower pace, with prices up 22.8 per cent compared with 25.7 per cent a month earlier, as the conflict in the Middle East continued to weigh on prices.

Excluding gasoline, consumer prices rose 2.4 per cent last month compared to a year earlier, up from 2.2 per cent in July.

Some economists note the recent oil and gas price spikes appear to be contained, at least for now.

“Headline inflation remained elevated in August, but core measures continued to show only limited evidence that high energy prices are spilling over into wider inflationary pressure,” said Cibc economist Andrew Grantham in a statement.

“With the economic outlook clouded by U.S. tariffs and related uncertainty we think that the Bank [of Canada] should, and will, keep interest rates on hold at the October meeting, particularly with core measures of inflation not exactly flashing warning signs.”

Abbey Xu, economist at the Royal Bank of Canada, also said, “There continued to be limited evidence that elevated energy costs were generating significant second-round inflation. Price growth remained high for energy-intensive categories such as air travel but had not spread materially across the broader consumer basket.”

Xu added: “The risk of greater pass-through will rise the longer oil prices remain elevated.”

Travel and tour costs surged 26.1 per cent in August from a year earlier, up from a 15.2 per cent increase in July, and Statistics Canada says rising fuel surcharges amid higher prices for jet fuel was one of the main reasons for this.

One of the other reasons for this sharp increase in travel and tour costs was what the agency says was a “base-year effect” when comparing to a year earlier. That’s because prices for flights and tours were significantly higher last month than they were 12 months before, when there was a notable decline in Canadian travel to the United States .

Housing costs were another hot spot for inflation last month, with rent prices increasing 2.8 per cent year-over-year in August, up from 2.5 per cent in July.

Grocery prices continued to rise by 2.8 per cent last month compared to a year earlier, down from 3.1 per cent in July.

August also marked the first time since July 2024 that retail food costs increased at a slower pace than the overall inflation reading, and Statistics Canada says grocery price growth increased at a slower pace than all the other categories in the August CPI report.

Dairy products like cheese and yogurt saw price growth decelerate the most in the grocery basket, rising 0.7 per cent year-over-year in August compared with a 3.1 per cent increase in July.

The agency also notes that although overall food price growth cooled off in August, food prices have increased 29 per cent since August 2021.

– with files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Networking group supports women through the AI shift
stories.summary: Monday Girl emerged after co-founders had grown frustrated with panels and conferences where they never saw themselves reflected as young professional women
stories.author: Nickie Shobeiry
stories.content:
As artificial intelligence (AI) proliferates in workplaces, there are different perceptions related to use of the tools. Toronto-based women’s networking group Monday Girl published research earlier this year that found only 36 per cent of women felt confident using AI compared with 52 per cent of men. Women were also more likely than men to worry about AI’s negative consequences.

“A lot of women feel like they’re cheating when it comes to using AI,” says Rachel Wong, co-founder of Monday Girl. The findings prompted Monday Girl to create AI-focused panels and workshops for its members. “Education is empowerment. Knowing how these tools work is so key.”

What might be a confidence gap today could turn into a career gap in the future, says Katrina Lawrence, a senior trainer and AI practice lead at Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst, Toronto Metropolitan University’s centre for technology security. “AI literacy is becoming more of a workplace skill rather than just like a bonus.”

Ms. Lawrence says when companies are looking to set up frameworks before adopting AI internally, they don’t need an unwieldy rulebook. “Start with four or five questions that everyone can use.”

Among them: What data is going into the tool? Is any of it sensitive? Is the output intended simply for brainstorming or will it ultimately reach a client? Crucially, who remains accountable for the result?

“If you are using the AI tool, then you are responsible for its output,” Ms. Lawrence says.

Buying licenses isn’t enough, she adds. She recommends company-wide training, opportunities to experiment, and practical instruction tied to actual jobs.

At Monday Girl, Ms. Wong is happy to let AI crunch the company’s numbers, pull dashboards and take meeting notes. That tech support has helped her five-person team expand the organization into the United States, where nearly 40 per cent of its 5,000-person membership is now based.

“Anytime we can use AI to automate the boring, not-so-glamorous things, that’s where we see it having a huge advantage for us,” Ms. Wong says.

Monday Girl emerged after Ms. Wong and her co-founder, Istiana Bestari, had grown frustrated with panels and conferences where they never saw themselves reflected as young professional women. In 2017, they founded Monday Girl as a Facebook group. The membership-based organization now includes mentorship, weekly newsletters, events and summits in Toronto, New York and San Francisco.

While they use AI for other purposes, they draw a hard line against it when it comes to brand voice. “We hate AI slop,” Ms. Wong says. They May use generative AI to mock up graphics, but Monday Girl’s graphic designer creates the final product.

Ms. Lawrence says AI should be for repetitive, transactional work – as Monday Girl’s team is using it – while protecting the parts of the job that rely on trust, creativity and judgement. “At our core, we’re all still human. We all still want to see each other and have those like real relationships, and not just virtual ones,” she says.

At one of their events, Monday Girl “vibe coded” a tool (building an app or website through word prompts rather than writing code) that allowed attendees to create profiles with their experience and interests. From there, users could find a mentor to meet on-site. Those with AI expertise were among the fastest to book up.

“A lot of people come to our platform with the hopes of self-improvement,” Ms. Wong says. “AI is not going to go away. How can they make sure that they themselves are prepared?”

stories.title: This person-centred approach to dementia could revolutionize long-term care in Canada
stories.summary: Dementia villages are part of a growing movement toward less institutionalized, more person-centred long-term care
stories.author: Sydney Loney
stories.content:
Josephine Loukes could no longer live on her own. The 86-year-old’s dementia affected every aspect of her health: She was incontinent. She’d begun wandering at night. She had fallen more than once. During the day, she became increasingly disoriented and, by evening, she was agitated and aggressive.

Three years ago, her daughter Merry Reynolds had moved from Alberta into Loukes’s two-bedroom home in a seniors’ complex in Courtenay, B.C. to care for her. “I was losing sleep,” she says, adding that after a few years she was burnt out. “I’d be up at 3 a.m. cleaning up after my mom and I was trying to juggle work with caregiving. It was 24/7.”

Loukes had been on a waitlist for long-term care for a year-and-a-half when, in April 2026, she landed a spot with Providence Living at The Views in Comox, B.C. “We literally won the lottery,” Reynolds says.

In this case, “winning the lottery” meant gaining access to a dementia village – a residential care community that looks, feels and functions like a regular neighbourhood. Modeled after dementia villages in the Netherlands, there are no locked doors, dead-end hallways or desolate common areas where reruns of I Love Lucy play perpetually on repeat.

Instead, residents at The Views live in 12-person homes and roam freely around the village, which includes a bistro, art studio, salon, cafe, chapel, grocery store, multiple gardens and an Indigenous gathering space. Staff wear street clothes instead of scrubs and dinner is prepared communally in shared kitchens, not served up on hospital trays.

The Views, which opened in 2024, is Canada’s first public, non-profit long-term care village. (The Village Langley, the country’s first private dementia village , opened in 2019 in Langley, B.C.) Providence Living is planning three additional villages in British Columbia, the first of which will open in Prince George in 2028.

Dementia villages are part of a growing movement toward less institutionalized, more person-centred long-term care, says Jennifer Gibson, Providence Living’s interim president and chief executive officer. She describes The View’s approach as social-relational, where the focus is on building a community around what people can still do, instead of what they’ve lost. “It’s a significant difference from an institutional model and it’s an investment that takes courage and persistence.”

A former critical care nurse, Gibson is quick to acknowledge the dedication of everyone working in long-term care, traditional or otherwise. “When I look at the potential of a social-relational model, it’s about building on the efforts that people are already making,” she says. “But I think we’re at a time now when we realize that it’s possible to do this better.”

It’s also necessary, she adds, given the numbers. Every day, more than 414 people in Canada develop dementia. By 2030, nearly 1 million Canadians will be living with Alzheimer’s and other forms of dementia.

Amid this rising need, less institutional approaches to dementia care are gaining traction across the country. The Manitoba government is backing the construction of several household-model long-term care homes, including a residence in Lac du Bonnet designed with seven self-sufficient, 12-person households that will open in 2027. In 2021, Milton, Ont. became home to Canada’s first Green Care Farm (GCF), offering outdoor programming on a working farm, as well as a sensory garden, for people living with dementia.

Sharon Kaasalainen, a professor at McMaster University’s School of Nursing in Hamilton, Ont. and co-lead of the Strengthening a Palliative Approach in Long-Term Care program in Canada, is one of many researchers fighting to bring GCFs to the country’s long-term care landscape.

Although the one in Milton is a day program, in the Netherlands many GCFs are incorporated into long-term residential care, often in conjunction with dementia villages. Studies show residents in GCFs are more physically and socially active and spend more time outdoors than people living in traditional nursing homes. Kaasalainen has witnessed the positive outcomes of GCFs in the Netherlands firsthand and is frustrated by the obstacles – largely funding- and regulatory-related – that are preventing them from becoming commonplace in Canada.

“We’re so afraid that residents are going to fall, but we do more harm thinking that way,” she says. “When we strap people in wheelchairs or lock them indoors, they stop moving. They become deconditioned and end up in pain. So we’re really working to partner with governments to provide some latitude for us to try these new innovations.

“To make long-term care truly person-centred, we need to work together to change the culture.”

Toronto-based Baycrest, recognized globally for its studies on aging and brain health, built its person-centred memory-care model, Possibilities by Baycrest, around customized experiences for its residents, based on input from its clinicians and research by its scientists.

“The losses associated with dementia are real and we can’t pretend that they’re not, but we also know that life doesn’t stop,” say Melissa Turzanski, executive director of residential living at Baycrest’s Jewish Home for the Aged. Turzanski is a co-developer of Possibilities by Baycrest, which now informs the care approach at the Terraces Memory Residence in Toronto.

The goal is to offer autonomy and independence around both routine care tasks and daily programming, Turzanski says. Smart sheets on beds and smart toilets in bathrooms feed key health information to clinical staff, alerting them to potential issues while respecting residents’ dignity. Standardized activities are replaced with personalized plans based on a resident’s history, interests, preferences and abilities. “Everybody has a different plan each day that is meaningful to them personally,” Turzanski says.

Loukes had been on a waitlist for long-term care for a year-and-a-half when, in April 2026, she landed a spot with Providence Living at The Views in Comox, B.C. “We literally won the lottery,” Reynolds says.

In this case, “winning the lottery” meant gaining access to a dementia village – a residential care community that looks, feels and functions like a regular neighbourhood. Modeled after dementia villages in the Netherlands, there are no locked doors, dead-end hallways or desolate common areas where reruns of I Love Lucy play perpetually on repeat.

stories.title: Watchdog called in to probe fatal shooting of man by Edmonton officers
stories.summary: Alberta's police watchdog has been called in to investigate the officer-involved fatal shooting of a man in west Edmonton.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Alberta’s police watchdog has been called in to investigate the fatal shooting of a man by police in west Edmonton this past weekend.

The Edmonton Police Service responded Sunday around 10 a.m. to a home near Donsdale Drive and 45 Avenue after it was reported that a man had entered a home, where a woman and infant were then shot.

Officers arrived to the Donsdale neighbourhood in the Lessard Road areas to find witnesses and the injured waiting for them.

Police set up containment around the home.

“During this time, the adult male suspect opened the front door with a firearm in his possession. Officers issued verbal direction to the man; however, he did not comply. Three officers then discharged their firearms,” a news release issued Sunday evening said.

The 36-year-old man was arrested but died at the scene. Police said two women and an infant were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

On Monday, police shared more information: one woman was shot, the other didn’t report physical injuries and the infant suffered other physical injuries.

They add the event is believed to be a case of domestic violence.

Police say no officers were injured, and the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team, or Asirt, has been notified.

The agency investigates matters involving police that result in serious injury or death to determine whether there was officer misconduct.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: How Google, Meta are implementing its ‘age assurance’ tech in Canada
stories.summary: The federal government has introduced digital safety legislation that would introduce a ban on social media for kids under 16.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
The federal government has introduced digital safety legislation that would introduce a ban on social media for kids under 16. Big tech companies are already using age assurance technology to estimate users’ age.

So what is “age assurance”?

Age assurance is the umbrella term used for efforts by tech platforms to determine the age of a user. It includes age declarations — those “click to verify you’re 18” boxes that internet users have been encountering for a long time.

But more recently, tech companies have been incorporating “age estimation.” That includes the use of AI technology to estimate a user’s age based on factors like their online behaviour or the images they post. “Age verification” is any method that requires a user to prove their age — the use of government ID, for example.

Google said last year it would begin rolling out age assurance in the U.S. On Monday, it announced it would expand the technology to Canada.

Google’s approach looks at factors like a user’s search queries and the types of videos they’ve looked at on YouTube. The company says it won’t collect any additional information for age assurance.

Users who are identified as underage by Google have additional protections placed on their accounts. They include measures like turning on tools that remind users to take a break, placing safeguards on content recommendations, disabling personalized advertising and restricting access to apps that are adults-only.

If the tech mistakenly identifies an adult as being under 18, they’ll be able to prove their age using such tools as a government ID, a selfie, or a credit card check.

Google says that for those users who use a government ID, it will store the date of birth in their account and delete the ID after a short period of time. It says it will use the service PrivateID to analyze selfies, which will tell Google whether it believes the user is of age. Google says PrivateID doesn’t provide it with the selfie or the precise age of the user, or retain the image.

If Meta suspects the person behind an account is under 18, it places them in a teen account. The settings on teen accounts include additional protections limiting who can contact the user and the content they can view. It uses AI to remove individuals it believes are under 13 from its services entirely.

Meta said in a blog post it uses AI to “analyze entire profiles for contextual clues — such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades — to determine if an account likely belongs to someone underage.”

That work includes looking at posts, comments, bios and captions. “If we determine an account May be underage, it will be deactivated and the account holder will need to provide proof of age through our age verification process to prevent their account from being deleted,” Meta said.

The company said in May it would also begin using visual analysis, which “allows our AI to scan photos and videos for visual clues about a person’s age.” It said the AI doesn’t identify the person in the image or use facial recognition.

stories.title: Live updates: Carney’s investment summit gears up to pitch Canada, welcome hundreds of global executives
stories.summary: The summit in Toronto is part of Ottawa’s plan to promote the country’s resources and major projects
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said in an interview Monday that his government’s investment summit is part of a strategy to line up foreign capital behind Canada’s manufacturing sector while boosting trade with Asia and Europe.

The summit, taking place Monday and Tuesday at the Four Seasons in Toronto, is being attended by global investors and watched closely by a domestic audience waiting to see Carney’s next move in the trade war with the United States.

On the first day of the event, Carney said capital is just one of many ingredients required to boost Canada’s economy.

“You need capital, you need deals, you need projects, you need the proper regulatory environment, you need a competitive tax environment, and you need ambition and action,” Carney said. He said the summit is meant to bring all these factors together, to the benefit of all Canadians, not just business leaders.

“We are launching the investment supercycle that the country needs,” he added, perched on the edge of a Four Seasons hotel chair and occasionally jabbing a finger in the air to drive home his point.

Hundreds of Toronto protesters who had promised to disrupt the investment summit’s evening events at the Art Gallery of Ontario have not gotten far.

An Ontario Provincial Police line of about 30 officers, fronted by metal gate barriers and backed by a dozen large, black police vehicles, has blocked off a downtown street just south of the gallery.

The police line is at McCaul Street, just outside the Ontario College of Art and Design University pencil box building. A standoff is under way with drumming, chanting, placard-waving protesters wanting to move forward and police blocking their path.

“Move, you clowns,“ one protester shouted.

– Stephanie Levitz

Hi, I’m Stephanie Levitz. Normally I cover politics from The Globe’s Ottawa bureau, but this Monday and Tuesday, I am in Toronto for the Canada Investment Summit.

The official list of participants for the summit circulated by the Prime Minister’s Office runs 22 pages. Tonight, many of them are likely at the Art Gallery of Ontario for the summit’s opening gala.

But the event is closed to media, so we don’t know exactly what is happening inside.

The formal program begins Tuesday morning around 8:30, with the Prime Minister slated to speak just before 9 a.m.

Sagard CEO Paul Desmarais Iii’s advice for foreigners looking to invest in Canada could be summarized in five words: Go big and be patient.

Speaking at the final session of the Cvca’s Canadian Global Growth Forum on Monday, the financial scion said early-stage investments here take a long time to attract money from elsewhere.

“If you’re a foreign investor, you’ve really got to think about the fact that if you’re going to bet early in Canada, you’d better be reserving a really big chequebook, because you will often be on your own until the Series C, Series D, until you’ve proven out the Canadian market as a scale opportunity,” he said.

Desmarais said that is what happened when he put $300-million into Wealthsimple during the Canadian fintech company’s first five years of operations.

“Many, many, many people thought I was certifiably crazy,” he said. “In fact, there were moments where I had a little bit of self-doubt.”
