content_blocks.text: Analysis: What’s Carney’s pitch? You can build things faster, and we’ll come along for the ride
content_blocks.html: Analysis: What’s Carney’s pitch? You can build things faster, and we’ll come along for the ride

content_blocks.text: For years, Canada has had a reputation as a tough place to build major resource and energy projects. There’s a graveyard of pipeline and oil sands projects to prove it.
content_blocks.html: For years, Canada has had a reputation as a tough place to build major resource and energy projects. There’s a graveyard of pipeline and oil sands projects to prove it.

content_blocks.text: Mark Carney’s pitch to the who’s who of global finance gathered in Toronto this week is that this environment is changing. Over the past year, Ottawa has made a series of regulatory, legislative and institutional changes aimed at speeding up project permitting and reducing the number of hurdles companies need to get over to get shovels in the ground – with more changes to come .
content_blocks.html: Mark Carney’s pitch to the who’s who of global finance gathered in Toronto this week is that this environment is changing. Over the past year, Ottawa has made a series of regulatory, legislative and institutional changes aimed at speeding up project permitting and reducing the number of hurdles companies need to get over to get shovels in the ground – with more changes to come.

content_blocks.text: It’s set up the Major Projects Office as a concierge service for big projects, signed “one project, one review” deals with provinces to reduce duplication for environmental review and First Nations consultation requirements, and it’s contemplating a range of other changes to environmental review rules and bureaucracy to reduce the amount of time projects spend in regulatory limbo.
content_blocks.html: It’s set up the Major Projects Office as a concierge service for big projects, signed “one project, one review” deals with provinces to reduce duplication for environmental review and First Nations consultation requirements, and it’s contemplating a range of other changes to environmental review rules and bureaucracy to reduce the amount of time projects spend in regulatory limbo.

content_blocks.text: Ottawa is also putting more skin in the game by promising to use its balance sheet to de-risk private-sector investments.
content_blocks.html: Ottawa is also putting more skin in the game by promising to use its balance sheet to de-risk private-sector investments.

content_blocks.text: It has tweaked the mandates and risk profiles of the various Crown corporations involved in financing projects: the Canada Infrastructure Bank, Canada Growth Fund, Export Development Canada and Business Development Bank of Canada. Each is being directed to invest in “nation building” projects and take on more risk, while the explicitly green lens the Trudeau government put on these organizations is taking a back seat.

content_blocks.text: There are also newer public finance tools, including the Canada Strong Fund, which Ottawa will use to take equity stakes in major projects, and the Indigenous Loan Guarantee Program, which looks to overcome opposition by helping Indigenous groups acquire an economic stake in major projects.

stories.title: Calgary legislature seat up for grabs in Alberta byelection
stories.summary: A longtime Tory stronghold, the riding of Calgary-Shaw has been without a legislature member since May, when former cabinet minister Rebecca Schulz resigned her seat.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 14, 2026 8:24 am

Updated September 14, 2026 3:02 pm

Voters in Calgary head to the polls Monday in a provincial byelection.

A longtime Tory stronghold, the riding of Calgary-Shaw has been without a legislature member since May, when former cabinet minister Rebecca Schulz resigned her seat.

Five candidates are in the running, including Mike Derry for Premier Danielle Smith’s United Conservative Party and Kyle Campbell for Naheed Nenshi’s NDP.

2:08 The byelection for the next Calgary-Shaw MLA is underway

Derry’s campaign has focused on affordability, education, health care and government transparency, while Campbell has made promises on health care.

Other candidates include teacher Kyle Joseph for the Progressive Tory Party of Alberta, lawyer John Roggeveen for the Liberal Party of Alberta, and Independent candidate Rolly Ashdown.

The election comes as the province prepares to vote Oct. 19 on whether to stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on quitting the country.

Polls open at 9 a.m. and close at 8 p.m.

stories.title: Value of unsold condos in Metro Vancouver put at $4.6-billion
stories.summary: By year’s end, 4,200 completed homes in the city will be sitting empty, a report says
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
The number of completed unsold homes across Metro Vancouver is expected to reach approximately 4,200 by year’s end and have a total estimated value of $4.6-billion, according to an internal industry report that has been circulated within the industry and obtained by The Globe and Mail.

Prepared by real estate advisory firm Rennie with data sourced from the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. and analytics firm Zonda Urban, the report is dated April 20, 2026 and is labelled “For Internal Use Only.”

Rennie confirmed the authenticity of the report, but declined to provide a more up-to-date version or commentary on the report.

The report highlights that there were 3,945 completed unsold condos in Metro Vancouver at the end of March, 2026, split between 3,080 units in concrete buildings – typically high-rise towers – and 865 units in low-rise wood-frame buildings. Townhomes and other building forms are not included.

By city, Burnaby had 1,118 completed but unsold units, with a total estimated valuation of $1.092-billion. The report splits Vancouver into three areas – Downtown, East, and West – with a total of 668 units valued at $1.334-billion. Richmond was third-most with 516 units valued at $521-million.

The smallest condos are being hit hardest by the market decline

Across Metro Vancouver, the 3,945 units have a total value of $4.351-billion. When including projects expected to complete construction by year’s end, however, Rennie estimates the total at 4,195 units valued at $4.577-billion.

Rennie estimates that the total is projected to dip to 3,812 by the end of 2027, before jumping to 5,330 by the end of 2028 and then 6,333 by the end of 2029, before falling to 6,063 by the end of 2030.

The report also identifies the developers with the most completed unsold condos, with Ledingham McAllister – a developer with a history dating to 1905 – at the top of the list with 701 units valued at $688-million across seven projects.

Second is Anthem Properties with 395 units with a total value of $368-million across eight projects. Rounding out the top five are Onni Group, Pinnacle International, and Westbank, the last of which has just 178 unsold units but a total value of $602-million. Some of those developers also operate in the Greater Toronto Area.

The report does not list the projects, but the projects were recently identified by The Realist , whose data was obtained from a different source and are generally in line with those in Rennie’s report.

How young condo owners became accidental landlords

This amount of completed unsold condos, sometimes also referred to as standing inventory, can create problems across the industry – not just for developers, but also investment firms and lenders – because the units remain on the books and, in effect, constitute trapped capital – $4.6-billion worth – that cannot be used elsewhere.

“From the developer perspective, there isn’t that return of capital and profit,” said James Paleologos, President of Realtech Capital Group, a Vancouver-based real estate lender. “They’re usually making their money on the last handful of sales, so it’s leaving profit and maybe even equity capital out in the market.”

Mr. Paleologos said that developers have to decide whether to drop their prices. Some May feel inclined to “get out” of the project, while others May not want to take a loss or cheapen their product. Oftentimes, the bigger developers – whose lenders are more often the big banks – May be able to afford holding on until the market bounces back.

“It’s a matter of motivation for these to move. There are some developers who don’t need to sell and probably won’t until prices recover – and that could be years. But that’s a very small slice of the market. For most of these groups, it’s gonna come down to whether they get to a point where they can’t hold out any longer.”

In some scenarios, the construction loan May have to be converted into an inventory loan, which typically carries a higher interest rate, says Mr. Paleologos. Either way, the loan can’t be fully repaid and will stay on the books for longer than anticipated. Developers also often raise equity from other investors, and there May be time constraints related to that money too.

Opinion: Buyers want houses, but housing policy keeps pushing condo shoeboxes

Assuming 60 per cent of the $4.6-billion in unsold condos is financed by debt with a 6 per cent interest rate, that would mean $165.6-million in the economy is going to lenders as interest, annually, instead of being deployed elsewhere. That May be why lenders – particularly the big banks – are not panicking quite yet.

“It’s considered a pretty benign loan, from a bank’s perspective, in terms of their stress,” said Mr. Paleologos. “They usually value the units initially at a pretty safe level, and they’re only lending 50- to 60- per cent of that, so there’s so much room before you end up being in trouble. Anything is possible, but I would say, right now, most lenders would probably tell you their inventory loans don’t cause them too much concern. But it’s still on their radar for sure. It’s not like land. Land terrifies lenders right now.”

Brad Newman-Bennett, a Vancouver-based VP at Cushman & Wakefield Structured Finance, says standing inventory is a problem, but he’s more concerned about the big picture.

“I think the bigger question is what this market will look like three, four, or five years from now? There’s a reset going on in terms of working through how to finance projects going forward and what that looks like.”

“There’s a trickle-down effect to all of this, as far as the broader economy. Developers are cutting staff. Lots of realtors aren’t earning commissions. Tradespeople were so busy, but I think now everybody is scrambling for work. Everything in the economy is impacted, especially because real estate in the Lower Mainland is such a massive part of our economy.”

stories.title: St. Thomas police detail weekend call that prompted large response
stories.summary: An investigation into intimate partner violence drew a large police response in St. Thomas over the weekend.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
An investigation into intimate partner violence drew a large police response in St. Thomas over the weekend.

Officers from several units, including the critical response team and the canine unit, were involved in the investigation that led to the arrest of a suspect without incident on Sunday, police said.

“Due to the circumstances of the investigation and to ensure the apprehension of the accused, additional police resources were deployed and containment of the residence was established,” police said in a statement, adding that they thanked “area residents for their patience and co-operation during the police response.”

The accused, whose name or age wasn’t released, is charged with assault causing bodily harm, uttering threats to cause death, three counts of failure to comply with a release order and failure to comply with a probation order.

A single-vehicle collision that left an Essex woman dead is under investigation, police say.

At around 11:40 p.m. on Friday, officers with the Ontario Provincial Police Essex detachment responded to a reported crash near County Road 15 and Fifth Concession Road.

Based on a preliminary investigation, police say that investigators believe that the sedan was travelling south on County Road 15 when it left the roadway and entered a field. Despite efforts to resuscitate her, a 39-year-old woman was pronounced dead at the scene, police said, adding that they continue to investigate.

Anyone who May have witnessed the collision, or who has dashboard-camera or surveillance footage from the area recorded at the time of the incident, is asked to contact Essex OPP at 1-888-310-1122.

-With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: Could a long-empty downtown jewel soon be turned into apartments?
stories.summary: Efforts are underway to turn the more than century-old Wright Lithographing building at 424 Wellington St. into housing, according to public property records
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
Is it possible one of downtown London’s most prominent historic buildings May be getting a new lease on life?

Efforts are underway to turn the more than century-old Wright Lithographing building at 424 Wellington St. into housing, according to public property records. The building, ON the east side of Wellington near Dundas Street, has been vacant for decades – but in recent weeks, yellow construction fencing has been erected around the property.

A search of the Farhi Holdings Corp.-owned building on the city hall property records online portal shows two recent applications, including for a heritage alteration permit from August and for a change-of-use application from July to convert all floors into multi-residential use.

The possibility is something that excites downtown Coun. David Ferreira.

“ I’m very excited to get one of the heritage properties in London that has been for a very long time vacant . . . brought through the motions to be brought back online,” he said. “I am one to say, I pull the politics out of our heritage properties, our built heritage completely, and we use any tools we can . . . to save the property.”

The Wright Lithographing building, located between Dundas Street and Queens Avenue, was built in 1902 and designed by London architects Hubert Carroll McBride & Frederick W. Farncomb for the Sanitary Dairy Co. The building was bought by London Life in 1906 and housed its head office until the company, now Canada Life, moved into its present-day building a stone’s throw away on Dufferin Avenue in 1927.

In 1909 Wright Lithographing moved in, buying the building from London Life as it moved.

Farhi Holdings Corp. bought the building in 2007, and it was designated as a heritage property in 2013.

Ferreira describes the building as one of the “keystone heritage properties” in the core that many Londoners recognize for its prominence, which he likens to Banker’s Row and the former library building on Queens Avenue.

“The history of the building, the history of the business, the clock itself, where its location is, and the built structure and form of it, and I see people talking about it all the time,” he said.

stories.title: Fined into bankruptcy: the small Montreal college at the forefront of the language battle
stories.summary: LaSalle College tries to bargain its way out of $30 million in punitive fines for excessive anglophone education
stories.author: Joseph Brean
stories.content:
For a panicked few days in early September, it looked like LaSalle College in downtown Montreal was going to close for good, forced into bankruptcy by the Quebec government for temporarily teaching too many students in English.

It was politically unusual. In the middle of any other provincial election, campaigning political parties would likely rally to support an institute of higher education that was dying, even indirectly, because of government punishment.

But Quebec, which goes to the polls Oct. 5, is determinedly unique.

In 2022, Quebec strengthened the province’s language charter to make French the sole language for communication between the government and citizens, and what the province calls “a common denominator in the public sphere.”

For private Montreal colleges like LaSalle, and smaller ones like Marionopolis, it required their graduating students to have at least three courses taught in French, excluding courses in French language instruction. It also put a strict quota on the number of students taking courses in English, to keep that under a set proportion of all college students, specified in law and varying in different cases between 11.7 per cent and 18.7 per cent.

But it offered no transition period before financial penalties would be imposed on violators. And it allowed no adjustment based on an unanticipated pandemic relief education program that artificially boosted the number of students in the short term retraining and skills development programs that lead to “Attestation of College Studies,” a lesser degree than a full diploma.

This led to what LaSalle calls a temporary, two-year “administrative imbalance,” now resolved, by which it exceeded the 2023-24 quota by 716 students, and the next year’s by 1,066. In response, the government levied far more in fines than LaSalle could afford to pay, and with the academic year about to start, the bill was due.

“It was a nightmare,” said the school’s director general Claude Marchand. “An existential crisis.”

In the end it did not close, and by court order it survives to teach another year. Classes, suspended for a tense week, finally started on Sept. 8. But legally, the reckoning has only been delayed. The central problem remains, along with the political curiosity, as the school tries to bargain its way out of $30 million in punitive fines for excessive anglophone education.

Students, 3,000 of whom would have been left in the lurch, rallied at the school in advance of a last-ditch court appearance, with signs declaring “Studying is a right, save our education/our future” and “Laissez-nous étudier.”

“They’re tied up in knots,” said Merwie Garzon, whose 20-year-old daughter is a second-year student of fashion design at LaSalle.

Garzon is “furious” at what she sees as a provincial government discriminating against a linguistic minority in ways that are “calculated” to bring about the closure of the college, and “actively trying to drive out anglophones.”

“It’s uncomfortable to live in a place that is always sending you messages, in big ways and small ways, that you are not welcome,” she said. “If you read a headline that stated ‘Government Shuts Down School For Accepting Too Many Minority Students,’ we as Canadians would probably be shocked and wonder in what oppressive regime this school is being shut down.”

More than 400 employees faced impending unemployment. There was a contingency plan that would have seen almost all of them lose their jobs, keeping only a skeleton team of 16.

And Marchand, who has run LaSalle for 18 years and whose family owns this private college founded on Sainte-Catherine St. in 1962, wondered whether the government would finally start returning his calls, or responding to settlement offers, of which there have been a full dozen.

Now, at least, they have to. On Sept. 4, Quebec Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ordered the province to pay the school its allocated subsidies, which allows the year of classes to go ahead. He also extended the school’s creditor protection, ordering the parties back to court later this month, just before the provincial election, in which the governing Coalition Avenir Québec is in a tight race.

There is only one creditor, the province.

“We don’t get it,” Marchand said. “We don’t get that there was no dialogue from day one…. It’s really strange.”

The school’s website now declares it “finds itself abandoned by the very organization with which it has collaborated for more than 67 years,” the province.

Marchand said he accepts the quota system as democratically legitimate, he just expected a period of transition within which to comply.

“I will not say that personally that’s my vision of the world, but I perfectly respect that a duly elected democratic government can act pretty much however they want,” he said.

As Marchand describes it, the school was abruptly in a dilemma, wishing to comply with the new law, but mindful of its duties to its students, seeking a compromise.

The school starts recruiting in early October, and by March 1 prospective students make their decisions. But the quota numbers arrive in mid-February, which is “really late to the game for Quebecer students, but absolutely late to the game for international students,” he said.

The first year quotas were in fact lower than the school’s actual population, he said, because they were based on the highest numbers of the previous three years, and it seemed impossible to comply.

As this was happening, then Premier Francois Legault launched a pandemic recovery program that made tuition free for Quebecers in LaSalle’s continuing education “Attestation of College Studies” stream, typically shorter than a diploma program.

The effect was what the school calls “an administrative imbalance in the distribution of English-speaking students between our (Attestation of College Studies) and (Diploma of College Studies) programs.”

The school now has fewer students studying in English than they have ever had, and fewer in their diploma programs, but because their anglophone class numbers exceeded the quota, they are being fined into bankruptcy.

In a statement, Quebec’s Minister of Higher Education, Martine Biron, told the Montreal Gazette that discussions between the government and school can continue through the court-monitored creditor protection process, and that “any settlement proposal submitted by the college can be analyzed in due course and through the proper process.”

The government offered no clarity, Marchand said, and his messages went unanswered. From the beginning in 2021, he told them he needed a transition period, which is a common element of many new laws, and a delay of application is often explicitly written into legal judgments that overturn old laws.

Instead, the school was fined $8,781,740 on June 28, 2024, and $21,113,864 on June 30, 2025.

In a sense, Marchand managed his own transition period, because after those first two years of non-compliance, LaSalle was fully compliant with the quota system in the school year just passed, and will be so this year too.

So the province has at least not recently added to the school’s debt. But the historical debt is crippling, and the total impact of the new law on the school was $50 million, more than enough to put it under. Marchand said he accepts $20 million of that debt as manageable and fair, but the rest — the two fines — he sees as unfair. His hypothesis is that the government doubled down on a narrative it invented to justify the initial fine.

“LaSalle cannot be depicted as the institution threatening French on the island of Montreal,” Marchand said. He supports protecting the French language, “but I refuse that Lasalle be instrumentalized for small politics like that.”

LaSalle College offers both diploma and certificate programs in animation, administration, hospitality, computer science, accounting, real estate and others.

It has an especially rich history educating workers in Montreal’s robust fashion and retail clothing industry.

In 2019, for example, the shoe company Aldo Group backed a shoe design course at LaSalle, which just this month has grown into the “Footwear and Accessory Design” specialization in its fashion diploma program.

When former Gov. Gen. Mary Simon was sworn in, in 2021, she wore a dress and jacket designed by Victoria Okpik of Nunavik, the first Inuk woman to graduate in fashion design at LaSalle.

The school is privately owned by Marchand and his family. His father Jacques was founding academic dean, ran the school for 40 years, and now sits on the board.

A separate campus in Laval has grown internationally with study abroad programs.

content_blocks.text: For a panicked few days in early September, it looked like LaSalle College in downtown Montreal was going to close for good, forced into bankruptcy by the Quebec government for temporarily teaching too many students in English.

It was politically unusual. In the middle of any other provincial election, campaigning political parties would likely rally to support an institute of higher education that was dying, even indirectly, because of government punishment.
But Quebec, which goes to the polls Oct. 5, is determinedly unique.

In 2022, Quebec strengthened the province’s language charter to make French the sole language for communication between the government and citizens, and what the province calls “a common denominator in the public sphere.”

For private Montreal colleges like LaSalle, and smaller ones like Marionopolis, it required their graduating students to have at least three courses taught in French, excluding courses in French language instruction. It also put a strict quota on the number of students taking courses in English, to keep that under a set proportion of all college students, specified in law and varying in different cases between 11.7 per cent and 18.7 per cent.

But it offered no transition period before financial penalties would be imposed on violators. And it allowed no adjustment based on an unanticipated pandemic relief education program that artificially boosted the number of students in the short term retraining and skills development programs that lead to “Attestation of College Studies,” a lesser degree than a full diploma.

This led to what LaSalle calls a temporary, two-year “administrative imbalance,” now resolved, by which it exceeded the 2023-24 quota by 716 students, and the next year’s by 1,066. In response, the government levied far more in fines than LaSalle could afford to pay, and with the academic year about to start, the bill was due.
“It was a nightmare,” said the school’s director general Claude Marchand. “An existential crisis.”

content_blocks.alt: LaSalle College Claude Marchand
content_blocks.caption: LaSalle College Claude Marchand speaks to the media at LaSalle College in Montreal, on Monday, August 25, 2025. Photo by Allen McInnis / Montreal Gazette

content_blocks.alt: LaSalle College Claude Marchand
content_blocks.caption: LaSalle College Claude Marchand speaks to the media at LaSalle College in Montreal, on Monday, August 25, 2025. Photo by Allen McInnis / Montreal Gazette

content_blocks.text: In the end it did not close, and by court order it survives to teach another year. Classes, suspended for a tense week, finally started on Sept. 8. But legally, the reckoning has only been delayed. The central problem remains, along with the political curiosity, as the school tries to bargain its way out of $30 million in punitive fines for excessive anglophone education.

Students, 3,000 of whom would have been left in the lurch, rallied at the school in advance of a last-ditch court appearance, with signs declaring “Studying is a right, save our education/our future” and “Laissez-nous étudier.”
“They’re tied up in knots,” said Merwie Garzon, whose 20-year-old daughter is a second-year student of fashion design at LaSalle.

Garzon is “furious” at what she sees as a provincial government discriminating against a linguistic minority in ways that are “calculated” to bring about the closure of the college, and “actively trying to drive out anglophones.”

“It’s uncomfortable to live in a place that is always sending you messages, in big ways and small ways, that you are not welcome,” she said. “If you read a headline that stated ‘Government Shuts Down School For Accepting Too Many Minority Students,’ we as Canadians would probably be shocked and wonder in what oppressive regime this school is being shut down.”
More than 400 employees faced impending unemployment. There was a contingency plan that would have seen almost all of them lose their jobs, keeping only a skeleton team of 16.

And Marchand, who has run LaSalle for 18 years and whose family owns this private college founded on Sainte-Catherine St. in 1962, wondered whether the government would finally start returning his calls, or responding to settlement offers, of which there have been a full dozen.

content_blocks.alt: LaSalle College in Montreal
content_blocks.caption: Collège LaSalle students, staff and supporters take part in a protest in Montreal on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Photo by Evan Buhler / Montreal Gazette

content_blocks.text: Now, at least, they have to. On Sept. 4, Quebec Superior Court Justice Martin Castonguay ordered the province to pay the school its allocated subsidies, which allows the year of classes to go ahead. He also extended the school’s creditor protection, ordering the parties back to court later this month, just before the provincial election, in which the governing Coalition Avenir Québec is in a tight race.
There is only one creditor, the province.
“We don’t get it,” Marchand said. “We don’t get that there was no dialogue from day one…. It’s really strange.”
The school’s website now declares it “finds itself abandoned by the very organization with which it has collaborated for more than 67 years,” the province.
Marchand said he accepts the quota system as democratically legitimate, he just expected a period of transition within which to comply.
“I will not say that personally that’s my vision of the world, but I perfectly respect that a duly elected democratic government can act pretty much however they want,” he said.
As Marchand describes it, the school was abruptly in a dilemma, wishing to comply with the new law, but mindful of its duties to its students, seeking a compromise.

The school starts recruiting in early October, and by March 1 prospective students make their decisions. But the quota numbers arrive in mid-February, which is “really late to the game for Quebecer students, but absolutely late to the game for international students,” he said.
The first year quotas were in fact lower than the school’s actual population, he said, because they were based on the highest numbers of the previous three years, and it seemed impossible to comply.

content_blocks.alt: LaSalle College in Montreal
content_blocks.caption: Collège LaSalle students, staff and supporters take part in a protest in Montreal on Thursday, August 27, 2026. Students are calling for the government to intervene and save the school. Classes have been suspended and the college has entered creditor protection after it was fined millions of dollars for allowing too ma

content_blocks.text: As this was happening, then Premier Francois Legault launched a pandemic recovery program that made tuition free for Quebecers in LaSalle’s continuing education “Attestation of College Studies” stream, typically shorter than a diploma program.

The effect was what the school calls “an administrative imbalance in the distribution of English-speaking students between our (Attestation of College Studies) and (Diploma of College Studies) programs.”

The school now has fewer students studying in English than they have ever had, and fewer in their diploma programs, but because their anglophone class numbers exceeded the quota, they are being fined into bankruptcy.

In a statement, Quebec’s Minister of Higher Education, Martine Biron, told the Montreal Gazette that discussions between the government and school can continue through the court-monitored creditor protection process, and that “any settlement proposal submitted by the college can be analyzed in due course and through the proper process.”

The government offered no clarity, Marchand said, and his messages went unanswered. From the beginning in 2021, he told them he needed a transition period, which is a common element of many new laws, and a delay of application is often explicitly written into legal judgments that overturn old laws.
Instead, the school was fined $8,781,740 on June 28, 2024, and $21,113,864 on June 30, 2025.

In a sense, Marchand managed his own transition period, because after those first two years of non-compliance, LaSalle was fully compliant with the quota system in the school year just passed, and will be so this year too.

content_blocks.alt: LaSalle College in Montreal
content_blocks.caption: People enter the LaSalle College building in Montreal, on Monday, August 25, 2025. Photo by Allen McInnis / Montreal Gazette

content_blocks.text: So the province has at least not recently added to the school’s debt. But the historical debt is crippling, and the total impact of the new law on the school was $50 million, more than enough to put it under. Marchand said he accepts $20 million of that debt as manageable and fair, but the rest — the two fines — he sees as unfair. His hypothesis is that the government doubled down on a narrative it invented to justify the initial fine.

“LaSalle cannot be depicted as the institution threatening French on the island of Montreal,” Marchand said. He supports protecting the French language, “but I refuse that Lasalle be instrumentalized for small politics like that.”
LaSalle College offers both diploma and certificate programs in animation, administration, hospitality, computer science, accounting, real estate and others.
It has an especially rich history educating workers in Montreal’s robust fashion and retail clothing industry.

In 2019, for example, the shoe company Aldo Group backed a shoe design course at LaSalle, which just this month has grown into the “Footwear and Accessory Design” specialization in its fashion diploma program.
When former Gov. Gen. Mary Simon was sworn in, in 2021, she wore a dress and jacket designed by Victoria Okpik of Nunavik, the first Inuk woman to graduate in fashion design at LaSalle.
The school is privately owned by Marchand and his family. His father Jacques was founding academic dean, ran the school for 40 years, and now sits on the board.
A separate campus in Laval has grown internationally with study abroad programs.

stories.title: Kelowna businesses raise concerns over crime on Commerce Avenue
stories.summary: One of the most recent incidents happened just two weeks ago when the Goertsens found themselves temporarily locked inside their own office building.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Businesses on Kelowna’s Commerce Avenue say a series of break-ins, vandalism and other incidents are leaving them increasingly concerned about safety.

Security cameras have captured a range of crime-related incidents, including a bicycle being stolen from an RV rack, a glass door being kicked in and open drug use.

“It’s unacceptable to steal, it’s unacceptable to vandalize people’s property,” said Janine Goertsen, who owns a business with her husband Gerald on Commerce.

One of the most recent incidents happened just two weeks ago when the Goertsens found themselves temporarily locked inside their own office building.

“All of a sudden my car alarm is going off and I go and run to the door, and the door was tied shut with a garbage bag,” Gerald Goertsen said. “We saw it on the camera after he tied it with a garbage bag and then went to break into our vehicle.”

The couple has operated a business on Commerce Avenue for more than a decade.

They say conditions have deteriorated significantly in recent years, a change they associate with the opening of Hearthstone Supportive Housing in 2018.

“They walk around with knives and needles and all this stuff. So you never know. Like it’s not safe,” Gerald Goertsen said. “The RCMP have told me, don’t touch them, even to take them off the property because they can stab you. They can hurt you and it’s not worth it.”

The couple says they are now regularly cleaning up drug paraphernalia, garbage and human feces around their business. They also say they have witnessed people carrying weapons and have been threatened multiple times.

Janine says she was nearly attacked by another woman.

“My husband had to step in and she kept trying to go around him to get to me,” she said.

2:14 Crime and disorder problems in Rutland getting more attention

Alicia Parsons, who works on Commerce Avenue, says she has also witnessed incidents that have left staff feeling unsafe.

“It’s absolutely wild,” Parsons said. “They actually locked themselves into the bathroom and broke in after hours. We’ve had people wander into the office while one of the staff was there alone and actually terrified her.”

Global News did not receive a response from the John Howard Society, which operates the facility.

In an email to Global News, a city spokesperson said the city is engaging with business operators to improve safety.

“While many of the root causes of the rise in crime across communities in British Columbia fall within provincial and federal jurisdiction, the City remains committed to doing everything within our authority to improve safety and livability in Kelowna,” said Kevin Duggan, Community Safety Services Manager.

The City says it has taken additional steps to improve safety for businesses, including Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design reviews at 129 Kelowna businesses this year, resulting in more than 800 recommendations.

It also pointed to a new rebate program, which offers businesses up to $3,000 for security improvements and the business Cctv Registry, which now includes 135 registered cameras.

The Goertsens say they believe more could and should be done at the local level.

Among their suggestions are a call centre that would allow bylaw officers to respond more quickly to complaints, as well as curfews for people staying in shelters.

“We should not have to deal with this,” Janine Goertsen said.

She also suggested community leaders travel to other countries that have much better control of social challenges.

“Visit Japan, visit Austria, visit Switzerland, visit the Middle East. What are they doing? What are some of these cities doing that they don’t have the high percentage of unhoused people?” said Goertsen.

stories.title: London retailers stock up, brace for fallout from Canada-U.S. tariff fight
stories.summary: Local businesses say customers are already looking for Canadian-made alternatives as trade tensions reshape buying habits.
stories.author: Norman De Bono
stories.content:
In the London Major Appliance warehouse, there are a lot more Whirlpool stoves and refrigerators than usual – about twice as many.

The retailer has packed its storage site with U.S.-made appliances in a race to dodge the counter-tariffs the Canadian federal government applied to some goods from America, with appliances among the items affected.

“We doubled our inventory to protect our customers,” said Jay Vanderhoeven, general manager of London Major Appliances. “We’re seeing more customers come in asking to buy Canadian products, anything not made in the U.S.”

Canada recently hit some U.S. goods imported into Canada with $27.6 billion in tariffs ranging from 15 to 25 and up to 50 per cent, ON about 700 items. This came after the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a long list of Canadian items sold in the U.S., including alcohol, dairy and sectors such as electronics and building materials.

The last time Canada slapped tariffs on incoming U.S. appliances in 2025, Whirlpool, a major U.S. manufacturer, did not pass the increases on to retailers, Vanderhoeven said.

“It May have an impact, but we haven’t received direct tariff notice yet,” he said of any upcoming additional fees.

The additional inventory will keep Vanderhoeven from ordering any new stock from south of the border for more than a month. By then, he is hoping for a resolution to the tariff dispute.

The retailer stocks appliances manufactured in other countries, including Stirling Marathon Appliances, a Canadian manufacturer, so there is an opportunity to avoid additional costs.

London Centre MP Peter Fragiskatos knows some retailers will be hurt by the tariffs, but “we have to defend Canada,” he said.

“We will stand up for Canadian sovereignty, we will not yield in defending this country’s interest,” Fragiskatos said.

If that sounds like a Churchillian wartime speech, that is no accident. Canada walked away from trade negotiations with the U.S. federal government after a series of late demands from Washington that would have impeded Canada’s ability to trade with other nations and even exempted U.S. products from French-language labelling, among other concerns.

In other words, U.S. President Donald Trump put Canada’s ability to govern itself on the table, Fragiskatos said.

“I realize how difficult it has been when we rely on the U.S. as a chief export market. It’s difficult,” he said. “But the economy of our country is sound, we’re in a good position.”

At Cellular Magician in London, the cellphone sales and repair business has seen prices steadily increase in recent weeks, and owner Chady Boutros is not sure how much is due to tariffs and how much is simply the rising cost of doing business.

“It’s very concerning, but I will figure it out. I’m more concerned about my customers, people will have less money. Phones are essential,” said Boutros, who owns stores in London, St. Thomas, Tillsonburg and Woodstock.

“I will figure it out but it means people will have less money.”

He has even seen some customers trade in new phones for older models so they can pocket the difference. That few hundred dollars is being used to pay bills, he has been told.

“People don’t have money, you can tell.”

Along with iPhones, Samsung also makes phones in the U.S., he added.

In the technology sector, many products come from Asia and Europe and are not hit by the new tariffs, but some are still manufactured in the U.S., and local retailers are bracing for increases.

“It’s out of our control. It’s frustrating. Any time there’s a trade war with our largest economic partner, there’s reason for concern,” said James Fitzsimmons of London Audio on Fanshawe Park Road.

“There are definitely some products that will be affected. High-fidelity audio equipment from the U.S. will likely be subject to tariffs. These are premium products and the addition of a 25 per cent tariff will make some buyers think twice about their purchases,” he said.

“The last time there was a tariff hit, sales of U.S. products plummeted, with buyers opting to wait rather than fork out an extra 25 per cent. It’s hard to imagine this time around being any different.”

But the store stocks enough Canadian, Asian and U.K.-made products that it anticipates remaining busy.

“Anthem, Paradigm and Bryston are all Canadian companies, and they make world-class products. People are looking to buy Canadian, and we’re proud to offer a range of great options.”

As for support for businesses dealing with tariffs, Ottawa will offer grants to help businesses expand into new markets and loans to buy new equipment and technology, Fragiskatos said. “The interests of our country are at stake. We will not be pushed around.”

The federal government recently announced it is also continuing its suspension of the gas tax, which May help ease the tariff sting, Fragiskatos added.

“It does provide relief and we will find ways to support farmers and (business) owners and workers,” he said.

Canada recently hit some U.S. goods imported into Canada with $27.6 billion in tariffs ranging from 15 to 25 and up to 50 per cent, ON about 700 items. This came after the U.S. imposed 50 per cent tariffs on a long list of Canadian items sold in the U.S., including alcohol, dairy and sectors such as electronics and building materials.
The last time Canada slapped tariffs on incoming U.S. appliances in 2025, Whirlpool, a major U.S. manufacturer, did not pass the increases on to retailers, Vanderhoeven said.
“It May have an impact, but we haven’t received direct tariff notice yet,” he said of any upcoming additional fees.
The additional inventory will keep Vanderhoeven from ordering any new stock from south of the border for more than a month. By then, he is hoping for a resolution to the tariff dispute.
The retailer stocks appliances manufactured in other countries, including Stirling Marathon Appliances, a Canadian manufacturer, so there is an opportunity to avoid additional costs.
London Centre MP Peter Fragiskatos knows some retailers will be hurt by the tariffs, but “we have to defend Canada,” he said.
“We will stand up for Canadian sovereignty, we will not yield in defending this country’s interest,” Fragiskatos said.

If that sounds like a Churchillian wartime speech, that is no accident. Canada walked away from trade negotiations with the U.S. federal government after a series of late demands from Washington that would have impeded Canada’s ability to trade with other nations and even exempted U.S. products from French-language labelling, among other concerns.
In other words, U.S. President Donald Trump put Canada’s ability to govern itself on the table, Fragiskatos said.
“I realize how difficult it has been when we rely on the U.S. as a chief export market. It’s difficult,” he said. “But the economy of our country is sound, we’re in a good position.”

At Cellular Magician in London, the cellphone sales and repair business has seen prices steadily increase in recent weeks, and owner Chady Boutros is not sure how much is due to tariffs and how much is simply the rising cost of doing business.

“It’s very concerning, but I will figure it out. I’m more concerned about my customers, people will have less money. Phones are essential,” said Boutros, who owns stores in London, St. Thomas, Tillsonburg and Woodstock.
“I will figure it out but it means people will have less money.”
He has even seen some customers trade in new phones for older models so they can pocket the difference. That few hundred dollars is being used to pay bills, he has been told.
“People don’t have money, you can tell.”
Along with iPhones, Samsung also makes phones in the U.S., he added.
In the technology sector, many products come from Asia and Europe and are not hit by the new tariffs, but some are still manufactured in the U.S., and local retailers are bracing for increases.
“It’s out of our control. It’s frustrating. Any time there’s a trade war with our largest economic partner, there’s reason for concern,” said James Fitzsimmons of London Audio on Fanshawe Park Road.

“There are definitely some products that will be affected. High-fidelity audio equipment from the U.S. will likely be subject to tariffs. These are premium products and the addition of a 25 per cent tariff will make some buyers think twice about their purchases,” he said.

“The last time there was a tariff hit, sales of U.S. products plummeted, with buyers opting to wait rather than fork out an extra 25 per cent. It’s hard to imagine this time around being any different.”
But the store stocks enough Canadian, Asian and U.K.-made products that it anticipates remaining busy.
“Anthem, Paradigm and Bryston are all Canadian companies, and they make world-class products. People are looking to buy Canadian, and we’re proud to offer a range of great options.”

As for support for businesses dealing with tariffs, Ottawa will offer grants to help businesses expand into new markets and loans to buy new equipment and technology, Fragiskatos said. “The interests of our country are at stake. We will not be pushed around.”
The federal government recently announced it is also continuing its suspension of the gas tax, which May help ease the tariff sting, Fragiskatos added.
“It does provide relief and we will find ways to support farmers and (business) owners and workers,” he said.

stories.title: From scandal to celebration: David Cronenberg’s evolving legacy at Tiff
stories.summary: Over the years, Tiff and Cronenberg developed together
stories.author: Rachel Ho
stories.content:
As the 51st Toronto International Film Festival takes over the city Sept. 10-20, this series of articles examines some of the Canadian directors whose lives and careers have been shaped by Tiff.

When David Cronenberg’s 1988 film Dead Ringers had its world premiere at Tiff to open the festival, it sparked a “classic festival scandal,” says current Tiff CEO Cameron Bailey, who was a film critic at the time.

Bailey points out that in 1988, Cronenberg was not yet “fully canonized” as one of the country’s most lauded filmmakers. The Fly had been a massive hit, pushing him into the mainstream, “but his films were still known to be a little bit shocking,” Bailey says.

“ Dead Ringers was a very polished film about wealthy people, which maybe suited the opening night context, but they did pretty outrageous things in the film, and it was too much for some people,” he remembers. The film stars Jeremy Irons playing twin gynecologists Beverly and Elliot, who take drugs and secretly swap identities with their lovers. It also focuses on Beverly’s fascination with “mutant women,” that is, women with abnormal genitalia.

Tiff would be vindicated for its bold move in championing in the film: Dead Ringers went on to receive glowing reviews, win 10 Genie Awards and become a revered Canadian classic.

Bailey notes that Tiff has introduced audiences “time and time again” to Cronenberg’s work, “to show the artistry, the vision, the daring of his work, and why it all matters.” In addition to Dead Ringers , international or North American premieres at Tiff have included M. Butterfly (1993), Eastern Promises (2007), Crimes of the Future (2022) and The Shrouds (2024).

“There’s nothing that approaches what Cronenberg does with the kind of film he makes,” adds Bailey. “He’s influenced so many filmmakers. There’s a whole school of filmmaking that is essentially born out of Cronenberg’s early films.”

In the late 70s, the Toronto-born Cronenberg made ripples with indie successes like Shivers and Rabid ; but by his own admission, filmmaking in Canada at that time amounted to “making low-budget American films, that was our model,” as he said during an interview with The Globe and Mail promoting The Shrouds in 2024.

Over the years, Tiff and Cronenberg developed together – Tiff transforming from a composite of other festivals into a bona fide tastemaker, and Cronenberg transitioning from indie filmmaker to a paragon of body horror with multiple international awards under his belt.

“Until I’ve shown the film in Toronto, I haven’t really shown the film, that’s the way it feels,” he told The Canadian Press on the red carpet of the Tiff Tribute Awards in 2024 when the festival presented him with the Tiff Norman Jewison Career Achievement Award.

Bailey, who joined Tiff as a seasonal programmer in 1990, has been witness to Cronenberg’s journey over the years. “Part of the trajectory with somebody like him is that they start on the fringes of society and culture, and then they slowly move their way into the mainstream,” he says.

Billie Anderson, a lecturer in disability studies at Western University, is currently writing a book about Cronenberg and the cross-section between his films and disability. She points to Cronenberg’s ability to reflect the country’s worries as a connection point between his films and his fellow Canadians.

“Every time he comes out with a movie, he’s tackling a very real crisis that Canadians are grappling with,” says Dr. Anderson.

For example, Cronenberg’s film Videodrome brought to life the concerns of Canadian media theorist Marshall McLuhan and the concept of “the medium is the message.” In Dead Ringers , Cronenberg reflected the significant changes in women’s health care in 1980s Canada when contraception options greatly expanded.

In 2013, Tiff announced that Cronenberg would be donating film artifacts from his personal collection, ranging from notes to set memorabilia, to the Toronto institution. (Those items would feature in a touring, Tiff-curated exhibition called “David Cronenberg: Evolution.”) At the press conference to announce the donation, Cronenberg recalled that Piers Handling, Tiff CEO at the time, told him , “David, let us be your garbage can.” He added, “Imagine someone saying that to you. It was fantastic!” One man’s trash is a cultural centre’s treasure, as the saying goes.

“I hope, and I believe, that David knows that he always has a home at Tiff,” says Bailey. “We’ve shown so many of his films. Sometimes his world premieres. Sometimes they’re coming fresh from Cannes or somewhere else. But he has had such a warm reception in recent years… I think people see him for the larger-than-life auteur that he is.”

As the dynamic between twin brothers Beverly and Elliot becomes increasingly fraught, Beverly, dealing with depression and paranoia, commissions a set of custom medical instruments to be used on the so-called mutant women in his care.

In the operating room, Beverly reveals the medieval-looking tools to his surgical team, much to their shock and horror.

It’s an unsettling scene. The nickel-plated brass instruments (currently housed in Tiff’s archive) make a tremendous thud when Beverly presents them in a burlap sleeve inside the otherwise silent operating room. The tools bear a frightening resemblance to actual implements used during gynecological examinations.

“For me, and maybe for other men in the audience, it’s squirm-inducing, even though it’s not male anatomy,” observes Bailey. “That’s the fascinating thing. Just through how he stages the scene, shoots it, edits it and the music, he makes you identify with what is happening from the perspective of the woman it’s happening to. That’s radical to me because men don’t spend a lot of time thinking about what it’s like to be in a woman’s body.”

For Dr. Anderson, the scene is also notable because it shows that from Beverly’s perspective, the women’s abnormalities must be eradicated. In the character’s mind, “We have to introduce new medical instruments to change it, rather than just accepting variability.”

She commends Cronenberg’s commitment to making films “about how we can sympathize and empathize with people who have disabilities, because we all understand what it means to have a body that behaves in a way we perhaps don’t want it to.”

stories.title: Jazz Aviation reaches tentative contract with flight attendants
stories.summary: Halifax — Jazz Aviation LP says it has reached a new tentative contract with the union representing its flight attendants.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Halifax — Jazz Aviation LP says it has reached a new tentative contract with the union representing its flight attendants.

The subsidiary of Chorus Aviation Inc. operates Air Canada Express flights for Air Canada to 65 destinations across North America.

Details of the agreement, which still must be ratified, were not immediately available.

The Canadian Flight Attendant Union represents more than 1,000 flight attendants at the company.

The flight attendants voted earlier this month to strike if a deal could not be reached.

They have been working without a contract since Jan. 1.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:CHR)

stories.title: B.C.'s drug decriminalization experiment didn't change overdose deaths: study
stories.summary: While police encounters for drug possession declined, there were no changes in drug-related hospitalizations or deaths, research shows.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
British Columbia’s contentious experiment decriminalizing fentanyl, cocaine and other hard drugs was hailed by provincial health leaders as a “vital” means of keeping people from dying from drug overdoses.

It appears it didn’t. New research found no significant changes in drug-related hospitalizations or toxic drug deaths compared with the rest of Canada, where the drug laws hadn’t changed.

“I think there’s a real risk of over-promising simple solutions” to the opioid crisis, said the study’s senior author, Dr. Daniel Myran, in an interview.

Although drug poisoning deaths dropped slightly in B.C. after decriminalization, the changes didn’t differ relative to other provinces, according to the study published in this week’s issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal.

Overdose deaths fell by 19 per cent in B.C. but were down 25 per cent in Ontario over the same period.

“There is no effect that you’re seeing in B.C. that is not occurring in Ontario,” said Myran, who is the Gordon F. Cheesbrough Research Chair at North York General Hospital and associate professor and scientist at the University of Toronto’s department of family medicine.

“I do think that the premise of ‘we’re going to see these very large health benefits related to acute overdoses’ has not been borne out by the data we’re presenting here.”

Under a pilot project that launched Jan. 31, 2023, B.C. allowed adults to possess up to 2.5 grams of heroin, fentanyl, crack or powder cocaine, methamphetamine and Mdma (ecstasy) for their personal use.

People found carrying drugs below the 2.5-gram threshold were no longer to be arrested, charged or have their drugs seized. Instead, police were directed to offer information on social supports and help with referrals to treatment, if requested.

The province was granted a time limited, three-year exemption from the federal government’s Controlled Drugs and Substances Act.

The intent was to reduce risky behaviours, such as using alone, or using in unsafe locations, and end the “shame and stigma” that can keep people with drug addictions from reaching out for life-saving help, BC’s ministry of health said in a news release at the time.

B.C.’s provincial health officer, Dr. Bonnie Henry, called the exemption “a vital step to keeping people alive and help connect them with the health and social support they need.”

Local communities, however, soon began raising the alarm over growing public disorder and open drug use in parks, playgrounds and other public spaces.

Midway through, the policy was partly rolled back: In May 2024, possession of any amount of drugs in all public places, including hospitals, ON transit and in parks, was re-criminalized, though possession below the 2.5 gram threshold remained legal for adults in certain designated spaces, including private homes and overdose prevention sites.

The 2.5-gram policy expired on Jan 31, 2026, and wasn’t renewed. “The pilot hasn’t delivered the results we hoped for,” Josie Osborne, then B.C.’s health minister, told reporters in announcing the experiment was over.

Osborne said it was “difficult, if not even (impossible) to attribute certain changes or increases directly to decriminalization,” including the number of people who sought treatment.

The shifts in policy — off-again, ON-again criminalization — allowed researchers to look at different outcomes using data that captured police-recorded drug incidents nationally, and drug-related hospitalizations and deaths in B.C., Alberta and Ontario.

They compared monthly changes in B.C. to the rest of the country between August 2020 and March 2025.

Over the five-year study period, researchers counted a total of 97,630 instances of police encounters for drug possession, 75,485 for drug trafficking, 161,278 opioid-related hospitalizations, 113,747 stimulant-related hospitalizations in Canada, and 29,730 drug toxicity deaths in B.C., Ontario and Alberta.

As predicted, B.C. saw a significant (39 per cent) drop in monthly rates of police-reported drug possession incidents after decriminalization, followed by a rapid uptick (68 per cent increase) following partial re-criminalization in public spaces.

But after decriminalization, B.C. didn’t differ significantly from other provinces and territories for changes in opioid-related hospitalizations or deaths, according to the study.

Hospitalizations and deaths fell during partial re-criminalization in B.C., but, again, similar declines occurred across the rest of Canada, as well as the U.S, and were more likely driven by “broader factors” such as changes in the drug supply and its toxicity, Myran and his co-authors wrote.

“It is important to recognize plausible reasons behind these non-effects; crucially, the decriminalization policy was not combined with additional interventions or services that could have effectively reduced exposure to toxic drugs or related risk behaviours to improve drug-related mortality and morbidity outcomes for people who use drugs,” the researchers wrote.

There are compelling reasons to decriminalize minor drug possession and increase support for people who use drugs, Myran said. A criminal record carries implications for education, housing and employment “and it’s not necessarily the case that it’s helping someone to enter recovery or use fewer drugs,” he said.

Decriminalization was associated with a large fall-off in both police encounters and police charges for minor drug possession. From that perspective, the policy worked, he said.

“The problem was that there was a promise saying that we’re going to do this, and it’s going to have these criminal justice benefits, but it’s also going to have major health benefits. We are going to see these big reductions in overdoses. And the data are not supporting that.”

Officials risk eroding public trust “if the thing you promised doesn’t materialize.”

The study wasn’t designed to look at other outcomes, like public drug use or community safety.

But Myran isn’t convinced that the criminal status of minor drug possession is a major driver of the overdose crisis. “There are other very meaningful drivers that are worth understanding and acting on. But it doesn’t seem to be the criminal status.”

Declining opioid-related deaths in Canada and the U.S. May be partly down to tightened controls on China’s export of fentanyl “precursors,” disrupting fentanyl production in North America, and fewer young people using opioids, Dr. Alexis Crabtree, of the BC Centre for Disease Control, wrote in an accompanying commentary.

stories.title: Multiple Myeloma Walk of Champions
stories.summary: More than 30 patients with Multiple Myeloma (MM) gathered at the Dorchester Fairgrounds for the annual Walk of Champions.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
More than 30 patients with Multiple Myeloma (MM) gathered at the Dorchester Fairgrounds for the annual Walk of Champions.

For 18 years, this event brings together survivors and families of loved ones who have passed away due to the rare blood cancer.

This year’s walk brought in around $150,000 pushing the total to nearly $1.5 million since its inception in support of Myeloma Cancer Research at London Health Sciences Centre.

Among those walking the track was Richard Zsoldos who was diagnosed with Multiple Myeloma in 2018.

“The symptoms were severe back pain to the point where I have eight fractures in my spine and they had to put plates in my neck here because nothing was holding up my neck due to the cancer eating away the calcium,” said Zsoldos.

“It (Cancer) sucks and I wouldn’t wish that on anybody. I certainly hope there is a cure.”

Walking the track isn’t easy after everything he’s been through.

“I basically had to learn to walk again,” said Zsoldos.

“I think we’re in the greatest area for research with London’s pain clinic here and specialized pain doctors and the Cancer clinic, I think we’re in a great spot.”

London Health Sciences Centre Hemotologist Dr. Martha Louzada says MM affects around 7,000 Canadian patients annually.

“It’s a disease that has been known as not having a cure because it’s based on a cell that is a very hard to reach cell,” said Louzada.

“With a lot of research, the mortality of patients have decreased over time and the overall survival has increased substantially. So about 25 years ago, patients would survive two to three years but right now, I’m thinking about 15-20 years of survival on average for people.”

To help fight his cancer Zsoldos is now on his second clinical trial.

“I was successful for about 18 months, and then I relapsed,” said Zsoldos.

“Then I went on to this other trial with the drug not available in Canada and I’m now three and a half years into it in remission. I really think trials are important because they’re giving forward and the people ahead of me had to go through trials and experiment to get where I am now, and I need to pay that forward”. Louzada calls the clinical trials are important because they give both the patient and doctor access to medication that wouldn’t otherwise be available.

“We never test in clinical trials,” added Louzada.

“People think they’re being guinea pigs. It’s not that sense. It’s the sense that you have the opportunity to use a state of the art medication that otherwise you wouldn’t be able to and that could be the key to keep you alive.”

stories.title: Ontario universities attracted more than $1-billion in private-sector investment in three years, report finds
stories.summary: They also supported more than 2,800 startups and spinoff companies in a single year
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Universities in Ontario attracted more than $1-billion in private-sector investment over the past three years and supported more than 2,800 startups and spinoff companies in just one of those years, according to a new report from the Council of Ontario Universities.

The new research, set to be published Monday, marks the first time the COU has put a dollar figure on collaborations between the province’s public research universities and private companies.

“We knew universities were very significant players in attracting capital for research and innovation, but what was striking was the breadth and depth of it,” said Steve Orsini, president of the COU, which represents universities across Canada’s most populous province.

Ontario announces 40,000 new seats at universities and colleges, with focus on practical job training

The council is releasing the report as Prime Minister Mark Carney kicks off a two-day international investment summit on Monday in Toronto, an event designed to shore up Canada’s economy as it fights a trade war started by U.S. President Donald Trump. Summit organizers hope the conference will attract $500-billion worth of new investments over five years in marquee projects ranging from mines to port expansions to pipelines.

Although universities aren’t participating in the summit, the COU decided to use the moment to quantify the postsecondary education sector’s record of attracting private capital. Major projects on offer at the summit will need engineers, geologists, scientists, artificial-intelligence developers and other experts trained at universities, Mr. Orsini said.

“These big investments need to be supported by a very strong ecosystem,” he added. “So a lot of our research enterprises are supporting those projects.”

The COU compiled the report by surveying member universities this month, and by drawing on reports to the provincial Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security.

That effort led the council to conclude that Ontario universities attracted $1.02-billion in private-sector investment between 2023-24 and 2025-26. The sector established more than 7,500 corporate partnerships in the same period, the research found.

The report also said that 2,840 new startups and spinoff companies came out of universities in a single year, 2024-25. University startups and spinoffs secured more than $15-billion in investments from 2023-24 to 2025-26.

Susan Tighe, the president and vice-chancellor of McMaster University, said it is “extremely important” that universities tout their partnerships with industry.

“I think universities, generally speaking, have not done a good job in stating what kinds of contributions we’re having to the local economy,” she said. More than 400 companies have been spun out from her Hamilton institution alone, Prof. Tighe said.

The nearby University of Waterloo just cracked the top 10 in Pitchbook’s international rankings of the best schools for entrepreneurs . Pitchbook, a market tracking company, counts the number of alumni entrepreneurs whose businesses have raised venture capital money in the past 10 years to produce its list.

Waterloo placed seventh globally in the 2026 rankings, released last week – the first time a Canadian school made the top 10. Eight Canadian schools made the top 100, including the University of Toronto at number 17 and McGill at 23.

stories.title: Sara Bareilles grieves both a friend and the U.S. on her new album
stories.summary: Good Grief is an elegant account of frustration and loss curated across 14 thoughtful tracks
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
The title of Sara Bareilles’s first album in seven years is Good Grief , which sounds either like an expression of exasperation ripped from a Peanuts comic strip, or a statement on the cathartic nature of mourning.

It’s both – the double meaning is intentional.

“It’s a phrase I use a lot,” she says, speaking on a video call. “I sound like my mom when I say it.”

The album is a reflection on the death of a close friend and a politically conscious reaction to a society going haywire. “This whole collection of songs felt like transmissions rather than a deliberate attempt to make sense of the world,” she said earlier this year when the record was announced.

A few months have passed. The album is out, and Bareilles is on a tour that brings her to Toronto’s Massey Hall on Sept. 15 and 16. How is she doing now?

“I’m fine,” the musician, actress and Broadway composer says with a smile. “I’ve figured it all out.” Sarcasm. “No, I’m not fine,” she continues, still smiling. “I don’t think there’s a solution here. It’s not an album of answers.”

What Good Grief is, then, is an elegant account of frustration and loss − melodic punches thrown in the air. The album’s first track and lead single is Home , an affecting ballad inspired by a conversation between Stephen Colbert and Anderson Cooper on the latter’s podcast about sorrow. The song serves as a rallying call for community: “So tell me your story, I’ll tell you mine.”

From her home in New York, the 46-year-old native of Northern California spoke about journeys − musical, emotional and otherwise.

When putting the album together, were you conscious of the whole 14-track experience as opposed to just putting out songs for playlists?

I’m an artist who has been around long before playlists. I’m schooled in a different way. I’m also someone who takes time between records. If I’m going to take the time to make an album, I’m going to curate the listening experience from top to bottom.

I should point out to the readers that the album is not a downer. The song Capsize Me is upbeat and Nervous Breakdown is probably the jazziest number about an acute mental health crisis ever written.

[Laughs] Well, it’s about taking the listener on a journey. I’m thinking thematically and tonally about what the sounds evoke, and what the tempos feel like next to each other. The tracking is a big undertaking.

What’s the takeaway? What do we learn about grief?

The whole point of this record is to try to capture the fullest embodied expression of grieving, which to me is not one thing. It is the paradox. It is the surprise and delight of what can sometimes feel monolithic or like dark matter. There is so much awe and mystery and joy and connection and fulfillment in grief as well.

And resilience?

Yes, and hopefulness. That is all embedded in the record as well. And humour. You brought up Nervous Breakdown .

I smiled at the line “keep the Novocaine out of my wisdom teeth” when I heard it.

Who doesn’t need a cheeky moment when they’ve having a hard time? I was trying to speak to grief in all its forms.

Let’s talk about Hands off My Body. When you performed it in 2024 at the Hollywood Bowl, you told the audience that the song would speak for itself. Now that I have you, can you speak for it?

I started writing it just after the women’s movement in Iran in 2022, after Mahsa Jina Amini’s death . Then the song began taking on different layers. Roe v. Wade fell, and women’s reproductive health was under attack in the United States and all over the world. There were just so many places in which I felt like we are witnessing the kind of monster of misogyny and what feels oppressive to me on behalf of women. So, the song is a plea for autonomy and independence and community.

Would you say community is a theme throughout the album?

Yes. I think so many of the songs on the record are about bringing your pain to each other so we can hold it together. I think Hands off My Body is a battle cry for women to come stand together and ask for freedom.

Speaking of women, tell me about Heartland. I love the Carole King feel, and it seems you’re singing about one woman in particular, the one with the torch.

Heartland is about grief of country. It’s a complicated feeling being American right now. I wrote the song from the perspective of what something like the Statue of Liberty actually represents. And from the perspective of the Constitution − these words on the page, what they embody and what they idealize. I still feel the ideas are worth pursuing.

What is America grieving over as you see it?

The cruelty. The greed. The competition. There’s just a lot of grief, and the powerlessness seems so big.

Where are you in your own grieving process?

I’m in the messy middle. I’m not healed. And I’m trying to share from that place.

This interview has been edited and condensed.
