stories.title: At Tiff, and in Washington, Quebec’s film industry finds itself in the hot seat
stories.summary: Rarely making a dent outside of the province, it has now become crucial to the existential battle for Canadian cultural sovereignty
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
In the new documentary Ladies and Gentlemen, Brian Mulroney – a madcap assemblage of archival footage from the acclaimed Montreal-based director Matthew Rankin ( Universal Language ), which will premiere Tuesday at the Toronto International Film Festival – Canada’s 18th prime minister is introduced with a telling quote.

Speaking with a reporter back in the eighties, Mr. Mulroney decries the diminished state of Canada’s “entrepreneurial spirit,” going on to insist that the farmers, fishermen and small business owners who risk their lives and capital will “get less of a tax break than somebody who wants to make a third-rate movie that you wouldn’t even show in your basement.”

What, one cannot help but wonder as Mr. Rankin’s delightfully surreal doc unfolds, would the late Mr. Mulroney think about this current moment for Canadian cinema? Especially the films coming out of his home province of Quebec, whose onscreen culture has become one of the thickest red lines that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government will not cross in trade negotiations with the United States.

Of course, it is doubtful that Mr. Rankin’s National Film Board production would have seen the light of day if Mr. Mulroney was in charge, given the politician’s affinity for cutting the budgets of the NFB, the CBC and all things culture.

Yet the fact that Mr. Rankin’s movie does indeed exist, and is premiering at TIFF alongside a handful of other buzzy French-language productions, offers a prime opportunity for moviegoers outside of the province to consider the current, sometimes contradictory state of Québécois cinema. It is an industry that thrives inside its own provincial borders, rarely makes a dent outside of them, and has now become crucial to the tremulous, fraught and existential battle for Canadian cultural sovereignty writ large.

“It’s an interesting moment for Québécois cinema, because you have a couple different things happening at the same time,” says Jason Anderson, TIFF’s lead programmer for Canadian films.

“There are more auteurist, personal films that are built for international festivals, but then you have, at the other end, more commercial work, which is still unusual in English-language Canada. Quebec has its own stars, its own dependable directors making films that hit really well at home, but don’t travel outside Quebec. And in the festival, we get that range.”

This diversity includes, on one hand, such smaller, art-house-geared work as Mr. Rankin’s film, plus L’Autre , a highly anticipated psychological thriller from Alexandre Franchi; Rémi St-Michel’s darkly comic crime story Toy Gun Bandit ; and a pair of films, Denis Côté’s dystopian drama Nobody’s Violence and Sophie Deraspe’s documentary The Final Act , which both pivot around the topic of assisted suicide. (Curiously, that’s a subject familiar to Quebec moviegoers thanks to the surprise box-office success of Louis Bélanger’s low-budget family drama 125, rue des Malaises , currently in theatres.)

But as TIFF’s Mr. Anderson notes, there is also room for big, glitzy crowd-pleasers. This includes the festival’s closing-night film, Yan Lanouette Turgeon’s Formula One-centric biopic Villeneuve: The Rise of a Legend (whose $15-million-plus budget makes it one of the most expensive Québécois films ever made), as well as Michael Dowse’s Quebec-accented comedy The Stunt Driver , starring Jay Baruchel as the Montreal-born daredevil Ken (The Mad Canadian) Carter, alongside Quebec star Laurence Leboeuf.

This year, there is also TIFF’s inaugural Market, a seven-day event running parallel to the festival that gathers buyers and sellers of film, television and interactive content under the roof of the Metro Toronto Convention Centre. When TIFF organizers were first considering launching the Market, chief programming officer Anita Lee met with Louise Lantagne, president and chief executive of Quebec’s cultural funding agency La Société de développement des entreprises culturelles (SODEC), to puzzle out what the initiative could do for the province’s industry.

“To give you an example, there will be approximately 200 Quebec delegates coming to the market, which is definitely an uptick from the year before,” Ms. Lee says. “It just shows the kind of pride that there is in championing Quebec cinema.”

Still, this year’s slate of Québécois productions will, like their English-language Canadian counterparts, have a tough time competing for attention at TIFF with the biggest titles coming out of Hollywood.

“Let’s say that it’s not what it used to be,” says prolific Montreal-based producer Pierre Even ( C.R.A.Z.Y. , Café de Flore ). “Not so long ago, a film playing at TIFF that got good reviews would have an impact on a release following in the coming weeks or months. Nowadays, we have the feeling that TIFF is even more focused on big American films and stars.”

“It’s more and more difficult to attract journalists, buyers and the audience for a French-language film. We consider TIFF as our own; they should treat Canadian films the same way Cannes does with French films. Put them at the forefront of their programming.”

Indeed, a TIFF premiere is nice in theory, but offers no promise of box-office success in return, even within Quebec.

“We’ll see with the Villeneuve movie. On the home front, the festival is well-regarded and a film finding success there will lend it prestige and recognition when it opens,” says Gabriel Pelletier, president of the Quebec director’s guild, L’Association des réalisateurs et réalisatrices du Québec (ARRQ). “Although I wish Quebec films would travel more in Canada. I don’t know if TIFF can help with that.”

And right now, the industry can use all the help it can get.

While French filmmakers are snapping up awards across the world stage, such as the Montreal team behind the Oscar-winning animated NFB short The Girl Who Cried Pearls , the situation at the box office is a different story.

In 2025, the Quebec box office – historically the strongest-performing market of any province – dropped 15 per cent compared with the year before, which marked a whopping 39-per-cent decline compared with the prepandemic year of 2019. And so far this year, things are even worse, with receipts currently tracking 4.8 per cent below 2025.

Industry players are mixed on the reasons. Some point to the fact that Villeneuve was supposed to be released this past July to buoy the summer market, but production delays forced the title to be punted to the fall. At the same time, such presumed sure-things as François.e , a modern-day trans spin on Tootsie starring comedy icon Louis Morissette, fell flat.

And then there are more macro concerns to consider, such as the shaky state of independent film worldwide, which has been dented owing to changing audience habits, and the challenge for any movie not boasting an Odyssey -level marketing machine to break through the pop-culture noise.

“I’m convinced that we could do much better very quickly if film financiers like Telefilm and SODEC decide to bring back ‘audience appeal’ as their initial criteria for financing films,” says Patrick Roy, founder of Immina Films, the most successful Quebec-owned distributor for the past two years.

“We’ve focused so much on discoverability of content, which is also important, that we kind of forgot that we are making films to appeal to audiences. I think we should be ambitious and set a box-office goal like the 5-per-cent market share for Canadian films that Telefilm had for a long time,” Mr. Roy says.

Not that Mr. Roy feels there isn’t room for smaller, more independent-minded films, too. “More successes at the box office also inspire audiences to be more adventurous and curious about artsier movies, so the entire industry benefits from popular success.”

On that rising-tide-lifts-all-boats sentiment, there are more than a few reasons to be optimistic about what’s coming down the pike later this year and into 2027.

On the art-house circuit, there are new features from such critically trusted directors as Charlotte Le Bon ( Falcon Lake , but perhaps best known for her performance in Season 3 of HBO’s The White Lotus ), Philippe Lesage ( Who By Fire ), Kim Nguyen ( Rebelle ) and Pascal Plante (whose dark 2023 thriller Red Rooms might have been the most talked-about movie on the American indie circuit that year).

In terms of more commercial fare, there is Villeneuve to look forward to, but also the fall-season release of Rafaël Ouellet’s family-friendly ghost story Hantée , written by the massively popular novelist India Desjardins. Anaïs Barbeau-Lavalette has a biopic on the beloved singer-songwriter and activist Pauline Julien, which should resonate both in Quebec and in other francophone markets around the world. And the culture-clash comedy Maudits Français , from box-office lucky charm Émile Gaudreault ( Menteur ), features the biggest stars from both Quebec (Patrick Huard, Antoine Bertrand) and France (Lambert Wilson, Suzanne Jouannet), and is being distributed in France and internationally by the French powerhouse StudioCanal, and in Canada by Immina Films.

Meanwhile, the industry has been galvanized over the promises of Quebec’s Bill 109 , which requires foreign-owned streamers to promote original French-language content and use French as their default interface language for Quebec subscribers. Similar in intention to the federal Online Streaming Act (Bill C-11), which compels foreign-owned streamers to contribute percentages of their Canadian revenues to the production and promotion of local content but has since been held up in court, both laws have reportedly become sticking points in Canada-U.S. trade talks. Bill 109 was passed into law late last year by Quebec’s National Assembly, though there has been little movement on it since then, largely due to the forthcoming provincial election.

“If everything goes well, it could be effective in 2028,” says ARRQ’s Mr. Pelletier, noting that it could be fought in court by the Motion Picture Association of Canada, as the industry group did with C-11. “Or it becomes the subject of trade negotiations once again. Or both.”

Others see the Bill 109 fight as indicative of larger political winds.

“Regardless of the outcome of the provincial election, I sincerely hope that the elected government will protect our culture,” says Tim Ringuette, founder and president of Entract Films and one of the producers of Villeneuve . “If Prime Minister Carney is standing up to President Trump when it comes to the French language, the Quebec government has every reason to do the same.”

Ultimately, the prevailing sentiment inside the industry is that, no matter the outsized impact that Québécois culture might currently be having on the larger geopolitical climate, the sector cannot continue along its current course without leaders addressing the systemic challenge of financing.

This past March, the Quebec government allocated $280.4-million to the audiovisual sector over five years, including $176.4-million to renew and increase funding for SODEC, Quebec’s cultural funding agency. Yet that bump in funding was not fully in line with the recommendations outlined in a report commissioned by the province’s Culture Minister, Mathieu Lacombe, in the fall of 2025, leaving producers frustrated.

“Not so long ago, we had established that the Quebec industry needed to produce between 22 to 25 films to obtain a critical mass of films released within a year in order to achieve any goals of success. With the postpandemic costs and inflation, we’re now down to 16 to 18 films per year financed with the same body of money,” Montreal producer Mr. Even says.

After all, if the industry cannot sustain itself, it also cannot be used as a bargaining chip in further trade negotiations.

“I am a big fan of our creators, I believe in their talent and judgment. I think that they have to show us the way, and for that they need more freedom,” Mr. Roy says. “So less political interference by our institutions, more rewards for success and more ambition can help us do much better very quickly.”

stories.title: Leading mental health hospital slashes wait times by reducing number of programs it offers
stories.summary: The Royal, in Ottawa, used to run 17 different mental health programs – now it’s just three
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
When senior staff at one of the country’s leading mental health hospitals looked at the lengthy wait times for the facility’s outpatient care, they decided to take an unusual step to address the issue: reducing the number of programs the hospital offers.

The Royal, located in Ottawa, used to run 17 different mental health programs, such as for anxiety disorders and mood disorders.

But members of the hospital’s senior leadership team say this led to siloed services that had different admission criteria, contributing to a backlog of patients who waited around two years to receive care.

Some patients qualified for more than one program, for instance if they were struggling with both anxiety and substance use, further complicating how patients received care.

Then, in January, the mental health hospital moved to deliver just three.

Emergency room wait times continue to climb in Canada as more medically complex patients seek care

The programs now include a general psychiatry stream for patients who live with a range of mental health concerns, including mood, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, trauma and personality disorders.

There is also a program to support patients with severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia.

Lastly, the integrated forensic program provides specialized treatment for patients who have come into contact with the criminal justice system or who are at risk of doing so.

The changes have already proven to be effective, along with other measures including hiring a dozen more psychiatrists and centralized data tracking on patient demand to better inform service delivery.

Since the beginning of the year, the Royal increased the number of outpatients seen from 407 in January to 800 in June. The number of patients waiting for care has also declined by 62 per cent from 1,498 to 574.

“We are providing more access to patients,” said Maiko Schneider, the hospital’s senior medical officer and deputy chief of staff.

Opinion: Ending the marathon of suffering in Canada’s emergency rooms

Dr. Schneider said the hospital can now see outpatients within about three to four months. Previously, the wait list was so long that many of the city’s care providers stopped referring patients to the hospital all together.

In the hospital’s annual report for 2024-25, it described how “long wait times, fragmented services, and the continued shortage of primary care providers have created a system under pressure.“

Too often, it added, people turn to emergency departments because they have nowhere else to go.

Dr. Schneider said patients who do not receive timely care become more difficult to treat, and often have more dysfunctional lives and struggle in the community.

The Royal’s new approach to improving patients’ access to care could serve as a roadmap for other institutions looking to reduce wait times while also facing financial constraints.

Cara Vaccarino, the Royal’s president and chief executive officer, said most hospitals are facing significant structural deficits. The Royal reported a $6.5-million deficit last March.

She said that while it can be a daunting proposition for hospital leaders to be ambitious and bold in this climate, that cannot “deter us from innovating, from advancing.”

On Sept. 21, the Royal is scheduled to open an urgent-care clinic where patients who are in distress can be seen by psychiatrists.

The hospital’s former urgent-care clinic shuttered in 2000 amid efforts in Ontario to streamline health care services.

At the clinic, patients would be admitted to hospital if needed or could have up to six outpatient appointments, said Stephanie Carter, executive director at the hospital.

The goal is to eventually scale up clinic services to include evening and weekend coverage.

Ms. Vaccarino said the Royal has drawn lessons from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health in Toronto, such as tracking patient intake to inform program delivery.

Ontario ER doctors raise alarm on hospital overcrowding

Camh is Canada’s largest mental health teaching hospital and also operates an urgent care clinic.

“A lot of us, including myself, worked at Camh for a long time,” she said. “Camh actually undertook a lot of the changes we’re doing now quite some time ago.”

At the Royal, Ms. Vaccarino said her team’s approach is to be “relentlessly focused and dogged.”

“We are not rocket scientists,” she said. “We’re just doing the right thing.”

She speaks from personal experience. When she was just 10-years-old, her mother, Joan, died by suicide.

Ms. Vaccarino shared how her mother encountered stigma and isolation while she was navigating what is now known as treatment-resistant depression.

“That kind of loss changes you forever,” Ms. Vaccarino wrote in an op-ed last year, describing the experience as her “guiding force.”

“I knew – even then – that I would spend my life working to ensure no other child had to lose a parent to an illness that could, and should, be treated with the same urgency and innovation as any physical health condition.”

“A lot of us, including myself, worked at Camh for a long time,” she said. “Camh actually undertook a lot of the changes we’re doing now quite some time ago.”
At the Royal, Ms. Vaccarino said her team’s approach is to be “relentlessly focused and dogged.”
“We are not rocket scientists,” she said. “We’re just doing the right thing.”
She speaks from personal experience. When she was just 10-years-old, her mother, Joan, died by suicide.
Ms. Vaccarino shared how her mother encountered stigma and isolation while she was navigating what is now known as treatment-resistant depression.
“That kind of loss changes you forever,” Ms. Vaccarino wrote in an op-ed last year, describing the experience as her “guiding force.”

“I knew – even then – that I would spend my life working to ensure no other child had to lose a parent to an illness that could, and should, be treated with the same urgency and innovation as any physical health condition.”

content_blocks.text: When senior staff at one of the country’s leading mental health hospitals looked at the lengthy wait times for the facility’s outpatient care, they decided to take an unusual step to address the issue: reducing the number of programs the hospital offers.
The Royal, located in Ottawa, used to run 17 different mental health programs, such as for anxiety disorders and mood disorders.

But members of the hospital’s senior leadership team say this led to siloed services that had different admission criteria, contributing to a backlog of patients who waited around two years to receive care.
Some patients qualified for more than one program, for instance if they were struggling with both anxiety and substance use, further complicating how patients received care.
Then, in January, the mental health hospital moved to deliver just three.

The programs now include a general psychiatry stream for patients who live with a range of mental health concerns, including mood, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive, trauma and personality disorders.
There is also a program to support patients with severe mental illness, such as schizophrenia.
Lastly, the integrated forensic program provides specialized treatment for patients who have come into contact with the criminal justice system or who are at risk of doing so.

The changes have already proven to be effective, along with other measures including hiring a dozen more psychiatrists and centralized data tracking on patient demand to better inform service delivery.

Since the beginning of the year, the Royal increased the number of outpatients seen from 407 in January to 800 in June. The number of patients waiting for care has also declined by 62 per cent from 1,498 to 574.

Too often, it added, people turn to emergency departments because they have nowhere else to go.
Dr. Schneider said patients who do not receive timely care become more difficult to treat, and often have more dysfunctional lives and struggle in the community.
The Royal’s new approach to improving patients’ access to care could serve as a roadmap for other institutions looking to reduce wait times while also facing financial constraints.

stories.title: Carney pitches Canada to the world’s biggest investors
stories.summary: The Canada Investment Summit runs Sept. 14 and 15 in Toronto
stories.author: The Decibel Staff, Sherrill Sutherland, James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Starting today, 300 big-money investors are descending upon Toronto to take part in the inaugural Canada Investment Summit . Prime Minister Mark Carney will try to convince them to fund development projects in the country, such as oil and gas pipelines, critical mineral mines and data centres . Getting their buy-in is a crucial plank in the prime minister’s plan to diversify and fortify the country.

James Bradshaw is The Globe’s institutional investment reporter. He’ll be covering the event. He’s on the show to explain what projects are being offered and what this means for Canada’s economy while we’re engaged in a trade war with the U.S.

Questions? Comments? Ideas? Email us at thedecibel@globeandmail.com

stories.title: Statistics Canada to report inflation figures for August this morning
stories.summary: Ottawa — Statistics Canada is set to report fresh inflation figures for August this morning.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Canada’s inflation rate held steady in August, suggesting higher energy costs have yet to spill over significantly into broader consumer prices.

The consumer price index report released Monday by Statistics Canada showed the annual rate of inflation was unchanged at three per cent last month.

The inflation reading was in line with economists’ forecasts and could ease speculation of a Bank of Canada rate hike next month, said Benjamin Reitzes, Bmo’s managing director of Canadian rates and macro strategist.

He said there was little in the inflation report to push the central bank toward an interest rate increase, potentially cooling market expectations of an October hike.

However, oil prices continued to be a real problem, which could “drive angst among policymakers and concern that it’s just a matter of time before we get some spillover into broader inflation,” Reitzes said in a note.

Financial odds of a hike at the central bank’s Oct. 28 meeting have jumped over the past week or so to 60 per cent as of midday Monday, according to Lseg Data & Analytics.

The conflict in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices in August but just at a slower pace, with prices up 22.8 per cent compared with 25.7 a month earlier, StatCan reported.

Excluding gasoline, consumer prices rose 2.4 per cent last month.

The slowdown in rising gas prices was offset by higher costs for rent, travel tours and air travel.

Canadians paid more for travel amid rising fuel surcharges and as airlines adjusted to the sharp decline in Canadian travel to the United States in 2025, the agency said.

Rent prices also trended higher, increasing 2.8 per cent year-over-year in August, up from 2.5 per cent in July.

Consumers found some relief at the grocery store as food prices rose more slowly than overall inflation for the first time since July 2024, climbing 2.8 per cent year-over-year, according to StatCan.

Prices for dairy products like cheese and yogurt led the deceleration in grocery prices. StatCan said dairy prices rose 0.7 per cent in August compared with a 3.1 per cent rise in July.

Smaller price hikes for pork, condiments, spices and vinegars also added to the year-over-year slowdown in grocery inflation.

Still, overall food affordability is still a challenge for households, Royal Bank of Canada economist Abbey Xu said.

“The direction has been somewhat more encouraging recently,” she said in an interview. “We have seen food inflation overall ticking slightly lower for several months.

“But consumers might still feel it’s expensive to fill up their gas tanks and go to the grocery store,” Xu added.

“We’re seeing improvements but it doesn’t really make the household cost of living pressure any less significant.”

Consumers paid less for clothing in August, with annual prices edging down 1.1 per cent last month due to a 2.3 per cent drop in men’s clothing prices and a 1.9 per cent decline in children’s clothing.

Across Canada, the Atlantic provinces had the highest rates of inflation in August, with prices accelerating in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Labrador, Statistics Canada said.

Overall, the August inflation data was “fairly reassuring” with core measures remaining around the Bank of Canada’s two per cent target and limited evidence that higher energy costs were spreading to other consumer prices, Xu said.

Yet the outlook for inflation and interest rates depends largely on how persistent higher energy prices prove to be, she said.

“If oil stays elevated for longer, then the risk of energy spillover will be higher” Xu said.

“So far we still have the Bank of Canada on hold for the remainder of 2026 and raising rates gradually beginning in 2027.”

stories.title: Prime Minister Carney to kick off first investment summit in Toronto
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney is welcoming the world's investors to Toronto on Monday for a high-stakes summit aimed at attracting new investment to Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Three prime ministers were on hand in Toronto to mark one of the largest private sector investments in Canadian history on Monday — the opening salvo in Mark Carney’s two-day summit aimed at attracting billions of dollars in capital to Canada.

The deal in question was a massive data centre expansion planned by Bell in Saskatchewan, a move that the Montreal-based telecom giant’s CEO Mirko Bibic said will require $50 billion in capital investment to complete.

In the room for the announcement was Carney and bipartisan pair of former prime ministers — Liberal Jean Chrétien and Conservative Stephen Harper — the latter of whom will deliver closing remarks at the inaugural investment summit on Tuesday.

The event is part of Carney’s bid to improve Canada’s reputation in the eyes of investors after years of stagnant business investment. The prime minister is trying to court the world’s investors as part of his lofty goal to attract $1 trillion in investments over the next five years.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe on Monday hailed Carney for his “renewed … sharp focus” on expanding Canada’s trading relationships and promoting the country’s international credibility.

Carney held up Bell’s investment as the kind of investment Canada needs to pivot the economy to growth. He didn’t directly mention headwinds from U.S. tariffs or other geopolitical shifts in his comments.

“The tone of Canadians is, let’s get on with it. Let’s build. Let’s control our future. Let’s be positive. Let’s come together. This is a fantastic example of that,” Carney told the room at the Fairmont Royal York in downtown Toronto.

Toronto is playing host to executives at some of the world’s largest asset managers this week as Carney, his cabinet ministers and premiers pitch the investors on major infrastructure projects.

Major Canadian banks and pension funds are also taking the opportunity to promote their domestic investment plans on the sidelines of the summit.

Tuesday marks the main programming of the summit, with sector-specific panels and an opening keynote by Carney.

Attendees were welcomed with a private dinner at the Art Gallery of Ontario on Monday night. The Prime Minister’s Office says the menu including smoked Arctic char, bison short rib and roasted pear was all Canadian-sourced.

The summit has attracted the heads of some of the world’s largest asset managers, including BlackRock CEO and chairman Larry Fink and Blackstone president Jon Gray. Other attendees hail from Australia, Singapore, Denmark, Qatar, Indonesia and more.

Police equipped with high-visibility green vests, batons and helmets shut down traffic in the blocks surrounding the gallery in downtown Toronto in the late afternoon as large black SUVs dropped off VIPs. Armoured vehicles, police buses and horse-mounted officers were also on hand around the art gallery.

Officers allowed some attendees arriving by foot to pass through the barricades. Housing Minister Gregor Robertson arrived via rental bike in a striped suit after a day of meetings about his infrastructure portfolio.

By 7:30 p.m., a group of around 100 demonstrators who had marched from Nathan Phillips Square amassed in front of police barricades. One attendee held a sign that read, “No deals behind closed doors.”

Organizers of the group, which included representatives of labour unions, Indigenous leaders, and climate and housing advocates, say they reject the idea of leaving Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs and they worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said in a social media post Monday that Canada would be attracting more investment right now if not for federal policies that add costs and delays to proposed projects.

He accused Carney of failing to deliver for Canadians over his first year and a half in office.

“Speeches, summits and symbolic signing ceremonies do not grow the economy, or pay people’s mortgages and groceries. That takes results,” Poilievre said.

Earlier Monday, Ottawa announced a tweak to tax policy aimed at making Canada more attractive to international investors.

The federal government said in a press release Monday that investors putting $1 billion or more into the Canadian economy will now get priority access to a program that offers binding decisions from the Canada Revenue Agency.

Through the existing Advance Income Tax Rulings program, qualifying investors can get clarity on how income tax law will apply before they commit capital.

“When investors are considering major projects, certainty matters,” Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said in a media statement.

“By prioritizing advance tax rulings for investments of $1 billion or more, we are giving them the clarity and predictability they need to invest with confidence, create opportunities and help build Canada’s economic future.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

— with files from David Baxter and Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa and Kathryn Mannie and Maan Alhmidi in Toronto

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: The deal in question was a massive data centre expansion planned by Bell in Saskatchewan, a move that the Montreal-based telecom giant’s CEO Mirko Bibic said will require $50 billion in capital investment to complete.

content_blocks.text: In the room for the announcement was Carney and bipartisan pair of former prime ministers — Liberal Jean Chrétien and Conservative Stephen Harper — the latter of whom will deliver closing remarks at the inaugural investment summit on Tuesday.

content_blocks.text: The event is part of Carney’s bid to improve Canada’s reputation in the eyes of investors after years of stagnant business investment. stories.title: Indigenous turnout remains low in Quebec amid calls for political inclusion
stories.summary: Montreal - There are a number of signs scattered along the suburban streets of the Mohawk community of Kahnawake, across the river from Montreal.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A few of them have messages that read “Every Child Matters” or “This is Mohawk Land.” Some feature the local language of Kanien’kéha.

But election campaign posters or signs are nowhere to be found in Kahnawake, even though a Quebec general election is only a few weeks away.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

“We don’t want to participate or be involved in (the elections) in any way, nor do we want it to be right in our face,” said Mohawk Council of Kahnawake Grand Chief Cody Diabo.

Turnout at provincial elections is close to nil in the Mohawk community of Kahnawake. Numbers from the province’s electoral oversight body, Élections Québec, show it has been under one per cent at almost every Quebec election since 2007, except in 2012, where it reached 1.87 per cent. (Sept. 14, 2026)

The Canadian Press

If someone tried to put up a sign, they’re swiftly taken down, said Diabo.

Recently, a video of someone tearing down a sign of Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon that had been installed at the outskirts of Kahnawake made the rounds online. In the video, a man appears to use a sledgehammer to knock out the wooden stakes propping up the poster at the edge of the highway.

Diabo said that most people in the community view both provincial and federal elections as if they were taking place in a different country.

Numbers compiled over the past two decades reflect how Kahnawake and many other Indigenous communities in Quebec have largely turned away from participating in Quebec elections.

In May, the province’s electoral oversight agency, Élections Québec, published data showing the average voter turnout for provincial elections in Indigenous communities in Quebec was at about 19 per cent since 2007, compared to close to 68 per cent provincewide.

These rates vary from community to community.

In Wendake, a community in the Quebec City region, 1012 out of 1691 registered voters cast their ballots in 2022.

Turnout has been much lower in Akwesasne, where no one voted in 2022 even though the community had 1423 registered voters. Over the past two decades, only one person has voted in a Quebec election in the community, which is located in the southwestern part of the province, overlapping with Ontario and New York. The single vote was cast in the 2018 election.

In Kahnawake in 2022, 20 out of 2313 registered voters cast their ballots in the provincial riding of Châteauguay. Overall, the voter turnout in Kahnawake has been under one per cent in every Quebec election since 2007, except for 2012, when there was a turnout of 1.87 per cent.

Despite the low turnout, the provincial agency isn’t campaigning to increase voter participation. Instead, it’s focusing on making sure that voting is accessible, spokesperson Julie St-Arnaud-Drolet said.

Part of those efforts include sending out trilingual documents with voting information in French, English and local languages to post office boxes in Inuit, Cree and Naskapi communities.

“We understand their history, and the goal is not necessarily to boost voter turnout, but rather to ensure that voting is accessible to those who wish to vote,” she said.

In Kahnawake, a number of community members approached by The Canadian Press seemed surprised when asked about the elections. They were quick to point out that they don’t vote on the provincial or federal levels.

Diabo explained that Kahnawake follows the principle of the Two Row Wampum, an agreement of mutual respect and non-interference with Quebec and Canada represented by a belt of parallel purple and white beads.

“We’re staying in our lane, and we expect the federal and provincial governments to stay in their lane. So that’s why we don’t participate in their governing system,” he said.

Ideally, he would like that principle to be applied to legislation as well, with the Quebec government staying out of the community’s affairs. But he knows the provincial government can make sweeping decisions that impact Kahnawake.

While Kahnawake is keeping its distance from provincial elections, some Indigenous politicians have embraced Quebec politics.

Alexis Wawanoloath is one of the few Indigenous people who were elected to represent ridings in Quebec’s national assembly.

Voters in the riding of Abitibi-Est riding elected Wawanoloath, who ran for the Parti Québécois, in 2007. He held that seat for a year, until the minority Liberal government triggered another election in 2008 and he lost his seat.

As he was campaigning to get elected, he received mixed responses from First Nations communities in his riding, with some of them showing support.

“For others, because of my position with a sovereigntist party, they saw it as a kind of betrayal. Others thought that just the fact that I was running, no matter the party, legitimized a system that shouldn’t be ours,” he said.

Once he was elected, he had more time to digest these messages.

“To be called a traitor and things like that, I found it hard. But to see that I could bring hope and be a spokesperson, it’s certain I felt driven by that mission,” he said.

Natural Resources Minister Kateri Champagne Jourdain, a member of the Innu nation, is seeking re-election in the north shore riding of Duplessis, where she grew up.

She said she understands those who choose not to participate in elections, but she believes Indigenous communities should make their voices heard by voting.

In Quebec, Indigenous people living on reserve got the right to vote in 1969, almost three decades after women got the right to vote in 1940, according to Élections Québec.

“Those rights were won through the sweat of struggle and advocacy — just like women’s right to vote, it was the same for Indigenous people. If we waged those battles, it was because it was important,” she said.

In the current campaign, party leaders have highlighted the need for communication with Indigenous communities.

“It’s up to us to pass on that passion for voting. I know that many Indigenous nations don’t fully identify with the Quebec political system, but it is up to politicians to encourage the exercise of that right to vote,” said Quebec liberal party leader Charles Milliard.

Québec Solidaire spokesperson Yssia Tormin said the party wants to decolonize the political system.

“In our view, First Nations and Inuit people participate little in elections because the other parties show no interest in them,” she wrote in an email to The Canadian Press.

For his part, St-Pierre Plamondon said he hopes to have a conversation with each nation to try to gauge their interest in the elections.

“I will make myself available for that, in which case maybe we will get higher participation. But some nations will say, ‘This is you. We are a separate nation and we’re not interested,’ in which case we have to respect that too,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

RR[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/tech-companies-are-implementing-age-assurance-tech-here-s-how-it-works/article_dd916a36-b819-5fbe-811c-243128e25f01.html)

By Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press

So what is “age assurance”?

Age assurance is the umbrella term used for efforts by tech platforms to determine the age of a user. It includes age declarations — those “click to verify you’re 18” boxes that internet users have been encountering for a long time.

But more recently, tech companies have been incorporating “age estimation.” That includes the use of AI technology to estimate a user’s age based on factors like their online behaviour or the images they post. “Age verification” is any method that requires a user to prove their age — the use of government ID, for example.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

What is Google doing?

Google said last year it would begin rolling out age assurance in the U.S. On Monday, it announced it would expand the technology to Canada.

Google’s approach looks at factors like a user’s search queries and the types of videos they’ve looked at on YouTube. The company says it won’t collect any additional information for age assurance.

Users who are identified as underage by Google have additional protections placed on their accounts. They include measures like turning on tools that remind users to take a break, placing safeguards on content recommendations, disabling personalized advertising and restricting access to apps that are adults-only.

If the tech mistakenly identifies an adult as being under 18, they’ll be able to prove their age using such tools as a government ID, a selfie, or a credit card check.

Google says that for those users who use a government ID, it will store the date of birth in their account and delete the ID after a short period of time. It says it will use the service PrivateID to analyze selfies, which will tell Google whether it believes the user is of age. Google says PrivateID doesn’t provide it with the selfie or the precise age of the user, or retain the image.

What is Meta doing?

If Meta suspects the person behind an account is under 18, it places them in a teen account. The settings on teen accounts include additional protections limiting who can contact the user and the content they can view. It uses AI to remove individuals it believes are under 13 from its services entirely.

Meta said in a blog post it uses AI to “analyze entire profiles for contextual clues — such as birthday celebrations or mentions of school grades — to determine if an account likely belongs to someone underage.”

That work includes looking at posts, comments, bios and captions. “If we determine an account May be underage, it will be deactivated and the account holder will need to provide proof of age through our age verification process to prevent their account from being deleted,” Meta said.

The company said in May it would also begin using visual analysis, which “allows our AI to scan photos and videos for visual clues about a person’s age.” It said the AI doesn’t identify the person in the image or use facial recognition.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Google to begin using age assurance tech to identify underage accounts in Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — Google is bringing its age assurance technology — which uses artificial intelligence to detect underage users — to Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Google is bringing its age assurance technology — which uses artificial intelligence to detect underage users — to Canada.

“Our age estimation model uses machine learning to interpret a variety of signals already associated with a user’s account, such as the types of information a user has searched for or the categories of videos they’ve watched on YouTube,” the company said in a blog post Monday.

The company says that if the technology identifies someone as underage, their Google account will be changed to include additional protections, such as safeguards on content recommendations.

If it mistakenly identifies an adult as being under 18, the company says that person will be able to prove their age using things like a government ID or a selfie.

“In the coming days, we’ll begin to gradually roll out this technology in Canada, carefully monitoring progress as we expand its availability,” Jeanette Patell, director of government affairs and public policy at Google Canada, said in the post.

She said the company won’t be collecting any new information that isn’t already associated with the user’s account.

“Age assurance technology is becoming more widely available, and we’re encouraged to see its increasing adoption by other companies in recent months,” Patell wrote.

“While some would like a system that imposes a universal arbiter of age, we believe that liability and responsibility rest with every service owner — the developer, the publisher, the app creator — because they know their users and services best.”

The increasing use of age assurance technology comes as governments around the world, including in Canada, move to implement age restrictions for social media.

Meta has already started using AI to identify underage users and place them in teen accounts in Canada. The company said in September it would expand testing of the technology to countries outside the United States., including Canada.

Meta uses AI to look at context clues, such as birthday celebrations, to identify accounts that May be underage. In May, it said it would add “visual analysis” as a technique — which involves AI scanning photos and videos for “visual clues” to a user’s age.

Meta promised to implement child protection measures, including stronger measures to identify underage users, as part of a massive recent legal settlement in the United States. But the company has confirmed those changes won’t be coming to Canada.

Google’s announcement comes after the Liberal government introduced digital safety Bill C-34.

The legislation, which has not yet become law, would force social media platforms to at least temporarily block access for kids under 16. The government has not yet decided how age verification would work and has said it will consult with platforms on specific methods.

In December, Australia became the first country to implement age restrictions for social media. It introduced a law that requires social media platforms to take reasonable steps to keep kids under 16 from using their services. The law doesn’t include standards for age verification.

In the United Kingdom, legislation sets out seven separate methods of age verification for legal access to adult content.

They include facial age estimation (which involves a third-party service using a live image to estimate age), a digital ID, or using a credit card, a mobile network operator or a bank to verify age. It also allows for the use of email to estimate age through a process that looks at where an email address has been used previously.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 14, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: The Star profiled Andrew Azevedo’s five years in isolation. Now his Ontario hospital has been ordered to take action
stories.summary: The Ontario Review Board has ordered Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care to implement a number of measures "recognizing the harm done by seclusion."
stories.author: Jacques Gallant
stories.content:
Family photos of Andrew Azevedo as a child. He’s spend the last five years in seclusion at Ontario’s Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care.

Arlyn McAdorey/Toronto Star

Investigations

20 Years in Isolation

The Ontario Review Board has ordered Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care to implement measures “recognizing the harm done by seclusion.”

Updated at 2:58 p.m.

Arlyn McAdorey/Toronto Star[](http://www.thestar.com/news/investigations/the-star-profiled-andrew-azevedo-s-five-years-in-isolation-now-his-Ontario-hospital-has-been-ordered-to-take-action/article_f7c85024-6f6a-49d8-b365-bfc9cd72bf7e.html)

ByJacques Gallant Courts and Justice Reporter

An independent oversight body has officially recognized that seclusion is harmful and has ordered Ontario’s only maximum-security psychiatric hospital to take action to reduce a mentally ill patient’s time in isolation.

It’s a stunning decision from the Ontario Review Board (ORB) — which had previously been criticized for its lax approach to the plight of patients in long-term seclusion — and one that could call into question the prolonged isolation of other patients at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care in Penetanguishene.

The decision comes amid the Star's continuing investigation, 20 Years in Isolation, which has revealed that Waypoint is locking patients up in sparsely furnished rooms alone, sometimes for years on end, a practice described as "egregious,"unlike anything done elsewhere in North America and akin to torture.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Andrew Azevedo, a 39-year-old man with schizophrenia who was profiled in the Star in April, has been deemed unfit to stand trial for allegedly assaulting a psychiatrist and has spent the last five years in seclusion due to what the hospital describes as persistent aggressive behaviour caused by his hallucinations.

Andrew Azevedo’s doctor at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care attributes his improvement to a change in medication — not the public attention.

In what’s known as a disposition, the ORB ordered Waypoint on Thursday to implement a number of measures in Azevedo’s case, “recognizing the harm done by seclusion.”

Among other things, the board ordered that Waypoint create a staff training program specific to Azevedo’s needs that will ensure “seclusion is minimized and liberty is maximized”; offer Azevedo a minimum of two hours of seclusion relief a day, not including family visits and showers; daily in-person examinations before deciding whether his seclusion should be continued; weekly communication between his treatment team and family; and clear documentation outlining why seclusion was deemed necessary.

The detailed reasons for the disposition from the five-member ORB panel will be released at a later date.

“It is certainly valuable and notable that the board has specifically acknowledged that there are harms associated with seclusion; I think that is new and very important,” said Azevedo’s lawyer, Anita Szigeti, an expert on mental health law who has frequently appeared before the board.

She said the Star’s investigation, coupled with “the public’s increasing awareness of the situation,” would not have been lost on the board.

“It seems obvious to most people that there are significant harms associated with seclusion, but it has been shockingly and remarkably difficult to get anyone with a position of authority or oversight to acknowledge that.”

Waypoint — which had urged the board to not make any orders — has the option of appealing to the Ontario Court of Appeal.Hospital CEO Dr. Nadiya Sunderji said they’re reviewing the disposition and awaiting the reasons “which will assist our review.”

The hospital has refused to say how many patients are in seclusion, though it was revealed at Azevedo’s ORB hearing last month that there are 11 secluded patients just in his 20-bed unit.

The Star’s investigation has revealed how Waypoint has been keeping patients in continuous isolation for as long as20 years and counting in the case of Camelott Hamblett. This despite the fact that seclusion is meant to be the option of last resort to deal with a patient who poses an imminent risk of bodily harm to themselves or others.

The ORB, made up of retired judges, lawyers, doctors and laypersons, annually reviews the cases of people found not criminally responsible or unfit to stand trial, to determine if they should remain detained in hospital or released and under what conditions.

The board also has a duty to inquire into a patient’s treatment and living conditions and has the legal authority to order the hospital to implement measures to assist patients in their rehabilitation.

The ORB also ordered Thursday that Azevedo is still unfit to stand trial and should remain detained at Waypoint — something agreed to by all the parties. The board ordered that Azevedo’s case come back before them early— in six months— “to obtain an update on progress made by Waypoint regarding the above directions and the accused’s seclusion status.”

The disposition is a marked departure from what other panels of the board did in previous years, when no orders were issued to try to end Azevedo’s time in seclusion, and some decisions made but a passing reference to his status.

In the wake of the Star’s reporting, Azevedo’s doctor declared at his ORB hearing last month that he was on the cusp of being released from seclusion— which could happen as early as this week— and Waypoint’s lawyer pointed to this progress in arguing that the board shouldn’t order the hospital to do anything further.

The board clearly disagreed, and Azevedo’s family said they were “deeply grateful,” saying the disposition validates their concerns that the hospital was not doing enough to help him.

The wording in the disposition is important, because for the last five years Waypoint “insisted that seclusion is absolutely clinically necessary,” said Azevedo’s sister-in-law, Susan.

The board “made specific orders with the intention of improving Andrew’s daily life, but the sad part is that all of these things should have already been a part of his care plan.”

Andrew Azevedo and his lawyer Anita Szigeti, ON the monitor, appear before the ORB panel.

Alexandra Newbould illustration

Some of the board’s orders are in line with recommendations made by Andrea Monteiro, who previously held senior roles in the correctional system and prepared an independent assessment of Azevedo’s case for his ORB hearing.

In her report, she said prolonged seclusion would meet the United Nations’ definition of solitary confinement and that patients at Waypoint are being held in conditions that the UN has “deemed to constitute torture” in similar settings.

Monteiro found that patients’ seclusion status was being maintained without them being seen in person by a doctor and without a reason being noted, and that due to a lack of staff, patients were sometimes spending an entire day in seclusion without any relief.

Sunderji has said the hospital “categorically” rejects Monteiro’s findings regarding torture, while the chair of the hospital’s board, Steve Parry, said he is “fully aligned” with the CEO.

Monteiro told the Star that she was “extremely pleased” to see some of her recommendations incorporated into the disposition. As she said during her testimony at Azevedo’s hearing, she is not a seclusion abolitionist, but said that when seclusion is used, it should not be indefinite, the impact on the patient must be “given extensive consideration,” and there must be rigorous oversight.

“I think the board recognized the importance of appropriately balancing the safety and security of the hospital and their staff while also acknowledging the harmful effects that long-term seclusion can have on an individual patient and their family,” she said.

Because the board’s decision only applies to Azevedo, it raises the question of whether the board will now take a similar approach when dealing with the cases of other secluded patients at Waypoint.

Jake Gordon is being released from seclusion at Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care. His mom credits the Star’s investigation for the change.

Richard Schneider, a clinical psychologist and semi-retired judge of the Ontario Court of Justice who chaired the ORB from 2012 to 2023, said he’s never seen a disposition with that much detail, saying any concerns a panel May have are usually reserved for the reasons that come out later.

“I was happy to see it and sort of thinking: ‘Why haven’t we done that in the past?’” Schneider said.

He said the Star’s investigation has “thankfully” put the issues surrounding long-term seclusion in the spotlight and on the board’s radar.

“My initial impressions are this is great,” he said. “Maybe it will signal a new level of specific direction to the hospital in future dispositions. This disposition could be a bit of an ice-breaker.”

But then there are also patients in seclusion at Waypoint who do not fall under the Orb’s jurisdiction, as they are not charged with any crimes, but are admitted involuntarily under the Mental Health Act. This includes Jake Gordon, a 30-year-old man with schizophrenia profiled by the Star last weekend who spent five years in seclusion.

Surveillance footage shared with the Star captured Gordon walking around his tiny room in circles during a six-and-a-half-hour period, leaving his mother, Diane Worden, “horrified.”

Szigeti reiterated her calls for an independent review of the use of seclusion at Waypoint.

“Ultimately, I think what the Star’s investigation is revealing is that the issues are bigger than one secluded individual,” she said.

The ORB, made up of retired judges, lawyers, doctors and laypersons, annually reviews the cases of people found not criminally responsible or unfit to stand trial, to determine if they should remain detained in hospital or released and under what conditions.

National Bank of Canada alleges that Keel Digital Solutions and its subsidiary Get A-Head as well as a third company, Amerimind AI, have not made payments on loans and Mastercard accounts since last March.

Ryan Remiorz/The Canadian Press file photo[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Ontario/bank-moves-to-place-company-linked-to-skills-fund-scandal-into-receivership/article_fe950279-b7ae-4710-abc3-391b64a36307.html)

ByMoira Welsh Queen's Park Bureau

A Canadian bank is going to court in an attempt to recoup $4.5 million by forcing receivership on a company caught in Ontario’s Skills Development Fund scandal.

In an application filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, National Bank of Canada alleges that Keel Digital Solutions and its subsidiary Get A-Head as well as a third company, Amerimind AI, incorporated in the United States, have not made payments on loans and Mastercard accounts since last March.

“It appears that there is no plan in place to repay indebtedness,” said National Bank’s application for a court-ordered “receiver” under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act,filed in late July. Receivers are considered neutral parties and can take control of a company’s assets and operations to protect creditors’ interests. In some cases, receivership can ultimately lead to bankruptcy or liquidation. National Bank did not respond to the Star’s request for comment.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

A virtual court hearing is now scheduled for Oct. 5.

Provincial Politics

The province alleges Keel Digital Solutions provided “false and misleading” claims related to its performance, expenses or unspent funds.

Keel Digital, the parent company of Get A-Head, offered government-funded virtual mental health supports for students and peer training for first responders, but last fall it was swept into the controversy that followed the auditor general’s scathing report on the apparent politicization of Premier Doug Ford’s $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund.

The public paper trail behind Keel’s troubles with the province did not begin with the fund, which falls under the Ministry of Labour.

Officially, it started last fall — with the Ministry of Colleges and Universities— when the government said it gave the Ontario Provincial Police the results of a forensic audit into payments to Keel. It was not until the new year, in January, that Keel’s contracts with the skills fund were questioned through a lawsuit that cited issues under both ministries.

During daily opposition attacks in the fall question period, Ford and then-labour minister David Piccini defended decisions to award millions of dollars to applicants despite low scores assigned by ministry staff evaluating funding applications.

Piccini is awaiting the findings of an investigation by integrity commissioner Cathryn Motherwell into alleged ethics breaches. However, in Thursday’s cabinet shuffle, Ford appointed him as minister of infrastructure, which oversees massive public construction projects and a 2026-2027 budget that is expected to reach $3.2 billion.

As the media storm about the fund ensued in 2025, the Ontario government announced it had sent the results of a forensic audit into Keel and Get A-Head’s 2023 contract with the Ministry of Colleges and Universities to the OPP for review by its anti-racket squad. The OPP later launched an investigation. Keel and Get A-Head claimed the government was using them as a political ”scapegoat” to deflect from the controversy.

National Bank’s legal documents note the audit, the criminal investigation — and the province’s next move.

In early January, Ontario filed a civil lawsuit against Keel and Get A-Head, claiming they owed $22.5 million to the colleges and universities ministry and another $2.7 million to the labour ministry’s skills development fund for “false and misleading reporting to artificially increase” the funding it received. Keel and Get A-Head filed a defence and a counterclaim for $98.7 million in damages.

“As a result of this litigation,” National Bank’s legal document noted, “the respondents have lost their primary source of revenue and have no other material customers.”

Amerimind AI was not named in the government lawsuits, but National Bank’s filing says it was incorporated in Delaware and that its president is Rob Godfrey, one of Keel’s directors.

In 2023, Amerimind AI guaranteed “all of the debts and liabilities” of Keel and Get A-Head, the bank’s court documents said.

The Star sent Godfrey three requests for comment through Keel’s spokesperson, who said he would not be responding.

Asked about National Bank’s attempt to force the companies into receivership, Keel’s former chief operating officer Jay Fischbach said, “Keel and Amerimind do not have any ongoing business activities and all employees, including myself and the CEO have been terminated. Over 100 employees also lost their jobs due to this baseless attack on the company.

The Star, simplified

“We were all terminated between Nov. 25 and Apr. 26,” Fischbach said, a decision “approved by the board.” Godfrey is listed as a director of Keel Digital Solutions.

Keel and Get A-Head, he wrote in an email, were “accused of fraud without evidence and without the government following its standard practice of providing its draft audit findings” for the company’s response.

“The real loser in this (are) the students and first responders who relied on the Keel platform for mental health,” he said. “To this end over 25,000 students and parents had signed a petition requesting these mental health supports to return.”

National Bank’s documents said that once Keel and the other companies stopped making payments late last March, the bank reviewed the account activity and found “the respondents May have diverted their banking activity to TD Bank, leaving (National Bank) with no visibility as to the respondents’ operations.” A TD Bank spokesperson said the company could not comment since “this is a matter before the courts.”

Keel, Get A-Head and Amerimind AI all shared a Toronto office on the 35th floor at 2 Bloor St. E., National’s documents said, but they “no longer occupy those premises.”

A virtual court hearing is now scheduled for Oct. 5.

The province alleges Keel Digital Solutions provided “false and misleading” claims related to its performance, expenses or unspent funds.

Keel Digital, the parent company of Get A-Head, offered government-funded virtual mental health supports for students and peer training for first responders, but last fall it was swept into the controversy that followed the auditor general’s scathing report on the apparent politicization of Premier Doug Ford’s $2.5-billion Skills Development Fund.

Officially, it started last fall — with the Ministry of Colleges and Universities— when the government said it gave the Ontario Provincial Police the results of a forensic audit into payments to Keel. It was not until the new year, in January, that Keel’s contracts with the skills fund were questioned through a lawsuit that cited issues under both ministries.

During daily opposition attacks in the fall question period, Ford and then-labour minister David Piccini defended decisions to award millions of dollars to applicants despite low scores assigned by ministry staff evaluating funding applications.

Piccini is awaiting the findings of an investigation by integrity commissioner Cathryn Motherwell into alleged ethics breaches. However, in Thursday’s cabinet shuffle, Ford appointed him as minister of infrastructure, which oversees massive public construction projects and a 2026-2027 budget that is expected to reach $3.2 billion.

Keel and Get A-Head filed a defence and a counterclaim for $98.7 million in damages.
“As a result of this litigation,” National Bank’s legal document noted, “the respondents have lost their primary source of revenue and have no other material customers.”
Amerimind AI was not named in the government lawsuits, but National Bank’s filing says it was incorporated in Delaware and that its president is Rob Godfrey, one of Keel’s directors.
In 2023, Amerimind AI guaranteed “all of the debts and liabilities” of Keel and Get A-Head, the bank’s court documents said.
The Star sent Godfrey three requests for comment through Keel’s spokesperson, who said he would not be responding.

Asked about National Bank’s attempt to force the companies into receivership, Keel’s former chief operating officer Jay Fischbach said, “Keel and Amerimind do not have any ongoing business activities and all employees, including myself and the CEO have been terminated. Over 100 employees also lost their jobs due to this baseless attack on the company.

“We were all terminated between Nov. 25 and Apr. 26,” Fischbach said, a decision “approved by the board.” Godfrey is listed as a director of Keel Digital Solutions.

Keel and Get A-Head, he wrote in an email, were “accused of fraud without evidence and without the government following its standard practice of providing its draft audit findings” for the company’s response.

“The real loser in this (are) the students and first responders who relied on the Keel platform for mental health,” he said. “To this end over 25,000 students and parents had signed a petition requesting these mental health supports to return.”

National Bank’s documents said that once Keel and the other companies stopped making payments late last March, the bank reviewed the account activity and found “the respondents May have diverted their banking activity to TD Bank, leaving (National Bank) with no visibility as to the respondents’ operations.” A TD Bank spokesperson said the company could not comment since “this is a matter before the courts.”
Keel, Get A-Head and Amerimind AI all shared a Toronto office on the 35th floor at 2 Bloor St. E., National’s documents said, but they “no longer occupy those premises.”

stories.title: Many people with nerve pain describe it as 'worse than death.' Can ketamine help?
stories.summary: Toronto studies see some success in treating pain, depression. But ketamine’s potential is still poorly understood.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
Carmelina Crudo said she experienced what some call “the opening” when she first tried ketamine therapy. While the therapy didn’t completely take her pain away, she said she learned to “surrender” to the pain, which has been transformative.

Nick Lachance/Toronto Star

Twitter

Supplied by Dr. Akash Goel

ByOmar Mosleh Staff Reporter

Most of Carmelina Crudo’s life has been etched in pain.

At 21, a major car accident left her with a spine injury. Then came fibromyalgia. A slipped disc. Lyme disease. More bacterial infections than she can count.

At one point, she was taking 52 pills a day, over 20 prescriptions, just to keep her head above water.

“The pain was a 10 out of 10 every minute of every day,” Crudo, 63, said from her home in Bolton, seated on a heating pad to soothe her nerve pain. “It was just 20 years of hell.”

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

But then she came across a clinical trial for a novel treatment that would change her life: ketamine combined with psychotherapy for nerve pain.

Ketamine is widely used in Canada as a general anesthetic for both humans and animals, and can be administered off-label by medical professionals in clinical settings for certain mental health conditions and pain management. A version called esketamine, a prescription nasal spray, was approved by Health Canada in 2020 for treatment-resistant depression. It’s also used recreationally for its psychedelic properties, and was widely publicized when “Friends” actor Matthew Perry’s abuse of the drug led to his death.

Ketamine has been a life-saver for people with certain mental disorders, experts say— but improper use can prove fatal.

But there is emerging evidence that ketamine could be “transformative” for treating pain and mental illnesses because of its unique properties and rapid onset of action, scientists say. Still, we’re only beginning to fully comprehend the therapeutic potential of ketamine; how exactly it works and what other conditions it could help is still not completely understood.

“We don’t know with the utmost certainty how these things are all coming together,” said Dr. Roger McIntyre, an international leading expert on ketamine therapy, based in Toronto.

It’s also being studied for conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

“What unites all these conditions is that they are associated with significant distress,” said Dr. Joshua Rosenblat, a psychiatrist and clinician investigator at University Health Network’s Krembil Brain Institute. With ketamine, “there seems to be a reduction in distress and sort of this dissociation between the pain, the suffering and the person.”

Rosenblat recently led a UHN clinical study, published this month in Jama Psychiatry, to explore the efficacy and safety of ketamine for Treatment-Resistant Bipolar Depression. Rosenblat said one in three patients do not get better with traditional medications, hence why more effective treatments are needed.

The randomized clinical trial, involving 68 adults with bipolar I or II disorder,found that repeated ketamine infusions, which are delivered via an intravenous drip under medical supervision,significantly improved symptoms in adults with treatment-resistant bipolar depression, with 35 per cent of participants experiencing a response, compared to 11.8 per cent in a control group.

He noted while it wasn’t the focus of the study, participants said the treatment “completely transformed their life, their quality of life is so much better, they’re engaging, they’re happy, everyone around them is noticing how much better they’re doing.”

What makes ketamine unique compared to conventional antidepressants and painkillers is that it targets multiple systems in the brain responsible not only for physical pain, but also how we perceive and process pain, said McIntyre, a professor at the University of Toronto and head of the Mood Disorders Psychopharmacology Unit at UHN.

“Pain is not just physical, but it’s also an emotional and psychological experience,” McIntyre said. “Ketamine is an equal opportunity employer.”

About one in 10 Canadians suffer from chronic pain, and about half of those patients have nerve pain. One study found that 17 per cent of people with chronic nerve pain described it as “worse than death.”

Dr. Akash Goel, an attending anesthesiologist and clinician — scientist at St. Michael’s Hospital and assistant professor at U of T, led a Unity Health pilot clinical study involving 30 people to explore combining ketamine treatment with psychotherapy to treat nerve pain.

The study found that 80 per cent of patients who combined the therapies experienced a “meaningful reduction in pain interference,” which is a different metric than pain intensity, looking at how pain affects a patient’s quality of life.

“When I see these patients, their suffering is extraordinary … This begins to tear apart their ability to communicate with their partner, their ability to work, to function,” Goel said.

“So how do we help this person reconstruct their life?”

Crudo said her pain was so constant that managing it became her full-time job. She tried many treatments over the years: a cornucopia of pharmaceuticals, physiotherapy, psychotherapy, to name a few.

When she learned of the Unity Health clinical trial, she was ready to try something new.

The ketamine infusions relieve her pain for about 24 hours. But it’s what came after that has been life-changing. She said during one of the treatments she had an experience that was “magical” — she describes floating on a cloud, the sun on her face, overcome with a sense of peace and calm.

“I realized as days went on, I could access this place in my brain,” she said. “And so I started using that as an anchor for when my body was too much.”

While Crudo still lives with pain and regularly undergoes various treatments to manage it, she said the ketamine therapy, combined with psychotherapy, has brought her to a place where it no longer consumes her.

“It has literally taken all the negative thoughts out of my head … I’m finally at a place now where I can live my life.”

Ketamine is believed to treat mood disorders by promoting neuroplasticity, the brain’s ability to create new neural pathways and strengthen connections between neurons (brain cells). It does this by targeting multiple receptors, leading to a rapid increase in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf), sometimes called the brain’s fertilizer, which plays an important role in memory, learning and the growth of new neurons.

This can help people break out of entrenched, negative thought patterns that underpin conditions such as depression. Goel compares it to clearing weeds from a garden.

“What we think the ketamine does … is kind of catalyze this removal of weeds so that you can plant seeds and allow new flowers to grow, which is the psychotherapy,” Goel said.

Most antidepressants take four to six weeks to reach their full effect. Ketamine works much more rapidly, potentially showing improvement within 24-48 hours.

The Star, simplified

Breaking news, interactive polls, video, and voice notes. Star stories you’ll want to share, delivered where you’re already chatting. Follow the Star on WhatsApp.

“Ketamine goes straight to the lesion. It’s a fast track, so to speak,” McIntyre said. “That is transformative in psychiatry. So I think we’re still realizing the potential of ketamine.”

Crudo is still unsure how ketamine led to a such paradigm shift in her life, but said the treatments have made her happier and more at peace, and have strengthened her connection to God. Her faith has always anchored her, and similar to spiritual teachings, she said she learned to “surrender” to the pain.

“I can’t make this go away, there’s no cure, but I can find things to help me find joy in my day,” Crudo said.

“It’s not about getting better. It’s about living a better life.”
