stories.title: Stephen Harper to deliver closing speech at Carney's Investment Summit
stories.summary: Stephen Harper will deliver the closing speech of Prime Minister Mark Carney's first Canada Investment Summit Tuesday.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper will deliver the closing speech of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s first Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday.

A senior government source confirmed Harper’s long-rumoured participation in the Liberal prime minister’s event to National Post on Sunday.

The Canada Investment Summit in Toronto is Carney’s flagship event to pitch foreign and domestic investors on investing in Canadian projects. As part of the pitch, the government has circulated a list of over 160 projects that are seeking investments ranging from $25 million to hundreds of millions of dollars.

Harper’s participation is meant to send the message that attracting foreign capital to Canada is a cross-partisan exercise, said the source who requested anonymity to speak freely.

Harper, who speaks to Carney regularly since the latter was elected prime minister last spring, is the chairman of the Alberta Investment Management Corp, the province’s pension plan that manages over $200 billion.

Over one decade since leaving politics, Harper remains a venerated figure in many conservative circles. So, his participation in Carney’s flagship investment summit will be perceived by many as a tacit endorsement of the Liberal government’s strategy to attract foreign investment and shift Canada’s economic dependency away from the U.S.

Harper’s speech is expected to be open to media, a rarity for the former prime minister who has delivered few open-access speeches since leaving politics.

Pension investment bodies will feature heavily during Carney’s Investment Summit that will be held Monday and Tuesday. The prime minister will deliver the opening speech for the evening and Harper will close it.

John Graham, the president and CEO of Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, is also expected to deliver a keynote speech.

Among the 250 invited guests from more than 25 nations expected to attend are BlackRock Inc. chairman Larry Fink, Barclays PLC chief executive C.S. Venkatakrishnan and senior managers of pension funds and sovereign wealth giants from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) to Norway’s Norges Bank Investment Management.

A full list of attendees to the invitation-only event has not yet been released. But a high-level program circulated by the government shows there will be panels on critical mineral, defence, energy and artificial intelligence and “frontier” technology projects.

National Post, with files from Financial Post’s Barbara Shecter cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Carney’s investment summit to be met with protests
stories.summary: Hundreds of executives and global asset managers are set to arrive in Toronto for Canada's first-ever investment summit to get a look at major projects in development.
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
Protests are planned for the prime minister’s high-stakes summit aimed at attracting new investment to Canada, with organizers saying Mark Carney is keeping company with business leaders they say are exacerbating global crises.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada has an unprecedented opportunity to build up the economy as global investors descend in Toronto for a high-stakes summit, and teased that a number of deals have already been signed.

Hundreds of executives and global asset managers are arriving in Toronto for Canada’s first-ever investment summit to get a look at major projects in various stages of development.

Speaking Sunday evening at the Royal Ontario Museum, Carney told Canadian business leaders and politicians that the world is looking at Canada different, and that Canada should do the same.

“We have what the world wants: the energy, the resources, the talent, the technology and the capital,” Carney said.

“And our greatest strength is something that cannot be found on any balance sheet: trust,” he said, in an apparent jab at U.S. President Donald Trump.

Among those in attendance were Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez and Canada’s chief trade commissioner, Sara Wilshaw.

The summit is a key part of Carney’s plan for stimulating $1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years.

Carney said while those in the room May not always agree, nor do they need to, they all align on where Canada is going.

“There is a new consensus from Iqaluit to Victoria to Quebec City and St. Johns: Canada is taking control of our future,” he said. “We will build more, we will trade more with each other and the world, and we will create more sustainable prosperity here at home.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said invitees come from Kuwait, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Singapore, Qatar, Norway, Japan and Australia.

“This is about building relationships, opening doors and making the case that Ontario is one of the most investable places anywhere in the world,” Ford said in a media statement.

He said 15 major projects in Ontario are up for offer, including energy production and transmission, critical minerals and mining, AI and advanced manufacturing.

“We are building an economy that can compete with anyone, anywhere. That’s going to be my message throughout the Canada Investment Summit,” Ford said.

“Ontario has what the world needs and we’re going to make sure the world knows it.”

While Ford and Carney pitched the summit as an opportunity for investments in Canada, civil society groups say they’re keeping company with business leaders that are exacerbating global crises.

Demonstrators, including labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates, will mobilize Monday carrying a banner reading “The Many vs. The Money,” and plan “direct intervention” with attendees.

Organizers say they reject Carney’s plan to put Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs, and that they worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

— With files from Craig Lord and Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa

stories.title: $5M donation to Bluewater Health to fund future cardiac care
stories.summary: Bluewater Health has received its largest individual donation in the hospital foundation’s history, with $5 million from The Gordon Foundation set to support cardiac care and other patient needs.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Bluewater Health has received its largest individual donation in the hospital foundation’s history, with $5 million from The Gordon Foundation set to support cardiac care and other patient needs.

The donation includes $2 million for the development of future cardiac care services at Bluewater Health and $3 million to establish a permanent endowment for the hospital’s highest-priority needs.

The donation will also result in the hospital’s London Building being renamed the Gordon Family Patient Care Building. New signage is expected to be installed in November.

The Gordon Foundation endowment is expected to generate ongoing funding for patient care, to support the hospital and community for years to come.

Bluewater Health says the $2-million cardiac investment will help strengthen and expand local services as the Sarnia-Lambton community grows and ages.

“As our community grows and ages, we know the need for cardiac care closer to home will continue to grow with it,” said Dr. Mike Haddad, chief of staff and vice-president of medical affairs at Bluewater Health.

The hospital says the goal is to allow more patients to access advanced cardiac care locally instead of travelling outside Sarnia-Lambton.

Ron Gordon of The Gordon Foundation said the family is honoured to invest in the hospital’s future.

“We are honoured to make this investment in its future and help ensure that patients and families can continue to receive excellent care close to home for generations to come,” Gordon said.

stories.title: ‘Capital-T tough guy.’ Boxing legend George Chuvalo remembered for his resilience
stories.summary: In almost 100 fights, Canadian boxing titan George Chuvalo was never knocked out and never fell to the canvas.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
In almost 100 fights, Canadian boxing titan George Chuvalo was never knocked out and never fell to the canvas.

A five-time Canadian heavyweight champion and two-time world heavyweight challenger, Chuvalo died Saturday in Toronto on his 89th birthday.

As tributes were posted online Sunday from around the world, Chuvalo’s son Mitchell recalled how his father was an extraordinarily resilient man — in and outside the ring.

“He was a capital-T tough guy in every way,” he said in an interview Sunday.

“I always think about him transcending sport and boxing into another realm where even more people could identify with his life and his achievements.”

He is perhaps best known for his iron chin and his two acclaimed fights with fast-talking boxing icon Muhammad Ali. But Chuvalo’s boxing career stood in sharp contrast with his private life, which was marked by a profound level of tragedy.

His son Jesse took his own life in 1985 after developing an addiction to painkillers. Another son, Georgie Lee, died from a drug overdose in 1993. Four days later, Chuvalo’s wife Lynne was found dead with a suicide note.

And in 1996, his son Steven died in a hotel room with a needle in his arm.

Chuvalo spoke openly about being barely able to function after his family’s unimaginable losses. In 2013, he said he felt like he was suffocating every time he went to sleep.

During that dark time, however, he began his decades-long “Fight Against Drugs” campaign that took him to schools across the country.

“For casual sports fans, he’s remembered for his efforts against Muhammad Ali, where he displayed tremendous courage and resilience,” said Mitchell Chuvalo.

“Those things were foundational in his being able to go out and talk about the tragedies … that destroyed our family in so many ways … That tells you what kind of a constitution he had.”

Mitchell Chuvalo said his father’s depth of character was something that resonated with people long after his prizefighting career was over.

“My dad’s post-boxing life and his boxing life are indelibly connected,” he said. “He will always be remembered as a very giving individual — giving his emotions, giving his time, giving up his story, even though to recount it over and over again was torturous for him.”

Chuck (Spider) Jones, a Toronto-based boxing expert and longtime Chuvalo friend, posted a statement on Facebook noting Chuvalo’s private challenges and thanking the boxer for helping with his broadcasting career.

“Rest well champ,” said Jones, a member of the Canadian Boxing Hall of Fame. “You faced so many heartbreaking challenges throughout your years on Earth. Thank you for opening so many doors for me.”

Russ Anber, a Montreal-based trainer recently inducted into the International Boxing Hall of Fame, said Chuvalo personified Canadian boxing for a half a century.

“George Chuvalo was a friend and an inspiration to everyone in the boxing world in Canada, and around the globe,” Anber said in a social media post. “He epitomised the grit, toughness, courage and persistence, which future generations tried to emulate. The best chin in the history of the sport!”

The World Boxing Council, based in Mexico, issued a statement Saturday saying Chuvalo was widely regarded as “Canada’s greatest warrior.”

“He went to war against true titans during the heavyweight division’s golden era,” the council said, noting his clashes with George Foreman and Joe Frazier.

As for Chuvalo’s famed fights with Ali in 1966 and 1972, Mitchell Chuvalo recalled Ali’s telling assessment of his stocky rival after their first fight.

“He’s the toughest guy I ever fought,” Ali said at the time, having won the closely fought match after 15 rounds.

Mitchell Chuvalo said the brief assessment was remarkable because Ali was at his athletic peak when the match was held at Toronto’s Maple Leaf Gardens.

“George gave him his most difficult battle,” he said, recalling how his father was impressed with Ali’s incredibly fast hands and feet.

“Things were very closely contested in many of the rounds, but George meted out a lot of punishment … (Ali) had to go to St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto because he was urinating blood after the fight.”

Mitchell Chuvalo said no dates had been set for a funeral, but he said plans are in the works for a public event that will make room for many personal tributes.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 13, 2026.

Michael MacDonald, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney, Macron to meet as talks of stronger Canada-EU relationship ramp up
stories.summary: Carney has made it no secret he wants closer economic, security and political ties with the EU as Canada's relationship with the U.S. continues to worsen amid the trade war.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with the French president this week, showcasing efforts to strengthen energy and defence ties with the European ally.

The Prime Minister’s Office announced Carney will visit Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador, ON Sept. 20 where he’ll meet with President Emmanuel Macron.

The PMO says the pair will discuss deepening the countries’ partnership in “strategic sectors,” including aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies such as quantum, satellites and supercomputing.

Carney’s planned visit comes as the Wall Street Journal reports the prime minister is speeding up Canada’s pivot to Europe. It’s reported he’s even suggested to European leaders that Canada take on the title: “Associate Member of the European Union.”

Global News has reached out to the PMO, Macron’s office and the European Parliament for comment.

Carney’s visit with Macron is set to take place just days after the prime minister meets with his U.K. counterpart for the first time, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Much like Macron, the two leaders are expected to discuss defence, security, energy and AI.

0:38 French foreign minister says Canada could join EU

During his trip to Europe that begins Tuesday, Carney will also address the European Parliament in Strasbourg and attend the State of the European Union address.

Earlier this week, the EU’s ambassador to Canada said the bloc is crafting a new partnership with Ottawa unlike anything that currently exists, but did not provide specifics.

“What we have in mind is something different from what we have with other countries,” Geneviève Tuts said in an interview Wednesday with The Canadian Press. “That will be something unique.”

That partnership is still being carved out, but Tuts said it won’t look exactly like the arrangements the EU has with its neighbours like Switzerland and the U.K.

Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who speaks with Carney regularly, signalled support for Canada having a stronger relationship with the EU.

“Wouldn’t it be lovely if Canada was the 28th state of the European Union rather than the 51st state of the United States,” Stubb said during a speech in June.

The idea will be discussed when Carney visits this week, an invitation Tuts said was a rare gesture for a non-European leader.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre criticized both Carney’s trip and the report the prime minister is pursuing Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU.

“Mark Carney could not be more out of touch,” Poilievre said Sunday in a post on X.

Poilievre went on to say any such deal would not be about diversifying trade, and questioned if European border policies would apply in Canada or if small businesses would be “buried under the red tape of Eurocrats.”

He added he would ask these questions in Parliament but said the House of Commons is on summer break until Sept. 21.

The Opposition leader called on Carney to confirm if the Wall Street Journal report was true.

“We will Never be the 51st U.S. state. And we will Never be the 28th EU state,” Poilievre said.

No deal is expected at the meeting, only discussions, but Tuts said Brussels would then consult with member states on the deal. Canada would do the same with its provinces and territories. A possible announcement could, however, come at a late-October summit.

Carney has made it no secret he wants closer economic, security and political ties with the EU as Canada’s relationship with the U.S. continues to worsen amid the trade war.

“We will be looking to use the coming months to explore a deepening of that partnership across a broad range of areas and we’ll have more to say to that (next week) in Strasbourg,” Carney told reporters in Banff, Alta., this past Thursday, where his cabinet was gathering for a planning session.

Experts have said the EU is the “most obvious partner” in diversifying Canada’s trading relationships.

Christian Leuprecht told Global News that just as Canada could benefit from sourcing more of its military purchases from Europe as it works to dramatically boost defence spending, Europe could benefit from Canada’s supply of liquefied natural gas, oil and critical minerals.

On Saturday, President Donald Trump said Canada wants to reach a deal with the U.S. “very badly” and suggested an agreement could come “fairly soon” if Ottawa addresses his concerns about agricultural trade.

5:06 Carney says he remains in regular contact with Trump despite trade war

— with files from Global News’ Alex Boutillier and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney wants Canada to be an ‘associate member’ of the EU: report
stories.summary: Canadian and European Union officials say Prime Minister Mark Carney is racing toward deeper integration across the Atlantic Ocean.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Officials on both sides say the prime minister is racing toward deeper integration as the Canada-U.S. relationship deteriorates

Canada is not seeking to join the European Union as a full-fledged member, but Prime Minister Mark Carney is reportedly testing how close the country can get via deeper economic and societal integration.

According to the Wall Street Journal , the Canadian leader has suggested to some of his European peers that Canada should become the EU’s first-ever “associate member,” a status that doesn’t yet legally exist within the enclave. Moreover, the Journal reported that unnamed officials on both sides said the 27-member EU, traditionally rigid about who joins its ranks, is amenable to the concept.

While early, Carney has reportedly informed his officials the result “will be the reorienting of an economy and a society that for half a century has been dominated by the U.S.”

The bureaucratic talks are “terribly unsexy,” one Canadian official told the Journal, but they are “terribly consequential nonetheless.”

The news comes as Carney is set to address the European Parliament and meet with members “to strengthen Canada’s ties with the EU in trade, investment, and security.” His speech will come the day after EU President Ursula von der Leyen announces a new deal with Canada to broaden collaboration on defence, trade and other areas.

Meanwhile, ON Sept. 20th, the prime minister will return to Europe when he meets French President Emmanuel Macron in Saint-Pierre-and-Miquelon, a French archipelago colony of France about 25 kilometres south of Newfoundland, where his office said the two will discuss “partnership in strategic sectors, including aerospace, energy and critical minerals, and advanced technologies such as quantum, satellites, and supercomputing.”

His visit is the first official one made by a Canadian prime minister, AFP reported.

Some of these discussions are a continuation of the many that Carney has reportedly had in response to the souring of Canada’s deeply integrated relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump and his administration.

Instead of pulling Canada closer to the U.S. on America’s terms, the trade war has pushed Ottawa towards the EU and its “$21 trillion single market.”

The concept would allow Canada’s goods, services and workers in defence, energy, AI, and critical minerals to “move frictionlessly” in Europe.

“While there are multiple hurdles to dance around, European officials envision major Canadian companies could effectively lock in as single market suppliers for decades to come,” the Journal reported.

Unnamed officials said Macron and Carney have discussed the possibility of Canadians living and working in Europe without requiring a visa and that the prime minister has also expressed an interest in joining the EU’s study-abroad program, Erasmus+ — an exchange program supporting education, training, youth, and sport across Europe.

Canada and the EU are also examining underwater cables, the joint construction of data centres, cloud storage and new satellite networks that don’t involve U.S. tech giants, the Journal said. Carney is also keen to lay gas pipelines across the Atlantic and utilize icebreakers so Canadian fertilizer can be shipped through the Northwest Passage.

A lot of discussion occurred on the sidelines of this year’s G-7 leaders meeting in France, where officials from both sides reportedly outlined “11 stack items” to allow for deeper collaboration and less reliance on U.S. technologies, defence equipment and trade. One French official told the Journal they were shocked at how quickly their Canadian counterparts wanted to proceed on several policy cooperation areas.

Still, there has been some skepticism among some European officials that Carney’s ambitions aren’t grounded in reality, noting that 10 nations — including France and Italy — have yet to formally ratify the Canada-EU Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) after almost a decade. Others are trying to determine if Canada is using the EU as leverage in trade negotiations with the Trump administration, and some are concerned that if Canada is offered too good a deal as a non-member, some member nations May leave and request a similar arrangement.

There was a healthy amount of doubt, bordering on incredulity, from some Conservative MPs on X responding to the Journal story.

“What fresh hell is this,” York Centre’s Roman Baber wrote , adding that the EU is “falling apart” due to over-regulation, bad immigration policies and censorship.

“We are Canadian, we are not European. @MarkJCarney did not campaign on joining the EU and he did not consult Parliament!”

Calgary MP Shuv Majumdar said becoming the 28th member of the EU is as bad an idea as becoming the 51st state was and that Canada’s “sovereignty is not for sale… to anyone.”

“Prime Minister, can we please just have the self respect to build our own country with our own money and our own people,” he wrote . “Can we get competitive with Washington and the world, and unleash the economic powerhouse that Canadians demand and deserve?”

The 51st state was a bad idea. So too would be the EU’s 28th state. Our sovereignty is not for sale, not to America, not to Europe, not to Beijing, not to anyone. Prime Minister, can we please just have the self respect to build our own country with our own money and our own… https://t.co/X4qr292H9c — Shuv Majumdar (@shuvmajumdar) September 13, 2026

Elgin—St. Thomas—London South’s Andrew Lawton called the idea “asinine.”

“Now is the time to assert our sovereignty, not cede it to one of the most over-regulated, heavy handed bureaucracies in the world,” he posted Sunday.

Deputy Conservative Leader Melissa Lantsman said Canada is not a “franchise” other countries can “buy into.”

“Oh, and Canadians again learned about this from the Wall Street Journal, not Ottawa,” she posted . Never an election issue. No debate. No vote. Parliament hasn’t said a word.”

While overseas this week, Carney will also travel to the U.K. for a first meeting with its new prime minister, Andy Burnham, ON “defence and security, energy, artificial intelligence, and critical minerals.”

stories.title: Celine Dion kicks off 1st show in 6 years at Paris residency: ‘I missed this’
stories.summary: The Quebec superstar opened her show before nearly 33,000 people at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre marking an emotional comeback after what she described as a “rocky road.”
stories.author: Anja Conton
stories.content:
After nearly six years away from the concert stage, Céline Dion returned Saturday night with a fitting message: “On ne change pas”– we don’t change.

The Quebec superstar opened her show before nearly 33,000 people at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, outside Paris, marking an emotional comeback after what she described as a “rocky road.”

Dion thrilled the crowd with a two-and-a-half-hour performance that began about 40 minutes late, revisiting her career and some of her biggest hits, including “My Heart Will Go On,” “J’irai où tu iras” and “Pour que tu m’aimes encore.”

She delivered powerful vocal performances throughout the night despite the health challenges she has faced. Fans who had travelled from around the world greeted her return with sustained applause as she wiped away tears.

“Thank you so much! I had promised myself I wouldn’t cry. I don’t keep my promises,” Dion told the crowd after her first song. “I missed this!”

Saturday night marked the beginning of a series of 26 performances at the Plenitude Arena this fall and next spring.

Dion’s last tour was cancelled in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and in 2022 she revealed that she was suffering from stiff-person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disease that prevented her from returning to the stage at the time.

Although the singer gave a moving performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics of “Hymne à l’amour” that lit up the Eiffel Tower, these will be her first full concerts in six years. Another 10 shows are scheduled for next year.

A number of celebrities attended Saturday night’s performance, including former U.S. first lady Michelle Obama.

3:51 Celine Dion surprises fans with a song on the streets of Paris

The concert moved through several different sections, some more emotional, with stripped-down piano-and-vocal performances, and others more festive and upbeat.

“Can you hear my heart beating?” Dion asked as “Destin” came to an end. “I am standing in this city that I love so much thanks to your support, your love.”

She thanked the audience before launching into “Because You Loved Me” as a tribute.

Dion spoke several times about the autoimmune disease she lives with and her determination to fight so she could sing and perform on stage again.

“I learned to live with this fragility,” Dion told the crowd. “By living alongside it, I learned to tame it. I turned it into my strength to live.”

She danced as she performed “Ne bouge pas,” “Dans un autre monde” and “I’m Alive.” She also surprised the crowd with a cover of Eurythmics’ “Sweet Dreams.”

Short set and costume changes took place throughout the show, accompanied by videos of Dion walking through the desert or dancing.

Throughout the concert, Dion was accompanied by musicians and backup singers, as well as musical director Scott Price, who has worked with her for nearly a decade.

She shared the stage with two of her backup singers during “J’irai où tu iras” and “Beauty and the Beast.” Despite some rumours, no other guests appeared on stage Saturday night.

She also sang “All By Myself” and “Un garçon pas comme les autres (Ziggy),” which drew particularly emotional reactions from the audience.

But perhaps the performance that made the biggest impression Saturday night was her rendition of the operatic aria “La Wally.”

Wearing a long pink coat, Dion stepped onto a large, rock-shaped pedestal and performed the classical piece as snowflakes fell from the arena ceiling.

Dion herself appeared deeply moved afterward, thanking the audience and saying that performing the piece was “a dream” for her.

Some Canadian fans made it to the show.

3:56 Celine Dion opens up about her battle with Stiff Person Syndrome

Frédérique Lauzon and Alexandrine Derome, two Montreal-based flight attendants, snagged last-minute tickets during a layover.

For Derome, it was her 24th time attending a Dion performance.

“I’ve seen her in Las Vegas, Montreal, Quebec City, Paris, and during the tapings of special TV shows in Montreal,” Derome said before the performance.

Dion closed the concert with some of her best-known French-language classics, including “Pour que tu m’aimes encore” and “S’il suffisait d’aimer,” as the crowd sang along.

“Des milliers de baisers” was the final song of the night.

Between songs, Dion repeatedly took time to speak directly to her fans.

She reminded them of the importance of dreaming big and paying attention to the people around them and what they May be going through, echoing her own experience.

“I love you. Take care of yourselves,” she repeated several times as she blew kisses into the crowd.

stories.title: Saskatoon rally for the unhoused calls for action on forced displacement
stories.summary: After ongoing discrepancy between unhoused people and the police, a rally was held outside Saskatoon's city hall. Attendees say there are little options for people to get help.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
A community rally outside Saskatoon’s City Hall Saturday called for changes to how the city and police respond to homeless encampments.

This follows ongoing interactions between people living in encampments and police, where people are ordered to move by police or risk tickets that carry fines of up to $10,000.

“That was their option, us is move or you’re going to get trespassing tickets,” said David Fineday from Sweetgrass First Nation. “Last time we got suckered into going into a meeting. While we all went to the meeting, they all rolled in there and tried to tear down our camp.”

Fineday is a 70-year-old man who has been homeless since he was 20, after leaving the child welfare system and surviving the Sixties Scoop.

He is currently living in an encampment with about 50 others.

“On one side, one whole side is people that work, but they have to live in a tent. Why? Because the rent’s too high.”

People have limited options when it comes to finding housing.

“There is things available in town and there’s many people that sign up, but there’s a waiting list… So, what do you do? You don’t get in there for six months,” said Fineday.

A former Prairie Harm Reduction worker and advocate, Marissa Livedotte, says homelessness can happen to anyone.

“I was working full-time. I had a very well-paying job, and I actually ended up unhoused for three months. It was just a quick change in circumstance, and you know people just they hear that you’re a paycheck away, but nobody takes it seriously. Nobody thinks that it’s going to happen to them.”

And she says it’s more prevalent than what is recorded.

“Right now, I think they said that it’s about 3,000 people that are living unhoused in our city,” said Livedotte. “But you could probably double that with the people who are experiencing hidden homelessness. Hidden homelessness is just, you know, people who were couch surfing, just going from place to place wherever they can.”

Fineday says he hopes decision-makers listen.

“I want to see the proper ears come here, the proper eyes that come here and can see what’s happening, that can hear what’s happening.”

stories.title: Protests planned for Carney’s Canada Investment Summit in Toronto
stories.summary: Organizers say they reject Carney’s plan to put Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
Protests are planned for the prime minister’s high-stakes summit aimed at attracting new investment to Canada, with organizers saying Mark Carney is keeping company with business leaders they say are exacerbating global crises.

Hundreds of executives and global asset managers are set to arrive in Toronto for Canada’s first-ever investment summit to get a look at major projects in various stages of development.

The summit is a key part of Carney’s plan for stimulating $1 trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years.

Demonstrators, including labour unions, Indigenous leaders and climate and housing advocates, will mobilize Monday carrying a banner reading “The Many vs. The Money,” and plan “direct intervention” with attendees.

Organizers say they reject Carney’s plan to put Canada’s economic future in the hands of CEOs, and that they worry about the future of public services, pipelines and arms manufacturing.

The prime minister’s event kicks off Sunday evening where he is scheduled to share brief remarks at the summit’s welcome reception.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says invitees come from Kuwait, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Singapore, Qatar, Norway, Japan and Australia.

“This is about building relationships, opening doors and making the case that Ontario is one of the most investable places anywhere in the world,” Ford said in a media statement.

He said 15 major projects in Ontario are up for offer, including energy production and transmission, critical minerals and mining, AI and advanced manufacturing.

“We are building an economy that can compete with anyone, anywhere. That’s going to be my message throughout the Canada Investment Summit,” Ford said.

“Ontario has what the world needs and we’re going to make sure the world knows it.”

stories.title: Carney to meet with Macron in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon next week to discuss energy, defence
stories.summary: The prime minister is also set to meet with his counterpart in the United Kingdom for the first time this week
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume
stories.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron will meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon next week to discuss energy and defence partnerships.

The prime minister’s office says Carney will travel to the French territory off the coast of Newfoundland on Sept. 20 for talks on aerospace, energy and critical minerals. The pair will also talk about quantum satellites and supercomputing.

Carney says the two countries share a history and common values, and that working together is to the benefit of both nations.

The prime minister is also set to meet with his counterpart in the United Kingdom for the first time this week during a three-day trip to Europe.

Carney is also set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg and attend the State of the European Union address during the trip, adding to a busy week for the prime minister who is hosting a two-day investment summit in Toronto on Monday and Tuesday.

By Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press

Ottawa - French President Emmanuel Macron will meet with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon next week to discuss energy and defence partnerships.

The prime minister’s office says Carney will travel to the French territory off the coast of Newfoundland on Sept. 20 for talks on aerospace, energy and critical minerals. The pair will also talk about quantum satellites and supercomputing.

Carney says the two countries share a history and common values, and that working together is to the benefit of both nations.

stories.title: Céline Dion makes emotional return to concert stage after nearly six years
stories.summary: After nearly six years away from the concert stage, Céline Dion returned Saturday night with a fitting message.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Anja Conton, The Canadian Press

Posted September 13, 2026 11:44 am.

Last Updated September 13, 2026 1:03 pm.

Paris — After nearly six years away from the concert stage, Céline Dion returned Saturday night with a fitting message: “On ne change pas”– we don’t change.

The Quebec superstar opened her show before nearly 33,000 people at the Plenitude Arena in Nanterre, outside Paris, marking an emotional comeback after what she described as a “rocky road.”

Dion thrilled the crowd with a two-and-a-half-hour performance that began about 40 minutes late, revisiting her career and some of her biggest hits, including “My Heart Will Go On,” “J’irai où tu iras” and “Pour que tu m’aimes encore.”

She delivered powerful vocal performances throughout the night despite the health challenges she has faced. Fans who had travelled from around the world greeted her return with sustained applause as she wiped away tears.

“Thank you so much! I had promised myself I wouldn’t cry. I don’t keep my promises,” Dion told the crowd after her first song. “I missed this!”

Saturday night marked the beginning of a series of 26 performances at the Plenitude Arena this fall and next spring.

Dion’s last tour was cancelled in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and in 2022 she revealed that she was suffering from stiff-person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disease that prevented her from returning to the stage at the time.

Although the singer gave a moving performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics of “Hymne à l’amour” that lit up the Eiffel Tower, these will be her first full concerts in six years. Another 10 shows are scheduled for next year.

A number of celebrities attended Saturday night’s performance, including former U.S. first lady Michelle Obama.

The concert moved through several different sections, some more emotional, with stripped-down piano-and-vocal performances, and others more festive and upbeat.

“Can you hear my heart beating?” Dion asked as “Destin” came to an end. “I am standing in this city that I love so much thanks to your support, your love.”

She thanked the audience before launching into “Because You Loved Me” as a tribute.

Dion spoke several times about the autoimmune disease she lives with and her determination to fight so she could sing and perform on stage again.

“I learned to live with this fragility,” Dion told the crowd. “By living alongside it, I learned to tame it. I turned it into my strength to live.”

She danced as she performed “Ne bouge pas,” “Dans un autre monde” and “I’m Alive.” She also surprised the crowd with a cover of Eurythmics’ “Sweet Dreams.”

Short set and costume changes took place throughout the show, accompanied by videos of Dion walking through the desert or dancing.

Throughout the concert, Dion was accompanied by musicians and backup singers, as well as musical director Scott Price, who has worked with her for nearly a decade.

She shared the stage with two of her backup singers during “J’irai où tu iras” and “Beauty and the Beast.” Despite some rumours, no other guests appeared on stage Saturday night.

She also sang “All By Myself” and “Un garçon pas comme les autres (Ziggy),” which drew particularly emotional reactions from the audience.

But perhaps the performance that made the biggest impression Saturday night was her rendition of the operatic aria “La Wally.”

Wearing a long pink coat, Dion stepped onto a large, rock-shaped pedestal and performed the classical piece as snowflakes fell from the arena ceiling.

Dion herself appeared deeply moved afterward, thanking the audience and saying that performing the piece was “a dream” for her.

Some Canadian fans made it to the show.

Frédérique Lauzon and Alexandrine Derome, two Montreal-based flight attendants, snagged last-minute tickets during a layover.

For Derome, it was her 24th time attending a Dion performance.

“I’ve seen her in Las Vegas, Montreal, Quebec City, Paris, and during the tapings of special TV shows in Montreal,” Derome said before the performance.

Dion closed the concert with some of her best-known French-language classics, including “Pour que tu m’aimes encore” and “S’il suffisait d’aimer,” as the crowd sang along.

“Des milliers de baisers” was the final song of the night.

Between songs, Dion repeatedly took time to speak directly to her fans.

She reminded them of the importance of dreaming big and paying attention to the people around them and what they May be going through, echoing her own experience.

“I love you. Take care of yourselves,” she repeated several times as she blew kisses into the crowd.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 13, 2026.

Anja Conton, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Popular farmers market shifts outside after fire officials order building shut
stories.summary: "The people are supporting us, (they're) so good."
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
A fire department-ordered closure of the main market building didn’t stop hundreds of people from flocking to the Trails End Farmers’ Market just east of London Saturday morning as they pivoted to an open-air format.

The market at 4370 Dundas St. in Thorndale announced late Friday it planned to run an outdoor market specifically for its produce vendors, while emphasizing the main building remains closed.

It was a welcome compromise for vendors, who said Saturday morning not only did they still have perishables to sell on behalf of their farms, but they were happy to serve loyal customers who depend on their more affordable products.

“The people are supporting us, (they’re) so good . . . they’re all giving us a word of solidarity,” said vendor Fred Sedat, who owns Fresh4Less, a Southwestern Ontario produce wholesaler. “I am so thankful to them, and they’re showing up and they still showed up for us with very little notice.”

The shift outdoors comes after the Thames Centre fire department ordered the market’s building closed, approved by the Ontario fire marshal, noting “serious and life safety deficiencies (were) identified on the premises.”

Entrances to the market building were taped off Saturday morning, and some confused attendees had to be turned away from the building by staff who told them the stucture was closed. Still, a steady stream of vehicles pulled into the premises and dozens of people shopped for produce and some artisan products.

The move earned praise from some patrons on Facebook, with one commenter saying: “Way to pivot in an unfortunate circumstance. Looks great.”

Sadat said he is especially grateful to have an outlet for his perishables that provides a way for the farms he serves to get their product to market, rather than turn them away just as growing seasons start for items like apples and squashes.

“It’s a compromise, but I wish we had an option – we don’t have an option,” he said. “We are in the perishable business, and in this business, I wish I could tell the apple on the tree: ‘Could you please wait for a couple of weeks or so for us to resolve issues, and then I’ll come back to get you?'”

Kelvin Bokor of Chatham-based produce wholesaler Greatview Orchard said as a long-term vendor, they weren’t sure what to expect after the news of the building closure emerged. But Bokor said it was a “relief” and “a nice change” to be able to sell outdoors – even if it was less busy than usual.

“You don’t know what to expect (with) turnouts, what it’s going to be. Sometimes we can pick based on last year’s sales and stuff, like how a weekend’s going to be,” he said. “But this is obviously an unknown that hasn’t happened to us before. So we were kind of like, you know what? We’re going to show up, hopefully people show up, because it’s a lot of work to come here.”

A representative of the market, who did not wish to be identified, said on Saturday the owners consulted with Thames Centre officials to make sure they could operate outdoors. They continue to comply with the fire marshal’s order, working on retrofits while engineers and contractors examine the building.

The Thames Centre fire department has said it recognizes that closing the building is a serious measure, but because of the conditions observed during the inspection process, Trails End required an intense response due to the fire and safety concerns identified.

Trails End Farmers’ Market is family-owned and has operated since 1983, according to its website, which lists 56 vendors.

stories.title: Canadian boxing icon George Chuvalo, known for his two Ali fights, dies at 89
stories.summary: George Chuvalo was a Canadian amateur champion at 17, held the national title as a pro for almost 20 years and was ranked as high as No. 2 in the world.
stories.author: Bill Beacon and Neil Davidson
stories.content:
George Chuvalo, a hard-nosed heavyweight who never hit the canvas despite taking on the world’s best boxers, has died.

Sully’s Boxing Gym in Toronto, where Chuvalo trained during his career, confirmed his death in a social media post Saturday. The gym said Chuvalo died on his 89th birthday.

“Today, Sully’s lost a piece of its history,” the gym said.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford also paid tribute to Chuvalo, calling him “a heavyweight boxing legend, a family friend and a Canadian icon.”

“My thoughts are with all of George’s family and loved ones as we mourn his passing,” Ford said in a social media post.

Chuvalo was a Canadian amateur champion at 17, held the national title as a pro for almost 20 years and was ranked as high as No. 2 in the world.

He was 73-18-2 as a pro with 64 knockouts in a pro career that stretched from 1956 to 1978.

His career was defined by two mega-bouts with Muhammad Ali, in 1966 at Toronto’s Maple Leaf Gardens and 1972 at the Pacific Coliseum in Vancouver, in which Chuvalo drew kudos for standing toe-to-toe with the most gifted and charismatic boxer of the era.

“When people think of me, they think of me fighting Muhammad,” Chuvalo said. “But I had close to 100 fights.”

Known for having one of the best chins in boxing, Chuvalo pointed out that it took more than the ability to absorb punches to record 73 wins and rank in the top 10 in the world in an age of heavyweight greats like Ali, Joe Frazier and George Foreman.

Chuvalo took pride in noting he had more knockouts than Joe Louis and Jack Dempsey, while also exceeding the total number of fights that Ali, Frazier, Rocky Marciano and Mike Tyson had.

Before retiring in 1978, Chuvalo wrote in his 2013 autobiography “Chuvalo: A Fighter’s Life: The Story of Boxing’s Last Gladiator, “I’ll be remembered as a guy who fought the best of his time, beat a lot of them and lost to some others.”

He was never knocked down as a pro.

“Not in the ring, anyway,” he says. “Outside the ropes has been a different story.”

Chuvalo lost three sons and his first wife Lynne to drugs and suicide.

“If you added up every punch I ever took and then multiplied the total by 10,000, it wouldn’t begin to equal the pain of losing three sons and a wife to drugs and suicide,” he wrote.

As for his fights with Ali, the American legend made most opponents look slow and predictable, but he could not finish Chuvalo, even though the stocky fighter who liked to get in close and work the body had only 17 days’ notice to prepare.

“They had a contest between a bull and a bumblebee at Maple Leaf Gardens last night,” Toronto Star columnist Milt Dunnell wrote at the time. Dunnell would add, “The bull came out of it with his face looking like a bucket of balls at a golf driving range.”

Ali went a full 15 rounds for the first time and had to go to the hospital for internal bleeding, while Chuvalo said, “I went dancing with my wife.”

When it came to his payday, Chuvalo said he ended up with $12,500, as manager Irving Ungerman took the lion’s share of the $49,000 purse, after expenses.

Chuvalo would also lose a rematch to Ali six years later by 12-round decision.

Despite the defeats, the Ali fights made Chuvalo a star in Canada and in the boxing world as the tough, unrelenting underdog.

“Icon — that’s the only way I can describe George Chuvalo,” said Lennox Lewis, a Canadian boxing star of another generation.

“He gave as good as he got, and then some,” reads Chuvalo’s Canada Sports Hall of Fame bio. “George Chuvalo was an extraordinary fighter and competitor — inside and outside of the boxing ring.”

Chuvalo was the son of Croat immigrants.

His mother worked in Toronto as a chicken plucker at Royce Poultry Packers, owned by Ungerman’s father, Chuvalo’s future manager. His father was a cattle skinner at Canada Packers.

George said he was drawn to boxing as a boy after seeing a copy of The Ring, a magazine known as “the Bible of boxing.” He egged his mother to get him boxing gloves, which she eventually bought at Eaton’s department store.

He found a local church that offered boxing training and had his first organized fight at age 10, an exhibition bout declared a draw. He eventually joined a boxing club and by 15 was a 198-pound heavyweight.

He fought 19 times as an amateur, losing just once. In May 1995, he knocked out Peter Piper in Regina to win the Canadian amateur title.

Chuvalo was chosen to represent Canada at the 1956 Olympics in Melbourne but turned pro instead.

He went on to become a five-time Canadian heavyweight champion, back when that title still counted, and held it for most of his 20-year pro career.

He lost a World Boxing Association championship bout to Ernie Terrell in 1965, a fight he always felt was fixed by mobsters.

A frequent fighter at Madison Square Garden during that time, going 3-6 against top pugilists like Frazier, Foreman, Floyd Patterson and Buster Mathis. The Ring named his bloody 1965 encounter with Patterson fight of the year.

2:36 Long-forgotten film of Muhammad Ali in B.C.

He hoped to challenge for the Commonwealth title, but could not convince English champion Henry Cooper to fight him. He felt the Canadian Boxing Federation also let him down by not insisting that Cooper face him.

His last bout was a TKO win over George Jerome, a logging camp cook from Vancouver, who was the No. 1 contender in Canada, in December 1978 at Toronto’s St. Lawrence Market to retain the Canadian title. Chuvalo was 41 and made just $7,500 for the bout.

A bloody Jerome lasted two rounds before the ring doctor stepped in.

Out of the ring, Chuvalo was a big, friendly man who loved telling stories and making jokes. But his painful moments were almost beyond imagination.

In 1985, his son Jesse, who began using painkillers after an accident and developed an addiction, committed suicide. In 1993, another son, Georgie Lee, died of a drug overdose. Four days later, his wife was found dead with a suicide note.

Then, in 1996, his son Steven was found dead in a hotel room with a needle in his arm.

“After Steven died, I was barely able to function,” Chuvalo wrote in Toronto Life in 2013. “I felt like I was suffocating every time I went to sleep in the dark.

“I blamed myself for my sons’ deaths — for letting them quit high school, for not putting them in rehab earlier.”

He remarried to Joanne O’Hara and began visiting schools across Canada to deliver an anti-drug message. He had two remaining children and said he turned to “mush” whenever he saw his grandchildren.

Chuvalo, inducted into Canada’s Sports Hall of Fame in 1990 and the World Boxing Hall of Fame in 1997, was named to the Order of Canada in 1998.

Canada added him to its Walk of Fame in 2005.

A statue of Chuvalo was erected in his family’s ancestral home in Ljubuski, Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 2011.

Some 24 years after his induction into Canada’s Sports Hall of Fame, Chuvalo took part in a new conference at Mattamy Athletic Centre, site of the old Gardens, honouring the 2014 inductees — and the bell he answered 15 times against Ali some 48 years earlier.

Chuvalo, then 77, rang the bell, gave the crowd a thumbs-up and then shadowboxed.

“I get reminded of it just about every day of the week,” he said of his first fight with Ali. “That makes me very, very proud to be a Canadian.”

The bell was donated to the Hall of Fame by Michael Shillolo, whose father, Frank Shillolo, used to be the official bellman for the Ontario Athletics Commission.

stories.title: Canadian air force rescues sick passenger on cruise ship off B.C. coast
stories.summary: The medical evacuation call prompted the Royal Canadian Air Force to deploy a Cormorant helicopter and a Kingfisher airplane in the pre-dawn hours of Saturday.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
When a person on board a cruise ship off the coast of British Columbia fell ill, the Royal Canadian Air Force responded quickly to airlift the patient, a travel companion and medical personnel from the ship to waiting emergency health services.

The rescue happened on Saturday morning, when the Rcaf’s 442 Transport and Rescue Squadron received a call that prompted a high-seas search and rescue mission.

A CH-149 Cormorant helicopter and a CC-295 Kingfisher airplane were deployed in the pre-dawn hours to a spot 200 km northwest of Port Hardy, B.C.

The Kingfisher arrived first and coordinated the medevac alongside the ship’s captain and provided “over-watch” for the helicopter, a news release said.

At the same time, the ship’s captain steered his vessel into the wind, turned off his radar and cleared an area on the bow so the chopper could safely approach.

Two search and rescue technicians were then lowered onto the ship from the helicopter to take over care of the patient and prepare them for a transfer onto the aircraft.

The patient, their companion and a member of the ship’s medical staff, along with the technicians, were then hoisted into the helicopter. The aircraft then flew to Comox where the patient was transferred to emergency health services awaiting their arrival.

stories.title: London Knights acquire local player in trade with Saginaw Spirit
stories.summary: Coming back to London in Sunday's deal is Carson Harmer, a native of Mitchell.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
Sarnia Sting player Easton Walos (11) tries to take the puck from Saginaw Spirit player Carson Harmer (13) during their OHL game at Progressive Auto Sales Arena in Sarnia on Sunday, March 15, 2026. Mark Malone/Postmedia Network

The London Knights traded away forward Braidy Wassilyn on Sunday in a deal with the Saginaw Spirit that netted a centre who grew up in nearby Mitchell, along with a draft pick.

Wassilyn, 18, was the first-round pick to Niagara in 2024 before being dealt to the Knights last fall in a trade that sent Noah Read back to the IceDogs. The six-foot, 194-pound Wassilyn, a left winger, had 17 goals and 24 assists for 41 points in 56 games for the Knights last season. He was held pointless in five playoff games.

Coming back to London in Sunday’s deal is Carson Harmer, a native of Mitchell. The 19-year-old centre, who stands five-foot-10 and weighs 195 pounds, has played 134 OHL games with Saginaw across two seasons after being picked in the third round of the 2023 draft.

Last season, Harmer had 18 goals and 26 assists for 44 points for the Spirit. He registered one assist in four playoff games.

Braidy Wassilyn of the London Knights passes the puck during their OHL game against the Kingston Frontenacs at Canada Life Place in London on Friday, Nov. 7, 2025. (Mike Hensen/The London Free Press)

The Knights will also get Ottawa’s 2027 fourth-round pick in the trade. Wassilyn is currently with the Montreal Canadiens’ rookie camp.

The Knights will begin the 2026-27 season this Friday, playing host to the Windsor Spitfires at Canada Life Place. The longtime rivals will then play again on Saturday night, in Windsor.

The Knights lineup includes one of the best collections of import players in junior hockey. The club signed Anaheim Ducks first-rounder Marcus Nordmark recently. The 18-year-old Swedish forward joins Russian blue-liner Maksim Sokolovskii, a first-round pick to the Philadelphia Flyers, and Luca Santala, a forward from Finland who is expected to be picked high in the 2027 NHL draft.

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney will hold his marquee investment summit in Toronto starting Monday. The two-day Canada Investment Summit is expected to be a gathering of global investors, top Canadian executives and government with a goal to help facilitate $1 trillion in total investment in Canada over the next five years.

Statistics Canada is set to release its latest reading for inflation on Monday morning when it publishes its consumer price index for August. The annual inflation rate rose to three per cent in July as higher gas prices helped push the key data point higher. Excluding gasoline, the annual inflation rate was 2.2 per cent in July.

A pair of key reports on the Canadian housing market are expected this week. The Canadian Real Estate Association is expected to release its home sales figures for August on Tuesday, followed by housing starts figures from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. on Wednesday.

Dollarama Inc. will report its second-quarter results and hold a conference call with investors and financial analysts on Wednesday morning. The retailer saw its first-quarter profit and sales rise compared with a year ago as it looked to grow in Canada and internationally.

The All In AI tech conference in Montreal starts on Wednesday. The event is expected to bring together experts, researchers and business and political leaders to talk about the Canadian AI ecosystem and building an AI-powered economy. The conference comes amid rising concerns about AI safety.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Summer-like Sunday ahead for London
stories.summary: London is in for a warm Sunday with a mix of sun and cloud, before cooler and more unsettled conditions move in through the week.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London is in for a warm Sunday with a mix of sun and cloud, before cooler and more unsettled conditions move in through the week.

Fog patches will dissipate this morning, with winds becoming west at 20 km/h and gusting to 40 near noon. The high is expected to reach 25 C, with a humidex of 29.

Tonight will be mainly cloudy with a 30 per cent chance of showers this evening before clearing overnight. Northwest winds will gust to 40 km/h, with a low of 11 C.

The week ahead will bring cooler temperatures, with highs generally around 20 to 26 C. Several days will carry a chance of showers, including Tuesday and Thursday, while overnight temperatures will dip into the single digits by Friday.

stories.title: Carney seeks closer ties with EU, including possible associate membership, report says
stories.summary: Canada and the EU are reportedly discussing a new form of association that could deepen co-operation on trade, defence, AI and critical minerals
stories.author: Inti Landauro
stories.content:
Canada wants to forge deeper trade , investment, security, data and labour ties with the European Union − but not at the expense of Canadian sovereignty.

That was the message from Ottawa ahead of Prime Minister Mark Carney ’s visit to Strasbourg, France, according to a senior government official with knowledge of the Canada-EU file. Mr. Carney will address the European Parliament there Thursday and pitch Canada as a viable EU partner, as Ottawa attempts to reduce the country’s overwhelming dependence on the United States for everything from manufacturing supply chains to defence products.

Talks are still at the exploratory stages but, without sacrificing autonomy, the outcome could be linking Canada more closely with the EU than any other country, the official said.

The source said, without providing details, that the talks include labour and student mobility, plus strengthening academic and research collaboration.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source because they were not authorized to discuss the progress of the ongoing talks.

On Sunday The Wall Street Journal reported that Mr. Carney had suggested to EU leaders that Canada take on the title “associate member of the European Union” and that the EU was open to the idea.

But the Canadian government source said it was the EU, not Mr. Carney, that floated the title, though determining what sort of official tie Canada would have to the EU is premature.

Mr. Carney addressed the matter while speaking to reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival late Sunday. “We’re not looking to become a member of the European Union,” he said.

“What we are looking — and will begin discussions for — is a unique alliance between Canada and the European Union. We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths.”

The source rejected the notion that Canada was seeking a “Norway” deal − that it would have formal links to the EU without official membership in the 27-country trading bloc.

Norway has rejected EU membership but joined the European Economic Area (EEA) in the 1990s. EEA status grants non-EU countries access to the EU’s single market while allowing them to pursue trade deals with other countries.

But even that came at the expense of some sovereignty – a “democratic deficit,” as it’s called. Norway had to incorporate thousands of EU laws and regulations into national law without having voting rights in the European Council, Commission or Parliament. Norway must also make payments to the EEA for cohesion grants, which are aimed at reducing economic and social gaps among EEA member states.

“There are issues of Canadian sovereignty to be carefully considered, but the important thing is the fact that the linkage concept is being discussed in Ottawa and Brussels and other EU capitals and apparently getting serious traction,” said international trade lawyer Lawrence Herman of Toronto’s Herman & Associates. “All of this signifies a major transatlantic shift, reflecting the serious decline in faith in the U.S. as a reliable strategic partner.”

Mr. Carney has focused on strengthening ties with Europe from the moment he became Prime Minister in March, 2025, though previous Canadian leaders have had similar goals. Under his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, Canada and the EU negotiated the Comprehensive Trade and Economic Agreement (Ceta), which the EU Parliament approved in 2017.

Ceta removed most tariffs between the two sides. But the trade deal has not been universally popular – 10 EU member states have yet to approve it.

Since then, the biggest move has been Canada’s agreement, signed in February, to join Safe – the Security Action for Europe. The €150-billion defence initiative is designed to help EU countries rearm by building up their weapon industries. Canada receives equivalent, non-discriminatory access to the program.

Former Quebec premier Jean Charest, who played a key role in championing the Ceta, said Canada will never be a member of the EU, but there are plenty of ways Canadians can grow closer to the bloc.

He said more intense and profound co-operation at all levels appears to be where relations are headed under Mr. Carney.

And he added that increased mobility for skilled European professionals could be invaluable to building Canada’s economy.

“Whether it’s France or other European countries, they represent a great pool of talent from which we can recruit,” Mr. Charest said.

“The United States will always be our No. 1 trading partner − that will not change. But this is about diversifying.”

Canadian cabinet ministers have adjusted their messages to tout the advantages of moving closer to the EU as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats against Canada intensify.

Two weeks ago, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand met with EU foreign ministers in Ireland, during which she touted Safe, the implementation of the Canada-EU Defence and Security Partnership, negotiations to create a Canada-EU digital trade agreement and collaboration on critical metals.

In an interview with eudebates.tv , she said, “We are always looking for ways to strengthen this absolutely essential relationship. … It is time for us to ensure that we are negotiating with, dealing with, reliable partners who will remain at the table, who share similar values.”

As part of the courtship of Europe, Mr. Carney is to meet Friday with French President Emmanuel Macron on Saint Pierre and Miquelon, the French islands about 25 kilometres off the south coast of Newfoundland and Labrador. The two leaders plan to discuss deepening ties in aerospace, energy, critical metals, satellites, AI and supercomputing.

Mr. Herman said that moving closer to the EU “recognizes that the EU countries are mostly liberal democracies while the U.S. is no longer and has parted company with its Western allies.”

With a report from Steven Chase in Ottawa

stories.summary: The leaders debates for the Quebec provincial election are set to get underway with the first on Tuesday and multiple parties have released their financial frameworks.
stories.author: Staff

By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted September 13, 2026 9:15 am

Updated September 13, 2026 9:06 pm

Quebec political leaders are entering their 18th day on the campaign trail today with their first debate approaching on Tuesday.

The Liberal party is expected to present its financial framework today.

The Parti Québécois will then be the only one left to present its financial framework.

2:13 Some Quebec election party leaders split on high-speed train

Party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said he would do so on Tuesday, the day of the first debate.

While the Parti Québécois has been favoured by some public opinion polls, recent surveys appear to show the Coalition Avenir Québec gaining momentum.

Quebec voters go to the polls Oct. 5.

Quebec political leaders are entering their 18th day on the campaign trail today with their first debate approaching on Tuesday.
The Liberal party is expected to present its financial framework today.
The Parti Québécois will then be the only one left to present its financial framework.

Party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said he would do so on Tuesday, the day of the first debate.
While the Parti Québécois has been favoured by some public opinion polls, recent surveys appear to show the Coalition Avenir Québec gaining momentum.
Quebec voters go to the polls Oct. 5.

stories.title: Dawson college shooting survivor now serves as Montreal police officer 20 years later
stories.summary: On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered Dawson college and opened fire on students in the hall. One student was killed and 16 people were injured.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Two decades ago, James Santos saw his friend die in a shooting at a Montreal college . Now, he is a Montreal police officer, working for the force he says saved his life that day.

Sunday marks the 20th anniversary of the shooting. On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered Dawson college and opened fire on students in the hall. He killed 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and injured 16 others, according to a coroner’s report from 2008.

Santos, then a 17-year-old student, was having lunch with De Sousa that day. The cafeteria was packed and the two found a free table close to the entrance, he recalled in an interview with The Canadian Press.

“We were talking about our weekend and what we did and we had laughs — and then, all of a sudden, I see the shooter walk in,” he said.

When he realized the man had a real weapon, Santos dove behind some chairs. De Sousa, who couldn’t see the shooter, stood up.

“She turned around facing the shooter and basically one of the first shots was directed to my friend,” recalled Santos.

Thinking De Sousa fainted, Santos crawled over to drag her to cover.

“That’s when I realized she got hit by one of the rounds near the abdomen. So I tried to console her, tell her that I was next to her and that everything will be alright,” he said.

Soon, the shooter turned his attention back to Santos. He told Santos to get up and get in front of him, essentially acting as a human shield. Santos obeyed.

“I didn’t want to anger him because I believed that Anastasia was still there, and I also had other friends that were trapped,” he said.

He tried to talk the shooter down. At that moment, Santos recalled, he accepted that he would die.

“I just didn’t want to take other students with me,” he said.

2:01 Remembering the victims of the Dawson College shooting

He fed the shooter white lies about the layout of the school, telling him one corridor led to a janitor’s closet or that another led nowhere.

When the shooter asked Santos how De Sousa was doing, Santos didn’t know what to say. At that point, he still hoped his friend was alive. So he told the shooter that he wasn’t sure and asked him to let him get her help.

“He didn’t say anything — he just loaded his magazine into a semi automatic and walked over to her, he unloaded all his 12 rounds on her, and then he came back and he told me, ‘Well, now you have nothing to worry about,’” said Santos.

Santos froze. Later, when the shooter held another student at gunpoint, Santos snapped, yelling at the shooter to leave the student be.

“I think I had enough with everything. Enough with the gunshots, the blood, the screaming of the students, just all of it,” said Santos.

“The shooter didn’t say anything, he just laughed.”

The shooter spared that other student. Moments later, police shot him in the leg. Santos was sure the angered gunman would shoot him. Instead, the shooter killed himself.

Santos ran off. He thought it had been hours since De Sousa was killed and the ordeal began.

“I found out a little later on that it was a dozen minutes that passed by,” he said.

In 2008, then-Governor General of Canada Michaelle Jean awarded Santos the Star of Courage for his actions that day.

Dawson College commemorated the shooting on Friday in a ceremony that brought De Sousa’s family, survivors and students together in the school’s Peace Garden. Loved ones remembered De Sousa’s cheerful and resilient character.

During the ceremony, De Sousa’s mother, Louise De Sousa, called on the federal government to tighten gun control laws.

Santos said the journey to becoming an officer was a challenging one, as he worked over years to overcome the trauma.

4:13 From Dawson College hero to WE Day

Talking about the events of that day two decades later, Santos seems calm, his voice never wavering.

“I have all the details in my mind. I recall everything, but I don’t put myself into it. I’m looking at it as a third person,” he said.

That wasn’t always the case, he said.

“Initially, saying it the first couple of times was extremely, extremely, extremely hard. There’s really no words to place it, just because you pretty much relive every second of it,” he said.

Nonetheless, as he tells the story, little details come up. The way De Sousa had wanted to go out for lunch, but Santos instead opted to eat at the cafeteria. The fact that she sat with her back to the door and couldn’t see the shooter coming in.

Santos said he fixated on some of these details after graduating from Dawson, filled with survivor’s guilt.

“What if I had given her the (other) chair?” he asked.

“It just goes down that spiral that it’s extremely hard to get out because you could think of anything, but it’ll never change what actually happened.”

He had considered a career in law enforcement before the event of 2006, and he said his experience during the shooting pushed him to want to join the Montreal police.

“I wanted to give back to the community that gave me another chance, right? The police (officers) gave me another chance at life.”

The path to get there wasn’t easy. Santos had vivid nightmares and panic attacks, and he knew he would have to address his trauma if he wanted to work as a police officer. He turned to therapy and set small goals, like watching an action movie, or one with a lot of shooting, until he could get through it calmly.

Then he joined the army. Training was a challenge, he said.

“The smell of gunpowder would bring me right back to the event of Dawson,” he said.

After about a decade in the military, Santos got into the police academy. He then worked for a year in a town outside of Montreal before joining the Montreal force in 2018.

“As a police officer, you never know what calls you’re getting. (If) I get a call, I’m not going to be having anxiety or sweating or anything, because of all the little things I did prior to get myself to where I am today,” he said.

stories.title: 5-year-old pedestrian seriously injured in Goderich collision
stories.summary: A 5-year-old pedestrian has been transported to a trauma centre after suffering serious injuries following a collision in the Town of Goderich Saturday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A 5-year-old pedestrian has been transported to a trauma centre after suffering serious injuries following a collision in the Town of Goderich Saturday.

Just before 2:30 p.m. the Huron County OPP, along with Huron County Emergency Medical Services (EMS) responded to a motor vehicle collision on Quebec Street.

The child was struck by a motor vehicle and suffered serious, non-life threatening injuries. The child was transported by EMS to a trauma centre and is in stable condition.

No one else was injured as a result of the collision.

Quebec Street was closed between Waterloo Street South and Wellington Street South as police investigated the collision. OPP have since cleared the area and the roadway has been reopened
