stories.title: 'Serious' critique of Carney is what loyalty to Canada looks like, Tory critic says
stories.summary: Opinion: “When people say debate is treasonous, they’re undermining what opposition parties exist to do,” Shuv Majumdar says.
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Being the loyal opposition when Trump’s tariffs are hitting Canada is a tricky job, Shuv Majumdar admits.

Some voices treat criticism of the prime minister in a crisis as close to treason. The Calgary Conservative MP, named shadow minister for Canada-U.S. relations on June 30 — days before the July 1 Cusma review deadline — rejects that.

“Our country is not too brittle to have a debate where the loyal opposition — loyal to the Crown, loyal to the debate for the country — wants the best outcomes for our government and for the prime minister in a tough and unpredictable negotiation,” he says.

Prime Minister Mark Carney walked away from the table. He has framed the choice as defending sovereignty and shown little public appetite to reverse course. That May be good short-term politics. It leaves Canada waiting on Washington to blink, or living with a protracted tariff war — while Parliament has not been recalled. The House does not sit again until Sept. 21.

I want to know how Conservatives would handle the same untenable situation. The messages from various conservative camps have not always been coherent. Majumdar, the point man on the file for eight or nine weeks, is more straightforward.

“My effort has been to be thoughtful, to be serious, to be level-headed, to not be incendiary,” he says. “To stay focused on the national interest and to hold the government accountable.”

He is not calling for silence. “Why would you not celebrate that we have a democracy where we can criticize, thoughtfully? When people say debate is treasonous, they’re undermining what opposition parties exist to do.” Civil society, journalists, think tanks and trade experts all have a role, he adds. “Maintaining freedom is very fragile. It’s so easy to concede freedom in a crisis. The harder work is to preserve that freedom through the crisis.” Canadians should have learned that during the pandemic.

In the meantime the government is preparing support for tariff-hit businesses and an investment summit. Majumdar says Conservatives have stood with Canada and the prime minister since the new tariffs landed in July; he’s “not confident that the government has reciprocated the same statesmanship.”

Alberta thinks it has a health care fix. Ottawa, as always, is skeptical

The fight for Alberta's 'soft separatists' — the conservatives who want to send Carney a message

He recalls how in the Harper years, the government briefed the opposition. Critics such as the late NDP MP Paul Dewar were taken into confidence on Ukraine, Isis, TPP and Ceta. Majumdar’s confident Harper did the same with Tom Mulcair. Justin Trudeau sent border-town MPs to Congress; Chrystia Freeland used a non-disclosure process with journalists and experts. “We have not seen any of that in a year and a half,” Majumdar says. Pierre Poilievre’s New York swing this week — apparently with PMO blessing — looks like a shift toward a common front. Fine; but it still leaves the Opposition unbriefed on the talks, the deal text unpublished, and Parliament un-recalled.

Majumdar’s core demand is simple: release the text. “Reveal the deal, share the deal, read the opposition or others into the deal so people actually have a better understanding of what was comprehensively on the table, what was the decision point to walk away, and let people judge for themselves.”

Carney has said Canada would not sacrifice economic or cultural sovereignty. Majumdar’s reply: show Canadians what was actually demanded. “Quebec’s cultural sovereignty is a core part of our conservative identity. But what exactly was on the table that would have cost us our cultural sovereignty?”

Counter-tariffs, he acknowledges, are a tool. Conservatives “will pay whatever the price it takes to ensure our sovereignty, our economic security and the livelihoods of our people.” The question is, “if you are going to impose counter-tariffs, explain how it’s going to get to the outcome you want”: a resolution, a long standoff, or a pivot to other markets — and who bears the cost. He wants clarity on aerospace, defence, F-35s, and Arctic or “Golden Dome” arrangements that May have been in play.

What would Conservatives have done differently? They would have moved faster on the “catalytic” decisions Carney was elected to make: defence production, critical minerals, competitiveness and getting government out of the way of resource development.

Parliament, he notes, already gave the prime minister wide authority to move quickly. Conservatives put legislation in front of him to repeal “anti-development” rules that keep investment away. “We’re getting accused of not being patriotic just because we don’t believe in a single hammer of counter-tariffs. We’re building a whole array of instruments.”

Canada’s strengths should have been taken to Washington in a clear order of national interest: first, the security of Canadians and the border; second, middle-class prosperity and a social safety net that holds the country together; third, alignment with countries that share our values.

He is unconvinced that turning off oil or gas taps is a serious strategy. It would feed separatist sentiment in Alberta and damage Canada’s reputation as a reliable supplier. A better idea, he says, is a strategic reserve of oil, gas and critical minerals used as a positive incentive for tariff-free trade with allies — “a carrot, not a stick.”

On China, Majumdar is unsparing. Carney went to Beijing, then spoke in Davos of partnering with “Beijing’s New World Order” while treating America as the global disruptor, “which is not entirely unfair,” he says, “but I think (the disruption) is principally initiated from Beijing.” The result, in his telling, was concessions without a comprehensive trade arrangement, “and then comes July and (Carney) gets hammered by unjustified tariffs because he’s in a position of weakness.”

Geography still binds Canada to Washington. “Our competition with the United States is very multi-layered,” he observes, “one of the most complex relationships between two countries in the world. We can’t escape whatever direction Washington chooses to go. Our country needs to have the self-respect to fight for our existence.”

He does not expect November’s U.S. midterms to rescue Canada. He has seen no signal from Democrats in Congress, Senate candidates or governors auditioning to be president that they would roll back these tariffs. “Waiting to see what an election May reveal is not as important as sharpening our pencil, drafting legislation that makes Canada the economic powerhouse it needs to be for the next half-century.”

Asking to see the deal is not disloyalty. It is the minimum a self-respecting country should require before it is told to absorb the cost. If the offer really threatened sovereignty, publish it; if it did not, say so. Canadians can handle the argument. What they should not have to handle is a nation-defining trade war on trust alone.

stories.title: Helen Mirren, Penélope Cruz and Seth Rogen to be honoured at Tiff Tribute Awards
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney is also expected to walk the red carpet on the fourth day of the festival
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
On a red carpet that featured Penelope Cruz and Helen Mirren, Prime Minister Mark Carney drew the loudest cheers from an assembled crowd.

The prime minister walked the carpet and stopped by the Tribute Awards at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday night after delivering remarks to business leaders the Canada Investment Summit reception.

Director Sian Heder, whose film “Being Heumann” opened Tiff on Thursday, said even she was star-struck by Carney, who greeted attendees but left before the awards ceremony began.

Seth Rogen got the second-warmest welcome from members of the public who lined Front Street outside the Fairmont Royal York, where the gala was held.

That prize is named after late filmmaker Norman Jewison and meant to recognize Canadians who have made a global impact.

The annual fundraiser gala also honoured Mirren with an award inspired by Tiff’s women’s empowerment initiative, Share Her Journey.

Cruz was set to receive the Special Tribute Award, which recognizes individuals who have made lasting and extraordinary contributions to film.

Rounding out the stars being celebrated at the Tribute Awards are French actress Isabelle Huppert, Chinese actor Fan Bingbing, Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong and Polish cinematographer Adam Pietkiewicz.

Tiff said proceeds from the gala will support expanded access to cinema and champion artists.

stories.title: London civic election: Labour group unveils city council endorsements
stories.summary: London's umbrella group for labour unions has come out with its slate of endorsements for mayor and city council ahead of the Oct. 26 vote
stories.author: Jack Moulton
stories.content:
London’s umbrella group for labour unions has come out with its slate of endorsements for mayor and city council ahead of the Oct. 26 vote, backing Josh Morgan for the second election in a row along with nearly half of the incumbent council.

At a Saturday morning event in Peace Park near the Fork of the Thames, the London and District Labour Council gathered many of its preferred picks for city council – a regular function every civic election cycle based on responses to their survey sent to all candidates “to identify their approach to the issues affecting working people.”

Patti Dalton, president of the labour group, described it as a way to reach out to union members and community organizations involved with the labour council in order to get them to pay attention and turn out the vote.

“Really the purpose was to highlight the talented people that we’ve endorsed, to give them a kind of a social media boost build up their profile,” she told The Free Press. “I’m convinced that if we get them all elected, we can have an incredible progressive city council.”

During the 2022 election cycle , eight of the labour council’s 15 endorsements went on to win election — including then-newcomers Hadleigh McAlister, Sam Trosow, Corrine Rahman, and Skylar Franke. All four secured endorsements from the labour council again for this year’s election, as did Mayor Morgan, Anna Hopkins, Elizabeth Peloza.

Morgan was in Ottawa for federal meetings Saturday according to a statement from the mayor’s office, while Hopkins was attending the Harvestfest Parade in Lambeth.

While not endorsed in 2022, incumbent David Ferreira was endorsed for this year’s campaign in downtown Ward 13. Ward 2 incumbent and deputy mayor Shawn Lewis lost the council’s endorsement this year, after securing it in 2022. His opponent Zack Ramsey was instead endorsed for Ward 2.

Alongside Ramsey, the endorsement lineup included several new faces: Leroy Osbourne in Ward 3, Tom Cull in Ward 4, Jonathan Sher in Ward 7, and Lois Ward in Ward 10. Sarah Lehman earned a second consecutive endorsement from the labour council for Ward 14, where she ran unsuccessfully in 2022.

Notably, there was no endorsement in Ward 8. While the race has three registered candidates, including incumbent Steve Lehman, Dalton said they only received one response to their survey which “did not demonstrate the knowledge of unions and labour,” she said, adding it was “unfortunate.”

The survey questions, posted online , includes questions on campaign contributions, thoughts on public sector workers and unions, and addressing affordability and housing. It also includes the candidate’s opinion on controversial large-scale AI data centres, something Dalton said candidates mostly rejected or wished to study more.

Speaking on the labour council’s endorsement tradition and its previous endorsements of successful candidates, Dalton believes they are a trusted organization among working people. The council finalized their choices at their general membership meeting after “significant and intelligent debate.”

stories.title: Carney pushes idea of making Canada ‘associate member’ of EU, WSJ reports
stories.summary: Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney wants closer links with the European Union and is exploring whether his country could become an “associate member” of the bloc, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content:
Editor’s Note - A senior government source tells CTV News Canada is not seeking European Union membership in any capacity, pushing back against reporting by The Wall Street Journal. Read more here .

Brussels - Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney wants closer links with the European Union and is exploring whether his country could become an “associate member” of the bloc, The Wall Street Journal reported on Sunday.

The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet to be created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada.

The Canadian embassy in Brussels and spokespeople at the European Commission did not respond to separate requests for comment.

Canada’s escalating trade war with the United States has added urgency to its strategic pivot towards other trading partners.

Canada’s relations with Washington have deteriorated sharply since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in early 2025, with disagreements on trade and other issues. The trade spat has led to tariffs on tens of billions of dollars in cross-border trade.

Canada and the EU are discussing ways to let Canada’s goods, services and workers involved in strategic supply chains such as energy, AI, defense and critical minerals move freely, thus effectively shifting the EU border, The Wall Street Journal said.

Canada and the EU are also talking about laying underwater cables, jointly constructing data centers, cloud storage and new satellite networks and infrastructure to ship Canadian energy to the EU, the newspaper said.

Carney has spoken regularly with several EU leaders, most notably French President Emmanuel Macron, about the possibility of letting Canadians live and work visa-free in the EU, WSJ said, citing two unnamed officials familiar with the matter.

Both leaders are set to meet later this month.

Macron’s press office did not respond to a request for comment.

The project to closely tie-up Canada and the EU is not such an easy feat, though, as fierce opposition to a more modest trade deal showed.

More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.

Reporting by Inti Landauro; Editing by Christina Fincher

By Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press

Montreal - Two decades ago, James Santos saw his friend die in a shooting at a Montreal college. Now, he is a Montreal police officer, working for the force he says saved his life that day.

Sunday marks the 20th anniversary of the shooting. On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered Dawson college and opened fire on students in the hall. He killed 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and injured 16 others, according to a coroner’s report from 2008.

Santos, then a 17-year-old student, was having lunch with De Sousa that day. The cafeteria was packed and the two found a free table close to the entrance, he recalled in an interview with The Canadian Press.

Article continues below

“We were talking about our weekend and what we did and we had laughs — and then, all of a sudden, I see the shooter walk in,” he said.

When he realized the man had a real weapon, Santos dove behind some chairs. De Sousa, who couldn’t see the shooter, stood up.

“She turned around facing the shooter and basically one of the first shots was directed to my friend,” recalled Santos.

Thinking De Sousa fainted, Santos crawled over to drag her to cover.

“That’s when I realized she got hit by one of the rounds near the abdomen. So I tried to console her, tell her that I was next to her and that everything will be alright,” he said.

Soon, the shooter turned his attention back to Santos. He told Santos to get up and get in front of him, essentially acting as a human shield. Santos obeyed.

“I didn’t want to anger him because I believed that Anastasia was still there, and I also had other friends that were trapped,” he said.

He tried to talk the shooter down. At that moment, Santos recalled, he accepted that he would die.

“I just didn’t want to take other students with me,” he said.

He fed the shooter white lies about the layout of the school, telling him one corridor led to a janitor’s closet or that another led nowhere.

When the shooter asked Santos how De Sousa was doing, Santos didn’t know what to say. At that point, he still hoped his friend was alive. So he told the shooter that he wasn’t sure and asked him to let him get her help.

“He didn’t say anything — he just loaded his magazine into a semi automatic and walked over to her, he unloaded all his 12 rounds on her, and then he came back and he told me, ‘Well, now you have nothing to worry about,’” said Santos.

Santos froze. Later, when the shooter held another student at gunpoint, Santos snapped, yelling at the shooter to leave the student be.

“I think I had enough with everything. Enough with the gunshots, the blood, the screaming of the students, just all of it,” said Santos.

“The shooter didn’t say anything, he just laughed.”

The shooter spared that other student. Moments later, police shot him in the leg. Santos was sure the angered gunman would shoot him. Instead, the shooter killed himself.

Santos ran off. He thought it had been hours since De Sousa was killed and the ordeal began.

“I found out a little later on that it was a dozen minutes that passed by,” he said.

In 2008, then-Governor General of Canada Michaelle Jean awarded Santos the Star of Courage for his actions that day.

Dawson College commemorated the shooting on Friday in a ceremony that brought De Sousa’s family, survivors and students together in the school’s Peace Garden. Loved ones remembered De Sousa’s cheerful and resilient character.

During the ceremony, De Sousa’s mother, Louise De Sousa, called on the federal government to tighten gun control laws.

Santos said the journey to becoming an officer was a challenging one, as he worked over years to overcome the trauma.

Talking about the events of that day two decades later, Santos seems calm, his voice never wavering.

“I have all the details in my mind. I recall everything, but I don’t put myself into it. I’m looking at it as a third person,” he said.

That wasn’t always the case, he said.

“Initially, saying it the first couple of times was extremely, extremely, extremely hard. There’s really no words to place it, just because you pretty much relive every second of it,” he said.

Nonetheless, as he tells the story, little details come up. The way De Sousa had wanted to go out for lunch, but Santos instead opted to eat at the cafeteria. The fact that she sat with her back to the door and couldn’t see the shooter coming in.

Santos said he fixated on some of these details after graduating from Dawson, filled with survivor’s guilt.

“What if I had given her the (other) chair?” he asked.

“It just goes down that spiral that it’s extremely hard to get out because you could think of anything, but it’ll never change what actually happened.”

He had considered a career in law enforcement before the event of 2006, and he said his experience during the shooting pushed him to want to join the Montreal police.

“I wanted to give back to the community that gave me another chance, right? The police (officers) gave me another chance at life.”

The path to get there wasn’t easy. Santos had vivid nightmares and panic attacks, and he knew he would have to address his trauma if he wanted to work as a police officer. He turned to therapy and set small goals, like watching an action movie, or one with a lot of shooting, until he could get through it calmly.

Then he joined the army. Training was a challenge, he said.

“The smell of gunpowder would bring me right back to the event of Dawson,” he said.

After about a decade in the military, Santos got into the police academy. He then worked for a year in a town outside of Montreal before joining the Montreal force in 2018.

“As a police officer, you never know what calls you’re getting. (If) I get a call, I’m not going to be having anxiety or sweating or anything, because of all the little things I did prior to get myself to where I am today,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

“We were talking about our weekend and what we did and we had laughs — and then, all of a sudden, I see the shooter walk in,” he said.
When he realized the man had a real weapon, Santos dove behind some chairs. De Sousa, who couldn’t see the shooter, stood up.
“She turned around facing the shooter and basically one of the first shots was directed to my friend,” recalled Santos.
Thinking De Sousa fainted, Santos crawled over to drag her to cover.
“That’s when I realized she got hit by one of the rounds near the abdomen. So I tried to console her, tell her that I was next to her and that everything will be alright,” he said.
Soon, the shooter turned his attention back to Santos. He told Santos to get up and get in front of him, essentially acting as a human shield. Santos obeyed.
“I didn’t want to anger him because I believed that Anastasia was still there, and I also had other friends that were trapped,” he said.
He tried to talk the shooter down. At that moment, Santos recalled, he accepted that he would die.
“I just didn’t want to take other students with me,” he said.
He fed the shooter white lies about the layout of the school, telling him one corridor led to a janitor’s closet or that another led nowhere.

When the shooter asked Santos how De Sousa was doing, Santos didn’t know what to say. At that point, he still hoped his friend was alive. So he told the shooter that he wasn’t sure and asked him to let him get her help.

“He didn’t say anything — he just loaded his magazine into a semi automatic and walked over to her, he unloaded all his 12 rounds on her, and then he came back and he told me, ‘Well, now you have nothing to worry about,’” said Santos.
Santos froze. Later, when the shooter held another student at gunpoint, Santos snapped, yelling at the shooter to leave the student be.
“I think I had enough with everything. Enough with the gunshots, the blood, the screaming of the students, just all of it,” said Santos.
“The shooter didn’t say anything, he just laughed.”
The shooter spared that other student. Moments later, police shot him in the leg. Santos was sure the angered gunman would shoot him. Instead, the shooter killed himself.
Santos ran off. He thought it had been hours since De Sousa was killed and the ordeal began.
“I found out a little later on that it was a dozen minutes that passed by,” he said.

Santos said the journey to becoming an officer was a challenging one, as he worked over years to overcome the trauma.

“I have all the details in my mind. I recall everything, but I don’t put myself into it. I’m looking at it as a third person,” he said.
That wasn’t always the case, he said.
“Initially, saying it the first couple of times was extremely, extremely, extremely hard. There’s really no words to place it, just because you pretty much relive every second of it,” he said.

Nonetheless, as he tells the story, little details come up. The way De Sousa had wanted to go out for lunch, but Santos instead opted to eat at the cafeteria. The fact that she sat with her back to the door and couldn’t see the shooter coming in.
Santos said he fixated on some of these details after graduating from Dawson, filled with survivor’s guilt.
“What if I had given her the (other) chair?” he asked.
“It just goes down that spiral that it’s extremely hard to get out because you could think of anything, but it’ll never change what actually happened.”
He had considered a career in law enforcement before the event of 2006, and he said his experience during the shooting pushed him to want to join the Montreal police.
“I wanted to give back to the community that gave me another chance, right? The police (officers) gave me another chance at life.”

The path to get there wasn’t easy. Santos had vivid nightmares and panic attacks, and he knew he would have to address his trauma if he wanted to work as a police officer. He turned to therapy and set small goals, like watching an action movie, or one with a lot of shooting, until he could get through it calmly.
Then he joined the army. Training was a challenge, he said.
“The smell of gunpowder would bring me right back to the event of Dawson,” he said.
After about a decade in the military, Santos got into the police academy. He then worked for a year in a town outside of Montreal before joining the Montreal force in 2018.

“As a police officer, you never know what calls you’re getting. (If) I get a call, I’m not going to be having anxiety or sweating or anything, because of all the little things I did prior to get myself to where I am today,” he said.

Building an economy less dependent on the U.S. is urgent. We need to prioritize not just GDP growth but also our sovereignty, writes Alex Himelfarb.

Updated Sept. 15, 2026

\_As the trade dispute with Donald Trump’s administration continues unpredictably, Canada’s economic prospects are changing quickly, even daily. Writers are not immune from being swept up. “Breaking Free of Neoliberalism,” the 2024 book by Canadian retired civil servant Alex Himelfarb — clerk of the privy council under three prime ministers — was updated and reissued last week as “Breaking Free of Neoliberalism in Trump Times.” That, however, was several days and several\_new tariffs ago. Below is the update to the update, freely adapted from the book on the stands \by the author\.

It is probably the conceit of every generation that they are at a turning point in history, that the choices we make will shape the lives of future generations. But Canada, under attack by our neighbour and closest trading partner, does indeed seem to face just such a defining moment. Are we still to be part of a continental economy with all its benefits and costs or are we ready to build a less dependent, more resilient Canada?

Mark Carney was elected with a near majority on the promise of Canada strong. By virtue of his demeanour, smarts and credentials, he looked like the perfect anti-Trump to take on the job. He said out loud what most leaders were reluctant or afraid to admit: that the America we had organized ourselves around no longer exists; the international order had been ruptured and Canada was on the front lines. His bold agenda to drive economic growth less dependent on the U.S. market won Canadians over.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

But it has never been entirely clear what elbows up means in practice. At the same time as Carney was making these arguments, his government was trying to get a deal with the Trump administration that would reduce the tariffs and secure our trading relationship. Whether to buy time or curry favour, the government made a series of concessions including compromising the small steps Canada was taking to secure digital sovereignty. Carney also took pains not “to poke the bear,” even offering comfort to Trump’s regime when it kidnapped the Venezuelan president, and when Israel and the U.S. launched the devastating and illegal war on Iran. Canada, of course, got nothing for the trail of concessions.

The prime minister seemed to be balancing two divergent strategies— reduced dependence and further integration, even apparently considering joining Trump’s ill-considered missile defence scheme and musing about “fortress North America.”

The government’s two tracks probably captured the combination of anxiety and patriotism Canadians were feeling. But it meant that Canadians were given little sense of where negotiations or Canada were headed. If rumours and leaks are to be believed we came close to trading off crucial elements of our sovereignty and locking in unsupportable and likely illegal tariffs for a deal that offered only the illusion of economic stability.

Of course, the chaos of the Trump administration ultimately saved us from any bad deal. Carney, in the face of increasingly outrageous demands from Trump negotiators and emboldened by an evident surge of patriotism among Canadians, did what no other world leader had done: he said no to Trump.

Most Canadians celebrated. That is not to say they weren’t worried about the consequences of the tariffs and the possibility of escalation, but they had had enough. No deal was to be trusted— written in pencil, as Carney concluded— nor was a reasonable deal even possible. This was not a trade war, Canadians understood, but an attack on Canadian sovereignty and identity.

No doubt this surge of patriotism— this willingness to imagine a future less reliant on the U.S., despite the risks— was intensified by the front row seat we have to American decline, to plutocracy run rampant. We have watched a few individuals and corporations accumulate so much wealth and power that they can shape and pollute public discourse, subvert public institutions for their own purposes, interfere in elections, steer world affairs, and accumulate yet more wealth and power. We have watched the often-violent stifling of dissent and the horrific abuse of immigrants. Most Canadians, with the exception of a small northern Maga rump, understand that the Trump regime represents a profound threat to democratic values, to humanity.

When Carney said no, he was thrust, whether he wants it or not, into a global leadership role in a fight that is taking place across much of the world today: against the threat of fascism and in defence of democracy.

Still, many of our corporate leaders (and the premier of Alberta) continue to push for a deal, urging the PM to do whatever it takes to restore our economic relationship with the U.S.— either in denial about who we are dealing with or prepared to sacrifice our sovereignty and values for their bottom line and the illusion of economic stability. All we need to do, they say, is the familiar recipe: drop our climate agenda, cut taxes, cut regulations, scale back the public sector, integrate with and be more like the U.S.

Trump didn’t create our dependency but by weaponizing it he made painfully evident the costs. Our sovereignty had been compromised for decades. We have always known that sharing a bed with an elephant comes with significant risks. When, in the 1980s, we cuddled in more closely, those risks grew. Now that the elephant has gone rogue, the threat is existential. The 1988 free trade election ushered in the Canadian version of the neoliberal counter-revolution of Reagan and Thatcher. That electrifying election asked whether we were willing to risk cultural, economic and democratic sovereignty for access to the American market. We never got the access we hoped for but we clearly compromised our sovereignty.

For the next four decades the priority of government shifted from the protection of its citizens to the pursuit of economic growth. Government’s main job became to create the conditions for the market to do its magic. What that meant practically was that governments were to create business-friendly policies, removing as many barriers to profit as politics allowed— cut taxes, deregulate, privatize.

After Nafta, our business class adapted their strategies overwhelmingly to the U.S. market, and organized around continental and global supply chains. Governments backed away from industrial policy, and Canada again became a resource hinterland to the United States. In the competition for investment, we allowed digital infrastructure and our cultural space to be dominated by foreign corporations, limiting our access to our own stories, undermining our ability to control and maintain the privacy of our data, and making us vulnerable to malign interference in our politics and our lives.

All of this contributed to record-breaking inequality, undermining solidarity and trust. Canada’s youth face rising tuitions, a precarious labour market and unaffordable housing. Deep conflicts about carbon taxes and pipelines, amplified by the powerful petroleum sector, have cramped our climate plans and threaten our unity. We have too often pursued development by trampling the rights of Indigenous Peoples instead of building partnerships based on respect. We have, for years, been less active in the international partnerships essential to managing global crises.

And now we face an existential crisis. The fight for survival is nothing new for Canada. Canada is an improbable country, bilingual, multicultural, built on French, English and Indigenous foundations, regionally diverse and geographically sprawling, next door to a giant. Pierre Trudeau once described Canada as “an act of defiance against the history of mankind.” Canada’s survival always took political will, and previous generations always rose to the challenge. Canada’s surge of patriotism in response to the Trump assault shows that spirit is alive. Now begins the fight to build a more resilient Canada.

The prime minister has clear sailing for leading a major reset. He has an almost unprecedented degree of public trust. He has his majority. The parliamentary opposition is relatively weak.

The latitude that all governments get during a crisis comes with considerable risks. In crisis, room for debate is often narrowed. We May accept decisions inconceivable in normal times. We May treat democracy as a luxury that can be sacrificed in the name of urgency. Many become reluctant to question the government. Governments, however, are at their best when challenged. This is no time for Canadians to be on the sidelines.

Building an economy less dependent on the U.S. is clearly urgent. But sovereignty is not just about our ability to grow the economy. How would our decisions on retaliation, the projects we choose or the investments we welcome change if we ask how will they contribute not just to GDP growth but to our sovereignty over our energy, water and natural resources, our digital and cultural spaces, our ability to determine our future and carve out our own place in the world?

Will the decisions we make move our economy up the value chain, create union jobs, help us meet our emission targets, keep wealth and intellectual property in Canada? Investments in mergers and acquisitions or foreign investments to pick off Canadian companies or public assets, for example, would erode sovereignty and democracy. As would allowing American tech giants free rein in Canada, especially given the disruptive power of AI.

We need to be wary of “progress traps,” decisions that get us through a tough moment but create even tougher moments down the road. Investing public funds in a major pipeline, for example, would divide the country, lock us into the past, end up as a stranded asset, and take up resources required for building the energy transformation we need but seem to be backing away from.

Canada is not powerless. We have the ninth largest economy in the world, a diverse, educated population, unique natural resources. We are reliable. Decades of neoliberalism May have blinded us to the range of tools we have successfully used to protect our sovereignty. For example, we used to own things together if they were crucial to our sovereignty and security or to the public good even if not privately profitable.

We need to take care of each other through these difficult times, to spend whatever it takes to protect workers, families and firms hurt by Trump’s assault — especially young Canadians, always hardest hit. Research warns that the combination of economic shocks, economic insecurity, and the absence of state protections fuels right-wing populism. Investing in our programs of education and care is essential for our economy and democracy.

We must not waste the unprecedented solidarity Trump has gifted us. This is a time for compassion, ambition, imagination and robust democracy.

stories.title: Delayed emergency room treatment caused the death of this Winnipeg woman. Now her family is seeking answers.
stories.summary: A Winnipeg family says they are now left with more questions than answers, after a critical incident report was released following the death of their loved one.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – A Winnipeg family says they are now left with more questions than answers, after a critical incident report was released following the death of their loved one.

Stacey Ross was just 55 years old when she died, after waiting several hours in Winnipeg St. Boniface Hospital in January.

On Jan. 3, Stacey was experiencing severe chest pain and went to the emergency room. Her sister, Sheri Ross said Stacey waited more than 12 hours before being told her sickness was a virus and was sent home.

But over time her condition worsened and she returned by ambulance to the same hospital on Jan. 15, where she waited more than 11 hours before being admitted.

A CT scan revealed pneumonia in Stacey’s lungs, but not long after, she went into cardiac arrest and died.

An investigation into the critical incident was launched, and eight months after Stacey’s death, findings into the incident were released to the family.

The report, obtained by CTV News, shows the investigation found “several factors” that contributed to delays in Stacey’s care.

“The long wait times and a shortage of available treatment spaces, resulted in a delay of approximately 12 hours, before Stacey was assessed by a physician,” the report read.

“The review also found that elevated troponin blood test results were not identified and escalated as they should have been,” it adds.

The findings also confirmed Stacey’s concerns regarding chest pains were also not reported to a physician on the night of her death.

In the report, the hospital says it is trying to reduce emergency room delays by improving how patients move through the ER, by making sure the sickest patients are seen first when it gets very busy and making sure critical blood-test results are communicated quickly.

Manitoba’s Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara told CTV News that the recommendations from the report are being taken “seriously” and has “given direction for all of them to be actioned.”

“No report can undo what Stacey’s family has been through, but they deserve to know that lessons are being learned and acted on,” Asagwara said in a statement.

“We will continue working with health-system partners to strengthen emergency care, including adding more staff and capacity and improving access to care across the system.”

A spokesperson with the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority (Wrha) says these recommendations are being implemented.

“As part of this work, a cardiologist is now providing rapid cardiology consultations in the St. Boniface Hospital emergency department, with the intent to expand the service as staffing allows,” the statement reads.

However, Sheri says her family is frustrated and disappointed with the results of the report.

“They’re taking blame for it, but that doesn’t fix anything,” she said. “It just makes me really angry that this happened because it never should have happened.”

“She should have received treatment right away, or at least within a reasonable amount of time. She should have received treatment or seen a doctor, or something should have been done, not 12 hours later,” she said.

Sheri has been speaking out about her sister’s death to try and prevent others from going through a similar loss. She says the report is making it harder for her family to get closure and does not believe it provides any real change.

“I’m not seeing that. Neither is anybody in my family. We just don’t see what the purpose of it (critical incident report) was,” she said. “There’s no change.”

“It’s very frustrating because we were promised answers to what happened and how it won’t happen again,” she said.

‘Status quo not acceptable’

According to numbers from the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority (Wrha) website, Winnipeg ED and urgent care median wait times have generally increased over time, rising from around two hours in 2021, to 4.4 hours in July 2026.

As of Friday afternoon, the wait time at St. Boniface Hospital was nine hours, where as the wait time at the city’s Grace Hospital was 8.5 hours.

“I do think that while it’s common in many parts of the country, we cannot accept this as a status quo, so we certainly can do better,” said Dr. Bolu Ogunyemi, who is the president of the Canadian Medical Association (CMA).

He says better access to primary care could alleviate long wait times in emergency departments.

“We need to train more family doctors, train more doctors in general, we also need to retain them,” he said.

“It’s one thing about training our own and recruiting folks from different parts of the world can be important, but we need to retain them.”

“We need urgency because people shouldn’t be waiting longer than they need to. We need all hands on deck when it comes to folks getting access to care,” he said.

stories.title: Quebec election campaign wraps third week as leaders’ debates approach
stories.summary: Montreal - Quebec political leaders are entering their 18th day on the campaign trail today with their first debate approaching on Tuesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - Quebec’s political leaders unveiled new promises on the economy and violence against women Sunday as they prepared for the campaign’s first televised debate.

Updated Sept. 15, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

jqb SDV[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/quebec/quebec-election-campaign-wraps-third-week-as-leaders-debates-approach/article_5026a47b-3765-55e3-8f73-b6e0f5247e0a.html)

By The Canadian Press

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard unveiled his party’s fiscal framework in Quebec City, promising a return to “economic realism” and a balanced budget by 2029-30.

“This is not the time for election goodies or tax cuts that May be appealing, but are not very realistic in the current context,” Milliard told reporters.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

The Liberals say they can close a $6-billion hole in the province’s finances and pay for their promises by reforming government, refocusing some tax credits and regulating illegal online gambling, among other measures.

The framework also anticipates a $4.36-billion increase in federal transfers by 2030-31 and includes $4 billion in contingency provisions because of uncertainty surrounding U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariff war.

Milliard has promised to cut 12,000 public service positions while maintaining services in health, education and culture. Departmental spending would increase by an average of 2.4 per cent over the next five years.

“I’m not afraid at all of the word austerity because what we’re proposing is not austerity, he said.

“It’s a return to economic realism.”

The Parti Québécois is now the only major party that has yet to present its fiscal framework. Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said he will release it Tuesday, the same day as the first leaders’ debate.

Meanwhile, Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette sought to rally supporters Sunday, telling hundreds of them that a third CAQ mandate remains within reach.

“This victory is within our reach,” Fréchette told an enthusiastic crowd at her first major rally of the campaign in Kingsey Falls, in the Centre-du-Québec region.

About 400 supporters and 88 of the Caq’s 125 candidates attended the rally.

Fréchette also promoted the Caq’s autonomist approach, which seeks greater powers for Quebec within Canada without pursuing independence.

The position has long allowed the CAQ to present itself as a third option between the federalist and sovereigntist camps that have traditionally dominated Quebec politics.

The CAQ fell to lows in public opinion polls earlier this year before making gains under Fréchette, though its momentum now appears to have stalled.

Fréchette is expected to take the rest of Sunday and Monday off the campaign trail to prepare for the debates.

The five party leaders will face off in Tva’s Face-à-Face on Tuesday and Noovo and Crave’s leaders’ debate Wednesday. A third debate will air on Radio-Canada the following week.

Elsewhere Sunday, Québec solidaire and the PQ both unveiled measures aimed at protecting women from violence.

QS Leader Ruba Ghazal proposed spending $10 million to create a first-line service for victims of online hate and harassment.

“Freedom of expression does not mean the freedom to intimidate, threaten or harass,” Ghazal told reporters in Montreal.

QS would also provide 10 days of paid leave, at the employer’s expense, to women experiencing domestic violence and spend $600 million to create up to 1,000 new spaces in women’s shelters.

The PQ, meanwhile, promised to build six new emergency shelters in Montreal, Outaouais, Laval, Lanaudière, Montérégie and the Capitale-Nationale, creating an estimated 70 to 80 spaces.

The party would also invest $35 million over four years in emergency shelters and increase funding for second-stage shelters by $52 million over four years.

St-Pierre Plamondon did not attend the announcement as he prepared for this week’s debates.

Quebec voters go to the polls Oct. 5.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 13, 2026.

— with files from Patrice Bergeron in Kingsey Falls and Thomas Laberge in Quebec City

stories.title: This Calgary realtor left China for a better life. Now she’s among the immigrants backing Alberta independence
stories.summary: “Did you guys register to vote?”
stories.author: Jeffrey Mo
stories.content:
Anand Chetty, seen selling corn from the back of his truck, was born in South Africa, came to Canada and now backs Alberta separatism.

Todd Korol for the Toronto Star

Courtesy of Hong Wang

Todd Korol for the Toronto Star[](http://www.thestar.com/news/insight/fea-alta-mo/article_da63476e-0230-4502-9a6f-041b7f01993c.html)

“Did you guys register to vote?”

I no longer live in Alberta, so I cannot vote in next month’s independence referendum. No matter — my parents could be my proxies, right?

My sister piped up with some amusement into our family Zoom call. “I don’t think you want Mom to vote.”

A semi-incredulous “What do you mean?” was soon followed by, “Mom, how are your church friends voting?”

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

My parents immigrated to Canada from Hong Kong. They didn’t, like the parents of a university classmate, randomly stab a pin onto a map of Canada and end up in a small town in Saskatchewan. My dad went to university in Ontario; my parents met in Manitoba; and a few weeks after I was born, my parents moved west from Saskatchewan to Alberta, ON the basis of my dad’s premonition that Alberta’s economy would take off. He was right.

When people ask about my family’s immigration history, they want to know when we landed in Canada, not when we moved to Alberta. The major decision was always Canada versus the rest of the world; we could just as easily have ended up in Vancouver or Toronto instead of in Calgary.

Immigrants and their children talk about how grateful they are to live in Canada, not Alberta in particular. I simply assumed that all immigrants — including my mom’s church friends — would vote for Alberta to stay in Canada. Surely, they didn’t move to Canada in order to no longer live in Canada, and surely, Alberta separation was a problem wrought by others.

According to my mom, the independence supporters at her church fell into two camps: (1) those who didn’t really want to leave but wanted to use the referendum as leverage against Ottawa, and (2) those who had been unable to immigrate to the United States, saw Canada as the next best option, and thought that Alberta independence would make it easier to achieve their original goal.

Surprisingly, to me at least, a poll by Janet Brown Opinion Research showed that immigrants and native-born Canadians didn’t differ too much in how likely they are to support independence. When I went back home this summer, I set about trying to understand those immigrants and visible minorities.

In a fit of racial profiling, I looked at two of the largest pro-independence Facebook groups, Alberta Separation and Alberta Independence Movement, and sent messages to some members with promising-looking names.

I was expecting to get all sorts of crazy and combative responses. Some of my interviewees did not disappoint. (One “applied health scientist” originally from India claimed to have healed a patient with Stage 4 brain cancer, yet he couldn’t remember what year it was.)

But then there’s Hong Wang. She moved to Ontario in the early 1990s and came to Calgary five years later, where she now works as a realtor.

“It’s ironic. When I left China, I saw no hope in our country,”because of a corrupt government, the lack of freedom, and a system that forced her and her then-husband to live apart from one another.

“I gave up everything, just hoping for a better life, and now I see this country is going down the drain. In the meantime, China’s GDP grew (often by 10 per cent or more per year). The country I left became a different country; the country I came to became a different country. I’ll be damned if, at the end of the day, I realized it was all a joke — if it was such a mistake to leave China.”

Immigrants, by definition, have experience elsewhere and thus often a different — and perhaps wider — perspective than many native-born Albertans, who might never have lived outside the province, let alone the country. Many of my interviewees compared Canada to their home countries in an unfavourable way.

Back in the Philippines, they could say anything they wanted to without worrying about being convicted in court (as long as it wasn’t intentionally offensive), claimed Luis Aragon, who immigrated with his wife and children in the early 2010s. (Aragon’s name is a pseudonym; many of my interviewees were hesitant to use their real names or to have their pictures taken, given the polarizing nature of this topic and, often, a desire to protect their children from having to explain their parents’ values and opinions.)

“Here, there are so many words I cannot say even if I don’t mean them in a bad way,” said Aragon. “Tell me, who’s really free?” (For context, the Philippines ranked 114 th out of 180 countries in this year’s World Press Freedom Index, while Canada ranked 20 th.)

“I wouldn’t know whether life in Canada (today) is better than that in the Philippines because I left it long ago. I didn’t like the corruption, the politicians leaving the people hungry. That’s the reason I thought it wasn’t a good place for kids, and suddenly I’m seeing that here.”

Wang’s justification for leaving was entirely economic, and the prospect of prosperity through Albertans taking control of their own economy and resources was almost universally important among the pro-independence immigrants I spoke to. Aragon, for instance, had worked for more than a decade in oil and gas in the Middle East, and moved to Alberta with the initial goal of staying in that field.

“Look at the conversion rate,” he said. “We send money to the Philippines but compared to our relatives from the U.S., we feel ashamed” at how much less it is.

“During the time of Harper and when Trudeau started, I was so proud to tell everyone I was Canadian but right now, I tell them that I’m not Filipino any more but I cannot be proud to say that I’m Canadian.”

Aragon said he began to feel the increasing cost of living around 2015, but only started seriously considering independence after the worst of the COVID pandemic, when the idea seemed more realistic. “I didn’t agree with much of what the left is doing. We are basically for common sense.” He cited, for instance, restricting Alberta’s oil development.

Anand Chetty, who moved as a child from South Africa to British Columbia in the mid-1970s before coming to Alberta in the early 1990s, also blamed the federal Liberal government for “very deliberately continuing to harm Alberta.”

“There could be substantial development and substantial economic benefits and that was stymied. The spending that the federal government has done is out of control. Somebody is going to end up paying and it’s not going to be me — it’s going to be the youth.” Chetty has supported independence from the start of Justin Trudeau’s time in office, deeming his economic policies “irresponsible.”

The bristling about the federal government strikes a familiar chord with Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta who came to Canada as a 12-year-old from the then-Communist Poland. “There’s a segment of the (immigrant) population that I would call anti-establishment, anti-system,” he said. “I often heard Polish people saying that Justin Trudeau was just as bad as the Communists (in 1980s Poland).”

Lukaszuk, the leader of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity initiative, says that like pro-independence immigrants, their pro-unity counterparts also have an incentive to not speak up too loudly.

He believes that, just as a certain segment of immigrants who have experienced repression in their homelands will fight against any perceived repression in Canada, another segment has a lingering fear of doing anything to oppose what they think the government wants them to do — and he added that there is a perception that Alberta’s Premier Danielle Smith supports independence, even though she has publicly and repeatedly said that she opposes it.

The provincial government also funds initiatives such as weekend language schools or faith-based schools, and “those ethnocultural groups are unlikely to cause any waves with the government because they feel obliged,” said Lukaszuk.

Earlier this summer, Rishi Nagar, a morning show presenter on Calgary’s RED FM, whose tag line is “Reflecting Ethnic Diversity,” hosted 10 days of discussions about the Oct. 19 referendum, devoting a day to each question and breaking down the issues to a listening audience that was majority South Asian. (The other nine questions deal with immigration and citizenship, and with efforts to amend Canada’s Constitution.)

The station reported that none of the 42 people who responded during the program said that they wanted to separate from Canada, though any biases that Nagar might have held could have affected his listeners.

Wang, the realtor in Calgary, doesn’t suffer from being uninformed or from being swayed by ethnic media. “I support the Conservatives but I don’t (want to) defund the CBC,” she said. “I listen to CBC Radio all the time. I’m not sure where to get Chinese news — even on social media, only a very few (things I watch) are Chinese videos.”

She said that she loves Canada — and I believe her. She might have wanted to get out of Toronto, but she liked Ottawa (where she first lived) and thought that living in Montreal might not have been “a bad idea,” with its “beautiful houses,” liveliness, and culture. She didn’t want Canada to become the 51 st state.

Aragon, ON the other hand, said that he’d thought about moving to the United States, but his children vetoed the idea. He didn’t see this as disloyalty to Canada. Instead, he thought that “Canada is betraying immigrants with a promise of a different world from where we came from, (but it keeps) changing for the worse, and that’s not the expectation of those who work hard.”

“I didn’t turn my back on the country,” said South African-born Chetty. “The country turned its back on me.”

Most of my interviewees started by talking about their strong support for independence and their intent to vote “yes” next month, but almost all of them — more emphatic voices like Aragon and Chetty included — didn’t believe that Alberta would separate from Canada during their lifetimes. Over the course of our talks, most gradually moderated what they said, telling me that they really just wanted more leverage for Alberta, like the first group of my mom’s church friends.(Chetty is still an ardent separatist.)

Ranj Shergill (another pseudonym), a Sikh lawyer and entrepreneur in his mid-30s who has lived and worked in rural Alberta and is now in Calgary,told me in late July that he wanted to use the referendum to renegotiate Confederation and give Alberta more of a say in how the country is run.

“I would definitely characterize myself as a Western Canadian,” said Shergill. “I think there’s a unique set of values and a way of life in the Canadian West … that is more pro-freedom and pro-enterprise, that’s more rugged and more pioneering.

“The Canadian experiment allows me to live my faith in a way that’s aligned with my values, and I think Alberta (wants) the same sovereignty and a way of living that’s aligned with its values.”

After the Canada-U.S. trade war intensified, though, Shergill told me that he no longer intends to vote for Alberta independence, as the world is too uncertain now and “entertaining these questions (about independence) right now … creates jeopardy for what kind of future we might have.” He thought that some parts of the Alberta independence movement were coalescing with Trump’s Maga movement and that there was a risk that it might take on some of Maga’s more ethnonationalist and anti-democratic elements.

The Star, simplified

Breaking news, interactive polls, video, and voice notes. Star stories you’ll want to share, delivered where you’re already chatting. Follow the Star on WhatsApp.

Writing this article has actually forced me to re-evaluate why I want Alberta to stay in Canada, especially since I don’t even live in Canada right now and don’t have concrete plans to return. I want to say it’s because I think that Canada is a family — diverse ethnoculturally and also ideologically, but a family nonetheless — and that it’s both Alberta’s responsibility and Alberta’s privilege to contribute to the welfare of the rest of this vast family.

Maybe, though, it’s just because I grew up loving Canada and can’t imagine returning to something that is no longer Canada. As another Chinese-Canadian man abroad once put it to me, “My heart bleeds red and white.” (I realize, of course, that I am not living through any economic pain in Alberta, nor can I personally feel it if the rest of the country is taking advantage of or not listening to us.)

Even if we might disagree about the way forward, I respect how much these pro-independence immigrants and visible minorities want to improve their adopted land, whether that be Alberta or Canada as a whole. As Wang said, “This is my patriotic act (for) Canada.” Perhaps it sounds counterintuitive, but I believe she’s sincere.

I just hope my parents’ votes will reflect what my patriotic act for Canada would be — and, for decency’s sake, that those in my mother’s congregation who don’t even want to be Canadian don’t vote. Let them vote with their feet and just leave.

Jeffrey Mo is a Canadian freelance writer based in Taipei.

Writing this article has actually forced me to re-evaluate why I want Alberta to stay in Canada, especially since I don’t even live in Canada right now and don’t have concrete plans to return. I just hope my parents’ votes will reflect what my patriotic act for Canada would be — and, for decency’s sake, that those in my mother’s congregation who don’t even want to be Canadian don’t vote. Let them vote with their feet and just leave.

stories.title: Why a team of Ontario student scientists is racing to the wreckages of Canada's worst storms
stories.summary: At Western University, a team of students with the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory investigated whether the severe storm was a tornado, after it hit.
stories.author: Janet Hurley
stories.content:
Manley, ONT. — As Kevin Murray stood on his porch, the sky suddenly turned dark and the wind surged, driving the rain sideways. He ordered his four children to the basement.

He watched as a trampoline careened across the yard; the house shook, and Murray knew it was time to follow the family downstairs.

Less than 15 minutes later, he emerged from his Perth County home to a scene of devastation across his two properties. Towering trees that once lined the long country driveway like a colonnade lay in ruins. The barn was reduced to kindling, save for one metal wall bearing a precariously affixed sign that was a wedding gift from his wife some 14 years ago.

“I was shocked but more sad because we have our name on the barn and now it’s gone,” Murray said.

Kevin Murray and his son Stephen among the trees and damage from the Sept. 2 storm that swept through their property.

The storm that rolled through southern Ontario on the afternoon of Sept. 2 cut a wide path. In Toronto, it twisted and tossed the bleachers at Rogers Stadium and flooded the streets of Vaughan. In farming communities west of Waterloo, it levelled barn after barn and flattened fields of corn. Debris and downed hydro lines blocked roads around Brodhagen, not far from Murray’s farm.

The question on everyone’s mind was: Had a tornado come through?

At Western University, a team of students with the Canadian Severe Storms Laboratory (Cssl) was getting ready to find the answer.

The severe weather forecast for Sept. 2 had proven all too accurate. Reports of property damage, particularly around Brodhagen, north of Stratford, were beginning to filter into the lab, established in 2024 to house the Northern Tornadoes , the Northern Hail and the Northern Mesonet research projects.

Matthew Woodward, a 22-year-old geography major, got tapped to assemble a team. The University of Waterloo student grabbed his go-bag — packed with water, food, a laptop and some overnight supplies just in case — and prepared to head out for what would be his 21st investigation this year.

For the past four summers, Woodward has served as a Cssl intern, returning each season to do forensic analysis and research in the wake of Canada’s worst storms, helping piece together the what and why.

Matthew Woodward, a University of Waterloo student who has spent four summers as a Cssl intern, checks out foundation connections on the Murray barn destroyed in the Sept. 2 storm.

The paid 17-week internship program, launched in 2022 and open to any university student in Canada, places teams in London, Ont., Winnipeg and Olds, Alta., known as “hailstorm alley.” This year, there were 270 applicants for 28 spots.

On Sept. 3, just after noon, Woodward and three graduate students pulled up to the Murray farm in a white pickup emblazoned with the Cssl logo. The team, which had already visited 20 sites that morning, had spotted the collapsed barn via drone images captured from another battered property more than a kilometre away.

Because tornado damage gets cleaned up quickly, speed matters, explained internship co-ordinator Connell Miller, who is also director of the Northern Mesonet Project. “The more preserved a site is by the time we get there, the more information we can glean from it.”

Even as the team arrived, Murray and his family were already clearing debris, a tractor scooping up downed branches.

With permission, the students fanned out, searching for clues.

One day, says a climatologist, Toronto will get a true “climatologically extreme” storm, says an expert, and the results will be “beyond

Their first questions were practical: Was the barn door open when the storm hit? No. How old was the structure? More than a century. The answers mattered. Construction quality is part of the calculus. The team examined the remnants, inspecting the nails and screws that had once connected the roof to the walls and the walls to the foundation.

They looked for splatter marks. A tornado generates significant uplift, throwing dirt and debris everywhere; the more common downburst, a powerful column of sinking air, pushes outward rather than upward, leaving no such signature.

They surveyed the field of damage trying to determine if it was wide and in the same direction like a downburst or narrow and convergent like a tornado.

They photographed everything and fed their observations into a program on an iPad, ranking the destruction of Murray’s property a 6 out of 8 and concluding the wind speed had likely been 130 km/h.

The final report would be done back at the lab with the ultimate goal of determining whether a tornado actually touched down and assigning a rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale , a measure of wind intensity similar to the Richter scale for earthquakes but with a key difference being that it’s damage-based and requiring humans trained in forensic assessment to, as Miller put it, “work backwards” from the wreckage.

Since the internship program began, the most catastrophic events recorded have been the derecho — a long-lived, fast-moving straight-line band of thunderstorms — that swept through Ontario and Quebec in May 2022 killing 16 people and the EF4 tornado, with a wind speed of 275 km/h , that hit Didsbury, Alta ., the next year.

“The biggest misconception is that Canada doesn’t receive that many tornadoes,” said Miller, adding it’s second in the world to the U.S. In 2025, there were 116 tornadoes .

Back in June, when Miller first spoke to the Star, he said 2026 was looking relatively quiet. “I was wrong. It started off slow, but it’s really picked up,” he admitted the day after the Sept. 2 storm. This could be “one of the busiest seasons since we started the Northern Tornadoes Project in 2017.”

In Ontario alone, with the season not yet over, there have been 29 tornadoes and 31 downbursts.

From left, Matthew Woodward, Daniel Butt, Jessica van den Heuvel and Jihan Pacer, a forensic team from Western University during their investigation of a possible tornado touchdown in Brodhagen, Ont.

The relentless pace takes a toll. There is a duality to the work, said Miller, in that such weather events are necessary to advance research but no one wants a tornado to occur. He tells the interns, “it’s OK to feel both of these things at the same time.”

It’s a tension the students navigate on site visits. “Being able to balance the curiosity of finding out what happens but then also approaching people where they’re at is really important,” said Catherine Walke, a 20-year-old Western psychology student who just completed her second summer internship. “People can feel really emotional about the loss of property.”

It’s that loss that drives the work. Nearly all tornadoes in Canada are rated EF2 or lower, and the lab has found through its research that a small change to roof-wall connection, costing as little as $200, can be enough to withstand that intensity. The lab is pushing for enhanced building code provisions to make structures more resilient. And being able to better understand and classify storms helps to build better warning systems, giving the next family more time to get to the basement.

Within days of the Sept. 2 storm, the lab results were in: Tornadoes had touched down in Wellesley , Tavistock , Shakespeare and Monkton ; downbursts in Orr Lake, Seaforth and Toronto.

In Brodhagen , it was a downburst rated EF1, not a tornado — a distinction meaningful on paper but less so on a country road in Perth County. “For a homeowner, damage is damage,” said Miller.

Murray was happy to help with the science, but it wouldn’t change what was in front of him. “The established trees are gone and it’s going to change the landscape of everything.”

Because tornado damage gets cleaned up quickly, speed matters, explained internship co-ordinator Connell Miller, who is also director of the Northern Mesonet Project. “The more preserved a site is by the time we get there, the more information we can glean from it.”
Even as the team arrived, Murray and his family were already clearing debris, a tractor scooping up downed branches.
With permission, the students fanned out, searching for clues.

Their first questions were practical: Was the barn door open when the storm hit? No. How old was the structure? More than a century. The answers mattered. Construction quality is part of the calculus. The team examined the remnants, inspecting the nails and screws that had once connected the roof to the walls and the walls to the foundation.

They looked for splatter marks. A tornado generates significant uplift, throwing dirt and debris everywhere; the more common downburst, a powerful column of sinking air, pushes outward rather than upward, leaving no such signature.
They surveyed the field of damage trying to determine if it was wide and in the same direction like a downburst or narrow and convergent like a tornado.
They photographed everything and fed their observations into a program on an iPad, ranking the destruction of Murray’s property a 6 out of 8 and concluding the wind speed had likely been 130 km/h.

The final report would be done back at the lab with the ultimate goal of determining whether a tornado actually touched down and assigning a rating on the Enhanced Fujita scale , a measure of wind intensity similar to the Richter scale for earthquakes but with a key difference being that it’s damage-based and requiring humans trained in forensic assessment to, as Miller put it, “work backwards” from the wreckage.

Since the internship program began, the most catastrophic events recorded have been the derecho — a long-lived, fast-moving straight-line band of thunderstorms — that swept through Ontario and Quebec in May 2022 killing 16 people and the EF4 tornado, with a wind speed of 275 km/h , that hit Didsbury, Alta ., the next year.
“The biggest misconception is that Canada doesn’t receive that many tornadoes,” said Miller, adding it’s second in the world to the U.S. In 2025, there were 116 tornadoes .

Back in June, when Miller first spoke to the Star, he said 2026 was looking relatively quiet. “I was wrong. It started off slow, but it’s really picked up,” he admitted the day after the Sept. 2 storm. This could be “one of the busiest seasons since we started the Northern Tornadoes Project in 2017.”
In Ontario alone, with the season not yet over, there have been 29 tornadoes and 31 downbursts.
From left, Matthew Woodward, Daniel Butt, Jessica van den Heuvel and Jihan Pacer, a forensic team from Western University during their investigation of a possible tornado touchdown in Brodhagen, Ont.

The relentless pace takes a toll. There is a duality to the work, said Miller, in that such weather events are necessary to advance research but no one wants a tornado to occur. He tells the interns, “it’s OK to feel both of these things at the same time.”

It’s a tension the students navigate on site visits. “Being able to balance the curiosity of finding out what happens but then also approaching people where they’re at is really important,” said Catherine Walke, a 20-year-old Western psychology student who just completed her second summer internship. “People can feel really emotional about the loss of property.”

It’s that loss that drives the work. Nearly all tornadoes in Canada are rated EF2 or lower, and the lab has found through its research that a small change to roof-wall connection, costing as little as $200, can be enough to withstand that intensity. The lab is pushing for enhanced building code provisions to make structures more resilient. And being able to better understand and classify storms helps to build better warning systems, giving the next family more time to get to the basement.
Within days of the Sept. 2 storm, the lab results were in: Tornadoes had touched down in Wellesley , Tavistock , Shakespeare and Monkton ; downbursts in Orr Lake, Seaforth and Toronto.
In Brodhagen , it was a downburst rated EF1, not a tornado — a distinction meaningful on paper but less so on a country road in Perth County. “For a homeowner, damage is damage,” said Miller.
Murray was happy to help with the science, but it wouldn’t change what was in front of him. “The established trees are gone and it’s going to change the landscape of everything.”
