stories.title: Canada to co-host conference on returning Ukrainian kids, detainees
stories.summary: Canada, Ukraine and Norway will host an international conference in Toronto focused on returning Ukrainian children, detained civilians and prisoners of war.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
Canada will co-host an international conference in Toronto later this month aimed at securing the return of Ukrainian children, detained civilians and prisoners of war held by Russia.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand announced Saturday that Canada, Ukraine and Norway will host the two-day conference on Sept. 28 and 29.

The event, called Pathways to Peace: Second International Conference on Returning Ukrainian Children, Detained Civilians, and Prisoners of War , will bring together foreign ministers, senior government representatives and international organizations.

“Canada, Ukraine and Norway are convening the conference to strengthen international support for efforts to bring people home, protect those who remain under Russian control and ensure that those who return can access rehabilitation and reintegration services,” Global Affairs Canada said in a statement.

Ukrainian authorities have documented 20,651 cases of possible unlawful deportation or forcible transfer of Ukrainian children by Russia, according to the federal government.

So far, 2,573 children have been returned from deportation, forcible transfer and temporarily occupied territories.

As of June, Ukraine’s parliamentary commissioner for human rights had confirmed 1,878 civilians were being unlawfully detained by Russia. Global Affairs Canada said the true number could be significantly higher, with some civil society organizations estimating that as many as 20,000 civilians could be detained.

Ukraine does not disclose the exact number of its prisoners of war being held by Russia.

As of August, 9,529 Ukrainian military personnel and civilians had been returned from Russian captivity, according to Global Affairs Canada.

Participants in Toronto will discuss ways to strengthen tracing and information sharing and establish pathways for people to return to Ukraine.

The conference will also focus on humanitarian access and family contact for those who remain under Russian control.

The gathering comes as Russia intensifies its air campaign against Ukraine.

Russian strikes killed eight civilians and wounded dozens more across Ukraine on Saturday, according to local officials.

Two people were killed when Russian drones struck a residential area in Zaporizhzhia, while another person was killed in Kryvyi Rih. In Odesa and the surrounding region, 35 people were wounded in what regional officials described as a “massive attack.”

Three people were also killed when drones struck vehicles in Kramatorsk, while two others died in a Russian attack on a grocery store in the Zhytomyr region.

The attacks came a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that the deployment of European troops to Ukraine would mean direct conflict with Russia.

“Now they’re talking about how they’re considering sending troops into Ukraine. That means a war with Russia,” Putin said Friday during a summit of the Brics group of emerging economies in India.

Some European leaders have pledged support for a potential peacekeeping force in Ukraine as part of a future peace agreement, a proposal Moscow has repeatedly rejected.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said in an interview published Saturday that he would be willing to meet Putin if both leaders were invited to the G20 summit in Miami in December.

Canada has committed more than $26 billion in multifaceted support to Ukraine since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, including more than $750 million for recovery and reconstruction, according to the federal government.

– With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Quebec party leaders talk transport, health care on campaign trail as first debate looms
stories.summary: The debate is scheduled for Tuesday in preparation for the Oct. 5 election
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Promises on transport, public safety and health care filled the air on the Quebec campaign trail on Saturday as leaders prepare to face off in debates next week.

The first of three debates between the leaders of the five major parties is scheduled for Tuesday in preparation for the Oct. 5 election.

Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Liberal Leader Charles Milliard both said they would put an increased focus on prevention to lighten the province’s health care system.

In a press conference in Montreal on Saturday morning, St-Pierre Plamondon said his party would invest $550 million over four years in prevention measures while encouraging physical activity and mental health care. He also promised to crack down on over-prescribing of medications.

“We’re shifting our approach and saying, if we invest money and time in preventing these problems, there will be less people in emergency rooms and less people throughout the system,” he said.

He also reiterated his promise to abolish Santé Québec, the province’s public health agency that was created in 2024 and became the sole employer in the health and social services network. He said not all the agency’s employees would be laid off by such a move, but did not specify how many would lose their jobs.

In Trois-Rivières, Milliard promised his party would invest five per cent of the province’s health care budget in 10 years in prevention services like vaccination, cancer screening and chronic disease prevention.

After a week marked by talks of sovereignty, Milliard tried to paint himself as the best candidate to negotiate with Ottawa on immigration. He accused Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette of not wanting to work with the rest of the country.

Québec Solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal said in a press conference in Montreal that, if elected, her party would make public transit free for those under 25 years old and those over 65 years old.

She said her party would also increase funding for public transit and highlighted the positive economic and environmental potential of such a measure.

“There are populations with an even greater need for public transit, and right now there are many barriers, whether in terms of service or affordability,” she said.

She accused the outgoing Coalition Avenir Québec administration of having “abandoned” public transit.

Meanwhile, Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime attended a protest in Quebec City against the ongoing tramway project and called for a clear estimate of the cost.

He repeated his disapproval of the project, casting instead its support to the so-called “third link” bridge project which has seen various iterations in recent years.

Fréchette, leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec, visited the province’s police school in Nicolet, close to Trois-Rivières. She promised her party would spend $196 million to hire 300 additional police officers and 50 prosecutors in the province.

She said online crime, homelessness and mental health issues have made police officers’ jobs more complex.

“Despite our many efforts, ...Quebecers remain worried,” she said.

While the Parti Québécois has been favoured by some public opinion polls, recent surveys appear to show the Coalition Avenir Québec gaining momentum.

In a press conference in Montreal on Saturday morning, St-Pierre Plamondon said his party would invest $550 million over four years in prevention measures while encouraging physical activity and mental health care. He also promised to crack down on over-prescribing of medications.
“We’re shifting our approach and saying, if we invest money and time in preventing these problems, there will be less people in emergency rooms and less people throughout the system,” he said.

He also reiterated his promise to abolish Santé Québec, the province’s public health agency that was created in 2024 and became the sole employer in the health and social services network. He said not all the agency’s employees would be laid off by such a move, but did not specify how many would lose their jobs.

In Trois-Rivières, Milliard promised his party would invest five per cent of the province’s health care budget in 10 years in prevention services like vaccination, cancer screening and chronic disease prevention.

After a week marked by talks of sovereignty, Milliard tried to paint himself as the best candidate to negotiate with Ottawa on immigration. He accused Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette of not wanting to work with the rest of the country.
Québec Solidaire spokesperson Ruba Ghazal said in a press conference in Montreal that, if elected, her party would make public transit free for those under 25 years old and those over 65 years old.
She said her party would also increase funding for public transit and highlighted the positive economic and environmental potential of such a measure.
“There are populations with an even greater need for public transit, and right now there are many barriers, whether in terms of service or affordability,” she said.
She accused the outgoing Coalition Avenir Québec administration of having “abandoned” public transit.
Meanwhile, Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime attended a protest in Quebec City against the ongoing tramway project and called for a clear estimate of the cost.
He repeated his disapproval of the project, casting instead its support to the so-called “third link” bridge project which has seen various iterations in recent years.

Fréchette, leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec, visited the province’s police school in Nicolet, close to Trois-Rivières. She promised her party would spend $196 million to hire 300 additional police officers and 50 prosecutors in the province.
She said online crime, homelessness and mental health issues have made police officers’ jobs more complex.
“Despite our many efforts, ...Quebecers remain worried,” she said.
While the Parti Québécois has been favoured by some public opinion polls, recent surveys appear to show the Coalition Avenir Québec gaining momentum.

stories.title: Carney to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham for first time during Europe trip
stories.summary: Carney is also set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg and attend the State of the European Union address
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet his counterpart in the United Kingdom for the first time.

The Prime Minister’s Office says Carney will meet Andy Burnham in Liverpool during a three-day trip to Europe set to start on Tuesday, and the two leaders will discuss Canada-U.K. relations on defence and security, energy, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

The Canadian leader congratulated Burnham after the U.K. prime minister took office on July 20, Carney’s office said at the time, but this will be the first time the two world leaders meet in person.

Burnham is the United Kingdom’s fourth prime minister in four years after a revolving door in the country’s top office has seen former Conservative leaders Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, and former Labour leader Keir Starmer, struggle to hold onto the job.

Starmer was forced out by his own party, and a leadership race within the governing Labour Party handed Burnham – former mayor of Greater Manchester – the keys to 10 Downing Street.

Carney is also set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg and attend the State of the European Union address during the trip, adding to a busy week for the prime minister who is hosting a two-day investment summit in Toronto on Monday and Tuesday.

The European Union’s ambassador to Canada said earlier this week in an interview that Carney and EU officials are looking to hash out a new partnership when he visits the European Parliament.

Carney has been pursuing deeper ties with countries in Europe and around the world as relations with the United States have worsened.

On Tuesday, Canadian counter tariffs on billions of dollars of U.S. products went into effect in a tit-for-tat response after Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down in late August.

paragraphs: A 39-year-old woman has died following a collision in Essex, near the community of Harrow, ON Friday evening, according to Ontario Provincial Police.
· Posted: Sep 12, 2026 3:51 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

stories.title: Ontario man completes 450-km ride in memory of brother & niece killed by a drunk driver
stories.summary: A four-day, more than 450-kilometre bike ride in memory of two family members killed by an impaired driver wrapped up in Dorchester Saturday afternoon.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A four-day, more than 450-kilometre bike ride in memory of two family members killed by an impaired driver wrapped up in Dorchester Saturday afternoon.

Jeff Wilson began the solo ride Sept. 9 at Brooks Falls in Emsdale, travelling by bike to Dorchester in support of Madd Canada.

Wilson was riding in memory of his brother, Scott, and his five-year-old niece, Leaira, who were killed by an impaired driver in 2018.

“He was that guy who everybody knew him. It didn’t matter where you went with him. There was always somebody that knew him,” said Jeff, of his late brother Scott.

The ride ended Saturday at the Dorchester Cornfest before Wilson made his way to Dorchester Cemetery, where his brother is buried.

Wilson, a personal trainer and owner of Rusted Iron Fitness, says physical fitness has helped him cope with grief and anxiety following the deaths.

He says the ride is about honouring Scott and Leaira, while keeping the conversation about impaired driving going.

“I just want everyone to know that there are always options. We don’t need to drink and drive home. There’s programs out there that can get you home, there are cabs, there’s always a sober friend. There’s so many people now are not drinking like they were in the past. So, call somebody and get a ride, and make sure you get home safe,” Wilson said.

Wilson’s goal was to raise at least $10,000 for Madd Canada, with all funds raised through the campaign going directly to the organization.

The ride was also intended to remind people that the consequences of impaired driving are devastating and preventable.

For Wilson, the journey was both a fundraiser and a personal tribute to two people whose lives were cut short.

Donations can be made online.

stories.title: London Labour Council announces municipal election endorsements
stories.summary: The London and District Labour Council (Ldlc) has announced its endorsed candidates for London city council ahead of the Oct. 26 municipal election.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
The London and District Labour Council (Ldlc) has announced its endorsed candidates for London city council ahead of the Oct. 26 municipal election. The endorsements were announced Saturday morning at Peace Park. The labour council says municipal decisions have a direct impact on working people, including issues such as housing affordability, public transit and access to good union jobs.

As part of its endorsement process, the Ldlc sent candidates a questionnaire asking about their priorities and approach to issues affecting working people. An election planning committee reviewed the responses, as well as the candidates’ past records, before making recommendations to the Ldlc executive and general membership.

Ldlc president Patti Dalton says the process involved lengthy discussions and a detailed review of each candidate’s responses. “We also invited every applicant to write about their priorities. So then the election planning committee went through all of those responses, and there were several with a fine tooth comb,” Dalton said.

Mayor Josh Morgan was among those endorsed by the labour council, although he was not present at today’s event. Dalton says Morgan’s support for collective bargaining was one of the factors considered during the endorsement process.

“Of the things that we discussed in our interview with Josh was that he is a strong supporter of collective bargaining. He ensured that with the firefighters’ union that they did engage in collective bargaining. And that doesn’t always happen.

It can go quickly to arbitration. So that was one measure of the mayor being pro-union,” Dalton said. Of the current council, Ldlc is endorsing 7 of eight councillors. The Ldlc endorsed candidates are as follows: Mayor Josh Morgan Ward 1 Hadleigh McAlister Ward 2 Zack Ramsey Ward 3 Leroy Osbourne Ward 4 Tom Cull Ward 5 Corrine Rahman Ward 6 Sam Trosow Ward 7 Jonathan Sher Ward 8 No recommendation Ward 9 Anna Hopkins Ward 10 Lois Ward Ward 11 Skylar Franke Ward 12 Elizabeth Peloza Ward 13 David Ferreira Ward 14 Sarah Lehman

stories.title: Flying this fall? You might get a good deal
stories.summary: Canadians planning a fall getaway could find cheaper flights as airlines compete for passengers after the busy summer travel season, even as airlines fly into fall in a real fix over the cost of fuel.
stories.author: Andrew Johnson
stories.content:
Vancouver – Canadians planning a fall getaway could find cheaper flights as airlines compete for passengers after the busy summer travel season, even as airlines fly into fall in a real fix over the cost of fuel.

Airline industry experts expect increased competition could lead to a price war this fall, as demand typically slows once Canadians return to work and school.

But lower fares could compound the problems facing Canadian airlines, which are already absorbing a major increase in the cost of jet fuel.

“This is just a very difficult time for the entire airline industry,” said Lorn Sheehan, an expert in tourism management at Dalhousie University. “And this industry has had to pivot and pivot and pivot again as we’ve had these global shocks.”

Smaller airlines bear the brunt

Fuel prices have doubled since February, when the United States went to war with Iran, which has turned up the pressure on airlines.

That pressure is particularly acute for leisure carriers such as Air Transat, which are more exposed to fluctuations in fuel prices and have fewer high-margin business travellers to help offset higher costs. Transat reported a loss of $106.6 million for the three months ended July 31.

Transat A.T. Inc., the parent company of Air Transat, announced Thursday it had secured an additional $250 million in federal financing to help offset the soaring energy costs. That follows a $150 million federal loan announced in July.

Porter Airlines has also received government assistance, with a $125 million federal bailout loan, according to the Canada Enterprise Emergency Funding Corp.

Experts say most airlines have cushioned the blow of soaring fuel costs by raising fares and could get away with it over the summer travel season with Canadians motivated to fly.

“Now we’re in a situation where everybody’s back at work, back at school,” said John Gradek, a lecturer at McGill University’s aviation management program. “Now you’re in the doldrums.”

Gradek expects airlines will have no choice but to lower fares to compete for passengers, despite fuel costs cutting deeply into profit. “There will be price wars in Canada, which means revenues will come down, which is not what you need when you are stuck with a fuel bill that keeps climbing,” he said.

Flight prices are particularly pivotal for carriers, Sheehan said, because of brand loyalty, or the lack of it, when Canadians are searching for cheap flights. “Customers are very willing to generally switch to another airline if the price is cheaper,” he said.

Gradek said he is already seeing what he calls some “spicy” fares for fall travel.

That’s good news for travellers, but potentially bad news for airlines. Smaller carriers in particular, experts say, May be in serious trouble. “It May lead to some carriers not being able to survive the fall and winter,” Gradek said.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Trump says Canada ‘wants to make a deal very badly’
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada wants a deal with Washington “very badly” and suggested an agreement could come “fairly soon” if trade concerns are resolved.
stories.author: Prisha Dev
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada wants to reach a deal with the United States “very badly” and suggested an agreement could come “fairly soon” if Ottawa addresses his concerns about agricultural trade.

Trump made the comments Saturday in Ireland, where he was asked whether he was considering withdrawing from the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement.

“No, we’re doing great. We’re gonna have a great relationship with Mexico,” Trump said.

He then turned his attention to Canada, saying the two countries have a good relationship while repeating his criticism of the trading relationship.

“We actually have a good one with Canada, but the United States has been ripped off for 50 years by Canada,” Trump said.

“We don’t need their product and they need our product. They do all of their business almost with us and we do very little with them.”

The Office of the United States Trade Representative says Canada is consistently one of the top trading partners for the U.S.

Trump said Canada “wants to make a deal very badly,” but suggested he does not believe Ottawa is ready yet.

The U.S. president then compared Canada’s desire to reach a deal with those of Iran.

“I hope Canada appreciates being in the same sentence with Iran,” Trump said. “It’s very interesting — Canada and Iran.”

“Canada wants to make a deal and Iran wants to make a deal. At the right time, both of those things could happen.”

Trump said agricultural trade remains among his concerns, repeating his criticism of Canadian tariffs on some U.S. agricultural products.

“Canada has to treat our farmers better and they can’t charge our farmers tariffs,” he said.

“When those things go away, and they’re willing to get rid of all of them, you’ll probably see a deal with Canada fairly soon.”

Trump’s comments came during a weekend visit to Ireland, where he also weighed in on the politically sensitive question of Irish reunification.

Speaking alongside Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said he would “love to see” the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland unified.

“I don’t want to cause any problems, but I’d love to see it unified,” Trump said. “It’s going to happen eventually. It May as well happen now.”

– With files from The Canadian Press and Reuters

stories.title: 'A legend': Celine Dion poised for emotional comeback in Paris
stories.summary: The cheering crowd chanted "Celine! Celine!", as the beaming star blew kisses and made a heart shape with her hands.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
Celine Dion is set to make her long-awaited return to the stage in Paris after years battling a rare neurological disorder, with anticipation among fans reaching fever pitch.

Just hours before she was scheduled to perform her first full concert in six years, the 58-year-old French Canadian singer greeted admirers outside her luxury hotel a short walk from the Arc de Triomphe.

The cheering crowd chanted “Celine! Celine!”, as the beaming star blew kisses and made a heart shape with her hands.

The opening show scheduled to begin at around 8 pm Saturday marks a major milestone in Dion’s comeback after Stiff Person Syndrome forced her to cancel shows and left her struggling to perform.

Around 30,000 fans were expected to pack the Plenitude Arena on the Western edge of Paris for the sold-out opening night of Dion’s 26-show run.

The show’s setlist has been kept under wraps.

“She’s a legend, she’s iconic,” said Chloe Rydquist, who travelled from London with her wife, Katy, to see Dion.

The French capital spared no effort in welcoming Dion, drawing thousands of fans from across the world, including some who flew in from as far away as the French Polynesian island of Tahiti.

For days Paris played host to costume contests, giant karaoke parties and tribute cruises on the Seine.

On Friday, the iconic cauldron rose above the Tuileries Garden, echoing the diva’s surprise appearance up the Eiffel Tower to perform “Hymn to Love” by Edith Piaf during the opening ceremony of the Paris Olympics in 2024.

A lyric from the song, “I’d go and fetch the moon if you asked me to”, along with the singer’s first name, was projected in big letters onto the balloon.

Canada welcome to send performer to Eurovision song contest: director

Celine Dion's Paris concerts could bring an additional US$585M into the city, industry expert says

“Paris is just as magical as ever,” Dion said on Instagram.

The suburban train station serving the arena has been temporarily renamed “Celine.”

Chloe and Katy Rydquist paid around 1,500 pounds ($2000) for their tickets. They said seeing Dion back onstage was worth the price. “It’s going to be very emotional for her and for everyone,” said Katy.

They “didn’t know if she was ever going to come back, so if you can get there, you get there,” she added.

The star’s residency is projected to generate hundreds of millions of euros in economic benefits.

“Celine Dion. Will she save the 2027 budget?” daily Liberation said on its front page, in a nod to France’s economic woes.

She kicks off her 26-date residency with 16 sold-out shows in September and October, before returning for another 10 next May.

Fans who missed out on tickets have found other ways to catch a glimpse of their idol.

Dion has regularly stepped outside the Royal Monceau hotel to greet waiting fans, at times breaking into song and dance with them well into the early hours.

On Friday, hundreds turned out for a free singalong in the city’s northeast, swaying and warbling along to some of Dion’s best-known tunes.

“I really wanted to go to her concert, but I didn’t get a ticket, so I thought I might as well have a massive karaoke session, sing all her songs again and have a good time,” said Eva Ingelaere, 24.

Over her four-decade career, Dion has sold around 260 million albums in English and French, with hits including “It’s All Coming Back to Me Now” and “Because You Loved Me”.

Dion’s return caps a remarkable journey back to the stage after years of uncertainty over whether she would perform again.

In December 2022, she revealed that she had been diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome, a rare and incurable autoimmune disorder that can cause severe muscle stiffness and agonizing spasms.

Dion has described the condition as making her feel as though she is being strangled, with cramps so intense they have left her with broken ribs.

The illness forced her to cancel concerts, but Dion remained determined to perform again.

In 2024, she spelt out her ambitions for a full comeback.

“I’m going to come onstage because I’m ready,” she told NBC at the time.

stories.title: ‘Céline is everywhere in my life’: Thousands gather in Paris for Dion’s big comeback
stories.summary: Thousands of Céline Dion fans gathered along the streets of Paris ahead of the singer's comeback concert Saturday evening at the Plenitude Arena.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Paris — Thousands of Céline Dion fans gathered along the streets of Paris ahead of the singer’s comeback concert Saturday evening at the Plenitude Arena.

For many, it was a test of patience and determination to get their hands on one of the highly coveted tickets to the first of the Quebec legend’s 16 sold-out shows in the city this year.

“I really had to fight for it,” said Elda Vauttier, 57, originally from the Yvelines region of France. “Unfortunately, I only got one ticket tonight, so I couldn’t bring my daughter, who’s also a fan. But luckily, I managed to buy more for May.”

Vauttier, whose son lives in Montreal, has been a fan of Dion since childhood. She has previously seen her perform twice in Paris and once in Las Vegas.

“I experience all my emotions with her — happiness, sadness,” she said. “Céline is everywhere in my life. She’s a beautiful person, a warm soul who always gives her all despite her own problems. You can’t help but love her.”

Other fans travelled far for the occasion.

Frédérique Lauzon and Alexandrine Derome, two Montreal-based flight attendants, took advantage of their layover to snag some last-minute tickets.

“I think she’s going to put on a spectacular show,” said Derome.

This will be Derome’s 24th time attending a Dion performance.

“I’ve seen her in Las Vegas, Montreal, Quebec City, Paris, and during the tapings of special TV shows in Montreal,” she said.

Marie-Caroline Honnet is attending her first Dion concert on Saturday at the 33,000-capacity indoor venue. She and her sister travelled from Caen, in Normandy, to share this moment.

“It’s a family passion,” Honnet said. “It even spans generations — my niece is already learning Céline’s songs.”

Nicolas Enème came from Avignon in southern France.

“It’s something extraordinary,” said Enème, delighted to be able to attend the performance. “We thought we’d never see her again. Tonight feels like a miracle.”

“I don’t have any particular expectations,” Enème added. “Just that she enjoys herself and that she makes us happy — that alone would be amazing!”

Dion’s last tour was cancelled in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and in 2022 she revealed that she was suffering from stiff-person syndrome, a rare autoimmune disease that prevented her from returning to the stage at the time.

Although the singer gave a moving performance at the 2024 Paris Olympics of “Hymne à l’amour” that lit up the Eiffel Tower, these will be her first full concerts in six years. Another 10 shows are scheduled for next year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 12, 2026.

Anja Conton, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta's Smith says Crown corporation for natural gas unlikely after report leaked
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says it's unlikely her government will launch a new Crown corporation to build out natural gas pipelines in the province.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Saturday that it’s “unlikely” her government will launch a new Crown corporation to build out natural gas pipelines in the province.

Updated at 5:20 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/alberta/alberta-s-smith-says-crown-corporation-for-natural-gas-unlikely-after-report-leaked/article_dff77521-c837-5105-b5c1-c7a675f3c614.html)

By Jack Farrell The Canadian Press

Smith, speaking on her provincewide radio call-in program “Your Province Your Premier” on QR Calgary and 880 Ched, said the government has heard from dozens of companies struggling to access natural gas and that the province is looking at solutions, though for now those conversations are sticking to the private sector.

The premier’s comments come after a leaked report to Smith’s cabinet recommended the province move forward with legislation and create two Crown corporations to spur new natural gas transmission lines to meet the demand for oil production and artificial intelligence data centres.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Smith’s government has been working to position Alberta as an ideal location for AI data centres, which are major computing complexes that require loads of power to operate. The cabinet report says Alberta risks data centre builders going elsewhere if a quick solution for natural gas supply isn’t secured.

The Crown corporations would cost between $53.9 million and $162.6 million, according to the report, while building a new major natural gas pipeline could have a price tag in the billions.

Smith — and the report — said the issue comes down to Calgary-based TC Energy, which owns and operates much of Alberta’s natural gas transmission infrastructure. The premier called it a “monopoly.”

The report says the company’s Nova Gas Transmission Ltd. — the biggest natural gas pipeline system in Alberta — is expected to be at full capacity until 2029 with limited plans to expand after 2030.

It says TC Energy doesn’t want to invest in further capacity unless it receives returns on investment at rates similar to its projects in the United States.

Smith said it’s an “active conversation” and that she has met with TC Energy leadership and other private sector companies.

“What we’re looking at is how do we get more competition, more choice, so that we can get more gas to more people so that it can be used,” she said.

“If one player isn’t able to feed our entire market ... then we’re going to look to some of the other private providers to do it.”

Smith said she believes there’s enough private sector interest for further development that “we would very unlikely have to create a Crown corporation to do it.”

Smith also brushed off concerns from Opposition NDP leader Naheed Nenshi, who noted on Friday that the cabinet report warns government intervention could lead to higher energy prices for Albertans.

The report says that current transmission bottlenecks mean natural gas from Alberta sells at lower rates when it reaches the market, but by boosting the province’s transmission capacity it could mean Alberta’s product sells for rates seen elsewhere in North America.

A higher selling price would be good for government royalty revenue, the report says, but it could also mean that Albertans pay more on their power bills.

Smith argued Saturday that boosting the supply of natural gas is what’s needed to avoid having Albertans’ bills go up, not keeping supply constrained as it is now.

“If you have constrained gas and there’s more demand than there is supply, that’s what causes prices to go up,” Smith said.

Nenshi didn’t buy the premier’s argument, saying in a statement Saturday that Albertans’ energy bills were still at risk.

”(The report) says that the government wishes to bully private companies into building infrastructure or spend billions of taxpayer dollars doing it themselves, with the express goal of increasing the price of natural gas,” he said.

Smith didn’t rule out her government moving forward with legislation to spur new natural gas infrastructure, something the cabinet report says could land the province in court with TC Energy.

The legislation recommended in the report would look to override federally approved co-operation agreements the company has in place with another major natural gas provider in Alberta, while also allowing the government to force companies to invest in new projects if deemed in the province’s best interest.

TC Energy did not respond to questions about the report on Friday. It also didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 12, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Childhood Cancer Canada calls for $15M from feds as demand rises
stories.summary: Childhood Cancer Canada says demand for its financial support programs has risen 40 per cent in two years as families face the long-term costs of a diagnosis.
stories.author: Prisha Dev, Meghan Cobb
stories.content:
A Canadian childhood cancer charity is calling on the federal government to provide more financial support to families whose children are undergoing cancer treatment.

The foundation has seen demand for its financial support programs rise 40 per cent over the past two years, but says government funding has not kept pace.

“This is the time to step up, talk to our parliamentary leaders, as well as make sure those families going through it have a helping hand,” said Kyle Smith with Childhood Cancer Canada.

The charity is asking Ottawa for $15 million in the next federal budget to sustain those programs, while also seeking changes to tax credits and employment insurance requirements to better support families dealing with childhood cancer.

About 1,500 children are diagnosed with cancer every year in Canada, according to the charity.

For many families, a diagnosis can mean a parent leaving work or reducing their hours to become a full-time caregiver, creating financial pressures that can continue long after a child’s treatment ends.

Smith said many parents caring for a child with cancer are under the age of 40, meaning time away from the workforce can have lasting consequences for their finances.

“That’s no RRSPs being built up, that is no other benefit,” he said, adding that decades later, “their retirement is impacted, the child’s retirement or education fund is impacted.”

For the Masikewich family, those pressures came after their daughter Sloane was diagnosed with stage 4 neuroblastoma in May 2023.

Treatment and a compromised immune system meant Sloane missed Grade 1 entirely, while Grades 2 and 3 were interrupted by trips to the hospital.

“It was hard not being in school and not being able to see my friends, but I enjoyed the time I got to spend with my mom and dad in the hospital,” Sloane said.

This school year marks a significant milestone for the family.

“This is the first year she doesn’t have to be in treatment, which is really incredible for our family and for Sloane,” her mother, Claire Masikewich, said.

Claire said families already coping with a child’s cancer diagnosis should not also have to contend with mounting financial pressures.

“The added financial stress for families on top of what you’re already going through is just not needed,” she said.

Childhood Cancer Canada raises awareness, funds research and provides support to families navigating a childhood cancer diagnosis.

The organization says financial stability is particularly important because it can allow parents to focus on caring for their children during treatment.

Beyond its $15-million funding request, the charity is calling for policy changes involving tax credits and EI requirements to provide more direct support to affected families.

For Sloane, being out of treatment has meant returning to the parts of childhood that cancer disrupted.

“I got to hang out with my friends, and I got to meet all my new classmates,” she said.

stories.title: Tiff 2026: Photos from the red carpet
stories.summary: Dozens of celebrities have made their way to Toronto to celebrate new film releases in the city’s Entertainment District.
stories.author: Denio Lourenco
stories.content:
Posted September 12, 2026 12:49 pm.

Last Updated September 16, 2026 4:52 pm.

The Toronto International Film Festival is back for its 51st edition.

Dozens of celebrities (and a former prime minister) have made their way to Toronto to announce new projects and celebrate film releases in the city’s Entertainment District.

This year’s festival is running from Sept. 10 to 20 and has already brought out big names like Courtney Cox, Rebel Wilson, Jennifer Coolidge, Seth Rogan and many more.

Dozens of celebrities (and a former prime minister) have made their way to Toronto to announce new projects and celebrate film releases in the city’s Entertainment District.
This year’s festival is running from Sept. 10 to 20 and has already brought out big names like Courtney Cox, Rebel Wilson, Jennifer Coolidge, Seth Rogan and many more.

stories.title: Peanuts recalled in Ontario, Quebec over possible salmonella contamination
stories.summary: Canadian food safety officials are warning that peanuts sold in Ontario and Quebec May be contaminated with salmonella.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has issued a recall for “Roasted Lemon N’ Chilli Peanuts” sold by the brand PK.

The recall, first issued on Thursday, instructs consumers to throw out the peanuts or return them to the location where they were purchased.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

The Cfia says food contaminated with salmonella May not look or smell spoiled but can still make a person sick.

They say people with weakened immune systems May contract serious and deadly infections after eating contaminated food, while healthy people May experience fever, headaches and vomiting.

The Cfia says there have so far been no reported illnesses associated with the recall.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 12, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: 79-year-old Arva man dies after two-vehicle crash
stories.summary: A 79-year-old male from Arva, Ont. is dead following a two-vehicle collision Friday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A 79-year-old male from Arva, Ont. is dead following a two-vehicle collision Friday in West Perth.

Just before 4:00 p.m. the Perth County OPP, along with Perth County Emergency Medical Services, and West Perth Fire Department responded to a two-vehicle collision on Perth Road 163 at the intersection of Perth Line 26.

The driver of one vehicle, a 79-year-old male from Arva, suffered life-threatening injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene.

The driver of the second vehicle suffered minor injuries and was transported to a local hospital.

All resources have since cleared, and the roads have been reopened.

This investigation remains ongoing.

stories.title: Trails End Market vendors move outside after fire department closure order
stories.summary: Vendors at the Trails End Farmers Market in Thorndale moved their operations outdoors Saturday after the market was ordered closed because of fire and life safety concerns.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Vendors at the Trails End Farmers Market in Thorndale moved their operations outdoors Saturday after the market was ordered closed because of fire and life safety concerns.

The market, located at 4370 Dundas St., was ordered to close Sept. 8 by the Thames Centre Fire Department after multiple inspections identified what the department called “serious fire and life safety deficiencies.” The closure order was approved by the Office of the Fire Marshal.

Some of the fire code concerns include the lack of a sprinkler system and issues related to fire exits, according to information provided by the fire department.

The building will remain closed until the outstanding inspection requirements are addressed and a follow-up inspection is completed.

Rather than cancel Saturday’s market altogether, management worked with vendors Friday evening to develop a temporary outdoor setup in the parking lot.

For vendors who rely on the weekly market for income, keeping their businesses running was important.

“We count on this, so many people count on this, so many people’s livelihoods. And it was a little alarming. But they made a way,” said Rene McIntyre, a Trails End vendor.

Sloane Liverman, another vendor, said her family depends on the income. “We’re a family run business and we have young kids. Food on the table is really important and it’s not an option. We have to show up”

Mina Harms, a longtime vendor, said the market is one of her family’s biggest sales outlets.

“We have a big farm, so this is one of our second biggest market we go to. So it would be a big impact. It would affect us a lot. Even our employees on farm.”

The closure came as a surprise to some longtime vendors. Fred Sadat has been selling at Trails End for 25 years. He said he had never felt unsafe inside the building but wants the concerns addressed quickly.

“Never had a feeling in here that something is not safe or something is going to it. This needs a serious attention.”

Despite the building being closed, regular customers came out Saturday to support the vendors and buy fresh produce.

“It’s cheap here and we can get like in less money, more quantity. As well, of course it’s a fresh and organic,” said customer Baljeet Ahluwalia.

But the outdoor setup did not include all the vendors who normally operate inside the market.

" I usually come here to get cheese and buns from a couple of vendors, but because they are not here, because the building is closed, I can’t buy from them and I am disappointed,” said frequent shopper Chris Bolt.

For farmers selling perishable products, vendors say they can’t afford a lengthy disruption.

“We are in a perishable business. I wish my farmer could tell the apple on the tree, ‘hey could you wait for a couple of weeks so we’ll come back, harvest you later, so we can sell you later?’ Unfortunately, the food industry has to continue,” Sadat said.

For now, vendors say they will continue operating outdoors while they wait for the building to be cleared for use.

The market, located at 4370 Dundas St., was ordered to close Sept. 8 by the Thames Centre Fire Department after multiple inspections identified what the department called “serious fire and life safety deficiencies.” The closure order was approved by the Office of the Fire Marshal.
Some of the fire code concerns include the lack of a sprinkler system and issues related to fire exits, according to information provided by the fire department.
The building will remain closed until the outstanding inspection requirements are addressed and a follow-up inspection is completed.
Rather than cancel Saturday’s market altogether, management worked with vendors Friday evening to develop a temporary outdoor setup in the parking lot.
For vendors who rely on the weekly market for income, keeping their businesses running was important.
“We count on this, so many people count on this, so many people’s livelihoods. And it was a little alarming. But they made a way,” said Rene McIntyre, a Trails End vendor.

Sloane Liverman, another vendor, said her family depends on the income. “We’re a family run business and we have young kids. Food on the table is really important and it’s not an option. We have to show up”
Mina Harms, a longtime vendor, said the market is one of her family’s biggest sales outlets.
“We have a big farm, so this is one of our second biggest market we go to. So it would be a big impact. It would affect us a lot. Even our employees on farm.”

The closure came as a surprise to some longtime vendors. Fred Sadat has been selling at Trails End for 25 years. He said he had never felt unsafe inside the building but wants the concerns addressed quickly.
“Never had a feeling in here that something is not safe or something is going to it. This needs a serious attention.”
Despite the building being closed, regular customers came out Saturday to support the vendors and buy fresh produce.
“It’s cheap here and we can get like in less money, more quantity. As well, of course it’s a fresh and organic,” said customer Baljeet Ahluwalia.
But the outdoor setup did not include all the vendors who normally operate inside the market.

" I usually come here to get cheese and buns from a couple of vendors, but because they are not here, because the building is closed, I can’t buy from them and I am disappointed,” said frequent shopper Chris Bolt.
For farmers selling perishable products, vendors say they can’t afford a lengthy disruption.

“We are in a perishable business. I wish my farmer could tell the apple on the tree, ‘hey could you wait for a couple of weeks so we’ll come back, harvest you later, so we can sell you later?’ Unfortunately, the food industry has to continue,” Sadat said.
For now, vendors say they will continue operating outdoors while they wait for the building to be cleared for use.

Overnight, cloudy periods and a 40 per cent chance of showers are expected, with a low of 10 C.

stories.title: Justin Trudeau says new production company aims to change minds
stories.summary: Former PM says 'storytelling' can get past ideology: 'Changing someone’s mind is actually trying to get them to change their very identity.'
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Justin Trudeau and longtime aide Katie Telford say they are “self-financing” their new production company, which aims to change people’s minds via “storytelling.”

The two announced their new multimedia entertainment company, Hope & Hard Work, at the Lightbox’s rooftop event space during the Toronto International Film Festival on Friday. They drew a crowd of media and entertainment press and personalities.

The former prime minister suggested that stories like the ones he and his former chief of staff will tell can get past ideological defences.

“It’s not just that you believe the Earth is flat,” he said. “You are a flat-Earther. So changing someone’s mind is actually trying to get them to change their very identity. And people are, rightly, resistant to that need to rethink who they are.”

He continued: “But storytelling can sneak through, get in behind people’s defences, and get them to actually feel connected to someone completely from them. And that’s what we need now more than ever.

“And unfortunately our algorithms and our technology are getting very, very good at ginning up outrage and division and separation instead of looking at ways of actually building human connections and experiences.”

Hope & Hard Work takes its name from a campaign slogan used by Trudeau and the Liberal party. It also seems to have taken a page from the playbook of Barack and Michelle Obama, who in 2018 launched a production company called Higher Ground. Prince Harry and Meghan, Duke and Duchess of Sussex, also founded a production company, Archewell Productions, in 2020.

“We got lots of advice,” Trudeau told National Post. “We took our time to really talk with all sorts of different people, including some of the ones with a similar path.”

Justin Trudeau to launch his own production company at Toronto film festival

Justin Trudeau still receives RCMP protection on personal trips: report

But he said he and Telford were not following a template. “This one we’re building from scratch,” he said. “We’re not starting with a big partnership … We’re actually self-financing.”

This gives them the freedom to find their own projects, he added. “Doing things that we want and being in control of it is really important to us.”

He said his fame gave him power as a politician, and will do the same in the film industry.

“In politics I had the advantage of my last name, which everyone knows,” he told National Post. “But one of the concrete advantages that people don’t think about is it meant I didn’t have to go cap in hand to all the elders and the power brokers around Canadian politics to get their blessing to do it. I just did it, and that was how we were able to completely reinvent the Liberal party from scratch and do it without owing anything to anyone.”

He added: “Similar approach that Katie and I want to do here, where we can come in and do the things that we want to do, that we believe in, and not feel like we have to deliver to the powers that be.”

Trudeau announced his resignation on Jan. 6, 2025, after nine years as prime minister, amid unrest in the Liberal caucus and historic lows in opinion polls. He has most recently made news for his relationship with American pop singer Katy Perry, and continues to give paid speeches around the world.

He told the crowd he wants to create stories that invite curiosity, challenge convention and expand people’s understanding of one another.

Justin Trudeau speaks during launch of Hope & Hard Work during Tiff 2026.“The time we’re in right now, the technologies we’re surrounded with, the world we’re surrounded with does a really good job of keeping people separate and disempowered,” he said.

“Technologies that were supposed to connect us to each other and empower us with knowledge and information instead end up dividing us and leaving us more isolated and feeling powerless.”

He continued: “In elections we used to say, ‘Whoever tells the best story about who we are and where we want to go wins the election.’ And those stories matter now more than ever before.”

Some of those stories are drawn from worlds Trudeau and Telford know well. The series Power Moves will be based on a novel by Australian writer Leesa Ronald, featuring an ambitious political advisor, a politician seeking reelection, and a persistent journalist.

Another series, Backchannels, is based on the book The Right Hand: Conversations with the Chiefs of Staff to the World’s Most Powerful People by another Australian, Phoebe Saintilan-Stocks, and in development with her twin sister, Chloe Saintilan.

Their plans also include some CanCon, including adaptations of Closer By Sea, the debut novel from writer and producer Perry Chafe (Republic of Doyle, Son of a Critch) and Detective Aunty by novelist Uzma Jalaluddin. Hope & Hard Work also has a partnership with Earth Tones, founded by Canadian sisters Aliya Jasmine and Aliza Sovani, which will produce documentaries and docu-series.

“These are stories that the world needs to hear,” Trudeau said at the launch.

stories.title: Healing in the Public Eye: Peloza’s final radiation treatment marks shift in her cancer journey
stories.summary: Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has shared her experience undergoing cancer treatments in a special CTV News series called Healing in the Public Eye.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Coun. Elizabeth Peloza has shared her experience undergoing cancer treatments in a special CTV News series called Healing in the Public Eye.

On Friday, she underwent her final radiation treatment inside the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC), a milestone that patients mark by striking a large gong inside the atrium.

It took only moments for applause from other patients, caregivers, and staff to drown out the resonating gong.

“Active treatment has wrapped up,” Peloza said shortly afterwards. “It’s definitely been a long road, we’ve been through a lot. Banging the gong was amazing.”

The mother of three, began her breast cancer journey with a diagnosis last October.

Her treatment included surgery late last year, dose-dense chemotherapy, and finally 19 rounds of radiation.

“When I started treatment, a survivor said to just write-off the next year of your life, you’re doing the next year of your life in treatment to make sure you have many more years ahead,” Peloza explained.

She hopes hearing the gong inspires patients and caregivers inside the cancer centre who are starting their own cancer journeys, “Every time someone bangs the gong, or rings the bell upstairs (for completing chemotherapy), other patients know that their day will hopefully come as well.”

“The gong is special for all patients,” explained Kirk Patterson, who survived a neck cancer diagnosis in 2012. “You bang the gong and people down there (in the atrium) realize you’ve been through a battle, and the hope is that you’re going to remain cancer free for the rest of your life.”

“It’s a lifelong journey, and I think once patients understand what they’re going through, they understand that ringing the bell or banging the gong is the end of one race, and it’s the beginning of another race,” Patterson added.

Peloza acknowledged that while her active treatments at the cancer centre are complete, follow-up care will continue, “My follow-up appointments are already booked. I’m back for another mammogram in February, and another meeting with my oncologist and cancer doctors in March. Some of the bloodwork still goes on (because) some of these medications are hard on your body and especially your liver.”

Eliot Archer, Director of Cancer Care believes Peloza’s decision to share her journey in the public eye increased awareness about many of the services available at the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre that extend beyond clinical treatments.

“I think it hopefully highlights that there are a number of different supports available for patients and families going through a cancer journey,” Archer said. “From the wig and turban boutique to some of our psychosocial oncology supports that try to embody person-centred care.”

Peloza admited reaching the milestone in her treatments hadn’t sunk in yet, “I’m needing to set aside some time to sit down and process what just concluded, what I’ve just accomplished, and what my body, my family, and my friends have just been through.”

She was reflective while rewatching an episode of Healing in the Public Eye that focused on her decision to shave her head after chemotherapy caused much of her hair to fall out.

Asked what advice she’d give herself on that difficult day in April she responded,” That it will be okay, and that you can help so many people along their journey if you just keep sharing.”

She recalled ringing the bell after finishing chemotherapy, “When I rang the bell upstairs, a lady shouted, ‘I know you from the news! I got my diagnosis after yours, but I’d already watched your story on the news, so when my hair started falling out, I already knew what to do.”

More than six months after the first episode of Healing in the Public Eye, Elizabeth Peloza says the series didn’t just document her cancer journey, it helped her to reach this milestone.

“Being so public about something that’s so private really helped to get me through it.”

Her treatment included surgery late last year, dose-dense chemotherapy, and finally 19 rounds of radiation.

“When I started treatment, a survivor said to just write-off the next year of your life, you’re doing the next year of your life in treatment to make sure you have many more years ahead,” Peloza explained.

She hopes hearing the gong inspires patients and caregivers inside the cancer centre who are starting their own cancer journeys, “Every time someone bangs the gong, or rings the bell upstairs (for completing chemotherapy), other patients know that their day will hopefully come as well.”

“The gong is special for all patients,” explained Kirk Patterson, who survived a neck cancer diagnosis in 2012. “You bang the gong and people down there (in the atrium) realize you’ve been through a battle, and the hope is that you’re going to remain cancer free for the rest of your life.”

“It’s a lifelong journey, and I think once patients understand what they’re going through, they understand that ringing the bell or banging the gong is the end of one race, and it’s the beginning of another race,” Patterson added.

Peloza acknowledged that while her active treatments at the cancer centre are complete, follow-up care will continue, “My follow-up appointments are already booked. I’m back for another mammogram in February, and another meeting with my oncologist and cancer doctors in March. Some of the bloodwork still goes on (because) some of these medications are hard on your body and especially your liver.”

Eliot Archer, Director of Cancer Care believes Peloza’s decision to share her journey in the public eye increased awareness about many of the services available at the Verspeeten Family Cancer Centre that extend beyond clinical treatments.

“I think it hopefully highlights that there are a number of different supports available for patients and families going through a cancer journey,” Archer said. “From the wig and turban boutique to some of our psychosocial oncology supports that try to embody person-centred care.”

Peloza admited reaching the milestone in her treatments hadn’t sunk in yet, “I’m needing to set aside some time to sit down and process what just concluded, what I’ve just accomplished, and what my body, my family, and my friends have just been through.”
She was reflective while rewatching an episode of Healing in the Public Eye that focused on her decision to shave her head after chemotherapy caused much of her hair to fall out.
Asked what advice she’d give herself on that difficult day in April she responded,” That it will be okay, and that you can help so many people along their journey if you just keep sharing.”

She recalled ringing the bell after finishing chemotherapy, “When I rang the bell upstairs, a lady shouted, ‘I know you from the news! I got my diagnosis after yours, but I’d already watched your story on the news, so when my hair started falling out, I already knew what to do.”
More than six months after the first episode of Healing in the Public Eye, Elizabeth Peloza says the series didn’t just document her cancer journey, it helped her to reach this milestone.
“Being so public about something that’s so private really helped to get me through it.”

stories.title: Trump sees Canada deal ‘fairly soon,’ downplays leaving Cusma
stories.summary: Trump was asked whether he intended to leave the Canada-US-Mexico Trade Agreement during a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
President Donald Trump expressed optimism about resolving a trade fight with Canada and downplayed the prospect of quitting a continental trade pact, in a potential sign of de-escalating tensions between the two countries.

Trump was asked Saturday whether he intended to have the US leave the Canada-US-Mexico Trade Agreement during a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin.

He went on to say that a deal with Canada could come “fairly soon,” but provided no details on whether formal talks between the two economies had resumed.

“Canada has to treat our farmers better, and they can’t charge our farmers tariffs. They’re charging our farmers 400% tariffs and many other things, so when those things go away, they’re willing to get rid of it all,” Trump said, adding, “You’ll probably see a deal with Canada fairly soon.”

The U.S. and Canada have been locked in a clash that has expanded well beyond tariffs and that threatens to rupture cross-border supply chains relied on by key industries like auto manufacturing. Talks in August on a broader trade deal collapsed at the last minute, leading Trump to follow through on threats to hit Canada with 50% levies on billions of dollars in goods.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney retaliated with tariffs on Sept. 8, hitting a score of U.S. consumer goods and raising duties on many US steel products to 50% from 25%. Trump, in turn, announced additional counter-measures against Canada, including bans on certain products while expanding duties on others.

Carney, however, recently signalled that another round of retaliation was unlikely, saying that the latest US measures against Canada would only have a “modest” impact overall. The prime minister also confirmed on Thursday that he had spoken to Trump recently on geopolitical issues, though it was not clear if that covered trade.

Trump attacks still good news for federal Liberals as lead increases among decided voters: new poll

Donald Trump has already seized one Canadian asset: our attention

Trump’s remarks Saturday and Carney’s earlier comments bolster hopes that the U.S. and Canada are looking to calm tensions and find an off-ramp to an economic dispute that has morphed into a broader confrontation.

The US president has repeatedly mocked Canada, threatening to make it a 51st state and deriding its prime minister as just a “governor,” comments that have fuelled anti-Trump sentiment north of the border and allowed Carney to cast himself as a defender of Canadian sovereignty.

As the relationship deteriorated, there were fears that Trump might threaten to withdraw from the Cusma, a dramatic move that could rewrite the rules governing trade across the continent. Any country can quit the trilateral pact on six months’ notice, though the deal’s language is ambiguous on the process.

The trade war with Canada has high stakes for Trump, whose Republican Party faces an uphill climb to retain control of Congress in November’s midterm elections. Trump’s popularity is at record lows with voters unhappy over his handling of the economy and Iran war.

The tit-for-tat exchange of tariffs also risks exacerbating high prices that have become a dominant concern for the electorate. Republicans in key border states, such as Michigan, which is hosting a crucial Senate race, face blowback.

—With assistance from Jennifer A. Dlouhy and Josh Wingrove.

stories.title: Carney to showcase Canada’s capital agenda at first-ever investment summit
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney will pitch Canada to hundreds of global and domestic investors at the country's first national investment summit in Toronto next week.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney will gather scores of deep-pocketed investors in Toronto next week in a bid to fix Canada’s “Achilles heel” — a persistent lack of business investment dragging down the economy.

Hundreds of global and domestic investors with trillions of dollars in assets under management will descend on a downtown Toronto hotel on Sept. 14 and 15 for Canada’s first-ever national investment summit.

Carney, cabinet members, premiers and other Canadian business leaders will be there with lists of major projects across the country.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she’s got a list of 34 proposed projects she’ll be shopping to investors at the summit; Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe plans to pitch his provinces’ energy, critical mineral, defence and agriculture sectors.

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said she will be pushing multiple projects including a port expansion, a data centre in Lorneville, and a rehabilitation project of a power plant known as the Mactaquac lifetime achievement project.

The investment event is being co-organized by the Prime Minister’s Office with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investments, two of the country’s largest asset managers.

The summit is, in many ways, the manifestation of the capital-focused agenda Carney laid out 18 months ago when he first took office. Since that time, he has reoriented federal policy and Ottawa’s budget framework to funnel spending to critical infrastructure and other major projects.

Carney has set what experts consider a lofty goal of “catalyzing” $1 trillion in investments in Canada over five years.

Mahmood Nanji, a fellow with the Ivey School of Business at Western University, said Canada has suffered from a well-documented dearth of business investment for much of the past decade, which has fed into weak productivity and sluggish growth.

“This has been a bit of Canada’s Achilles heel over the last couple of decades. And this is why I think Prime Minister Carney, upon being elected, this was his big bet on rebuilding the Canadian economy,” Nanji said.

Critics usually blame that investment shortfall on a history of regulatory burdens and the long timelines and uncertainty facing project approvals in Canada.

The CPP Investment Board’s Insights arm published a report Monday surveying 65 of the world’s largest asset managers on how they view Canada’s investment opportunities.

While the energy sector stands out globally as Canada’s most attractive realm for investment, it also comes with the sharpest risks. Fears of policy reversals, regulatory fragmentation and scale or liquidity constraints were cited prominently by those surveyed.

The Conservative party points to what it calls “anti-development laws” and levies like the industrial carbon price as Liberal policies holding back the resource extraction and manufacturing sectors.

Cpp’s survey of asset managers also highlighted Canada’s relative strengths in the competition for global capital.

Canada ranked well on openness to capital and execution in the energy transition, and trailed only Singapore when it came to policy stability and predictability. Nearly 70 per cent of investors ranked predictability as extremely important or essential in decisions about where to park their money.

Jeremy Kronick, president and CEO of the C.D. Howe Institute, said Carney has taken a number of steps to show that Canada is “open for business” since taking office in March 2025. The major projects office and One Canadian Economy Act look to streamline approvals for nation-building projects, for example.

Kronick said that’s enough to start shifting conversations about Canada as a destination for investment. But he suggested there’s more work to be done on other problems such as interprovincial trade barriers — the kind of regulatory snarls that can cause uncertainty about an otherwise viable project.

“I think there’s been enough done on the change in tone. I think regulatory processes are harder to change,” Kronick said.

Political opinion also has shifted in a way that could make it easier to win public approval for major projects, Nanji said.

Angus Reid polling from July suggested broad support for a new pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast, for instance. But major projects like these are also common targets for litigation, and Nanji said officials will need to do more to ensure Indigenous stakeholders are on board before making too many promises to investors.

“There are still risks. They’ve not been eliminated, but they’re not as big as they were perhaps a decade ago,” he said.

There are signs that external capital is already taking a renewed interest in Canada. Statistics Canada said foreign direct investment hit $96.8 billion in 2025, the highest level since 2007.

BMO chief economist Doug Porter said most of this inflow of foreign money so far has come in the form of mergers and acquisitions — not the kind of greenfield investments that organizers of the upcoming summit hope can get new projects off the ground.

The foreign direct investment figures are all the more encouraging given the backdrop of the Canada-U.S. trade war, Porter said. He said that, all other things being equal, he would have expected investment inflows to fall off in the face of President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariff agenda, which puts access to the U.S. market at risk.

All of the experts who spoke to The Canadian Press said the escalation of the tariff war over the past few weeks will definitely be part of the conversation at the summit. But it might not be a deal-breaker.

Summit participants are being presented with a list of projects that is likely to include ports, pipelines and critical mineral extraction. Nanji argued that means many of the opportunities being put in front of investors will be about getting Canadian goods to markets other than the United States.

paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney will gather scores of deep-pocketed investors in Toronto next week in a bid to fix Canada’s “Achilles heel” — a persistent lack of business investment dragging down the economy.

Hundreds of global and domestic investors with trillions of dollars in assets under management will descend on a downtown Toronto hotel on Sept. 14 and 15 for Canada’s first-ever national investment summit.
Carney, cabinet members, premiers and other Canadian business leaders will be there with lists of major projects across the country.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she’s got a list of 34 proposed projects she’ll be shopping to investors at the summit; Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe plans to pitch his provinces’ energy, critical mineral, defence and agriculture sectors.

New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt said she will be pushing multiple projects including a port expansion, a data centre in Lorneville, and a rehabilitation project of a power plant known as the Mactaquac lifetime achievement project.

The investment event is being co-organized by the Prime Minister’s Office with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and Public Sector Pension Investments, two of the country’s largest asset managers.

The summit is, in many ways, the manifestation of the capital-focused agenda Carney laid out 18 months ago when he first took office. Since that time, he has reoriented federal policy and Ottawa’s budget framework to funnel spending to critical infrastructure and other major projects.
Carney has set what experts consider a lofty goal of “catalyzing” $1 trillion in investments in Canada over five years.

Mahmood Nanji, a fellow with the Ivey School of Business at Western University, said Canada has suffered from a well-documented dearth of business investment for much of the past decade, which has fed into weak productivity and sluggish growth.

“This has been a bit of Canada’s Achilles heel over the last couple of decades. And this is why I think Prime Minister Carney, upon being elected, this was his big bet on rebuilding the Canadian economy,” Nanji said.
Critics usually blame that investment shortfall on a history of regulatory burdens and the long timelines and uncertainty facing project approvals in Canada.
The CPP Investment Board’s Insights arm published a report Monday surveying 65 of the world’s largest asset managers on how they view Canada’s investment opportunities.

While the energy sector stands out globally as Canada’s most attractive realm for investment, it also comes with the sharpest risks. Fears of policy reversals, regulatory fragmentation and scale or liquidity constraints were cited prominently by those surveyed.
The Conservative party points to what it calls “anti-development laws” and levies like the industrial carbon price as Liberal policies holding back the resource extraction and manufacturing sectors.
Cpp’s survey of asset managers also highlighted Canada’s relative strengths in the competition for global capital.

Canada ranked well on openness to capital and execution in the energy transition, and trailed only Singapore when it came to policy stability and predictability. Nearly 70 per cent of investors ranked predictability as extremely important or essential in decisions about where to park their money.

Jeremy Kronick, president and CEO of the C.D. Howe Institute, said Carney has taken a number of steps to show that Canada is “open for business” since taking office in March 2025. The major projects office and One Canadian Economy Act look to streamline approvals for nation-building projects, for example.

Kronick said that’s enough to start shifting conversations about Canada as a destination for investment. But he suggested there’s more work to be done on other problems such as interprovincial trade barriers — the kind of regulatory snarls that can cause uncertainty about an otherwise viable project.
“I think there’s been enough done on the change in tone. I think regulatory processes are harder to change,” Kronick said.
Political opinion also has shifted in a way that could make it easier to win public approval for major projects, Nanji said.

Angus Reid polling from July suggested broad support for a new pipeline from Alberta to the B.C. coast, for instance. But major projects like these are also common targets for litigation, and Nanji said officials will need to do more to ensure Indigenous stakeholders are on board before making too many promises to investors.
“There are still risks. They’ve not been eliminated, but they’re not as big as they were perhaps a decade ago,” he said.
There are signs that external capital is already taking a renewed interest in Canada. Statistics Canada said foreign direct investment hit $96.8 billion in 2025, the highest level since 2007.

BMO chief economist Doug Porter said most of this inflow of foreign money so far has come in the form of mergers and acquisitions — not the kind of greenfield investments that organizers of the upcoming summit hope can get new projects off the ground.

The foreign direct investment figures are all the more encouraging given the backdrop of the Canada-U.S. trade war, Porter said. He said that, all other things being equal, he would have expected investment inflows to fall off in the face of President Donald Trump’s aggressive tariff agenda, which puts access to the U.S. market at risk.

All of the experts who spoke to The Canadian Press said the escalation of the tariff war over the past few weeks will definitely be part of the conversation at the summit. But it might not be a deal-breaker.

Summit participants are being presented with a list of projects that is likely to include ports, pipelines and critical mineral extraction. Nanji argued that means many of the opportunities being put in front of investors will be about getting Canadian goods to markets other than the United States.

“Some of the investors might be a little bit jittery about this relationship with the United States … but if some of these projects are going to be exporting goods to other markets, that May not necessarily factor into their decision,” he said.
Speaking to reporters at the Liberal cabinet retreat in Banff on Thursday, Carney suggested that his pitch to investors will focus on Canada’s reliability as a supplier in an uncertain world.
“Canada is about so much more than being next to the United States, OK? We have what the world wants,” he said.

stories.title: Chris Rock, Michelle Yeoh and Seth Rogen among biggest stars to catch at Tiff today
stories.summary: Several of the festival’s highest-profile premieres hit Toronto screens as crowds gather along Festival Street for the third day
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Opportunities for celeb-spotting at the Toronto International Film Festival peaked Saturday as the red carpet rolled out for some of the most high-profile films of the year.

Among those premiering are Chris Rock’s “Misty Green,” which is about a down-on-her-luck actress trying to make a Hollywood comeback. The comedian wrote, directed and stars in the film.

Seth Rogen walked the carpet outside Roy Thomson Hall for “Babies,” a relationship comedy written and directed by his wife, Lauren Miller Rogen. The film follows a couple, played by Rogen and Anna Kendrick, who are deciding whether to have kids.

Miller Rogen said the film is very personal. She and Seth Rogen chose not to have kids.

“The idea for this movie – scenes, lines – has been a living document on my phone for probably seven or eight years,” Miller Rogen said on the carpet. “And so a lot of it went in there in real time. A friend would say something, I’d write it down. Someone would say to me, and I’d write it down.”

Issa Rae, Dan Stevens and Ed Helms are also in the film, and walked the carpet.

Other high-profile premieres include “Closing Night,” starring Sarah Paulson, Naomi Watts and Dianne Wiest, which follows a movie star reconnecting with her family.

And there’s “I Play Rocky,” about the making of the classic sports flick, starring Anthony Ippolito, Stephan James and Matt Dillon.

Meanwhile, Michelle Yeoh is in town to promote the thriller “The Surgeon,” which sees the Academy Award-winner play a kidnapped doctor, while Mahershala Ali is in the thriller “Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.”

The closed-off portion of King Street, known as Festival Street, has been bustling with film enthusiasts from near and far in the opening days of the event that bills itself as “the people’s festival” because of its accessibility to the public.
