stories.title: Brain injury survivors find friendship, ‘rejuvenation’ at London camp
stories.summary: A $30,000 donation is allowing 100 acquired brain injury survivors to attend the four-day program free of charge.
stories.author: Heather Rivers Davey
stories.content:
Brain fog. Cognitive deficits. Dizziness. Nausea.

Following a 2019 car crash outside Ingersoll, Carly Piett, 36, was left with injuries including an acquired brain injury.

“My executive functioning was really compromised and it still is – I am still struggling today,” she said.

But the Seaforth resident says spending time at Camp Dawn – being held at Easter Seals Camp Woodeden in London from Thursday until Sunday – gives her a chance to build friendships, enjoy a myriad of activities and the outdoors.

Camp Dawn is a registered non-profit organization that provides a four-day program including activities such as rock climbing, swimming, arts and crafts, campfires and karaoke.

“I feel rejuvenated, is the word. I wait every year to come back and see my friends,” Piett said. “I absolutely adore it – getting to be around people that understand me without having to talk about it.”

One hundred acquired brain injury (ABI) survivors are attending the London camp free of charge for the first time, following a donation from a Toronto-area law firm specializing in personal injury law.

To mark its 90th anniversary last year, Thomson Rogers LLP pledged to cover the fees for all campers during the 2026 session of Camp Dawn with a $30,000 donation.

“We do a lot of brain injury cases so we were connected with Camp Dawn, which gives four days for people with various types of brain injuries to come and just live a normal kind of stress-free life,” said Matt Sutton, a partner with the law firm.

Sutton said after visiting the camp a few years ago, he was so impressed he decided to become a camp leader.

“I came to visit the campsite to see what they were doing, toured it and just fell in love with the idea of it all,” he said. “There are a lot of people facing adversity, but you don’t see one person who is not happy – it’s really something special.”

Camp-style programs bring moments of joy to sick children in London

Sixty people rappel down One London Place to raise money for Easter Seals

Stephen D’Agostino, managing partner at Thomson Rogers, described the anniversary gift as “something rare.”

“It’s the kind of opportunity that doesn’t come along often,” he said in a release. “We wanted to mark our 90th year with a lasting contribution that removes barriers and ensures the full camp community can participate.”

The camp provides opportunities for ABI survivors aged 18–80 “to build independence, develop social skills, and participate in recreational activities in a supportive, outdoor environment,” the law firm said.

The donation will ensure there are “no financial barriers for all 2026 participants,” said Camp Dawn president Julie Dickison.

“This means more ABI survivors can benefit from the friendships, activities, and skill-building that makes Camp Dawn unique,” she said.

Campers can attend independently or with a personal care assistant at no extra cost, she said.

stories.title: Carney’s pitch, Trump’s latest trade blow and Rbc’s new fund for Canadian tech investments: Must-read business and investing stories for the week of Sept. 12
stories.summary: Plus, Canadian business travel to the U.S. still going strong even as trade war intensifies
stories.author: Abigale Subdhan
stories.content:
Getting caught up on a week that got away? Here’s your weekly digest of The Globe’s most essential business and investing stories, with insights and analysis on the biggest headlines, stock tips, personal finance strategies and more.

The escalating trade war between Canada and the United States took on a new face this week. On Tuesday, Ottawa introduced countertariffs on roughly $28-billion of U.S. goods, and President Donald Trump hit back with new executive orders that will ban imports of certain Canadian goods, including alcohol, motorcycles and some dairy products, and expanded tariffs to include more goods. Most of the new U.S. bans and tariffs are set to take effect on Sept. 29.

On the surface, Trump’s latest counterpunch against Canada looks painful. But Mark Rendell and Jason Kirby looked at the numbers to find that the economic consequences appear relatively minor, and there are signs that this bout is more about recalibrating existing tariff policy than outright escalation.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government is still studying whether to retaliate against the latest countermeasures, but played down the severity of the most recent salvo from Washington. “We’re looking closely at the measures that the Americans have just recently announced,” he told reporters in Banff on Thursday.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to host some 300 CEOs and senior executives from many of the world’s largest global investment organizations at the first-ever Canada Investment Summit in Toronto next week.

The summit is part of the Carney government’s plan to pitch Canada as an attractive, stable place to invest. Officials organizing the summit, in a 66-page prospectus , identified more than 160 projects in various stages of development across different asset classes for attendees to consider, including a $10.9-billion Edmonton-Calgary high-speed rail link and a $57-billion Port of Churchill expansion. It is framed as “a snapshot of the diverse opportunities available across multiple asset classes, sectors and stages of development.”

The high-profile nature of the event has many on Bay Street keeping close tabs. Here’s everything we know so far about the summit, including the guest list, agenda and more.

The trade war May be keeping Canadian tourists away from the U.S., but business travel is moving in the opposite direction . Air bookings by Canadian business travellers to the United States increased by 16.5 per cent year-over-year in August, even as leisure travel remains down roughly 25 to 30 per cent since the trade war began in 2025.

Companies say long-term contracts, clients and investment ties mean they simply can’t afford to stay away. The technology sector remains an especially major source of U.S.-bound corporate trips, Chris Lynes, president of Corporate Traveller for the Americas, told The Globe and Mail. Tech firms still rely heavily on raising capital in California and New York, where investors in later-stage financing rounds require in-person pitch meetings to write million-dollar cheques.

Royal Bank of Canada is launching a $1.4-billion fund aimed at investing in up to 15 Canadian technology companies in sectors including AI, health tech, defence and energy.

The country’s largest lender said the RBCx Growth Fund will focus on sectors where it believes the country’s greatest strengths lie, as a way to help Canadian entrepreneurs grow their businesses in Canada.

The fund has already attracted significant interest from investors. The bank has had initial, conceptual conversations with domestic and foreign investors, including those in the Middle East and the U.S. RBC chief executive officer Dave McKay plans to pitch the fund to foreign investors at next week’s Canada Investment Summit.

Foreign direct investment into Canada reached nearly $100-billion last year, the highest level of FDI since 2007. And global investors are keen to snap up Canadian-issued bonds at lower yields than comparable debt in other rich countries – an indication that Canada is a safe destination to park investment dollars.

But a closer look shows that the foreign investment boom is largely being driven by Americans acquiring Canadian companies – a fraught outcome during the trade war, where sovereignty is top of mind.

Reporter Jameson Berkow takes a look at the numbers around foreign capital in Canada and why Prime Minister Carney will need to focus on courting new sources of cash from beyond the United States.

Prepare for the week ahead with The Globe’s investing calendar .

stories.title: Detention order issued for killer found naked and screaming at Ontario lake
stories.summary: A man who was found not criminally responsible for killing his girlfriend and got a conditional discharge is subject to a new detention order.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Toronto man found not criminally responsible for killing his girlfriend who got a conditional discharge earlier this year from the Ontario Review Board is subject to a new detention order after police found him this summer roaming naked around a Simcoe County lake screaming about God.

Subsequent urine testing found that Michal Nowaczek-Said was not taking his anti-psychotic medication, according to a recent decision from the ORB, an independent tribunal that regularly reviews the status of individuals found not criminally responsible due to mental disorder.

“In this case, the nature and degree of Mr. Nowaczek-Said’s risk to public safety, including the speed and intensity of a relapse of his illness, compels the conclusion that a conditional discharge … is insufficient to protect the public,” according to an Aug. 25 ORB decision.

Nowaczek-Said, now 33, was found not criminally responsible in December 2020 for his girlfriend’s murder three years previous.

The panel heard that on the day Nowaczek-Said introduced his girlfriend to his mother, Sept. 10, 2017, the couple began arguing in his mom’s apartment.

They had only met a week before at the Canadian National Exhibition.

Their argument evolved into a physical fight, and his mom tried to intervene to separate the two.

“While doing so, (her son) punched her in the head multiple times resulting in her nose bleeding profusely,” said the ORB decision, which notes his mother then fled her apartment and called police.

When police arrived on the scene, they learned Nowaczek-Said was armed with a knife.

“The accused exited the apartment with no shirt on and covered in blood.”

Police found his girlfriend lying on the blood-soaked kitchen floor.

Cannabis-smoking Ontario stabber gets day passes despite 'significant threat'

Toronto man not criminally responsible for killing his grandmother is free despite psychiatrist's warning

The woman had 11 stab wounds to her abdomen, a significant stab wound to her neck and several defensive wounds.

“The victim was conscious and kept saying she couldn’t breathe. The initial officer asked the victim who did this and she replied, ‘Michael did it.’ The victim then went unconscious and the officer realized that she had no pulse.”

Paramedics rushed her to St. Michael’s Hospital, but she died two days later.

This past February, the ORB gave Nowaczek-Said a conditional discharge that required him to report not less than twice monthly to the person in charge of Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Camh).

Other conditions included that he abstain from the non-medical use of drugs, alcohol and other intoxicants, “submit samples for testing for same,” and agree to prescribed treatment.

Nowaczek-Said, who has criminal convictions related to previous domestic relationships, reported once fighting with a former girlfriend, who bore his child. “Mr. Nowaczek-Said tied her to a chair and threatened her with a gun. As a result, he was charged with several offences and received a penitentiary sentence in 2013.”

He was hospitalized at Camh following the NCR verdict from January 2021 until his discharge to community living in November 2023.

By the spring of 2023, his “behaviour, participation, and engagement were described as ‘outstanding,’” said the decision.

His transition to community living “went very well,” it said.

“He attended his appointments with the Hospital’s Forensic Outpatient Service, continued to take his oral antipsychotic medication on his own, submitted consistently negative urine drug screen samples and displayed no indications of returning to cannabis or other substance use, and remained free of symptoms of his illness.”

The hospital recommended a conditional discharge as “necessary and appropriate” at a hearing this past February.

Nowaczek-Said was living with his father, and “considering moving in with his fiancée at some point,” said the decision.

Nowaczek-Said, who has been diagnosed with schizophrenia and cannabis use disorder “in sustained remission,” reported to his transitional case manager every two weeks.

Visits with his psychiatrist were reduced to once every two months “due to his continued stability.”

But during a meeting with his handlers this past May, “he presented with notable changes in his mental state from the meeting’s outset,” said the decision.

“He was loud, restless, talkative, and overinclusive. He repeatedly interrupted and dominated the interview, and there was evidence of underlying irritability when challenged.”

When his handlers pointed out the change, Nowaczek-Said “became increasingly defensive,” said the decision. “He insisted that to the contrary, he felt more like himself than he had in a long time and that he was becoming more like the version of himself that he was before he became ill.”

On June 2, Nowaczek-Said’s psychiatrist got test results back indicating his patient had not taken his antipsychotic medication “for several days.”

Nowaczek-Said “was adamant that he had been compliant,” said the decision.

In a lengthy phone conversation with his psychiatrist, Nowaczek-Said reported that his father had recently been diagnosed with cancer and things weren’t going smoothly with his fiancée.

On June 3, after the call with his psychiatrist, Nowaczek-Said “was apprehended by the police at Orr Lake in Simcoe County and brought, initially, to the Georgian Bay Hospital.”

The panel heard Nowaczek–Said had been “roaming the area around Orr Lake while nude, repeatedly going in and out of the water, and screaming about God, including that he was God.”

He was placed in “mechanical restraints” at some point “due to his level of agitation.”

When the restraints were removed, Nowaczek–Said punched a camera.

“Multiple staff members and security personnel were required to contain him during what is recorded as a ‘very agitated outburst.’ Mr. Nowaczek-Said was placed back in mechanical restraints and given two injections. A third medication was later administered when the first two medications did not settle him.”

On June 4, he was moved to the Waypoint Centre for Mental Health Care but discharged on June 8 after contesting his admission.

“He declined to remain in hospital longer or to further optimize his medication.”

Nowaczek-Said “clearly represents a significant threat to the safety of the public,” said the ORB decision.

“The evidence compels a finding that absent the board’s oversight, there is a real risk that he would engage in criminal conduct that would result in serious physical and/or psychological harm.”

The panel determined that a “detention order is necessary and appropriate.”

“When unwell, his mental state can fluctuate drastically, and he can superficially present as better than his actual mental state. Absent rapid interventions, this instability can deteriorate quite abruptly into acutely aggressive and agitated behaviours that pose a serious risk of violence to others.”

stories.title: How to choose a comfortable – yet stylish – kitchen stool, according to design experts
stories.summary: Plus, six options that might be right for your kitchen
stories.author: Matthew Hague
stories.content:
Montreal interior designer Paule Bourbonnais knows the value of a good kitchen stool. She has two teenage daughters, who, after school, often pull up to the counter. “They do homework and I cook dinner,” she says. “It’s been like this since kindergarten.”

For the past 10 years, Bourbonnais has had X Stools from Italian brand Alma. The seat and back are one piece of moulded plastic, no cushion. The curving, scoop shape acts as something of a cradle. “People think comfort is all about upholstery,” she says. “But the ergonomics are more important – the way the seat meets the back. A flat seat with a pad is still pretty hard.” (In general, a back-to-seat angle of 105 degrees works well.)

While Bourbonnais recommends the X Stools, she doesn’t repeat them in clients’ homes. “I pick something different for every project,” she says, noting a near dizzying variety of options on the market, including different heights, materials and options such as armrests and swivels.

Tommy Smythe, co-founder of Toronto’s TOM Design, understands why there are so many styles. “I always say that a kitchen counter stool is kind of like eggs,” he says. “People are very particular with how they like them. If fact, stools can be as tricky to pin down as sofas and beds.”

Smythe suggests a smart place to start: picking the right height. “A kitchen counter stool is not a bar stool,” he says. “A bar stool is taller, so you really have to measure and make sure that you’re getting something that fits your space.” In general, he says, a bar is 40 to 42 inches off the ground, with stools that are 28 to 34 inches tall, whereas a kitchen counter is 36 inches off the ground, with stools that are 24 to 27 inches.

To further narrow down the options, Smythe asks his clients a long list of questions about their preferences and habits.

If someone needs a place to perch briefly with a glass of wine, Smythe says a sleek, backless option is adequate. “That’s your photoshoot counter stool,” he says. “It doesn’t interrupt the sightlines, looks great in a showpiece kitchen. But people who are going to sit there on their laptop for two hours need a soft landing – a back, maybe arms and a cushy seat.”

The issue with armrests, like swivels, is that they can take up precious space. “They don’t necessarily improve comfort,” says Bourbonnais. “Armrests can be bulky, and swivels need room to operate without knocking into a neighbour, so they can require a longer counter.”

While Smythe notes that a good stool doesn’t have to be expensive – “I’m a fan of Ikea,” he says – they should be well engineered since they are in daily use. “A metal footrest might be nice, so it doesn’t scuff and look dirty after a while. And they shouldn’t be too heavy. People get angry if their stool is 150 pounds and they are struggling to pull it in and out.”

Then there are materials. According to Vancouver designer Kelly Deck, who will be speaking alongside Smythe at Vancouver’s Interior Design Show at the end of September, leather is a durable, easy-to-clean choice. “It is undeniably practical, particularly for families,” she says. “Leather has a way of reading heavy, though, so I keep the frame fine to counteract that.”

Wood can also work well. “It can be surprisingly comfortable especially if it has a soft, rounded edge,” says Toronto designer Shirley Meisels. “They are practical because they are easy to wipe clean and generally not as bulky as upholstered stools.”

Fabric can be a bit “tricky if you have little kids or messy eaters,” according to designer Sarah McBean of Toronto’s RW Interiors. “But ultimately, the best thing to do is to test-sit the stools and see what works best for you and your bum.”

When shopping for kitchen stools, look for options that match your lifestyle.

The Alta Swivel Counter Stool has been described as the Switzerland of stools for its versatility. Made by Vancouver-based brand Article, its simple, white oak legs and cream-coloured seat work in both contemporary and traditional kitchens. $439

The Montrealaise Stool, from Gatineau, Que.-based furniture maker ref., is named for a city but has a certain, country house charm. The spindle back, tapered legs and smooth seat are all handmade using traditional techniques. Made to order with either white oak, walnut or maple. $844

The Slow Mornings Stool, from Vancouver-based Sundays, is minimal with thoughtful touches. The low-back rest, with a padded leather cushion, profiles support as does the moulded wood seat and metal foot rest. $550

The MacKenzie Custom Stool, from Winnipeg-based EQ3, appears backless for a clean, modern profile. But the moulded foam seat with a short back improves the sit-ability. The upholstery is customizable with over 100 fabric options, including leather. Available in both bar and counter heights. $399

The Lyndoe Bar Stool, from Toronto maker Mary Ratcliffe, is ideal for avid collectors of high-end design. This low-slung option is exquisitely produced by hand with a durable leather seat while the sculptural form, fashioned from either ash or oak, is just beautiful to behold in showpiece kitchens. $3,090

Ikea’s Glenn Stool is a practical option for a family kitchen. The moulded plastic seat and chrome footrest are designed for easy cleaning. It’s also lightweight and stackable so can tuck away when the floor below needs to be swept and mopped. $120

stories.title: ‘Super awesome’: Student’s Chinese ballads break barriers, win fans and lamb chops
stories.summary: When Kieran Michael MacNeill started going door to door in Richmond, B.C., serenading householders in Mandarin, he was worried they might think he was a “weirdo.”
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When Kieran Michael MacNeill started going door to door in Richmond, B.C., serenading householders in Mandarin, he was worried they might think he was a “weirdo.”

But instead, they embraced the efforts of the 22-year-old student, who spent summer singing to residents at the urging of Chinese Canadian friends who were “blown away” when he sang a classic Mando-pop tune in a car with them one day.

MacNeill’s renditions of the sentimental 1980s ballad, “A Spray of Plum Blossoms,” videoed by friend Jason Chen, have received millions of views online, drawing fascination for both his singing and the reactions to it.

Some residents join in the song, rich in symbolism about hardship and longing. Others have shared food with MacNeill and Chen.

“When you see a white guy at your door, you don’t expect him to speak Chinese,” said Chen, “Just seeing Michael want to learn Chinese and actually going out there and speaking it, I think it’s super awesome.”

MacNeill, who is studying computer science at Queen’s University in Ontario but is originally from Calgary, learned the song to kill time while on a flight in 2024.

But after mastering the song, it wasn’t until this May when he came to B.C. for a summer job that he got a chance to show off his talent in Richmond, which has the highest proportion of residents of Chinese descent of any municipality in Canada, making up more than half of the city’s population.

He was driving to a restaurant in Richmond with Chen and another friend when MacNeill started singing.

“They are like, you have to sing that to the aunties and uncles in Richmond, and they’re gonna be blown away that you could do that,” laughed MacNeill.

They started their project in June, MacNeill overcoming a sense of awkwardness and “being a weirdo” as the Chinese community warmed to his efforts.

At the first house they tried, the resident was so impressed she gave them dinner.

“She’s like, OK, hold on one second, and then she came out with two plates of lamb chops,” said MacNeill.

“We were just expecting a granola bar probably, not her dinner.”

A performance for an 81-year-old Chinese woman who immigrated to Canada in the 1980s received 1.8 million likes and almost 14 million views on Instagram.

She told MacNeill it was the first time a white person had sung in Chinese to her.

“If I moved to China 44 years ago and I didn’t speak Chinese, and then some random Chinese kid came up to me and sang ‘Sweet Caroline’ to me, that would be a real culture shock for sure,” said MacNeill.

Not everyone has been appreciative. MacNeill said he had visited 300 to 400 homes over the summer, some residents thinking he was a salesman and closing the door in his face.

But MacNeill said he had been overwhelmed with “over the top reactions” from those who enjoyed his performances — which have also included a song for Cantonese speakers, “Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies” by Beyond.

“They kind of go from not really wanting to talk to you or being very shy to then all of a sudden wanting to ask me a million questions,” said MacNeill.

Some guessed that he learned Chinese because he had a Chinese girlfriend, which he doesn’t.

MacNeill said he learned Chinese by using Google Translate and watching YouTube videos, testing out his language skills by ordering food at a Chinese restaurant. His B.C. friends have also mentored him.

But the reactions of Richmond householders to his singing have provided incentive to keep learning.

“The best way to learn a language is to actually be motivated … so when people have these good reactions and they’re always so impressed even if you just know really basic Chinese … that was good motivation to learn the language,” said MacNeill.

He said the idea that Chinese immigrants could be “closed off” was a false impression created by cultural and language barriers, with some worried about causing offence if they don’t speak English well.

But show interest in their culture, and true personalities shone through, he said.

“They’re very welcoming. Chinese people are some of the kindest people I’ve ever met in my life,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 12, 2026.

Nono Shen, The Canadian Press

stories.title: In a small B.C. town, a grizzly family stirs unease
stories.summary: A mother grizzly and her three yearlings are an unusual sight in Pender Harbour, a community more accustomed to black bears
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
Around noon on Thursday, the elementary school at the heart of a quiet coastal town issued a shelter-in-place order. Staff kept students inside. A road to the local marina was blocked off.

Phone lines and Facebook groups erupted with warnings: Strangers with fierce reputations had come to town and residents worried about a confrontation.

But it soon became clear that the newcomers – a mama grizzly and her three yearlings – wanted little to do with humans. They gorged on apples before galumphing down the highway.

Their appearance has left an uneasy feeling in Pender Harbour, British Columbia, a community of roughly 3,000 people. While Pender is comfortable with its teeming black bear population, grizzlies are novel.

Provincial maps list the species as eradicated in this region, which is located a 40-minute ferry ride and a twisty one-hour drive north of Vancouver. But the bears refuse to abide by cartography. For all kinds of possible reasons – wildfires, climate change, a hunting ban – B.C. grizzlies are pushing back into territory where there is no living memory of their presence.

Not everyone is welcoming the new arrivals. While many residents are preaching coexistence by removing attractants and bear-proofing properties with animal-resistant garbage cans, electric fences and even wolf hair, others want the family relocated before someone, or something, gets hurt.

“I really hope the conservation officer can relocate them,” said Lesley Durrant, who runs a bed and breakfast overlooking a bay where the family has been spotted. “They won’t do well in this community.”

In the first week of August, the mama bear led her yearlings down to the shellfish-rich Oyster Bay. There, they crunched clams and oysters in full view of dozens of waterfront residents.

On Aug. 14, Tammy Trefry, who runs a local animal rescue service, alerted the community on Facebook and urged everyone to give the family space. She also passed along tips for grizzly encounters. Don’t bang pots or yell like you might with black bears, she says, just stay calm and let grizzlies move on.

The very next day, Amelia Dunn was outside feeding her two pigs, when she looked up and saw the mama grizzly and three yearlings trotting straight toward her.

“My first instinct was ‘Oh my god, they know it’s feeding time. They’re coming to eat me. They’re coming to get the pigs.’”

Then, she recalled reading Ms. Trefry’s advice.

She had two bowls in her hands. Rather than banging them together like she might have for black bears, she dropped them to the ground, made sure the bears could see her, and calmly repeated “Off you go, bears. Off you go.”

The bears stood up, assessed Ms. Dunn for a few seconds, and then walked back from where they had come.

“She wanted nothing to do with me,” Ms. Dunn said about the mama bear. “She was gone. She’s not here to take down a bunch of humans.”

Ms. Dunn then contacted Ms. Trefry, who arrived armed with an array of eclectic deterrents: wolf hair, Pine-Sol, strobe lights, air-filled garbage bags and a static-blaring radio.

“She had some really good ideas,” Ms. Dunn said. “We never saw the bears again.”

Not everyone has been so receptive. People have sicced dogs on the bears, and others have refused to set up electric fences or remove fruit, Ms. Trefry said.

Generational habits are hard to change. When Andy Pestraschuk saw the grizzlies early Thursday morning, he banged a pot to keep them away from his livestock. It worked. “They freaked out and took off towards the water,” he said.

Decades ago, B.C. paid bounties for killing large carnivores. It wasn’t until the 1960s that the province started regulating grizzly hunting with a tag and limited-entry restrictions. In 1975, the U.S. listed them as a threatened species, prompting concerns of overhunting in B.C.

In 2017, the B.C. government banned trophy hunting of grizzlies.

“The population is coming back,” said Evelyn Kirkaldy, who leads the Sunshine Coast Bear Alliance and lives in Pender Harbour. “We really wiped them out at the turn of the century.”

She says many communities would quietly dispatch bears, an approach she calls “SSS,” or shoot, shovel, shut up. But those days are largely gone.

The hunting ban is just one possible reason the species is moving in. In the nineties, the government reintroduced elk, which can attract the apex predators, to the area. Recent low snowpacks have made for poor berry foraging, pushing bears into settled areas. There are also constant wildfires forcing populations into unfamiliar terrain.

Whatever the reason, the Pender grizzlies decided to vacate the harbour in late August, walking about 15 kilometres north before swimming to sparsely populated shores.

“That was a big relief,” said Sergeant Dean Miller, local field supervisor for the BC Conservation Officer Service. “But I always suspected that they might be back, just like the bear that swam over to Texada Island last year.”

That bear, popularly known as Tex , has become an infamous cautionary tale. The young male was relocated multiple times after wandering near downtown areas of two other area towns, Gibsons and Sechelt. Each time, it returned to populated areas and reportedly began stalking people. In May, 2025, it swam at least five kilometres to Texada Island, where it was eventually shot and killed by farmers who said Tex was attacking their dairy cows.

They later pleaded guilty for failing to promptly report the accidental or protective killing of wildlife, and were fined $6,000.

Sgt. Miller’s suspicions were correct. This week, several people photographed the family marching south along the S-bends of Highway 101 toward Pender’s main commercial hub, Madeira Park.

On Thursday, they turned up on Madeira’s shores, where they feasted on apples at a marina and seemed generally unfazed by human onlookers. Even though they eventually marched out of town, Sgt. Miller said their return is worrisome.

“Obviously, the level of human habituation has increased in just two weeks,” he said by phone as he drove to check on the grizzlies on Thursday. “That just shows the trajectory of where these bears are going, and getting these apples – and who knows what else – from yards.”

With the bears so close to a school, some locals on Facebook called for conservation officers to relocate the animals.

Sgt. Miller said the process would require complex logistics and the involvement of provincial biologists.

There are other options. Conservation officers “destroyed” 24 grizzlies last year and have so far killed three in 2026 for public safety reasons, according to provincial figures.

“Shooting them is such a lazy human approach,” said Ms. Dunn, who had the close encounter. “Heaven forbid that humans have to adjust.”

stories.title: Canada's young entrepreneurs are fleeing south. We need to keep them here
stories.summary: Are they leaving because of high taxes? Red tape? Funding shortfalls? Experts say we can stop the U.S. swallowing up our young talent.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
Naila Moloo, 19, won the 2022 Canadian Youth Innovation Award at the age of 16 for creating a flexible solar panel prototype when she was a Grade 11 student at Elmwood School in Ottawa. She plans to become an entrepreneur, pursuing her own AI-startup, Periodwise, which assists with menstrual management for women.

She’s attending the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill — and considering living in the United States permanently to pursue her dream.

Why not Canada? “There are a lot of opportunities in the U.S., especially in the tech scene,” she says.

Moloo is not alone in that thinking, studies suggest. Last year, Canada lost about 65,000 residents to net emigration , according to Statistics Canada. A paper by the Canadian Labour Economics Forum suggests it is mostly young, high-skilled workers who are being lost. A 2025 report by the Leaders Fund warned that Canada risks “missing out on the next Shopify.”

“We’re seeing a pretty significant exodus of our most ambitious entrepreneurs. They are leaving Canada and moving to the U.S., and that’s intensified over the last decade,” says Charles Lammam, Senior Fellow at the Montreal Economic Institute (MEI), a free-enterprise thinktank.

Nearly one in two Canadian company founders who raised over $1 million in 2024 are now based in the U.S., he notes, citing the Leaders Fund study.

It’s a problem politicians, economists and the business community want to solve. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s planned Investment Summit Sept. 14 and 15 is part of the strategy, aiming to stem the outflow of investment dollars from Canada and attract new capital – particularly at a time when acrimonious trade talks with the U.S. have added instability. Boosting investment could help keep Canadian innovators at home, building successful businesses here.

Canada’s tech industry warns 'entrepreneurs are leaving in droves' for U.S.

Canada's economy posts fastest growth in three years

Why are young innovators — tomorrow’s successful entrepreneurs — leaving Canada? Hint: It’s not about their ideas.

“There’s no shortage of smart, talented people in Canada,” says Michael Buhr, a serial entrepreneur and executive director of C100 – an association of Canadian tech veterans from Silicon Valley dedicated to building up Canadian innovation. Buhr says Canada has great educational and research institutions.

Canadian talent has, in the past, created giants such as Nortel, Research in Motion, Shopify and more. A new report by Cbre, a real estate corporation, writes that of the top 15 tech talent markets in North America, six are in Canada. (Toronto ranks third, with Vancouver and Waterloo Region also in the top 10. Montreal weighs in at 11, Ottawa 14 and Calgary 15.)

But great research, talent and ideas are not enough, says Daniel Debow, founder of DMI – Debow Musical Instruments, company producer at Ambitious Adventurers and a board director at Loblaw Companies Limited, based in Toronto. “Innovation … is not invention, innovation is applying an invention to a market.” In other words, it has to be successfully “commercialized.”

The critical players in this field are incubators, which give very early-stage companies access to mentorship, investors and other support, as the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) describes them.

University of British Columbia, as one example among many, has three flagship programs: Hatch Venture Builder , Lab2Market and Venture Founder . According to the university, these have helped create 296 spin-off companies, 91 per cent of which remain in Canada.

But by themselves, incubator programs are not enough.

There are “517 American companies started by Canadians. They’ve raised about $414 billion,” wrote Lucy Hargreaves in a recent LinkedIn post, citing statistics in The Dominion List . “Nearly all of the founders went to school in Canada.”

Canada is paying for their schooling, and they are taking their ideas across the border.

Examples of major American companies founded by Canadians who emigrated to Silicon Valley include Instacart’s Apoorva Mehta, Uber’s Garrett Camp and Slack’s Stuart Butterfield.

One reason, argues Lammam, is Canada’s tax policy, which is “not competitive globally – and certainly not more attractive than the U.S.” Canadians “are paying the fifth highest marginal tax rate in the entire set of Oecd economies,” he says.

Canada used to be relatively competitive on corporate taxation, but this advantage has dwindled since 2017 when the U.S. cut its rates, he says. Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act further strengthened U.S. tax advantages” for entrepreneurs, he adds.

Even Canada’s Small Business Deduction has been only a limited help to starting entrepreneurs, according to Lammam.

While some taxes might be lower in the U.S., the costs of doing business in certain cases might still be higher than in Canada, however.

Buhr, who moved to Silicon Valley after university for a job with Apple, has lived in the U.S. for decades, founding his companies, Bridge Strategies and Voice Over IT, there. He says private health care insurance and other mandatory expenses south of the border even the playing field: “In the U.S., 38 per cent of your (company) fundraising goes to paying for employees. You raise $10 million, $3.8 million of that goes to paying health care for your employees. ”

Too much red tape and regulation is also cited as a reason young Canadians leave for the South.

Chathura Fernando, CEO of FDO Energy, a Canadian startup developing portable garbage incinerators, is entering his final year of engineering at Western University in London, Ont. He’s frustrated by Canada’s slow regulatory speed: “In some other jurisdictions, things are a lot faster. You don’t need four approvals or three approvals to build something. You can just go and build it and get quick approval.”

“Less entrepreneurship happens when markets are overly regulated or protected from competition,” says Lammam. “Contrast us with the U.S. where it’s a bit more cutthroat, you have to innovate or run the risk of becoming obsolete.”

Regulations and taxes aren’t necessarily the top of the list of obstacles facing startups.

The core requirements of any successful expanding business, Buhr says, boil down to supports such as mentorship, networking and capital.

Natasha Penzo, CEO of Homekin, which specializes in the home design marketplace, says the Toronto Metropolitan University incubator DMZ provided her with “support, collaboration with other startups” and advice for creative solutions.

But funding to scale her business remains a particular challenge. “I found that (in) any conversations with Canadian venture, they really wanted to focus more on Fintech and health tech.”

Even in those sectors, however, things aren’t easy. Saumik Biswas, co-founder and CEO of Tenomix, a Canadian health tech startup focused on cancer diagnostics through AI and automation for lymph node examinations in biopsy samples, says he also had problems attracting capital.

Biswas said he had to pitch to “205 investors, and we ended up getting 16 of them.” Even that required “a lot of resilience.”

“We ended up raising … just north of $2.1 million Canadian. And it was all Canadian route, which is awesome,” he said.

Even so, there’s often an investment ceiling in Canada. “Once you reach a certain scale, if you’re a tech company, moving to (Silicon) Valley makes a material difference because to get that next round of funding, you need the right people on your board,” says Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont.

Buhr, though, notes the fierce competition in Silicon Valley for capital. “What you don’t see is there are 1,000 times as many companies chasing that money.”

Keeping talent in a company matters as well and is as tough for individual companies in the U.S. as it is here, he adds.

“All those great employees that you’re hiring … will last on average 12 to 18 months because there’s always somebody sexier, shinier who’s going to pay you more,” says Buhr. “By coming (to the U.S.) you’re going to trade off problems you know about for problems you don’t know about.”

Among other challenges, ironically, are sometimes the very programs governments in Canada offer to boost innovation and provide more capital.

As of July 2024, the federal government had invested $2.4 billion in AI. And it says it plans to commit $180 billion in defence procurement with a further $290 billion in defence-related capital investment through The Defence Industrial Strategy.

In the emerging fields such as AI, Daley says, placing multiple bets on numerous firms, is “the right approach,” because it “give(s) everyone enough that they have a chance to make it to the next level.”

But MEI research concludes that a higher level of government venture capital can crowd out private venture capital. “If BDC is competing with private providers, the unintended impact can be (that) the private providers of venture capital retrench,” says Lammam.

He also points to the confusion of having multiple support programs at federal, provincial, and municipal levels.

Penzo says she has experienced this with her company. “I’m hiring a consultant to help me with it; these programs and grants take a lot of time out of a founder’s already very busy schedule,” she says.

“I often hear some people don’t even end up going for them because they’re just so time-consuming.”

Still, Daley argues, Canada has had real successes. “We still have lots of great startup companies; we have Cohere (Canadian AI firm).”

However, for Buhr, the issue is that “you get a Shopify or a Cohere every 10 years. We need those every month.”

The biggest — and hardest to avoid — factor is Canada’s proximity to the US, both a blessing and a curse, experts say. “The money is concentrated geographically,” like the people who control it, says Daley.

Matt Bazely, the Entrepreneurship Department Director at Huron University College in Ontario, believes that the problem of entrepreneurs leaving the country as soon as their business gets to a certain size is “a very specific Canadian phenomenon.”

“It’s much easier to move offices and business operations into the States from Canada than, let’s say, from Australia or New Zealand.”

To stay in Canada, there would have to be Canadian customers. But caution about the unknown has always been “part of the natural DNA” here in Canada, Buhr says.

“You can talk to a lot of companies that say their first customers were not in Canada,” says John MacRitchie, president of the Canadian Council for Small Business and Entrepreneurship and co-founder of incubator Lab2Market, noting that it makes a profound impact on international credibility “if you don’t have those (customer) references back in your home country.”

Debow recalls that some of the businesses he has run relied substantially on foreign customers. “In the case of Rypple (which was a social media monitoring platform) … virtually every customer came from the United States for a very long time,” he says.

“What will typically happen is if that U.S. customer becomes the first customer; those companies then start to get dragged more into the U.S. to a certain point that some of them just get acquired by US companies,” Buhr says.

Penzo says expanding to the U.S. “makes most sense for our business model, and the market is so much bigger.”

“Canadians sometimes are a little more hesitant … to use a technology until it’s really gotten off the ground or has that track record of success,” she adds.

With a critical mass of talent and capital, mentoring and support are added advantages for the United States.

“The people that are successful are very good at tapping into the right resources and talking about what they’re doing and getting feedback,” MacRitchie says. In other words, they rely on a like-minded community.

In Silicon Valley “you’re naturally surrounded by people who inspire you,” says Buhr, and who will tell you “how you should get to $150 million or … a billion.”

“Canadian entrepreneurs aren’t surrounded by that,” he says, adding that the lack of mentorships leads many to sell their companies too early and too cheap, because “$50 million is a lot of money,” and there is no one to say “you’ve got a $5 billion company in front of you. You should not even consider that offer.”

Fernando says it’s important to have links to an innovative community post-graduation: “There’s a lot of early-stage help. It’s just from the middle to kind of the end… there’s not as much.”

But it’s not just about taxes, regulation, geography, or the critical mass of entrepreneurial peers and mentors south of the border.

Buhr says that out of 40 early-stage entrepreneurs who came to Silicon Valley for a bootcamp with C100, many expressed doubts about whether their own country needs or wants them.

Sustained criticism in part is what drives people south. “They keep saying how what we’re doing is bad and, you know, technology is not good,” and that is a big discouragement for many, Buhr says.

Meanwhile, “Silicon Valley cares about what we are doing,” so many end up leaving, thinking “I’m a proud Canadian, I want to build Canada, but I just don’t hear that my country wants me there,” he says.

“It has everything to do with this sheer human nature of ‘do you want me to build this thing in Canada or not?’ ”

Some aren’t concerned with these critiques; they plan to build here regardless.

Biswas started his health tech company after losing a close family member to cancer. He was inspired to become an innovator after a surgeon used transformative technology to regrow leg bones for his younger brother, who was born without a tibia. Through the process, Biswas had to translate what the doctor was saying to his Bangladeshi parents. His brother recovered.

So he wants to give back to Canada: “I made a promise to myself that whatever I do in this life, I’d love to give back to this community, through medical innovation.”

Buhr’s convinced “what Canada needs to do is … to celebrate the (entrepreneurial) ecosystem on a national scale.”

Arguably, the federal government has made efforts in this direction — for instance, through innovation hubs and the appointment of a minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation.

Additionally, Carney’s planned Investment Summit this month aims to “catalyse $1 trillion in total investment in Canada over the next five years,” according to a government press release . The federal government wants to do that by investing $280 billion over five years, hoping to attract the rest in foreign investment.

Buhr does not believe this is enough; in the U.S., he says, entrepreneurs are encouraged to just “go build something exciting.”

Daley, though, considers government involvement a cornerstone of a successful innovation policy. “Silicon Valley exists because of policy decisions made by the U.S. government after Wwii,” particularly military investment.

Indeed, “For the people and institutions in the business of researching cutting-edge science and technology, the US government was the original venture capitalist,” Margaret Pugh O’Mara, professor of American History at the University of Washington, once wrote , highlighting that this investment was mostly made between 1939 and late 1960s through military contracts.

“We should be thinking on that time scale,” Daley says, arguing that as AI becomes more prevalent, Silicon Valley’s capital advantage will wane. “Tech companies are cheaper than manufacturing companies, and AI-native tech companies are cheaper still.”

Lammam thinks it would be more valuable “to focus on getting the framework conditions right” — specifically the tax system, which hasn’t been comprehensively reviewed for 60 years. It has become “not only uncompetitive” but is “holding back entrepreneurs,” he says.

Yet Bazely argues the system is not broken; it is “producing exactly what it’s designed to produce,” which is stability. “We do not have the economic downturns that the United States might have, for example,” he says.

For him, the debate revolves around a conscious tradeoff between stability and innovation. Embracing the degree of market freedom involved in U.S. innovation might also mean tolerating such consequences as “people losing their houses,” and “banks failing.”

“The States is a great place to be if you’re successful. It’s an awful place to be if you’re not,” he adds.

For Canada, more and better entrepreneurial education is among Bazely’s suggestions.

Marie-Claire Wasson, a co-founder of Oncolinc Therapeutics, a Halifax biotech startup that focuses on immune therapy cancer treatment, went through Lab2Market training. She says such guidance from a university incubator of this sort is “invaluable.”

Graduate students are perfect targets for such training “because they’re motivated by the work that they’re doing in the research” and “they need a path forward that’s not necessarily in the academic range,” says MacRitchie.

Incubators in post-secondary institutions can play “a wider role in introducing entrepreneurship, providing a real training environment and potentially supporting commercialization,” he notes.

Debow is unsure that entrepreneurship is “purely a set of skills that you learn,” in a classroom, comparing it to a demanding sport. “I could take a class on triathlon. But you have to go run a triathlon… before you actually know what it is to be a triathlete.”

Another piece is risk reduction. “You don’t have the pension, (and) you don’t have the benefits,” says Bazely. Even creating the arrangements for entrepreneurs to be enrolled in the CPP could go a long way, Bazely suggests.

Next-generation entrepreneurs do see hope in the Canadian landscape.

“We’re very proud to be Canadian,” says Biswas, adding that it is his heartfelt hope to launch commercially in Canada and keep his company rooted in the country as it expands to global markets.

Wasson says innovators’ successes can inspire future innovators: “If I see other people do it … we can do it too.”

“There just need to be a way where we can maintain Canadian ownership, hiring more Canadian talent, and advancing an economy in a way of solving global problems.” Biswas says, adding that he believes this is what “generates billion-dollar ideas.”

In other words, says Daley, “Canada’s moment is right now.”

She plans to become an entrepreneur, pursuing her own AI-startup, Periodwise, which assists with menstrual management for women.
She’s attending the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill — and considering living in the United States permanently to pursue her dream.
Why not Canada? “There are a lot of opportunities in the U.S., especially in the tech scene,” she says.

Moloo is not alone in that thinking, studies suggest. Last year, Canada lost about 65,000 residents to net emigration , according to Statistics Canada. A paper by the Canadian Labour Economics Forum suggests it is mostly young, high-skilled workers who are being lost. A 2025 report by the Leaders Fund warned that Canada risks “missing out on the next Shopify.”

“We’re seeing a pretty significant exodus of our most ambitious entrepreneurs. They are leaving Canada and moving to the U.S., and that’s intensified over the last decade,” says Charles Lammam, Senior Fellow at the Montreal Economic Institute (MEI), a free-enterprise thinktank.
Nearly one in two Canadian company founders who raised over $1 million in 2024 are now based in the U.S., he notes, citing the Leaders Fund study.

It’s a problem politicians, economists and the business community want to solve. Prime Minister Mark Carney’s planned Investment Summit Sept. 14 and 15 is part of the strategy, aiming to stem the outflow of investment dollars from Canada and attract new capital – particularly at a time when acrimonious trade talks with the U.S. have added instability. Boosting investment could help keep Canadian innovators at home, building successful businesses here.
Canada’s tech industry warns 'entrepreneurs are leaving in droves' for U.S.
Canada's economy posts fastest growth in three years
Why are young innovators — tomorrow’s successful entrepreneurs — leaving Canada? Hint: It’s not about their ideas.

“There’s no shortage of smart, talented people in Canada,” says Michael Buhr, a serial entrepreneur and executive director of C100 – an association of Canadian tech veterans from Silicon Valley dedicated to building up Canadian innovation. Buhr says Canada has great educational and research institutions.

Canadian talent has, in the past, created giants such as Nortel, Research in Motion, Shopify and more. A new report by Cbre, a real estate corporation, writes that of the top 15 tech talent markets in North America, six are in Canada. (Toronto ranks third, with Vancouver and Waterloo Region also in the top 10. Montreal weighs in at 11, Ottawa 14 and Calgary 15.)

But great research, talent and ideas are not enough, says Daniel Debow, founder of DMI – Debow Musical Instruments, company producer at Ambitious Adventurers and a board director at Loblaw Companies Limited, based in Toronto. “Innovation … is not invention, innovation is applying an invention to a market.” In other words, it has to be successfully “commercialized.”

The critical players in this field are incubators, which give very early-stage companies access to mentorship, investors and other support, as the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC) describes them.

University of British Columbia, as one example among many, has three flagship programs: Hatch Venture Builder , Lab2Market and Venture Founder . According to the university, these have helped create 296 spin-off companies, 91 per cent of which remain in Canada.
But by themselves, incubator programs are not enough.

There are “517 American companies started by Canadians. They’ve raised about $414 billion,” wrote Lucy Hargreaves in a recent LinkedIn post, citing statistics in The Dominion List . “Nearly all of the founders went to school in Canada.”
Canada is paying for their schooling, and they are taking their ideas across the border.
Examples of major American companies founded by Canadians who emigrated to Silicon Valley include Instacart’s Apoorva Mehta, Uber’s Garrett Camp and Slack’s Stuart Butterfield.

One reason, argues Lammam, is Canada’s tax policy, which is “not competitive globally – and certainly not more attractive than the U.S.” Canadians “are paying the fifth highest marginal tax rate in the entire set of Oecd economies,” he says.

Canada used to be relatively competitive on corporate taxation, but this advantage has dwindled since 2017 when the U.S. cut its rates, he says. Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act further strengthened U.S. tax advantages” for entrepreneurs, he adds.
Even Canada’s Small Business Deduction has been only a limited help to starting entrepreneurs, according to Lammam.
While some taxes might be lower in the U.S., the costs of doing business in certain cases might still be higher than in Canada, however.

Buhr, who moved to Silicon Valley after university for a job with Apple, has lived in the U.S. for decades, founding his companies, Bridge Strategies and Voice Over IT, there. He says private health care insurance and other mandatory expenses south of the border even the playing field: “In the U.S., 38 per cent of your (company) fundraising goes to paying for employees. You raise $10 million, $3.8 million of that goes to paying health care for your employees. ”
Too much red tape and regulation is also cited as a reason young Canadians leave for the South.

Chathura Fernando, CEO of FDO Energy, a Canadian startup developing portable garbage incinerators, is entering his final year of engineering at Western University in London, Ont. He’s frustrated by Canada’s slow regulatory speed: “In some other jurisdictions, things are a lot faster. You don’t need four approvals or three approvals to build something. You can just go and build it and get quick approval.”

“Less entrepreneurship happens when markets are overly regulated or protected from competition,” says Lammam. “Contrast us with the U.S. where it’s a bit more cutthroat, you have to innovate or run the risk of becoming obsolete.”
Regulations and taxes aren’t necessarily the top of the list of obstacles facing startups.
The core requirements of any successful expanding business, Buhr says, boil down to supports such as mentorship, networking and capital.

Natasha Penzo, CEO of Homekin, which specializes in the home design marketplace, says the Toronto Metropolitan University incubator DMZ provided her with “support, collaboration with other startups” and advice for creative solutions.
But funding to scale her business remains a particular challenge. “I found that (in) any conversations with Canadian venture, they really wanted to focus more on Fintech and health tech.”

Even in those sectors, however, things aren’t easy. Saumik Biswas, co-founder and CEO of Tenomix, a Canadian health tech startup focused on cancer diagnostics through AI and automation for lymph node examinations in biopsy samples, says he also had problems attracting capital.
Biswas said he had to pitch to “205 investors, and we ended up getting 16 of them.” Even that required “a lot of resilience.”
“We ended up raising … just north of $2.1 million Canadian. And it was all Canadian route, which is awesome,” he said.

Even so, there’s often an investment ceiling in Canada. “Once you reach a certain scale, if you’re a tech company, moving to (Silicon) Valley makes a material difference because to get that next round of funding, you need the right people on your board,” says Mark Daley, chief AI officer at Western University in London, Ont.
Buhr, though, notes the fierce competition in Silicon Valley for capital. “What you don’t see is there are 1,000 times as many companies chasing that money.”
Keeping talent in a company matters as well and is as tough for individual companies in the U.S. as it is here, he adds.

“All those great employees that you’re hiring … will last on average 12 to 18 months because there’s always somebody sexier, shinier who’s going to pay you more,” says Buhr. “By coming (to the U.S.) you’re going to trade off problems you know about for problems you don’t know about.”
Among other challenges, ironically, are sometimes the very programs governments in Canada offer to boost innovation and provide more capital.

As of July 2024, the federal government had invested $2.4 billion in AI. And it says it plans to commit $180 billion in defence procurement with a further $290 billion in defence-related capital investment through The Defence Industrial Strategy.

In the emerging fields such as AI, Daley says, placing multiple bets on numerous firms, is “the right approach,” because it “give(s) everyone enough that they have a chance to make it to the next level.”

But MEI research concludes that a higher level of government venture capital can crowd out private venture capital. “If BDC is competing with private providers, the unintended impact can be (that) the private providers of venture capital retrench,” says Lammam.
He also points to the confusion of having multiple support programs at federal, provincial, and municipal levels.

Penzo says she has experienced this with her company. “I’m hiring a consultant to help me with it; these programs and grants take a lot of time out of a founder’s already very busy schedule,” she says.
“I often hear some people don’t even end up going for them because they’re just so time-consuming.”
Still, Daley argues, Canada has had real successes. “We still have lots of great startup companies; we have Cohere (Canadian AI firm).”
However, for Buhr, the issue is that “you get a Shopify or a Cohere every 10 years. We need those every month.”

The biggest — and hardest to avoid — factor is Canada’s proximity to the US, both a blessing and a curse, experts say. “The money is concentrated geographically,” like the people who control it, says Daley.

Matt Bazely, the Entrepreneurship Department Director at Huron University College in Ontario, believes that the problem of entrepreneurs leaving the country as soon as their business gets to a certain size is “a very specific Canadian phenomenon.”
“It’s much easier to move offices and business operations into the States from Canada than, let’s say, from Australia or New Zealand.”
To stay in Canada, there would have to be Canadian customers. But caution about the unknown has always been “part of the natural DNA” here in Canada, Buhr says.

“You can talk to a lot of companies that say their first customers were not in Canada,” says John MacRitchie, president of the Canadian Council for Small Business and Entrepreneurship and co-founder of incubator Lab2Market, noting that it makes a profound impact on international credibility “if you don’t have those (customer) references back in your home country.”

Debow recalls that some of the businesses he has run relied substantially on foreign customers. “In the case of Rypple (which was a social media monitoring platform) … virtually every customer came from the United States for a very long time,” he says.

“What will typically happen is if that U.S. customer becomes the first customer; those companies then start to get dragged more into the U.S. to a certain point that some of them just get acquired by US companies,” Buhr says.
Penzo says expanding to the U.S. “makes most sense for our business model, and the market is so much bigger.”
“Canadians sometimes are a little more hesitant … to use a technology until it’s really gotten off the ground or has that track record of success,” she adds.
With a critical mass of talent and capital, mentoring and support are added advantages for the United States.

“The people that are successful are very good at tapping into the right resources and talking about what they’re doing and getting feedback,” MacRitchie says. In other words, they rely on a like-minded community.
In Silicon Valley “you’re naturally surrounded by people who inspire you,” says Buhr, and who will tell you “how you should get to $150 million or … a billion.”

“Canadian entrepreneurs aren’t surrounded by that,” he says, adding that the lack of mentorships leads many to sell their companies too early and too cheap, because “$50 million is a lot of money,” and there is no one to say “you’ve got a $5 billion company in front of you. You should not even consider that offer.”
Fernando says it’s important to have links to an innovative community post-graduation: “There’s a lot of early-stage help. It’s just from the middle to kind of the end… there’s not as much.”
But it’s not just about taxes, regulation, geography, or the critical mass of entrepreneurial peers and mentors south of the border.
Buhr says that out of 40 early-stage entrepreneurs who came to Silicon Valley for a bootcamp with C100, many expressed doubts about whether their own country needs or wants them.
Sustained criticism in part is what drives people south. “They keep saying how what we’re doing is bad and, you know, technology is not good,” and that is a big discouragement for many, Buhr says.

Meanwhile, “Silicon Valley cares about what we are doing,” so many end up leaving, thinking “I’m a proud Canadian, I want to build Canada, but I just don’t hear that my country wants me there,” he says.
“It has everything to do with this sheer human nature of ‘do you want me to build this thing in Canada or not?’ ”
Some aren’t concerned with these critiques; they plan to build here regardless.

Biswas started his health tech company after losing a close family member to cancer. He was inspired to become an innovator after a surgeon used transformative technology to regrow leg bones for his younger brother, who was born without a tibia. Through the process, Biswas had to translate what the doctor was saying to his Bangladeshi parents. His brother recovered.
So he wants to give back to Canada: “I made a promise to myself that whatever I do in this life, I’d love to give back to this community, through medical innovation.”
Buhr’s convinced “what Canada needs to do is … to celebrate the (entrepreneurial) ecosystem on a national scale.”
Arguably, the federal government has made efforts in this direction — for instance, through innovation hubs and the appointment of a minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation.

Additionally, Carney’s planned Investment Summit this month aims to “catalyse $1 trillion in total investment in Canada over the next five years,” according to a government press release . The federal government wants to do that by investing $280 billion over five years, hoping to attract the rest in foreign investment.
Buhr does not believe this is enough; in the U.S., he says, entrepreneurs are encouraged to just “go build something exciting.”

Daley, though, considers government involvement a cornerstone of a successful innovation policy. “Silicon Valley exists because of policy decisions made by the U.S. government after Wwii,” particularly military investment.

Indeed, “For the people and institutions in the business of researching cutting-edge science and technology, the US government was the original venture capitalist,” Margaret Pugh O’Mara, professor of American History at the University of Washington, once wrote , highlighting that this investment was mostly made between 1939 and late 1960s through military contracts.

“We should be thinking on that time scale,” Daley says, arguing that as AI becomes more prevalent, Silicon Valley’s capital advantage will wane. “Tech companies are cheaper than manufacturing companies, and AI-native tech companies are cheaper still.”

Lammam thinks it would be more valuable “to focus on getting the framework conditions right” — specifically the tax system, which hasn’t been comprehensively reviewed for 60 years. It has become “not only uncompetitive” but is “holding back entrepreneurs,” he says.

Yet Bazely argues the system is not broken; it is “producing exactly what it’s designed to produce,” which is stability. “We do not have the economic downturns that the United States might have, for example,” he says.

For him, the debate revolves around a conscious tradeoff between stability and innovation. Embracing the degree of market freedom involved in U.S. innovation might also mean tolerating such consequences as “people losing their houses,” and “banks failing.”
“The States is a great place to be if you’re successful. It’s an awful place to be if you’re not,” he adds.
For Canada, more and better entrepreneurial education is among Bazely’s suggestions.

Marie-Claire Wasson, a co-founder of Oncolinc Therapeutics, a Halifax biotech startup that focuses on immune therapy cancer treatment, went through Lab2Market training. She says such guidance from a university incubator of this sort is “invaluable.”

Graduate students are perfect targets for such training “because they’re motivated by the work that they’re doing in the research” and “they need a path forward that’s not necessarily in the academic range,” says MacRitchie.
Incubators in post-secondary institutions can play “a wider role in introducing entrepreneurship, providing a real training environment and potentially supporting commercialization,” he notes.

Debow is unsure that entrepreneurship is “purely a set of skills that you learn,” in a classroom, comparing it to a demanding sport. “I could take a class on triathlon. But you have to go run a triathlon… before you actually know what it is to be a triathlete.”

Another piece is risk reduction. “You don’t have the pension, (and) you don’t have the benefits,” says Bazely. Even creating the arrangements for entrepreneurs to be enrolled in the CPP could go a long way, Bazely suggests.
Next-generation entrepreneurs do see hope in the Canadian landscape.
“We’re very proud to be Canadian,” says Biswas, adding that it is his heartfelt hope to launch commercially in Canada and keep his company rooted in the country as it expands to global markets.
Wasson says innovators’ successes can inspire future innovators: “If I see other people do it … we can do it too.”

“There just need to be a way where we can maintain Canadian ownership, hiring more Canadian talent, and advancing an economy in a way of solving global problems.” Biswas says, adding that he believes this is what “generates billion-dollar ideas.”
In other words, says Daley, “Canada’s moment is right now.”

Debow recalls that some of the businesses he has run relied substantially on foreign customers. “In the case of Rypple (which was a social media monitoring platform) … virtually every customer came from the United States for a very long time,” he says.
content_blocks.html: Debow recalls that some of the businesses he has run relied substantially on foreign customers. “In the case of Rypple (which was a social media monitoring platform) … virtually every customer came from the United States for a very long time,” he says.

content_blocks.text: “What will typically happen is if that U.S. customer becomes the first customer; those companies then start to get dragged more into the U.S. to a certain point that some of them just get acquired by US companies,” Buhr says.
Penzo says expanding to the U.S. “makes most sense for our business model, and the market is so much bigger.”
“Canadians sometimes are a little more hesitant … to use a technology until it’s really gotten off the ground or has that track record of success,” she adds.
The community matters too
With a critical mass of talent and capital, mentoring and support are added advantages for the United States.

“The people that are successful are very good at tapping into the right resources and talking about what they’re doing and getting feedback,” MacRitchie says. In other words, they rely on a like-minded community.
In Silicon Valley “you’re naturally surrounded by people who inspire you,” says Buhr, and who will tell you “how you should get to $150 million or … a billion.”

“Canadian entrepreneurs aren’t surrounded by that,” he says, adding that the lack of mentorships leads many to sell their companies too early and too cheap, because “$50 million is a lot of money,” and there is no one to say “you’ve got a $5 billion company in front of you. You should not even consider that offer.”
Fernando says it’s important to have links to an innovative community post-graduation: “There’s a lot of early-stage help. It’s just from the middle to kind of the end… there’s not as much.”
But it’s not just about taxes, regulation, geography, or the critical mass of entrepreneurial peers and mentors south of the border.

content_blocks.text: Buhr says that out of 40 early-stage entrepreneurs who came to Silicon Valley for a bootcamp with C100, many expressed doubts about whether their own country needs or wants them.

content_blocks.text: Sustained criticism in part is what drives people south. “They keep saying how what we’re doing is bad and, you know, technology is not good,” and that is a big discouragement for many, Buhr says.

Meanwhile, “Silicon Valley cares about what we are doing,” so many end up leaving, thinking “I’m a proud Canadian, I want to build Canada, but I just don’t hear that my country wants me there,” he says.
“It has everything to do with this sheer human nature of ‘do you want me to build this thing in Canada or not?’ ”
Some aren’t concerned with these critiques; they plan to build here regardless.

Biswas started his health tech company after losing a close family member to cancer. He was inspired to become an innovator after a surgeon used transformative technology to regrow leg bones for his younger brother, who was born without a tibia. Through the process, Biswas had to translate what the doctor was saying to his Bangladeshi parents. His brother recovered.

Through the process, Biswas had to translate what the doctor was saying to his Bangladeshi parents. His brother recovered.

content_blocks.text: So he wants to give back to Canada: “I made a promise to myself that whatever I do in this life, I’d love to give back to this community, through medical innovation.”

content_blocks.text: Maybe a better attitude?
Buhr’s convinced “what Canada needs to do is … to celebrate the (entrepreneurial) ecosystem on a national scale.”
Arguably, the federal government has made efforts in this direction — for instance, through innovation hubs and the appointment of a minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation.
content_blocks.html: Arguably, the federal government has made efforts in this direction — for instance, through innovation hubs and the appointment of a minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation.

content_blocks.text: Additionally, Carney’s planned Investment Summit this month aims to “catalyse $1 trillion in total investment in Canada over the next five years,” according to a government press release . The federal government wants to do that by investing $280 billion over five years, hoping to attract the rest in foreign investment.
content_blocks.html: Additionally, Carney’s planned Investment Summit  this month aims to “catalyse $1 trillion in total investment in Canada over the next five years,” according to a government press release. The federal government wants to do that by investing $280 billion over five years, hoping to attract the rest in foreign investment.

content_blocks.text: Buhr does not believe this is enough; in the U.S., he says, entrepreneurs are encouraged to just “go build something exciting.”

Daley, though, considers government involvement a cornerstone of a successful innovation policy. “Silicon Valley exists because of policy decisions made by the U.S. government after Wwii,” particularly military investment.

Indeed, “For the people and institutions in the business of researching cutting-edge science and technology, the US government was the original venture capitalist,” Margaret Pugh O’Mara, professor of American History at the University of Washington, once wrote , highlighting that this investment was mostly made between 1939 and late 1960s through military contracts.
content_blocks.html: Indeed, “For the people and institutions in the business of researching cutting-edge science and technology, the US government was the original venture capitalist,” Margaret Pugh O’Mara, professor of American History at the University of Washington, once wrote, highlighting that this investment was mostly made between 1939 and late 1960s through military contracts.

content_blocks.text: “We should be thinking on that time scale,” Daley says, arguing that as AI becomes more prevalent, Silicon Valley’s capital advantage will wane. “Tech companies are cheaper than manufacturing companies, and AI-native tech companies are cheaper still.”

Lammam thinks it would be more valuable “to focus on getting the framework conditions right” — specifically the tax system, which hasn’t been comprehensively reviewed for 60 years. It has become “not only uncompetitive” but is “holding back entrepreneurs,” he says.
content_blocks.html: Lammam thinks it would be more valuable “to focus on getting the framework conditions right” — specifically the tax system, which hasn’t been comprehensively reviewed for 60 years. It has become “not only uncompetitive” but is “holding back entrepreneurs,” he says.

content_blocks.text: Yet Bazely argues the system is not broken; it is “producing exactly what it’s designed to produce,” which is stability. “We do not have the economic downturns that the United States might have, for example,” he says.

For him, the debate revolves around a conscious tradeoff between stability and innovation. Embracing the degree of market freedom involved in U.S. innovation might also mean tolerating such consequences as “people losing their houses,” and “banks failing.”

content_blocks.text: “The States is a great place to be if you’re successful. It’s an awful place to be if you’re not,” he adds.
For Canada, more and better entrepreneurial education is among Bazely’s suggestions.

Marie-Claire Wasson, a co-founder of Oncolinc Therapeutics, a Halifax biotech startup that focuses on immune therapy cancer treatment, went through Lab2Market training. She says such guidance from a university incubator of this sort is “invaluable.”

Graduate students are perfect targets for such training “because they’re motivated by the work that they’re doing in the research” and “they need a path forward that’s not necessarily in the academic range,” says MacRitchie.
content_blocks.html: Graduate students are perfect targets for such training “because they’re motivated by the work that they’re doing in the research” and “they need a path forward that’s not necessarily in the academic range,” says MacRitchie.

content_blocks.text: Incubators in post-secondary institutions can play “a wider role in introducing entrepreneurship, providing a real training environment and potentially supporting commercialization,” he notes.

Debow is unsure that entrepreneurship is “purely a set of skills that you learn,” in a classroom, comparing it to a demanding sport. “I could take a class on triathlon. But you have to go run a triathlon… before you actually know what it is to be a triathlete.”

Another piece is risk reduction. “You don’t have the pension, (and) you don’t have the benefits,” says Bazely. Even creating the arrangements for entrepreneurs to be enrolled in the CPP could go a long way, Bazely suggests.
Next-generation entrepreneurs do see hope in the Canadian landscape.
“We’re very proud to be Canadian,” says Biswas, adding that it is his heartfelt hope to launch commercially in Canada and keep his company rooted in the country as it expands to global markets.
Wasson says innovators’ successes can inspire future innovators: “If I see other people do it … we can do it too.”

“There just need to be a way where we can maintain Canadian ownership, hiring more Canadian talent, and advancing an economy in a way of solving global problems.” Biswas says, adding that he believes this is what “generates billion-dollar ideas.”
In other words, says Daley, “Canada’s moment is right now.”
