And while there isn’t necessarily a straight line between the number of applications a program receives and the number of students it admits, about 2,500 fewer students have accepted offers to start undergraduate computer science degrees in Ontario this fall compared to two years ago.
“This is true all over the world,” said Mark Daley, the chief AI officer at Western University in London.

Government funding and university priorities factor into the number of students admitted to computer science, and emerging specializations in AI are becoming more popular. But computer science leaders at universities in other provinces are seeing the same overall drop in applications. This suggests Ontario’s figures aren’t an outlier.

Teenagers raised in the just-learn-to-code era worry that AI can already do much of a junior software engineer’s job, and they’re not sure that making “artisanal bespoke human code, like it’s the sourdough bread from the local bakery, is going to be a great job market,” Prof. Daley said.

Waning interest in computer science degrees is to be expected. Big Tech stalwarts such as Meta, Google, Shopify, Oracle, Amazon and others have laid off tens of thousands of workers in recent years. The internet is awash in stories of young tech workers struggling in a brutal job market. And it’s not the first time a broad technological shift has caused students to feel skittish.

In another sense, it’s a surprise. Artificial intelligence threatens jobs of all kinds. But it was born of computer science, and leaders in the field say students will still be the vanguard; programs are tailoring their offerings as such. Surely young people who understand how generative AI works and know how to build with it have the best shot at a safe future?

Either way, trends in computer science education underscore a dilemma facing many teenagers and twentysomethings, regardless of what they want to be when they grow up. AI is improving so fast that no students know what awaits them on the other side of a degree.

“We don’t know what the labour market is going to look like five or 10 years from now,” said Prof. Daley, who was also vice-chair of the Council of Ontario Universities’ AI Task Force . “I don’t think there’s going to be a complete apocalypse of jobs and there’ll be nothing for humans to do. But I think the nature of what we do is going to change.”

Richard Zhao is acting co-head of computer science at the University of Calgary. Students entering the program used to graduate high school with averages in the high 80s. That’s fallen to an average of 79.6 this fall as fewer students apply to computer science. Todd Korol/The Globe and Mail

Luigi Benedicenti, a professor and dean in the Faculty of Computer Science at the University of New Brunswick, used to be greeted by big groups of students and their eager parents when he spoke at high-school recruitment fairs or university orientation events a few years ago.

Computer science – where students typically studied coding, computer architecture, advanced algorithms and computational theory, among other subjects – was a hot program. His audience viewed it as a ticket to the good life.

That began to change recently, Prof. Benedicenti said. Although UNB, like many Canadian universities, does not disclose application figures for individual programs, the dean said applications plunged two years ago. That’s when computer science suffered the one-two punch of federal restrictions on international student visas and a growing public recognition of AI’s coding prowess, he explained.

“Before we had a room full of parents when we were working on orientation,” Prof. Benedicenti said. “Last year, we had far fewer parents than we would have liked, and that is because, in my opinion, there is this perception that artificial intelligence is, if not a present, then a future danger to the career of young computer scientists.”

While some university officials, particularly outside Ontario, agree with Prof. Benedicenti that Ottawa’s curbing of international student visas contributed to the decline, federal policy changes don’t seem to be the driving factor behind fewer students applying to university computer programs in Canada’s most populous province.

Ouac reports separately on applications from students coming straight out of an Ontario high school and all other applicants, a category that includes international, out-of-province and mature students. Applications to computer programs fell similarly for both streams between 2023 and 2026.
Fewer applications don’t necessarily translate to fewer students majoring in computer science.
Take the University of Calgary, where the number of applications to computer science peaked for entry in the fall of 2023, and has dropped since, a university spokesman said by e-mail.

Despite the decline, registration in computer science was up to 1,745 students last fall from 1,483 three years earlier. That’s partly because the Alberta government funded an expansion of high-demand programs, including computer science, colleges and universities beginning in the fall of 2022.

At the University of Alberta, registrations rose 32.7 per cent between the autumns of 2020 and 2025 across computer-science related programs at the graduate and undergraduate level, a school spokesman said.
In other words, regardless of softening demand, there are still enough students interested in computer science to fill the seats – even in a province that recently increased the supply.
They might just be able to get in with lower marks.

Richard Zhao, the acting co-head of computer science at the University of Calgary, said the average student starting his program this fall graduated high school with a 79.6 average, down from the high 80s at the peak of computer science’s popularity a couple of years ago.
“We are aware of students coming with slightly lower averages, and we’ve essentially adapted our curriculum to account for them,” he said. “We provide more support.”

There are upsides to some Canadian computer science programs being less selective. It opens the door to talented young people who love the logical problem-solving that defines the work, but who couldn’t at age 17 or 18 pull off the A+ marks to earn a spot.

“If you’re getting fewer applications and you’re accepting the same number of students, then the quality is probably going to go down a bit,” said Joanne Atlee, a computer science professor at the University of Waterloo. “I think it’s also true that a lot of the students who might have applied and are choosing not to probably had less of a passion for the field.”
Still, getting into computer science programs remains a cutthroat game at the country’s most prestigious schools.

Dina Dawoud, the associate dean of undergraduate admissions and outreach at the University of Waterloo, said the school continues to receive 12 applications for every computer science student it admits.

Spokespeople for McGill University and the University of Toronto, where undergraduate computer science enrolments have been stable over the past couple of years, also say their applicant pools remain strong.

Eyal de Lara, chair of the Department of Computer Science at U of T, said the department froze undergraduate enrolment about a decade ago because it had already grown “quite large” for a selective program. Applications skyrocketed nonetheless until the volume started to taper off two years ago, he added.
“We had, effectively, an enormous applicant pool,” Prof. de Lara said. “Some students realize it’s going to be impossible to get to U of T and apply to other universities.”

That’s another possible explanation for the drop in applications. As top Canadian computer science programs developed reputations for turning away academic superstars with intimidating resumes, some high-school seniors might have considered applying futile – or simply not worth it if the degree no longer guaranteed a six-figure salary straight out of school.

The reputed competitiveness of computer science played a part in 17-year-old Ella Poku’s decision to pursue a degree in physics instead. She started first-year classes in the discipline at U of T last week.
Although Ms. Poku had marks in the low 90s, coding experience, and two older brothers studying computer science at McMaster University, she feared she wouldn’t get into computer science.

She and her family had recently moved from Ghana to Ancaster, Ont., near Hamilton. “I only moved to Canada in 2023. I didn’t have as many extracurriculars or connections as other people, so that was, like, a big factor for me since I wasn’t too sure about if I would get in or not,” she said. “And if I didn’t, it would be a big problem.”

The job market for computer science graduates worried her, too, and led her to conclude she’d be better off with a more general hard science degree. “I still wasn’t too sure about going to computer science because I’m not the type of person who wants to always be nervous about my job or my stability.”

Are students like Ms. Poku right to be worried? There’s a fierce debate about whether, in the long run, artificial intelligence, which can already write and debug basic code, will steal jobs from computer scientists or create lucrative new opportunities for them.

In the short run, Statistics Canada reported last January that between the launch of ChatGPT in November, 2022, and December of 2025, coding-intensive jobs such as software engineering and web design grew at the same rate as other jobs. But the gains were concentrated among Canadian coding professionals aged 30 to 49; job opportunities stagnated for their counterparts under 30.

In the U.S., a trio of economists at Stanford University mined payroll data to report a widening employment gap between young workers in AI-exposed professions, such as software engineering, customer service, accounting and secretarial work, and their peers in less-exposed industries. As of last month, they pegged the gap for U.S. workers aged 22-25 at 19 per cent. There wasn’t a comparable gap for older workers.
Leo Tenenbaum, 22, found the Canadian tech job market much tougher to crack than expected when they were applying to computer science programs in the fall of 2020.

Although they graduated from the University of Toronto in June, 2025, with a first-place win in an undergraduate student research contest under their belt, their resumes and cover letters went unanswered for months. They applied for about 50 jobs online before a friend of a friend opened the door at Mozilla, where Tenenbaum started as a software engineer in February.
“It was very discouraging at that time,” Tenenbaum said. “I was feeling like I’d never get anywhere.”

If job hunting is harder for new computer science grads today than it was a few years ago, all the blame shouldn’t be pinned on AI, said Tracy Camp, the executive director and CEO of the Computing Research Association, a U.S. non-profit made up of academic computer science departments, industry and government.
Some high-profile tech companies over-hired during the pandemic, then made AI a scapegoat for layoffs, she argued.

Still, Prof. Camp conceded that computer science undergraduates can no longer expect multiple six-figure job offers before they don a cap and gown. “So then the narrative is, ‘all the jobs are gone.’ But no, that’s not true at all. It just is a little bit more difficult to find a job, which is similar to how other students have been struggling for decades.”

In the U.S., enrolment in computer and information science programs as of this spring fell by 8.4 per cent at four-year institutions and 11.2 per cent at two-year colleges compared to spring of 2025, according to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center. The drop followed nearly two decades of growth.

The Computing Research Association, which conducts regular surveys of university computer science departments in the U.S. and Canada, says the topline enrolment figures obscure rising interest in some subdisciplines of computer science. Software engineering and information systems are down, but data science, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence are up.
“That tells us that students are shifting their interest to more specialized disciplines,” said Kari George, a senior research associate at the association.

Indeed, postsecondary institutions north and south of the border are rushing to add AI courses earlier in their computer science curriculum, and to launch concentrations or degrees with artificial intelligence right in the name, according to Northeastern University’s Center for Inclusive Computing. It just added Canada to its map of AI programs in computer science at universities.
Applications could rebound as computer science departments rebrand their offerings for the AI era. If history is any guide, a rebound is inevitable, according to Prof. de Lara of U of T.

Applications and enrolments dropped in the early 1980s and again in the early 2000s, when personal computers and the early internet’s dot-com crash scared students into believing there would be fewer jobs for computer scientists. Both technologies created many more jobs for computer scientists than they killed.

“If you’re in any other degree, innovations in AI are happening to you,” Prof. de Lara said. “If you’re in computer science, you’re actually among the people driving the revolution. You’re an active agent making this new reality happen.”

stories.title: Is Carney a closer? The Canada Investment Summit will be the ultimate test
stories.summary: The PM and top Canadian CEOs plan to pitch the country’s untapped potential to global investors. Will that be enough to secure billions of dollars in new deals?
stories.author: James Bradshaw, Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to bring the world’s most powerful investors to Toronto next week was always a gambit to ease the economic pressure from the Trump administration’s trade crusade by pitching Canada as an alternative, more reliable place to put money to work.

What event planners could not have predicted is the way a feud over tariffs would boil over into a full-blown trade war just days before those money managers are set to touch down, and the intense spotlight it is shining on Canada – for better and for worse.

It is Mr. Carney’s reputation and relationships, backed by a co-ordinated push from some of Canada’s most influential chief executives, that have convinced the masters of the world’s deepest pools of capital to gather for two days at the Canada Investment Summit , at a scale never seen before on Canadian soil.

The event Monday and Tuesday will mark the biggest test yet of a project to reframe the way global investors see Canada. The pitch is that the country has an increasingly competitive business environment, a pipeline of investable major projects and middle-market deals and deserves investors’ attention not just as the junior part of a North American market, but on its own terms.

It’s one thing to get CEOs to attend a summit. It’s another for Mr. Carney and Canadian corporate leaders to convince them to invest huge amounts of capital.

“It’s a choice opportunity, when you’re getting this type of a group together, to hear directly from the people at the helm about what’s happening and what’s going to change,” David Layton, CEO of US$186-billion Swiss asset manager Partners Group AG and a summit guest, said in an interview.

“You have a lot of businesspeople coming and they want to talk business. They want to understand what the business environment is going to be like there, so it’s an opportunity to set those expectations.”

The potential trade fallout is sure to loom large. Mr. Carney and business leaders will urge global investors to look past the trade war and focus on the country’s long-term prospects, citing the White House’s scattershot tariff strategy as proof that there is merit in building other, more stable alliances.

But investors crave certainty before they commit dollars to a project or a business. “It’s not something that you look through. I think it’s something you need to understand,” Mr. Layton said.

The Globe and Mail spoke to more than two dozen sources from the financial sector and government, including summit attendees and organizers, and is not identifying those who are not authorized to discuss the event publicly. They expressed excitement about the flurry of activity and attention that is coming, and cautious optimism that Canada will meet the moment. It’s clear Mr. Carney has captured investors’ interest. Will that be enough to close billions of dollars in new deals?

Canada will need to back up its message that it’s open to investment by showing there is an investable pipeline of deals available – and, crucially, that it can get agreements signed and projects off the ground without delays, several sources said.

Federal, provincial and territorial political leaders will need to demonstrate that they are removing friction points such as interprovincial trade barriers, redundant permitting processes and onerous regulations. Federal cabinet ministers directly responsible for those files are expected to attend, such as Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and Dominic LeBlanc, who also leads the Canada-U.S. trade file. Most premiers are expected as well.

Investors also look for a competitive tax regime, but a senior government source said it is unlikely any changes to tax policy would be revealed before the next federal budget is set to be released later this fall.

The federal government is taking steps to reduce duplication in the approval process for several types of large energy projects, including through new legislation expected this fall.

Policymakers also need to give investors confidence that the rules in Canada won’t change suddenly. Choosing former prime minister Stephen Harper, a Conservative politician who chairs the board of the Alberta Investment Management Corp. pension fund, to be the summit’s last speaker is intended to signal that the course Canada is on will be lasting, not partisan, two sources said.

Some investors, including massive sovereign wealth funds in the Middle East, are keen to put money to work quickly and want to see full-fledged projects that are ready for an investment decision, two other sources said.

A 66-page prospectus pitching more than 160 potential projects that summit organizers circulated to the event’s guests this week describes only 15 investment opportunities as “shovel-ready” or “fully permitted.” They include the US$28.5-billion Ksi Lisims floating liquefied natural gas export terminal in northern British Columbia.

But other projects in the catalogue don’t look quite so ready to investors, one source said, lacking the contractual details they need to assess risk and potential returns.

Though Mr. Carney, pension fund CEOs and industry leaders have used their credibility to pique investor interest in Canada, it will likely be months before it is clear whether that leads to action.

“Investment can beget more investment,” Toronto-Dominion Bank chief economist Beata Caranci and deputy chief economist Derek Burleton wrote in an August research report. “If Canada executes well on major projects over the coming years, it will boost confidence in the private sector to undertake new projects without as much support from the public purse, driving a self-reinforcing feedback loop.”

The report suggests Canada could unlock “an investment supercycle” underpinned by $1-trillion of early-stage and proposed spending on projects through 2035, by increasing competitiveness on taxes and regulations, scaling high-growth companies and expanding a skilled workforce. The bank’s most optimistic scenario envisions $1.5-trillion to $1.7-trillion in investment over the next decade.

Behind the scenes, the summit’s organizers have managed expectations, describing the event as a starting point. Two sources said the summit could be repeated, possibly as soon as next year. Attendees expect some deals, investment commitments or policy promises could be announced, but not many.

Rather, the summit’s core goal is to make Canada a distinctive part of investors’ strategies going forward. Global investors have historically approached North America as a single region, steering the lion’s share of capital to the U.S. with little deliberate thought for Canada.

“If the chief investment officer doesn’t have a perspective on what role Canada can play, and what role the Canadian opportunity set can contribute to his or her broader strategic objectives, then no deal team is going to roll in with an actionable idea,” Northleaf Capital Partners Ltd. managing partner Stuart Waugh, who is speaking at the summit, said in an interview.

After the summit, influential global executives need to “walk away saying, ‘I need to get a team engaged on this because this actually will be accretive to what I’m doing,’” he said.

What CIOs and deal teams want to see to move forward are concrete contractual terms such as supply and offtake agreements, where a buyer agrees to specific purchases in advance, sources said. Those fine details May not come up at the summit, but they will be important in follow-up meetings to help investors assess expected risks and returns.

There is no doubt that global investors’ curiosity about Canada is at its highest level in recent memory.

Summit organizers have fielded a wave of requests to get in, and a source familiar with the planning said the guest list has expanded from about 100 initial invitations sent on the Prime Minister’s letterhead to include roughly 300 attendees.

Plenty of senior financial executives have had requests for a ticket turned down. And dozens of dinners, receptions, lunches and other side events have sprung up in downtown Toronto next week to meet huge demand to be near the action.

After the latest Canada-U.S. tariff drama, summit organizers and some CEOs have quietly wondered whether some U.S. CEOs or companies might drop out to avoid drawing unwanted attention from the White House. So far, the biggest names appear to be committed.

Multiple sources said current uncertainty around Canada-U.S. trade could be a double-edged sword. In the near term, it will make it harder for investors to know what to expect, at the summit and afterward.

“I do think it’ll have some sway with regards to how investment decisions actually get made, if there’s clarity around that or not in the coming quarters,” Mr. Layton said. “Being able to avoid surprises is as important to an investor as just about anything.”

Mr. Carney was asked ahead of a cabinet meeting in Banff, Alta., ON Thursday what his pitch was to investors at a time of Canada-U.S. tensions. He said Canada has far more to offer than being next to the U.S., citing the country’s natural resources, skilled workforce and respect for the rule of law, among other attributes.

“That combination is pretty rare in the world, and it’s an attractive combination,” Mr. Carney said.

At the same time, many investors are reassessing their desire to make new investments in the United States, relative to other markets.

“People are definitely taking a harder look, not to say, ‘we’re not going to invest in the U.S.,’ but to say, ‘Do I need a different risk-return profile or a different premium than I might have a decade ago?’” Mr. Waugh said.

With the summit’s attendees managing roughly $120-trillion in assets, if some of them invested even an additional 1 or 2 percentage points of their portfolios in Canada, it could deliver a massive boost to the country’s foreign investment.

“We need, at the margin, to be considered on our own merits,” Mr. Waugh said. “We don’t need a fundamental shift in people’s capital allocations to really move the needle.”

The timing of a recent leadership overhaul at Invest in Canada is no accident. Ottawa installed Dominic Barton as chair and hired private equity executive Gurinder Grewal as CEO, giving the agency charged with attracting foreign investment a more ambitious mandate that starts in earnest at the summit next week, two sources said.

Mr. Barton is chair of mining company Rio Tinto Group and a former consultant and ambassador to China who has close ties to the previous Trudeau government, and his appointment exposes Mr. Carney to opposition attacks that he is rewarding Liberal insiders and wealthy friends. Activist groups are also expected to protest against the summit, suggesting that Canada’s prized resources are being put up for sale, with the proceeds flowing increasingly to foreign coffers.

That will turn the summit into a moment to benchmark the Carney government’s political promise to Canadians when it came into office last year: that a rebooted Liberal machine would equally reboot the Canadian economy and that doing so through waves of new private investment would benefit all Canadians, not just those in certain sectors or tax brackets.

The event’s core themes of energy, critical minerals, defence and advanced technologies are intended to echo the sectors where there is most demand for investment capital, and where some global investors already have a track record of deals in Canada.

For example, Partners Group has an established presence with Canadian clients, offices in Toronto and Montreal , partnerships with large Canadian banks and a track record of deals with major pension funds. With the company’s roots in Switzerland - a multilingual, export-oriented economy that has prospered in tandem with larger European neighbours - Mr. Layton said there is “obvious resonance” in Canada’s message urging middle powers to forge more diverse relationships.

“I always felt like we could find more investment opportunities [in Canada] and so this could be a catalyst for that,” he said.

A key challenge for Ottawa is to get global investors to widen the lens of what they consider investable, sources said. That would mean looking beyond buying existing assets and companies in Canada, which are seen as less risky, to consider investing in greenfield infrastructure projects. Those could include new pipelines or expanded ports, energy and transmission assets, or new mining ventures.

Projects starting from scratch are more prone to run into delays or go over-budget, and major pension funds in Canada have been hesitant to invest in them. To make them more enticing to global capital, the government is likely to highlight existing federal financing tools designed to reduce risk, such as the Canada Infrastructure Bank and the Canada Growth Fund.

The summit prospectus mostly consists of energy projects - in oil and gas, as well as clean technologies such as wind and solar - and mining ventures for minerals and metals.

Some are still in early stages. The prospectus lists several projects for which final investment decisions are pending or expected as late as 2028 or 2029. A greenfield on- and offshore wind platform linking Atlantic Canada to Quebec, proposed by Novatron Energy at a cost of US$36-billion, is still in development. So are a pair of multi-billion-dollar data-centre projects seeking financing in Saint John, N.B., and Redcliff, Alta.

Some global investors are also eagerly awaiting specifics about how Ottawa might open up federal assets such as airports to private investments.

There is growing awareness that many of Canada’s investment opportunities are not major projects, but rather middle-market deals with smaller ticket sizes. The prospectus contains nearly 30 projects needing US$200-million or less in capital expenditures and some as small as US$25-million.

Canadian private equity and infrastructure funds and mid-sized asset managers will be lining up to present themselves as potential partners for global investors, offering exposure to companies that are too small and numerous for the largest asset managers to assess on their own. Some of those deals can close much faster than major projects.

“Large-scale opportunities are relatively few, and they’re long-dated. So how do you access the very attractive opportunity set that resides in the mid-market? That’s a solvable challenge,” Mr. Waugh said.

Mr. Carney’s previous career in business suggests he knows what it takes to get investors to commit capital. As head of transition investing at Brookfield Asset Management Ltd., he was instrumental in raising billions of dollars for climate transition funds from investors on Wall Street, in the Middle East and in Canada.

Still, landing even larger cheques to finance rapidly changing industries in the midst of a trade war with the country’s dominant economic partner is a more daunting task. And much as his government will be judged for the measurable outcomes of the summit, putting heavy hitters in front of each other for 48 hours in Toronto can only serve as a starting point.

“The government does need to continue the positive momentum. They need to put some points on the board in terms of some of the very worthwhile initiatives they’ve announced and the things that they’ve started to do,” Mr. Waugh said.

But Canada’s leading companies know that “it’s on us to then move that along the investment process.”

With Canada’s countertariffs coming into effect on roughly $28-billion worth of U.S. goods, the trade war between Canada and the U.S. is heating up. Tim Shufelt , the Globe’s investment reporter, joins the show to talk about whether Carney’s bet on foreign investment is working, which sectors are seeing an increase in investments and what this says about the resilience of Canada’s economy.

“If the chief investment officer doesn’t have a perspective on what role Canada can play, and what role the Canadian opportunity set can contribute to his or her broader strategic objectives, then no deal team is going to roll in with an actionable idea,” Northleaf Capital Partners Ltd. managing partner Stuart Waugh, who is speaking at the summit, said in an interview.
After the summit, influential global executives need to “walk away saying, ‘I need to get a team engaged on this because this actually will be accretive to what I’m doing,’” he said.

What CIOs and deal teams want to see to move forward are concrete contractual terms such as supply and offtake agreements, where a buyer agrees to specific purchases in advance, sources said. Those fine details May not come up at the summit, but they will be important in follow-up meetings to help investors assess expected risks and returns.
There is no doubt that global investors’ curiosity about Canada is at its highest level in recent memory.

Summit organizers have fielded a wave of requests to get in, and a source familiar with the planning said the guest list has expanded from about 100 initial invitations sent on the Prime Minister’s letterhead to include roughly 300 attendees.

Plenty of senior financial executives have had requests for a ticket turned down. And dozens of dinners, receptions, lunches and other side events have sprung up in downtown Toronto next week to meet huge demand to be near the action.

After the latest Canada-U.S. tariff drama, summit organizers and some CEOs have quietly wondered whether some U.S. CEOs or companies might drop out to avoid drawing unwanted attention from the White House. So far, the biggest names appear to be committed.

Multiple sources said current uncertainty around Canada-U.S. trade could be a double-edged sword. In the near term, it will make it harder for investors to know what to expect, at the summit and afterward.

“I do think it’ll have some sway with regards to how investment decisions actually get made, if there’s clarity around that or not in the coming quarters,” Mr. Layton said. “Being able to avoid surprises is as important to an investor as just about anything.”

Mr. Carney was asked ahead of a cabinet meeting in Banff, Alta., ON Thursday what his pitch was to investors at a time of Canada-U.S. tensions. He said Canada has far more to offer than being next to the U.S., citing the country’s natural resources, skilled workforce and respect for the rule of law, among other attributes.
“That combination is pretty rare in the world, and it’s an attractive combination,” Mr. Carney said.
At the same time, many investors are reassessing their desire to make new investments in the United States, relative to other markets.

“People are definitely taking a harder look, not to say, ‘we’re not going to invest in the U.S.,’ but to say, ‘Do I need a different risk-return profile or a different premium than I might have a decade ago?’” Mr. Waugh said.

With the summit’s attendees managing roughly $120-trillion in assets, if some of them invested even an additional 1 or 2 percentage points of their portfolios in Canada, it could deliver a massive boost to the country’s foreign investment.
“We need, at the margin, to be considered on our own merits,” Mr. Waugh said. “We don’t need a fundamental shift in people’s capital allocations to really move the needle.”

The timing of a recent leadership overhaul at Invest in Canada is no accident. Ottawa installed Dominic Barton as chair and hired private equity executive Gurinder Grewal as CEO, giving the agency charged with attracting foreign investment a more ambitious mandate that starts in earnest at the summit next week, two sources said.

Mr. Barton is chair of mining company Rio Tinto Group and a former consultant and ambassador to China who has close ties to the previous Trudeau government, and his appointment exposes Mr. Carney to opposition attacks that he is rewarding Liberal insiders and wealthy friends. Activist groups are also expected to protest against the summit, suggesting that Canada’s prized resources are being put up for sale, with the proceeds flowing increasingly to foreign coffers.

That will turn the summit into a moment to benchmark the Carney government’s political promise to Canadians when it came into office last year: that a rebooted Liberal machine would equally reboot the Canadian economy and that doing so through waves of new private investment would benefit all Canadians, not just those in certain sectors or tax brackets.

The event’s core themes of energy, critical minerals, defence and advanced technologies are intended to echo the sectors where there is most demand for investment capital, and where some global investors already have a track record of deals in Canada.

For example, Partners Group has an established presence with Canadian clients, offices in Toronto and Montreal , partnerships with large Canadian banks and a track record of deals with major pension funds. With the company’s roots in Switzerland - a multilingual, export-oriented economy that has prospered in tandem with larger European neighbours - Mr. Layton said there is “obvious resonance” in Canada’s message urging middle powers to forge more diverse relationships.
“I always felt like we could find more investment opportunities [in Canada] and so this could be a catalyst for that,” he said.

A key challenge for Ottawa is to get global investors to widen the lens of what they consider investable, sources said. That would mean looking beyond buying existing assets and companies in Canada, which are seen as less risky, to consider investing in greenfield infrastructure projects. Those could include new pipelines or expanded ports, energy and transmission assets, or new mining ventures.

Projects starting from scratch are more prone to run into delays or go over-budget, and major pension funds in Canada have been hesitant to invest in them. To make them more enticing to global capital, the government is likely to highlight existing federal financing tools designed to reduce risk, such as the Canada Infrastructure Bank and the Canada Growth Fund.
The summit prospectus mostly consists of energy projects - in oil and gas, as well as clean technologies such as wind and solar - and mining ventures for minerals and metals.

Some are still in early stages. The prospectus lists several projects for which final investment decisions are pending or expected as late as 2028 or 2029. A greenfield on- and offshore wind platform linking Atlantic Canada to Quebec, proposed by Novatron Energy at a cost of US$36-billion, is still in development. So are a pair of multi-billion-dollar data-centre projects seeking financing in Saint John, N.B., and Redcliff, Alta.
Some global investors are also eagerly awaiting specifics about how Ottawa might open up federal assets such as airports to private investments.

There is growing awareness that many of Canada’s investment opportunities are not major projects, but rather middle-market deals with smaller ticket sizes. The prospectus contains nearly 30 projects needing US$200-million or less in capital expenditures and some as small as US$25-million.

Canadian private equity and infrastructure funds and mid-sized asset managers will be lining up to present themselves as potential partners for global investors, offering exposure to companies that are too small and numerous for the largest asset managers to assess on their own. Some of those deals can close much faster than major projects.

“Large-scale opportunities are relatively few, and they’re long-dated. So how do you access the very attractive opportunity set that resides in the mid-market? That’s a solvable challenge,” Mr. Waugh said.

Mr. Carney’s previous career in business suggests he knows what it takes to get investors to commit capital. As head of transition investing at Brookfield Asset Management Ltd., he was instrumental in raising billions of dollars for climate transition funds from investors on Wall Street, in the Middle East and in Canada.

Still, landing even larger cheques to finance rapidly changing industries in the midst of a trade war with the country’s dominant economic partner is a more daunting task. And much as his government will be judged for the measurable outcomes of the summit, putting heavy hitters in front of each other for 48 hours in Toronto can only serve as a starting point.

“The government does need to continue the positive momentum. They need to put some points on the board in terms of some of the very worthwhile initiatives they’ve announced and the things that they’ve started to do,” Mr. Waugh said.
But Canada’s leading companies know that “it’s on us to then move that along the investment process.”

With Canada’s countertariffs coming into effect on roughly $28-billion worth of U.S. goods, the trade war between Canada and the U.S. is heating up. Tim Shufelt , the Globe’s investment reporter, joins the show to talk about whether Carney’s bet on foreign investment is working, which sectors are seeing an increase in investments and what this says about the resilience of Canada’s economy.

stories.title: ‘The Final Act’ offers an intimate look at death through people who chose Maid
stories.summary: Deraspe aims to share that feeling with a broader audience with her documentary "The Final Act," which is premiering at Tiff on Sunday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press

Posted September 12, 2026 4:01 am.

Last Updated September 12, 2026 7:37 am.

Toronto — After filming 69-year-old Céline Carpentier take her final breaths before a medically assisted death, Sophie Deraspe couldn’t help but notice, in sharp focus, all the life around her.

On the hour-long drive back home, the Montreal filmmaker said mundane scenes seemed to vividly come to life — the light shining, people talking, cars moving, and even the person mowing the lawn.

Her son was the first person she saw when she arrived home. She told him she had just filmed a person dying.

“My experience was so soothing and so, it was so peaceful that I wasn’t afraid of telling him. And the first thing he said: ‘I want to see it.’”

Deraspe showed him the footage and she began to cry.

“I felt emotional. Yes, sad she’s gone. She’s not in this world anymore. But also emotional because it was so beautiful.”

Deraspe aims to share that feeling with a broader audience with her documentary “The Final Act,” which is premiering at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday.

Carpentier’s death is shown in the documentary, along with those of others who chose medically assisted deaths.

Their circumstances vary, but they all said they didn’t want to suffer any longer. She captures the final moments of their lives as they say goodbye to family and impart their last reflective thoughts.

Deraspe wants to be clear – this is not a movie about the political and legal debates that have arisen around Maid in the decade since it was legalized in Canada.

People who are suffering intolerably with a serious and incurable illness or disability are eligible to apply for a medically assisted death. Their death does not have to be reasonably foreseeable, a criteria that was eliminated in 2021, and has been divisive since. Some people say death should not be offered as a solution to suffering, while others want more people who are suffering to have access.

However, Deraspe’s film does not delve into the controversies surrounding the end-of-life procedure, and instead is a philosophical interrogation of the place that death has in society, through the eyes of those who have chosen it and the health providers who assist them.

Her previous French-language feature films and documentaries, such as “Antigone” and “Shepherds,” often explore shared elements of humanity.

“Maid made it possible to have a conversation about death with people who know they are going to die rather soon,” Deraspe said.

She was surprised by how many people wanted her to film their deaths, not just allowing her to be there with her camera, but welcoming her to share how they were feeling right before they died.

“That’s why we came into the world, to share,” a 101-year-old named Paulette Fiset-Germain says in the documentary before receiving Maid.

Deraspe said she tried to make her presence inconspicuous while filming, but sometimes found it impossible to be invisible.

She recalls her heart pounding when she realized she forgot to remove the microphone from Carpentier, who was about to die. She was tucked into bed surrounded by loved ones.

Deraspe did not want to disrupt such an intimate moment, but then Carpentier herself reminded the filmmaker to remove it.

Though Carpentier’s diagnosis is not discussed, she describes not wanting to end life in a steep decline. “It’s a relief to go like this,” she says in the film.

Deraspe’s hands shook as she unclipped the microphone from Carpentier’s bra strap. They hugged goodbye.

“I get emotional when I think about that moment,” Deraspe said.

“I don’t know her much, we had met twice, you know. But what we shared was, well, it was something so real and we were two human beings being real.”

“The Final Act” screens Sunday, Sept. 13 and Tuesday, Sept. 15 at Tiff. It’s set for theatrical release in April.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Student's door-to-door Chinese ballads break down barriers, win fans and lamb chops
stories.summary: When Kieran Michael MacNeill started going door to door in Richmond, B.C., serenading householders in Mandarin, he was worried they might think he was a "weirdo."
stories.author: Nono Shen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
When Kieran Michael MacNeill started going door to door in Richmond, B.C., serenading householders in Mandarin, he was worried they might think he was a “weirdo.”

But instead, they embraced the efforts of the 22-year-old student, who spent summer singing to residents at the urging of Chinese Canadian friends who were “blown away” when he sang a classic Mando-pop tune in a car with them one day.

MacNeill’s renditions of the sentimental 1980s ballad, “A Spray of Plum Blossoms,” videoed by friend Jason Chen, have received millions of views online, drawing fascination for both his singing and the reactions to it.

Some residents join in the song, rich in symbolism about hardship and longing. Others have shared food with MacNeill and Chen.

“When you see a white guy at your door, you don’t expect him to speak Chinese,” said Chen, “Just seeing Michael want to learn Chinese and actually going out there and speaking it, I think it’s super awesome.”

MacNeill, who is studying computer science at Queen’s University in Ontario but is originally from Calgary, learned the song to kill time while on a flight in 2024.

But after mastering the song, it wasn’t until this May when he came to B.C. for a summer job that he got a chance to show off his talent in Richmond, which has the highest proportion of residents of Chinese descent of any municipality in Canada, making up more than half of the city’s population.

He was driving to a restaurant in Richmond with Chen and another friend when MacNeill started singing.

“They are like, you have to sing that to the aunties and uncles in Richmond, and they’re gonna be blown away that you could do that,” laughed MacNeill.

They started their project in June, MacNeill overcoming a sense of awkwardness and “being a weirdo” as the Chinese community warmed to his efforts.

At the first house they tried, the resident was so impressed she gave them dinner.

“She’s like, OK, hold on one second, and then she came out with two plates of lamb chops,” said MacNeill.

“We were just expecting a granola bar probably, not her dinner.”

A performance for an 81-year-old Chinese woman who immigrated to Canada in the 1980s received 1.8 million likes and almost 14 million views on Instagram.

She told MacNeill it was the first time a white person had sung in Chinese to her.

“If I moved to China 44 years ago and I didn’t speak Chinese, and then some random Chinese kid came up to me and sang ‘Sweet Caroline’ to me, that would be a real culture shock for sure,” said MacNeill.

Not everyone has been appreciative. MacNeill said he had visited 300 to 400 homes over the summer, some residents thinking he was a salesman and closing the door in his face.

But MacNeill said he had been overwhelmed with “over the top reactions” from those who enjoyed his performances — which have also included a song for Cantonese speakers, “Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies” by Beyond.

“They kind of go from not really wanting to talk to you or being very shy to then all of a sudden wanting to ask me a million questions,” said MacNeill.

Some guessed that he learned Chinese because he had a Chinese girlfriend, which he doesn’t.

MacNeill said he learned Chinese by using Google Translate and watching YouTube videos, testing out his language skills by ordering food at a Chinese restaurant. His B.C. friends have also mentored him.

But the reactions of Richmond householders to his singing have provided incentive to keep learning.

“The best way to learn a language is to actually be motivated … so when people have these good reactions and they’re always so impressed even if you just know really basic Chinese … that was good motivation to learn the language,” said MacNeill.

paragraphs: When Kieran Michael MacNeill started going door to door in Richmond, B.C., serenading householders in Mandarin, he was worried they might think he was a “weirdo.”

But instead, they embraced the efforts of the 22-year-old student, who spent summer singing to residents at the urging of Chinese Canadian friends who were “blown away” when he sang a classic Mando-pop tune in a car with them one day.

MacNeill’s renditions of the sentimental 1980s ballad, “A Spray of Plum Blossoms,” videoed by friend Jason Chen, have received millions of views online, drawing fascination for both his singing and the reactions to it.
Some residents join in the song, rich in symbolism about hardship and longing. Others have shared food with MacNeill and Chen.

“When you see a white guy at your door, you don’t expect him to speak Chinese,” said Chen, “Just seeing Michael want to learn Chinese and actually going out there and speaking it, I think it’s super awesome.”
MacNeill, who is studying computer science at Queen’s University in Ontario but is originally from Calgary, learned the song to kill time while on a flight in 2024.

But after mastering the song, it wasn’t until this May when he came to B.C. for a summer job that he got a chance to show off his talent in Richmond, which has the highest proportion of residents of Chinese descent of any municipality in Canada, making up more than half of the city’s population.
He was driving to a restaurant in Richmond with Chen and another friend when MacNeill started singing.
“They are like, you have to sing that to the aunties and uncles in Richmond, and they’re gonna be blown away that you could do that,” laughed MacNeill.
They started their project in June, MacNeill overcoming a sense of awkwardness and “being a weirdo” as the Chinese community warmed to his efforts.
At the first house they tried, the resident was so impressed she gave them dinner.
“She’s like, OK, hold on one second, and then she came out with two plates of lamb chops,” said MacNeill.
“We were just expecting a granola bar probably, not her dinner.”
A performance for an 81-year-old Chinese woman who immigrated to Canada in the 1980s received 1.8 million likes and almost 14 million views on Instagram.
She told MacNeill it was the first time a white person had sung in Chinese to her.

“If I moved to China 44 years ago and I didn’t speak Chinese, and then some random Chinese kid came up to me and sang ‘Sweet Caroline’ to me, that would be a real culture shock for sure,” said MacNeill.
Not everyone has been appreciative. MacNeill said he had visited 300 to 400 homes over the summer, some residents thinking he was a salesman and closing the door in his face.

But MacNeill said he had been overwhelmed with “over the top reactions” from those who enjoyed his performances — which have also included a song for Cantonese speakers, “Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies” by Beyond.
“They kind of go from not really wanting to talk to you or being very shy to then all of a sudden wanting to ask me a million questions,” said MacNeill.
Some guessed that he learned Chinese because he had a Chinese girlfriend, which he doesn’t.

MacNeill said he learned Chinese by using Google Translate and watching YouTube videos, testing out his language skills by ordering food at a Chinese restaurant. His B.C. friends have also mentored him.
But the reactions of Richmond householders to his singing have provided incentive to keep learning.

“The best way to learn a language is to actually be motivated … so when people have these good reactions and they’re always so impressed even if you just know really basic Chinese … that was good motivation to learn the language,” said MacNeill.

He said the idea that Chinese immigrants could be “closed off” was a false impression created by cultural and language barriers, with some worried about causing offence if they don’t speak English well.
But show interest in their culture, and true personalities shone through, he said.
“They’re very welcoming. Chinese people are some of the kindest people I’ve ever met in my life,” he said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 12, 2026.

stories.title: The Globe and Mail crosswords: Breaking down the Weekender's 'Record Sleeves,' cryptic clues and more
stories.summary: It’s not you, it’s me
stories.author: Jess Shulman
stories.content:
Puzzle Pieces is my weekly column for discussing the Globe’s Saturday Weekender and Weekender Cryptic crossword puzzles. I show clues in [square brackets] and grid entries in Capital Letters. And remember, if you plan to solve today’s crosswords, you’ll want to do that before reading this spoiler-filled piece.

Today’s Weekender, Record Sleeves , comes to us from Toronto crossword constructor Ada Nicolle. Ada is also a comedian, and you can find her jokes and music on Instagram and TikTok under @adanicklmao (do yourself a favour and go watch her viral song about the font on bags of Arctic Glacier Ice).

Favourite moments in today’s crossword

28A contains one of the funniest clues I’ve seen in a while: [Practice that stretches out sweaters?] As a weekly-or-so practitioner of HOT Yoga, the very thought of woolly sweaters juxtaposed with the dripping-wet reality of those classes gives me heat exhaustion.

I like it when a fairly short, standard word is given a particularly evocative clue. At 57D, [“Get into positions!” at a surprise party] is a neat way to clue Hide, a little bonus to add to your solving pleasure. 81D’s [Commit a Christmas faux pas] is a similarly perfect description of Peek.

And did you spot the mini sequence in 17D and 18D, with two unrelated fictional best friends mentioned in a row? It takes a special kind of mind to think of connecting Frog and Ernie because they’re [Toad’s best friend] and [Bert’s best friend].

Breaking down today’s theme

One reason I wanted to start a column about our crossword themes is that they’re new to many Globe readers. Themes are far more common in North American crosswords than in the U . K . , and until we launched our new Games program in February we ran syndicated, unthemed British puzzles.

One question I hear often from readers is: “What am I supposed to do with the circles in the grid?” Today’s puzzle is a good example.

When you see squares that contain circles, they’re pointing you toward the theme. The theme May be so simple that it’s easy to miss entirely, and the circles are there to highlight what’s going on. Here, the key entry is at 115A: Break-UP Albums, clued as [Recordings made after failed relationships … or, read another way, what the theme entries in this puzzle do?]

Each of the theme answers has circles at its beginning and end, highlighting how it BREAKs UP an Album title. Without the circles, that would be a lot harder to spot. Do you need to notice it to solve the puzzle? Technically no. But since each theme clue also gives the album’s artist in parentheses, spotting the gimmick means you can use that extra hint to help you solve those long entries.

Together, the theme entries make a pretty cool list of popular albums that span generations and genres:

20A: W ALK-IN FR Eezer - breaking up any one of Weezer’s seven self-titled albums

31A: DA ILY Colu MN - Kendrick Lamar’s Damn

38A: RUM S Ours - Fleetwood Mac’s Rumours

55A: BRA Nches OU T - Charli Xcx’s Brat

65A: SU GAR We’re GOI N Down - Gordon Lightfoot’s Sundown

74A: PUR PLE PR OSE - Justin Bieber’s Purpose

93A: HER E G OES - David Bowie’s Heroes

101A: BL ANK Cheq UE - Joni Mitchell’s Blue

A note from today’s constructor, Ada Nicolle

So excited to be back in The Globe and Mail! This puzzle was inspired by pop icon Olivia Rodrigo’s most recent quasi-breakup album You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love , which is ironic, since it’s the one album of hers whose name wouldn’t work for a theme like this. I’d like to thank Jess for pushing me to include more Canadian artists! In an industry centred mostly around Americana, it’s refreshing to be able to include so much local stuff. Thanks for having me!

Some scrapped theme entries:

D Igestive C Ookie (Green Day’s Dookie )

Disney’s BL Izzard B Each (Nirvana’s Bleach )

The Left at London song Revol Ution LO VER (The Beatles’s Revolver )

JA Cqui ZZ Rodgers (Queen’s Jazz )

COL Lege MAJ ORS (Beck’s Colors , though we’d prefer if he’d spelled it with a U)

Cryptic clue of the week

From today’s Weekender Cryptic , let’s look at a clue that sent me down the entirely wrong path: 23A [Committee’s head left unfinished hot drink (4)].

My first thought was that “committee’s head” referred to the first letter of committee , giving C. That’s such a common device in cryptics that I barely questioned it. “Left” is often L, and I wondered if “unfinished hot” could be HO. Clho, however, is not a drink.

Back to the drawing board. Maybe “left unfinished” meant LEF, giving Clef. A word! But not a hot drink.

Next, I tried using “committee’s head” as the definition and “left unfinished hot drink” as the wordplay. “Hot drink” could become SAK or CHA ( sake or chai without their endings), but Lsak and Lcha didn’t seem like committee heads in any way I could see.

Then it clicked. A committee’s head is a chair , and “left unfinished” turns chair into Chai – a hot drink!

It was a simple deletion clue disguised as something trickier, and I just followed it on down the garden path. Did you fall for it?

As always, if you’re new to cryptics, check out Fraser Simpson’s article: How to solve The Globe’s cryptic crossword .

stories.title: LFP Letters to the Editor: September 12, 2026
stories.summary: Cindy Chrisjohn remembers her sister, 10 years after her death.
stories.author: Free Press Readers
stories.content:
Ten years ago this week, my sister, Debra Chrisjohn, died in hospital after she was in the custody first of London police, then the OPP. Debra had been in distress for two hours before being brought to the hospital, when it was too late to save her life.

I’ve watched, during the last 10 years, police and paramedic service members who came in contact with her that day refuse to take responsibility or make meaningful changes beyond record keeping that would indicate my sister’s death was not in vain.

After seven years of criminal proceedings against an officer charged in Debra’s death , we finally are expecting a coroner’s inquest next year. Recommendations will be made by the inquest jury to try to prevent similar tragedies but ultimately, it will be up to our local institutions to decide whether to adopt them and how seriously to take them.

Debra’s life was not easy and she was not perfect. Attending an Indian day school and being subject to the child welfare system, Debra knew that receiving public services comes at a cost. But she tried and sometimes failed. She was 39 when she died and I know there was still time for her to try again, when it maybe would have been enough.

I am Oneida, Debra was Oneida. In Oneida, our daily prayer translates as:

I give thanks for this day. It is a good day. And I’m glad that I’m here.

Ten years after my sister’s death, I still give thanks for this day. I still say it is a good day. And I am still glad to be here. But it doesn’t mean that I’m not angry and it doesn’t mean I’m not sad. It does mean I see each day as a new chance to remember my sister and to make sure you remember her, too, so that others May not have to suffer the same fate.

Cindy Chrisjohn, London

It is time to stop the constant taxpayer handouts to the London Transit Commission.

Ridership is down, yet taxpayers continue to be asked to provide more and more money to support transit operations. At some point, the organization needs to look at its own budget and identify where costs can be reduced rather than continually turning to taxpayers.

The bus rapid transit project is an example of spending that many taxpayers question. When ridership is declining and residents already are struggling with the rising cost of living, it is difficult to justify continuing to pour additional taxpayers’ dollars into expensive transit initiatives without demonstrating clear value and measurable results.

Everyone is facing higher fuel costs, higher grocery bills, higher housing costs and increased operating expenses.

Taxpayers do not have the ability simply to ask for more money. We have to adjust our budgets, make difficult choices and live within our means.

Government should be held to the same standard.

If the city has accumulated a surplus as a result of collecting more in taxes than was necessary to cover its expenses, now is not the time to expand the purse strings. It is time to provide relief to taxpayers and exercise fiscal responsibility.

It is time for the city and LTC to live within their means, review their priorities, reduce unnecessary spending and stop treating taxpayers as an unlimited source of funding.

The answer to every financial shortfall cannot continue to be another request for money from taxpayers.

It seems, when people look out on the world, they typically see themselves.

With people like U.S. President Donald Trump, this is magnified and his comments become a mirror on his self-perception.

For example, calling Prime Minister Mark Carney “a weak and ineffective leader” shows Trump’s feelings of being overwhelmed by his own failures.

His contention and chaos routine is a mask. No one sees America like a “piggy bank” more than Donald Trump.

Our trade issue could be resolved overnight if Canadians would authorize Carney to make a deposit to Trump’s crypto diplomacy account. Judging by the Windsor bridge re-negotiations, the starting donation is $1 ­million.

Graeme MacLean, St. Thomas

Ontario’s spending of $25,000 on Lake Ontario signs is needless. Our reaction should be silence.

Our best recourse is not to invest in frivolous expenses but out-strategize the ­opponent.

We have things he needs, including electricity th U.S. wants Let us use our greatest resource to our benefit, until the mid-terms define a new House.

Not only are Canadians quiet and polite, we are resilient and have common sense.

Mary Anne Reid, London

stories.summary: A ballyhooed summit in Toronto and a big speech in Europe offer opportunities to seize business and diplomatic opportunities, but there are hazards.

Sean Kilpatrick The Canadian Press[](http://www.thestar.com/news/analysis/next-week-mark-carney-faces-his-biggest-tests-as-pm-here-s-why/article_e35a74e3-0407-4784-9b6c-06e3f2ddf4ba.html)

ByAllan Woods Staff Reporter

It’s been 18 months since Mark Carney was sworn in as prime minister, but the week ahead will be his real coming out.

With his much-touted investment summit in Toronto and his planned speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, it will be the moment when much of what the prime minister has been preaching and promising since he took power is put into practice.

Think of the investment summit as the grand opening of a heavily advertised new store.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 10Image 11Image 12Image 13

The Carney government first created the Major Projects Office to develop and evaluate a series of big-ticket energy, infrastructure and mining projects seen as capable of boosting a Canadian economy under threat from Donald Trump’s tariffs.

They include a new oil pipeline out to the B.C. coast, a high-speed rail line from Toronto to Quebec and a deep-water port upgrade in northern Manitoba.

On Monday and Tuesday, they will be among the 167 projectsthe Carney government puts on the shelves, creating a shopping experience for some of the world’s deepest-pocketed investors.

Think of it as an epic ”Dragons’ Den” episode meant to turbocharge the Canadian economy.

We know from an abundance of opinion polling that the Canadian public trusts Carney to run the country at this fraught moment. The investment summit could tell us if the world of global finance has the same level of confidence in the pitches that will be made.

The prime minister has set a goal of attracting $1 trillion in foreign investment from the summit over five years.

But with days to go before the summit convenes, there are questions about the projected costs of some of these projects, and about the strength of the business case if Canada no longer holds the promise of tariff-free access to American markets.

Carney pushed back on the latter suggestion on Thursday, saying: “Canada is about so much more than being next to the United States.”

He touted Canada’s natural resources, energy and critical minerals, but also its stability and reliability, respect for the rule of law and the education and talents of the population.

“The individuals and organizations that are coming to that summit … are coming because of Canada. If they wanted to go to the United States, they would go to the United States.”

The next week will also test the power of Carney’s political persuasion.

We refer to it too often, perhaps, but the prime minister inspired his fellow world leaders to think about the world in a new way with his JanuaryDavos speech to the World Economic Forum.

He spoke about middle-power nations banding together to insulate themselves from the impact and influence of superpower bullies like the U.S. and China.

Do we need a global order? Did we even believe in the old one?

His challenge as he heads to the European Parliament on Wednesday and Thursday of next week, where he will be a guest of honour at the annual State of the Union address and then give a speech to European lawmakers, is to demonstrate that he is able to craft something more than just an inspiring political speech.

Officials in both Ottawa and Brussels have promised details about how they intend to take the economic and security relationship to a new level. The challenge is to come up with measures more substantial and tangible than the raft of bilateral agreements, strategic partnerships and memoranda of understanding that currently exist.

If Canada is to meet the Carney government’s goal of doubling trade to non-U.S. markets, the high-level transatlantic love-in needs to become concrete and reach a point at which Canadians naturally shift their gazes east to Europe rather than south to the U.S. — not just in protest of or in reaction to American tariffs.

In a paper released this week, the European Council on Foreign Relations urged deeper integration in transatlantic defence ties, including joint military exercises, co-operation in the Arctic and — perhaps most daringly — an agreement to jointly defend against threats to territorial sovereignty, whether it is challenged along the 49 th parallel dividing Canada from the U.S., or in Greenland.

The paper’s author, Anand Sundar, warned that Ottawa and Brussels “should expect increasing pushback if they embark on this joint course.”

That’s a reference to the other potential bump in the path that Carney is leading the country along: the wrath of Donald Trump’s America.

The Trump administration has already signalled that it is keeping a close eye on Carney’s ambitions.

In May, a senior U.S. Defense Department official, Elbridge Colby, announced the suspension of a joint Canada-U.S. defence forum, saying there were “gaps between rhetoric and reality” on Canada’s defence spending and urging Ottawa to begin “recognizing our shared geography.”

In July, he followed it up with a social media post referring to the middle powers strategy credited to Carney as “a great deal of hubbub.”

“We are not concerned that this is a serious possibility. Rather, we are more concerned that a few allies and partners will think it is and waste valuable time, money, and political capital on a distraction.”

That is a clear warning — one that suggests Carney’s coming out next week could be seen in some quarters less as a celebratory grand opening, more as the opening round of a boxing match.

And that will put the Prime Minister up against the maxim of the seasoned former heavyweight slugger, Mike Tyson: that everyone has a plan until they get hit.

Allan Woods is a Paris-based staff reporter for the Star. He covers global and national affairs. Follow him on X: @WoodsAllan.

It’s been 18 months since Mark Carney was sworn in as prime minister, but the week ahead will be his real coming out.

stories.summary: Five university professors explain the new ways they’re using to gauge students’ understanding, and where AI fits in.

Ashley Fraser for the Toronto Star[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/inside-the-creative-ways-Ontario-professors-are-grading-now-this-is-the-class-where-ai-goes-to-die/article_ab7e7e52-5759-4687-b4bd-3af77237834f.html)

ByJanet Hurley Senior Writer

There will be no take-home essays in Stuart Chambers’ university courses this fall.

Tired of trying to detect AI usage, the University of Ottawa sociology professor is replacing the traditional means of assessment with an in-person 75-minute handwritten paper. “I was becoming too much of a police officer and less of a professor. I want to go back to being a professor.”

Chambers’ dilemma is playing out in classrooms everywhere. Since ChatGPT’s public launch in 2022, generative AI has rapidly gained traction: Last fall, 73 per cent of Canadian students reported relying on it for schoolwork, up from 52 per cent in 2023. And while some educators have responded by banning the technology, just over half of Canadian post-secondary students say they are permitted to use it.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Meanwhile, cheating scandals have come to dominate the discourse, from a Western University professor who sought to invalidate an exam over suspected widespread AI misuse, to an American prof whose ruse to hide the word “Madagascar” in a midterm question revealed nearly all students had fed the query to a chatbot.

As educational institutions grapple with how to harness AI ethically without sacrificing critical thinking, classrooms have become petri dishes for a period of intense experimentation in teaching and assessment.

“Our credibility as a university is dependent on how accurately we can assess grades,” says Chambers. “And if we’re not accurate in assessing grades, the diploma is worthless.”

Here’s how five Ontario professors are transforming their practice.

For the first 15 minutes of each class, University of Toronto Prof. Kyle Smith conducts what he calls “proof of human thinking.”

He hands out a question, typed on paper, based on that week’s reading materials. He recognizes students May use AI to study, but once in his lecture hall, there’s no hiding behind a screen. Students “have to show up in class and, without any sort of device other than a pencil, be able to respond in a coherent way.”

Instead of banning AI or grudgingly tolerating it, the history of religions professor has redesigned how he measures student understanding. “A lot of colleagues maybe still have their heads in the sand and think we can do the same things,” he says, but AI is “impacting post-secondary education, particularly in the humanities, in ways that are unwelcome.”

Instead of a written final, Smith now conducts a “viva voce,” an oral exam in which students meet with him and roll a 12-sided die three times, randomly selecting three of the course’s 12 weeks of topics for discussion. Students must also pose one hard question to Smith to demonstrate they have synthesized the material.

“The vast majority of students have never had this sort of assessment,” says Smith. “The pressure to perform live is a little scary … but the feedback I have consistently gotten is, ‘I was really worried about this; it turned out I was super-prepared, eager for the conversation and it went really well.’ ”

That final is worth 20 per cent; the in-class questions a total of 40. The remaining grade consists of two multilayered, sophisticated take-home assignments in which AI is not just permitted but potentially necessary, enabling students to create such things as a religious shrine using digital tools.

But as AI improves, the balance between human and machine keeps shifting: “I’m reacting to the changes I’m seeing,” Smith says, noting he May need to pivot again this fall.

When Sharon Ferguson put her first-year students into randomized groups for projects, she noticed something striking: their finished work contained almost no AI-generated content.

Not because they couldn’t use it. But students who might have happily thrown the assignment into a chatbot found themselves working alongside peers who wanted to do their own thinking. The group kept itself honest.

The result confirmed something Ferguson, an assistant professor in management science and engineering at the University of Waterloo, has already built into her practice: the most effective response to AI isn’t restriction, it’s design.

“A large majority of our students go into tech, and the philosophy in most tech companies is use as much AI as you can, gain as much efficiency as you possibly can with this tool … So, it doesn’t make sense to say you absolutely cannot use it.”

As a researcher of human-AI interaction and in her second year of teaching, Ferguson has always inherently thought about generative AI. Her approach is to teach responsible and effective use while demanding transparency, asking students to sign a declaration and show their chat history. She has also built a grading rubric tied to the exact terminology and concept applications she uses in lectures, making generic AI work easier to spot. And she introduced frequent quizzes with thought-provoking questions that can’t just be memorized.

In foundational year courses, she still does as many in-person, hands-on activities as possible: “If we never let them become experts because they’re never learning, because they are just using AI all of the time, then that’s a very dangerous future.”

Rahul Kumar is teaching the teachers. And there’s great responsibility in that.

“Without themselves knowing (AI), how can they guide their students?” says the associate professor of educational studies at Brock University.

When Kumar’s research revealedself-disclosed AI use among post-secondary students had risen from 74 per cent in 2023 to 94 in 2025, he found himself at a critical juncture: “How do we ensure the degrees we are conferring actually ensure people are learning and not subcontracting the work to generative AI?”

His answer was to overhaul his teaching and assessment practices, without banning AI. “It is our responsibility to prepare our students for their future, not our past.”

He asked students to disclose their usage, with no repercussions, and added 15-minute interviews. “If you can have an intelligent conversation and demonstrate your learning, that ought to be sufficient.”

He likens his approach to “Swiss cheese,” accepting that any single assessment May have holes where students turn to AI. But by stacking several assessments— an outline, a conversation, multiple drafts, a final paper— “you get a relatively solid piece of cheese,” he says, giving him greater assurance his students can apply their knowledge.

This fall, he also plans to introduce debates, grading students on their position and how they listen and respond in the moment.

But these solutions are time-consuming and not always practical, workable for Kumar’s small graduate student cohort, but for a class of 40, “probably not.”

His ongoing research is only deepening his resolve: He’s finding some Ontario teachers personally use AI but ban it in class. “The duplicity of that further gives me confidence that these steps I’m taking are worthwhile,” Kumar says. “Changes in our practice are a must.”

When students in Emily Kuang’s third-year course in user interfaces built their own websites with AI last winter, the project average was over 90 per cent. Then came the closed-book, in-person exam, and grades dropped to the 60s and 70s.

That gap was hard to ignore. So this fall, the York University assistant professor of electrical engineering and computer science is making two changes.

Kuang, whose research focuses on human-computer collaboration, says her graduates will be expected to use AI on the job, so the question shouldn’t be “how do we make our assessments AI-proof, but how can we make our students more AI-literate?” Still, she is expanding the declaration form students submit with each assignment, adding more detailed questions about fact-checking and whether results matched what was envisioned. She also plans to share the grade discrepancy with new classes as a warning that “you still need to learn the material.”

She believes foundational coding and debugging skills still matter and need to be mastered without AI assistance, but in the upper-year courses she teaches, the focus shifts to application and judgment. It’s a distinction that shapes her philosophy: “Humans are not going to be replaced by AI, but humans are going to be replaced by humans who know how to use AI. So, the viewpoint I take is we need to prepare them.”

Assessment also looks different depending on class size. In her fourth-year multimedia technology course, with just 20 students, she replaced the closed-book test with in-person presentations. In her third-year course of 120, that wasn’t possible. “The scalability issue is a big one.”

The first red flag was the sudden appearance of near-perfect papers from a couple of students who had failed the earlier multiple-choice midterm. It was a pattern Stuart Chambers hadn’t seen before. Usually, grades dropped on the take-home essay “because writing is a harder skill,” says the University of Ottawa professor.

That was 2023. This past winter, suspect submissions increased eightfold. When Chambers confronted the students, most couldn’t remember a single detail of their written arguments and admitted using ChatGPT. “The only thing valid on the paper was their name,” he says. “By doing nothing, we’re complicit in cheating, so I decided I had to do something.”

This fall, his students will write closed-book essays under his watch. Chambers spent months testing the format, gauging what students can realistically communicate with pen and paper in the allotted time. He has reduced the weighting from 40 per cent to 30 to account for constraints.

He believes the approach will preserve the writing and critical-thinking skills central to a university’s mission. Worried about AI’s effect on reading too, he introduced a bonus assignment last year, offering five per cent to those who read a book from a list and sparred with him for 30 minutes. It worked well and was manageable with 10 per cent of the class taking him up on it.

Chambers will be emailing expectations to his incoming students: when it comes to assignments, they’re on their own.

“This,” he says, “is the class where AI goes to die.”

Janet Hurley is a Toronto Star journalist and senior writer covering culture, education and societal trends. She is based in Toronto. Reach her via email: jhurley@thestar.CA.
