Tired of trying to detect AI usage, the University of Ottawa sociology professor is replacing the traditional means of assessment with an in-person 75-minute handwritten paper. “I was becoming too much of a police officer and less of a professor. I want to go back to being a professor.”

Chambers’ dilemma is playing out in classrooms everywhere. Since ChatGPT’s public launch in 2022, generative AI has rapidly gained traction: Last fall, 73 per cent of Canadian students reported relying on it for schoolwork, up from 52 per cent in 2023. And while some educators have responded by banning the technology, just over half of Canadian post-secondary students say they are permitted to use it.
Article continues below
Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Meanwhile, cheating scandals have come to dominate the discourse, from a Western University professor who sought to invalidate an exam over suspected widespread AI misuse, to an American prof whose ruse to hide the word “Madagascar” in a midterm question revealed nearly all students had fed the query to a chatbot.

As educational institutions grapple with how to harness AI ethically without sacrificing critical thinking, classrooms have become petri dishes for a period of intense experimentation in teaching and assessment.
“Our credibility as a university is dependent on how accurately we can assess grades,” says Chambers. “And if we’re not accurate in assessing grades, the diploma is worthless.”
Here’s how five Ontario professors are transforming their practice.
Roll of the dice
For the first 15 minutes of each class, University of Toronto Prof. Kyle Smith conducts what he calls “proof of human thinking.”

He hands out a question, typed on paper, based on that week’s reading materials. He recognizes students May use AI to study, but once in his lecture hall, there’s no hiding behind a screen. Students “have to show up in class and, without any sort of device other than a pencil, be able to respond in a coherent way.”

Instead of banning AI or grudgingly tolerating it, the history of religions professor has redesigned how he measures student understanding. “A lot of colleagues maybe still have their heads in the sand and think we can do the same things,” he says, but AI is “impacting post-secondary education, particularly in the humanities, in ways that are unwelcome.”

Instead of a written final, Smith now conducts a “viva voce,” an oral exam in which students meet with him and roll a 12-sided die three times, randomly selecting three of the course’s 12 weeks of topics for discussion. Students must also pose one hard question to Smith to demonstrate they have synthesized the material.

“The vast majority of students have never had this sort of assessment,” says Smith. “The pressure to perform live is a little scary … but the feedback I have consistently gotten is, ‘I was really worried about this; it turned out I was super-prepared, eager for the conversation and it went really well.’ ”

That final is worth 20 per cent; the in-class questions a total of 40. The remaining grade consists of two multilayered, sophisticated take-home assignments in which AI is not just permitted but potentially necessary, enabling students to create such things as a religious shrine using digital tools.
But as AI improves, the balance between human and machine keeps shifting: “I’m reacting to the changes I’m seeing,” Smith says, noting he May need to pivot again this fall.
Positive peer pressure
When Sharon Ferguson put her first-year students into randomized groups for projects, she noticed something striking: their finished work contained almost no AI-generated content.

Not because they couldn’t use it. But students who might have happily thrown the assignment into a chatbot found themselves working alongside peers who wanted to do their own thinking. The group kept itself honest.

The result confirmed something Ferguson, an assistant professor in management science and engineering at the University of Waterloo, has already built into her practice: the most effective response to AI isn’t restriction, it’s design.

“A large majority of our students go into tech, and the philosophy in most tech companies is use as much AI as you can, gain as much efficiency as you possibly can with this tool … So, it doesn’t make sense to say you absolutely cannot use it.”

As a researcher of human-AI interaction and in her second year of teaching, Ferguson has always inherently thought about generative AI. Her approach is to teach responsible and effective use while demanding transparency, asking students to sign a declaration and show their chat history. She has also built a grading rubric tied to the exact terminology and concept applications she uses in lectures, making generic AI work easier to spot. And she introduced frequent quizzes with thought-provoking questions that can’t just be memorized.

In foundational year courses, she still does as many in-person, hands-on activities as possible: “If we never let them become experts because they’re never learning, because they are just using AI all of the time, then that’s a very dangerous future.”
Plugging the holes
Rahul Kumar is teaching the teachers. And there’s great responsibility in that.
“Without themselves knowing (AI), how can they guide their students?” says the associate professor of educational studies at Brock University.

When Kumar’s research revealedself-disclosed AI use among post-secondary students had risen from 74 per cent in 2023 to 94 in 2025, he found himself at a critical juncture: “How do we ensure the degrees we are conferring actually ensure people are learning and not subcontracting the work to generative AI?”
His answer was to overhaul his teaching and assessment practices, without banning AI. “It is our responsibility to prepare our students for their future, not our past.”

He asked students to disclose their usage, with no repercussions, and added 15-minute interviews. “If you can have an intelligent conversation and demonstrate your learning, that ought to be sufficient.”

He likens his approach to “Swiss cheese,” accepting that any single assessment May have holes where students turn to AI. But by stacking several assessments— an outline, a conversation, multiple drafts, a final paper— “you get a relatively solid piece of cheese,” he says, giving him greater assurance his students can apply their knowledge.
This fall, he also plans to introduce debates, grading students on their position and how they listen and respond in the moment.
But these solutions are time-consuming and not always practical, workable for Kumar’s small graduate student cohort, but for a class of 40, “probably not.”

His ongoing research is only deepening his resolve: He’s finding some Ontario teachers personally use AI but ban it in class. “The duplicity of that further gives me confidence that these steps I’m taking are worthwhile,” Kumar says. “Changes in our practice are a must.”
Mind the AI gap

When students in Emily Kuang’s third-year course in user interfaces built their own websites with AI last winter, the project average was over 90 per cent. Then came the closed-book, in-person exam, and grades dropped to the 60s and 70s.
That gap was hard to ignore. So this fall, the York University assistant professor of electrical engineering and computer science is making two changes.

Kuang, whose research focuses on human-computer collaboration, says her graduates will be expected to use AI on the job, so the question shouldn’t be “how do we make our assessments AI-proof, but how can we make our students more AI-literate?” Still, she is expanding the declaration form students submit with each assignment, adding more detailed questions about fact-checking and whether results matched what was envisioned. She also plans to share the grade discrepancy with new classes as a warning that “you still need to learn the material.”

She believes foundational coding and debugging skills still matter and need to be mastered without AI assistance, but in the upper-year courses she teaches, the focus shifts to application and judgment. It’s a distinction that shapes her philosophy: “Humans are not going to be replaced by AI, but humans are going to be replaced by humans who know how to use AI. So, the viewpoint I take is we need to prepare them.”

Assessment also looks different depending on class size. In her fourth-year multimedia technology course, with just 20 students, she replaced the closed-book test with in-person presentations. In her third-year course of 120, that wasn’t possible. “The scalability issue is a big one.”
Where AI goes to die

The first red flag was the sudden appearance of near-perfect papers from a couple of students who had failed the earlier multiple-choice midterm. It was a pattern Stuart Chambers hadn’t seen before. Usually, grades dropped on the take-home essay “because writing is a harder skill,” says the University of Ottawa professor.

That was 2023. This past winter, suspect submissions increased eightfold. When Chambers confronted the students, most couldn’t remember a single detail of their written arguments and admitted using ChatGPT. “The only thing valid on the paper was their name,” he says. “By doing nothing, we’re complicit in cheating, so I decided I had to do something.”

This fall, his students will write closed-book essays under his watch. Chambers spent months testing the format, gauging what students can realistically communicate with pen and paper in the allotted time. He has reduced the weighting from 40 per cent to 30 to account for constraints.

He believes the approach will preserve the writing and critical-thinking skills central to a university’s mission. Worried about AI’s effect on reading too, he introduced a bonus assignment last year, offering five per cent to those who read a book from a list and sparred with him for 30 minutes. It worked well and was manageable with 10 per cent of the class taking him up on it.
Chambers will be emailing expectations to his incoming students: when it comes to assignments, they’re on their own.
“This,” he says, “is the class where AI goes to die.”
Janet Hurley is a Toronto Star journalist and senior writer covering culture, education and societal trends. She is based in Toronto. Reach her via email: jhurley@thestar.CA.

stories.title: 26-91602 - Missing Person
stories.summary: General Releases
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
UPDATE - LONDON, ON (September 14, 2026) - Updated information in relation to missing person Kirsty Ortmanns, 38, has been obtained.

The missing person was reportedly last seen on September 1, 2026, in the 200-block of Dundas Street.

Investigators continue to appeal to the public for information in relation to her whereabouts.

Anyone with information in relation to the missing person’s whereabouts is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

ORIGINAL - LONDON, ON (September 12, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 38-year-old Kirsty Ortmanns, of London.

The missing person is described as a White female who is approximately 5’8” with a slim build and long black hair. The missing person was last seen wearing a black sweater, brown pants, and black shoes.

The missing person was last seen on August 25, 2026, at approximately 10:00 a.m., in the area of Dudas Street and Clarke Road and was reported missing on September 12, 2026.

Family and police are concerned for the missing person’s welfare.

A person can be reported missing at any time. You do not need to wait 24 hours before you report someone missing. If you are concerned for someone’s immediate safety, call 9-1-1. Otherwise, you can report a person as missing to the London Police Service by calling the non-emergency number 519-661-5670.

ByFrédérik Plante Investigative Reporter

U.S. President Donald Trump put Canada and Iran side by side when discussing potential deals on Saturday, apparently equating the United States’ relationship with one of its closest allies to that of an enemy nation.

Asked by a reporter whether he was considering withdrawing from the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma) on trade entirely, Trump said that “Canada wants to make a deal very badly, just like Iran wants to make a deal very badly.”

Trump made his comments during a meeting in Dublin with Ireland’s taoiseach Micheál Martin, the country’s head of government.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

“I just don’t think they’re ready,” Trump added, saying that both countries could get a deal “at the right time” with the United States. “But Canada wants to make a deal. I hope Canada appreciates being in the same sentence with Iran.”

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said Friday that no formal trade talks were scheduled, although he said conversations between Canadian and American officials have not stopped. His office declined to comment on Trump’s Saturday remarks.

The president started by saying that the United States has a “good” relationship with Canada and followed this with his oft-repeated assertion that his country “has been ripped off for 50 years by Canada.”

The North American neighbours have been embroiled in an escalating trade war since Prime Minister Mark Carney summoned negotiators home on Aug. 21, accusing the American side of making last-minute demands that would undermine Canada’s sovereignty. The two countries appeared to be on the verge of a deal earlier that week, to settle some outstanding trade irritants and prevent the United States from imposing a new round of punishing tariffs on Canada.

Trump’s numbers keep changing because they were never real, writes Jim Stanford. Here’s a point-by-point rebuttal of his wildest arguments — and

Trump then imposed 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $28 billion in Canadian goods. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs, ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on hundreds of products, took effect on Tuesday; later that same day, Trump signed new orders to ban imports of some Canadian products, including most alcohol. He also vowed to include steel, aluminum and automotive products — already facing steep import duties — in tariffs from which they had previously been excluded.

Both sides have blamed each other for the impasse. In a statement issued Tuesday, U.S. Trade Rep. Jamieson Greer said the escalation was a “natural consequence” of Canada discriminating against American exports and choosing “senseless retaliation” over an almost final trade deal. In a video posted that day, Prime Minister Carney accused the Trump administration of trying to make Canadian industries dependent on the U.S.

In parallel, the United States has been at war with Iran since it launched joint strikes with Israel on the Islamic Republic on Feb. 28, starting a months-long conflict that spread to neighbouring states and rocked the global economy.

Iran continues to attack some ships trying to transit the Strait of Hormuz, which has become an important source of leverage for Tehran in the war. The U.S. has been introducing new measures to increase the economic pain on Iran after negotiations collapsed and no end to the intermittent fighting appears in sight.

With files from the Canadian Press and the Associated Press

Frédérik Plante is a Toronto-based investigative reporter for the Star. You can reach him at fplante@thestar.CA, @fx_plante on X or @fxplante.bsky.social on Bluesky.

stories.title: Chrétien touts Canada’s values, strength in speech at 9/11 ceremony in Gander
stories.summary: Former prime minister spoke at a ceremony to remember 3,000 people, including 24 Canadians, who were killed on Sept. 11, 2001
stories.author: Lindsay Jones
stories.content:
In a fiery and impassioned speech, former prime minister Jean Chrétien sounded off against the United States at an emotional ceremony commemorating 25 years since 9/11 in Gander, N.L., ON Friday, drawing roars of applause and a standing ovation.

“I have a message for American friends,” he said, as U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra looked on with a tepid smile.

“Yes, Canada is generous, open country. And Canadians are tolerant and kind, but never mistake our generosity for weakness, never, never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination, and never, never mistake our kindness for softness. We know who we are and we are proud of it.”

About 1,000 people, mostly seniors, sprang to their feet at his words, loudly cheering, whistling and applauding.

The event was to honour first responders and remember the nearly 3,000 people, including 24 Canadians, who were killed on Sept. 11, 2001, when terrorists crashed planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, into the Pentagon in Virginia and a field in Pennsylvania.

After officials closed U.S. airspace, the tiny airport in Gander was the landing spot for 38 passenger planes – part of an operation that diverted more than 200 flights to airports across Canada. Gander, a town of less than 10,000, took in nearly 7,000 stranded strangers.

The event highlighted the people of Gander and nearby communities who dropped everything to welcome passengers into their homes, create makeshift shelters in schools and community halls, and provide thousands of hot meals, paving the way to lifelong friendships. Many of those “plane people” had returned to Gander for the service on Friday, sitting alongside their found families in the local arena.

Up until the end of the two-hour service when Mr. Chrétien spoke, the event had been largely apolitical with performances from The Ennis Sisters and Alan Doyle, remarks from Governor-General Louise Arbour that focused on the friendship between the two countries, and a meandering speech from Mr. Hoekstra.

But the 92-year-old Mr. Chrétien addressed the issue that overshadowed the event, one that has fractured a long-standing friendship between the two countries that Gander had come to symbolize.

President Donald Trump’s escalating trade war has fuelled anti-American sentiment, as has his repeated threats to annex Canada and the barrage of disrespectful memes targeting Prime Minister Mark Carney. Mr. Hoekstra has amplified some of the threats from the White House.

The crowd remained riveted as Mr. Chrétien delivered more of his impassioned rallying cry for Canada.

“We embrace our friends and we help them in their moment of need, but we bow to no one,” he said to booming applause. “The more we are insulted, are threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united.”

He finished by saying he wasn’t speaking in anger but as one friend to another. Friends need to be honest with each other, he added.

“Just as the people here in Gander and anywhere else in Newfoundland and Labrador, they will give you the shirt off their back, like they did 25 years ago,” he said. “They will always show you the respect of telling you the truth. So, my friends, here is to truth, to respect, to friendship and to good neighbours.”

Then, to more resounding applause, he said in French long live the United States and long live Canada.

As he turned away from the podium, Mr. Hoekstra embraced Mr. Chrétien, who patted him on the back.

Later that evening, Mr. Hoekstra, ON his way into the internationally acclaimed musical Come From Away showing in Gander, he declined to share his thoughts on Mr. Chrétien’s speech, shrugging his shoulders twice with his palms up as he went into the theatre. When asked what he took from the ceremony, he said. “Wonderful ceremony for 9/11 absolutely.”

Others however said Mr. Chrétien’s speech was historic. Michael Rubinoff, the originating producer of Come from Away and the producer of the Gander production said the former prime minister met the moment and spoke for many Canadians.

“To hear somebody speak up so strongly and articulate what those Canadian values are on this day, at this moment in time, at this intersection of this tension between the two countries was really profound,” said Mr. Rubinoff.

“I think it’s one of those moments that the people in the room, the people watching – we won’t forget.”

At the event, Mr. Hoekstra opened his speech by saying where he was when the 9/11 attacks occurred: “talking about asparagus to asparagus farmers as any good parliamentarian would do.”

He also talked about the shared sacrifices that Canada and the United States have had as countries, standing side by side during the Afghanistan war and on 9/11 when diverted planes came to Gander and the locals “did extraordinary things,” welcoming thousands of stranded passengers that nearly doubled the town’s population. “You did it all. You stood up. You did what needed to be done,” Mr. Hoekstra said.

“Thank you for your friendship. Thank you for standing up. To the nation of Canada, thank you. Thank you for being a partner. Thank you for the shared sacrifices.”

The Governor-General did not address the current animosity between the U.S. and Canada, but her speech highlighted the history of friendship and allyship between Canada and the United States, including during 9/11.

Ms. Arbour spoke about the “exceptional” relationship forged over generations – fighting alongside one another in two world wars, and standing together in defence, freedom and democracy throughout the Cold War.

“We have helped one another through natural disasters and difficult times, time and time again,” she said. “And entire communities from Windsor to Detroit, Vancouver to Seattle, have grown side by side, always in solidarity.”

stories.title: London firefighters mark 25th anniversary of 9/11
stories.summary: A solemn ceremony was held in London Friday to honour fallen firefighters and those who lost their lives 25 years ago on 9/11.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A solemn ceremony was held in London Friday to honour fallen firefighters and those who lost their lives 25 years ago on 9/11.

The ceremonial ‘3 bells’ rang out as the firefighters last alarm. It was in honour of the 49 London firefighters who gave their lives in service to their community. This year, two more names were added to the London firefighter memorial.

The families of Cpt. Dennis McCallum and Cpt. Douglas Perryman were presented with medals for their sacrifice.

“It means a lot to us, at the dedication, and honouring the ones that fell in 9/11, as well as my dad’s honour. He passed away earlier this year,” said Niki Bowyer, daughter of Cpt. Douglas Perryman.

“Oh. I can’t explain it. Fantastic. Great. I just wish he was here to enjoy it,” said Helen McCallum, the widow of Cpt. Dennis McCallum, who passed away in 2007.

A couple hundred first responders took part in the gathering at London Fire Dept. Memorial Headquarters on Horton Street, including area police and ambulance services, as well as military personnel.

Dignitaries and civic leaders of all political colours were also on hand. They were remembering the 343 first responders and the thousands of citizens who lost their lives on 9/11.

“I think about the bravery and the heroism that every firefighter and every first line responder exhibits on behalf of every person in our city,” said London Mayor Josh Morgan.

Lpffa President, Jason Timlick says while most on the job that day 25 years ago would have retired by now, those still active with the London Professional Firefighters Assn. remember it well. First responders of all stripes were on high alert, ready to serve.

“I’ll never forget the captain saying, ‘okay guys, we’re just going to do this all day.’ And we sat there and watched, barring alarms, to going out to do our duty. And it was horrific and unreal all at the same time,” Timlick said.

Lpffa secretary Randy Evans explained some London firefighters were mobilizing, trying to get to New York to help. A dozen local firefighters were preparing to fly down by helicopter, but the border and air space had been shut down.

“And so, all we did was, we turned our attention to serving our own community. Putting Canadian flags, American flags on our trucks, and really embracing that,” Evans said.

stories.title: Despite the trade war, some consumer prices are better in Canada than in the U.S.
stories.summary: Cashmere sweaters and Teslas are among the items that are more affordable north of the border
stories.author: Nathan VanderKlippe
stories.content:
Apple’s release of new iPhones this week confronted Canadians with a long familiar problem: sky-high prices. The top-end version of the new iPhone Duo will cost over $350 more in Canada than in the U.S. Such disparities have often turned Canadians into ambitious cross-border shoppers.

But, at this moment, the iPhone pricing is an anomaly.

After years of inflation, months of rising tariffs in the U.S. and a weak loonie, it is Canada that is now the haven for cheap buys.

Across a swath of goods – from home appliances to baby cribs, cashmere turtlenecks, Coca-Cola and pickup trucks – Canadian prices are consistently lower than those in the U.S.

The Globe and Mail compared pretax prices this week for more than 40 goods using the websites of more than a dozen retailers that operate on both sides of the border. In some cases, such as the Storkcraft Beckett convertible crib in natural wood carried by Walmart, the same product is for sale in the U.S. for a higher sticker price than in Canada. Factor currency conversion, and Canadians can purchase that crib for nearly 40 per cent less.

In Canada, the price of a Tesla Model 3 premium rear-wheel drive is nearly 45 per cent lower. Microsoft has priced the base model Xbox Series X nearly 10 per cent cheaper. A men’s Patagonia Nano Puff hoody is 15 per cent less. A base-model Ford F-150 pickup sells in Vancouver, B.C., for $4,200 below the price in Vancouver, Wash., a difference of 8.5 per cent. For both a base-model Honda Civic and a top-spec GMC Terrain, Canadian prices are nearly 15 per cent lower.

Meanwhile in the U.S., Home Depot lists a KitchenAid over-the-range microwave for US$1 more – making it 38 per cent pricier with the currency conversion. An LG French door fridge costs an additional 15 per cent. Banana Republic sells its featherweight cashmere Henley, a women’s fitted top, for 10 per cent more and a pair of Nike Air Max 270 is 22 per cent costlier.

What’s true for bigger items is true for smaller items as well.

Triscuits are nearly a third cheaper at Safeway in Canada.

And a Swiffer WetJet mop at Walmart sells for 20 per cent more in the U.S., a 500-caplet bottle of Tylenol extra strength gets a premium of 27 per cent. Even a 12-pack of Coca-Cola cans at Walmart costs nearly 30 per cent more south of the border.

Retail pricing is fraught with complexity. Sticker tags reflect wholesale costs, logistics expenses and market conditions. For many years, those worked against Canada. Retail consultant Clay Parnell recalled working with shoe retailer Aldo in the late 2010s. At the time, Canada’s immense geography and smaller market worked against it.

“Historically, Canadian prices have been higher,” said Mr. Parnell, who is chief executive of The Parker Avery Group.

No longer. At Aldo, the Kristof men’s loafer is 14 per cent cheaper in Canada; the Ayrah women’s ballet flat is 16 per cent less.

Retailers in the U.S. have contended with higher rates of inflation and a blanket of tariffs, which have both raised import costs and offered cover for price hikes. “On the tariff side, most of it generally is being passed through,” Mr. Parnell said. Some retailers, too, are raising prices even outside of tariff increases, padding profit margins.

In Canada, meanwhile, the economy has tended to be more sluggish than the U.S. in recent years, while Americans on average enjoy a higher disposable income.

Companies that sell across borders tend to price for local markets, “setting prices based on local consumer demand and purchasing power rather than strictly converting currency,” said Hakan Yilmazkuday, a professor of economics at Florida International University.

He sees lower Canadian prices as a reflection of more straitened northern circumstances.

“If companies fully applied the exchange rate difference, Canadian sales volumes would collapse. To maintain their market share, these retailers potentially absorb some of the currency penalty by accepting lower profit margins in Canada,” he said.

Currency matters, too, of course. When major retailers set prices for a given country, “they do not change them very frequently,” said Jeffrey Campbell, an economist at the University of Notre Dame. When the loonie drops, U.S. prices tend to grow more expensive by comparison.

“It is tempting to look at Canadian domestic developments as a source of loonie weakness, but in this case the fault is really in the stars rather than with ourselves,” he said. The U.S. dollar remains a haven in times of risk, “so while the Iran war has been good for the price of oil, it has also been good for the greenback.”

Price disparities between the U.S. and Canada have cycled as circumstances change – and today’s price gaps will almost certainly be reshaped by shifting policies and economic performance on both sides of the border.

This isn’t the first time, either, that Canadians have found themselves with a price advantage. In the early 1980s, around the time of price controls imposed under the National Energy Program, gas was considerably cheaper in Canada. And Americans flocked north.

“I remember my Dad taking us from Detroit to buy gas in Windsor during that time,” Prof. Campbell said.

Nearly a half-century later, a raft of different circumstances has again tilted the pricing landscape in favour of Canada – at least, outside of the fuel pump and the Apple store.

Add up the strong U.S. dollar, tariffs and less favourable economic circumstances in Canada, and the U.S. is now “the more expensive retail environment for many items,” Prof. Yilmazkuday said.

stories.title: How Canada’s military and first responders supported the U.S. months and years after 9/11
stories.summary: Canada was among the Nato nations that joined a global fight against terrorism after the attacks in the United States on Sept. 11, 2001.
stories.author: Nick Westoll
stories.content:
By Nick Westoll

Posted September 11, 2026 8:47 pm.

As many mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the United States, the solemn occasion also comes almost a quarter century after Canadian Armed Forces personnel joined a global fight against terrorism.

On Sept. 11, 2001, nearly 3,000 people died when hijackers forcibly took control four aircraft. The first two aircraft crashed into the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

The attacks prompted Canada’s ambassador to NATO ( North Atlantic Treaty Organization ) to move for the alliance to, for the first time ever, invoke Article Five – the clause in the NATO treaty that says an attack on one member country constitutes an attack on all.

Canada went to war with its allies to support the United States and overthrow the Taliban regime which was harbouring the terror group led by Osama bin Laden that was behind the 9/11 attacks.

Canadian Armed Forces special forces personnel were sent to Afghanistan in December 2001, marking the beginning of 13 calendar years of fighting and training operations. By the time the military ended its presence in the country in 2014, more than 40,000 soldiers rotated through – the longest tenure in Canadian history and the largest deployment since the Second World War. In addition to civilian deaths, 158 soldiers died in Afghanistan.

Private Demetrios Diplaros , a 24-year-old former Scarborough resident, was among the Canadians who died in the line of duty. For nearly 18 years now, Anargyros ”Jerry” Diplaros and members of his family have mourned the loss of Demetrios.

“He was typical young boy, you know, with the sports and the video games,” Jerry said during a recent interview with CityNews while showing a collection of photos of Demetrios.

The pair worked together at Cineplex before Demetrios pursued his dream of being a soldier, following in the footsteps of his father.

“‘You like it or not, but that’s up to you, all right … [there’s] going to be moments where you’re going to be like 1,000 miles far from from your family, and you’re going to face the danger,'” Jerry recalled telling his son.

“He was so proud when he was wearing the uniform.”

Jerry said one of the last, brief conversations Demetrios had was with his sister. He said his family remembered hearing gunfire at the time of the call.

“‘Sorry, I love you, but I have to go.’ Like (he) hang up the phone,” he said.

Lt.-Col. Trevor Norton is assigned to the Canadian Forces College in Toronto, but served multiple deployments in Afghanistan over two years. He described the intensity of fighting as being similar to the First World War and the Second World War albeit on a smaller scale.

“When I look back at 9/11 and realizing we are the 25th anniversary, I see a direct line from that event straight through my two deployments and to who I am now,” he said while speaking with CityNews on Friday.

“It’s the visceral environment of combat sort of brings that everything is extreme. The jokes are extreme. The sort of back and forth communications on the radio, everything is extreme because you’re you’re in an active war zone, and you know it’s the threat of serious injury and death.

“There’s also you know moments I remember about dealing with the Afghan population and getting to know them, especially in Kabul, where we would be walking through the city regularly and you would have engagements with with civilians … they impressed me in many ways.”

The losses of fellow soldiers, Norton said, had an effect on him.

“You’ve gone through the same system, wear the same uniform. You know, you have the same sense of patriotism that is pervasive in the Canadian Forces, obviously. So it it hurts each one of them, even if you didn’t know them,” Norton said.

“How do you maintain morale? It really is a focus on the mission, and it really is when you’re on the ground. It is a focus on supporting your brothers and sisters on your left and right, up and down the chain.”

He also remembered multiple repatriation ceremonies at CFB Trenton where fallen service members were flown to before a journey on the ‘Highway of Heroes,’ which saw personnel transferred to the coroner’s office in Toronto.

“Just seeing all the Canadians there holding their placards, holding the flags, and paying their respects, it it really really meant something. When you go back to Afghanistan or you’re talking to other soldiers about you know the support that Canadians are giving you, it gives you that vivid image, and which really does give you strength to know that truly the country is standing behind you,” Norton said, adding that type of support is more important than ever as approximately 3,000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel rotate annually through Latvia as part of Operation Reassurance .

As the extensive search for survivors and the remains of victims carried on at the World Trade Center in the days, weeks and months after the attack on Sept. 11, former Toronto Professional Fire Fighters’ Association (TPFFA) president Jim Lee was in contact with his counterparts in New York City.

“We knew it was going to be very, very labour-intensive (and) that it was going to take a number of firefighters to go up to where those planes had crashed in, and try and put the fire out and rescue the people. There were thousands of people in that building that obviously wanted to get out,” Lee recalled thinking at the time.

At the time, Lee said fire and police union officials asked emergency personnel here not to come due to logistical concerns involving an influx of outside help. He noted some still went down on their own accord, but the TPFFA shifted to fundraising.

“We started to raise money for the orphans and the widows of the fallen firefighters, and I’ll tell you the citizens of Canada really stepped up to the plate. They started to make money like never before, and it sent a great message to our firefighters in the U.S. that Canada was behind them 100.per cent,” Lee told CityNews.

He also recalled a large effort to bring New York City firefighters to Ontario as part of an effort to help them “regroup and have other things to think about other than trying to rescue or recover bodies.” The contingent eventually made their way to Toronto where they played a baseball game on the field at Rogers Centre, go to a Toronto Blue Jays game against the New York Yankees later on, and then a golf trip to a course near Gravenhurst.

“I think the firefighters that came in really appreciated the Toronto firefighters reaching out to them and trying to help them cope,” he said.

“It’s a brother and sisterhood.”

CityNews recently spoke with Joseph Dittmar, a retired insurance executive, about his harrowing experience escaping the World Trade Center South Tower on Sept. 11, 2001 . He talked about what it was like to see Canadians offer support in the aftermath of the devastation.

“It means the world to me … every bit of help, every ounce of help that we got from everybody, especially our great friends in Canada, was greatly appreciated by those of us that were able to escape,” he said.

“The folks that went and served their countries and served those who love freedom, those who love democracy, those who want to live in a free world-unbelievable feelings of thankfulness for them willing to do this.

“Like I said about the first responders, I don’t know how people can be that brave and that strong. I don’t know how many people — Americans, Canadians, no matter what — that I met along the way who said, “Yeah, I volunteered to go in the service. I volunteered to go to Afghanistan after 9/11 because of 9/11.

“Did we make the world a safer place? A little bit more. Do we still have a lot to go? Absolutely, positively. But every ounce of effort that any of those folks made was not in vain. It’s helped to make the world just a little bit of a better place each day as we go by.”

Meanwhile, back in Scarborough, Jerry had a message for all about remembering the sacrifices made by so many.

“On November 11, just wear the poppy, say thank you — (a) simple thank you, and keep one moment silent,” he said.

Files from The Canadian Press were used in this report

“It’s the visceral environment of combat sort of brings that everything is extreme. The jokes are extreme. The sort of back and forth communications on the radio, everything is extreme because you’re you’re in an active war zone, and you know it’s the threat of serious injury and death.

“There’s also you know moments I remember about dealing with the Afghan population and getting to know them, especially in Kabul, where we would be walking through the city regularly and you would have engagements with with civilians … they impressed me in many ways.”
The losses of fellow soldiers, Norton said, had an effect on him.

“You’ve gone through the same system, wear the same uniform. You know, you have the same sense of patriotism that is pervasive in the Canadian Forces, obviously. So it it hurts each one of them, even if you didn’t know them,” Norton said.

“How do you maintain morale? It really is a focus on the mission, and it really is when you’re on the ground. It is a focus on supporting your brothers and sisters on your left and right, up and down the chain.”

He also remembered multiple repatriation ceremonies at CFB Trenton where fallen service members were flown to before a journey on the ‘Highway of Heroes,’ which saw personnel transferred to the coroner’s office in Toronto.

“Just seeing all the Canadians there holding their placards, holding the flags, and paying their respects, it it really really meant something. When you go back to Afghanistan or you’re talking to other soldiers about you know the support that Canadians are giving you, it gives you that vivid image, and which really does give you strength to know that truly the country is standing behind you,” Norton said, adding that type of support is more important than ever as approximately 3,000 Canadian Armed Forces personnel rotate annually through Latvia as part of Operation Reassurance .

As the extensive search for survivors and the remains of victims carried on at the World Trade Center in the days, weeks and months after the attack on Sept. 11, former Toronto Professional Fire Fighters’ Association (TPFFA) president Jim Lee was in contact with his counterparts in New York City.

“We knew it was going to be very, very labour-intensive (and) that it was going to take a number of firefighters to go up to where those planes had crashed in, and try and put the fire out and rescue the people. There were thousands of people in that building that obviously wanted to get out,” Lee recalled thinking at the time.

At the time, Lee said fire and police union officials asked emergency personnel here not to come due to logistical concerns involving an influx of outside help. He noted some still went down on their own accord, but the TPFFA shifted to fundraising.

“We started to raise money for the orphans and the widows of the fallen firefighters, and I’ll tell you the citizens of Canada really stepped up to the plate. They started to make money like never before, and it sent a great message to our firefighters in the U.S. that Canada was behind them 100.per cent,” Lee told CityNews.

He also recalled a large effort to bring New York City firefighters to Ontario as part of an effort to help them “regroup and have other things to think about other than trying to rescue or recover bodies.” The contingent eventually made their way to Toronto where they played a baseball game on the field at Rogers Centre, go to a Toronto Blue Jays game against the New York Yankees later on, and then a golf trip to a course near Gravenhurst.
“I think the firefighters that came in really appreciated the Toronto firefighters reaching out to them and trying to help them cope,” he said.
“It’s a brother and sisterhood.”

CityNews recently spoke with Joseph Dittmar, a retired insurance executive, about his harrowing experience escaping the World Trade Center South Tower on Sept. 11, 2001 . He talked about what it was like to see Canadians offer support in the aftermath of the devastation.

“It means the world to me … every bit of help, every ounce of help that we got from everybody, especially our great friends in Canada, was greatly appreciated by those of us that were able to escape,” he said.

“The folks that went and served their countries and served those who love freedom, those who love democracy, those who want to live in a free world-unbelievable feelings of thankfulness for them willing to do this.

“Like I said about the first responders, I don’t know how people can be that brave and that strong. I don’t know how many people — Americans, Canadians, no matter what — that I met along the way who said, “Yeah, I volunteered to go in the service. I volunteered to go to Afghanistan after 9/11 because of 9/11.

“Did we make the world a safer place? A little bit more. Do we still have a lot to go? Absolutely, positively. But every ounce of effort that any of those folks made was not in vain. It’s helped to make the world just a little bit of a better place each day as we go by.”
Meanwhile, back in Scarborough, Jerry had a message for all about remembering the sacrifices made by so many.
“On November 11, just wear the poppy, say thank you — (a) simple thank you, and keep one moment silent,” he said.

stories.title: Lethbridge firefighters honoured at annual memorial: ‘What we signed up to do’
stories.summary: Twenty-five years after the 9/11 terrorist attacks killed hundreds of firefighters, members across North America still gather to honour the fallen.
stories.author: Justin Sibbet
stories.content:
It’s been 25 years since terrorists attacked the United States by crashing two commercial passenger jets into the World Trade Centres, one into the Pentagon and another that was taken down by passengers over a field in Pennsylvania.

Thousands of people died that day. Many who lived through witnessing it remember the tragedy as if it was yesterday.

“I was still in high school. I was in math class, so I remember exactly where I was,” said Brent Nunweiler.

A few short years later, Nunweiler himself would become a firefighter, saying he was influenced by those in service to change his career plans.

Now, he is the president of the Local Iaff 237 Firefighters Union in Lethbridge.

Far removed from the attacks in the northeastern US, Lethbridge’s brothers and sisters in the red trucks still honour the fallen every year.

“Twenty-five years ago, our profession changed forever,” Nunweiler said. “We’re honoured to recognize those from, not only New York, but our own members here who have given their lives for the community.”

During the annual event, every Iaff member across North America who passed away in the last year is honoured by having their name called.

In Lethbridge, all local members are read aloud, whether they passed away this past year, or decades ago.

“A lot of those names we read locally I worked with, (my colleagues) worked with. Their families are here, so to let their families know we are still thinking about them and that their service is honoured is extremely important,” said Nunweiler.

Most of the names of people called died, not actively battling a blaze, but to cancer.

It’s a silent killer that has claimed so many firefighters in the years since 9/11, and for generations before the attacks.

“Our risks stay with us long after we stay home. It’s a dangerous profession, one of the most dangerous in the world.

“None of us would choose a different profession, this is what we signed up to do.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "None of us would choose a different profession, this is what we signed up to do."

As this year marks a quarter-century since the attacks, it felt different for those involved in the ceremony.

“We always feel it every year, but this year we knew it was in the public awareness and lots of people have that history in their hearts,” said Neil Laboske, commander of the Iaff 237 honour guard.

He says sadness and grief is felt fully, but it’s not the only emotion relit every year on September 11.

“Immediately after the events of 9/11, everybody was very much together and working together on building a future,” he said.

That unity in the face of rubble and smoke defined the days, weeks and years after the attack.

Now, Laboske says it’s more important than ever to remain unified while honouring the fallen.

“We just hope it’s an opportunity for people to stop, look around and remember what’s really important.”

stories.title: Bruce County ready to host 100,000 visitors at International Plowing Match
stories.summary: A perfect first furrow by Canadian Plowing Champion, Tom Evans, kicks off the unofficial opening of the 2026 International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A perfect first furrow by Canadian Plowing Champion, Tom Evans, kicks off the unofficial opening of the 2026 International Plowing Match (IPM) near Walkerton.

“This marks the 50th anniversary of when it was here first. So, this is the fourth time in Bruce County and quite an honor. Until 1976, the Plowing Association didn’t think there was enough people in Bruce County to put on a plowing match. And in 1976 they broke all attendance records, so we’re hoping to do that again,” said IPM 2026 Local Committee Chair, Gord Lang, who was at the first Bruce County IPM back in 1976.

The annual celebration of agriculture has taken over 100 acres of farmland, west of Walkerton, and turned it into a tented city with cell towers, and 14 kilometres of hydro wires, and water pipes. It’s actually, the same parcel of land used to host Bruce County’s IPM in 1993.

“Well, it’s an honour. There’s no question about it. It is an honor. Now, in fairness, we didn’t own this property in 1993. We bought it shortly after 1993. But still, we’re just really proud that they decided to come back here. It’s a good spot for a match. It can rain next week. And if the rain stops by Sunday, Tuesday, it’ll be all perfect,” said Tony and Elaine Lang, the host farmers for this year’s IPM.

The five day celebration of agriculture and rural living runs from Sept. 22-26. A place for farmers and rural residents to revel in their way of life, and a place for those that don’t live in the countryside to learn more about how and why Ontario grows some of the best food and commodities in North America.

“This is a heartland for beef production and cash crops. So for us to be able to highlight that, especially in these troubled times, trade wise, it’s a perfect positive event for all,” said Executive Director of the Ontario Plowmen’s Association, Kathy Lasby.

Teeswater’s Square Dancing Tractors are coming out of retirement, as one of the main sources of IPM entertainment over the five day event, one that hopes to bounce back from a few down years in terms of attendance.

“It’s been off for the last couple of years, but this year we’re hoping to get close to 100,000 visitors, if we can,” said local organizer, Lang.

“We’ll have people from all across the province, but we also will have people from other countries. And sometimes that’s all it takes, is somebody sees something they like and relocate to our county and start their own agriculture business or any kind of a business. It’s a huge spin off for the county to have this match located right here,” said Bruce County’s Deputy Warden Don Murray.

Organizers say none of this would be possible, without the 1600 volunteers who have organized, and will run the 2026 International Plowing Match later this month.

stories.title: Mark Carney meets with ‘Forever Canadian’ campaigners in Banff
stories.summary: The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.
stories.author: Kyle Duggan and Bill Graveland
stories.content:
The head of the Forever Canadian group campaigning for Alberta to remain in the federation said Friday Prime Minister Mark Carney has been a “calm” and “reassuring” presence for Albertans.

Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta, said Carney is showing “there is someone at the helm” by standing up for Canadians in trade negotiations with the White House.

Carney shook hands with volunteers from the Forever Canadian campaign on Friday in Banff, Alta. They were invited to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on the final day of the federal cabinet retreat.

The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.

The prime minister wrote “Canada is everyone and for everyone” with a black marker on the campaign’s promotional bright pink recreational vehicle, which it’s using to travel around the province.

The crowd then broke out in a rendition of O Canada .

Alberta is set to hold a referendum on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a second vote on leaving Canada.

Carney has called for national unity but has not gone out on the campaign trail to loudly make the case for Albertans to stay in Canada.

The prime minister did not take questions from reporters on Friday.

On Thursday, Carney said he sees his role primarily as delivering on his economic agenda for Alberta and Canada to further the cause of co-operative federalism.

He also encouraged Albertans to get out to the polls next month.

“Canada is worth fighting for, and fighting for in this regard means showing up on the 19th or mailing in your ballot or participating in early voting,” Carney told reporters on Thursday.

Lukaszuk said he expects there will be “a stage in the campaign” when the prime minister will become “much more personally engaged.”

Lukaszuk also said he hopes to see the federal Conservatives get more involved in the campaign.

“The leader of the Official Opposition, Mr. Pierre Poilievre, says that his MPs from Alberta are behind us. You know, I keep looking in the rear-view mirror of this RV. I don’t see them,” he said.

“But I certainly hope that they get engaged because this is not a partisan issue and this is the time where all hands are on deck.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "But I certainly hope that they get engaged because this is not a partisan issue and this is the time where all hands are on deck."

While the federal cabinet chose to hold their meeting this week in Alberta and to meet with some of the province’s mayors, ministers did not spell out any future plans to take part in the remain campaign.

At a closing news conference on Friday, Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, who represents an Edmonton riding, said it’s not the job of the federal government to tell Alberta what to do.

“Our role with respect to this referendum certainly is not to tell Albertans how to do anything. It’s not to tell Albertans how to vote. It is to make sure that we are a strong partner with Alberta, that we collaborate in terms of projects and other steps that we’re taking to build a unified country together,” she said.

Olszewski said the federal government’s actions “speak a lot more loudly than if we just stand at a microphone and say some platitudes about Alberta.”

But she also said her colleagues are “absolutely” calling for Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

“We are talking to Albertans about the importance of remaining in Canada,” she said. “We’re showing Albertans that Canada works, that we’re doing our best to ensure that our country works for all regions across the country.”

On Thursday, Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas credited Carney and his cabinet for putting in “hard work” in his province and for not taking an off-putting approach to the debate over separation.

“If they had just diminished this to transactions, if they had asked Albertans, ‘Well, what’s it going to take to keep you?’ then I think Albertans are smart. We would have been able to see through that,” Farkas told reporters.

“They have been present not just in major events like Stampede but also … visiting rural communities in Alberta. There’s many areas of Alberta that haven’t seen a member of Parliament from outside of the province — let alone a Liberal member of Parliament — in many, many decades.

“They’re showing up to listen, to learn and to be able to support common cause.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "They're showing up to listen, to learn and to be able to support common cause."

Thomas Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier of Alberta, said Carney is showing “there is someone at the helm” by standing up for Canadians in trade negotiations with the White House.

Carney shook hands with volunteers from the Forever Canadian campaign on Friday in Banff, Alta. They were invited to the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity on the final day of the federal cabinet retreat.
The prime minister was cheered by about 50 supporters of the Forever Canadian campaign, almost all holding red and white signs and some wearing the maple leaf.
The prime minister wrote “Canada is everyone and for everyone” with a black marker on the campaign’s promotional bright pink recreational vehicle, which it’s using to travel around the province.
The crowd then broke out in a rendition of O Canada.
Alberta is set to hold a referendum on Oct. 19 on whether to hold a second vote on leaving Canada.
Carney has called for national unity but has not gone out on the campaign trail to loudly make the case for Albertans to stay in Canada.

The prime minister did not take questions from reporters on Friday. On Thursday, Carney said he sees his role primarily as delivering on his economic agenda for Alberta and Canada to further the cause of co-operative federalism.
He also encouraged Albertans to get out to the polls next month.
“Canada is worth fighting for, and fighting for in this regard means showing up on the 19th or mailing in your ballot or participating in early voting,” Carney told reporters on Thursday.
Lukaszuk said he expects there will be “a stage in the campaign” when the Prime Minister will become “much more personally engaged.”
Lukaszuk also said he hopes to see the federal Conservatives get more involved in the campaign.
“The leader of the Official Opposition, Mr. Pierre Poilievre, says that his MPs from Alberta are behind us. You know, I keep looking in the rearview mirror of this RV. I don’t see them,” he said.
“But I certainly hope that they get engaged because this is not a partisan issue and this is the time where all hands are on deck.”

While the federal cabinet chose to hold their meeting this week in Alberta and to meet with some of the province’s mayors, ministers did not spell out any future plans to take part in the remain campaign.
At a closing news conference on Friday, Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, who represents an Edmonton riding, said it’s not the job of the federal government to tell Alberta what to do.

“Our role with respect to this referendum certainly is not to tell Albertans how to do anything. It’s not to tell Albertans how to vote. It is to make sure that we are a strong partner with Alberta, that we collaborate in terms of projects and other steps that we’re taking to build a unified country together,” she said.
Olszewski said the federal government’s actions “speak a lot more loudly than if we just stand at a microphone and say some platitudes about Alberta.”
But she also said her colleagues are “absolutely” calling for Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

“We are talking to Albertans about the importance of remaining in Canada,” she said. “We’re showing Albertans that Canada works, that we’re doing our best to ensure that our country works for all regions across the country.”
On Thursday, Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas credited Carney and his cabinet for putting in “hard work” in his province and for not taking an off-putting approach to the debate over separation.

“If they had just diminished this to transactions – if they had asked Albertans, ’Well, what’s it going to take to keep you?’ – then I think Albertans are smart. We would have been able to see through that,” Farkas told reporters.

“They have been present not just in major events like Stampede but also ... visiting rural communities in Alberta. There’s many areas of Alberta that haven’t seen a member of Parliament from outside of the province – let alone a Liberal member of Parliament – in many, many decades.
“They’re showing up to listen, to learn and to be able to support common cause.”

stories.title: They were strangers when grounded in Newfoundland on 9/11. But they soon fell in love
stories.summary: A real life inspiration for the ‘Come From Away’ musical, one couple told CTV News Channel how they fell in love in the midst of one of America’s worst terrorist attacks.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
A real life inspiration for the “Come From Away” musical, one couple shared how they fell in love in the midst of the worst terrorist attack in U.S. history.

Nick and Diane Marson explained in an interview with CTV News Channel Friday how their flight was diverted to the Newfoundland town of Gambo , after planes struck the World Trade Center in New York on Sept. 11, 2001.

That’s where their love story began.

“For the longest time we had survivor’s guilt, we didn’t feel comfortable with what happened to us,” Nick said, adding his and Diane’s stay in Gambo “turned out to be a wonderful five days.”

He said he felt for the families of the victims of the attack, but now was grateful for how his life turned out.

“We would’ve never met otherwise,” Diane added.

The couple was waiting in line for blankets at a shelter 40 kilometres from Gander, N.L.

“And this attractive American lady stood in line next to me,” Nick, who speaks with an English accent, said.

“She turned to me and said ‘they smell like–‘,” he added, before Diane chimed in with “mothballs,” finishing his sentence.

“It turned out to be quite a good pick-up line,” Nick said.

The couple said they had never heard of Gander before and needed to pull out maps to locate Newfoundland when it was announced their flight was being diverted. But once they landed, they were treated with kindness.

“We had no expectations, but we were met with angels, we were put down in Heaven, these angels looking after us,” Nick said. “They fed us, they gave us somewhere to sleep, they gave us a hug, they started to entertain us.

“If it hadn’t been for all that, Diane and I would have never got together.”

The locals even “Screeched” their visitors, a Newfoundland tradition that Diane explained makes a person an “honourary Newfoundlander.”

The term “Screech” comes from Newfoundland fishers who would sail to other ports to sell their fish, loaded in barrels, then bring back rum in those same barrels, which supposedly negatively affected the taste of the rum, she said.

“They were trying to lighten the mood and entertain us,” Diane said about her hosts. She also confirmed that she did kiss a cod fish, an Atlantic Canada rite of passage.

It was on the school bus to the airport after their five-day stay that they decided to start living the rest of their lives together.

“I actually put my arm around her to kiss her on the forehead, because that was as advanced as a British guy would dare be,” Nick said.

“And I just grabbed him and kissed him on the mouth,” Diane said. “Because I knew if I didn’t, I would never see him again.”

Nick called Diane’s smooch “her ace card.” He said that kiss made its way into the award-winning musical “Come From Away,” which the couple claimed to have seen more than 160 times, where a flight attendant offers an older couple a cold towel, rather than a hot towel, as they were “canoodling.”

“It actually really happened,” he said.

The romance continued after the couple’s flight out of Newfoundland. They used phone calls and email, until Nick proposed over the phone.

“And I said yes,” Diane said, adding that a house was bought two weeks later. They got married on Sept. 7, 2002, and honeymooned in Gambo.

stories.title: Dawson community marks 20 years since college shooting
stories.summary: Survivors and family members reflected on the tragedy's legacy and ongoing calls for stronger gun-control measures.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Elizabeth Zogalis
stories.content:
Twenty years after a shooting at Dawson College claimed the life of 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa and injured 19 others, survivors, family members and members of the college community gathered Friday to remember the victims and reflect on how the tragedy has shaped their lives.

The commemoration at the college’s Peace Garden brought together alumni, friends, relatives, dignitaries and first responders, many of whom continue to carry the impact of Sept. 13, 2006.

For survivor Hayder Kadhim, memories of that day remain vivid.

“It feels like 20 days ago,” he said. “Like I am still 17 years old.”

Kadhim was shot three times during the attack, in the leg, neck and head. Despite the passage of two decades, he said the anniversary was also a reminder of the resilience that emerged in its aftermath.

“Seeing everyone here today, the fact that 20 years later we are still able to make something great out of this, I think it feels inspiring,” he said.

Kadhim said he continues to draw inspiration from De Sousa, whom he remembers for her positivity.

“Losing a friend that had such a good vibe … having survived it and knowing that I was given a second chance, it almost felt like a duty or a mission that I had to continue spreading the positivity that she had,” he said.

Another survivor, Meaghan Hennegan, said the anniversary highlights how remembrance has evolved into action.

“We’re far enough removed from the actual tragedy that remembrance is being turned into action,” she said.

Hennegan has spent the past two decades advocating for stronger gun-control laws, a cause she says is deeply personal.

“It’s something that is very personal to me and I feel like I am making a positive contribution to the safety of not only students at school, but our society and country as a whole,” she said.

Following the ceremony, De Sousa’s mother, Louise De Sousa, helped plant three pink heather plants in her daughter’s honour.

“I am sure she is very happy with the garden we have growing here,” she said.

De Sousa said her family continues to keep Anastasia’s memory alive through stories and conversations.

“All the good and the bad things she did. She was a normal teenager,” she said. “I always said, yes, she had a beautiful smile, she was fun and loving, but she was also a little brat,” she said jokingly.

Now, 20 years later, De Sousa said she still finds herself wondering what kind of woman her daughter would have become. She also continues to advocate for stronger gun-control laws, saying the work remains unfinished long after the anniversary ceremonies end.

stories.title: ‘We didn’t know if we would get locked out, fined, or the place would burn down’: Trails End vendor speaks out
stories.summary: Gates and barricades now block the entrances to Trail’s End Farmer’s Market.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Gates and barricades now block the entrances to Trails End Farmer’s Market.

And while some go around, vendor Alex Schelhaas, no longer worries about access.

He is now on the outside looking in.

This week he cleared out his Trails End business Legacy Gems Co. after the Thames Centre Fire Department (Tcfd) posted a closure order for what it called, “Potentially catastrophic fire code violations.”

Given the action, Schelhaas felt he had no other option but to close his stall.

“We just didn’t feel safe leaving our stuff behind. We didn’t know if we would get locked out, fined, or the place would burn down.”

But while he has packed up, he said other vendors are still questioning their futures while worrying about their ability to make ends meet.

“It’s their lives. It’s not just a hobby or a side gig. For some people, it’s everything. For them, it’s their bread and butter. And without that, they’re going to be homeless.”

Schelhaas tells CTV News there were ‘rumblings’ of concern inside the market for the last several weeks.

“You know, one thing led to another. And I guess there are a lot more problems than people understood there were. So, it’s devastating.”

Schelhaas said inspectors of varying types visited the main building his stall was located in.

At the same time, he said the operators of Trail’s End were conducting cosmetic and facility upgrades.

“They were updating stuff as they go. So, while we were there, the floors were getting updated. The lights were getting updated.”

But it was not enough to satisfy fire inspectors, who again cautioned Friday that anyone disobeying the closure order is “guilty of an offence.”

Tcfd Chief Neil Dorken added that the inspectors will monitor activities on the site this weekend.

Meanwhile, Shelhaas said he understands the directive, but reiterated his concern for fellow vendors and the on-site manager.

“People are hanging on by a thread in this economy, especially in a place near London, where it’s the highest unemployment rate. So, we can’t really afford to lose something small like this because it might mean everything to somebody.”

CTV News has again reached out to officials with Trails End. A phone call was answered and a message left, but we have not received a reply.

Chief Dorken confirmed Trails End management reached out to Tcfd on Friday afternoon.

stories.title: How 9/11 changed Canadian airport security
stories.summary: "If you want to fly, you have to be prepared to accept the security regime."
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
A travelling parent with kids cannot take a 460-millilitre jar of peanut butter through airport security. It’s not an allergen issue, but rather it is too large: a spreadable food, treated like a liquid. But any number of containers of it less than 100 ml is OK.

At one airport, a blazer comes off; at another, it stays on. The same thing with shoes and laptops, all according to the rules that can look arbitrary or capricious to onlookers.

For Margaret Bloodworth, the former deputy minister of transport who helped manage Canada’s response on Sept. 11, 2001, that apparent regulatory mismatch is not entirely a design flaw.

“In any human system, there’s going to be some inconsistencies,” Bloodworth said. And in airport security, she argues, the reality is that the machinery itself keeps changing: newer equipment can see things older equipment cannot, while smaller airports May not have the same technology as Toronto or Vancouver.

Still, many travellers’ questions remain: Why must so much of flying now involve a hodgepodge ritual of belts, bins, scans, re-scans and Ziploc-ing bite-sized toothpaste tubes? It goes to the heart of how Canada built a modern security apparatus in a crisis, what trade-offs it accepted, and whether a system designed during an emergency has adequately distinguished genuine protection from permanent habit.

Though the inconsistencies are real, so is the risk that a perfectly standardized system becomes perfectly learnable.

“If you are predictable, then it’s dangerous,” said Jacques Duchesneau, the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority’s founding president and CEO, who led Catsa from 2002 to 2008. “If you are predictable, you are unsafe.”

Security can look different from one airport or lane to another, because officials do not want a would-be attacker to know precisely what to expect, he told the Post.

We’re saving lives

'There's Been A Tragedy': The untold history of Canada's 9/11 response

How Canada's best-known 9/11 widow became a fierce advocate for terrorist victims

“We’re not searching people,” he said. “We’re saving lives.”

The post-9/11 system was born in a fog of fear, urgency and incomplete (at the time) information. Bloodworth, who later became national security adviser to then prime minister Stephen Harper, said that officials had to make urgent calls, with little certainty about the scale of the threat.

“We really did know very little to begin with,” she said. “And yet had to make decisions, first of all to land planes, then what we do when we get them on the ground, and then when do we let them up, and on what grounds do we let them fly again?”

David Collenette, then the federal transport minister, was one of the few people with statutory authority under the Aeronautics Act to issue the orders that grounded and redirected aviation traffic over Canada. He estimates that roughly 500 flights and 85,000 people were involved as aircraft were told not to proceed into the United States and, in many cases, to return across the Atlantic.

The attacks did not reveal merely a gap in airport screening. They exposed a seismic change in the threat model. Earlier aviation-security regimes had been built to confront hijackers seeking leverage, or bombers placing luggage on an aircraft while remaining behind. Air India and Lockerbie had already taught governments the necessity of matching bags to passengers and removing unaccompanied baggage.

Then came 9/11 and attackers prepared to die with the aircraft and turn it into a weapon.

“That required another rethink,” Bloodworth said. “You had to think, ‘Well, okay, we’ve got to watch people that want to get on a plane. They not only want to bring the plane down; they’re prepared to go down with us.’”

The changes were swift. Canada created Catsa in 2002 as a publicly funded national authority to screen passengers, baggage and non-passengers entering restricted airport areas. Before that, Bloodworth said, airlines often hired local screening companies themselves, producing uneven training and standards.

“It might be the commissionaires of the office building down the street,” she said of the pre-9/11 arrangement. Catsa and the U.S. Transportation Security Administration were meant to replace that patchwork with common training, specialized equipment and centralized accountability.

New decisions were required, and at breaking speed. Collenette said a regulation that would normally take “about two years of consultation” was reviewed within two weeks. He recalls a scramble to obtain baggage-screening equipment that had to be manufactured quickly. Canada also hardened cockpit doors, an obvious vulnerability in retrospect, but one that had encountered resistance before the attacks.

A year prior, Collenette said, he had raised concerns about open cockpit doors. At the time, “it was the world of goodwill.” Children might be invited forward to see the cockpit; pilots might allow visitors in. “I had an uneasy feeling,” he said.

In the weeks and months that followed, governments expanded airport screening, and new province-wide offices with expanded mandates. New money, powers and institutions flowed to the RCMP, Csis, the Canada Border Services Agency and other parts of the federal apparatus. Anne McLellan, Canada’s first minister of public safety and emergency preparedness from 2003 to 2006, said the post-9/11 challenge was to build an architecture that had been missing pieces — and, above all, to get agencies to cooperate in exchanges of crucial data.

“Agencies were not sharing relevant information,” McLellan said. The priority was building the capacity and culture for intelligence and law-enforcement bodies to share it “in real time” and get it “to the front lines where people could use it.”

By McLellan’s account, agencies did not always mesh smoothly. She described the relationship between the RCMP and the newly created Cbsa as “not a frictionless relationship.” At one point, she said, Cbsa officers sought to be armed while the RCMP opposed it, creating a substantial dispute.

More fundamentally, McLellan recalled resisting pressure to make a new screening system serve a broader policing purpose. Police wanted access to screening information to identify people wanted for any offence. Her response was sharp.

“We’re protecting planes,” she said. “We’re not trying to find pickpockets here.”

McLellan says ministers and legislators must continually balance safety gains against the risk of eroding rights and privacy. “That is a constant tension,” she said. “It has to be managed.”

Duchesneau’s perspective is, the system must react to real threats, even when the reaction later looks to some as over the top. One example: A 2006 transatlantic aircraft plot was thwarted, as terrorists tried to detonate liquid explosives disguised as soft drinks on multiple flights travelling from the United Kingdom to the United States and Canada.

With it, aviation security around the world changed almost overnight, he said. He was called at 2 a.m.; by 5 a.m. new liquid-and-gel directives were in place across Canada. Thus, no inflight peanut butter jars for the kids.

“We always need to wait for something bad to happen to put measures in place,” Duchesneau lamented. “We were, let’s say, fighting the last war instead of being proactive.”

The passenger who sees a rule as irrational May be looking at the fossil of a plot, an attack, an intelligence warning or a technological limitation. Security is “reactive by nature,” Duchesneau said, and “when you react, you’re always one step behind.”

Yet the official case for the system is not solely based on fear or history. Catsa says its mandate is to detect, prevent and respond to threats while keeping people and goods moving through the air-transportation network. In its statement to the Post, Catsa said 96 per cent of passengers at Canada’s busiest airports waited less than 15 minutes for screening in 2025-26; 91 per cent reported a positive screening experience and 89 per cent expressed confidence in security screening.

Transport Canada says aviation security is now a multi-layered system involving Catsa, the RCMP, Cbsa, Csis, local authorities and international partners. It points to measures including non-passenger screening, U.S. preclearance, the Passenger Protect Program, Verified Traveller lanes, cargo targeting and computed-tomography X-ray technology for carry-on baggage.

And still, not everything’s in sync. Bloodworth notes that the first explosive-detection equipment was expected to be overtaken technologically within five years. A quarter-century later, airports are using “different generations of machines,” often within the same country.

All of the hoops, the regulations, the minutia, are “sort of like the price of admission,” Collenette said. “If you want to fly, you have to be prepared to accept the security regime.”

By The Canadian Press

Niagara-ON-THE-Lake - Police in Niagara Region say they have charged one of their own officers with impaired driving after he allegedly fled an attempted traffic stop and collided with another vehicle.

Police say they responded to reports of an impaired driver in Niagara-on-the-Lake around 8:20 p.m. on Thursday and tried to stop a grey Dodge Ram pickup truck in the area of Glendale Avenue and Taylor Road.

They say the driver failed to stop and police began pursuing the vehicle, but the chase was called off for public safety reasons.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Minutes later, police say the pickup collided with another vehicle and the driver was arrested at the scene and taken to hospital with serious injuries.

They say the suspect, a 54-year-old man from Fort Erie, Ont., has been a member of the Niagara regional police force for 21 years.

The officer is facing several charges including impaired operation of a conveyance, flight from a peace officer and dangerous operation.

He has been suspended with pay pending an investigation, and police say the Special Investigations Unit has invoked its mandate due to injuries he sustained in the crash.

Niagara police say no other injuries were reported.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.
