stories.title: Peace Garden ceremony at Canada-U.S. border marks 25th anniversary of 9/11 attacks
stories.summary: Hundreds gathered at the International Peace Garden to remember the 9/11 terrorist attacks in a ceremony that also affirmed close bonds between Canada and the United States.
stories.author: Ian Bickis
stories.content:
Hundreds gathered Friday on a remote stretch of the Prairies to remember the 9/11 terrorist attacks in a ceremony that also affirmed close bonds between Canada and the United States.

Firefighters from across southern Manitoba marched to the skirl of a bagpipe at the International Peace Garden, a park straddling the Canada-U.S. border at Manitoba and North Dakota.

Salvaged beams from the destroyed World Trade Center in New York City sit in the garden as part of a permanent memorial to the attacks 25 years ago.

Jason Shaw, a deputy fire chief in Winnipeg, said communities and countries came together on Sept. 11, 2001, and that the love and compassion shown to neighbours pierced the darkness of the day.

“Canadians and Americans have always reached across the border in support of each other.”

In the final prayer of the ceremony, 1st Lt. J. Nathan Haugen with the U.S. air force called the garden a place of enduring fellowship and the sacred steel of the beams a testament to resilience, courage and sacrifice.

“Lord, as we stand along this quiet border, where two nations meet not in division, but in shared purpose, we thank you for that unbreakable bond,” said Haugen.

In the crowd were high school students who had not yet been born in 2001.

Audrey Emerson said her parents have told her how they vividly remember being in their school classrooms on 9/11, and that it was good to hear more at the ceremony Friday.

She was decked out in her crown and sash as the North Dakota contestant for this year’s Miss Teen USA pageant.

“Getting to hear about all the stories is amazing. Even though I was not born at that time, (it was interesting) just hearing about it and being educated on all the different stories,” she said.

“And now I think about Sept. 11 in a different way.”

Retired auditor Mae Streich of Bottineau, N.D., said she has been to every 9/11 ceremony at the garden.

“If we don’t remember and keep remembering the past, we can’t move on to the future,” said Streich, wearing an American flag coat.

She said she’s proud of Canada for doing so much to make the ceremony happen and to have been instrumental in making the memorial at the site.

It’s a testament of what the relationship could be during the current Canada-U.S. trade war, she said.

“I’m very sad that we’re acting the way we are,” said Streich.

Also in attendance were Terry and Kathy Harder. Along with marking the solemn day, they were also celebrating their 55th wedding anniversary.

The couple, who recently moved to the area from Tennessee, said it’s hard to keep the two apart.

“I don’t think you separate it. Sept. 11 is a big day now of sadness for a lot of people,” said Kathy Harder.

But she said it was good to mark the day with so many people.

“We’re just happy to be here.”

stories.title: Lake Ontario merchandise turns Trump order into fundraiser to protect the lake
stories.summary: A Lake Ontario-inspired phrase is being turned into merchandise, with part of the proceeds going toward protecting and restoring the lake.
stories.author: Prisha Dev, Germain Ma
stories.content:
A lighthearted quip sparked by U.S. President Donald Trump’s labelling of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” has turned into a fundraiser aimed at protecting the lake itself.

Lloyd Rang, who lives in the municipality of Clarington, Ont., a short walk from Lake Ontario, describes it as peaceful and an important part of his community.

So when Trump first floated a new name for the lake amid trade tensions with Canada, Rang had a response.

“I thought about it, ‘Aw come on, like really? This again?’” he said in an interview Global News.

“Oh, my hydronyms are Lake and Ontario.”

A hydronym is the proper name for any body water. Prime Minister Mark Carney brought the term into the national conversation in an Aug. 27 statement responding to Trump’s executive order seeking to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America.”

Rang, a municipal councillor of Clarington who is not seeking re-election, thought the phrase could work on sweatshirts, T-shirts and hats.

“I’ve only ever gotten laughs,” Rang said.

However, he also saw an opportunity to turn the attention surrounding Lake Ontario into something more meaningful.

“And I thought, how can I take this idea which I think might take off, and put it to some good use that might actually protect the lake?” he said.

Rang reached out to Swim Drink Fish, a Canadian non-profit focused on protecting water, and put forward a plan to donate $10 from the sale of each item.

The organization said the attention comes as Lake Ontario faces environmental pressures that extend far beyond the political debate surrounding its name.

“Aquatic invasive species, the impacts of climate change, water levels are a big issue of concern on Lake Ontario,” said Gregory Ford with Swim Drink Fish. “We see shoreline erosion. We see flooding.”

Money raised through the merchandise will support the organization’s restoration projects, water monitoring and advocacy work.

Ford said the unusual political attention surrounding the lake has also created an opportunity to get more people thinking about its future.

“People are talking about Lake Ontario for the first time in a long time, in a really positive way, and I would like to see this keep going,” he said.

Rang said the merchandise has been successful so far, with interest coming from well beyond the shores of Lake Ontario.

“What I understand from the distributor is, they’ve had calls from as far away as Australia, Asia, and calls from all over Canada,” he said. “They’re shipping orders to the United States, even.”

For Rang, the humour behind the merchandise is also a distinctly Canadian way of responding to a political dispute with the country’s closest geographical neighbour.

“The border is sometimes like a bit of a one-way mirror where we see them more clearly than they see us,” he said.

“The ability to laugh in the face of something that’s potentially quite serious is actually a sign of strength.”

stories.title: Sovereignty referendum becomes the latest focus of Quebec election campaign
stories.summary: PQ’s St-Pierre Plamondon promises to hold a vote even with a minority government
stories.author: Maura Forrest, Eric Andrew-Gee
stories.content:
The Parti Québécois’s commitment to a third referendum on independence took centre stage in the Quebec election campaign this week, despite the party’s best efforts to shift the attention of a nervous electorate away from the question of sovereignty.

On Friday, the PQ confirmed it will cost at least $130-million to hold an independence referendum in a first mandate, as Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to do if his party forms government on Oct. 5.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also said this week that he would pursue a referendum even without a majority government – a challenging proposition that would require support from members of opposition parties.

Meanwhile, Christine Fréchette, leader of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s chief rival, tripped up over the independence question this week when she refused – not for the first time – to say if she is a sovereigntist despite her opposition to a referendum.

Sovereignty is broadly unpopular in Quebec, with support for independence stuck around 30 per cent as the escalating Canada-U.S. trade war looms over the campaign. Last month, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon announced he would not hold a referendum until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office . Mr. Trump’s current term is meant to end Jan. 20, 2029. The move was the PQ Leader’s bid to focus the campaign elsewhere.

For a while, that seemed to work. In the early days of the campaign, other issues were shunted aside as the major party leaders jockeyed to position themselves as best equipped to defend Quebec’s interests against a hostile U.S. administration.

But the PQ Leader faced repeated questions this week about his insistence on a referendum. In an interview with The Canadian Press published Friday, he said the party has budgeted $20-million for a travelling commission that would consult on the adoption of a provisional constitution.

Holding a referendum in 2029 or 2030 would cost at least $110-million, he said. The party has confirmed the figures to The Globe and Mail.

The PQ has been leading in the polls for the better part of three years, but currently seems unlikely to form a majority government. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon maintained several times this week that his commitment to a referendum would not change in a minority context.

“I think I have a responsibility to keep my promises,” he told a panel of Radio-Canada journalists during a televised event Wednesday featuring interviews with each of the five main party leaders.

In Quebec, the National Assembly must adopt the text of a referendum question drafted by the government, meaning a PQ minority would require support from opposition parties to trigger a vote on independence.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon suggested that some members of the nationalist CAQ, the sovereigntist Québec Solidaire and the Quebec Conservatives could support a PQ minority. “There are plenty of scenarios,” he said.

However, Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime was quick to say this week that if his party holds the balance of power in a minority government, he would “block any referendum project.” The Conservatives are projected to win seats in the provincial legislature for the first time this fall.

Ms. Fréchette has also said repeatedly that this would be the “worst moment” in the 50 years since the Parti Québécois first formed government to hold a referendum, given the tariff war with the United States.

But on Thursday, she refused to say whether she herself remains a sovereigntist. “My personal position doesn’t matter,” she told reporters.

Ms. Fréchette worked as a staffer for the Parti Québécois between 2012 and 2014. This is not the first time she has refused to say how she would vote in a third referendum on independence.

“What I’ve observed is that 70 per cent of Quebeckers don’t want a referendum,” she said in a video posted later to social media.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, who has cast his party as the only federalist option, demanded that Ms. Fréchette clarify her position, calling her answer “shameful.”

When QS Leader Ruba Ghazal was asked if she would support the PQ’s sovereignty referendum, she said her party would campaign for an independent Quebec, but also advocate for broad public consultations to ensure “everyone is on board.”

The “most plausible ally” for the PQ in launching a referendum is the QS, said Patrick Taillon, professor of constitutional law at Laval University.

However, given their strong disagreements over everything from government spending to immigration, and QS’s weaker emphasis on independence as opposed to social justice, there is no guarantee the parties would work together on a referendum project.

It is also unclear how many of their 11 seats QS will retain after the election, given the party’s weak position in the polls currently.

On top of unreliable support in the legislature, the PQ faces a number of self-imposed hurdles to launching a referendum in its first mandate, Prof. Taillon noted.

“The PQ’s roadmap includes several steps before the referendum: consultations on a provisional constitution, adoption of that constitution by the National Assembly, and dialogue with First Nations. Even apart from the question of a minority government, this represents a fairly demanding timetable.”

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney reaches out to pro-Canada referendum campaigners in Banff
stories.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney met with a Canadian sovereignty group in Banff as a federal cabinet planning session ends.
stories.author: Bill Kaufmann
stories.content:
Banff — Amid criticism that he’s not doing enough to boost anti-separatist forces in Alberta, Prime Minister Mark Carney met with pro-Canada supporters outside a cabinet gathering in this Rocky Mountain resort town.

On Thursday at the cabinet planning forum, Carney wouldn’t commit to injecting federal money into the pro-Canada side, but urged people to vote in the Oct. 19 referendum that includes a question on Alberta’s future in Confederation.

Anti-separatist, Forever Canadian crusader Thomas Lukaszuk pulled up outside the cabinet meeting Friday in his campaign RV for a brief chat with Carney. The prime minister, he said, invited him to the gathering.

He said he’s not concerned that Carney hasn’t made a major effort to counter separatists in Alberta ahead of the referendum, which asks Albertans if they want to proceed to a binding vote on independence.

“I know the prime minister will become much more visible when the right time comes,” said Lukaszuk.

“The prime minister made comments (Thursday) about the importance of the referendum and voter turnout. That means you’re doing your job.”

But he said Conservative politicians who have pledged support have yet to show it.

Just before he departed Banff, Carney chatted and joked with a throng of Forever Canadian volunteers before leading a rendition of O Canada with them.

He scrawled “Canada is everyone and for everyone,” on the side of the Forever Canadian RV.

When asked if her government will become more actively involved in the referendum campaign, one of Alberta’s three Liberal MPs said Ottawa is doing that by ensuring vital infrastructure projects, such as signing an MOU on a new oil pipeline to the B.C. coast, benefit Albertans.

“Our role, really, as the federal government is to act as a partner and to make sure with respect to Alberta that we are engaged with them collaboratively, that we’re working on projects,” said Eleanor Olszewski, MP for Edmonton Centre and Minister Responsible for Prairies Economic Development.

“We’ve had a lot of discussions to the effect that Alberta is central to our vision of building Canada strong.”

There’s some concern among pro-Canada ranks that their foes are badly outspending them as the referendum campaign

Meanwhile, Canadian leaders in Banff offered an olive branch to their U.S. counterparts in recalling the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks 25 years on.

Speaking at their cabinet forum in Banff, Internal Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said he was in touch with U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who lost a brother in the World Trade Center after two hijacked passenger planes slammed into it. About 600 people in Lutnick’s business also died in the attack.

“Early this morning, I sent a text message to Secretary Howard Lutnick telling him I was thinking of his family on this anniversary of 9/11,” LeBlanc told reporters just before the two-day gathering ended.

“He has talked to me often about what that meant for him and his family, so I sent him a message.”

That exchange underlined the reality that both sides in the Canada-U.S. trade impasse are speaking to one another, though no return to the negotiating table is planned after Ottawa suspended talks Aug. 21, with the Canadian side saying they were presented with unacceptable last-minutes terms threatening the country’s sovereignty.

Since then, both sides have traded retaliatory tariffs.

On Thursday in Calgary, Carney said he still speaks with U.S. President Donald Trump, though he added those conversations haven’t centred on the trade war.

Minutes before LeBlanc spoke, a sombre-sounding Carney also commented on the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks that claimed nearly 3,000 lives, including 24 Canadians.

While he acknowledged the trauma Americans suffered that day, he reiterated how Canadians didn’t hesitate to assist their southern neighbour.

He recalled that Gander, N.L., took in thousands of stranded American air passengers, and that Canada sacrificed 158 soldiers in the Afghanistan war that followed 9/11.

“The lesson, I’d suggest, of these events is the response is to reach out, to support, to stand in solidarity, as Canadians did, with our American neighbours, to reach out to strangers,” said Carney.

Federal cabinet ministers are in Banff to chart a path forward in the face of the trade war with the U.S., seeking to hammer out ways of speeding approval of infrastructure projects and diversifying trade.

On Thursday, Ukraine and Canada signed agreement to assist that country in its war with Russia, as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke with cabinet members in Calgary and Banff.

LeBlanc on Friday said in the absence of trade talks, the country is working toward streamlining government approvals of nation-building infrastructure projects, while also breaking down interprovincial trade barriers. Legislation toward streamlining is coming this fall, said ministers.

“The reason we’re doing this is because of the economic headwinds the country’s facing,” he said.

And he dismissed reports the U.S. and Mexico are hastening toward a bilateral agreement that could leave Canada out in the cold.

“They’ve been at this for a number of months, and speeding toward a deal two months from now doesn’t feel like speed,” said LeBlanc.

“But they are having those conversations as we did, and we May again, at some point.”

When asked if the government is concerned bilateral talks with Mexico could scuttle the wider Canada-U.S.-Mexico trade pact, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said they’re focused on what they can control.

“That includes being less reliant on one trading partner and more reliant on the rest of the world, and building the structures, the rules and the kind of government you need to make sure Canada gets the world it needs and wants,” said Champagne.

In that spirit of economic development, the federal government is hosting an investment summit in Toronto next week, hoping to attract $1 trillion in international investments for nearly 170 projects across the country.

First Nations are ready to benefit from the effort to fast-track projects, said Mark Podlasly, a member of an Indigenous stakeholder group pushing for Indigenous participation. But Podlasly, who presented to cabinet members, said there are roadblocks.

“(First) Nations are not generally opposed to projects, Nations want to see projects that are in their benefit, help their populations,” said Podlasly, chief sustainability officer at the First Nations Major Projects Coalition.

“The No. 1 issue is access to affordable capital. Indigenous people do not have easy access to capital like other Canadians.”

stories.title: Senior dead after two-vehicle crash in West Perth
stories.summary: An 89-year-old Stratford woman is dead following a two-vehicle collision in West Perth on Friday morning.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
An 89-year-old Stratford woman is dead following a two-vehicle collision in West Perth on Friday morning.

Perth County OPP, along with Perth County and Huron County paramedics and the West Perth Fire Department, responded to the collision on Perth Road 180 at the intersection of Perth Line 36 shortly after 9 a.m.

Police say the woman, who was driving one of the vehicles, suffered life-threatening injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene.

No one else was injured as a result of the collision.

The roadways have since reopened.

stories.title: Globe journalists share their 9/11 experiences from New York and beyond, 25 years later
stories.summary: What our reporters remember from their time spent covering the Sept. 11 attacks
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
In the minutes and hours following the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Globe journalists flew into action – some heading immediately for the U.S. border from Toronto, others surveying the landscape in Ottawa and elsewhere. It was a day when their professional responsibilities had to outweigh their personal concerns as the world changed around them.

Twenty-five years later, they can still remember every detail. Here, they recollect those moments.

On Sept. 11, 2001, I was among a team of Globe reporters who drove from Toronto to New York City. We crossed the border in the afternoon and arrived at midnight.

I remember it being the first time I ever saw the Manhattan skyline. As big as it was, it was absolutely dwarfed by an enormous smoke plume that was still growing. Nearly 3,000 people were underneath the rubble of what had been the World Trade Center.

To see this was to feel as if New York had been hit by an inscrutable bolt from the blue. The strike was actually affected by Boeing 767s commandeered by a handful of terrorists armed with box cutters. A quarter century later, my impressions of the aftermath remain.

I remember a sun-dappled Sept. 12 spent partly in a midtown playground where a group of moms pointed at a playing four-year-old, saying he was unaware his firefighter dad had likely perished. I remember the people who began posting myriad photocopies of their missing loved ones’ faces around town, holding out all hope against odds. I remember the resigned families starting to queue around the block, bringing hair and toothbrushes to forensic officials for future DNA matches of whatever might eventually be exhumed underneath the burned and collapsed wreckage.

I remember that week’s shock and grief, and also the rage that was starting to brew in America, as a counterpoint to a document I acquired several months later.

In small-town Florida, I obtained a copy of the lead al-Qaeda terrorists’ flight school invoices. These itemized bills showed the enemy agents had methodically embedded in America for months, patiently logging their hours flying Cessnas. This was done in preparation for their eventual terrorist attacks on New York and Washington. – Colin Freeze , reporter

I was still at home on the morning of Sept 11. I turned on the TV to see smoke coming out of the World Trade Center. Then I watched the second plane hit. The phone rang, and my colleague Jeff Sallot asked, “Are you watching this?” I said yes, and he told me to go to the American embassy. At that point there was a palpable fear that there were probably more attacks coming, and maybe in Canada.

Employees were leaving the U.S. embassy on Sussex Drive en masse. Staff at the Revenue Canada building next door left, too, worried they might be close to a target. I walked to the office past the Prime Minister’s Office, where the Mounties were shutting down the street across from Parliament. I remember seeing a Mountie from Prime Minister Chretien’s protective detail furiously directing traffic away. And that he looked scared. – Campbell Clark , political writer

It was just before 9 a.m. and I was in the Tiff press office, chatting to other journalists and publicists, getting ready for a day of back-to-back interviews. A rumour started that a plane had just crashed into the World Trade Centre. The room, which had been buzzing, started to go quiet. Everyone looked confused. A person beside me asked if it was some kind of joke. A television was turned on to CNN. Smoke was billowing from the side of the first building.

While we all stood there trying to make sense of the impossible, a second plane flew across the screen, smashing into the second tower. The room went deathly still. One woman, a journalist from New York, screamed that her husband worked in that building. Then the first building started to crumble. Over the next few hours, the room filled with journalists, actors, directors, and their handlers – no one knew where to go or what to do. They only knew they did not want to be alone. – Gayle MacDonald , senior feature writer

I first heard about Rev. Mychal Judge’s death about 15 hours after the 9/11 attacks. I was in Toronto packing to drive to Manhattan with Globe and Mail colleague Jan Wong when I heard New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani on the radio. He was talking about the firefighters and police officers who had been killed in the Twin Towers. His voice was tight, deliberate and controlled as he tried to hold his emotions.

Father Judge, the chaplain of the Fire Department of New York, was among the dead, he said. I felt that I had been punched in the gut and ran upstairs to tell my wife, Karen Zagor. She bent over double and wept. We knew Father Judge. He and a rabbi – Karen is Jewish – together married us in New York in 1994. I covered his funeral and interviewed his firefighter colleagues, but otherwise spent the whole week in tears. On the 10th anniversary of the attacks, Karen and I wrote a remembrance piece about ‘St. Mychal of Ground Zero’ . – Eric Reguly , European bureau chief

I was at the Toronto Star on Sept. 11, 2001, as a young intern. That morning I was sent out to the Financial District to collect voices and mood. As I reached Bay Street, it was a struggle to move against the tide of thousands of people heading in the opposite direction towards the subway and GO station. Everyone was trying to get home. You could almost hear a pin drop, a silence borne out of fear – no one knew if Toronto was a target too. I wandered in and out of the lobbies of the big banks and American financial institutions, interviewing people. Huddled around one television screen were men and women trying to reach colleagues at Cantor Fitzgerald in New York. The TV was showing on repeat the collapse of the World Trade Center’s North Tower. One woman I spoke to was on her knees and could not stop screaming. The firm was based there, and lost hundreds of staff that day . I had no idea that the horror unfolding in New York was to have extraordinary consequences for the country of my birth, Afghanistan. – Hamida Ghafour, deputy foreign editor

I was on a media charity flight with kids headed to Walt Disney World in Orlando. We were in the air when the world changed forever. Most of the media stayed, but I was told to get to New York City by however means. I thought about driving, but ended up finding a train heading north. The handful of other passengers and I had no idea if the train was going to bypass NYC. We did arrive, a day and a half after Sept. 11. By then the city was zipped up drum tight. I met my Globe colleagues and tried to plan our coverage. It was very surreal, as life seemed to go on in other areas of Manhattan, like the Upper East and West sides. New Yorker stoicism in the face of terror. – Fred Lum , photojournalist

stories.title: Ottawa begins rolling out long-awaited supplemental funding for national sport groups
stories.summary: Alpine Canada receives an additional $2.77-million to its funding for the year
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
The federal government is rolling out more money for amateur sports organizations and will host a national “playground to podium” summit for stakeholders this fall.

Secretary of state for sport Adam van Koeverden announced Friday that Alpine Canada will be the first group to get supplementary funding, adding $2.77-million to its funding for the year, which will now be $8-million.

Last year Alpine Canada received $5-million.

Ottawa announced plans in its spring economic update to inject more money into Canada’s national sport organizations.

That promise came after the Future of Sport in Canada Commission’s final report, issued in March, found the country’s sport system was facing a “funding crisis” as federal funding had not kept up with inflation.

Organizations were invited to submit applications in July for supplemental funding from a pot of $112-million available this year.

The federal government is also planning to bring together representatives from nearly all corners of Canada’s amateur sport landscape for a two-day conference in Ottawa in November.

Dubbed “the playground to podium summit,” the event aims to foster an ongoing conversation about how to strengthen Canada’s sport system, and where best to direct the new injection of in federal money.

Van Koeverden said the event will be the first of its kind and have “an ambitious agenda.”

“We are really focused on this team effort of collective action and listening and making sure that we are bringing every sport and every sport leader along for the journey of rebuilding our sport system,” van Koeverden told The Canadian Press.

“At its core this is to highlight and to focus on the direction for this novel $1-billion investment in support.”

In April’s spring economic update, Ottawa injected $755-million over five years, with another $118-million each year after, to help host international sporting events, support athletes and boost participation in sport.

The government also issued a call in April for national sport organizations to work with private sector partners to get Canadians more involved in sport.

Van Koeverden announced on Friday that Edmonton-based Capital Power is partnering with Alpine Canada. And while private sector money flowing to amateur sport in Canada is not new, van Koeverden’s office is touting the partnership as the first sign of the private sector stepping up since the call-out.

“The details are forthcoming. But Alpine Canada is thrilled, and I know some of the athletes are really excited as well,” van Koeverden said.

Van Koeverden also announced details this week about several events Ottawa is supporting, including the 2026 Men’s Continental Volleyball Championships in Moncton, N.B., and the Davis Cup international team tennis events, both taking place next week.

“These events are awesome,” van Koeverden said, reminiscing on the Fifa World Cup that Canada co-hosted earlier this summer.

“They bring us together, we’re cheering for the same team. So we want to do more of that.”

Van Koeverden announced on Friday that Edmonton-based Capital Power is partnering with Alpine Canada. stories.title: London firefighters mark 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks
stories.summary: Firefighters in London, Ont., gathered Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and add more names to a local memorial.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Firefighters in London, Ont., gathered Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and add more names to a local memorial.
· Posted: Sep 11, 2026 4:44 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
London firefighters gathered Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and honour firefighters who have died in the line of duty.

The ceremony at the London Fire Department Memorial Headquarters on Horton Street East honoured the 343 firefighters and other emergency responders who died in the World Trade Center attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.
In photos | Remembering 9/11 25 years later
London Professional Fire Fighters Association president Jason Timlick said he was working a shift when the attacks happened.
“I think what was witnessed on 9/11 was so tragic and large that any first responder that could help wanted to help,” said Timlick.

“And that overwhelming urge to go to help those that were in danger and suffering drove people to get in their cars, drive down to New York and help. And we had a number of London firefighters that did that, and a number of first responders from across North America did that.
“And that is what community is. We come together to support each other regardless of borders.”
The monument at London Fire Department Memorial Headquarters, 400 Horton Street East. (Matt Allen)
Politicians and community leaders also paid tribute to the 51 London firefighters who have died in service to the community.
Two names were recently added to the memorial monument: Capt. Dennis McCallum and Capt. Douglas Perryman.
Their families were presented with memorial medals during Friday's ceremony.
Natalie Lovie, with files from Matt Allen

stories.title: New accessible playground opens in Saskatoon
stories.summary: A new playground in Saskatoon was revealed September 10th, allowing Makenna Hiebert to play without barriers. Something her mom says should be the standard.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
It’s a day a long time in the making for Makenna Hiebert and her family.

A ribbon cutting ceremony on Sept. 10 officially marked the opening of Saskatoon’s second accessible playground at St. Anne Catholic School.

“It was a dream turned to reality, so it’s very exciting. We’ve had an exciting couple of weeks since it’s been open and seeing all the kids run out and even meeting some friends here has been really exciting,” said Brittany Hiebert, Makenna’s mom and project lead for the playground.

Makenna sustained a brain injury when she was just three years old.

Her family quickly learned how few accessible play spaces there were in Saskatoon.

Brittany says this new playground will serve plenty more people beyond the St. Anne’s school community.

“We actually got to meet friends here on the weekend and they have a young child that uses a walker. So, we’re able to have it be a gathering place and people from all over the city have even said like, ‘I’m definitely coming, my child’s in a wheelchair’.”

There are ramps and a rubber ground to make play easier and more independent.

And while it May look like any old playground for some, it means a whole lot more to others.

Brittany says she thinks this should be the standard.

“I think that we want to create a city and a culture where play is accessible and we don’t have to fight for it when there’s maybe an accident or someone specific starts recognizing the need.”

Watch the video above to see how much the new playground brings joy to the community.

stories.title: CTV News in Gander: Stranded passengers on 9/11 arrived as strangers. When they left, they were family
stories.summary: For 25 years Karen Mills has held the memories of 9/11 in her heart and in a binder full of photos she flips through while speaking with CTV News. Mills says she recalls the time like it was yesterday.
stories.author: Heather Butts
stories.content:
Gander, N.L.- For 25 years Karen Mills has held the memories of 9/11 in her heart and in a binder full of photos she flips through while speaking with CTV News.

When the tragedy occurred 25 years ago, she was the manager at a Comfort Inn hotel in Gander, N.L. that housed thousands of “plane people” who were stranded when the FAA closed American airspace forcing all planes to land.

That sent 38 planes to Gander with more nearly 7,000 passengers. In a town of roughly 10,000, that meant Gander’s population nearly doubled in size overnight.

With no committee or association available to help, the people of Gander and surrounding communities stepped up, for those in need.

Mills says she recalls the time like it was yesterday.

“Our switchboard had 12 lines and it (lit up) just like a Christmas tree, it was just buzzing,” Mills said about the time when passengers landed in Gander and need a place to stay.

Although some hotel rooms were already filled with scheduled tourists, when the town declared a “State of Emergency” hotels in Gander were required to give flight crews first access to rooms.

With 7,000 passengers in need of shelter, the few hundred hotel rooms in the entire town were filled in minutes.

“Do you know how many times we had to say, ‘gosh so sorry,’ we felt so bad, you knew people probably slept on the floor somewhere,” said Mills.

The ‘basement boys’

As the so-called “plane people” kept coming, two young men caught a break.

The former Comfort Inn manager of 33 years recalled two young men who were desperate for a safe place to rest their heads.

“They walked in and once again they were like ‘we know you don’t have anything sorry,’” Mills recounted.

“And it was like a boom moment… and I was like ‘wait I got a box spring mattress and a cot you guys can come sleep down in the basement, downstairs in the gym in the fitness centre.’”

The two men accepted with delight, telling Mills the box spring was better than the pool table they had slept on the night before.

Mills dubbed the two men the “Basement Boys,” and even drove them across town to fulfill one simple request: they needed fresh underwear.

The group developed a fond relationship that has run the course of 25 years.

“Every year on 9/11 flowers show up at the hotel. They call themselves the ‘Liverpool Lads,’ they don’t know they’re the ‘Basement Boys,’” she said.

“I did get an email (from them) once and I told them, ‘Do you know how many times I’ve told your story?’”

25 years later, Mills and the community of Gander remains steadfast in their message.

“My god, if we can just be kind, what a world eh… I mean seriously think about it… I think anyone would do what we did.” Mills said. It’s a message she hopes continues to bloom in uncertain times.

Open heart, open home

Decades-old stories of kindness and empathy are commonly shared around the anniversary of 9/11 in the community of Gander.

“I got a call from the (The Royal Canadian) Legion asking to bring a tray of sandwiches to the Legion. I didn’t ask what (it was) for, they wanted a tray, I brought a tray,” said Beulah Cooper, a Gander resident and executive at the local Legion.

Her efforts extended well beyond a tray of sandwiches. With dozens of people sleeping on the floor of the Legion, in community centres and schools, she offered comfort.

“I took them to make phone calls and I asked them if they wanted to come up to my home and get a good night’s sleep,” Cooper said.

One of the people who accepted Cooper’s invitation was American passenger Monica Burke. She is among the many “plane people” who have returned to Gander for the 25th anniversary of 9/11, marking her fifth visit to the community.

“I was kind of shocked that she invited me into her house but I was also very relieved, because I needed some rest and was emotional and exhausted,” Burke said while sitting in Cooper’s living room 25 years after they first met.

Burke had spent 16 hours on the plane, parked on the tarmac and had no real sense of what happened until she arrived at the Legion.

She called her boss in the U.S. to say she wouldn’t be coming back anytime soon. All she knew was that she was somewhere in Canada.

As the world witnessed extraordinary horror, people in Gander gave those in need remarkable hope.

“It kept happening at the Legion. People would just show up and say, ‘I have two beds. Who wants to come home?’ After a while, it was like, ‘Oh, okay, that’s what they do here.’” said Burke.

The bonds capture a strength that is hard for many to describe, people who would otherwise have never met, with seemingly nothing in common, now like family.

Former Gander mayor Claude Elliott “put it right,” Cooper said.

“He said when they arrived, they were strangers, by the middle of the week they were friends and when they left they were family.”

Well into her 80s now, Cooper is still active with the Legion and welcoming “Plane People” into her home. She says she’s humbled by helping so many in such an uncertain time and shares this advice with others:

“If you see someone who needs help, or you can help them do it. Open your home or your heart to them. It makes you feel good it really does, I’d do it in a heartbeat again.”

“I was kind of shocked that she invited me into her house but I was also very relieved, because I needed some rest and was emotional and exhausted,” Burke said while sitting in Cooper’s living room 25 years after they first met.
Burke had spent 16 hours on the plane, parked on the tarmac and had no real sense of what happened until she arrived at the Legion.
She called her boss in the U.S. to say she wouldn’t be coming back anytime soon. All she knew was that she was somewhere in Canada.
As the world witnessed extraordinary horror, people in Gander gave those in need remarkable hope.
“It kept happening at the Legion. People would just show up and say, ‘I have two beds. Who wants to come home?’ After a while, it was like, ‘Oh, okay, that’s what they do here.’” said Burke.
The bonds capture a strength that is hard for many to describe, people who would otherwise have never met, with seemingly nothing in common, now like family.
Former Gander mayor Claude Elliott “put it right,” Cooper said.
“He said when they arrived, they were strangers, by the middle of the week they were friends and when they left they were family.”

Well into her 80s now, Cooper is still active with the Legion and welcoming “Plane People” into her home. She says she’s humbled by helping so many in such an uncertain time and shares this advice with others:
“If you see someone who needs help, or you can help them do it. Open your home or your heart to them. It makes you feel good it really does, I’d do it in a heartbeat again.”

stories.title: Drunk driver gets 30 months for ‘frightening and horrendous’ London crash
stories.summary: The judge said the crash was no accident, rejecting a conditional sentence and stressing the need to deter impaired driving.
stories.author: Jane Sims
stories.content:
Shona Ivany had tears in her eyes as she left the London courtroom where the drunk driver who seriously injured her 17 months ago was sent to prison.

“I thought I would be happy with the outcome of him going to jail, but I still don’t feel that,” she said after Mitchell Gauthier-Neville, 32, was dealt a 30-month sentence for impaired driving causing bodily harm.

“You still feel sad for his family, for him and for his son. I do know that he needs to pay the price. He did harm to me. He did a lot of harm to me,” she said.

“But I still feel sorry for him because I know he didn’t do it intentionally. But that does not mean he should walk away free. He still needs to pay for it.”

Her reaction reflected much of what Ontario Court Justice Jason Miller said in his decision Friday to reject Gauthier-Neville’s pitch for a conditional sentence that would have kept him out of jail and allowed him to continue as the single parent to his 10-year-old son with special needs.

“I know this wasn’t the result you were looking for. I do think this is the result the law requires that I impose,” the judge said to Gauthier-Neville.

“I take no pleasure in incarcerating people and separating them from their family. The public, however, has to get the message. These offences must stop.”

Miller reiterated what many judges see in local courtrooms – that too many people are choosing to drive after drinking or consuming intoxicants.

Gauthier-Neville fits the profile of most people charged with impaired driving, described by Miller as “a law-abiding, pro-social member of their community.”

“Regrettably, it seems too many otherwise good people are still not properly considering the potentially lethal consequences” of drinking and driving, he said, despite large-scale education campaigns and increased sentences imposed by the courts.

Miller said Gauthier-Neville made a “tragic” decision on March 24, 2025, at about 7 a.m. when he sped south at 148 km/h in the 40 km/h community safety zone on McNay Street near Blessed Sacrament elementary school in his 2021 Dodge Ram 1500 pickup truck. He ran through the red light at Oxford Street and into the side of Ivany’s pickup truck, which was heading east on a green light.

The impact, all caught on surveillance video, was catastrophic. There was no evidence that he tried to brake. Upon impact, Ivany’s truck rolled onto the passenger side and Ivany, 57, was trapped inside.

‘Driving is a privilege’: Woman faces drunk driver who nearly killed her

London mom faces 'long road' to recovery after violent crash: Friend

When she was finally freed 40 minutes later, Ivany was rushed to hospital with serious injuries. Gauthier-Neville wasn’t injured, but he failed a roadside breath test. Further testing after his arrest showed a reading of 140 milligrams of alcohol in 100 millilitres of blood, nearly double the legal limit of 80 milligrams.

At the sentencing hearing last month, assistant Crown attorney Jeremy Carnegie argued for a three-year prison sentence, while defence lawyer Nick Cake asked Miller to consider a conditional sentence that would have kept Gauthier-Neville at home with his son. Instead, the boy is expected to move out of London and away from his doctors to relocate to Kirkland Lake with Gauthier-Neville’s family.

“But for the collateral consequences to Mr. Gauthier-Neville’s family, particularly his son who will no doubt be harmed by losing his father for any period, I would have imposed the three-year sentence sought by the Crown,” Miller said.

In addition to the 30-month sentence, Miller ordered a DNA sample and imposed a five-year driving prohibition to begin once the sentence is completed, which will keep Gauthier-Neville off the road for 7.5 years.

At the time of the crash, Gauthier-Neville was struggling after his father’s death and his sister’s cancer diagnosis. He lost a brother to lung disease. A sister-in-law and a pet also died.

His inability to deal with his grief led him to become a daily heavy drinker. Since his arrest, he has quit drinking and participated in rehabilitative programming for addiction. He also completed 200 hours of community service.

Ivany continues to recover. She suffered fractures in the neck area of her spine, lower spine, collarbone, sacrum, both sides of her pelvis, both hip sockets, ribs and breastbone. Her internal organs were bruised and she had a laceration to her liver.

She required several surgeries and needs more. During the first few months of her recovery, she needed assistance with her daily needs, plus a wheelchair, then a walker, then a cane. She gets injections for pain management.

Ivany was unable to travel to see her ailing father until shortly before he died. She doesn’t feel safe anymore and is anxious while driving.

Her daughter, Ashley, planned to surprise her on the day of the crash with news of a pregnancy. “It turned what was to be a beautiful moment between mother and daughter … into one of fear that she would never see her mother again,” Miller said.

Ivany hasn’t fully returned to work as a home painter and drew on her retirement funds after a GoFundMe campaign gave her initial financial help.

The judge noted that Gauthier-Neville has been remorseful since the moment of the crash. However, his driving was “frightening and horrendous,” and his breathalyzer readings were very high.

Offenders like Gauthier-Neville “do not intend the harm they cause, but they, in fact, cause harm,” he said through their choice to get behind the wheel after consuming alcohol and without thought of potential tragic consequences.

Miller addressed Ivany and her family directly. “I’m very sorry this happened to you. It’s always regrettable to have people come to this building simply because they were in the wrong place at the wrong time and have suffered significant harm.”

He said the courts must continue to increase sentences in impaired driving cases “until law-abiding, pro-social people in the public get the message.”

People with drinking problems should “get help” and “leave your car at home. If they simply make that decision, so much suffering would be eliminated,” he said.

Miller was clear that the crash should not be called “an accident” because “an accident is an unforeseeable event. Calamity caused by drinking and driving is hardly unforeseeable.”

Outside the courtroom, Ivany agreed. “This was not an accident,” she said. “To me, when I look at that video, it looks like I was preyed upon.”

stories.title: How a Newfoundland town’s 9/11 compassion built a bond lasting 25 years
stories.summary: It’s been a quarter-century since New Yorker Tom McKeon was stranded and whisked off a grounded plane by school bus to a small community in central Newfoundland.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
Appelton, N.L. - It’s been a quarter-century since New Yorker Tom McKeon was stranded and whisked off a grounded plane by school bus to a small community in central Newfoundland.

Twenty-five years later, McKeon is crashing in the same basement, with the same family who hosted him for those few emotional and troubled days in Appleton — just as he’s done on his many visits back to the province, at host Derm and Dianne Flynn’s insistence.

“I try to insist to Dianne that I want to get a hotel, I don’t want to impose,” McKeon said. “The first time we did that, I think I might have insulted them.”

McKeon was one of the thousands of “plane people” who were stranded in Gander after American authorities shut down the country’s airspace following the Sept. 11 attacks.

‘We really love each other’

Derm Flynn — the then mayor of Appleton — was one of many in the town and the region that opened their homes to the stranded travellers in the days after they arrived.

“I, as mayor, made the decision because people were asking me,” Flynn recalls. “They were saying, ‘Derm, how come there’s people staying, sleeping on the floor? I’ve got two bedrooms at my house!’”

So, McKeon spent a first sleepless night at Appleton’s small-town hall. For the second, he was invited — by either Derm or Dianne — to stay at the mayor’s house, along with five of the other “plane people” who were stuck in the community.

Among the chaos of that second day, the Flynns found a small moment of respite with their new guests – a moment that sparked a friendship that lasts to this day.

“We got back here to this room,” McKeon said from the Flynns’ basement bar. “Derm said, I think it’s time we had a drink.”

“I think he was sorry about that, because he had probably one, and then all of his guests drank him dry.”

The relationship between the two men only grew — McKeon was so moved by the kindness that he came back to visit the community again in the spring of 2002. The Flynns even travelled to New York to visit and would call to mark milestones, births and deaths in their families.

“We really love each other. We’ve been part of each other’s lives since that day.”

Nearly 7,000 people on 38 planes were diverted to Gander in the morning of 9/11, the first arriving minutes after American officials shut down their airspace.

‘My life was changed’

In response, Gander and surrounding communities launched an ad-hoc hosting campaign — finding places for passengers to sleep, eat and call home. The “plane people,” as they are still called, dwarfed the region’s hotel and restaurant capacity.

“The second question wasn’t asked, ‘can you feed them?’ or ‘how are you going to feed them?’ or that sort of thing,” Mac Moss remembers.

Moss was an administrator at the College of the North Atlantic in Gander when hundreds of “plane people” showed up at his door.

“It was just, ‘will you take care of them?’ and everybody said they would, of course.”

Among them was Kevin Tuerff, who was diverted to Gander while travelling from Paris to New York City.

“My life was changed by the amazing compassion of the people who volunteered to help every single one of us who needed food, clothing, shelter,” Tuerff said.

stories.title: Nova Scotia to expand protections for people affected by AI-generated intimate images
stories.summary: The Nova Scotia government says new legislation will expand protections for people affected by intimate images created or altered by AI without their consent.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government says new legislation will expand protections for people affected by intimate images created or altered by AI without their consent.

The government introduced the new bill on Thursday.

It amends the provincial Intimate Images and Cyber-protection Act, which provides legal protection for victims of cyberbullying and the sharing of intimate images online.

Provincial Justice Minister Scott Armstrong told The Canadian Press in an interview that the proposed changes expand the definition of an intimate image and ensure that victims do not have to prove intimate images were shared without their consent.

This would reduce the burden on victims, when applying for a court order for an image to be taken down.

“Prior to these changes … if someone uploaded an intimate image of a victim, it was on the victim to actually prove that they did not give consent,” Armstrong said. “That’s not trauma informed. The victim shouldn’t have to do the work here.”

Armstrong says the amendments also make it illegal for someone to threaten to share an intimate image online.

He says the changes align with those made to the Canadian Criminal Code in June, which made it illegal to threaten to share intimate images, including sexual deepfakes, without consent.

The proposed legislation also includes amendments to the Safer Communities and Neighbourhoods Act.

One of the changes would give the provincial government expanded powers to take control of a property that is suspected of hosting serious criminal activity.

“This is another tool we’re using to be able to combat human trafficking, in particular,” Armstrong said.

The legislation includes other amendments to improve public safety in the province, including modernizing 911 services.

stories.title: In photos: Around the world with Western
stories.summary: Western students travelled around the world on international study trips and exchange opportunities throughout the summer.
stories.author: Western Communications
stories.content:
As Western students return to classes for a new academic year, many are reflecting on summer experiences abroad. From international study trips to research projects to exchanges at other universities, Western students explored multiple countries this summer.

New locations offered unique perspectives and introduced students to diverse cultures. The desire to explore the world is growing, with an increase of more than 70 per cent reported in international exchange applications at Western.

Western News highlights a few of the fascinating places students visited this summer:

Ivey Businss School student Ben King, an Hba’26 candidate, was on exchange at Thammasat University in Thailand. (L to R) Iyanu Dosunmu and King on a United Nations field trip. (Submitted)

Engineering students took a two-week trip to Karlsruhe Institute of Technology in Germany, an institution building research partnerships with Western. The trip offered hands-on exposure to modern manufacturing through factory and research facility tours. Cultural experiences in Heidelberg, the Black Forest, Karlsruhe and Strasbourg were also popular among students. (Submitted)

The Faculty of Education’s two-week Alternative Field Experience in Orléans, France offers teacher candidates in the French as a Second Language specialization the opportunity to strengthen their language skills and cultural understanding while experiencing daily life as locals through homestays, university courses and cultural excursions. “ The lessons I learned in Orléans will stay with me forever and continue to shape the way I teach, learn and experience the world,” said Faye Guadalupe, a teacher candidate and trip participant. (Submitted)

Two Ivey Emba participants, (L to R) Weina Chong and Ann Wu, wearing traditional Vietnamese conical hats during the Ivey Emba Discovery Expedition in Vietnam. The Discovery Expedition brings participants to either Chile or Vietnam to learn about international business practices and operations first-hand. (Emman Price/Ivey)

Each year, 80 to 90 students from Western travel to Rondine and Arezzo, Italy for an immersive experiential learning program combining Italian language and culture with intercultural learning. Through local experiences and engagement with Rondine Cittadella della Pace, students explore dialogue, peacebuilding and conflict transformation alongside an international community. (Submitted)

A two-week faculty-led study trip to Vienna, Austria gives students the opportunity to experience the city’s culture and history while earning a management and organizational studies credit in a condensed format. Students also collaborate with peers from the Vienna University of Economics and Business. (Submitted)

stories.title: Toronto’s new country bar pays tribute to the late, great Dolly Parton
stories.summary: Dolly’s channels the icon’s glamour and generous spirit to celebrate her legacy
stories.author: Photography and story by Joel Rodriguez
stories.content:
The Dolly Parton cutout was hard to miss.

Life-sized and permanently cheerful, she stood at the entrance to Dolly’s, a new country bar on Toronto’s Esplanade, watching over a steady stream of guests in cowboy hats, blond wigs and varying degrees of rhinestone commitment.

This week, the affection for Dolly Parton, who died on Aug. 25 at the age of 80, has been visible across Canada, from Halifax to Vancouver . Parton’s estate has also announced Dollyfest, a major celebration planned for 2027. The Globe and Mail spent a night at Dolly’s this week for a special celebration in tribute to the queen of country.

The bar takes its name and inspiration from Parton.

“The idea behind Dolly’s was to create a country bar in the city where women would feel safe,” said Taruna Daya, a staff member who welcomed guests as they arrived.

Among the guests was Ayah Conic, Dolly’s main drag performer and host for the evening.

“Dolly didn’t have a mean bone in her body. She was love,” Conic said. “When she could’ve gone and just become a billionaire, she started a charity. I adore her.”

That generosity was part of the tribute itself. The night was raising funds for Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library , the program she founded to provide free books to children.

It was an appropriate way to celebrate someone whose public life has always extended beyond music. Parton built a career as a songwriter and performer, while using her success to give back to the communities around her.

But perhaps that is part of what makes Dolly Dolly. The glamour was never the whole story. There was always something given away, whether it was a song, a joke, a book or simply a reason for people to feel welcome.

stories.title: Survivors and families of victims of Dawson College shooting gather 20 years later
stories.summary: Montreal - Nearly 20 years after being shot three times, Hayder Kadhim still asks himself why he survived and not his friend Anastasia.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
On Sept. 13, 2006, a gunman entered the Montreal college where he was studying and opened fire on students in the hall. Kadhim, then 17 years old, was shot in the head, neck and calf.

Today, he says it’s crucial for people to take care of one another.

“Maybe just these small gestures could prevent a tragedy from happening and some lonely and depressed person from waking up with crazy thoughts, just because one of us did a small gesture of care,” he said.

Twenty years after the Sept. 13, 2006, shooting at Montreal's Dawson College, survivors remember 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa. (Sept. 11, 2026)

The Canadian Press

He spoke to a crowd gathered in the garden at Dawson College commemorating the shooting that killed 18-year-old Anastasia De Sousa. Sixteen others were injured in the attack, according to a coroner’s report from 2008.

The gunman killed himself after being shot by police.

Kadhim remembers Anastasia, whom he affectionately nicknamed Stacy, as someone cheerful, fun-loving and with a gorgeous smile. He says he remains inspired by Anastasia’s resilience, as she struggled with her health as a teenager.

“When I remember her now and knowing that, how can I not also push through? How can I also not try as much as possible to have that positive vibe?” he said.

The garden where the ceremony was held was named the Peace Garden in the aftermath of the attack, according to Toby Harper-Merrett, the director of Dawson College.

Harper-Merrett said students, faculty and members of the Montreal community would regularly leave bouquets at the school gates. A white post with black lettering that reads “May peace prevail on Earth” was installed in the garden.

After the ceremony, Louise De Sousa, Anastasia’s mother, helped plant three pink heather plants in her honour. Students, politicians and faculty also took handfuls of wildflower seeds to plant in the garden.

De Sousa wore a pink lace dress in honour of her daughter.

“Pink was her favourite colour. Her friends in high school called her Malibu Barbie,” she told journalists after the ceremony. “Even her room was bubblegum pink.”

De Sousa says she still thinks about her daughter every day, wondering what kind of woman Anastasia would have become.

“Would she be married, would she have children?” she mused.

She added that she especially misses her daughter during big family milestones.

“Two years ago when my son got married, it really hit me that his big sister wasn’t there. So, there are moments that are harder than others, but life goes on. And we talk about her and that’s what keeps us going,” she said.

De Sousa said anniversaries are always emotional but that it’s comforting to spend time commemorating the tragedy with the other victims and families.

But Sunday will be different.

“That day is mine,” she said.

Every year, De Sousa and her family visit Anastasia’s grave on the hour of her death. They then share stories about Anastasia over a meal. De Sousa says her grandkids still get to know their aunt even though they never met her.

“She was a normal teenager,” she said. “She had a beautiful smile, and she was fun and loving, but she was also a little brat.... We remember everything that she did. That’s how we continue.”

De Sousa is also calling on the federal government to tighten gun control laws. She was one of the signatories of a letter sent to Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier this week demanding the government complete its ban on assault-style firearms and tighten rules around large-capacity magazines and handguns.

During the ceremony, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada and police Chief Fady Dagher drew parallels between the Dawson tragedy and a shooting in June that left a police officer, a bystander and the gunman dead.

“This kind of weapon that’s in circulation, assault weapons, we can’t afford it in Canada, not in this community in which we live,” said Dagher.

Ian Lafrenière, Quebec’s internal security minister, was working as a spokesperson for Montreal police in 2006. He remembers his partner, brother and best friend — all police officers — were sent to the scene of the Dawson shooting.

He said he was emotional seeing the faces of young students who May not have been born at the time attending the ceremony.

“To see the next generations here and to continue to keep this memory alive, it reassures me,” he said. “We’ll never forget what happened, because this is the only way to prevent that from happening in the future.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

Note to readers: This is a corrected story: A previous version said that 19 people were injured in the Dawson shooting. A coroner’s report from 2008 said that 16 people were injured in the shooting.

stories.title: Gas prices are expected to drop soon, but geopolitical risks remain
stories.summary: Consumers in Canada could see some relief at gas pumps starting next week as gas refineries go through regular seasonal changes, but how much prices will drop is unclear.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Consumers in Canada could see some relief at gas pumps starting next week as gas refineries go through regular seasonal changes, but how much gas prices will drop is unclear as geopolitical risks keep analysts guessing about the long-term outlook.

A drop in available oil supplies worldwide typically leads to higher gas prices, unless demand falls significantly, while the opposite effect usually will see lower gas prices.

Gas prices in Canada, and worldwide, have skyrocketed ever since the United States and Israel launched joint attacks on Iran at the end of February. The conflict has been ongoing ever since, with a temporary ceasefire in June unravelling after just a few weeks, and all the while keeping the vital Strait of Hormuz shipping channel virtually closed to most oil and gas shipments.

The Strait of Hormuz normally sees about a fifth of the world’s oil supply pass through on a daily basis.

But a switch to winter gasoline blends in Canada could see prices drop starting Sept. 16, as the new fuel starts arriving at retail pumps. In addition, gas prices typically fall during colder weather months because demand for gasoline decreases as Canadians do less driving compared to warmer months.

“Demand for gasoline declines across North America as Canadians and Americans drive less as temperatures progressively cool off. So that drop in demand usually gives us some drop in price,” says petroleum analyst Patrick De Haan at GasBuddy.

“In addition, next week, we make the switch back to cheaper winter gasoline.”

Winter blends of gasoline, De Haan says, are typically cheaper than what is sold during warmer months because the blending components like butane are relatively low cost, but help improve vehicle performance in colder temperatures. The trade off is that butane contributes to more air pollution when temperatures are warm, and as temperatures cool off, more butane is allowed.

The national average price for regular grade gasoline sits at about $1.77 per litre as of publication, according to CAA, up from around $1.75 last week and $1.42 a year ago.

Without global volatility stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions and other economic factors contributing to gas price changes, De Haan says these seasonal changes can usually result in a five to 20 cent per litre drop in the price of regular grade gasoline.

This means filling a 50-litre gas tank could see savings of about $10.

“It does vary year to year, but typically that would be a noticeable amount of relief. This year though, obviously a part of the traditional downturn could be offset by new action overseas,” says De Haan.

“Where we go, whether it’s higher or lower, it’s tough to know based on the balance of all these geopolitical tensions.”

stories.title: Former PM Chretien tells U.S. to ‘never mistake our generosity for weakness’ in 9/11 speech
stories.summary: Former prime minister Jean Chretien, during a speech commemorating the 25-year anniversary of Sept. 11, delivered what he called 'a message for our American friends.'
stories.author: Luca Caruso-Moro
stories.content:
Former prime minister Jean Chretien, during a speech commemorating the 25-year anniversary of Sept. 11, delivered what he called “a message for our American friends.”

“Never mistake our generosity for weakness,” he said.

“We embrace our friends, and we help them in their moment of need. But we bow to no one. And the more we are insulted and threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united,” he later added to applause in the room.

“I say that not in anger, but as one friend to another.”

Chretien, who was prime minister in 2001, was one of several speakers participating in a memorial event in Gander, N.L., where locals took in thousands of travellers who were grounded during the terror attacks.

U.S. authorities closed American airspace following the attack, forcing all planes to land. Thirty-eight aircraft touched down in Gander, a town of roughly 10,000. Nearly 7,000 passengers were left stranded. Gander residents stepped up to provide shelter to the new arrivals, putting them in hundreds of hotel rooms.

In a preamble to his remarks to the U.S., he said he was not representing “any government.” Rather, he said he was speaking as a 92-year-old former prime minister and a “very proud Canadian.”

“Friends need to be honest with each other. Just as the people in Gander, and anywhere else in Newfoundland and Labrador, they will give you the shirt off their backs. Like they did 25 years ago.

“But they will always show you the respect of telling you the truth. So, my friends, here is to truth, to respect, to friendship and to good neighbours: Vive les États-Unis, et vive le Canada.”

Canada and the U.S. have been in a protracted trade war since February 2025. Both countries have mounted escalating restrictions on a variety of goods, ranging from booze, dairy, metals, softwood lumber and others, affecting billions of dollars in products.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford told business leaders he stands with the prime minister against Donald Trump's trade moves.

U.S. President Donald Trump has also repeatedly called Prime Minister Mark Carney “governor” – a reference to threats from the U.S. administration to pressure Canada to relinquish its own sovereignty to become a U.S. state.

The two countries appeared close to a deal in late August, but talks fell apart after the U.S. tried to introduce last-minute adjustments , according to Carney. Those changes included restrictions on Canada’s trade deals with other countries and its ability to protect the French language, the prime minister claimed.

stories.title: Stellantis, Unifor break off contract talks as automaker pursues sale of Brampton assembly plant
stories.summary: Stellantis confirmed to union it has signed MOU with defence industry supplier Roshel, which wants to buy the factory near Toronto
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Automaker Stellantis NV Stla-N says it has signed a preliminary agreement to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to armoured carmaker Roshel.

The Brampton factory stopped production in 2023 to retool to make the Jeep Compass, but the work was paused shortly after the U.S. placed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars in 2025. Stellantis last year said the Compass would instead be made in the U.S., leaving the future of the plant and 2,200 laid-off workers up in the air.

Stellantis said on Friday it has reached a memorandum of understanding with Brampton-based Roshel.

“Stellantis believes that Roshel represents a strong path to restoring sustainable operations at Brampton assembly, preserving the site’s strategic role in Canada’s advanced manufacturing sector and helping to avoid a prolonged period of inactivity,” Stellantis said in a statement.

Roshel makes armoured vehicles for military and law enforcement agencies, as well as making aftermarket modifications to existing commercial trucks.

The Unifor union said it walked away from contract negotiations with Stellantis on Friday after Stellantis told it of the Roshel agreement. The future of the plant was a priority for the union as it seeks a three-year deal for its 9,000 Canadian members.

“The persistence of the company’s proposal to close and sell the Brampton plant has hindered the bargaining process,” Unifor said.

Unifor said the proposed shutdown of the Stellantis plant is a “devastating blow to Canada’s industrial sector” and threatens wages, pensions and other benefits of Unifor members.

Ottawa has been boosting defence spending to reach Nato’s target of 2 per cent of gross domestic product and pushing buy-Canadian policies amid the trade war with the U.S. However, a small-production security vehicle plant cannot replace the jobs and economic heft of an auto assembly plant, Unifor said.

“There is no economic substitute for automotive assembly in Canada, including the extensive supply chain, regional economic activity, and high-quality, union jobs connected to it,” the union said.

The two sides began bargaining on Sept. 1, with the union seeking a three-year deal by Sept. 11 that matched the gains made in recent negotiations with Ford and General Motors. Those agreements provided raises of 3 per cent in each year of the deal.

The union said it is “actively considering next steps.”

Stellantis declined to provide more details of the sale process, citing the Unifor negotiations.

“For more than 100 years, Stellantis has invested in and grown with Canada, and we remain committed to supporting Canadian jobs, innovation and the long-term competitiveness of the country’s automotive sector,” the company said.

Riyadh Nazerally, a spokesman for Innovation, Science and Economic Development, said the federal government continues to talk with the automaker, Unifor and Ontario about the plant’s future.

“The government will continue to use the tools available to protect workers, secure production, and preserve Brampton’s long-term role in Canada’s manufacturing sector,” he said.

Patrick Brown, mayor of Brampton, said if the sale to Roshel happens, it is “a betrayal of our workers, their families, and every Canadian taxpayer.”

“Stellantis accepted hundreds of millions of dollars in public support on the promise of a future for this plant,” he said. “Instead, it moved production to the United States and left roughly 3,000 workers, along with the suppliers and small businesses that depend on them, waiting for answers.”

Marit Stiles, the leader of Ontario’s New Democratic Party, said Stellantis is failing the very workers who helped build the company.

“At a time when Ontario families are dealing with economic uncertainty thanks to Donald Trump’s unjustifiable tariffs, Stellantis continues to turn its back on the workers who have powered its business in Ontario,” Ms. Stiles said.

Before Stellantis announced Jeep production would move to Belvidere, Ill., the Brampton plant was being retooled with millions of taxpayers’ dollars. The federal government gave as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor. The province of Ontario committed more than $500-million but withheld the money when work slowed.

Ottawa last year declared Stellantis in violation of the funding agreement and launched a dispute resolution proceeding. “We will get our money back from Stellantis,” Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in February.

The federal government recently rejected a proposal by Stellantis’s Chinese partner, Leapmotor, to assemble kit cars at the factory, saying the work would create few jobs and contribute little to the local economy.

The Brampton plant was built in 1986 and acquired by Chrysler Corp., as Stellantis was then called, with the purchase of American Motors Corp. The factory, which sprawls over 109 hectares, has produced several models over the years, including the Chrysler 300, Dodge Magnum and Dodge Charger. The plant employed more than 3,000 people when it closed for retooling.

With reports from Jeff Gray
