stories.title: Supreme Court rejects strict deadlines during criminal sentencing
stories.summary: Friday’s judgment answers specific questions amid broader issue of delays in the justice system
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday clarified how the justice system should handle delays after a person is convicted of a crime but before they are sentenced, ruling that such situations must be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Friday’s judgment, called R.B.-C., involved a conviction for sexual assault where it took more than a year to deliver the sentence.

The unanimous court took a relatively narrow approach to answer specific questions in the R.B.-C. appeal.

The case intersected with major legal issues: the protection in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to be tried within a reasonable time when charged with a crime, and what happens when that right is violated.

Such questions are usually focused on the process of a criminal trial. The Supreme Court a decade ago, in the landmark Jordan ruling, set strict deadlines for trials to be completed, from charge to conviction. If there’s an unreasonable delay that violates the Charter, a Supreme Court precedent from 1987 called Rahey means that the only outcome is a stay of proceedings. The accused is freed without a verdict.

Delays plague Canada’s justice system. Parliament and the Supreme Court in recent months have wrestled with the challenge. The Supreme Court earlier this year said it might reconsider its Rahey precedent.

Friday’s R.B.-C. judgment zeroed in on delays between conviction and sentencing. It was written by Justice Sheilah Martin in her final months of work as she retires this year.

If there is a Charter violation of unreasonable delay after conviction, the top court said the remedy in most cases is a reduction in the sentence levied on the offender. The court noted that it had not previously provided such precise guidance.

The court further said that delays after conviction should not be measured against a strict deadline, the way Jordan is used to consider trial delays. The key difference between the two phases is a person at trial is presumed innocent.

In the R.B.-C. case, a man studying for his PhD at a university in Ontario assaulted his new girlfriend one evening in 2019. The Ontario Court of Justice convicted him in 2021, but it took more than a year to render the punishment: a conditional sentence of two years less a day.

The man asked the Ontario Court of Justice for a stay of the proceedings because of unreasonable delay. The court said no. But the Ontario Court of Appeal in 2024 ruled that there was an unreasonable delay. Both courts were working with a rule applicable only in Ontario, a five-month deadline to deliver a sentence after conviction.

The Ontario appeal court reduced his conditional sentence by four months.

At the Supreme Court, the man, R.B.-C., once more sought a complete stay of the proceedings – which would wipe out his conviction.

On Friday, the top court said no.

The Supreme Court agreed that there was an unreasonable delay in his sentencing, engaging the Charter of Rights. The top court also agreed with the Ontario appeal court’s move to reduce the conditional sentence by four months.

The Supreme Court, however, rejected the idea of a five-month deadline between conviction and sentencing.

Justice Martin, invoking the central rationale of the Jordan ruling, said trial deadlines were established to address a “proven culture of complacency in bringing accused persons to trial.”

On delays between conviction and sentencing, she said strict deadlines didn’t make sense because “no comparable evidentiary foundation has been established.”

Lawyers for R.B.-C. on Friday said they were disappointed that the Supreme Court will allow sentencing proceedings to continue “even after they have become unconstitutional” because of unreasonable delay.

“Courts, more than any other institution, should respect constitutional rights,” said lawyers Arash Ghiassi and Julia Kirby of Savards LLP in a statement.

They said that allowing cases to drag on beyond the point of unreasonable delay “will not fix the system.” They also said Friday’s ruling means that R.B.-C., an Iranian, May be deported back to Iran because of his conviction and his immigration status.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, an intervener in the case, ON Friday said sentence reductions are not a meaningful remedy for a violation of the Charter right on delay. The advocacy group added that the vagueness of the remedy does not “provide the clarity necessary” to push the justice system to render sentences in a timely manner.

Beyond the R.B.-C. case itself, the broader question of how the Supreme Court May grapple with the issue of cases stayed because of unreasonable trial delays is not yet answered.

In May, in another Jordan-related ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said the court might reconsider its Rahey precedent, which dictates that a stay is the only remedy for an unreasonable trial delay.

“It May be that the time is near at hand when Rahey should be revisited,” the Chief Justice wrote.

Friday’s R.B.-C. judgment zeroed in on delays between conviction and sentencing. It was written by Justice Sheilah Martin in her final months of work as she retires this year.

If there is a Charter violation of unreasonable delay after conviction, the top court said the remedy in most cases is a reduction in the sentence levied on the offender. The court noted that it had not previously provided such precise guidance.

The court further said that delays after conviction should not be measured against a strict deadline, the way Jordan is used to consider trial delays. The key difference between the two phases is a person at trial is presumed innocent.

In the R.B.-C. case, a man studying for his PhD at a university in Ontario assaulted his new girlfriend one evening in 2019. The Ontario Court of Justice convicted him in 2021, but it took more than a year to render the punishment: a conditional sentence of two years less a day.

The man asked the Ontario Court of Justice for a stay of the proceedings because of unreasonable delay. The court said no. But the Ontario Court of Appeal in 2024 ruled that there was an unreasonable delay. Both courts were working with a rule applicable only in Ontario, a five-month deadline to deliver a sentence after conviction.
The Ontario appeal court reduced his conditional sentence by four months.
At the Supreme Court, the man, R.B.-C., once more sought a complete stay of the proceedings – which would wipe out his conviction.
On Friday, the top court said no.

The Supreme Court agreed that there was an unreasonable delay in his sentencing, engaging the Charter of Rights. The top court also agreed with the Ontario appeal court’s move to reduce the conditional sentence by four months.
The Supreme Court, however, rejected the idea of a five-month deadline between conviction and sentencing.
Justice Martin, invoking the central rationale of the Jordan ruling, said trial deadlines were established to address a “proven culture of complacency in bringing accused persons to trial.”
On delays between conviction and sentencing, she said strict deadlines didn’t make sense because “no comparable evidentiary foundation has been established.”

Lawyers for R.B.-C. on Friday said they were disappointed that the Supreme Court will allow sentencing proceedings to continue “even after they have become unconstitutional” because of unreasonable delay.
“Courts, more than any other institution, should respect constitutional rights,” said lawyers Arash Ghiassi and Julia Kirby of Savards LLP in a statement.

They said that allowing cases to drag on beyond the point of unreasonable delay “will not fix the system.” They also said Friday’s ruling means that R.B.-C., an Iranian, May be deported back to Iran because of his conviction and his immigration status.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, an intervener in the case, ON Friday said sentence reductions are not a meaningful remedy for a violation of the Charter right on delay. The advocacy group added that the vagueness of the remedy does not “provide the clarity necessary” to push the justice system to render sentences in a timely manner.
Beyond the R.B.-C. case itself, the broader question of how the Supreme Court May grapple with the issue of cases stayed because of unreasonable trial delays is not yet answered.

In May, in another Jordan-related ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said the court might reconsider its Rahey precedent, which dictates that a stay is the only remedy for an unreasonable trial delay.
“It May be that the time is near at hand when Rahey should be revisited,” the Chief Justice wrote.

stories.title: Sovereignty referendum would cost at least $130-million, Parti Québécois leader says
stories.summary: Figures will be included in the financial framework that Paul St-Pierre Plamondon plans to make public on Sept. 15
stories.author: Caroline Plante
stories.content:
The Parti Québécois’s commitment to a third referendum on independence took centre stage in the Quebec election campaign this week, despite the party’s best efforts to shift the attention of a nervous electorate away from the question of sovereignty.

On Friday, the PQ confirmed it will cost at least $130-million to hold an independence referendum in a first mandate, as Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to do if his party forms government on Oct. 5.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon also said this week that he would pursue a referendum even without a majority government – a challenging proposition that would require support from members of opposition parties.

Meanwhile, Christine Fréchette, leader of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s chief rival, tripped up over the independence question this week when she refused – not for the first time – to say if she is a sovereigntist despite her opposition to a referendum.

Sovereignty is broadly unpopular in Quebec, with support for independence stuck around 30 per cent as the escalating Canada-U.S. trade war looms over the campaign. Last month, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon announced he would not hold a referendum until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office . Mr. Trump’s current term is meant to end Jan. 20, 2029. The move was the PQ Leader’s bid to focus the campaign elsewhere.

For a while, that seemed to work. In the early days of the campaign, other issues were shunted aside as the major party leaders jockeyed to position themselves as best equipped to defend Quebec’s interests against a hostile U.S. administration.

But the PQ Leader faced repeated questions this week about his insistence on a referendum. In an interview with The Canadian Press published Friday, he said the party has budgeted $20-million for a travelling commission that would consult on the adoption of a provisional constitution.

Holding a referendum in 2029 or 2030 would cost at least $110-million, he said. The party has confirmed the figures to The Globe and Mail.

The PQ has been leading in the polls for the better part of three years, but currently seems unlikely to form a majority government. Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon maintained several times this week that his commitment to a referendum would not change in a minority context.

“I think I have a responsibility to keep my promises,” he told a panel of Radio-Canada journalists during a televised event Wednesday featuring interviews with each of the five main party leaders.

In Quebec, the National Assembly must adopt the text of a referendum question drafted by the government, meaning a PQ minority would require support from opposition parties to trigger a vote on independence.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon suggested that some members of the nationalist CAQ, the sovereigntist Québec Solidaire and the Quebec Conservatives could support a PQ minority. “There are plenty of scenarios,” he said.

However, Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime was quick to say this week that if his party holds the balance of power in a minority government, he would “block any referendum project.” The Conservatives are projected to win seats in the provincial legislature for the first time this fall.

Ms. Fréchette has also said repeatedly that this would be the “worst moment” in the 50 years since the Parti Québécois first formed government to hold a referendum, given the tariff war with the United States.

But on Thursday, she refused to say whether she herself remains a sovereigntist. “My personal position doesn’t matter,” she told reporters.

Ms. Fréchette worked as a staffer for the Parti Québécois between 2012 and 2014. This is not the first time she has refused to say how she would vote in a third referendum on independence.

“What I’ve observed is that 70 per cent of Quebeckers don’t want a referendum,” she said in a video posted later to social media.

Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, who has cast his party as the only federalist option, demanded that Ms. Fréchette clarify her position, calling her answer “shameful.”

When QS Leader Ruba Ghazal was asked if she would support the PQ’s sovereignty referendum, she said her party would campaign for an independent Quebec, but also advocate for broad public consultations to ensure “everyone is on board.”

The “most plausible ally” for the PQ in launching a referendum is the QS, said Patrick Taillon, professor of constitutional law at Laval University.

However, given their strong disagreements over everything from government spending to immigration, and QS’s weaker emphasis on independence as opposed to social justice, there is no guarantee the parties would work together on a referendum project.

It is also unclear how many of their 11 seats QS will retain after the election, given the party’s weak position in the polls currently.

On top of unreliable support in the legislature, the PQ faces a number of self-imposed hurdles to launching a referendum in its first mandate, Prof. Taillon noted.

“The PQ’s roadmap includes several steps before the referendum: consultations on a provisional constitution, adoption of that constitution by the National Assembly, and dialogue with First Nations. Even apart from the question of a minority government, this represents a fairly demanding timetable.”

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: ‘I like to walk’: Japanese man traverses Canada purely for the joy of it
stories.summary: For Nobuaki Okumura, happiness can be a borrowed Habs jersey, making friends with total strangers, or a well-earned meal after a long day of walking across Canada.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
By Jack Rabb

Posted September 11, 2026 2:44 pm.

For Nobuaki Okumura, happiness can be a borrowed Habs jersey, making friends with total strangers, or a well-earned meal after a long day of walking across Canada.

Okumura, who also goes by “Nobby,” just strolled into Vancouver this week after leaving Halifax — on foot — four and a half months ago.

When asked why he began his journey, he said, “For my happiness; just for fun.”

“I’m not Terry Fox,” he said.

“I like to walk, very much.”

Canada is the fifth country he has traversed just because he felt like it. He even set a Guinness World Record in 2024 for the fastest walk across his native Japan.

“Canada’s nature is very good for me, so anywhere I love, but B.C. is very good,” he said.

Okumura documented his journey thoroughly, taking in incredible natural features and wildlife.

He also made friends everywhere he went, saying his success wouldn’t have been possible without the support he received along the way.

“Many people help me,” he said. “I’m very happy. Without their help and support, I can not walk this long way, I think.”

While his venture was ultimately for his own contentment and well-being, Nobby hopes he is able to inspire others to follow their passions and prioritize their own happiness.

“I walk for my happiness, but if that challenge encourages someone, it’s my pleasure,” he said.

stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia legislator Teresa Wat says she has joined the still-unnamed party co-founded by former B.C. Conservative leadership candidate and Opposition finance critic Peter Milobar, becoming its sixth member.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - The newest member of a still-unnamed party acknowledged she and five other former provincial Conservative legislators are in for the “long-haul” if they want to throw out British Columbia’s NDP government, while urging others to join them.

By Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press

Teresa Wat became the sixth member of the new party co-founded by former Opposition finance critic Peter Milobar, another B.C. Conservative defector, saying Friday that his experience and competency were factors in her decision.

The legislator from Richmond, B.C., said she was asking anyone right-of-centre who wanted to defeat Premier David Eby’s New Democrats to follow her.

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

Image 9Image 10Image 11Image 12

“Our common enemy is the NDP,” she said in an interview Friday.

Milobar, who is serving as the interim leader of the new party, welcomed Wat to its ranks, saying there was a “clear appetite” for its brand of right-of-centre politics.

He said Wat’s decision showed there was momentum behind the new outfit, which will have the third-largest caucus in the provincial legislature after the NDP and the Conservatives when sitting resumes next month.

“Our team is growing, because there is a clear appetite for a serious alternative to the NDP,” Milobar said in a statement.

“British Columbians are tired of out-of-control spending and a government who is responsible for the decline of so many sectors in our province.”

The new party’s members are all among nine legislators who have quit the Conservative caucus in recent weeks, citing a range of concerns about party leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay.

Milobar, a former B.C. Conservative leadership candidate, was the first to leave last month, followed by Ian Paton. They announced they would form a new party that grew last week to include Rosalyn Bird, Bruce Banman and A’a:liya Warbus.

Wat said in the initial statement announcing her move that she joined because she believes the new party can unite people and unseat the governing New Democrats.

“British Columbians want a strong, credible alternative to the NDP that is focused on affordability, competent government,” she said.

Wat’s move comes ahead of a Sept. 26 byelection that will determine whether Findlay will have a seat in the legislature as the MLA for Abbotsford-Mission.

The Richmond MLA announced her decision to leave the Conservatives on Aug. 26.

Wat said at the time that Findlay had failed to apologize over “serious and unfounded accusations” that questioned her allegiance to Canada. Remarks attributed to Findlay called Wat “CCP,” a reference to the Chinese Communist Party.

Findlay later said she had a private conversation with Wat and apologized directly.

The leader’s statement also called Wat’s decision to leave the caucus a “betrayal of the hardworking volunteers, campaign workers and voters,” who helped her get elected as a Conservative in 2024.

Wat was first elected to the legislature as a member of the former provincial Liberal Party in 2013.

Some of Findlay’s critics have said she is driving the Conservatives further to the right after her narrow win in the leadership ballot in May.

Banman has called Findlay “unelectable” and levelled scathing criticism about the direction of the party under her leadership, calling out those around her for creating a “purity test” of whether legislators were “hard right enough.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Researchers confirm sixth tornado in early September southwestern Ontario storms
stories.summary: Researchers at Western University have confirmed yet another tornado that happened during a series of significant storms that swept across southwestern Ontario last week.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Researchers at Western University have confirmed yet another tornado that happened during a series of significant storms that swept across southwestern Ontario last week.
· Posted: Sep 11, 2026 2:12 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

This drone photo shows what researchers call the worst damage point west of Monkton, which includes a partially destroyed farm building, several destroyed grain bins, and a tornado path through the crops.(Northern Tornadoes Project)
Researchers at Western University have confirmed another tornado from a series of significant storms across southwestern Ontario last week.
The Northern Tornadoes Project (NTP) said it found evidence a tornado touched down in the area of Monkton, Ont., ON Sept. 2, alongside evidence of a downburst in Seaforth, Ont.
This brings the tally of tornadoes that touched down in southwestern Ontario on Sep. 2 and 3 to six, and brings the number of downbursts confirmed to three.
Storm that hammered south, southwestern Ontario leaves 'significant' damage, outages as cleanup continues
EF1 tornado confirmed in Wellesley Township, 2 others confirmed in Tavistock
The tornadoes and downbursts now confirmed include:
An EF0 tornado, an EF1 tornado and an EF0 downburst in the Tavistock area on Sept. 2.
An EF1 tornado in Wellesley on Sept. 2.
An EF1 tornado near Monkton and an EF1 downburst in Seaforth on Sept. 2.
An EF1 tornado in Windsor on Sept. 3.
An EF1 tornado and an EF1 downburst in Wheatley on Sept. 3.
Researchers classify these events on the Enhanced Fujita Scale, which ranks tornadoes and downbursts based on wind speed and damage. The the lowest rating is EF0 and the maximum rating is EF5.
This farm located west of Monkton faced a partially destroyed barn, several destroyed grain bins, and a tornado path through the crops. (Northern Tornadoes Project)
The newly-confirmed tornado near Monkton caused damage to crops, trees and manmade structures, according to a report from the NTP.
"An NTP ground and drone survey was completed on September 8, 2026, documenting the reported damage along with damage to two farm buildings," the report reads.
The tornado began in the west travelling 4.91 kilometres toward Monkton with wind speeds of 150 km/h and a width of roughly 50 metres.
This drone photo shows a farm building that was destroyed near Seaforth, days after much of the debris was cleaned. (Northern Tornadoes Project)
In Seaforth, west of Monkton, the downburst caused damage to several farm buildings, trees and power poles, the report reads.
The downburst is reported to have an estimated maximum wind speed of 165 km/h, with damage found across an area roughly 8.5 kilometres long and up to 3 kilometres wide.
NTP officials said in the latest report that no further surveys looking at damage reported during the storms are planned.

stories.content:
Middlesex County Warden’s Statement on the 25th Anniversary of September 11

September 11, 2026

MIDDLESEX COUNTY: On September 11, 2026 Warden Sue Clarke issued the following statement regarding the 25 th Anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

Today, we pause to remember the lives lost on September 11, 2001, and to honour the courage, sacrifice, and resilience shown in the face of tragedy. As we mark this anniversary, we reflect on how that day changed the lives of families, communities, and people around the world. We remember the courage of first responders, the compassion shown by ordinary people, and the resilience that emerged. Twenty-five years later, the events of that day continue to remind us how we can come together and support one another, even in times of profound loss. We will never forget those who lost their lives, or the sacrifices made in the days and years that followed.

MEDIA CONTACT: Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division @email

stories.title: Gander gathers to commemorate 25th anniversary of 9/11 and town’s rush to help passengers
stories.summary: Thirty-eight planes carrying more than 6,500 passengers were grounded in Newfoundland town during the attacks
stories.author: Sarah Smellie
stories.content:
In a fiery and impassioned speech, former prime minister Jean Chrétien sounded off against the United States at an emotional ceremony commemorating 25 years since 9/11 in Gander, N.L., ON Friday, drawing roars of applause and a standing ovation.

“I have a message for American friends,” he said, as U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra looked on with a tepid smile.

“Yes, Canada is generous, open country. And Canadians are tolerant and kind, but never mistake our generosity for weakness, never, never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination, and never, never mistake our kindness for softness. We know who we are and we are proud of it.”

About 1,000 people, mostly seniors, sprang to their feet at his words, loudly cheering, whistling and applauding.

The event was to honour first responders and remember the nearly 3,000 people, including 24 Canadians, who were killed on Sept. 11, 2001, when terrorists crashed planes into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, into the Pentagon in Virginia and a field in Pennsylvania.

After officials closed U.S. airspace, the tiny airport in Gander was the landing spot for 38 passenger planes – part of an operation that diverted more than 200 flights to airports across Canada. Gander, a town of less than 10,000, took in nearly 7,000 stranded strangers.

The event highlighted the people of Gander and nearby communities who dropped everything to welcome passengers into their homes, create makeshift shelters in schools and community halls, and provide thousands of hot meals, paving the way to lifelong friendships. Many of those “plane people” had returned to Gander for the service on Friday, sitting alongside their found families in the local arena.

Up until the end of the two-hour service when Mr. Chrétien spoke, the event had been largely apolitical with performances from The Ennis Sisters and Alan Doyle, remarks from Governor-General Louise Arbour that focused on the friendship between the two countries, and a meandering speech from Mr. Hoekstra.

But the 92-year-old Mr. Chrétien addressed the issue that overshadowed the event, one that has fractured a long-standing friendship between the two countries that Gander had come to symbolize.

President Donald Trump’s escalating trade war has fuelled anti-American sentiment, as has his repeated threats to annex Canada and the barrage of disrespectful memes targeting Prime Minister Mark Carney. Mr. Hoekstra has amplified some of the threats from the White House.

The crowd remained riveted as Mr. Chrétien delivered more of his impassioned rallying cry for Canada.

“We embrace our friends and we help them in their moment of need, but we bow to no one,” he said to booming applause. “The more we are insulted, are threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united.”

He finished by saying he wasn’t speaking in anger but as one friend to another. Friends need to be honest with each other, he added.

“Just as the people here in Gander and anywhere else in Newfoundland and Labrador, they will give you the shirt off their back, like they did 25 years ago,” he said. “They will always show you the respect of telling you the truth. So, my friends, here is to truth, to respect, to friendship and to good neighbours.”

Then, to more resounding applause, he said in French long live the United States and long live Canada.

As he turned away from the podium, Mr. Hoekstra embraced Mr. Chrétien, who patted him on the back.

Later that evening, Mr. Hoekstra, ON his way into the internationally acclaimed musical Come From Away showing in Gander, he declined to share his thoughts on Mr. Chrétien’s speech, shrugging his shoulders twice with his palms up as he went into the theatre. When asked what he took from the ceremony, he said. “Wonderful ceremony for 9/11 absolutely.”

Others however said Mr. Chrétien’s speech was historic. Michael Rubinoff, the originating producer of Come from Away and the producer of the Gander production said the former prime minister met the moment and spoke for many Canadians.

“To hear somebody speak up so strongly and articulate what those Canadian values are on this day, at this moment in time, at this intersection of this tension between the two countries was really profound,” said Mr. Rubinoff.

“I think it’s one of those moments that the people in the room, the people watching – we won’t forget.”

At the event, Mr. Hoekstra opened his speech by saying where he was when the 9/11 attacks occurred: “talking about asparagus to asparagus farmers as any good parliamentarian would do.”

He also talked about the shared sacrifices that Canada and the United States have had as countries, standing side by side during the Afghanistan war and on 9/11 when diverted planes came to Gander and the locals “did extraordinary things,” welcoming thousands of stranded passengers that nearly doubled the town’s population. “You did it all. You stood up. You did what needed to be done,” Mr. Hoekstra said.

“Thank you for your friendship. Thank you for standing up. To the nation of Canada, thank you. Thank you for being a partner. Thank you for the shared sacrifices.”

The Governor-General did not address the current animosity between the U.S. and Canada, but her speech highlighted the history of friendship and allyship between Canada and the United States, including during 9/11.

Ms. Arbour spoke about the “exceptional” relationship forged over generations – fighting alongside one another in two world wars, and standing together in defence, freedom and democracy throughout the Cold War.

“We have helped one another through natural disasters and difficult times, time and time again,” she said. “And entire communities from Windsor to Detroit, Vancouver to Seattle, have grown side by side, always in solidarity.”

stories.title: ‘I thought we were done’: Former MP recalls witnessing WTC south tower collapse while working in NYC on 9/11
stories.summary: Former Member of Parliament Francesco Sorbara stands in front of his Woodbridge home clutching a black backpack covered in soot. The grey dust that still clings to the material conjures conflicting emotions. On one hand, it reminds him how lucky he was. One the other, it’s a symbol of the cruel fate inflicted on thousands. […]
stories.author: Michael Talbot
stories.content:
Former Member of Parliament Francesco Sorbara stands in front of his Woodbridge home clutching a black backpack covered in soot.

The grey dust that still clings to the material conjures conflicting emotions. On one hand, it reminds him how lucky he was. One the other, it’s a symbol of the cruel fate inflicted on thousands.

The soot is from the carcinogenic storm cloud that covered everything in its path when the World Trade Center’s south tower collapsed after it was struck by a plane commandeered by terrorists on September 11, 2001.

Sorbara, who was living in New York City at the time while working for JPMorgan Chase, stood in horror and watched as it toppled before his eyes. Then he ran for his life.

Twenty-five years later, he’s still shaken by the memories.

“It’s something I’ll never forget,” he said of that ill-fated day. “I don’t think about it all the time of course, but at the same time … it left its mark on many of us in different ways.”

Sorbara says September 11, 2001 started as a “beautiful sunny September day where you wanted to be outside.”

He rode the subway towards the World Trade Center for a training session at a building that was directly across the street from the iconic twin towers.

By the time he emerged from the subway system, both towers had been struck by planes.

“When I exited the subway … there seemed to be a lot of confusion … you could see there was some panic, I remember that.”

“I was watching the firefighters walk down toward the twin towers and all of a sudden, it seemed like maybe after five minutes of standing there … the first (south) tower collapses. I thought we were done, there was no way we would survive that.”

He ran as clouds of debris and soot swept over the area.

“It became dark, very, very dark,” he remembered. “I just threw myself near a big cement flower pot and the screams I heard I still remember from people that were near me, because we all had the same inclination that there was no way we are going to make it.”

Eventually he ran into a burger joint that was offering water “to clear your throat because it was all full of soot.”

He then walked to a nearby church on the lower east side that offered a hose to wash off with, and a change of clothes.

Bewildered by the jarring experience, he started walking back to his apartment on the upper east side — a trek through the frantic and eerie streets of New York City that took him around two hours.

At the time, the full scope of what transpired wasn’t clear. But now, 25 years later, he realizes the magnitude.

“It changed history,” he said of the infamous attacks orchestrated by Osama bin Laden.

“The sounds of the screams when the tower collapsed … I will never forget that.”

stories.title: Police seek public’s help identifying suspect in two London business arsons
stories.summary: London police are asking for the public’s help to identify a suspect believed to be responsible for two arson incidents targeting a business in the city’s west end last month
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police are asking for the public’s help to identify a suspect believed to be responsible for two arson incidents targeting a business in the city’s west end last month.

Police say the first incident occurred around 4 a.m. on Aug. 23 near Oxford Street West and Westdel Bourne. Investigators allege a man approached the business, ignited a Molotov cocktail and threw it at the front of the building, causing an explosion and property damage.

A second arson was reported in the same area around 3 a.m. on Aug. 29. Police believe the same suspect was involved in both incidents.

Officers responded to each call and searched the area, but the suspect was not located.

Investigators have obtained surveillance video and are releasing images of the suspect in hopes that someone can identify him.

Police say that during the Aug. 23 incident, the suspect was wearing a black tracksuit, black shoes and a red-and-white brimmed hat.

During the Aug. 29 incident, the suspect was described as wearing a grey tracksuit, grey slide sandals and black socks.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the London Police Service or Crime Stoppers anonymously.

stories.author: Shawn Knox
stories.content:
Canada

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette hops on her campaign bus in Quebec City on Thursday, August 27, 2026.Photo by Francis Vachon /Montreal Gazette

Amid an ongoing trade war with the U.S., Quebec voters will head to the polls this fall.

Will new CAQ leader Christine Fréchette manage to repeat what Mark Carney did for the federal Liberals, renewing a long-standing government for a new mandate? Or will the resurgent Parti Québécois unseat the CAQ after eight years in government?

Phil Authier, political correspondent with the Montreal Gazette, joins host Dave Breakenridge to discuss how the political landscape in Quebec has changed in the last eight years, how the trade war has factored into this race, and what a PQ win could mean when it comes to the debate around Quebec separatism.

stories.title: LeBlanc says no meetings scheduled with U.S. while Mexico works towards a deal
stories.summary: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there are no meetings scheduled in Washington.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Canada

Canadian Politics

LeBlanc said he has been in touch with his U.S. counterparts

Last updated 30 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/leblanc-says-no-meetings-scheduled-with-u-s-while-mexico-works-towards-a-deal#comments-area)

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc speaks during a press conference at the federal cabinet retreat in Banff on Sept. 11, 2026. Photo by Gavin Young /Postmedia

Ottawa — Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said there are no meetings scheduled in Washington, even as Mexico and the United States are reportedly working towards a completed bilateral deal by November.

“They’ve been at this for a number of months, and speeding towards a deal two months from now doesn’t feel like speed,” said LeBlanc, during a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., ON Friday. “But they are they are having those conversations as we did, as we May again at some point.”

Reuters reported on Friday that Mexican and American negotiators are working towards a bilateral trade agreement before the U.S. midterms on Nov. 3.

LeBlanc said he has been in touch with United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick recently. The minister said he had reached out to Lutnick to offer his thoughts for him and his family during the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

LeBlanc said he was encouraged by recent comments made by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum last week that all three countries should be at the negotiating table for the renewal of the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (Cusma). The U.S. declined to renew the trade pact in July, which means all three parties are now subject to mandatory annual reviews.

The trade conflict between the U.S. and Canada has intensified in recent weeks, following the collapse in trade negotiations between both sides last month. U.S. President Donald Trump then imposed a 50 per-cent tariff on nearly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, with Canada matching those tariffs, imposing levies ranging from 15 to 50 per cent on $27.6 billion worth of U.S. imports this week.

The U.S. tariffs represent about five per cent of Canadian exports to the U.S.

On Tuesday, Trump announced he would impose import bans on some Canadian alcohol products, dairy products and motorcycles, effective Sept. 29. Trump also removed items from the Section 338 tariff list, like cement, road salt, and added new items.

Economists have said the impact from the bans will be minimal on the Canadian economy.

Carney said Thursday evening that Trump’s import bans and changes to Section 338 tariffs were “relatively modest” compared to the president’s previous trade actions. He added that his government was still studying Trump’s latest trade actions and would not confirm whether he plans to retaliate.

Risks also remain that Trump could escalate further. The president has threatened to ban aerospace company Bombardier from selling in the U.S. and intends to impose a 50 per-cent tariff on Canadian autos and trucks on Jan. 1, 2027.

Carney has said Canada’s red lines in relation to negotiations with the Americans remain, including protections of the French language and its sovereignty.

Lutnick and Greer have disputed that the French language was ever a red line for American negotiators.

LeBlanc was asked if that means Canada can return to the negotiating table given the French language is no longer an issue in trade discussions. The minister reiterated that he would be pleased to set aside the matter, should negotiations resume.

stories.summary: The annual ceremony honoured 51 London firefighters and remembered those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
stories.author: Dale Carruthers
stories.content:
The annual ceremony honoured 51 London firefighters and remembered those killed in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

London Professional Firefighters Association president Jason Timlick presents the Martin E. Pierce commemorative medal to Niki Perryman, whose father, former London fire captain Douglas Ian Perryman, died in January, during the annual firefighters’ memorial at the Horton Street station on Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (Dale Carruthers/The London Free Press)

Emergency responders, politicians and community members gathered Friday at the Horton Street fire station for London’s annual firefighters’ memorial, honouring 51 local firefighters who died in the line of duty. The ceremony also marked the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed 343 emergency responders and thousands of civilians in New York. Photos by Lfp’s Dale Carruthers.

London firefighters stand at attention during the national anthem at the annual firefighters’ memorial.

Retired London fire captain Phill King sounds the bell – a firefighting tradition used to signal shifts, alarms and the final return of a fallen firefighter – during the memorial.

London Professional Firefighters Association president Jason Timlick presents the Martin E. Pierce commemorative medal to Helen McCallum, whose husband, former London fire captain Dennis McCallum, died in 2007.

London police Chief Thai Truong and other members of the police force attend the annual firefighters’ memorial.

stories.title: Edmonton Gurdwara attack suspect had history of random violence linked to conspiracy theories: parole board
stories.summary: Man accused of stabbing men at Edmonton Sikh temple has history of violent outbursts fuelled by paranoia, parole documents state.
stories.author: Jonny Wakefield
stories.content:
The man accused of stabbing two people at an Edmonton Sikh temple has a history of paranoia-fuelled violence linked to conspiracy theories, as well as a track record of breaching bail and parole conditions.

Austin Sim-Pelletier, 27, was charged with assault and weapons possession earlier this month after the Aug. 21 attack at Nanaksar Sikh Gurdwara. The victims, aged 51 and 75, are recovered after suffering non-life-threatening injuries, police said during a press conference Thursday.

While many feared the violence was a hate crime, police said there is no evidence suggesting Sim-Pelletier was motivated by hatred.

According to a series of parole decisions reviewed by Postmedia, Sim-Pelletier has been in and out of prison since 2020, when he shot a man in a Red Deer school parking lot after meeting up for a fight.

Overall, the parole decisions paint a picture of a man driven by paranoid thinking and “extreme jealously” who is quick to resort to violence.

“Your actions appear to be linked to underlying and unmanaged mental health concerns, particularly delusions and paranoia focused on your and your family’s safety,” reads a July 8 decision setting conditions for Sim-Pelletier’s most recent statutory release.

“Your delusions, which are (centred) around new world conspiracies and government control, have contributed to a profound distrust of authority, which can manifest as anti-authority behaviour, leading to defiant or hostile actions against perceived threats from government figures or policies.”

Sim-Pelletier was raised by his grandparents. According to the Parole Board of Canada, it was a happy home free from abuse. He began experimenting with alcohol, marijuana and Mdma as a teenager. He later worked as a mall janitor after suffering a shoulder injury working at a slaughterhouse. During one parole hearing, he talked about his Instagram following and his interest in a music career.

On April 9, 2020, Sim-Pelletier agreed to fight another man in the parking lot of Red Deer’s Holy Family School. The two wanted to settle “a dispute over a young lady,” the parole board states. When the other man arrived, he saw Sim-Pelletier carrying a sawed-off shotgun.

“You fired once in the air, and then fired a second shot towards the victim,” the parole board wrote. Several 12-gauge pellets struck the man, piercing his back, neck and scalp.

Sim-Pelletier was at his mother’s house a short time later. He claimed the victim threatened his grandmother, and that he got the shotgun “on the street because of the first wave of COVID as there (were) a lot of break-ins.”

Sim-Pelletier was released after his grandmother put up $10,000 for bail, but he soon reoffended. According to parole documents, Sim-Pelletier was rearrested July 4, 2020, after spraying his girlfriend with pepper spray and threatening to kill her. The charge was later withdrawn.

Sim-Pelletier was ultimately sentenced to four years in prison for the parking-lot shooting after pleading guilty to assault causing bodily harm and weapons offences.

He was granted day parole a year later, after a hearing in which his grandmother argued he deserved “a second chance.”

The parole board agreed. Three days later, though, officials suspended Sim-Pelletier’s parole after receiving reports he sent threatening messages to the shooting victim. Sim-Pelletier was rearrested, and was soon accused of assaulting a peace officer at the Calgary Remand Centre.

“You made no progress while in the community and it appears you were able to hold it together long enough to jump through the hoops to get an early release,” the parole board stated in a February 2022 decision.

By mid-2023, Sim-Pelletier was up for statutory release on the shooting charge. Statutory release typically occurs two-thirds of the way through a federal sentence, allowing authorities to monitor offenders after they are released from prison. Correctional Service Canada says statutory release “is not a choice or discretionary decision” and is required by law.

Sim-Pelletier received statutory release for the Red Deer shooting. Within a month, though, electronic monitoring revealed Sim-Pelletier had left his approved residence multiple times, including after curfew. He was arrested again. This time, Sim-Pelletier’s grandmother told parole authorities she no longer felt safe around her grandson. She said Sim-Pelletier broke her door, a safe and her necklace after she refused to give him $250 to send to a woman he was messaging online.

Sim-Pelletier later told corrections authorities he wakes up every day “in mental torture” and feared he was becoming a “menace.” He also spoke about JFK and the Illuminati and said he wished someone would kill him. The parole board revoked Sim-Pelletier’s statutory release in December 2023.

After serving the rest of the four-year sentence for the Red Deer shooting, Sim-Pelletier continued to behave violently.

In August 2024, he attacked a woman after she picked him up and brought him to her home. Sim-Pelletier quickly became paranoid and accused the woman of stealing money. He tried to “tie the doors” of her home closed, then punched the woman in the face five or six times, causing “severe facial injuries.”

After the attack, Sim-Pelletier ran outside and called police. Officers found him in the driveway with the victim, who was bleeding “profusely.” Sim-Pelletier had a large steak knife in his pocket and was later found to have been using marijuana and cocaine.

The following month, while in remand, Sim-Pelletier lashed out again, this time at a corrections worker. Sim-Pelletier was being interviewed in his cell, approached the worker and “without any warning” punched them in the face.

Sim-Pelletier was ultimately sentenced to just over two-and-a-half years in prison for the 2024 assaults. He came up for statutory release on those charges this summer.

In a July 8 decision, parole board member Andrea Menard said her hands were tied when it came to statutory release, but agreed to require Sim-Pelletier to live in a halfway house.

Menard cited a May 2025 psychological assessment which linked Sim-Pelletier’s offending to his “general unpredictable nature when experiencing paranoia and delusions.”

“The author of the report noted that given concerns in your case, as well as the extensive reporting of relevant risk factors within your file information, it could be argued that your propensity to engage in future violent actions, as well as your risk for returning to custody for any reason, is high,” Menard wrote.

Menard also noted that while in custody, Sim-Pelletier racked up 13 infractions, including fighting, possession of contraband, disruptive behaviour and threats toward staff. He also has a history of being disruptive in court, including interrupting a judge during sentencing.

Shortly before the attack at the gurdwara, Sim-Pelletier was released and ordered to report to a halfway house in Edmonton but did not show up. The following day, he was spotted in the middle of Highway 15 near the gurdwara just before 5 a.m. He went inside a short time later and attacked two men with a screwdriver before being subdued by other worshippers, police say.

During Thursday’s news conference, Edmonton police Staff Sgt. Eric Stewart said detectives are still piecing together how Sim-Pelletier ended up at the temple. Police have not specified the institution Sim-Pelletier was released from, but confirmed it was not Edmonton Institution, the maximum security prison near the gurdwara.

Sim-Pelletier is next due in court Sept. 18. He remains in custody.

stories.title: N.S. premier invites the public to build and submit their own provincial budgets
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is launching a new budget consultation process inviting the public to build and submit their own plans for the province’s finances.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is launching a new budget consultation process inviting the public to build and submit their own plans for the province’s finances.

Updated at 2:55 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

Out of gifts for the month

GAC[](http://www.thestar.com/news/Canada/nova-scotia/n-s-premier-invites-the-public-to-build-and-submit-their-own-provincial-budgets/article_9723838c-a8e6-5ba9-8de6-5108478b69a2.html)

By Devin Stevens The Canadian Press

Houston’s plan would allow members of the public to build their budget and submit their proposals to the government through a new provincial website.

“We’re putting the actual government numbers in front of Nova Scotians and showing them this is where the money goes, these are the pressures that we face,” Houston told reporters on Friday. “And then we will ask them a simple question: what would you do? If you spend more here, where do you spend less? … If you want something new, how would you pay for it?”

Article continues below

Who’s downloading photos of your kid at dance competitions?

The invitation comes a few months after the Houston government’s last budget provoked a public outcry and days of protests around the legislature. The public pressure drove Houston to reverse about $53 million worth of grant reductions before the revised budget was adopted in March.

Protesters also surrounded a car carrying Houston and some of his staff after a speech at Wolfville, N.S.‘s Acadia University in July, with one man charged after allegedly climbing on top of the vehicle and smashing the windshield.

On Friday, Houston said that the government’s budgeting process is similar to how families plan their own finances at the kitchen table. He said there are necessities such as rent, groceries and power that must be covered first, and other things that families want to spend money on, but aren’t necessarily vital.

But he also noted that some options would be off the table for anyone who participates in the new consultation.

For instance, the website won’t allow people to hike taxes or fees, increase the deficit or reduce funding for the Department of Health and Wellness. Houston said that’s so responses are realistic and don’t come in asking the government to double taxes or cut 100 per cent of health funding.

Besides health, Nova Scotians can increase or decrease all other department budgets by five per cent, and adjust funding for individual programs. If a person wants to increase funding in one area, they must find savings in another.

The Houston government’s last budget initially reduced discretionary grants by about $130 million, many of which supported the arts, First Nations, African Nova Scotians and people with disabilities.

The budget also landed with a record $1.2-billion deficit, despite having more than $304 million in cuts, before Houston agreed to reverse some of the spending reductions.

“We got too clinical (in the last budget) with spreadsheets and less human with understanding the desires of Nova Scotians,” Houston said. “And my commitment was not to let that happen again, so this is a very clear move toward delivering on that commitment. This is the opportunity for people to have your say. To say ‘Lift your head up from your spreadsheet and listen to how I think, and how I feel about how money should be spent.’”

Houston said he and Finance Minister John Lohr can be lightening rods at public meetings and he doesn’t want to be a distraction, which is why Public Service Commission Minister Twila Grosse is leading the consultation process.

He said he still hopes to attend some of the meetings, joking that he might hide behind a curtain.

Liberal caucus chair Becky Druhan said in a statement Friday that the premier is asking the public to fix a problem he created, and that this year’s controversial budget was part of a broader pattern of disregard for the public.

“That gives Nova Scotians every right to question whether this consultation is genuine,” she said. “A few weeks of pre-budget meetings cannot erase the government’s record of shutting people out.”

An independent committee, led by Grosse, will go through the budget submissions and submit a report to the finance minister as the government prepares its next fiscal plan. In-person consultations wrap up on Oct. 8.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 11, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: London police seek suspect in two west-end arsons
stories.summary: Officers searched the area but couldn’t find the suspect.
stories.author: Free Press staff
stories.content:
London police are asking for the public’s help identifying a suspect connected to two arsons at a west-end business last month.

At about 4 a.m. on Sunday, Aug. 23, a male suspect lit a Molotov cocktail and threw it at the front of a business near Oxford Street West and Westdel Bourne. The Molotov cocktail exploded and caused damage to the property, police said.

At about 3 a.m. on Saturday, Aug. 29, the male suspect returned to the area and committed a second arson, police said.

Officers searched the area but couldn’t find the suspect.

After obtaining video surveillance footage, investigators said they believe the same suspect May be responsible for both arsons.

During the first incident, the suspect was wearing a black tracksuit, black shoes and a red-and-white brimmed hat, police said.

During the second incident, the suspect was wearing a grey tracksuit, grey slide sandals and black socks.

Anyone with information about either incident, or who can identify the suspect, is asked to call London police at 519-661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477).

A total of 48 charges have been laid against two youths after Windsor police say they were involved in a series of vehicle thefts and attempted thefts across the city.

Officers responded to 11 incidents between July 26 and Aug. 19 involving attempts to steal vehicles.

Police said suspects tried to get into the vehicles by prying off door handles or punching the locking mechanisms on the driver’s side doors.

Two vehicles were successfully stolen during the series of attempted thefts.

Police said one vehicle was taken Aug. 13 from a parking lot in the 200 block of Tecumseh Road East. Another was stolen the following day from a parking lot in the 900 block of Ottawa Street.

Both vehicles were later recovered, police said.

Investigators with the Windsor Police Service’s Target Base Unit identified two youths as suspects.

A 13-year-old boy was arrested Aug. 19 at a residence on the city’s west side, while a 12-year-old boy was arrested Sept. 1 at a separate west-end residence.

The youths cannot be identified under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Each youth is charged with 11 counts of mischief under $5,000, 11 counts of attempted theft of a motor vehicle and two counts of theft of a motor vehicle.

With files from The Windsor Star

stories.title: Toronto police make another arrest in 2022 Scarborough shooting death
stories.summary: Toronto police say it has made another arrest in connection to the shooting death of a man in a Scarborough plaza nearly four years ago.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police say it’s made another arrest in connection to the shooting death of a man in Scarborough nearly four years ago.

On Nov. 12, 2022, 31-year-old Toronto resident Ding Pang Wang was shot while he was inside a vehicle in a parking lot near Midland and Passmore avenues.

He was approached by an unknown suspect, who opened fire and fled.

Police announced on Aug. 24 that 39-year-old Toronto resident Justin Longshaw was arrested and charged with first-degree murder.

On Thursday, 30-year-old Christopher Atkins-Price was arrested and charged with first-degree murder.

He was also charged with attempted murder in connection to a shooting on March 10, 2023.

That day, a 40-year-old man was inside a vehicle in the same plaza parking lot when he was approached and shot at several times.

The man, who suffered serious injuries, was able to escape and drive away.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: A Niagara winery makes its New York debut under the looming threat of a U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol
stories.summary: Restocking could prove impossible if the U.S.’s proposed ban takes effect later this month
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
This week, the first shipments of Canadian Leaning Post wines were sent out for delivery from their U.S. distributor to fine dining restaurants and wine bars in New York and New Jersey. Restocking the expressive pinot noirs and chardonnays from the family-owned craft winery in Stoney Creek, Ont., ON the edge of the Niagara region, could prove impossible if the U.S.’s proposed ban on importing Canadian alcohol comes into effect on Sept. 29 .

Steve Remming, sales director at New York distributor Lieber Fine Wines, had approached Leaning Post winery after being impressed by a bottle of their pinot noir about a year and a half ago. At a blind wine tasting where bottles are wrapped to disguise their origin, the group of collectors he was with believed it was an extremely high-quality, expensive red from Burgundy until its label was revealed.

Canadian alcohol producers face a U.S. ban, but some shipments can still cross the border

Lieber’s initial order, a 56-case mix of chardonnay, riesling and pinot noir, as well as the single vineyard Senchuk Pinot Noir that first convinced Remming, arrived at the company’s temperature-controlled warehouse in suburban New Jersey last month. Soon after, U.S. and Canadian negotiators failed to reach a trade agreement, and President Donald Trump’s 50-per-cent tariff on a range of goods, including many types of alcohol, took effect on Aug. 22.

“It’s sad for the wine drinking community in New York, who will love wines with this profile at this quality and price point but won’t be able to buy them or will only be able to buy them at a dramatically increased price,” says Remming.

While there is always risk involved in launching an unknown brand, an outright ban would be the worst-case scenario for establishing Leaning Post in his market. If their wines are available, he anticipates a positive reception and intends to expand his range to include other Leaning Post labels.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Leaning Post Wines (@leaningpostwine)

“The typical pinot noir drinker at a Michelin-star restaurant in Manhattan or a wine bar in Brooklyn isn’t wearing a Maga hat,” he says. “Even with the 50-per-cent tariff, the wines from Leaning Post and other producers of similar quality from Niagara are still worth the money. They are less expensive than their counterparts from Burgundy and California.”

Here are six Canadian wines to drink instead of U.S. labels

For Leaning Post co-owner Nadia Senchuk, exporting the wines her husband, Ilya, makes isn’t strictly about turning a profit, it helps build a strong reputation for Niagara wines and other Canadian producers. “Oregon didn’t only sell its wine in Oregon. Those winemakers sold to other markets right from the start and now Oregon pinot noir is established around the world,” she says.

Leaning Post is participating in an upcoming trade mission to Singapore and has completed industry trips to the United Kingdom to help open markets abroad while increasing sales to the Lcbo. Senchuk says sales through Ontario’s provincial liquor stores went from 300 cases in 2024, to nearly 4,000 cases this year.

“We continue to change people’s minds about the quality of local wines a glass and bottle at a time,” she says. “Building our reputation by selling our wine abroad helps sell our wine at home.”

stories.title: Supreme Court rules no need to set time limit for sentencing proceedings
stories.summary: It says a man is entitled to a reduction in his sentence for sexual assault because the post-verdict sentencing phase of the case took too long
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada on Friday clarified how the justice system should handle delays after a person is convicted of a crime but before they are sentenced, ruling that such situations must be considered on a case-by-case basis.

Friday’s judgment, called R.B.-C., involved a conviction for sexual assault where it took more than a year to deliver the sentence.

The unanimous court took a relatively narrow approach to answer specific questions in the R.B.-C. appeal.

The case intersected with major legal issues: the protection in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to be tried within a reasonable time when charged with a crime, and what happens when that right is violated.

Such questions are usually focused on the process of a criminal trial. The Supreme Court a decade ago, in the landmark Jordan ruling, set strict deadlines for trials to be completed, from charge to conviction. If there’s an unreasonable delay that violates the Charter, a Supreme Court precedent from 1987 called Rahey means that the only outcome is a stay of proceedings. The accused is freed without a verdict.

Delays plague Canada’s justice system. Parliament and the Supreme Court in recent months have wrestled with the challenge. The Supreme Court earlier this year said it might reconsider its Rahey precedent.

Parliament and Supreme Court eye major shift on trial delays

Friday’s R.B.-C. judgment zeroed in on delays between conviction and sentencing. It was written by Justice Sheilah Martin in her final months of work as she retires this year.

If there is a Charter violation of unreasonable delay after conviction, the top court said the remedy in most cases is a reduction in the sentence levied on the offender. The court noted that it had not previously provided such precise guidance.

The court further said that delays after conviction should not be measured against a strict deadline, the way Jordan is used to consider trial delays. The key difference between the two phases is a person at trial is presumed innocent.

In the R.B.-C. case, a man studying for his PhD at a university in Ontario assaulted his new girlfriend one evening in 2019. The Ontario Court of Justice convicted him in 2021, but it took more than a year to render the punishment: a conditional sentence of two years less a day.

The man asked the Ontario Court of Justice for a stay of the proceedings because of unreasonable delay. The court said no. But the Ontario Court of Appeal in 2024 ruled that there was an unreasonable delay. Both courts were working with a rule applicable only in Ontario, a five-month deadline to deliver a sentence after conviction.

The Ontario appeal court reduced his conditional sentence by four months.

Court delays in sex-assault cases increase despite Supreme Court deadlines, report finds

At the Supreme Court, the man, R.B.-C., once more sought a complete stay of the proceedings – which would wipe out his conviction.

On Friday, the top court said no.

The Supreme Court agreed that there was an unreasonable delay in his sentencing, engaging the Charter of Rights. The top court also agreed with the Ontario appeal court’s move to reduce the conditional sentence by four months.

The Supreme Court, however, rejected the idea of a five-month deadline between conviction and sentencing.

Justice Martin, invoking the central rationale of the Jordan ruling, said trial deadlines were established to address a “proven culture of complacency in bringing accused persons to trial.”

On delays between conviction and sentencing, she said strict deadlines didn’t make sense because “no comparable evidentiary foundation has been established.”

Lawyers for R.B.-C. on Friday said they were disappointed that the Supreme Court will allow sentencing proceedings to continue “even after they have become unconstitutional” because of unreasonable delay.

“Courts, more than any other institution, should respect constitutional rights,” said lawyers Arash Ghiassi and Julia Kirby of Savards LLP in a statement.

They said that allowing cases to drag on beyond the point of unreasonable delay “will not fix the system.” They also said Friday’s ruling means that R.B.-C., an Iranian, May be deported back to Iran because of his conviction and his immigration status.

The Canadian Civil Liberties Association, an intervener in the case, ON Friday said sentence reductions are not a meaningful remedy for a violation of the Charter right on delay. The advocacy group added that the vagueness of the remedy does not “provide the clarity necessary” to push the justice system to render sentences in a timely manner.

Beyond the R.B.-C. case itself, the broader question of how the Supreme Court May grapple with the issue of cases stayed because of unreasonable trial delays is not yet answered.

In May, in another Jordan-related ruling, Chief Justice Richard Wagner said the court might reconsider its Rahey precedent, which dictates that a stay is the only remedy for an unreasonable trial delay.

“It May be that the time is near at hand when Rahey should be revisited,” the Chief Justice wrote.

stories.title: Giant MapQuest directions to Lake Ontario appear on billboards across Canadian and U.S. cities
stories.summary: MapQuest has erected billboards across Canada and the U.S. detailing directions to Lake Ontario, in an act of defiance against Donald Trump.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Navigation app MapQuest has put up billboards across Canada and the U.S. detailing directions to Lake Ontario, in its latest act of defiance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s executive order renaming the body of water “Lake America.”

The app collaborated with creative agency Quality Meats to install the billboards, and the company shared in an email with National Post that the six-foot posts have been erected in six cities: Toronto, Chicago, New York City, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Washington, D.C.

The designs recreate details from old-school MapQuest printed directions — the company having launched in 1996 as one of the first mapping services on the web — with old highway icons, a banner advert and a long URL running across the bottom of each page.

Canada’s billboard is located at 43 Lower Jarvis St., in Toronto, and includes just one page of directions, as opposed to the other cities’ three pages, owing to its proximity to the lake.

Meanwhile, Chicago’s board is found at State Street and Hubbard Street; Los Angeles’ is on Main Street in Santa Monica; and New York’s board is on East 38th St.; San Francisco’s board is at 490 Brannan St. and Washington, D.C.’s board is in the northwest quadrant of the District at Dupont Circle.

MapQuest’s new campaign comes after the company previously confirmed it has no intention of using the name “Lake America” in a social media post , after Trump’s Aug. 27 executive order directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name.

Both Google Maps and Apple Maps have adopted the name change for users based in the U.S., but MapQuest’s refusal to do the same resulted in a surge of people downloading the app in support of its stance.

In an email to National Post, MapQuest said it has since reached number one in the U.S. App Store in both the navigation category and overall, surpassing two million downloads as the app’s usage rose to roughly 50 times the normal amount.

In a recent interview with CNN , Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest, said he has been “blown away” by the response.

When asked what he would do if Trump were to ask MapQuest to change the lake’s name, he said: “We’re fully committed to our users right now, and the users are showing what they believe in by downloading our app.”

He added that MapQuest’s recent actions were not intended to be a political stance, but to give people the names of lakes that they’re familiar with. “It’s fun that we’re talking about geography,” he said.

The company also expanded a feature allowing users to rename Lake Ontario within the app themselves, building on a tool it launched after Trump renamed the Gulf of Mexico in February 2025. It’s now selling Lake Ontario-themed merch, too, including a sweater with “We’re not changing it” written above a graphic of the lake and a tote bag and T-shirt reading “It’s Lake Ontario on MapQuest.”

Meanwhile, Robert Corradino, a Republican and mayor of Oswego, a city in New York State on the shore of Lake Ontario, has also taken a stance against the name change.

He previously told National Post that his community is taking the renaming of Lake Ontario “very personally” and said Oswego won’t alter any signage, tourism materials or official communications to reflect the new name.

In Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford erected a Lake Ontario sign at a cost of $25,000 in Winona, near Hamilton, shortly after Trump signed the executive order.

Unveiling the sign in a video posted on X, Ford said: “Long before President Trump, this lake was called Lake Ontario. And long after President Trump is gone, it will still be called Lake Ontario. But just in case President Trump or anyone else forgets, we have set up a sign to remind them, it’s Lake Ontario now and forever.”

More recently, B.C. has unveiled plans to install signs at its border crossings informing travellers that they are entering territory that is “Never the 51st state” in a rejection of Trump’s rhetoric around Canada.

The worsening of relations between Canada and the U.S. comes after a breakdown in trade negotiations between the two countries last month, which saw 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian goods imposed on Aug. 22, followed by Canadian counter-tariffs which came into effect on Tuesday.

Later that day, Trump unveiled a series of executive orders to ban certain Canadian goods, including some dairy products, motorcycles and alcoholic beverages, from being imported to the U.S.

T he U.S. president appeared to suggest renaming New Mexico to “New America” in a post on Truth Social over the weekend, while David Maloney, a Republican congressman from Pennsylvania, plans to put a resolution before the U.S. House of Representatives urging the renaming of Lake Erie to “Lake Pennsylvania.”

content_blocks.text: The app collaborated with creative agency Quality Meats to install the billboards, and the company shared in an email with National Post that the six-foot posts have been erected in six cities: Toronto, Chicago, New York City, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Washington, D.C.

The designs recreate details from old-school MapQuest printed directions — the company having launched in 1996 as one of the first mapping services on the web — with old highway icons, a banner advert and a long URL running across the bottom of each page.
Canada’s billboard is located at 43 Lower Jarvis St., in Toronto, and includes just one page of directions, as opposed to the other cities’ three pages, owing to its proximity to the lake.

Meanwhile, Chicago’s board is found at State Street and Hubbard Street; Los Angeles’ is on Main Street in Santa Monica; and New York’s board is on East 38th St.; San Francisco’s board is at 490 Brannan St. and Washington, D.C.’s board is in the northwest quadrant of the District at Dupont Circle.

MapQuest’s new campaign comes after the company previously confirmed it has no intention of using the name “Lake America” in a social media post , after Trump’s Aug. 27 executive order directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name.

stories.title: Why are rising bond yields spurring alarm? And what do they mean for you?
stories.summary: Consumers could be facing higher borrowing costs for longer as bond markets are once again signalling rising economic risk to the finance and investing community.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Consumers could be facing higher borrowing costs for longer as bond markets are once again signalling rising economic risk to the finance and investing community amid the Iran war, rising government debt and an escalating trade war.

A bond is essentially a loan that governments and companies use to borrow money from the general public, and in return for providing funding, those that purchase bonds expect to earn interest.

The yield on the 10-year U.S. government bond increased to about 4.9 per cent as of publication — the highest since 2023, an increase of 0.8 percentage points since the start of September. This also comes after the 30-year bond yield spiked over five per cent in July , the highest since 2007.

Meanwhile, Canada’s 10-year government bond yield was at about 3.9 per cent, the highest in nearly two years, with most of the spike happening at the start of the month. This was at the same time that Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods took effect, and raised inflation risks.

Bond yields tend to fluctuate for a variety of reasons, but a sudden sharp rise in bond yields can signal that investors are concerned about inflation, government debt or economic uncertainty and are choosing to sell their bonds because of the increased perceived risk.

Higher yields can also drive up interest rates on mortgages, corporate loans, consumer credit and other products to protect lenders like banks from a higher risk environment. Although the Bank of Canada’s interest rate policy can affect borrowing costs in the short-term, bond market changes have more of an affect on long-term rates.

“You have these higher oil prices because of the Iran war and that’s stoking inflation fears, you’re seeing treasury yields in the U.S. spike, and that’s because investors are demanding a higher return on lending the government their money because they see so much risk there,” says mortgage and personal finance expert Clay Jarvis at NerdWallet Canada.

“That can be tied to the Iran war and the amount of money that is being spent there and the inflationary impact that it’s having on U.S. consumers.”

Bonds are priced based mostly on supply and demand, but the reasons for those changes can vary.

According to a statement released Wednesday from Kana Norimoto, an allocation of assets researcher at Fidelity Investments, long-term bond investors are trying to guess about what will happen with interest rates, inflation, government debt and spending, and says, “When the future feels unpredictable, investors want a bigger payout to take on the risk of holding onto long-term bonds.”

“People are starting to look a little nervous if they’re holding large amounts of government bonds,” says economics professor Moshe Lander of Concordia University.

“That’s not the type of thing that attracts people then, that could actually make them run away, and it could actually exacerbate the problem.”

There are several risks economies worldwide are exposed to, with the U.S. at the centre of it all because it is the world’s largest economy. This includes the war with Iran, which has led to spiking prices for oil and other commodities, and has led to higher inflation.

“As the ceasefire in the Middle East dissolved, oil prices jumped back above US$90 per barrel—the highest level since early June—stoking inflation concerns,” said Vikram Rai, senior economist at TD Bank, in a report on Thursday.

Rai added: “Since the relative low in yields before the conflict with Iran, 10-year yields have risen by about 80 basis points in the U.S. and 60 basis points in Canada.”

Rising U.S. debt is another area of concern for investors.

“The U.S. government is borrowing more as some traditional buyers step back,” said Rai.

“Private investors must therefore absorb a growing share of government debt and are demanding higher yields to do so. ”

Although higher bond yields can present an investing opportunity for certain investors, it can also present affordability challenges for consumers, especially with long-term loan products.

Higher bond yields can effect the interest rates on certain mortgages, car loans, lines of credit and student debt.

With mortgages, for example, if government bond yields are rising, that could result in higher fixed-term mortgages offered by commercial banks and other lenders.

“When these bond yields increase, you often see banks and other lenders increasing their three and five-year fixed rates.”

Higher borrowing costs as a result of spiking bond yields could also indirectly lead to higher prices for some goods and services in Canada.

If a business is faced with higher costs, they May make changes to maintain profits. This can be through increasing productivity, reducing costs elsewhere, or potentially passing along those higher costs to consumers.

“There should still be lots of concerns here for businesses and consumers. If the yields are higher, then that means when the government has to refinance its debt, it’s going to have to refinance it at a higher rate,” says Lander.

“This all of a sudden becomes more expensive than for businesses to raise cash, to pay for capital expansion, to pay for trying to find new markets or new suppliers or to try and take on more workers or replace existing equipment. So all of those things raise the cost of doing business in Canada .”

Lander also says it’s Canadian businesses that don’t have as much market competition, like with groceries, telecommunications and banking, which May find it easier than other sectors to raise prices for consumers when faced with higher costs.

“Will it spill over to the consumer? Yeah, it’s gonna spill over because firms aren’t afraid to pass along that cost to the consumer because there’s nobody there to come and steal their business by undercutting them.”
